shelves.title: The 365-day supply evidence base Deposit #5 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: How big is the treatment gap, how many people have diabetes — and what happens when medicines are dispensed in longer supplies?
shelves.balance: The gap is measured: statin use after heart disease or stroke is 14.6% worldwide, and no low- or middle-income region reaches the WHO 50% target. The population is counted: 589 million adults with diabetes, 42.8% undiagnosed. Longer supplies travel with better continuation wherever observed — 90 vs 30 days after heart procedures, and a full year of contraception. What does not exist anywhere on this shelf is a randomized trial of a full year’s supply of chronic medicines — that empty space is the trial this project exists to run.

cards.headline: PURE: who actually takes preventive medicines after heart disease or stroke?
cards.summary: Statin use 14.6% after cardiovascular disease; 66.5% in high-income vs 3.3% in low-income countries; no preventive drugs 11.2% vs 80.2% — 153,996 adults, 17 countries.
cards.type: Prospective epidemiological survey (PURE study), community-based, Lancet 2011
cards.people: 153,996 adults aged 35–70 in 17 countries
cards.result: Statin use 14.6% ; 66.5% in high-income vs 3.3% in low-income countries; no preventive drugs 11.2% vs 80.2%
cards.watchOut: Disease history and drug use were self-reported by questionnaire, so both may be misclassified
cards.source: Yusuf et al., Lancet 2011; PMID 21872920
cards.search: pure yusuf 2011 preventive medicines cardiovascular disease coronary heart stroke statins treatment gap high-income low-income countries lancet pmid 21872920 survey

cards.headline: Statin use in low- and middle-income countries
cards.summary: Statin use 8.0% for primary prevention and 21.9% for secondary prevention; the WHO 50% target was met nowhere — 116,449 adults, 41 countries.
cards.type: Pooled nationally representative health surveys, Lancet Glob Health 2022
cards.people: 116,449 non-pregnant adults aged 40–69 in 41 countries
cards.result: Statin use 8.0% for primary prevention and 21.9% for secondary prevention; WHO 50% target met by no region or income group
cards.watchOut: Statin use and prior disease were self-reported; primary-prevention eligibility was estimated from risk scores
cards.source: Marcus et al., Lancet Glob Health 2022; PMID 35180420
cards.search: marcus 2022 statin use low middle income countries lmic primary secondary prevention who 50 percent target pooled surveys lancet global health pmid 35180420

cards.headline: How many don’t know they have it? (IDF undiagnosed)
cards.summary: 42.8% of adults with diabetes were undiagnosed — 251.7 million people; 58.7% in low-income vs 28.9% in high-income countries.
cards.type: Modelled estimates, 2025 IDF Diabetes Atlas, Diabetes Care 2026

cards.headline: 90-day vs 30-day fills after a heart attack
cards.summary: Adherence with 90- vs 30-day fills: statins 83.1% vs 75.3% ; beta blockers 72.7% vs 62.9% ; ACEi/ARB 71.1% vs 60.9% ; P2Y12 78.5% vs 66.6% — 353,259 post-PCI patients.
cards.type: Observational registry linked to pharmacy fill data, J Am Heart Assoc 2021
cards.people: 353,259 patients with myocardial infarction treated with PCI
cards.result: Adherence, 90- vs 30-day fills: statins 83.1% vs 75.3% ; beta blockers 72.7% vs 62.9% ; ACEi/ARB 71.1% vs 60.9% ; P2Y12 78.5% vs 66.6%
cards.watchOut: Patients on 90-day fills differed from those on 30-day fills, so the gap may reflect who gets 90 days, not the supply length
cards.source: Rymer et al., J Am Heart Assoc 2021; PMID 33342227
cards.search: rymer 2021 90-day 30-day fills supply after myocardial infarction heart attack pci adherence statins beta blockers ace arb p2y12 registry pharmacy journal american heart association pmid 33342227

cards.headline: A year of contraceptive pills at once — continuation and cost
cards.summary: Women given 13 cycles received 14.5 vs 9.0 cycles over the year; wastage 6.5% vs 2% ; the program paid $99 more per woman given 3 cycles — 82,319 women.
cards.type: Retrospective analysis of paid claims data, Obstet Gynecol 2006
cards.people: 82,319 women dispensed oral contraceptive pills through California’s Family PACT program
cards.result: 14.5 vs 9.0 cycles over the year; wastage 6.5% vs 2% ; program paid $99 more per woman given 3 cycles than per woman given 13 cycles
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised claims comparison — differences in who received 13 cycles may account for some of the effect
cards.source: Foster et al., Obstet Gynecol 2006; PMID 17077231

cards.headline: A year of pills at once — pregnancy and abortion
cards.summary: Pregnancy 1.2% with a 1-year supply vs 3.3% (three packs) and 2.9% (one pack); about 30% lower odds of unplanned pregnancy and 46% lower odds of abortion — 84,401 women.
cards.type: Retrospective cohort linking dispensing records to Medi-Cal pregnancy events, Obstet Gynecol 2011
cards.people: 84,401 women who received oral contraceptives through the California family planning program
cards.result: Pregnancy 1.2% vs 3.3% vs 2.9% ; about 30% lower odds of unplanned pregnancy and 46% lower odds of abortion
cards.watchOut: Women were not randomised to supply length, so unmeasured differences between groups may remain
cards.source: Foster et al., Obstet Gynecol 2011; PMID 21343759

shelves.title: Statin compliance and continuation Deposit #12 · Oct 23, 2026
shelves.question: What actually works to keep patients on their statins?
shelves.mesh: Medication Adherence · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Acute Coronary Syndrome · Secondary Prevention · Reminder Systems · Humans
shelves.balance: Intensity works, nudges barely do: pharmacist-led multifaceted care after a heart event lifted statin adherence to 93.2% vs 71.3%, while automated reminders bought only 2–3 points, decision support was borderline (OR 1.18), texts did nothing (RR 0.93), a reminder device and a risk mailer were both null — and pharmacist counseling’s early persistence benefit was gone by 12 months.

cards.headline: Pharmacist-supported care after a heart event
cards.summary: Multicenter RCT, 232 VA patients in the statin analysis — statin adherence 93.2% vs 71.3% (P<.001), an absolute difference of 22 percentage points .
cards.type: Multicenter randomized controlled trial of a multifaceted adherence intervention vs usual care, JAMA Intern Med 2014
cards.people: 253 patients hospitalized with acute coronary syndrome at VA medical centers; the published statin analysis included 232 patients
cards.result: Statin adherence 93.2% vs 71.3% (P<.001), an absolute difference of 22 percentage points (95% CI 12 to 32); adherence threshold was proportion of days covered >0.80
cards.watchOut: Participants were overwhelmingly male veterans, and dispensing coverage does not establish medication ingestion
cards.source: Ho et al., JAMA Intern Med 2014; PMID 24247275 · NCT00903032
cards.search: pharmacist supported care heart event acute coronary syndrome ho jama internal medicine 2014 multicenter randomized trial veterans statin adherence proportion days covered pmid 24247275 acute coronary syndrome cardiotonic agents follow-up studies interprofessional relations medication adherence patient discharge patient education as topic physician-patient relations prognosis retrospective studies secondary prevention time factors humans nct00903032 i25.1 e11.9 ba52 5a11

cards.headline: Automated refill reminders — small gains at scale (PATIENT)
cards.summary: Pragmatic RCT, 21,752 patients — statin coverage rose 2.2 points with voice reminders and 3.0 points with enhanced reminders vs usual care.
cards.type: Pragmatic randomized trial — usual care, automated voice reminders, and enhanced reminders with additional outreach, Am J Manag Care 2014
cards.people: 21,752 adults with diabetes or atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease and suboptimal adherence; 16,380 qualified for the statin analyses
cards.result: Statin coverage rose 2.2 percentage points (95% CI 1.1 to 3.4) with automated voice reminders and 3.0 percentage points (95% CI 1.9 to 4.2) with enhanced reminders vs usual care; the two reminder groups did not differ significantly from each other
cards.watchOut: Pharmacy coverage measures medication availability, and the clinical impact of these small gains remains uncertain
cards.source: Vollmer et al., Am J Manag Care 2014; PMID 25811824
cards.search: automated refill reminders patient trial vollmer american journal managed care 2014 pragmatic randomized voice enhanced reminders statin coverage adherence pmid 25811824 age factors aged anticholesteremic agents blood pressure cardiovascular agents cardiovascular diseases electronic health records female health maintenance organizations humans lipids male middle aged reminder systems sex factors socioeconomic factors telephone drug monitoring i25.1 e11.9 ba52 5a11

cards.headline: Decision support + pharmacist outreach — borderline
cards.summary: Randomized trial, 2,600 in the dyslipidemia cohort — statin PDC ≥80% in 55.1% vs 50.9% ; adjusted OR 1.18 (0.99–1.41) , interval includes no difference.
cards.type: Patient-randomized parallel-group clinical trial, JAMA Network Open 2025
cards.people: 5,421 adults across the cardiometabolic trial; the dyslipidemia cohort comprised 1,324 intervention and 1,276 usual-care participants (2,600 total)
cards.result: Statin PDC ≥80% in 55.1% vs 50.9% ; adjusted OR 1.18 (0.99–1.41) — the confidence interval includes no difference
cards.watchOut: The adherence endpoint was restricted to participants currently prescribed the medication at follow-up, limiting interpretation as an outcome for everyone randomized
cards.source: O’Connor et al., JAMA Network Open 2025; PMID 39786775 · NCT03748420
cards.search: decision support pharmacist outreach borderline oconnor jama network open 2025 randomized trial dyslipidemia statin pdc adherence odds ratio pmid 39786775 humans middle aged male female decision support systems, clinical medication adherence aged adult glycated hemoglobin cholesterol, ldl hydroxymethylglutaryl-coa reductase inhibitors hypoglycemic agents primary health care cardiovascular diseases pharmacists antihypertensive agents blood pressure nct03748420 i25.1 e11.9 ba52 5a11

cards.headline: Supportive texts after a heart event — no effect (TEXTMEDS)
cards.summary: RCT, 1,424 patients, Australia — combined medication adherence RR 0.93 (0.84–1.03) , not significant; statin adherence 95% vs 95% .
cards.type: Single-blind multicenter randomized controlled trial of text-message support plus usual care vs usual care, Circulation 2022
cards.people: 1,424 patients after acute coronary syndrome, recruited from 18 Australian public teaching hospitals
cards.result: Combined medication adherence RR 0.93 (0.84–1.03) , not significant (P=.15); statin adherence at 12 months 95% vs 95% . The primary RR is a combined medication outcome, not a statin-specific RR
cards.watchOut: The adherence outcome was self-reported, with high statin adherence in both groups
cards.source: Chow et al., Circulation 2022; PMID 35533220 · ACTRN12613000793718
cards.search: supportive texts heart event textmeds chow circulation 2022 randomized trial australia text messages medication adherence acute coronary syndrome pmid 35533220 acute coronary syndrome australia female humans male medication adherence middle aged secondary prevention single-blind method text messaging actrn12613000793718 i25.1 e11.9 ba52 5a11

cards.headline: Pharmacist counseling — early benefit, gone by a year
cards.summary: Dutch RCT, 899 new statin users — discontinuation HR 0.66 (0.46–0.96) at 6 months; 0.84 and not significant at 12 months; refill adherence >99% in both arms.
cards.type: Multicenter, open-label randomized controlled trial, Ann Pharmacother 2010
cards.people: 899 evaluable new statin users from 26 Dutch community pharmacies; 439 intervention and 460 usual care
cards.result: The intervention lowered discontinuation within 6 months (hazard ratio 0.66 ; 95% CI 0.46–0.96), but the 12-month difference was not significant (hazard ratio 0.84 ; 95% CI 0.65–1.10). Median medication possession ratio was >99% in both groups and did not differ
cards.watchOut: Very high refill adherence created a ceiling effect, and the early persistence benefit was not statistically sustained at 12 months
cards.source: Eussen et al., Ann Pharmacother 2010; PMID 21119098
cards.search: pharmacist counseling early benefit gone year eussen annals pharmacotherapy 2010 dutch randomized trial new statin users discontinuation lipid feedback pmid 21119098 adolescent adult community pharmacy services female humans hydroxymethylglutaryl-coa reductase inhibitors male middle aged netherlands outcome and process assessment, health care patient education as topic drug monitoring i25.1 e11.9 ba52 5a11

cards.headline: Reminder device did not fix adherence
cards.summary: Three-arm RCT, 399 older adults — adherence ≥80%: 69.2% counseling+device, 72.4% device alone, 64.8% usual care; not significant overall; only half the counseling arm actually received it.
cards.type: Three-arm, multicenter, community-pharmacy randomized controlled trial, Front Pharmacol 2013
cards.people: 399 adults aged ≥65 years with pre-baseline statin refill adherence of 50%–80%, randomized in 24 Dutch pharmacies
cards.result: The proportion with 360-day refill adherence ≥80% was 69.2% with counseling plus the device, 72.4% with the device and written instructions, and 64.8% with usual care; neither intervention significantly improved adherence overall. In a subgroup of women using statins for secondary prevention, adherence was 86.1% with the device vs 52.6% with control (P<.005)
cards.watchOut: Intervention fidelity was poor: only 54 of 130 eligible participants in the counseling arm actually received counseling and the device
cards.source: Kooy et al., Front Pharmacol 2013; PMID 23755014
cards.search: reminder device adherence kooy frontiers pharmacology 2013 three-arm randomized trial older adults statin refill counseling pmid 23755014 i25.1 e11.9 ba52 5a11

cards.headline: Personalized risk mailer — null
cards.summary: Pragmatic RCT, 207 veterans starting statins — LDL-goal attainment RR 0.95 at 12 months and 1.03 at 18 months; no improvement.
cards.people: 207 US veterans initiating statin therapy; 95 received the educational mailer and 112 received usual care
cards.result: LDL-goal attainment did not improve at 12 months (RR 0.95 ; 95% CI 0.77–1.17) or 18 months (RR 1.03 ; 95% CI 0.84–1.25). Having statin coverage for ≥70% of days was numerically more common with the mailer, but not clearly significant (RR 1.33 ; 95% CI 1.00–1.78)
cards.watchOut: This small, single-system pragmatic trial may have been underpowered for modest adherence effects
cards.source: Nord et al., eGEMs 2017; PMID 28203610
cards.search: personalized risk mailer null nord egems 2017 pragmatic randomized trial veterans statin initiators ldl goal attainment pmid 28203610 i25.1 e11.9 ba52 5a11

shelves.title: A1C compliance
shelves.question: What actually moves A1c — and how many recommendations can a patient carry?
shelves.balance: Remote diabetes care works when it adjusts medicines: DiaTel −1.7 vs −0.8 points, comprehensive telehealth −0.61 against monitoring alone, pharmacist-coach mobile health −0.62, Thai tele-insulin titration −0.65 — but gains fade (EMPOWER-D’s advantage gone by 12 months) and teleconsultation is non-inferior to in-person care. Underneath all of it, the burden literature, shelved in full on Shelf #135: one ‘most important’ label doubled implementation, five or more recommendations cut action, and delayed recall collapses at 3–4 instructions — with one large dissent (Press) arguing the bottleneck is the patient’s memory, not the physician’s list.

cards.headline: Telemonitoring with active medication management (DiaTel)
cards.summary: RCT, 150 veterans — HbA1c fell 1.7 points vs 0.8 points at 6 months (P<.001).
cards.people: 150 veterans with type 2 diabetes and entry HbA1c ≥7.5%; 73 active management plus telemonitoring, 77 monthly care-coordination calls
cards.result: HbA1c fell 1.7 points vs 0.8 points at 6 months (P<.001)
cards.watchOut: Short trial in predominantly male veterans; telemonitoring was evaluated together with more intensive medication management
cards.source: Stone et al., Diabetes Care 2010; PMID 20009091
cards.search: telemonitoring active medication management diatel stone diabetes care 2010 randomized trial veterans hba1c home telemonitoring pmid 20009091

cards.headline: Online diabetes management — early gain, faded (EMPOWER-D)
cards.summary: RCT, 415 patients — HbA1c change −1.32 vs −0.66 points at 6 months (P<.001); not significant at 12 months ( −1.14 vs −0.95 ).
cards.type: Parallel-group randomized controlled trial, J Am Med Inform Assoc 2013
cards.people: 415 adults with type 2 diabetes and baseline HbA1c ≥7.5%; 202 intervention, 213 usual care
cards.result: HbA1c change −1.32 vs −0.66 points at 6 months (P<.001); at 12 months −1.14 vs −0.95 , not significant (P=.133)
cards.watchOut: The early between-group benefit was not statistically significant at the final assessment, and participation required internet access
cards.source: Tang et al., JAMIA 2013; PMID 23171659
cards.search: online diabetes management empower-d tang jamia 2013 randomized trial hba1c internet care team faded benefit pmid 23171659

cards.headline: Specialist teleconsultation is non-inferior (TELECONSULTA, Brazil)
cards.summary: Randomized non-inferiority trial, 278 patients — HbA1c difference −0.5 points (90% CI −0.9 to 0.0) at 6 months, within the 0.5-point margin.
cards.type: Pragmatic, open-label, single-center randomized non-inferiority trial, Lancet Reg Health Am 2024
cards.people: 278 adults with type 2 diabetes referred from primary care to specialist care in Brazil’s public health system
cards.result: HbA1c change difference −0.5 points (90% CI −0.9 to 0.0) at 6 months, favoring teleconsultation numerically — within the 0.5-point non-inferiority margin
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-center comparison using imputed outcomes; does not isolate teleconsultation vs ordinary primary care. The reported interval is 90%, not 95%
cards.source: Rodrigues et al., Lancet Reg Health Am 2024; PMID 39507367
cards.search: specialist teleconsultation non-inferior teleconsulta brazil rodrigues lancet regional health americas 2024 randomized non-inferiority trial hba1c pmid 39507367

cards.headline: Comprehensive telehealth beat monitoring alone
cards.summary: VA RCT, 200 patients with persistently poor control — A1c −1.59 vs −0.98 points at 12 months; difference −0.61 (−1.12 to −0.11).
cards.type: Parallel randomized clinical trial with an active comparator, JAMA Intern Med 2022
cards.people: 200 adults with persistently poorly controlled type 2 diabetes; 101 received comprehensive telehealth, 99 telemonitoring/care coordination
cards.result: At 12 months, estimated HbA1c was 8.58% with comprehensive telehealth and 9.19% with telemonitoring/care coordination. HbA1c changed by −1.59 vs −0.98 percentage points; the between-group difference was −0.61 percentage points (95% CI −1.12 to −0.11; P=.02)
cards.watchOut: The multicomponent intervention was tested in integrated Veterans Affairs systems, so the effective component and generalizability are uncertain
cards.source: Crowley et al., JAMA Intern Med 2022; PMID 35877092
cards.search: comprehensive telehealth monitoring alone crowley jama internal medicine 2022 veterans affairs randomized trial hba1c persistently poor control nurse pmid 35877092

cards.headline: Pharmacist-coach mobile health in Black and Latinx patients
cards.summary: RCT, 221 adults, A1c ≥8% — treatment effect −0.62 points (−1.04 to −0.19).
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial with a waiting-list control, JAMA Network Open 2023
cards.people: 221 African American or Latinx adults with type 2 diabetes and baseline HbA1c ≥8%
cards.result: During the first 12 months, mean HbA1c changed by −0.79 percentage points in the intervention group vs −0.24 in the waiting-list control group. The treatment effect was −0.62 percentage points (95% CI −1.04 to −0.19; P=.005)
cards.watchOut: This was a multicomponent intervention in one urban health system, so its individual active component cannot be isolated
cards.source: Gerber et al., JAMA Network Open 2023; PMID 37773498
cards.search: pharmacist coach mobile health black latinx gerber jama network open 2023 randomized trial hba1c health coaches waiting list pmid 37773498

cards.headline: Telemonitoring with guided insulin titration
cards.summary: Open-label RCT in Thailand, 151 patients — A1c −1.14 vs −0.49 at 24 weeks; difference −0.65 .
cards.type: Six-month, single-center, open-label randomized controlled trial, Diabetes Obes Metab 2024
cards.people: 151 adults aged 18–65 years with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes and baseline HbA1c 7.5%–10.5%
cards.result: At 24 weeks, HbA1c changed by −1.14 percentage points (95% CI −1.38 to −0.89) with tele-iPDM vs −0.49 (95% CI −0.73 to −0.25) with control care. The between-group difference was −0.65 percentage points (95% CI −0.99 to −0.30; P<.001). Weight, BMI, and hypoglycemic events did not differ significantly
cards.watchOut: The trial was open-label and single-center, with only 24 weeks of follow-up
cards.source: Saetang et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2024; PMID 39161074
cards.search: telemonitoring guided insulin titration saetang diabetes obesity metabolism 2024 thailand open-label randomized trial hba1c tele-ipdm pmid 39161074

shelves.title: How much of the plan gets done: recommendation adherence
shelves.mesh: Geriatric Assessment · Referral and Consultation · Patient Compliance · Primary Health Care · Aged · Humans
shelves.balance: What an agent should take from this shelf: only part of any plan gets done — completion ran from 38.3% of recommendations in one follow-up to 69.7% adherence in inpatient consults — and volume is the recurring suspect: five or more recommendations cut GP action (OR 0.58), each added consult recommendation lowered adherence (OR 0.51), and poor recall rose steeply at three instructions (OR 26.1); what helps: label one recommendation ‘most important’ (implementation OR 2.4), deliver it written plus verbal (OR 2.4), and have the physician implement it (85% followed) rather than leave it as self-care (46%); one large cohort dissents — there, count alone did not predict implementation (P=.27) and only comorbidity burden did.

cards.headline: Label one recommendation ‘most important’
cards.summary: Observational analysis, 139 patients, 528 geriatric-assessment recommendations — prioritized recommendations: implementation OR 2.4 (1.3–4.5) ; more recommendations overall meant less patient adherence (OR 0.7 ).
cards.type: Observational predictor analysis within a geriatric-assessment intervention study, Am J Med 1996
cards.people: 139 older patients receiving 528 recommendations after comprehensive geriatric assessment
cards.result: Recommendations labeled most important: physician implementation OR 2.4 (1.3–4.5) . Separately, more recommendations overall were associated with less patient adherence (OR 0.7 , 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9) — different outcomes
cards.watchOut: These associations do not establish a causal recommendation-count threshold; recommendation count was not randomized
cards.source: Reuben et al., Am J Med 1996; PMID 8610732

cards.headline: How many recommendations do patients complete?
cards.summary: Observational follow-up, 45 MS patients — 44 of 115 recommendations completed ( 38.3% ); 11% completed all, 36% completed none.
cards.type: Observational telephone follow-up with retrospective medical-record review, Int J MS Care 2019
cards.people: 45 adults with multiple sclerosis interviewed after neuropsychological evaluation
cards.result: 44 of 115 recommendations completed ( 38.3% ); 11% completed all, 53% completed some, 36% completed none
cards.watchOut: Small observational sample relying on self-reported completion; cannot establish that reducing recommendation count improves adherence
cards.source: Stimmel et al., Int J MS Care 2019; PMID 31049037
cards.search: recommendations completed patients stimmel international journal ms care 2019 observational follow-up multiple sclerosis neuropsychological completion pmid 31049037

cards.headline: Pharmacist recommendations to GPs — volume cuts action
cards.summary: Cohort, 384 recommendations, Sweden — GPs acted on 63.8% ; five or more recommendations per patient: OR 0.58 (0.37–0.91) ; written plus verbal beat written alone (OR 2.4 ).
cards.type: Uncontrolled cohort study with multivariable logistic regression, BMC Prim Care 2023
cards.people: 109 community-dwelling primary-care patients in Sweden; 384 pharmacist recommendations analyzed for implementation
cards.result: GPs acted on 245/384 recommendations ( 63.8% ); five or more recommendations per patient vs one to four: OR 0.58 (0.37–0.91) ; written plus verbal communication vs written alone: OR 2.4 (95% CI 1.52 to 3.79)
cards.watchOut: The outcome includes partial implementation, plans, and alternative measures; the observational comparison cannot establish causation
cards.source: Dobszai et al., BMC Prim Care 2023; PMID 38042778
cards.search: pharmacist recommendations gps volume action dobszai bmc primary care 2023 cohort sweden medication review written verbal implementation pmid 38042778 humans medication review cohort studies independent living general practitioners primary health care

cards.headline: Recall collapses at three instructions
cards.summary: Prospective cohort, 250 primary-care patients — poor delayed recall vs one instruction: OR 26.1 after three instructions, OR 56.8 after four.
cards.type: Prospective observational study with adjusted logistic regression, BMC Fam Pract 2011
cards.people: 250 primary-care patients who received 1–4 instructions; mean follow-up was 47.4 days
cards.result: Compared with one instruction, poor delayed recall was much more likely after three instructions (OR 26.1 ; 95% CI 3.15–215.24; P=.002) and four instructions (OR 56.8 ; 95% CI 5.91–546.12; P<.001)
cards.watchOut: The study measured recall rather than completed clinical behavior, and the confidence intervals were very wide
cards.source: Selic et al., BMC Fam Pract 2011; PMID 22204743
cards.search: recall collapses three instructions selic bmc family practice 2011 prospective cohort primary care delayed recall slovenia pmid 22204743 adult aged aged, 80 and over female general practitioners humans logistic models male memory middle aged multivariate analysis patient education as topic patients physician-patient relations prospective studies risk factors slovenia social class surveys and questionnaires time factors urban health services

cards.headline: More recommended: more recalled, smaller share
cards.summary: Two randomized online experiments ( 193 + 266 people) — each added recommendation raised the number recalled but lowered the proportion recalled, for intentions too.
cards.type: Two randomized online experiments, Clin Psychol Sci 2017
cards.people: Experiment 1 enrolled 193 participants; Experiment 2 enrolled 266 participants
cards.result: In Experiment 1, each increase in presented recommendation count increased the number recalled (B= 0.333 ; 95% CI 0.254–0.412) but reduced the proportion recalled (B= −0.016 ; 95% CI −0.024 to −0.008). Experiment 2 replicated this for recall number (B= 0.291 ) and recall proportion (B= −0.049 ), and found the same pattern for intended behaviors
cards.watchOut: These were online experiments measuring immediate recall and intentions, not real-world adherence or health outcomes
cards.source: McDonald et al., Clin Psychol Sci 2017; PMID 32292643
cards.search: more recommended recalled smaller share mcdonald clinical psychological science 2017 randomized online experiments recommendation count recall proportion intentions pmid 32292643

cards.headline: Inpatient consults: more recommendations, less adherence
cards.summary: Multicenter cohort, 278 patients 75+ — overall adherence 69.7% ; each increase in recommendation count lowered adherence (OR 0.51 ); medication recommendations only 53.2% followed.
cards.type: Multicenter observational study, Eur Geriatr Med 2021
cards.people: 278 adults aged ≥75 years admitted to acute non-geriatric wards; median 3 recommendations per patient (range 1–13)
cards.result: Overall adherence was 69.7% . Medication recommendations had 53.2% adherence and nutritional recommendations 59.1% . Adherence decreased when more recommendations were given (OR 0.51 ; 95% CI 0.33–0.80), and increased when recommendations were directed to allied health professionals (OR 6.37 ; 95% CI 1.15–35.35) or came from more experienced teams (OR 1.34 ; 95% CI 1.04–1.72)
cards.watchOut: Recommendation burden was observational and could be confounded by patient complexity and recommendation difficulty
cards.source: Deschodt et al., Eur Geriatr Med 2021; PMID 32978747
cards.search: inpatient consults recommendations adherence deschodt european geriatric medicine 2021 multicenter cohort geriatric consultation medication pmid 32978747 aged aged, 80 and over cross-sectional studies female geriatric assessment hospitalization humans inpatients male referral and consultation

cards.headline: Doctor-ordered beats self-care, 85 to 46
cards.summary: Prospective series, 150 older adults — patient adherence 85% for physician-implemented recommendations vs 46% for self-care.
cards.type: Prospective case series after community-based comprehensive geriatric assessment, J Am Geriatr Soc 1997
cards.people: 150 community-dwelling older adults; 528 total recommendations, of which 212 were related to four target geriatric conditions
cards.result: Of the 212 target-related recommendations, 59% required a physician order and 41% were self-care. Overall physician implementation was 70%. Patient adherence was 85% for physician-implemented recommendations vs 46% for self-care recommendations
cards.watchOut: This was an uncontrolled case series limited to four geriatric conditions and 3-month follow-up
cards.source: Shah et al., J Am Geriatr Soc 1997; PMID 9100708

cards.headline: A cooperative PCP makes adherence happen
cards.summary: Prospective analysis, 81 patients, 50 physicians — greater physician cooperation predicted higher patient adherence (R²= 0.21 , P=.02).
cards.type: Prospective observational analysis nested within a randomized prevention program, J Am Geriatr Soc 1995
cards.people: 81 intervention-group patients and 50 primary-care physicians; physicians had 179 contacts with program nurse practitioners over 3 years
cards.result: Greater physician cooperation predicted higher patient adherence to recommendations that involved physicians (R²= 0.21 ; P=.02). Cooperation did not predict overall patient satisfaction with health care (multivariable R²= 0.21 ; P=.23)
cards.watchOut: Nurse practitioners rated both physician cooperation and patient adherence, creating potential common-rater bias

cards.headline: The dissent: count alone didn’t predict implementation
cards.summary: 8-year record cohort, 488 patients, 3,434 recommendations — 47.6% implemented; mean counts near-identical across implementation quartiles (P=.27); only comorbidity burden predicted less.
cards.type: Eight-year retrospective medical-record cohort, Isr J Health Policy Res 2017
cards.people: 488 older adults assessed in an outpatient comprehensive geriatric unit; 3,434 recommendations
cards.result: Primary-care physicians implemented 1,634/3,434 recommendations ( 47.6% ). Mean recommendation counts were similar across implementation quartiles: 7.2, 7.1, 7.3, and 6.5 recommendations (P=.27). In the multivariable model, only higher Charlson comorbidity score predicted lower implementation (OR 0.82 ; 95% CI 0.706–0.968; P=.018)
cards.watchOut: The retrospective design measured physician implementation, not patient adherence, and residual confounding is likely

shelves.title: An LLM at the doctor’s elbow: management scores up, diagnosis scores flat — in vignettes
shelves.question: Does giving physicians a large language model improve their clinical reasoning?
shelves.mesh: Clinical Competence · Clinical Reasoning · Humans · Language · Patient Care · Physicians
shelves.balance: Two randomized trials, one honest split result. For diagnosis, GPT-4 access did not significantly improve physicians’ reasoning scores (76% vs 74% per case). For management — choosing tests and treatments under uncertainty — it did (+6.5 points), at a cost of about two extra minutes per case. Both trials graded written vignettes against expert rubrics; neither touched a real patient, and in both, the LLM alone matched or beat the physicians who were given it. POSSIBLE for the vignette claim as fenced; no card here supports a claim about real-world diagnostic safety. (No ICD-10 code is printed for this shelf: a clinician-tool question has no single principal condition, and this library does not guess codes.) Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Diagnosis trial (Goh 2024, JAMA Network Open): giving doctors GPT-4 did not significantly improve diagnostic reasoning — 76% vs 74% per case — but the LLM alone outscored both
cards.summary: 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents; family medicine, internal medicine, emergency medicine) randomized to an LLM (GPT-4) plus conventional resources, or conventional resources alone, working up to 6 clinical vignettes in 60 minutes. Median diagnostic-reasoning score per case: 76% with the LLM vs 74% without — adjusted difference 2 percentage points [−4 to 8]; P=.60 . Time per case did not differ significantly (519 vs 565 seconds). In the exploratory comparison, the LLM alone scored 16 percentage points higher [2–30] than the conventional-resources group (P=.03) .
cards.type: Single-blind randomized clinical trial, JAMA Network Open 2024. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT06157944.
cards.people: 50 physicians with training in family medicine, internal medicine, or emergency medicine (26 attendings and 24 residents; median 3 years in practice [IQR 2–8]), participating remotely and at one in-person site, each reviewing up to 6 structured clinical vignettes.
cards.result: The median diagnostic reasoning score per case was 76% (IQR, 66%–87%) for the LLM group and 74% (IQR, 63%–84%) for the conventional resources-only group, with an adjusted difference of 2 percentage points (95% CI, −4 to 8 percentage points; P=.60). The median time spent per case was 519 seconds (IQR, 371–668) for the LLM group versus 565 seconds (IQR, 456–788) for the conventional resources group (difference −82 seconds; 95% CI, −195 to 31; P=.20). The LLM alone scored 16 percentage points (95% CI, 2 to 30 percentage points; P=.03) higher than the conventional resources group on the primary outcome.
cards.watchOut: Vignettes are not patients: the information arrives complete, legible, and curated, nobody interrupts, and the score rewards a well-built differential rather than a correct outcome in a messy real encounter. The result that launched a thousand headlines — the model alone beating doctors — comes from an exploratory secondary analysis against the conventional group, not from a randomized three-way contest; treat it as the trial’s most interesting hypothesis, not its finding.
cards.source: Goh E et al. Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2024;7(10):e2440969. PMID 39466245 · NCT06157944. DOI 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.40969
cards.search: diagnosis trial (goh 2024, jama network open): giving doctors gpt-4 did not significantly improve diagnostic reasoning — 76% vs 74% per case — but the llm alone outscored both 50 physicians (26 attendings, 24 residents; family medicine, internal medicine, emergency medicine) randomized to an llm (gpt-4) plus conventional resources, or conventional resources alone, working up to 6 clinical vignettes in 60 minutes. median diagnostic-reasoning score per case: 76% with the llm vs 74% without — adjusted difference 2 percentage points [−4 to 8]; p=.60 . time per case did not differ significantly (519 vs 565 seconds). in the exploratory comparison, the llm alone scored 16 percentage points higher [2–30] than the conventional-resources group (p=.03) . does access to a large language model improve physicians' diagnostic reasoning compared with conventional resources? single-blind randomized

cards.headline: Management trial (Goh 2025, Nature Medicine): GPT-4 assistance did improve management reasoning — scores 6.5 points higher — at the cost of more time per case
cards.summary: 92 practicing physicians randomized to GPT-4 plus conventional resources or conventional resources alone, answering five expert-developed management vignettes built from real, de-identified encounters, with information revealed sequentially. Total rubric score: 6.5 percentage points higher with the LLM [2.7 to 10.2]; P<0.001 . LLM users spent 119 seconds longer per case [17.4 to 221.2]. And again: physicians with the LLM scored no better than the LLM alone (difference −0.9 points [−9.0 to 7.2]).
cards.type: Prospective, randomized, controlled trial, Nature Medicine 2025. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT06208423. The record’s abstract does not print an age or sex mix for participants, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 92 practicing physicians, randomized November 2023 to April 2024 to use either GPT-4 plus conventional resources or conventional resources alone, each answering five expert-developed clinical vignettes in a simulated setting.
cards.result: Physicians using the LLM scored significantly higher than those using conventional resources alone (mean difference 6.5%; 95% CI, 2.7 to 10.2; P<0.001). LLM users spent more time per case (mean difference 119.3 seconds; 95% CI, 17.4 to 221.2; P=0.02). There was no significant difference between LLM-augmented physicians and the LLM alone (−0.9%; 95% CI, −9.0 to 7.2; P=0.8). The authors concluded that LLM assistance can improve physician management reasoning in complex clinical vignettes and should be validated in real clinical practice.
cards.watchOut: Same fence as Card 1 — simulated cases, rubric scores, no patients, no outcomes — plus a new trade: the gain came with two extra minutes per case, and in real clinics time is the scarcest input. The two trials also used the same model family at one moment in its development; whether the numbers describe GPT-4 in 2024 or a durable property of LLM assistance is unknowable from these data.
cards.source: Goh E et al. GPT-4 assistance for improvement of physician performance on patient care tasks: a randomized controlled trial. Nat Med. 2025;31(4):1233–1238. PMID 39910272 · NCT06208423. DOI 10.1038/s41591-024-03456-y
cards.search: management trial (goh 2025, nature medicine): gpt-4 assistance did improve management reasoning — scores 6.5 points higher — at the cost of more time per case 92 practicing physicians randomized to gpt-4 plus conventional resources or conventional resources alone, answering five expert-developed management vignettes built from real, de-identified encounters, with information revealed sequentially. total rubric score: 6.5 percentage points higher with the llm [2.7 to 10.2]; p<0.001 . llm users spent 119 seconds longer per case [17.4 to 221.2]. and again: physicians with the llm scored no better than the llm alone (difference −0.9 points [−9.0 to 7.2]). does large language model assistance improve physician performance on management reasoning — treatment and testing decisions under risk? prospective, randomized, controlled trial, nature medicine 2025. registry id from the record's own

cards.headline: Reading the two Goh trials together: the model helps doctors decide what to do more than what it is — and keeps matching the doctors who use it
cards.summary: Same investigators, same model, same vignette method — two different answers by task. Diagnosis: no significant improvement (adjusted difference 2 points, P=.60). Management: a significant improvement (+6.5 points, P<0.001). In both trials the LLM working alone scored at least as well as physicians given the LLM — the collaboration the tools are sold for has not yet beaten the tool.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 together and states what vignette evidence can and cannot carry.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1 and 2: 142 physicians in total (50 and 92), in family medicine, internal medicine, and emergency medicine, reasoning over structured written cases.
cards.result: Randomized evidence supports a narrow claim: LLM assistance improves physician scores on management-reasoning vignettes, does not significantly improve diagnostic-reasoning vignette scores, and takes more time per case. No trial on this shelf measured diagnostic error in real care, treatment appropriateness in real patients, or any patient outcome.
cards.watchOut: The shelf’s honest summary is the authors’ own: these tools ‘should be validated in real clinical practice.’ A rubric point is not a prevented error, and an agent or clinician citing this shelf for bedside benefit is citing past the evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 39466245; PMID 39910272).

shelves.title: Hospital at home: cheaper and better liked — the mortality claim depends on which trials you pool [Tier C]
shelves.question: For acutely ill adults, is hospital-level care at home as safe and effective as care in a hospital building?
shelves.mesh: Cost-Benefit Analysis · Home Care Services, Hospital-Based · Hospitalization · Humans · Length of Stay · Mortality · Patient Discharge · Patient Readmission · Patient Satisfaction
shelves.balance: The consistent findings are operational: in the one modern US randomized trial, home care cost 38% less, used far fewer tests, got patients moving, and readmitted fewer of them (7% vs 23%) — in 91 selected patients, most of whom had refused or been screened out of the alternative. The disputed finding is mortality, and it is why this shelf is Tier C: the broad 61-trial pool finds a mortality advantage (OR 0.81, relative; NNT 50), while the stricter Cochrane early-discharge pool finds little or no mortality difference (RR 1.07 in mixed conditions). Both pools are printed; the shelf takes no side. Proposed grade: POSSIBLE for the cost/readmission/satisfaction package, mortality unsettled. Tier C — mortality claim: built Nov 7, 2026 and held for the developer’s personal verdict; no approval stamp is claimed for this shelf. (No ICD-10 code is printed: hospital at home is a place of care across many principal conditions, and this library does not guess codes.)

cards.headline: The US randomized trial (Levine 2020, Annals of Internal Medicine): hospital-level care at home cost 38% less, with fewer readmissions (7% vs 23%) — in 91 highly selected patients
cards.summary: 91 adults admitted via the emergency department with selected acute conditions at two Boston-area hospitals, randomized to hospital-level care at home (nurse and physician visits, IV medicines, remote monitoring, video, point-of-care testing) or usual hospital care. Adjusted mean cost of the acute episode: 38% lower at home [24–49] . Home patients got far fewer laboratory orders (median 3 vs 15 per admission) and imaging studies (14% vs 44%), spent less of the day sedentary (12% vs 23%), and were readmitted within 30 days less often ( 7% vs 23% ).
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial, Annals of Internal Medicine 2020. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT03203759.
cards.people: 91 adults (43 home, 48 control) admitted through the emergency departments of an academic medical center and a community hospital with selected acute conditions. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: The adjusted mean cost of the acute care episode was 38% (95% CI, 24% to 49%) lower for home patients than control patients. Compared with usual care patients, home patients had fewer laboratory orders (median per admission, 3 vs. 15), imaging studies (median, 14% vs. 44%), and consultations (median, 2% vs. 31%). Home patients spent a smaller proportion of the day sedentary (median, 12% vs. 23%) or lying down (median, 18% vs. 55%) and were readmitted less frequently within 30 days (7% vs. 23%).
cards.watchOut: Selection is the whole fence: 63% of potentially eligible patients refused, the trial ran at 2 sites with a small number of home physicians, and the readmission comparison (7% vs 23%) rests on a handful of events in 91 patients. This is a proof that the model can work, in patients who have a home, a phone, and a condition expected to behave — not an estimate of what happens when a health system offers it to everyone at the ED door.
cards.source: Levine DM et al. Hospital-Level Care at Home for Acutely Ill Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Ann Intern Med. 2020;172(2):77–85. PMID 31842232 · NCT03203759. DOI 10.7326/M19-0600
cards.search: the us randomized trial (levine 2020, annals of internal medicine): hospital-level care at home cost 38% less, with fewer readmissions (7% vs 23%) — in 91 highly selected patients 91 adults admitted via the emergency department with selected acute conditions at two boston-area hospitals, randomized to hospital-level care at home (nurse and physician visits, iv medicines, remote monitoring, video, point-of-care testing) or usual hospital care. adjusted mean cost of the acute episode: 38% lower at home [24–49] . home patients got far fewer laboratory orders (median 3 vs 15 per admission) and imaging studies (14% vs 44%), spent less of the day sedentary (12% vs 23%), and were readmitted within 30 days less often ( 7% vs 23% ). for acutely ill adults who would otherwise be admitted, does hospital-level care at home reduce cost and improve outcomes compared with usual hospital care?

cards.headline: All the trials pooled, broad definition (Caplan 2012, Medical Journal of Australia): hospital-in-the-home associated with lower mortality (OR 0.81, relative) and fewer readmissions across 61 RCTs
cards.summary: 61 randomized trials of hospital-in-the-home services that significantly substitute for in-hospital time. Mortality: OR 0.81 [0.69–0.95], relative (42 trials, 6,992 patients; P=0.008), a number-needed-to-treat of 50 to prevent one death. Readmissions: OR 0.75 [0.59–0.95], relative (41 trials, 5,372 patients). Costs lower (mean difference −1,567 [−2,070 to −1,065], in the studies’ reported terms). Patient satisfaction was higher at home in 21 of 22 studies; carer burden did not differ significantly.
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Medical Journal of Australia 2012. (A meta-analysis — no single age or sex mix applies; no registry ID applies to the analysis itself.)
cards.people: 61 randomized trials in patients older than 16 years comparing hospital-in-the-home care with in-hospital treatment, across a range of acute and subacute conditions (literature to February 2012).
cards.result: Hospital-in-the-home care led to reduced mortality (odds ratio, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69 to 0.95; P=0.008; 42 RCTs with 6,992 patients), readmission rates (OR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.59 to 0.95; P=0.02; 41 RCTs with 5,372 patients) and cost (mean difference, −1567.11; 95% CI, −2069.53 to −1064.69; P<0.001; 11 RCTs with 1,215 patients). The number needed to treat at home to prevent one death was 50. No heterogeneity was observed for mortality, but heterogeneity was present for readmission and cost results. Patient satisfaction was higher in 21 of 22 studies reporting it.
cards.watchOut: Two cautions before quoting the mortality number. The pooled OR of 0.81 sits inside this library’s 0.5–2.0 caution band for small effects — statistically significant, clinically modest, and assembled from many small trials of varying quality across decades and health systems. And Card 3, pooling a narrower slice of the same literature, does not find it. A mortality claim that appears and disappears with the inclusion criteria is a Tier C claim by definition.
cards.source: Caplan GA et al. A meta-analysis of “hospital in the home”. Med J Aust. 2012;197(9):512–519. PMID 23121588. DOI 10.5694/mja12.10480
cards.search: all the trials pooled, broad definition (caplan 2012, medical journal of australia): hospital-in-the-home associated with lower mortality (or 0.81, relative) and fewer readmissions across 61 rcts 61 randomized trials of hospital-in-the-home services that significantly substitute for in-hospital time. mortality: or 0.81 [0.69–0.95], relative (42 trials, 6,992 patients; p=0.008), a number-needed-to-treat of 50 to prevent one death. readmissions: or 0.75 [0.59–0.95], relative (41 trials, 5,372 patients). costs lower (mean difference −1,567 [−2,070 to −1,065], in the studies' reported terms). patient satisfaction was higher at home in 21 of 22 studies; carer burden did not differ significantly. pooling all randomized trials of hospital-in-the-home that substitute for hospital time, what happens to mortality, readmissions, cost, and satisfaction? meta-analysis of randomized controlled

cards.headline: The same literature, narrower slice (Cochrane 2017): early-discharge hospital at home — mortality essentially unchanged (RR 1.07 mixed conditions; RR 0.92 after stroke)
cards.summary: 32 randomized trials, 4,746 participants , restricted to early discharge hospital at home (patients admitted first, then sent home early with hospital services). Mortality at 3–6 months probably differs little or not at all: after stroke, RR 0.92 [0.57–1.48], relative (11 trials, 1,114 patients; moderate-certainty); in mixed medical conditions, RR 1.07 [0.76–1.49], relative (8 trials, 1,247 patients; moderate-certainty). Readmission after stroke: RR 1.09 (low-certainty). Hospital-at-home patients were discharged from the intervention about 7 days earlier ; cost evidence was very low certainty.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (CD000356, 2017 update; searches to January 9, 2017). (A systematic review — no single age or sex mix applies; no registry ID applies to the review itself.)
cards.people: 32 randomized trials (4,746 participants), mainly in high-income countries, comparing early discharge hospital at home with acute inpatient care in adults recovering from stroke, with mixed medical conditions, or after surgery. Obstetric, pediatric, and mental-health schemes were excluded.
cards.result: Early discharge hospital at home probably makes little or no difference to mortality at three to six months after stroke (risk ratio 0.92; 95% CI, 0.57 to 1.48; moderate-certainty evidence) and probably makes little or no difference to mortality in people with a mix of medical conditions (risk ratio 1.07; 95% CI, 0.76 to 1.49; moderate-certainty evidence). It may lower the risk of living in an institutional setting at six months (RR 0.63) and probably reduces the duration of hospital-based care by about seven days. The reviewers judged the effect on cost uncertain (very low-certainty evidence).
cards.watchOut: Cards 2 and 3 are not contradicting each other so much as answering different questions: Caplan pools admission-avoidance and early-discharge schemes across six decades of ‘hospital in the home,’ Cochrane pools early discharge only, with stricter methods, and finds no mortality signal. When two competent pools of the same field disagree by inclusion criteria, the honest shelf quotes both and grades the disputed outcome — mortality — as unsettled.
cards.source: Gonçalves-Bradley DC et al. Early discharge hospital at home. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017;(6):CD000356. PMID 28651296. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD000356.pub4

shelves.title: Text-message programs: small nudges, honestly sized — adherence and risk factors improve a little
shelves.question: Do text-message programs improve medication adherence and the numbers adherence is meant to move?
shelves.mesh: Cell Phone · Coronary Disease · HIV Infections · Humans · Hypertension · Medication Adherence · Reminder Systems · Telemedicine · Text Messaging
shelves.balance: Three randomized trials, three diseases, one consistent size of effect: small. TEXT ME modestly improved LDL cholesterol and other risk factors at 6 months in coronary disease; StAR’s adherence texts bought about 2 mmHg of systolic pressure over a year; WelTel’s weekly nurse text — the most human and most interactive program here — produced the strongest yield, an NNT of 9 for adherence and 11 for viral suppression. No trial measured heart attacks, strokes, or deaths. POSSIBLE: texts are a cheap, safe nudge with real but modest effects on adherence-linked measures — an adjunct, never a treatment. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: TEXT ME (Chow 2015, JAMA): four texts a week for six months modestly improved LDL cholesterol and other risk factors after coronary disease
cards.summary: 710 patients with proven coronary heart disease (mean age 58; 82% men; 53% current smokers) at a Sydney tertiary hospital, randomized to usual care plus a semipersonalized text program — 4 messages a week for 6 months , drawn from a message bank matched to baseline characteristics — or usual care alone. The primary endpoint, LDL cholesterol at 6 months, was significantly lower in the intervention group, with concurrent significant reductions in systolic blood pressure and BMI, increased physical activity, and reduced smoking. The authors’ own summary word for the LDL effect is ‘modest’. 91% of recipients found the messages useful.
cards.type: Parallel-group, single-blind, randomized clinical trial (TEXT ME), JAMA 2015. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: ACTRN12611000161921.
cards.people: 710 patients (352 intervention, 358 control) with proven coronary heart disease (prior myocardial infarction or angiographically proven), recruited 2011–2013. Mean age 58 years (SD 9.2); 82% men; 53% current smokers.
cards.result: At 6 months, levels of LDL cholesterol were significantly lower in intervention participants, with concurrent reductions in systolic blood pressure and body mass index, significant increases in physical activity, and a significant reduction in smoking. The majority of intervention participants reported the text messages to be useful (91%), easy to understand (97%), and appropriate in frequency (86%). The authors concluded that the program produced a modest improvement in LDL cholesterol and greater improvement in other risk factors, and that whether the effects endure — and hence improve clinical outcomes — remained to be determined. (This card prints the effects as the record’s abstract states them; the abstract reports them qualitatively.)
cards.watchOut: Surrogates at six months, in volunteers at one hospital, from a program that was not interactive. Nothing here shows fewer heart attacks or deaths, and risk-factor gains from reminders commonly fade when the messages stop — TEXT ME’s own authors flag duration as the open question. Card it as what it is: the field’s flagship proof that texts can move numbers that matter, modestly, for a while.
cards.source: Chow CK et al. Effect of Lifestyle-Focused Text Messaging on Risk Factor Modification in Patients With Coronary Heart Disease: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2015;314(12):1255–1263. PMID 26393848 · ACTRN12611000161921. DOI 10.1001/jama.2015.10945

cards.headline: StAR (Bobrow 2016, Circulation): adherence-support texts in South African hypertension — systolic pressure 2.2 mmHg lower with information-only messages; interactive messages added nothing
cards.summary: 1,372 adults treated for hypertension at a Cape Town primary care clinic, randomized to information-only SMS, interactive SMS, or usual care for 12 months. Systolic blood pressure change vs usual care: −2.2 mmHg [−4.4 to −0.04] with information-only messages ; −1.6 mmHg [−3.7 to 0.6] — not significant — with interactive messages . The odds of achieving blood pressure <140/90 were higher in both message groups (OR 1.42 and 1.41, relative). The authors describe the blood-pressure effect as small.
cards.type: Pragmatic, single-blind, three-arm randomized trial (SMS-Text Adherence Support [StAR]), Circulation 2016. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT02019823.
cards.people: 1,372 participants treated for high blood pressure at a general outpatient clinic in South Africa (457 information-only SMS, 458 interactive SMS, 457 usual care); primary outcome data available for 1,256 (92%) at 12 months. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: At 12 months, the mean adjusted change in systolic blood pressure compared with usual care was −2.2 mm Hg (95% CI, −4.4 to −0.04) with information-only SMS and −1.6 mm Hg (95% CI, −3.7 to 0.6) with interactive SMS. Odds ratios for blood pressure <140/90 mm Hg were 1.42 (95% CI, 1.03–1.95) for information-only and 1.41 (95% CI, 1.02–1.95) for interactive messaging versus usual care. There was no evidence that the interactive intervention increased the effect.
cards.watchOut: The shelf’s humility card: a well-run, year-long, pragmatic trial of exactly the adherence-by-text idea, in exactly the kind of clinic where it should help most — and the yield is about 2 mmHg, with the fancier interactive version doing no better than plain information. Small is not nothing (2 mmHg across a population is real), but anyone promising transformation from a message bank should be shown this card.
cards.source: Bobrow K et al. Mobile Phone Text Messages to Support Treatment Adherence in Adults With High Blood Pressure (SMS-Text Adherence Support [StAR]): A Single-Blind, Randomized Trial. Circulation. 2016;133(6):592–600. PMID 26769742 · NCT02019823. DOI 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.115.017530

cards.headline: WelTel Kenya1 (Lester 2010, Lancet): a weekly nurse text improved antiretroviral adherence (NNT 9) and viral suppression (NNT 11)
cards.summary: 538 adults starting antiretroviral therapy at three Kenyan clinics, randomized to a weekly SMS from a clinic nurse — with a required reply within 48 hours — or standard care. Self-reported adherence (>95% of doses, at both 6 and 12 months): 168 of 273 with SMS vs 132 of 265 without (RR for non-adherence 0.81 [0.69–0.94], relative; P=.006). Viral suppression (<400 copies/mL) at 12 months: 156 of 273 vs 128 of 265 (RR for virologic failure 0.84 [0.71–0.99], relative; P=.04). Numbers needed to treat: 9 for adherence, 11 for suppression .
cards.type: Multisite randomized clinical trial, Lancet 2010. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT00830622.
cards.people: 538 HIV-infected adults initiating antiretroviral therapy at three clinics in Kenya (273 SMS intervention, 265 standard care), randomized May 2007 to October 2008. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: Adherence to antiretroviral therapy was reported in 168 of 273 patients receiving the SMS intervention compared with 132 of 265 in the control group (relative risk for non-adherence, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.69–0.94; P=.006). Suppressed viral loads were reported in 156 of 273 patients in the SMS group and 128 of 265 in the control group (relative risk for virologic failure, 0.84; 95% CI, 0.71–0.99; P=.04). The number needed to treat to achieve greater than 95% adherence was 9 (95% CI, 5.0–29.5) and to achieve viral load suppression was 11 (95% CI, 5.8–227.3).
cards.watchOut: The strongest result on this shelf — and note its ingredients: a human nurse, a required reply, a new-treatment start line, and a setting where the alternative was little support. The relative effects (0.81 and 0.84) sit inside this library’s caution band, yet the absolute yields (NNT 9–11 on a hard biological endpoint, viral suppression) are clinically meaningful. Adherence itself was self-reported; the viral load was not, and it moved the same way.
cards.source: Lester RT et al. Effects of a mobile phone short message service on antiretroviral treatment adherence in Kenya (WelTel Kenya1): a randomised trial. Lancet. 2010;376(9755):1838–1845. PMID 21071074 · NCT00830622. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61997-6

shelves.title: What moves vaccine uptake: reminders add ~8 points; a presumptive ‘announcement’ added 5.4
shelves.question: What actually moves vaccine uptake: patient reminders, and how clinicians offer?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Correspondence as Topic · Humans · Immunization · Immunization Programs · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Reminder Systems · Telephone · Text Messaging
shelves.balance: Two different levers, both randomised. Patient reminder and recall systems — letters, postcards, calls, texts — raise immunisation receipt by a pooled 8 percentage points across 55 trials and 138,625 participants (RR 1.28; Cochrane, moderate certainty). And how the clinician opens the conversation matters: training clinics to make a presumptive ‘announcement’ rather than open a discussion raised HPV vaccine initiation by 5.4 percentage points in a 30-clinic randomised trial, while conversation training did nothing. LIKELY for the uptake claim as asked — the reminder half rests on one of the largest randomised evidence bases in implementation science. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Patient reminder & recall (Cochrane, Jacobson Vann 2018): across 55 randomised trials, reminders raise immunisation by 8 percentage points (RR 1.28)
cards.summary: The Cochrane review pooled 75 studies of patient reminder or recall (letters, postcards, telephone and autodialer calls, text messages, and combinations, with or without outreach) across children, adolescents and adults in 10 countries. In the randomised trials ( 55 studies, 138,625 participants ), reminders probably improve immunisation receipt: risk ratio 1.28 [1.23–1.35], a risk difference of 8 percentage points , moderate-certainty evidence. Single-method effects with high-certainty evidence include postcards (RR 1.18 [1.08–1.30]; 8 studies, 27,734 participants).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials and other controlled studies (CD002959), 2018. No registry ID applies to the review itself.
cards.people: Children, adolescents and adults due or overdue for immunisation in outpatient, community and primary-care settings in 10 countries; the pooled randomised estimate covers 138,625 participants in 55 trials.
cards.result: Patient reminder or recall interventions probably improve the proportion of participants who receive immunization (risk ratio of 1.28, 95% confidence interval 1.23 to 1.35; risk difference of 8%) based on moderate certainty evidence from 55 studies with 138,625 participants. Three types of single-method reminders improve receipt of immunizations based on high certainty evidence, including the use of postcards (RR 1.18, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.30; eight studies; 27,734 participants).
cards.watchOut: An 8-point absolute gain is modest per person and large per population — and it is an average across decades, vaccines and health systems; the effect in any one clinic depends on how many of its patients are merely forgetful versus hard to reach, a distinction reminders cannot fix. The review’s certainty language (‘probably’) is the reviewers’ own and is kept on the card.
cards.source: Jacobson Vann JC et al. Patient reminder and recall interventions to improve immunization rates. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018;(1):CD002959. PMID 29342498. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD002959.pub2

cards.headline: The presumptive offer (Brewer 2017, Pediatrics): training clinicians to ‘announce’ rather than ‘discuss’ raised HPV vaccine initiation by 5.4 percentage points
cards.summary: A parallel-group cluster-randomised trial in 30 North Carolina clinics : one hour of training in ‘announcements’ (a brief statement that presumes the parent is ready to vaccinate) vs ‘conversations’ (open-ended discussion) vs no training. Among 17,173 adolescents aged 11–12 , six-month HPV vaccine initiation rose 5.4 percentage points more in announcement clinics than control [1.1–9.7] (girls +4.6, boys +6.2). Conversation training did not differ from control. Neither training changed other vaccines’ coverage or initiation at ages 13–17 (n=37,796).
cards.type: Parallel-group cluster-randomised clinical trial, Pediatrics 2017. The record prints no registry ID; none is printed here.
cards.people: 30 paediatric and family-medicine clinics in central North Carolina (29 open at follow-up); the primary outcome covers 17,173 adolescents aged 11 or 12 attributed to those clinics in the state immunisation registry.
cards.result: Six-month increases in HPV vaccination coverage were larger for patients in clinics that received announcement training versus those in control clinics (5.4% difference, 95% confidence interval: 1.1%–9.7%). Stratified analyses showed increases for both girls (4.6% difference) and boys (6.2% difference). Patients in clinics receiving conversation training did not differ from those in control clinics with respect to changes in HPV vaccination coverage. The authors concluded that training providers to use announcements resulted in a clinically meaningful increase in HPV vaccine initiation among young adolescents.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one vaccine, one state, one age band — and an effect that did not generalise even within the trial (not to 13–17-year-olds, not to other vaccines). The lead author reports commercial research grants from vaccine makers (Merck, Pfizer, GSK), disclosed on the record and printed here; the trial itself was not run with Merck resources. The finding’s plausibility is its mechanism — default-framing is a well-replicated behavioural effect — but the card’s fences are the trial’s own boundaries.
cards.source: Brewer NT et al. Announcements versus conversations to improve HPV vaccination coverage: a randomized trial. Pediatrics. 2017;139(1):e20161764. PMID 27940512. DOI 10.1542/peds.2016-1764

cards.headline: Reading the uptake evidence together: small percentages, honestly earned — reminders nudge systems, framing nudges moments
cards.summary: The two interventions work at different joints of the same pathway. Reminders and recall act on the system’s memory: across 55 randomised trials they recover about 8 additional vaccinations per 100 people due — unglamorous, replicated, and exactly the size of effect that, multiplied by a whole panel, outperforms most campaigns. The presumptive announcement acts on the consultation’s default: in its one large trial it added 5.4 points to HPV initiation in 11–12-year-olds, while the more respectful-sounding open conversation added nothing measurable. Neither is a mandate, an incentive or an education programme — this shelf cards what it cards — and neither effect should be quoted without its absolute size attached.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 together and fences the claim to uptake, not attitudes or mandates.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1 and 2: 138,625 trial participants due for immunisation across 10 countries, and 17,173 adolescents in 29–30 North Carolina clinics.
cards.result: The evidence establishes that patient reminder/recall systems produce a small, reliable increase in immunisation receipt, and that presumptive (‘announcement’) clinician framing increased HPV vaccine initiation in one cluster-randomised trial. It does not compare these against incentives, mandates, school-entry requirements or mass campaigns, which are different shelves’ questions where they are carded at all.
cards.watchOut: Quote the absolute numbers (8 points; 5.4 points), not the relative ones — in implementation science the relative figure is the one that travels and the absolute figure is the one that plans a clinic’s year.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 29342498; PMID 27940512).

shelves.title: Telemedicine versus in-person care: what holds condition-by-condition, and the untested wholesale switch
shelves.question: Does delivering care by telemedicine (video/phone), as a substitute for in-person visits, improve or worsen clinical outcomes in primary care and urgent/emergency care — and has switching a practice to mostly-telemedicine ever been randomised?
shelves.mesh: Communication · Diabetes Mellitus/therapy · Heart Failure/therapy · Mental Disorders/therapy · Monitoring, Physiologic/methods · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Physician-Patient Relations
shelves.balance: Split (PROPOSED, Tier C — the developer's personal verdict is required): POSSIBLE that telemedicine substituted condition-by-condition performs about as well as in-person care — 93 randomised trials in the Cochrane synthesis (heart-failure mortality relative risk 0.89, confidence interval crossing 1) and a 19-study primary-care review finding similar or lower service use and prescribing. MAYBE (weak evidence) for any claim that switching a practice wholesale to mostly-telemedicine improves outcomes: that switch has never been randomised; the one practice-cluster trial's mortality result (Whole System Demonstrator: 4.6% vs 8.3%) is implausibly large for remote monitoring and was flagged by its own team as a possible recruitment artefact; and commercial direct-to-consumer care carries a prescribing-quality cost (antibiotics at 52% of visits vs 31% in offices).

cards.headline: Flodgren 2015 (Cochrane, 93 RCTs): interactive telemedicine matched usual care on heart-failure mortality (relative risk 0.89, interval crossing 1)
cards.summary: Flodgren 2015 (Cochrane, 93 RCTs, 22,047 participants): interactive telemedicine matched usual care — heart-failure mortality relative risk 0.89 (95% CI 0.76 to 1.03).
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane EPOC)
cards.people: 93 randomised trials, 22,047 participants, across cardiovascular disease (36 trials), diabetes (21), respiratory conditions (9), mental health (7) and other conditions. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For heart failure, no difference in all-cause mortality (16 studies; N=5,239; relative risk 0.89, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.03; P=0.12) at a median of six months. Hospital admissions ranged from a 64% relative decrease to a 60% relative increase across studies. Quality of life improved modestly (5 studies; mean difference −4.39 points, 95% CI −7.94 to −0.83). Telemedicine was delivered in addition to usual care in 32% of studies, as an alternative in 57%, and partly substituted in 11%.
cards.watchOut: Almost every trial tested telemedicine for ONE defined condition, usually remote monitoring added to care or swapped for selected visits — none randomised a whole practice to mostly-telemedicine. Telephone-only and wholly automatic self-management interventions were excluded, so this does not cover those either.
cards.source: Flodgren G, et al. Interactive telemedicine: effects on professional practice and health care outcomes. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015;(9):CD002098. PMID: 26343551. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — systematic review.

cards.summary: Whole System Demonstrator 2012: telehealth cut admissions (OR 0.82); mortality was 4.6% vs 8.3% (OR 0.54) — a Tier C mortality claim its own team flagged.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multisite, cluster randomised trial (179 general practices randomised)
cards.people: 3,230 people with diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or heart failure in three areas of England, recruited between May 2008 and November 2009. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The proportion admitted to hospital within 12 months was lower with telehealth (odds ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.70 to 0.97; P=0.017 — a relative odds measure). Mortality at 12 months was 4.6% on telehealth vs 8.3% on usual care (odds ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.75; P<0.001 — a relative odds measure, printed beside its absolute rates). Emergency admissions per head: 0.54 vs 0.68.
cards.watchOut: TIER C card — it carries a mortality claim. A near-halving of mortality is implausibly large for remote monitoring alone, and the trial team flagged a possible recruitment-process artefact: practices knew their allocation while recruiting patients, so the two arms may not have recruited comparable people. One trial, one country, 2008–09 technology.

cards.headline: Bracken 2025 (19 studies): physician-led synchronous telemedicine in primary care — similar or fewer ED visits, hospital visits and prescriptions than face-to-face care
cards.summary: Bracken 2025 (19 studies): synchronous telemedicine in primary care showed similar or fewer ED visits, hospital visits and prescriptions than face-to-face care.
cards.type: Systematic review with narrative synthesis (19 included studies, mostly US)
cards.people: 19 studies comparing physician-led synchronous (video/telephone) telemedicine with face-to-face primary care; 78.9% conducted in the US; video plus telephone in 57.9%. The abstract does not state a pooled patient count, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Narrative synthesis: telemedicine visits were associated with similar or fewer emergency-department visits, hospital visits and prescribing than face-to-face visits, and with fewer diagnostic tests and imaging. No pooled effect sizes are reported.
cards.watchOut: The review's own caution: the included studies were susceptible to selection bias and confounding, with limited applicability to other health systems and time periods — patients who choose telemedicine differ systematically from patients who attend in person, and most underlying studies were not randomised.
cards.source: Bracken K, et al. Physician-Led Synchronous Telemedicine Compared to Face-To-Face Care in Primary Care: A Systematic Review. Evaluation & the Health Professions. 2025;48(3):279-290. PMID: 39140652. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — systematic review.

cards.headline: Ray 2019: direct-to-consumer telemedicine prescribed antibiotics more often (52% of visits) and less guideline-concordantly (59%) than urgent care or office visits
cards.summary: Ray 2019: direct-to-consumer telemedicine prescribed antibiotics at 52% of children's respiratory visits vs 31% in offices, and less often guideline-concordantly.
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study of matched national commercial claims (NOT randomised)
cards.people: Acute respiratory infection visits by children aged 0–17 years, 2015–2016: 4,604 direct-to-consumer telemedicine, 38,408 urgent care and 485,201 primary-care office visits, matched on age, sex, chronic medical complexity, state, rurality, health plan type and diagnosis category.
cards.result: Antibiotics were prescribed at 52% of direct-to-consumer telemedicine visits vs 42% of urgent-care and 31% of primary-care office visits (P<0.001 for both comparisons). Guideline-concordant antibiotic management: 59% vs 67% and 78% (P<0.001 for both). Absolute rates printed; the comparison is observational despite matching.
cards.watchOut: Claims data from one insurer, 2015–16, paediatric respiratory infections only; residual confounding by parental demand and case mix is likely. This is a quality signal about one commercial model of telemedicine, not a randomised verdict on telemedicine itself.
cards.source: Ray KN, et al. Antibiotic Prescribing During Pediatric Direct-to-Consumer Telemedicine Visits. Pediatrics. 2019;143(5). PMID: 30962253. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — observational study.

cards.headline: Synthesis: condition-by-condition telemedicine performs about as well as in-person care; the wholesale switch has never been randomised — split stamp, Tier C
cards.summary: Condition-by-condition substitution looks equivalent; the wholesale switch has never been randomised — Split: POSSIBLE · MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C, proposed only.
cards.people: See the cards above.
cards.result: Three layers of evidence: (1) condition-specific interactive telemedicine across 93 RCTs matched usual care on the hard outcome that could be pooled (heart-failure mortality relative risk 0.89, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.03); (2) the one large practice-cluster trial reported fewer admissions and a mortality difference (4.6% vs 8.3%) too large to take at face value and flagged by its own team; (3) prescribing quality slipped in a commercial direct-to-consumer model (antibiotics at 52% of visits vs 31% in offices). No trial — among the anchors or in the 2026 currency sweep — has randomised a practice to mostly-telemedicine versus mostly-in-person care.
cards.watchOut: The POSSIBLE half covers telemedicine substituted for defined conditions and visit types. The MAYBE (weak evidence) half is the question health systems are actually deciding — wholesale switching — for which the evidence is extrapolation from narrower trials, not experiment.
cards.source: Synthesis of the four records carded on this shelf (PMIDs 26343551, 22723612, 39140652, 30962253).
