shelves.title: Community health workers for hypertension control: COBRA-BPS and the Argentina trial
shelves.question: Do multicomponent interventions led by community health workers lower blood pressure in low- and middle-income settings?
shelves.mesh: Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Asia, Western · Blood Pressure · Blood Pressure Determination · Checklist · Community Health Workers · Developing Countries
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large cluster-randomised trials in low- and middle-income settings found concordant blood-pressure gains from community-health-worker-led multicomponent programmes — COBRA-BPS (rural Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka): systolic BP fell 5.2 mm Hg more than usual care at 24 months, with control (<140/90) in 53.2% versus 43.7%; Argentina (He): systolic BP fell 6.6 mm Hg more at 18 months, with control rising to 72.9% versus 52.2%. The interventions are unblindable by nature and were bundles — home visits plus physician training and system supports — so the shelf credits the programme, not the home visit alone. No mortality claim is made: COBRA-BPS's mortality figures were a secondary, unpowered outcome and are reported on its card as such.

cards.headline: COBRA-BPS: CHW-centred multicomponent intervention lowered systolic BP 5.2 mm Hg more than usual care at 24 months
cards.summary: COBRA-BPS: CHW-centred multicomponent intervention lowered systolic BP 5.2 mm Hg more than usual care at 24 months.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised, controlled trial (30 communities, rural South Asia)
cards.people: 2,645 adults with hypertension in rural districts of Bangladesh, Pakistan and Sri Lanka; baseline mean systolic BP 146.7 mm Hg (intervention) and 144.7 mm Hg (control); follow-up at 24 months exceeded 90%. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Systolic BP fell by 9.0 mm Hg on the intervention versus 3.9 mm Hg on usual care (mean reduction 5.2 mm Hg greater, 95% CI 3.2 to 7.1; P<0.001); diastolic reduction was 2.8 mm Hg greater (95% CI 1.7 to 3.9). BP control (<140/90) was achieved by 53.2% versus 43.7% (relative risk 1.22, relative, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.35 — inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, printed with its absolute rates). All-cause mortality was 2.9% versus 4.3% — a secondary outcome the trial was not powered for; no mortality claim is made on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: The bundle (CHW home visits for monitoring and counselling, physician training, public-sector care coordination) cannot be decomposed; effects were achieved inside publicly financed systems in three specific countries.
cards.source: Jafar TH et al. A Community-Based Intervention for Managing Hypertension in Rural South Asia. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(8):717-726. PMID: 32074419. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02657746, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: He (Argentina): CHW-led multicomponent intervention lowered systolic BP 6.6 mm Hg more than usual care at 18 months
cards.summary: Argentina: CHW-led multicomponent intervention lowered systolic BP 6.6 mm Hg more than usual care at 18 months.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial (18 primary-care centres, national public system)
cards.people: 1,432 low-income adults with uncontrolled hypertension (743 in 9 intervention centres, 689 in 9 usual-care centres); mean age 55.8 years (SD 13.3); 772 women (53.0%); 1,357 (94.8%) completed the trial. Baseline mean systolic BP was 151.7 mm Hg (intervention) and 149.8 mm Hg (usual care).
cards.result: Systolic BP fell 19.3 mm Hg on the intervention versus 12.7 mm Hg on usual care (difference in reduction 6.6 mm Hg, 95% CI 4.6 to 8.6; P<.001); diastolic fell 12.2 versus 6.9 mm Hg (difference 5.4 mm Hg, 95% CI 4.0 to 6.8). Controlled hypertension rose from 17.0% to 72.9% on the intervention versus 17.6% to 52.2% on usual care (difference in increase 20.6%, 95% CI 15.4% to 25.9%). No adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Again a bundle — CHW health coaching, home BP monitoring and audit-and-feedback, plus a physician intervention and text messaging — delivered where medications and care were free; which component carried the effect is unknown, as the authors state.

shelves.title: Remote monitoring and telemedical management in heart failure: TIM-HF2 versus BEAT-HF
shelves.question: Does structured remote patient management reduce hospitalisation and death in heart failure — the positive German TIM-HF2 system against the null Californian BEAT-HF programme?
shelves.mesh: Heart Failure/classification,mortality,physiopathology,therapy · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Telemedicine/methods,statistics & numerical data · Confounding Factors, Epidemiologic · Heart Failure
shelves.balance: PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — TIM-HF2's outcomes include all-cause mortality): POSSIBLE. The two large trials discord: TIM-HF2's intensive, physician-centre remote patient management reduced days lost to unplanned cardiovascular admission or all-cause death (4.88% vs 6.64% of days; ratio 0.80, relative; P=.046) and all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.70, relative; P=.028), with cardiovascular mortality not significant (hazard ratio 0.671, relative; P=.056) — mortality is printed beside the hospitalisation figures throughout this shelf. BEAT-HF's lighter post-discharge coaching-plus-telemonitoring changed nothing: 180-day readmission 50.8% versus 49.2% (adjusted hazard ratio 1.03, relative) and no mortality difference. Intensity and population, not the label 'telemonitoring', separate the two. FENCE: telemedicine as a substitute for in-person visits is drafted Shelf #709 — a visit-substitution question, not a monitoring-system question; no #709 material is carded here.

cards.headline: TIM-HF2: remote patient management cut days lost to CV admission or death (4.88% vs 6.64%) and all-cause mortality (HR 0.70, relative)
cards.summary: TIM-HF2: remote patient management cut days lost to CV admission or death ( 4.88% vs 6.64% ) and all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 0.70, relative); CV mortality was non-significant.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, controlled, parallel-group, unmasked multicentre trial (Germany)
cards.people: 1,571 patients with heart failure (NYHA class II–III, hospitalised for heart failure within the previous 12 months, LVEF 45% or lower or on oral diuretics if higher) assigned to remote patient management plus usual care (796) or usual care alone (775); 1,538 started assigned care and formed the full analysis set. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Days lost due to unplanned cardiovascular hospital admissions or all-cause death: 4.88% (95% CI 4.55–5.23) on remote management versus 6.64% (6.19–7.13) on usual care (ratio 0.80, relative, 95% CI 0.65–1.00; P=.046) — a mean of 17.8 versus 24.2 days lost per year. All-cause mortality was 7.86 versus 11.34 per 100 person-years (hazard ratio 0.70, relative, 95% CI 0.50–0.96; P=.028), printed beside the admission outcome as this shelf requires. Cardiovascular mortality did not differ significantly (hazard ratio 0.671, relative, 95% CI 0.45–1.01; P=.056). All relative measures sit inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band.
cards.watchOut: Unmasked trial of an intensive, centrally staffed system in a selected post-hospitalisation population (major depression excluded); the primary ratio's interval reaches 1.00 and the mortality findings are secondary outcomes — which is why this shelf is Tier C, proposed only.
cards.source: Koehler F et al. Efficacy of telemedical interventional management in patients with heart failure (TIM-HF2): a randomised, controlled, parallel-group, unmasked trial. cards.summary: BEAT-HF: post-discharge coaching plus telemonitoring did not reduce 180-day readmissions ( 50.8% vs 49.2% ).
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (6 academic medical centres, California)
cards.people: 1,437 patients aged 50 years or older hospitalised with decompensated heart failure (715 intervention, 722 usual care), followed for 180 days; median age 73 years; 46.2% female; 22.0% African American.

shelves.question: Does an intensive, relationship-based care-management programme for super-utilisers reduce hospital readmissions?
shelves.mesh: Ambulatory Care/statistics & numerical data · Chronic Disease/therapy · Health Care Costs · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · House Calls · Linear Models · New Jersey
shelves.balance: LIKELY the null: In the Camden Coalition randomised trial, 180-day readmission was 62.3% with the hotspotting programme versus 61.7% with usual care (adjusted difference 0.82 percentage points, 95% CI -5.97 to 7.61 — not significant). The trial also documents the trap it was designed to test: a before-and-after comparison inside the intervention group misleadingly suggested a 38-percentage-point decline, because the control group declined similarly. A single large randomised null carries LIKELY for the null, per the library's stated reasoning. Readmission was the primary outcome; no mortality claim is made on this shelf.

cards.result: The 180-day readmission rate was 62.3% in the intervention group and 61.7% in the control group (adjusted between-group difference 0.82 percentage points, 95% CI -5.97 to 7.61 — not significant). A within-group before-and-after comparison in the intervention arm suggested a 38-percentage-point decline in admissions, which the randomised comparison showed to be misleading because the control group declined similarly.

cards.summary: The flagship super-utiliser programme failed its randomised test — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on readmission.

shelves.title: Early supported discharge after stroke
shelves.question: Do early supported discharge services reduce death or dependency and shorten hospital stay after acute stroke?
shelves.mesh: Cost-Benefit Analysis · Home Care Services, Hospital-Based/economics,organization & administration · Home Nursing/economics,organization & administration · Length of Stay · Patient Discharge/economics · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane synthesis of 17 randomised trials (2,422 participants) found early supported discharge (ESD) reduced death or long-term dependency (odds ratio 0.80, relative, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.95; about five fewer adverse outcomes per 100 patients) and shortened hospital stay by about 5.5 days, with death alone unchanged (odds ratio 1.04, relative) — the dependency benefit is printed beside the null mortality figure, and no standalone mortality-benefit claim is made. Benefits concentrated in trials with a co-ordinated multidisciplinary ESD team and in patients with mild-to-moderate disability; death or institutional care was also reduced (odds ratio 0.75, relative).

cards.headline: Langhorne (Cochrane): early supported discharge — death or dependency odds ratio 0.80 (relative), stay about 5.5 days shorter, death alone unchanged
cards.summary: Cochrane review: early supported discharge after stroke — death or dependency odds ratio 0.80 (relative) , stay about 5.5 days shorter, death alone unchanged (odds ratio 1.04).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 17 trials recruiting 2,422 participants (a selected, mostly elderly group of stroke survivors with moderate disability); the primary outcome was available for 16 trials (2,359 participants) at a median follow-up of 6 months. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Death or dependency at end of follow-up: odds ratio 0.80 (relative, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.95; P=0.01; moderate-grade evidence), equating to five fewer adverse outcomes per 100 patients receiving ESD. Death alone: odds ratio 1.04 (relative, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.40 — null), printed beside the composite as required. Death or requiring institutional care: odds ratio 0.75 (relative, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.96). Length of hospital stay was reduced by a mean of 5.5 days (95% CI 3 to 8). Extended activities of daily living improved slightly (standardised mean difference 0.14) and satisfaction rose (odds ratio 1.60, relative); readmission risk was similar (odds ratio 1.09, relative, low-quality evidence). Estimated costs ranged from 23% lower to 15% greater than usual care. The death-or-dependency odds ratio sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band; the absolute translation (5 per 100) is printed with it.
cards.watchOut: Benefit was weaker at 1- and 5-year follow-up and concentrated in co-ordinated multidisciplinary-team services (subgroup interaction P=0.06) and in mild-to-moderate disability (P=0.04); results are inconclusive for ESD services without a co-ordinated team, and participants were a selected group.
cards.source: Langhorne P et al. Early supported discharge services for people with acute stroke. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017;7(7):CD000443. PMID: 28703869. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — systematic review.

shelves.title: Audit and feedback to change professional practice
shelves.question: Does giving clinicians audit-and-feedback reports on their own performance improve the care they deliver — and what makes feedback work harder?
shelves.mesh: Education, Medical, Continuing · Feedback, Psychological · Health Personnel/standards · Health Services Research · Medical Audit/standards · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Practice Patterns, Physicians'/standards
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE that audit and feedback produces small improvements in professional practice — across 140 randomised trials the weighted median adjusted risk difference was a 4.3% absolute increase in compliance with desired practice (IQR 0.5% to 16%) — and MAYBE (weak evidence) that it improves patient outcomes, where the weighted median risk difference was -0.4% (IQR -1.3% to 1.6%) for dichotomous outcomes. Feedback appears more effective when baseline performance is low, it comes from a supervisor or colleague, is given more than once, is delivered in both verbal and written formats, and includes explicit targets and an action plan.

cards.headline: Ivers (Cochrane): audit and feedback — median 4.3% absolute increase in compliance with desired practice across 140 trials
cards.summary: Cochrane review (140 trials): audit and feedback — median 4.3% absolute increase in compliance with desired practice.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials
cards.people: 140 randomised trials of audit and feedback included and analysed; the main practice analysis covered 108 comparisons from 70 studies (82 comparisons from 49 studies with dichotomous outcomes after excluding high risk of bias), weighted by the number of health professionals in each study. The abstract does not state patient mean age or sex mix (a professional-practice population).
cards.result: For dichotomous practice outcomes, the weighted median adjusted risk difference was a 4.3% (IQR 0.5% to 16%) absolute increase in compliance with desired practice; for continuous outcomes the weighted median adjusted change relative to control was 1.3% (IQR 1.3% to 28.9% — a relative measure). For patient outcomes, the weighted median risk difference was -0.4% (IQR -1.3% to 1.6%) across 12 comparisons from 6 studies with dichotomous outcomes, and the weighted median percentage change was 17% (IQR 1.5% to 17%, relative) across 8 comparisons from 5 studies with continuous outcomes. Meta-regression suggested greater effects with low baseline performance, a supervisor or colleague as source, repeated delivery, verbal plus written formats, and explicit targets with an action plan.
cards.watchOut: Effects are small and highly variable (IQR spans near-zero), the patient-outcome evidence base is a small subset of the trials, and the review's searches closed in 2010–2011 — later digital feedback methods are outside it.
cards.source: Ivers N et al. Audit and feedback: effects on professional practice and healthcare outcomes. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012;(6):CD000259. PMID: 22696318. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — systematic review.

shelves.title: Computerised clinical decision support at the point of care
shelves.question: Do computerised decision-support systems improve practitioner performance and patient outcomes, and which features predict success?
shelves.mesh: Clinical Pharmacy Information Systems · Clinical Trials as Topic · Decision Support Systems, Clinical · Medication Systems, Hospital · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Quality Assurance, Health Care · Software
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE that computerised clinical decision support improves practitioner performance — it did so in 62 of 97 studies (64%) assessing that outcome in the Garg systematic review of 100 controlled trials — and MAYBE (weak evidence) that it improves patient outcomes, reported in only 7 of 52 trials (13%) that assessed them. Systems that prompted users automatically succeeded more often than systems users had to activate (73% vs 47% of trials; P=.02). The patient-outcome evidence is thinner than the process evidence, as the topic file directed be labelled.

cards.headline: Garg: decision support improved practitioner performance in 64% of studies, but patient outcomes in only 13% of trials that measured them
cards.summary: Decision support improved practitioner performance in 64% of studies, but patient outcomes in only 13% of trials that measured them.
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised and non-randomised controlled trials
cards.people: 100 controlled trials of computerised clinical decision support systems met inclusion (searches to September 2004); 97 studies assessed practitioner performance and 52 assessed one or more patient outcomes. The abstract does not state patient mean age or sex mix (a practitioner-and-system population).
cards.result: Practitioner performance improved in 62 of 97 studies (64%): diagnostic systems 4 of 10 (40%), reminder systems 16 of 21 (76%), disease-management systems 23 of 37 (62%), drug-dosing or prescribing systems 19 of 29 (66%). Of 52 trials assessing patient outcomes, 7 (13%) reported improvements. Automatic prompting predicted success (73% of trials vs 47% for user-activated systems; P=.02), as did author-developed software (74% vs 28%; P=.001) — the latter a warning about developer-run evaluations.
cards.watchOut: A vote-counting synthesis (no pooled effect size), including non-randomised trials, from a 2004 search — pre-dating modern EHR-embedded and machine-learning support; 'improved performance' is a process judgement, not patient benefit.
cards.source: Garg AX et al. Effects of computerized clinical decision support systems on practitioner performance and patient outcomes: a systematic review. JAMA. 2005;293(10):1223-1238. PMID: 15755945. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — systematic review.

shelves.title: Patient-centred care for multimorbidity in primary care: the 3D trial

shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease/psychology,therapy · England · Interdisciplinary Communication · Intersectoral Collaboration · Multimorbidity · Patient Care Team · Patient-Centered Care
shelves.balance: LIKELY the null on quality of life: In the 3D trial — the largest test of the international consensus model for multimorbidity — quality of life at 15 months was identical between the patient-centred 3D approach and usual care (adjusted difference in EQ-5D-5L 0.00, 95% CI -0.02 to 0.02; P=0.93). shelves.title: Group medical visits (shared medical appointments) for chronic conditions
shelves.question: Do group medical visits improve glycaemic and blood-pressure control in diabetes and other chronic conditions versus usual one-to-one care?
shelves.mesh: Blood Glucose/metabolism · Body Mass Index · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood,therapy · Hypoglycemic Agents/therapeutic use · Life Style · Retrospective Studies · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The randomised evidence is thinner and more mixed than the model's popularity suggests. Adding intensive weight management to group medical visits was non-inferior to group visits alone for HbA1c at 48 weeks (8.2% vs 8.3%; difference -0.1%) and superior for weight (-3.7 kg), medication intensity and hypoglycaemic events (incidence rate ratio 0.49, relative) — a comparison of two group-visit variants, not of group visits versus usual care. In Kenya (BIGPIC), group visits with or without microfinance lowered systolic BP numerically more than usual care (extra reductions of 3.3 and 3.9 mm Hg) but no pairwise comparison met its significance threshold. Hence POSSIBLE, not higher. FENCE: the lay-led Expert Patients COURSE (Shelf #888) is a different intervention — education outside consultations, not a shared consultation — and is not carded here.

cards.headline: Group visits plus intensive weight management: non-inferior HbA1c (8.2% vs 8.3%), 3.7 kg more weight loss, half the hypoglycaemic events
cards.summary: Group visits plus intensive weight management: non-inferior HbA1c ( 8.2% vs 8.3% ), 3.7 kg more weight loss, half the hypoglycaemic events.
cards.type: Randomised clinical non-inferiority trial (VA medical centres, North Carolina)
cards.people: 263 outpatients with type 2 diabetes, uncontrolled HbA1c and BMI of 27 or higher, started the intervention (136 group medical visits alone, 127 group visits plus intensive weight management with a low-carbohydrate diet); mean age 60.7 years (SD 8.2); 235 (89.4%) men; 143 (54.4%) Black; baseline HbA1c 9.1% and BMI 35.3.
cards.result: At 48 weeks HbA1c was 8.2% with weight management plus group visits versus 8.3% with group visits alone (mean difference -0.1%, 95% CI -0.5% to 0.2%; non-inferiority margin 0.5% met; P=.44). The weight-management arm used less diabetes medication (medication effect score difference -0.5; P<.001), lost more weight (difference -3.7 kg, 95% CI -5.5 to -1.9; P<.001), and had approximately 50% fewer hypoglycaemic events (incidence rate ratio 0.49, relative, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.71; P<.001) — just below the 0.5 boundary of the caution band, printed as relative.
cards.watchOut: There is no usual-care arm: the trial compares two flavours of group visit, so it cannot show group visits themselves improve glycaemia; the population was 89% male veterans, and visit frequency differed between arms (13 vs 9 visits).
cards.source: Yancy WS Jr et al. cards.headline: BIGPIC (Kenya): group medical visits with microfinance — systolic BP fell most, but pairwise significance was not met
cards.summary: BIGPIC (Kenya): group medical visits with microfinance — systolic BP fell most, but pairwise significance was not met.
cards.people: 2,890 individuals with diabetes or hypertension in Kenya (708 usual care, 709 usual care plus microfinance, 740 group medical visits, 733 group visits integrated into microfinance); 69.9% women; average baseline systolic BP 157.5 mm Hg. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Mean systolic BP fell by 11.4 mm Hg on usual care, 14.8 on microfinance, 14.7 on group visits and 16.4 on group visits plus microfinance. Adjusted extra reductions versus usual care were 3.9 mm Hg for the combined arm (98.3% CI -8.5 to 0.7), 3.3 for group visits (-7.8 to 1.2) and 2.3 for microfinance (-7.0 to 2.4) — none met its pairwise significance threshold, though intervals for the combined arm ranged from substantive benefit to neutral. Group visits tended to benefit women, and microfinance arms tended to benefit poorer individuals.
cards.watchOut: The usual-care group itself fell 11.4 mm Hg, and the trial's own conclusion rests on interval interpretation rather than significant pairwise tests; group visits were bundled with a financial intervention in the best-performing arm.

shelves.title: Lay-led self-management programmes for long-term conditions (Expert Patients Programme)
shelves.question: Does a lay-led, group self-management course for people with long-term conditions improve health status, self-efficacy, and health-care use versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease/rehabilitation · Cost-Benefit Analysis · England · Health Services/statistics & numerical data · Health Status · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Self Care/economics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the single large pragmatic randomised evaluation of England's Expert Patients Programme, immediate access to the lay-led course produced considerably greater self-efficacy and energy at 6 months, but no statistically significant reduction in routine health-service use; the economic analysis found greater health-related quality of life and a small cost reduction, with a 70% probability of cost-effectiveness at a £20,000-per-QALY threshold. A single pragmatic trial with self-reported primary outcomes caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. FENCE: clinician-led group medical VISITS (Shelf #887) are a consultation format; this shelf is a lay-led course outside consultations.

cards.headline: Expert Patients Programme: lay-led course raised self-efficacy and energy at 6 months, with no significant fall in service use
cards.summary: Expert Patients Programme: the lay-led course raised self-efficacy and energy at 6 months, with no significant fall in service use.
cards.type: Two-arm pragmatic randomised controlled trial with waiting-list control, plus cost-effectiveness analysis
cards.people: 629 patients with a wide range of self-defined long-term conditions in community settings in England, assigned to immediate course access (six weekly lay-led sessions teaching self-care skills) or waiting-list control. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 months, patients with immediate access reported considerably greater self-efficacy and energy than controls (the record's abstract reports these qualitatively, without figures). There were no statistically significant reductions in routine health-services utilisation. The cost-effectiveness analysis showed considerably greater health-related quality of life and a small reduction in costs with immediate access; at a willingness to pay of £20,000 per quality-adjusted life year, there was a 70% probability the intervention was cost-effective.
cards.watchOut: Primary outcomes were self-reported in an unblindable trial with a waiting-list control (expectation effects possible), the abstract gives no numerical effect sizes, and 6 months says nothing about durability.
cards.source: Kennedy A et al. The effectiveness and cost effectiveness of a national lay-led self care support programme for patients with long-term conditions: a pragmatic randomised controlled trial. J Epidemiol Community Health. 2007;61(3):254-261. PMID: 17325405. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era pragmatic trial.

shelves.title: Lay health counsellors for common mental disorders in low-resource primary care: MANAS and the Friendship Bench
shelves.question: Can trained lay counsellors deliver effective psychological treatment for depression and anxiety in primary care where specialists are scarce?
shelves.mesh: Allied Health Personnel · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Anxiety Disorders/drug therapy,therapy · Cooperative Behavior · Counseling · Depressive Disorder/drug therapy,therapy · Directive Counseling/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two cluster-randomised trials in low-resource primary care found lay-counsellor psychological treatment improved common mental disorders — MANAS (Goa): recovery at 6 months 65.0% versus 52.9% (risk ratio 1.22, relative; risk difference 12.1%), with the effect concentrated in public facilities (risk ratio 1.55, relative) and absent in private facilities (risk ratio 0.95, relative); Friendship Bench (Zimbabwe): symptom scores far lower with problem-solving therapy (SSQ-14 3.81 vs 8.90; adjusted risk ratio 0.21, relative) and depression symptoms in 13.7% versus 49.9% (adjusted risk ratio 0.28, relative). Both interventions were supervised, structured and embedded in primary care — not unsupported volunteers. FENCE: collaborative care in US primary care (drafted Shelf #533) uses care managers under specialist supervision in a high-income staffing model; it is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: MANAS: lay-counsellor collaborative stepped care raised recovery from common mental disorders (65.0% vs 52.9%) — in public facilities
cards.summary: MANAS: lay-counsellor collaborative stepped care raised recovery from common mental disorders ( 65.0% vs 52.9% ) — in public facilities.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised controlled trial (24 primary-care facilities, Goa, India; assessor masked)
cards.people: Adults screening positive for common mental disorders in 24 public and private primary-care facilities; 1,160 of 1,360 (85%) intervention patients and 1,269 of 1,436 (88%) control patients completed the 6-month outcome assessment. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Recovery from ICD-10 common mental disorders at 6 months: 620 (65.0%) on the lay-counsellor collaborative stepped-care intervention versus 553 (52.9%) on enhanced usual care (risk ratio 1.22, relative, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.47; risk difference 12.1%, 95% CI 1.6% to 22.5%) — the relative ratio sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, so the absolute difference is the firmer figure. The effect was strong in public facilities (65.9% vs 42.5%; risk ratio 1.55, relative) and absent in private facilities (64.1% vs 65.9%; risk ratio 0.95, relative). Deaths: 3 versus 6; suicide attempts: 4 versus 6; no death was by suicide.
cards.watchOut: The overall interval touches 1.00 and the benefit is a public-facility finding; the intervention was a package (counsellor case management and psychosocial therapy, physician-prescribed antidepressants, specialist supervision), not counselling alone.
cards.source: Patel V et al. Effectiveness of an intervention led by lay health counsellors for depressive and anxiety disorders in primary care in Goa, India (MANAS): a cluster randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2010;376(9758):2086-2095. PMID: 21159375. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00446407, from the record's databank fields.

cards.people: 573 clinic attenders aged 18 years or older screening positive for common mental disorders (286 intervention, 287 control); 495 (86.4%) women; median age 33 years (IQR 27–41); 238 (41.7%) HIV-positive; 521 (90.9%) completed 6-month follow-up.

shelves.title: Behavioural nudges against inappropriate antibiotic prescribing (Meeker; stewardship by audit)
shelves.question: Do behavioural interventions in primary care — accountable justification and suggested alternatives in the record, and peer comparison against top performers — cut inappropriate antibiotic prescribing for respiratory infections, and does a paediatric outpatient stewardship programme with audit-and-feedback do the same?

shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two cluster-randomised trials in US primary care networks both cut inappropriate antibiotic prescribing. In Meeker 2016 (47 practices, 248 clinicians), accountable justification (difference-in-differences −7.0 percentage points, P<0.001) and peer comparison (−5.2 points, P<0.001) worked; suggested alternatives did not reach significance (P=0.66 for trajectories) — the shelf credits only the two interventions that worked. In Gerber 2013 (paediatric network), one education session plus quarterly personalised audit-and-feedback cut broad-spectrum prescribing more than controls (difference of differences 6.7%, P=0.01), driven by pneumonia and sinusitis prescribing, with no effect on viral-infection prescribing. These are prescribing-process outcomes; neither trial measured resistance or patient outcomes.

cards.headline: Meeker 2016: accountable justification and peer comparison cut inappropriate prescribing; suggested alternatives did not
cards.summary: Meeker 2016: accountable justification and peer comparison cut inappropriate antibiotic prescribing; suggested alternatives did not.
cards.type: Cluster randomised clinical trial (47 primary care practices, 18-month intervention)
cards.people: 248 clinicians in 47 primary care practices in Boston and Los Angeles, randomised to receive 0, 1, 2 or 3 behavioural interventions, all after guideline education at enrolment. Outcomes covered 14,753 visits (mean patient age 47 years; 69% women) for antibiotic-inappropriate acute respiratory infections in the baseline period and 16,959 visits (mean age 48 years; 67% women) in the intervention period.
cards.result: Mean inappropriate prescribing fell in all arms, including controls (24.1% to 13.1%; absolute difference −11.0%). Against that trend: suggested alternatives fell 22.1% to 6.1% (difference-in-differences −5.0% [95% CI −7.8% to 0.1%]; P=0.66 for differences in trajectories — not significant); accountable justification fell 23.2% to 5.2% (difference-in-differences −7.0% [−9.1% to −2.9%]; P<0.001); peer comparison fell 19.9% to 3.7% (difference-in-differences −5.2% [−6.9% to −1.6%]; P<0.001). There were no significant interactions between interventions.
cards.watchOut: A strong secular trend (controls improved by 11 points on education and observation alone) does much of the work in every arm; the card credits only the two interventions that beat that trend, and the trial says nothing about clinical outcomes or resistance.
cards.source: Meeker D et al. Effect of Behavioral Interventions on Inappropriate Antibiotic Prescribing Among Primary Care Practices: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016 Feb 9;315(6):562-570. PMID: 26864410. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01454947, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Gerber 2013: education plus quarterly audit-and-feedback cut broad-spectrum prescribing in children's primary care (26.8% to 14.3% vs 28.4% to 22.6% in controls)
cards.summary: Gerber 2013: education plus quarterly audit-and-feedback cut broad-spectrum prescribing in children's primary care ( 26.8% to 14.3% ).
cards.type: Cluster randomised trial of outpatient antimicrobial stewardship (25-practice paediatric network)
cards.people: A network of 25 paediatric primary care practices in Pennsylvania and New Jersey using a common electronic health record; 18 practices (162 clinicians) participated, randomised to a 1-hour on-site education session followed by one year of personalised quarterly audit-and-feedback, or usual practice. Prescribing was tracked for targeted acute respiratory infections from 20 months before to 12 months after the intervention, in children without chronic conditions, antibiotic allergy or prior antibiotic use.
cards.result: Broad-spectrum (off-guideline) antibiotic prescribing fell from 26.8% to 14.3% in intervention practices versus 28.4% to 22.6% in controls (difference of differences 6.7%; P=0.01 for differences in trajectories). Off-guideline prescribing for pneumonia fell 15.7% to 4.2% versus 17.1% to 16.3% (difference of differences 10.7%; P<0.001) and for acute sinusitis 38.9% to 18.8% versus 40.0% to 33.9% (14.0%; P=0.12 — not significant). Prescribing changed little for streptococcal pharyngitis and did not change for viral infections (7.9% to 7.7% vs 6.4% to 4.5%; difference of differences −1.7%; P=0.93).
cards.watchOut: One network, one health record, bacterial diagnoses only: the intervention improved guideline adherence where baseline off-guideline prescribing was high (pneumonia, sinusitis) and had nothing to fix where it was already low or the diagnosis was viral.
cards.source: Gerber JS et al. Effect of an outpatient antimicrobial stewardship intervention on broad-spectrum antibiotic prescribing by primary care pediatricians: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2013 Jun 12;309(22):2345-2352. PMID: 23757082. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01806103, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two of Meeker's three nudges worked, and audit-and-feedback worked in children — on prescribing, not outcomes
cards.summary: Two of Meeker's three nudges worked, and audit-and-feedback worked in children — on prescribing, not outcomes — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Meeker 2016 (248 clinicians, adult primary care, three behavioural interventions) and Gerber 2013 (162 clinicians, paediatric primary care, education plus audit-and-feedback).
cards.result: The convergent finding across two cluster trials is that showing clinicians their own prescribing — against a justification requirement, against top-performing peers, or as quarterly personal feedback — reduces inappropriate antibiotic prescribing by roughly 5–7 percentage points beyond background improvement; prettier order sets (suggested alternatives) did not significantly beat the trend. The currency sweep found a newer pragmatic peer-comparison trial in the same family (2024–2026 window); it is fenced here, not carded, and does not displace these anchors. Audit-and-feedback as a general implementation strategy is drafted at Shelf #884 and point-of-care decision support at Shelf #885; CRP testing to guide the same decisions is Shelf #1003 and delayed prescribing is Shelf #1004 — none re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Prescribing rates are a process surrogate: neither trial shows fewer complications, less resistance, or happier patients, and both ran inside US networks with shared electronic records — transport elsewhere is an assumption, not a result.
cards.source: Synthesis of Meeker D et al. JAMA. 2016;315(6):562-570. PMID: 26864410; Gerber JS et al. JAMA. 2013;309(22):2345-2352. PMID: 23757082. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Patient decision aids: what the Cochrane evidence actually shows
shelves.question: Do patient decision aids improve knowledge, risk perception and decisional conflict — and change uptake of screening and surgery — across the Cochrane review's hundred-plus trials, in its 2017 analysis and its 2024 update?
shelves.mesh: Communication · Conservative Treatment · Decision Support Techniques · Elective Surgical Procedures · Health Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice · Patient Education as Topic/methods · Patient Participation
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane review of patient decision aids — 105 trials and 31,043 participants in 2017, growing to 209 trials and 107,698 participants in the 2024 update — consistently finds that decision aids increase knowledge (mean difference about 12–13 points on a 100-point scale, high-certainty), improve accuracy of risk perceptions, and reduce decisional conflict about feeling uninformed and unclear about values, with more people making choices congruent with their informed values. Effects on what people actually choose are decision-specific and smaller: fewer chose major elective surgery (relative risk 0.86) and PSA screening (relative risk 0.88) in 2017, more started diabetes medication (relative risk 1.65), and most other choices did not change. There was no difference in decision regret (2024). The two editions are one living review, carded as versions — the update confirms and enlarges the 2017 findings rather than independently replicating them.

cards.headline: Stacey 2017: across 105 trials (31,043 participants), decision aids raised knowledge by 13.27 points and halved-to-doubled the accuracy of risk perception
cards.summary: Stacey 2017: across 105 trials (31,043 participants), decision aids raised knowledge by 13.27 points and improved risk-perception accuracy.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (2017 edition)
cards.people: 105 studies involving 31,043 participants facing health treatment or screening decisions, comparing decision aids with usual care and/or alternative interventions; 12 of the 105 studies were at high risk of bias. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age.
cards.result: Decision aids increased knowledge (mean difference 13.27/100; 95% CI 11.32 to 15.23; 52 studies; N=13,316; high-quality evidence), accuracy of risk perceptions (relative risk 2.10, 1.66 to 2.66; 17 studies; N=5,096; moderate-quality evidence) and congruence between informed values and care choices (relative risk 2.06, 1.46 to 2.91; 10 studies; N=4,626; low-quality evidence) — relative risks printed as relative. They decreased decisional conflict about feeling uninformed (MD −9.28/100, −12.20 to −6.36; high-quality) and indecision about personal values (MD −8.81/100, −11.99 to −5.63; high-quality), and the proportion passive in decision-making (relative risk 0.68, 0.55 to 0.83). Fewer people chose major elective invasive surgery (relative risk 0.86, 0.75 to 1.00; significant only after removing the prophylactic-mastectomy study, 0.84, 0.73 to 0.97) or PSA screening (relative risk 0.88, 0.80 to 0.98); more started new diabetes medication (relative risk 1.65, 1.06 to 2.56). Consultations ran a median 2.6 minutes longer.
cards.watchOut: Process outcomes (knowledge, conflict, perceived risk) are where the effects are large and certain; the choice outcomes that systems care about are small, mixed and decision-specific — and the 2017 surgery result was fragile to one study's removal, as the abstract itself discloses.
cards.source: Stacey D et al. Decision aids for people facing health treatment or screening decisions. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017 Apr 12;4(4):CD001431. PMID: 28402085. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Stacey 2024 update: the same review at 209 trials (107,698 participants) — knowledge +11.90 points, values-congruent choices relative risk 1.75, no difference in regret
cards.summary: Stacey 2024 update: the same review at 209 trials — knowledge +11.90 points, values-congruent choices up (relative risk 1.75).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (2024 update of the 2017 review)
cards.people: 209 studies involving 107,698 participants across 71 different decisions (most commonly cardiovascular treatments, cancer screening and treatments, mental health treatments and joint replacement); 34 studies had at least one item at high risk of bias. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age.
cards.result: Compared with usual care: congruence between informed values and care choices probably increased (relative risk 1.75, 95% CI 1.44 to 2.13; 21 studies, 9,377 participants; moderate-certainty evidence — a relative figure). High-certainty evidence showed improved knowledge (MD 11.90/100, 10.60 to 13.19; 107 studies, 25,492 participants), more accurate risk perceptions (relative risk 1.94, 1.61 to 2.34; 25 studies, 7,796 participants), less decisional conflict about feeling uninformed (MD −10.02, −12.31 to −7.74; 58 studies, 12,104 participants) and about personal values (MD −7.86, −9.69 to −6.02; 55 studies, 11,880 participants), and fewer people passive in decision-making (relative risk 0.72, 0.59 to 0.88; 21 studies, 4,348 participants). There was no difference in decision regret (MD −1.23, −3.05 to 0.59; 22 studies, 3,707 participants; high-certainty evidence), and no difference in consultation length when aids were used before the consultation.
cards.watchOut: This is the same living review seven years on, not an independent body of evidence: the 2024 edition contains the 2017 trials. Its value is that doubling the evidence base barely moved the estimates — the gains are stable, and so are their limits.
cards.source: Stacey D et al. Decision aids for people facing health treatment or screening decisions. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2024 Jan 29;1(1):CD001431. PMID: 38284415. Registry ID: none for the review itself — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: decision aids reliably make people better informed — they do not reliably change what people choose
cards.summary: Decision aids reliably make people better informed — they do not reliably change what people choose — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Stacey 2017 (105 trials, 31,043 participants) and Stacey 2024 (209 trials, 107,698 participants) — two editions of one Cochrane review (CD001431), carded as versions within this shelf only.
cards.result: The estimates barely moved as the evidence doubled: knowledge up roughly 12–13 points on a 100-point scale, decisional conflict down about 8–10 points on its subscales, risk perception and values-congruent choice improved with relative risks between 1.75 and 2.10. That stability across 209 trials carries LIKELY for the decision-quality claim. The honest boundary: uptake effects are few, small and decision-specific (surgery relative risk 0.86; PSA screening 0.88; diabetes-medication starts 1.65), most choices showed no difference, and decision regret was unchanged. A decision aid is an information intervention with proven information effects — not a lever for steering uptake in either direction.
cards.watchOut: Every relative risk on this shelf sits inside or near the library's 0.5–2.0 caution band on its own; the LIKELY grade rests on the consistency and certainty of the pooled mean differences, not on any single ratio.
cards.source: Synthesis of Stacey D et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017;4(4):CD001431. PMID: 28402085; Stacey D et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2024;1(1):CD001431. PMID: 38284415. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Mailed faecal testing outreach for colorectal cancer screening (STOP CRC)
shelves.question: Does mailing FIT kits to patients due for colorectal screening raise completion — in community health clinics in the STOP CRC cluster trial, and in the Systems of Support programme whose economic evaluation priced the strategy?
shelves.mesh: Ambulatory Care Facilities/organization & administration · Colonoscopy/methods · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis,epidemiology · Community-Institutional Relations · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Electronic Health Records · Mass Screening/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Mailed FIT outreach works, modestly and unevenly. STOP CRC (26 federally qualified health centre clinics, 41,193 adults) raised FIT completion by 3.4 percentage points over usual care (13.9% vs 10.4%) and any screening by 3.8 points — a real gain on a low base, but with clinic-level effects ranging from −7.4 to +17.6 percentage points and implementation (proportion actually mailed a FIT) ranging from 6.5% to 68.2%: the mailing is easy to prescribe and hard to deliver well. The Systems of Support economic evaluation (Meenan 2015, of the Green programme's stepped EHR-linked mailings trial) supplies the price side: delivery cost $21–$27 per participant brought up to date on screening, with the automated and assisted arms cost-saving once induced testing costs were counted. One effectiveness trial plus one programme's economic evaluation is a POSSIBLE base, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: STOP CRC 2018: mailed FIT outreach raised FIT completion to 13.9% versus 10.4% in usual care — with clinic effects from −7.4 to +17.6 points
cards.summary: STOP CRC 2018: mailed FIT outreach raised FIT completion to 13.9% versus 10.4% in usual care — with clinic effects from −7.4 to +17 points.
cards.type: Cluster randomised pragmatic clinical trial (26 clinics, 8 federally qualified health centres)
cards.people: 41,193 adults overdue for colorectal cancer screening (mean [SD] age 58.5 [6.3] years; 22,994 women) at 26 clinics in Oregon and California, randomised by clinic to an EHR-embedded mailed FIT programme (13 clinics; 21,134 patients — introductory letter, mailed FIT, reminder letter, with training and facilitation) or usual care (13 clinics; 20,059 patients).
cards.result: Intervention clinics had a significantly higher adjusted clinic-level proportion completing a FIT (13.9% vs 10.4%; difference 3.4 percentage points; 95% CI 0.1% to 6.8%) and completing any colorectal cancer screening (18.3% vs 14.5%; difference 3.8 points; 0.6% to 7.0%). Effectiveness varied widely across health centres (FIT-completion differences −7.4 to +17.6 percentage points), as did implementation (proportion mailed a FIT, 6.5% to 68.2%). The number needed to mail to achieve a completed FIT was 4.8 overall, and 4.0 in clinics that mailed a reminder.
cards.watchOut: A pragmatic trial of a programme, not of an envelope: where clinics barely implemented it, it barely worked. The average +3.4 points should always be quoted with its range, and screening completion is a process outcome — no cancer or mortality outcome is claimed.
cards.source: Coronado GD et al. Effectiveness of a Mailed Colorectal Cancer Screening Outreach Program in Community Health Clinics: The STOP CRC Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2018 Sep 1;178(9):1174-1181. PMID: 30083752. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01742065, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Meenan 2015 (Systems of Support economic evaluation): stepped mailed screening cost $21–$27 per person brought up to date — and saved money in its lighter arms
cards.summary: Meenan 2015: stepped mailed screening cost $21–$27 per person brought up to date.
cards.type: Economic evaluation based on a parallel-design randomised trial (stepped interventions vs usual care)
cards.people: Participants in the Systems of Support screening programme in primary care, randomised to EHR-linked automated mailings, automated mailings plus telephone assistance, automated and assisted support plus nurse navigation, or usual care (data August 2008 to November 2011; implementation resources micro-costed, research costs excluded). The abstract does not state the total participant number or mean age.
cards.result: Intervention delivery cost per participant current for screening ranged from $21 (automated) to $27 (navigated). Including induced testing costs, the automated arm (incremental cost-effectiveness ratio −$159) and the assisted arm (−$36) cost less than usual care over 2 years — savings arising because increased faecal occult blood testing substituted for more expensive colonoscopies in usual care. More intensive interventions were consistently likely to be cost-effective versus less intensive ones, with willingness-to-pay values of $600–$1,200 for an additional person current for screening yielding at least 80% probability of cost-effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: This card prices the strategy; it is not itself an effectiveness report — the screening gains it monetises come from its parent trial, and 2-year cost-effectiveness in one US system (2008–2011 prices and practice) is not a transferable tariff.
cards.source: Meenan RT et al. An economic evaluation of colorectal cancer screening in primary care practice. Am J Prev Med. 2015 Jun;48(6):714-721. PMID: 25998922. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00158639, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: mail the kit — expect single-digit gains, budget tens of dollars per screened person, and mind the implementation gap
cards.summary: Mail the kit — expect single-digit gains, budget tens of dollars per screened person, and mind the implementation gap — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: STOP CRC 2018 (26 clinics, 41,193 adults overdue for screening) and Meenan 2015 (economic evaluation of the Systems of Support stepped-mailing trial).
cards.result: Together they describe a cheap, real, small effect: +3.4 percentage points of FIT completion in safety-net clinics (STOP CRC), at a delivery cost of about $21–$27 per person brought up to date, with the lighter automated versions cost-saving over two years in the Systems of Support accounting (Meenan). The currency sweep found a fresh cohort of mailed-outreach trials in the 2024–2026 window (a community-health-centre FIT outreach trial and the CARES pragmatic cluster trial among them); they are fenced here — they confirm the strategy is still being tested at scale but were not carded over the anchors. The screening shelves that test FIT and colonoscopy accuracy and strategy themselves are a different question and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: The variance is the finding clinics should plan around: STOP CRC's centre effects ran from −7.4 to +17.6 points, so 'we mail FITs' describes intentions whose yield depends on mailing nearly everyone, and reminding them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Coronado GD et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(9):1174-1181. PMID: 30083752; Meenan RT et al. Am J Prev Med. 2015;48(6):714-721. PMID: 25998922. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Point-of-care C-reactive protein testing to guide antibiotics
shelves.question: Does CRP point-of-care testing safely reduce antibiotic prescribing — for COPD exacerbations in Butler's NEJM trial, and for respiratory infections when paired with communication-skills training in Cals's factorial trial?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Biomarkers/blood · C-Reactive Protein/analysis · Health Status · Inappropriate Prescribing/prevention & control · Point-of-Care Testing · Practice Patterns, Physicians'/standards,statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in primary care, a decade apart and in different clinical problems, both found large reductions in antibiotic prescribing with no signal of harm. Butler 2019 (653 patients with COPD exacerbations, 86 practices) cut patient-reported antibiotic use from 77.4% to 57.0% (adjusted relative odds 0.31) while meeting non-inferiority on COPD health status. Cals 2009 (431 patients with lower respiratory tract infection, factorial design) cut prescribing at the index consultation from 53% to 31% with CRP testing, and communication-skills training independently did as well or better (54% to 27%), with recovery and satisfaction unchanged. Safety here means 'no evidence of harm' on symptom and health-status outcomes in these trials — neither was powered for rare complications, and Butler recorded two deaths in the usual-care group, judged unrelated to participation.

cards.headline: Butler 2019: CRP-guided care cut antibiotic use in COPD exacerbations to 57.0% from 77.4% — with COPD health status non-inferior
cards.summary: Butler 2019: CRP-guided care cut antibiotic use in COPD exacerbations to 57.0% from 77.4% — with COPD health status non-inferior.
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, randomised controlled trial (86 general practices, England and Wales)
cards.people: 653 patients with a COPD diagnosis in their primary care record consulting for an acute exacerbation, randomised to usual care guided by CRP point-of-care testing or usual care alone; co-primary outcomes were patient-reported antibiotic use within 4 weeks (superiority) and COPD health status at 2 weeks on the Clinical COPD Questionnaire (non-inferiority). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Fewer CRP-guided patients reported antibiotic use (57.0% vs 77.4%; adjusted odds ratio 0.31; 95% CI 0.20 to 0.47 — a relative odds figure, printed beside its absolute rates). The adjusted mean difference in Clinical COPD Questionnaire score at 2 weeks was −0.19 points (two-sided 90% CI −0.33 to −0.05) in favour of the CRP-guided group, meeting non-inferiority. Clinicians prescribed antibiotics at the initial consultation to 47.7% versus 69.7% (difference 22.0 percentage points; adjusted odds ratio 0.31, 0.21 to 0.45) and over 4 weeks to 59.1% versus 79.7% (difference 20.6 points; adjusted odds ratio 0.30, 0.20 to 0.46). Two patients in the usual-care group died within 4 weeks, from causes the investigators judged unrelated to trial participation.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the 'use' outcome is patient-reported; the trial shows a testing strategy can support clinicians to withhold antibiotics in exacerbations — many of which are viral or non-infective — without measurable short-term harm, not that CRP identifies bacterial infection in an individual.
cards.source: Butler CC et al. C-Reactive Protein Testing to Guide Antibiotic Prescribing for COPD Exacerbations. N Engl J Med. 2019 Jul 11;381(2):111-120. PMID: 31291514. Registry ID: ISRCTN24346473, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Cals 2009: CRP testing cut prescribing from 53% to 31% — and communication-skills training cut it from 54% to 27%
cards.summary: Cals 2009: CRP testing cut prescribing from 53% to 31% — and communication-skills training cut it from 54% to 27%.
cards.type: Pragmatic, 2×2 factorial, cluster randomised controlled trial (20 general practices, Netherlands)
cards.people: 40 general practitioners in 20 practices recruited 431 patients with lower respiratory tract infection; practices were randomised to CRP point-of-care testing, training in enhanced communication skills, both, or neither (usual care). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: General practitioners in the CRP-test group prescribed antibiotics to 31% of patients versus 53% in the no-test group (P=0.02); those trained in communication skills prescribed to 27% versus 54% without training (P<0.01); the combined group prescribed to 23% (interaction non-significant). cards.watchOut: A 2009 trial of 431 patients — the smaller half of this shelf — and its second factor carries a message the testing literature often omits: the consultation skill performed at least as well as the biomarker.

cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Butler 2019 (653 patients, COPD exacerbations) and Cals 2009 (431 patients, lower respiratory tract infections), both randomised trials in primary care.

The currency sweep's newer paediatric CRP point-of-care trials are fenced here, not carded. shelves.title: Delayed antibiotic prescribing as a safety-net strategy
shelves.question: For respiratory infections, does a delayed-prescription strategy (collect later if not improving) cut antibiotic use without worsening symptoms or complications versus immediate or no antibiotics?
shelves.mesh: Common Cold/drug therapy,complications · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Cough/drug therapy · Respiratory Tract Infections/drug therapy · Pharyngitis/drug therapy · Otitis Media/drug therapy · Fever/drug therapy,etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The Cochrane individual-study evidence (Spurling 2023: 12 trials, 3,968 participants) and the large pragmatic Little 2014 factorial trial (889 patients) agree: delayed prescribing slashes antibiotic use compared with immediate prescribing (Cochrane relative odds 0.03 — an extreme ratio from few studies, printed with its caution on the card; in Little, 33–39% used antibiotics across delayed strategies versus 97% with immediate prescriptions), symptom severity and duration are broadly similar, satisfaction is preserved, and complication rates do not differ. The honest edges: delayed beats no-prescription on satisfaction but not on use (more delayed patients end up taking antibiotics than no-prescription patients — relative odds 2.52), and for sore throat and acute otitis media some symptom outcomes modestly favour immediate antibiotics. Delayed prescribing is a safety-net for the uncertain middle, not a universal default.

cards.headline: Spurling 2023 (Cochrane): delayed prescribing cut antibiotic use versus immediate (relative odds 0.03) with no difference in complications
cards.summary: Spurling 2023 (Cochrane): delayed prescribing cut antibiotic use versus immediate prescribing, with no difference in complications.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials (2023 update; living review to August 2022)
cards.people: 12 studies with 3,968 participants (data from 3,750 analysed) of all ages with respiratory tract infections — acute otitis media (3 studies), streptococcal pharyngitis (3), cough (2), sore throat (1), common cold (1) and mixed infections (2); six studies in children only, two in adults only, four in both; settings were primary care (6), paediatric clinics (4) and emergency departments (2). The abstract does not state a pooled mean age.
cards.result: For many clinical outcomes there were no differences between strategies; symptoms for acute otitis media and sore throat were modestly improved by immediate over delayed antibiotics, and there were no differences in complication rates. Antibiotic use: delayed probably reduced use versus immediate antibiotics (odds ratio 0.03, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.07; 8 studies, 2,257 participants; moderate-certainty evidence — a relative odds figure of unusual size, driven by near-universal use in immediate arms). Delayed was probably more likely to result in antibiotic use than no antibiotics (odds ratio 2.52, 1.69 to 3.75; 5 studies, 1,529 participants; moderate-certainty — relative). Satisfaction probably favoured delayed over no antibiotics (odds ratio 1.45, 1.08 to 1.96) and probably did not differ between delayed and immediate (odds ratio 0.77, 0.45 to 1.29). No study evaluated antibiotic resistance.
cards.watchOut: The headline odds ratio of 0.03 sits far outside the library's usual caution band because the comparator (immediate prescription) produces near-100% use — quote the Little trial's absolute percentages beside it, and note the review mixes children and adults across six infection types.
cards.source: Spurling GK et al. Immediate versus delayed versus no antibiotics for respiratory infections. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2023 Oct 4;10(10):CD004417. PMID: 37791590. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Little 2014: across four delayed strategies, 26–39% used antibiotics versus 97% with immediate prescriptions — symptoms indistinguishable
cards.summary: Little 2014: across four delayed strategies, 26–39% used antibiotics versus 97% with immediate prescriptions — symptoms indistinguishable.
cards.type: Open, pragmatic, parallel-group, factorial randomised controlled trial (UK primary care)
cards.people: 889 patients aged 3 years and over with acute respiratory tract infection, recruited by 53 health professionals in 25 practices, judged not to need immediate antibiotics and randomised to one of four delayed strategies (recontact for a prescription, post-dated prescription, collection of the prescription, or patient-led — prescription given with advice to delay), with a no-prescription strategy added as a further randomised comparison and immediate prescribing compared secondarily. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean symptom severity at days 2–4 ranged narrowly across the no-prescription and four delayed strategies (scores 1.60 to 1.82 on a 0–6 scale; likelihood ratio test P=0.625), and duration of symptoms rated moderately bad or worse did not differ between no prescription and the delayed strategies combined (median 3 vs 4 days; P=0.368). Antibiotic use was 26% with no prescription and 33–39% across the delayed strategies (37% recontact, 37% post-dated, 33% collection, 39% patient-led; differences among strategies non-significant, P=0.292), versus 97% use in patients given immediate antibiotics — who had no benefit in symptom severity (1.76) or duration (median 4 days) but stronger belief in antibiotics (93%). Satisfaction and beliefs in antibiotics did not differ significantly among the delayed and no-prescription strategies.
cards.watchOut: Open and pragmatic, in patients clinicians had already judged safe to wait: it validates the strategy in exactly the population where guidelines recommend it, and cannot extend it to patients who look like they need antibiotics now.

cards.headline: Synthesis: delay is the middle strategy that works — most patients never collect, symptoms run the same course
cards.summary: Delay is the middle strategy that works — most patients never collect, symptoms run the same course — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Spurling 2023 (Cochrane review, 12 trials, 3,968 participants) and Little 2014 (889 patients, four delayed strategies factorially compared).
cards.result: The absolute numbers carry the shelf: in Little, about a third of delayed-prescription patients used antibiotics versus 97% of immediate-prescription patients, with symptom severity scores within 0.2 points of each other and no satisfaction penalty; the Cochrane pooling adds no difference in complications across 12 trials. Hence LIKELY for the strategy in patients judged not to need immediate antibiotics. Two fences keep it honest: no-prescription used even fewer antibiotics (26%) — delay is the option for clinician or patient uncertainty, not the minimum-use option — and sore-throat and ear symptoms ran modestly better with immediate antibiotics in parts of the Cochrane evidence. Prescriber-side nudges are Shelf #1000 and CRP testing is Shelf #1003; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: No trial or review here measured antibiotic resistance — the population-level rationale for the strategy remains an inference from reduced use, and the cards say so.

shelves.title: Making professionals change: educational outreach visits and local opinion leaders
shelves.question: Do educational outreach visits (academic detailing) change prescribing and practice — and do local opinion leaders change compliance with desired practice — across the two Cochrane syntheses of randomised trials?
shelves.mesh: Education, Medical, Continuing · Health Personnel/education · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Patient Compliance · Practice Patterns, Physicians' · Professional Practice/standards · Attitude
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two Cochrane reviews of randomised trials find small, real improvements in professional compliance with desired practice. Educational outreach visits (O'Brien 2007: 69 studies, over 15,000 health professionals) produced a median adjusted risk difference of +5.6 percentage points in compliance (interquartile range 3.0% to 9.0%), most consistent for prescribing (+4.8%). Local opinion leaders (Flodgren 2019 update: 24 studies) produced a median adjusted risk difference of +10.8 percentage points (interquartile range 3.5% to 14.6%; moderate-certainty evidence), with patient-outcome effects uncertain (very low certainty). The grade is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY because the outreach-visits review is old (2007), effects are heterogeneous and unexplained in both reviews, and neither base shows what these strategies do to patient outcomes or costs. Small absolute gains, reliably in the right direction, at unknown price.

cards.headline: O'Brien 2007 (Cochrane): outreach visits improved compliance by a median 5.6 percentage points — most consistently for prescribing (4.8%)
cards.summary: O'Brien 2007 (Cochrane): outreach visits improved compliance by a median 5.6 percentage points — most consistently for prescribing.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials (educational outreach visits)
cards.people: 69 studies involving more than 15,000 health professionals, of which 28 studies (34 comparisons) contributed to the main median effect estimate — randomised trials in which an educational outreach visit was compared with no intervention, with baseline data and low or moderate risk of bias.
cards.result: The median adjusted risk difference in compliance with desired practice was +5.6% (interquartile range 3.0% to 9.0%). Effects were highly consistent for prescribing (median +4.8%, IQR 3.0% to 6.5%; 17 comparisons) but varied for other types of professional performance (median +6.0%, IQR 3.6% to 16.0%; 17 comparisons). For continuous outcomes (18 comparisons) the median adjusted relative improvement was 21% (IQR 11% to 41%) — a relative figure. Interventions including outreach visits appeared slightly superior to audit and feedback in the eight head-to-head trials (12 comparisons). Meta-regression found no compelling explanation for the variation in effects.
cards.watchOut: A 2007 review: the strategy's trial base is old, the effect is a median across heterogeneous small trials, and the review could not say which visit formats work best or what patient outcomes follow — consistency of direction is the finding, not precision.
cards.source: O'Brien MA et al. Educational outreach visits: effects on professional practice and health care outcomes. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2007 Oct 17;2007(4):CD000409. PMID: 17943742. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Flodgren 2019 (Cochrane): local opinion leaders improved compliance by a median 10.8 percentage points (moderate-certainty)
cards.summary: Flodgren 2019 (Cochrane): local opinion leaders improved compliance by a median 10.8 percentage points (moderate certainty).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised controlled trials (local opinion leaders; 2019 version)
cards.people: 24 studies involving more than 337 hospitals, 350 primary care practices, 3,005 healthcare professionals and 29,167 patients, mostly from North America and all in high-income countries; 18 studies (21 comparisons, 71 compliance outcomes) contributed to the main median estimate, with median follow-up of 12 months.
cards.result: Opinion-leader interventions probably improve healthcare professionals' compliance with evidence-based practice: median adjusted risk difference +10.8% (interquartile range 3.5% to 14.6%; moderate-certainty evidence). Secondary comparisons pointed the same way (opinion leaders alone vs no intervention: +9.15%, IQR −0.3% to 15%; opinion leaders plus other interventions vs the same interventions: +7.1%, IQR −1.4% to 19%). Whether opinion leaders improve patient outcomes is uncertain (3 studies; 5 dichotomous outcomes; very low certainty). No study reported costs or cost-effectiveness. The review could not determine how best to identify opinion leaders or which educational methods they should use, as methods were poorly described.
cards.watchOut: Some interquartile ranges cross zero and the occasional negative effect is unexplained in the review itself; the identification method (usually sociometric) is part of the intervention, so 'appoint a champion' is not automatically the trialled strategy.
cards.source: Flodgren G et al. Local opinion leaders: effects on professional practice and healthcare outcomes. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2019 Jun 24;6(6):CD000125. PMID: 31232458. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: expect single-digit-to-low-double-digit compliance gains — direction reliable, size and price uncertain
cards.summary: Expect single-digit-to-low-double-digit compliance gains — direction reliable, size and price uncertain — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: O'Brien 2007 (69 trials of educational outreach visits) and Flodgren 2019 (24 trials of local opinion leaders) — two Cochrane reviews of distinct strategies.
cards.result: Both strategies move professional behaviour in the desired direction by amounts that matter at scale and disappoint at the bedside: median +5.6 points for a trained visitor with data in hand, +10.8 points for a respected local peer. The currency sweep's newer academic-detailing trial in diabetes prescribing is fenced here, not carded. Audit-and-feedback as its own strategy is drafted at Shelf #884, and the prescribing-specific behavioural trials (Meeker, Gerber) are Shelf #1000 — not re-carded here. What neither review can support is a claim about patients: compliance is measured, outcomes and costs largely are not, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE despite two concordant syntheses.
cards.watchOut: Plan on heterogeneity: interquartile ranges in both reviews include near-zero effects, and neither review could explain which implementations land at the top of the range.

shelves.title: Comprehensive medication review in hospital, with post-discharge follow-up
shelves.question: Does a hospital-based comprehensive medication review — pharmacist-led, with post-discharge follow-up — reduce readmissions and emergency visits in older, polymedicated patients?
shelves.mesh: Aftercare/methods · Cluster Analysis · Cross-Over Studies · Emergency Service, Hospital/statistics & numerical data · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Medication Reconciliation/methods · Patient Discharge Summaries/standards
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — the single-centre ward-pharmacist model (Gillespie) · LIKELY — hospital CMR with post-discharge follow-up does not reduce unplanned hospital visits (MedRev, the null). The two trials disagree in an instructive way. Gillespie 2009 (400 patients aged 80+, one Swedish hospital, ward-based pharmacists embedded in the team) cut all hospital visits by a relative 16% and drug-related readmissions by a relative 80%, and saved money. The MedRev trial (Kempen 2021: 2,637 patients, 8 wards, 4 hospitals, cluster crossover) tested the exportable version — comprehensive medication review in hospital, with or without structured post-discharge follow-up — and found no reduction in unplanned hospital visits (adjusted rate ratios 1.04 and 1.15), with emergency department visits actually higher in the follow-up arm (1.29). The modern multicentre null governs the general claim; Gillespie stands as evidence that an intensive, single-centre, pharmacist-in-the-team model can differ — a POSSIBLE, not a transferable promise. OPERAM (structured review aimed at drug-related admissions) is drafted at Shelf #930 and is a different service design, not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Kempen 2021 (MedRev): hospital medication review, even with post-discharge follow-up, did not reduce unplanned hospital visits (rate ratios 1.04 and 1.15)
cards.summary: Kempen 2021 (MedRev): hospital medication review, even with post-discharge follow-up, did not reduce unplanned hospital visits.
cards.type: Cluster randomised crossover trial (8 wards, 4 hospitals, Sweden; 12-month follow-up)
cards.people: 2,644 patients aged 65 or older admitted at least one day (2,637 analysed: 1,357 female [51.5%]; median age 81 [IQR 74–87] years; median 9 medications [IQR 5–13]); wards rotated through comprehensive medication review (922 patients), CMR plus post-discharge follow-up (823), and usual care without a clinical pharmacist (892), with outcome assessors blinded to allocation.
cards.result: The primary outcome — incidence of unplanned hospital visits (admissions plus emergency department visits) within 12 months (crude rate 1.77 per patient-year overall) — did not differ from usual care for CMR (adjusted rate ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.22) or for CMR plus post-discharge follow-up (1.15, 0.98 to 1.34) — relative rate ratios, both null. CMR plus follow-up was associated with more emergency department visits (adjusted rate ratio 1.29, 1.05 to 1.59). There were no differences in other secondary outcomes. The authors conclude the findings do not support hospital-based CMRs as conducted in this trial.
cards.watchOut: One trial programme, however large: it tested CMR as an add-on service by multiprofessional ward teams in Swedish hospitals — it does not test pharmacists fully embedded in ward care of the Gillespie type, which is why this shelf splits rather than simply nulling the older trial.
cards.source: Kempen TGH et al. Effects of Hospital-Based Comprehensive Medication Reviews Including Postdischarge Follow-up on Older Patients' Use of Health Care: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open. 2021 Apr 1;4(4):e216303. PMID: 33929523. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02986425, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Gillespie 2009: ward-based pharmacists cut drug-related readmissions by a relative 80% and all hospital visits by 16% in patients 80 and older
cards.summary: Gillespie 2009: ward-based pharmacists cut drug-related readmissions (relative estimate 0.20) and all hospital visits by 16%.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (single university hospital, Uppsala, Sweden)
cards.people: 400 patients aged 80 years or older, randomised to ward-based pharmacist intervention (199) or standard care without direct ward-level pharmacist involvement (201); 368 patients were analysed (182 intervention, 186 control) over 12 months of follow-up. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The intervention group had a 16% reduction in all visits to hospital (visits per patient 1.88 vs 2.24; estimate 0.84, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.99), a 47% reduction in emergency department visits (0.35 vs 0.66; estimate 0.53, 0.37 to 0.75) and an 80% reduction in drug-related readmissions (0.06 vs 0.32; estimate 0.20, 0.10 to 0.41) — all relative estimates, printed beside their absolute rates. Including intervention costs, total cost per patient was $230 lower in the intervention group.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, 400 patients, 2005–2006 practice: the effect sizes (especially the 80% relative reduction in drug-related readmissions, on small absolute rates of 0.06 vs 0.32 visits) are exactly the kind that shrink on multicentre replication — and MedRev is that replication attempt, with a null.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the service model, not the review itself, decides — embedded pharmacists helped once; the add-on review did not
cards.summary: The service model, not the review itself, decides — embedded pharmacists helped once; the add-on review did not — Split: POSSIBLE · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Gillespie 2009 (400 patients aged 80+, single centre, ward-embedded pharmacists) and Kempen 2021 MedRev (2,637 patients, 8 wards, CMR with or without post-discharge follow-up).
cards.result: Read in chronological order this shelf is a familiar implementation story: a striking single-centre result (drug-related readmissions relative estimate 0.20) followed by a larger, more generalisable trial of a lighter-touch version that found nothing (rate ratios 1.04 and 1.15, emergency visits up at 1.29). The split stamp preserves both facts without averaging them: POSSIBLE for the intensive embedded model in the very old, LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for hospital CMR with post-discharge follow-up as a general service. The currency sweep's stepped-wedge collaborative pharmaceutical care trial (2025) is fenced here, not carded; it does not yet displace either anchor. OPERAM is drafted at Shelf #930 and single-drug-class deprescribing sits at Shelves #132/#500 — not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote Gillespie's 80% without MedRev beside it, and do not quote MedRev's null against pharmacist roles it did not test (prescribing is Shelf #1009).
