shelves.title: Nurses as substitutes for doctors in primary care (Laurant; Mundinger)
shelves.question: Can trained nurses deliver primary care with outcomes, satisfaction and resource use comparable to doctors — across the Cochrane substitution review, anchored on Mundinger's randomised trial of nurse-practitioner versus physician panels?
shelves.mesh: Family Practice/economics,organization & administration · Health Services Needs and Demand/economics,organization & administration · Nurse Practitioners/organization & administration · Nursing Staff/organization & administration · Personnel Delegation/organization & administration · Practice Patterns, Nurses' · Primary Health Care/economics,organization & administration
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Across 18 randomised trials (Cochrane review, Laurant 2018), trained nurses substituting for doctors in primary care probably achieve similar or better health outcomes for a broad range of conditions (low- to moderate-certainty evidence), probably slightly higher patient satisfaction, and probably slightly better blood-pressure outcomes — at the price of probably longer consultations and slightly more return visits, with little or no difference in prescriptions or emergency attendance (high-certainty) and uncertain effects on costs and process of care. The anchor trial, Mundinger 2000 (1,316 patients randomised to nurse practitioners with physician-equivalent independence or to physicians), found no differences in health status, diabetes or asthma measures, or utilisation at 6 months and 1 year. The review's mortality signal is low-certainty and inconsistent (nurse-led care 'may lead to slightly fewer deaths among certain groups' but may make little or no difference) — this shelf makes no mortality claim on it, and it is reported on the card as the uncertainty it is.

cards.headline: Laurant 2018 (Cochrane): across 18 trials, nurse-led primary care probably matches or slightly beats doctor-led care on outcomes and satisfaction
cards.summary: Laurant 2018 (Cochrane): across 18 trials, nurse-led primary care probably matches or slightly beats doctor-led care on outcomes and satisfaction.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (nurses as substitutes for doctors in primary care)
cards.people: 18 randomised trials of nurses working as substitutes for doctors in primary healthcare services providing first-contact and ongoing care (excluding mental health problems); all but one study in high-income countries; nursing level and preparation often unclear or variable between and within studies. The abstract does not state pooled participant totals or mean age.
cards.result: The review finds nurse-delivered care, compared with doctor-delivered care, probably generates similar or better health outcomes for a broad range of patient conditions (low- or moderate-certainty evidence). Blood pressure outcomes are probably slightly improved in nurse-led care; other clinical and health-status outcomes are probably similar (moderate-certainty). Patient satisfaction is probably slightly higher (moderate-certainty) and quality of life may be slightly higher (low-certainty). On mortality, the review is explicit about uncertainty: nurse-led care may lead to slightly fewer deaths among certain groups, but results vary and it is possible it makes little or no difference (low-certainty) — no mortality claim is made on this shelf. Consultations are probably longer with nurses (moderate-certainty) and attended return visits slightly higher (high-certainty); there is little or no difference in prescriptions or accident-and-emergency attendance (high-certainty). Effects on process of care and costs are uncertain (very low certainty).
cards.watchOut: Substitution in these trials usually meant trained, often advanced-practice nurses with doctor backup available — the review cannot say what level of nursing education produces these results, which is the implementation question that matters most.
cards.source: Laurant M et al. Nurses as substitutes for doctors in primary care. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018 Jul 16;7(7):CD001271. PMID: 30011347. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Mundinger 2000: patients randomised to nurse practitioners or physicians had indistinguishable outcomes at 6 months and 1 year
cards.summary: Mundinger 2000: patients randomised to nurse practitioners or physicians had indistinguishable outcomes at 6 months and 1 year.
cards.type: Randomised trial (single urban academic medical centre, 1995–1997)
cards.people: 1,316 adults (mean age 45.9 years; 76.8% female; 90.3% Hispanic) with no regular source of care who kept an initial appointment after an emergency department or urgent care visit, randomised to primary care follow-up and ongoing care with a nurse practitioner (806; 7 NPs in one clinic, with the same degree of independence as physicians) or a physician (510; 17 physicians in four clinics).
cards.result: No significant differences were found in health status at 6 months (P=0.92). Physiologic test results for patients with diabetes (P=0.82) or asthma (P=0.77) did not differ; for patients with hypertension, diastolic blood pressure was statistically significantly lower in nurse-practitioner patients (82 vs 85 mm Hg; P=0.04). There were no significant differences in health services utilisation after 6 months or 1 year, and no differences in satisfaction ratings following the initial appointment.
cards.watchOut: One centre, one NP practice model with full independence and a largely Hispanic, previously unconnected patient population: a strong test of that model, a weak basis for generalising to every substitution arrangement — the Cochrane card above carries the breadth.
cards.source: Mundinger MO et al. Primary care outcomes in patients treated by nurse practitioners or physicians: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2000 Jan 5;283(1):59-68. PMID: 10632281. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (2000).

cards.headline: Synthesis: substitution is safe and satisfying in the trials — the gain is capacity, not superiority
cards.summary: Substitution is safe and satisfying in the trials — the gain is capacity, not superiority — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Laurant 2018 (Cochrane review, 18 randomised trials) and Mundinger 2000 (1,316 patients, nurse-practitioner vs physician panels).
cards.result: The review and its landmark trial tell one story: outcomes and satisfaction are as good or marginally better with trained nurses, consultations run longer, patients come back slightly more often, and nothing in the high-certainty outcomes (prescriptions, emergency attendance) worsens. That is a workforce-capacity result, not a quality revolution, and LIKELY attaches to the comparability claim, not to any superiority. The review's low-certainty mortality passage is deliberately not promoted to a claim on this shelf. Lay counsellors for mental disorders in low-resource settings (drafted Shelf #889) are a different workforce and task and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Costs remain the open question both sources leave: longer consultations and more return visits could consume the salary differential, and the review rated cost evidence very low certainty.

shelves.title: Financial incentives for weight loss: lotteries, deposits and groups
shelves.question: Do lottery-based and deposit-contract incentives produce more weight loss than control — and do group-based incentives beat individual incentives at the same expected value?
shelves.mesh: Health Behavior · Health Promotion/economics · Motivation · Overweight/economics,psychology,therapy · Risk Reduction Behavior · Token Economy · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small randomised trials show financial incentives increase weight loss while the money is live. Volpp 2008 (57 participants) found lottery and deposit-contract groups lost about 13–14 lb in 16 weeks against 3.9 lb in controls, with about half the incentive participants hitting a 16-lb target versus 10.5% of controls — but by 7 months, three months after incentives ended, the between-group differences were no longer statistically significant. Kullgren 2013 (105 employees) found group incentives beat both control (by 4.4 kg) and individual incentives (by 3.2 kg) at 24 weeks, with the group advantage over control partly maintained 12 weeks after incentives ended (2.9 kg). POSSIBLE, not LIKELY: two small, single-employer/single-centre trials, short horizons, and Volpp's regain pattern is the central unanswered question for this whole strategy. Financial incentives for smoking cessation are drafted at Shelf #966 and workplace wellness programmes at Shelf #537 — different questions, not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Volpp 2008: lottery and deposit-contract groups lost 13.1 and 14.0 lb in 16 weeks versus 3.9 lb in controls — but the advantage faded after payments stopped
cards.summary: Volpp 2008: lottery and deposit-contract groups lost 13.1 and 14.0 lb in 16 weeks versus 3.9 lb in controls — but the advantage faded after payments ended.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (single VA medical centre, Philadelphia)
cards.people: 57 healthy participants aged 30–70 years with body mass index 30–40, randomised to monthly weigh-ins (control), a lottery incentive programme, or a deposit contract with participant matching, all aiming at 1 lb (0.45 kg) per week for 16 weeks, with follow-up to 7 months. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The incentive groups lost significantly more weight than control (whose mean loss was 3.9 lb): the lottery group lost a mean of 13.1 lb (P=0.02 for the difference versus control) and the deposit-contract group 14.0 lb (P=0.006). About half of each incentive group met the 16-lb target (deposit 47.4%; lottery 52.6%) versus 10.5% of controls (P=0.01). At 7 months — after incentives had ended — net weight loss remained numerically larger in the incentive groups (lottery 9.2 lb; deposit 6.2 lb; control 4.4 lb) but the between-group differences were not statistically significant (P=0.23 and P=0.61).
cards.watchOut: Fifty-seven participants at one centre, and the trial's own follow-up is its strongest caveat: incentives bought weight loss during payment and the groups converged once payment stopped — durability is unproven, not disproven.
cards.source: Volpp KG et al. Financial incentive-based approaches for weight loss: a randomized trial. JAMA. 2008 Dec 10;300(22):2631-2637. PMID: 19066383. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00520611, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Kullgren 2013: group incentives beat individual incentives — 4.4 kg more than control and 3.2 kg more than individual at 24 weeks
cards.summary: Kullgren 2013: group incentives beat individual incentives — 4.4 kg more than control at 24 weeks.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (single employer, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia)
cards.people: 105 employees with body mass index 30–40 kg/m², randomised to 24 weeks of monthly weigh-ins (control; n=35), an individual incentive ($100 per person per month for meeting or exceeding weight-loss goals; n=35), or a group incentive ($500 per month split among members of 5-person groups who met or exceeded goals; n=35), with follow-up to 36 weeks.
cards.result: Group-incentive participants lost more weight at 24 weeks than control participants (mean between-group difference 4.4 kg; 95% CI 2.0 to 6.7; P<0.001) and than individual-incentive participants (3.2 kg; 0.9 to 5.5; P=0.008). Twelve weeks after incentives ended, the group arm maintained greater weight loss than control (2.9 kg; 0.5 to 5.3; P=0.016, after adjustment for the three-group comparisons). The authors note the single-employer setting and short follow-up as limitations.
cards.watchOut: The group design's edge may be social (shared pot, peer visibility) as much as financial — the trial cannot separate those — and 105 employees of one children's hospital is a narrow base for employer policy.
cards.source: Kullgren JT et al. Individual- versus group-based financial incentives for weight loss: a randomized, controlled trial. Ann Intern Med. 2013 Apr 2;158(7):505-514. PMID: 23546562. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01208350, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: incentives work while they run — group designs work best, and nobody has shown the loss survives the payments
cards.summary: Incentives work while they run — group designs work best, and nobody has shown the loss survives the payments — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Volpp 2008 (57 participants, lottery and deposit designs) and Kullgren 2013 (105 employees, individual vs group designs).
cards.result: Both trials point the same way during the incentive window: roughly 9–10 lb (Volpp) or about 4 kg (Kullgren group arm) of extra loss over control, with the group/shared-pot design the strongest single result in either trial. The shelf's POSSIBLE grade is set by what happens next — Volpp's between-group differences were non-significant three months after payments ended — and by the small, single-site samples. The currency sweep's larger newer trial of text-message plus financial incentives for men with obesity (Game of Stones) is fenced here, not carded: it tests a combined digital-plus-incentive package, a different intervention from the pure incentive designs on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Any employer quoting these trials should quote the denominators too: 57 volunteers at a VA centre and 105 employees at one hospital, over 16–24 weeks.

shelves.title: Pharmacist prescribing for hypertension and cardiovascular risk (RxACTION, RxEACH)
shelves.question: Does pharmacist prescribing — assessing, prescribing and following up — lower blood pressure in community patients (RxACTION) and reduce cardiovascular risk in high-risk patients (RxEACH) versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Alberta/epidemiology · Antihypertensive Agents/therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects,physiology · Drug Prescriptions · Hypertension/diagnosis,drug therapy,epidemiology · Pharmacists/statistics & numerical data · Professional Role
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for blood pressure and risk-factor improvement; not for cardiovascular events): Two randomised trials from the same Alberta programme show community pharmacists with prescribing authority improving the numbers they targeted. RxACTION (248 patients with above-target blood pressure) found an extra 6.6 mm Hg systolic reduction at 6 months versus usual care (adjusted difference; P=0.0006) and higher odds of reaching target. RxEACH (723 high-risk patients) found greater improvement in estimated cardiovascular risk over 3 months, with systolic pressure down 9.37 mm Hg more, LDL cholesterol 0.2 mmol/L (≈8 mg/dL) lower, HbA1c 0.92% lower and more smoking cessation in the intervention group. The boundary is explicit: RxEACH's primary outcome is a change in a risk score (the greater of Framingham, International or UKPDS estimates), not observed heart attacks or strokes, and neither trial reports event outcomes — this shelf claims risk-factor control only. Home blood-pressure self-monitoring with self-titration (drafted/built Shelf #529) is patient-led and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: RxACTION 2015: pharmacist prescribing lowered systolic blood pressure by an extra 6.6 mm Hg at 6 months
cards.summary: RxACTION 2015: pharmacist prescribing lowered systolic blood pressure by an extra 6.6 mm Hg at 6 months.
cards.type: Patient-level randomised controlled trial (23 Alberta communities; community pharmacies, hospitals and primary care teams)
cards.people: 248 adults with above-target blood pressure by Canadian guidelines (mean age 64 years; 49% male; baseline mean blood pressure 150±14/84±11 mm Hg), randomised to pharmacist care — assessment, cardiovascular risk assessment, hypertension education, prescribing of antihypertensive medication, laboratory monitoring and monthly follow-up for 6 months — or control (wallet blood-pressure card, written information, usual pharmacist and physician care).
cards.result: Systolic blood pressure fell by a mean 18.3±1.2 mm Hg in the intervention group versus 11.8±1.9 mm Hg in controls — an adjusted difference of 6.6±1.9 mm Hg (P=0.0006). The adjusted odds of achieving blood-pressure targets were 2.32 (95% CI 1.17 to 4.15) in favour of the intervention — a relative odds figure, printed beside the absolute pressure changes above.
cards.watchOut: The control group also improved by nearly 12 mm Hg (enrolment, measurement and usual care at work), the pharmacists practised under Alberta's expanded scope of practice, and follow-up was 6 months — the trial tests a legal framework as much as a profession.
cards.source: Tsuyuki RT et al. Randomized Trial of the Effect of Pharmacist Prescribing on Improving Blood Pressure in the Community: The Alberta Clinical Trial in Optimizing Hypertension (RxACTION). Circulation. 2015 Jul 14;132(2):93-100. PMID: 26063762. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00878566, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: RxEACH 2016: pharmacist case-finding and prescribing improved estimated cardiovascular risk — systolic pressure −9.37 mm Hg, HbA1c −0.92%, LDL −0.2 mmol/L (≈-8 mg/dL) versus usual care
cards.summary: RxEACH 2016: pharmacist case-finding and prescribing improved estimated cardiovascular risk — systolic pressure −9.37 mm Hg.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (56 community pharmacies, Alberta)
cards.people: 723 adults at high risk for cardiovascular disease recruited by their pharmacists (mean age 62 years; 58% male; 27% smokers), randomised to usual pharmacist care or intervention: medication therapy management review, cardiovascular risk assessment and education, pharmacist prescribing and laboratory ordering to treatment targets, with monthly follow-up for 3 months. The primary outcome was the between-group difference in change in estimated cardiovascular risk (the greater of the Framingham, International or UKPDS risk scores).
cards.result: After adjustment for baseline values and centre effect, there was a 21% difference in change in estimated risk for cardiovascular events between groups (P<0.001) in favour of intervention — the authors' relative summary of a risk-score change, not a count of events. Component improvements were greater in the intervention group: LDL cholesterol −0.2 mmol/L (≈-8 mg/dL) (P<0.001), systolic blood pressure −9.37 mm Hg (P<0.001), HbA1c −0.92% (P<0.001), and smoking cessation 20.2% (P=0.002). The authors describe RxEACH as the first large randomised trial of cardiovascular risk reduction by community pharmacists.
cards.watchOut: Three months of follow-up and a surrogate primary outcome: the risk score improved because its inputs improved, which is encouraging and circular in equal measure — no patient in this trial was followed to a heart attack or stroke outcome.

cards.headline: Synthesis: give pharmacists the pen and the follow-up, and risk factors move — events remain unmeasured
cards.summary: Give pharmacists the pen and the follow-up, and risk factors move — events remain unmeasured — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: RxACTION 2015 (248 patients, hypertension) and RxEACH 2016 (723 patients, high cardiovascular risk), both randomised trials of Alberta community pharmacists with prescribing authority.
cards.result: The two trials are consistent across their shared measurements — systolic pressure fell an extra 6.6 mm Hg when hypertension was the target (RxACTION) and 9.37 mm Hg more when it was one of several targets (RxEACH) — which carries LIKELY for risk-factor improvement under this scope of practice. Both trials come from one province, one research programme and one permissive prescribing framework; transport depends on law and workflow, not just willingness. And the event question stays open by design: RxEACH's headline 21% is a difference in an estimated risk score, and this shelf does not convert it into prevented heart attacks or strokes.
cards.watchOut: Quote the component numbers (mm Hg, mmol/L, HbA1c) rather than the 21%: they are measured, and the percentage is a model's arithmetic on top of them.

shelves.title: Finding domestic violence in primary care, and having somewhere to send her: IRIS and WEAVE
shelves.question: Does a primary-care training and support programme with a referral pathway to advocacy (IRIS) increase identification of women experiencing domestic violence and referrals to specialist support — and does screening plus brief counselling (WEAVE) improve women's outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Cluster Analysis · Domestic Violence/prevention & control · Education, Medical, Continuing · General Practice/education · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Primary Health Care · Referral and Consultation
shelves.balance: LIKELY for identification and referral: In IRIS (48 UK general practices, cluster-randomised), a training-and-support programme with a named advocate pathway produced 223 recorded referrals to advocacy versus 12 in control practices over a year (adjusted intervention rate ratio 22.1, a relative figure) and recorded disclosures of 641 versus 236 (rate ratio 3.1). WEAVE (52 Australian doctors, 272 women screening positive) is the necessary counterweight: screening plus brief counselling improved no primary outcome — quality of life, safety planning, or mental health at 12 months — though depression caseness fell (odds ratio 0.3). The shelf's claim is a service claim: training plus a pathway finds women and refers them; it makes no claim that identification alone reduces violence or mortality. Both trials are unblindable by nature.

cards.headline: IRIS (Feder 2011): referrals to advocacy 223 versus 12 in a year (relative adjusted rate ratio 22.1); recorded disclosures 641 versus 236 (3.1)
cards.summary: IRIS (2011): referrals to advocacy 223 vs 12 in a year (adjusted rate ratio 22.1 relative); recorded disclosures 641 vs 235.
cards.type: Cluster randomised controlled trial (51 general practices in Hackney, London, and Bristol; 48 analysed)
cards.people: General practices randomised to a training and support programme (practice-based training, a medical-record prompt to ask about abuse, and a referral pathway to a named domestic violence advocate who also delivered training) or control; outcomes are practice-recorded referrals and identifications in the year after the second training session. Patient numbers and sex mix are practice-level and are not stated in the abstract (the programme concerned women experiencing domestic violence).
cards.result: One year after the second training session, the 24 intervention practices recorded 223 referrals of patients to advocacy versus 12 referrals in the 24 control practices (adjusted intervention rate ratio 22.1, 95% CI 11.5 to 42.4 — a relative figure, absolute counts beside it), and recorded 641 disclosures of domestic violence versus 236 (adjusted rate ratio 3.1, 2.2 to 4.3). No adverse events were recorded. The authors note that screening of women patients was not a necessary condition for the improvement — training plus a pathway, not a screening form, did the work.
cards.watchOut: Process outcomes (recording and referral), not safety outcomes: IRIS does not show the referred women became safer. Rate ratios on very small control counts (12 referrals) are inherently unstable — the absolute counts are the honest headline, and they are printed.
cards.source: Feder G et al. Identification and Referral to Improve Safety (IRIS) of women experiencing domestic violence with a primary care training and support programme: a cluster randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2011;378(9805):1788-95. PMID: 22000683. Registry ID: ISRCTN: ISRCTN74012786.

cards.summary: WEAVE (2013): screening plus brief counselling improved no primary outcome at 12 months; depression caseness fell (OR 0.6 relative).
cards.type: Cluster randomised controlled trial (52 family doctors in Victoria, Australia)

shelves.title: A medical emergency team for the deteriorating ward patient (MERIT)
shelves.question: Does introducing a medical emergency team, summoned by calling criteria before arrest, reduce cardiac arrests, unexpected deaths or unplanned ICU admissions across a hospital?
shelves.mesh: Emergency Service, Hospital/organization & administration · Heart Arrest/epidemiology · Hospital Mortality · Intensive Care Units/statistics & numerical data · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Patient Care Team
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled YES at build: unexpected death is a named component of the primary composite, so the mortality surface returns to the developer; the trial's result was null and no mortality-benefit claim is made). One pivotal cluster-randomised trial (MERIT, 23 Australian hospitals) found the system greatly increased emergency calling (8.7 vs 3.1 per 1000 admissions) without reducing the composite of cardiac arrest, unexpected death or unplanned ICU admission (5.31 vs 5.86 per 1000, p=0.640). A single cluster trial caps the null at POSSIBLE. (The record carries a published erratum, PMID 17470891; not a retraction.)

cards.headline: MERIT 2005: introducing a medical emergency team multiplied calling (8.7 vs 3.1 per 1000 admissions) but did not reduce arrests, unexpected deaths or unplanned ICU admissions (5.31 vs 5.86 per 1000, p=0.640)
cards.summary: MERIT (2005): introducing a medical emergency team multiplied calling ( 8.7 vs 3.1 per 1000 admissions) but did not reduce arrests, unexpected deaths or unplanned ICU admissions (composite 5.31 vs 5.48 per 1000).
cards.type: Cluster-randomised controlled trial (23 hospitals randomised; 6-month study period after activation; intention-to-treat)
cards.people: 23 hospitals in Australia randomised to introduce a medical emergency team system (12) or continue as usual (11). Patient-level denominators are admissions; the abstract does not state the total number of patients, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Calling incidence rose from 3.1 to 8.7 per 1000 admissions with the MET system (p=0.0001), yet the composite primary outcome was similar: 5.31 per 1000 admissions in MET hospitals vs 5.86 in controls (p=0.640). Components likewise did not differ: cardiac arrests 1.31 vs 1.64 per 1000 (p=0.736), unplanned ICU admissions 4.19 vs 4.68 (p=0.599), and unexpected deaths 1.06 vs 1.18 (p=0.752) — the mortality component printed beside the composite, per the library's pairing rule. The MET was called to only 30% of patients who fulfilled calling criteria and were subsequently admitted to ICU. Rates of cardiac arrest and unexpected death fell from baseline in both groups combined (p=0.003 and p=0.01).
cards.watchOut: Twenty-three clusters is a small number of randomised units for hospital-level effects, the study period was 6 months after activation, and calling reached only a minority of qualifying patients — the trial tests an immature implementation as much as the concept.
cards.source: Hillman K et al. Introduction of the medical emergency team (MET) system: a cluster-randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2005;365(9477):2091-7. PMID: 15964445. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial (2005).

shelves.title: Coaching the WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist into use (BetterBirth)
shelves.question: Does a coaching-based implementation programme for the WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist improve maternal and neonatal outcomes, or only the practices on the list?
shelves.mesh: Checklist/statistics & numerical data · Chi-Square Distribution · Delivery, Obstetric/education,standards · Guideline Adherence · India/epidemiology · Infant, Newborn · Intention to Treat Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled YES at build: maternal and perinatal mortality sit inside the primary composite; no mortality benefit was shown and none is claimed). One large cluster-randomised trial (BetterBirth, 120 facilities in Uttar Pradesh, 157,689 enrolled women) found the programme substantially improved adherence to 18 essential birth practices (72.8% vs 41.7% at 2 months) but did not improve the composite of perinatal death, maternal death or severe maternal complications (15.1% vs 15.3%; relative risk 0.99). The practices-versus-outcomes gap is the shelf. A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: BetterBirth 2017: checklist coaching raised essential-practice adherence (72.8% vs 41.7% at 2 months) but not outcomes — composite 15.1% vs 15.3% (relative risk 0.99)
cards.summary: BetterBirth (2017): checklist coaching raised essential-practice adherence ( 72.8% vs 41.7% at 2 months) but not outcomes — the maternal/perinatal composite was 15.1% vs 15.0%.
cards.type: Matched-pair, cluster-randomised, controlled trial (60 pairs of facilities, 24 districts of Uttar Pradesh, India; 8-month coaching programme)
cards.people: 157,689 women enrolled of 161,107 eligible (97.9%), with 7-day outcomes determined for 157,145 (99.7%) mother-newborn dyads; adherence observed in 4,888 births in 15 matched facility pairs. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Birth attendants' mean adherence to 18 essential birth practices was significantly higher with the programme: 72.8% vs 41.7% at 2 months and 61.7% vs 43.9% at 12 months (P<0.001 for both). The composite primary outcome (perinatal death, maternal death, or maternal severe complications within 7 days) did not differ: 15.1% in the intervention group vs 15.3% in controls (relative risk 0.99; 95% CI 0.83 to 1.18; P=0.90), and neither did secondary maternal or perinatal adverse outcomes. The composite's mortality components are not reported separately in the abstract, so none are printed separately.
cards.watchOut: Practices improved where coaching was active and decayed by 12 months (61.7% vs 72.8%): the trial shows a checklist-plus-coaching programme changing measured behaviour without changing outcomes — whether the listed practices, their fidelity, or the surrounding system's capacity is the binding constraint is exactly what the null leaves open.
cards.source: Semrau KEA et al. Outcomes of a Coaching-Based WHO Safe Childbirth Checklist Program in India. The New England journal of medicine. 2017;377(24):2313-2324. PMID: 29236628. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02148952, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Making the serious-illness conversation happen: the Serious Illness Care Program trials
shelves.question: Does a system intervention — clinician training, a structured conversation guide, and prompts — produce earlier, better-documented serious-illness conversations and less patient anxiety in advanced cancer?
shelves.mesh: Advance Care Planning/organization & administration · Critical Illness/psychology,therapy · Medical Oncology · Neoplasms/psychology,therapy · Palliative Care/organization & administration · Patient Acceptance of Health Care/psychology,statistics & numerical data · Patient Satisfaction/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One programme tested in cluster-randomised trials at a single cancer centre, reported in two companion papers (counted as one programme): the communication-outcomes report found documented conversations in 96% of intervention patients vs 79% of controls, a median 2.4 months earlier (143 vs 71 days before death), more comprehensive and far more accessible in the record (61% vs 11%); the patient-outcomes report found its coprimary outcomes (goal-concordant care, peacefulness) null, but significantly fewer patients with moderate-to-severe anxiety (5.0% vs 10.2% at 14 weeks) and depression (10.6% vs 20.8%). Conversation, documentation and mood outcomes; no mortality claim is made — survival did not differ.

cards.headline: Bernacki 2019: the programme's coprimary patient outcomes were null, but moderate-to-severe anxiety (5.0% vs 10.2%) and depression (10.6% vs 20.8%) were significantly lower at 14 weeks
cards.summary: Bernacki (2019): the programme's coprimary patient outcomes were null, but moderate-to-severe anxiety (5.0% vs 10.2%) and depression (10.6% vs 18.0%) were lower.
cards.type: Cluster randomised clinical trial (outpatient oncology; 91 clinicians in 41 clusters; intention-to-treat)
cards.people: 278 patients with advanced cancer (134 intervention, 144 control; 53.2% women) and 91 oncology clinicians (48 intervention, 43 control), enrolled 2012-2016 at one cancer institute. Mean patient age is not stated in the abstract. Of 39 clinicians who received a reminder, 34 (87.2%) completed at least one conversation (median duration 19 minutes).
cards.result: The coprimary outcomes — goal-concordant care and peacefulness at the end of life, evaluated in 64 patients — showed no significant differences. However, the proportion of patients with moderate-to-severe anxiety was significantly lower in the intervention group at 14 weeks (5.0% vs 10.2%; P=0.05), as was moderate-to-severe depression (10.6% vs 20.8%; P=0.04); the anxiety reduction was sustained at 24 weeks (4.2% vs 10.4%; P=0.02) but the depression reduction was not (12.5% vs 17.8%; P=0.31). Survival and therapeutic alliance did not differ between groups. The authors note methodologic challenges (measure selection, sample size for the coprimaries) limit the conclusions.
cards.watchOut: The positive mood results are secondary outcomes in a trial whose coprimaries were null and evaluable in only 64 patients: hypothesis-strengthening, not proof, and the percentages are of patients assessed at each wave.
cards.source: Bernacki R et al. Effect of the Serious Illness Care Program in Outpatient Oncology: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2019;179(6):751-759. PMID: 30870563. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01786811, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Paladino 2019: documented serious-illness conversations rose to 96% vs 79%, came a median 2.4 months earlier, and were accessible in the record in 61% vs 11%
cards.summary: Paladino (2019): documented serious-illness conversations rose to 96% vs 79% and came a median 2.4 months earlier.
cards.type: Cluster randomised clinical trial (same programme and trial population as the companion report — one programme, counted once)
cards.people: 91 clinicians (48 intervention, 43 control) and 278 patients (134 intervention, 144 control) at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute; the documentation analysis covers the 161 patients (58%) who died during the study, cared for by 76 clinicians; among decedents, mean age 62.3 years and 55% were women.
cards.result: After death, record review showed a documented serious-illness discussion in 96% of intervention patients vs 79% of controls (P=0.005), occurring a median of 143 days before death vs 71 days (P<0.001) — a median 2.4 months earlier. Intervention documentation was more comprehensive and patient-centred: values or goals in 89% vs 44% (P<0.001), prognosis or illness understanding 91% vs 48% (P<0.001), and life-sustaining-treatment preferences 63% vs 32% (P=0.004). Documentation about end-of-life care planning did not differ (80% vs 68%, P=0.08). Documentation was accessible in the electronic record for 61% vs 11% (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Documentation is a process outcome: more and earlier recorded conversations show the system changed clinician behaviour, and only the companion report's mood findings connect it — secondarily — to patient experience.

shelves.title: ICU diaries and post-traumatic stress: Jones 2010 and the French ICU-diary trial
shelves.question: Does keeping a diary of a patient's ICU stay, written by staff and family and given to the patient afterwards, prevent post-traumatic stress after critical illness?
shelves.mesh: Critical Care/methods · Critical Illness/epidemiology,therapy · Medical Records · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/epidemiology,etiology,prevention & control · Critical Care/psychology · Family/psychology · Health Personnel/psychology
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — the treatment made no difference in the larger 2019 trial · MAYBE (weak evidence) — benefit in Jones 2010. Two randomised trials of the same intervention disagree: Jones 2010 (352 randomised) found new-onset PTSD in 5% with a diary vs 13% without (P=0.02), while the larger, assessor-blinded French trial (657 randomised, 339 assessed) found significant PTSD symptoms in 29.9% vs 34.3% (risk difference -4%, CI -15 to 6; P=0.39). The discordance is the shelf: the later, larger, blinded-assessment trial outranks the earlier positive one, and the benefit claim is stamped MAYBE (weak evidence). Psychiatric-symptom outcomes; no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: Jones 2010: an ICU diary reduced new-onset PTSD at 3 months — 5% vs 13% (P=0.02)
cards.summary: Jones (2010): an ICU diary reduced new-onset PTSD at 3 months — 5% vs 13% (P=0.02).
cards.type: Randomised, controlled trial (diary given at 1 month after critical-care discharge; assessment at 3 months)
cards.people: 352 patients with an ICU stay longer than 72 hours, randomised at 1 month following critical illness. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix, nor the per-group denominators for the PTSD outcome, so only the printed percentages are given.
cards.result: The incidence of new cases of post-traumatic stress disorder was 5% in the diary (intervention) group vs 13% in control patients (P=0.02) — absolute percentages as printed in the abstract; the underlying group counts are not stated in the abstract and are not reconstructed here. The authors conclude the diary aids psychological recovery and reduces new PTSD.
cards.watchOut: A single positive trial with percentages but no printed denominators in the abstract, using a diagnostic-style PTSD ascertainment — and its result was not reproduced by the larger blinded-assessment trial below, which is why the benefit side of this shelf is MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.source: Jones C et al. Intensive care diaries reduce new onset post traumatic stress disorder following critical illness: a randomised, controlled trial. cards.headline: Garrouste-Orgeas 2019: in 35 French ICUs, an ICU diary did NOT reduce PTSD symptoms at 3 months (29.9% vs 34.3%, P=0.39) in patients or families
cards.summary: Garrouste-Orgeas (2019): in 35 French ICUs, an ICU diary did NOT reduce PTSD symptoms at 3 months ( 29.9% vs 34.3% ; P=0.39) in patients or families.
cards.type: Assessor-blinded, multicentre, randomised clinical trial (35 ICUs; follow-up to 3 months after discharge)
cards.people: 657 adult patients randomised (355 diary, 354 usual care) who had received mechanical ventilation within 48 hours of ICU admission for at least 2 days, each with one family member; 339 patients (51.6%) completed the trial and were assessed at 3 months; among assessed patients the median age was 62 years (IQR 51-70) and 126 (37.2%) were women.
cards.result: Significant PTSD symptoms (Impact of Event Scale-Revised score >22) at 3 months were reported by 49 of 164 patients (29.9%) in the diary group vs 60 of 175 (34.3%) in the control group (risk difference -4%; 95% CI -15 to 6; P=0.39). Median IES-R scores were 12 (IQR 5-25) vs 13 (6-27). None of the 6 prespecified secondary comparisons — PTSD symptoms in family members, anxiety and depression symptoms in patients and family, or ICU memories — differed significantly. The authors conclude the findings do not support ICU diaries for preventing PTSD symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Only 51.6% of randomised patients were assessed at 3 months: attrition this large can hide effects in either direction, though it does not rescue the intervention — the burden of proof sits with the diary.
cards.source: Garrouste-Orgeas M et al. Effect of an ICU Diary on Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Symptoms Among Patients Receiving Mechanical Ventilation: A Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: the small early positive meets the large later null — split stamp, benefit MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the small early positive meets the large later null — split POSSIBLE the null / MAYBE (weak evidence) benefit.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Jones 2010 (352 randomised) and Garrouste-Orgeas 2019 (657 randomised, 339 assessed).
cards.result: The ICU-diary literature's arc in miniature: a promising single trial (PTSD 5% vs 13%) followed by a larger, multicentre, assessor-blinded trial finding nothing (29.9% vs 34.3%). Note the outcome measures also differ — new-onset PTSD diagnosis vs a symptom-scale threshold — which softens, but does not remove, the contradiction. shelves.title: Rapid multiplex PCR for bloodstream infection, with a steward at the elbow (Banerjee)
shelves.question: Does rapid multiplex PCR identification of blood-culture organisms, reported with antimicrobial-stewardship review, shorten time to effective and optimal therapy versus conventional identification?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Banerjee 2015, 617 patients with positive blood cultures) in a three-arm design showed the test alone cut identification time (1.3 vs 22.3 hours) and reduced contaminant treatment, but the stewardship-paired arm — not the test alone — was fastest to antimicrobial de-escalation (21 vs 34 hours for control and 38 for test alone). Mortality, length of stay and cost did not differ, and none is claimed. The confirmatory rapid-diagnostic randomised report sought at build could not be pinned to a verified record, so the shelf rests on Banerjee alone (see summary). Process and antibiotic-use outcomes only.

cards.headline: Banerjee 2015: rapid multiplex PCR identified organisms in 1.3 vs 22.3 hours, but only the stewardship-paired arm sped de-escalation (21 vs 34 hours); mortality, stay and cost did not differ

cards.people: 617 patients with positive blood-culture bottles, stratified-randomised to control (207), rmPCR (198) or rmPCR plus stewardship (212). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Time from Gram stain to organism identification was 1.3 hours in the intervention groups vs 22.3 hours in controls (P<0.001). Both intervention groups reduced broad-spectrum piperacillin-tazobactam duration (control 56 hours; rmPCR 44; rmPCR/AS 45; P=0.01), increased narrow-spectrum beta-lactam use (42; 71; 85 hours; P=0.04), and reduced treatment of contaminants (25%; 11%; 8%; P=0.015). Time to de-escalation was shortest in the stewardship arm (21 hours vs 34 control and 38 rmPCR alone; P<0.001) and escalation was fastest with rmPCR/AS and rmPCR (5 and 6 hours vs 24 control; P=0.04). The groups did not differ in mortality, length of stay, or cost (rates not separated in the abstract).
cards.watchOut: A single-centre process-outcome trial from 2015, on that era's panel: the lesson is the pairing (test speed needs a steward to convert into prescribing speed), and de-escalation was paradoxically slowest in the test-alone arm — the finding the shelf exists to preserve.

shelves.title: Housing First for homeless adults with mental illness (At Home/Chez Soi, Stergiopoulos)
shelves.question: For homeless adults with mental illness and moderate support needs, does scattered-site housing with rent supplements and intensive case management — offered without treatment preconditions — produce more stable housing than treatment as usual?
shelves.mesh: Canada · Case Management/economics · Community Mental Health Services/economics · Costs and Cost Analysis · Ill-Housed Persons/psychology · Mental Disorders/rehabilitation · Public Housing
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Stergiopoulos 2015, 1,198 participants) found scattered-site Housing First with intensive case management increased housing stability over 24 months versus usual care — the adjusted difference varied by site, and the trial record's abstract reports the primary outcome through its table rather than a single pooled figure, so no pooled days-housed number is printed — while generic quality of life did not improve (EQ-5D difference in mean change 0.10, P=0.95). A single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Gate note: the topic file framed this as the Toronto site trial; the verified record is the programme's randomised trial of participants with moderate needs recruited in four Canadian cities (see summary). The At Home/Chez Soi national-programme primary report sought at build could not be pinned to a PubMed record — it is a programme report, not a journal article — so the shelf rests on this trial (see summary). No mortality claim is made.

cards.result: The primary outcome — percentage of days stably housed over 24 months — was higher in the intervention group on adjusted analysis, with adjusted mean differences varying across sites (the abstract reports the site-specific figures in its table rather than a pooled number, and no pooled figure is reconstructed here). Generic quality of life did not differ: mean EQ-5D change difference 0.10 (95% CI -2.92 to 3.13; P=0.95), with scores rising in both groups (intervention 60.5 at baseline to 67.2 at 24 months; usual care 62.1 to 68.6).

shelves.title: Nurses initiating and managing HIV treatment: STRETCH and CIPRA-SA
shelves.question: Can primary-care nurses initiate and manage antiretroviral therapy as safely as doctors, on mortality and viral suppression, in South African primary care?
shelves.mesh: Anti-HIV Agents/therapeutic use · CD4 Lymphocyte Count · Delivery of Health Care/organization & administration · Drug Prescriptions/nursing · HIV Infections/drug therapy,immunology,mortality,nursing · Primary Care Nursing/methods · Primary Health Care/organization & administration
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate ruled YES at build: mortality sits inside both trials' outcome frames — STRETCH's cohort-1 primary outcome was time to death and CIPRA-SA's composite includes mortality; the claims are equivalence of a delivery model, not superiority of a treatment). Two randomised trials agree: STRETCH (16,481 patients in two cohorts, cluster design) found time to death did not differ (hazard ratio 0.94) and viral suppression was equivalent (71% vs 70%); CIPRA-SA (812 patients) found nurse-monitored care noninferior on its composite of treatment-limiting events (hazard ratio 1.09, CI within the 1.40 margin), with deaths 10 vs 11. Unblindable by nature, as care-delivery trials are.

cards.headline: STRETCH 2012: nurse-led ART initiation and represcription did not change time to death (hazard ratio 0.94) and matched doctors on viral suppression (71% vs 70%, equivalent)
cards.summary: STRETCH (2012): nurse-led ART initiation and represcription did not change time to death (HR 0.94 relative) and matched doctors on viral suppression.
cards.type: Pragmatic, parallel, cluster-randomised trial (31 primary-care ART clinics, South Africa; two cohorts)
cards.people: Cohort 1 (ART-naive adults with CD4 at most 350 cells/µL): 5,390 patients in intervention clinics and 3,862 in control clinics; cohort 2 (adults already on ART for at least 6 months): 3,029 and 3,202. Median follow-up 16.3 months (cohort 1) and 18.0 months (cohort 2). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In cohort 1, 997 (20%) of 4,943 analysed intervention patients and 747 (19%) of 3,862 controls with known vital status had died; time to death did not differ (hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.76 to 1.15) — a relative measure with the absolute death proportions beside it. In a preplanned subgroup with baseline CD4 201-350, mortality was slightly lower with nurse-led care (0.73, 0.54 to 1.00; p=0.052) but not at CD4 of 200 or less (0.94, 0.76 to 1.15). In cohort 2, viral suppression (<400 copies/mL) at 12 months was equivalent: 2,156 (71%) of 3,029 vs 2,230 (70%) of 3,202 (risk difference 1.1%, -2.4 to 4.6; prespecified equivalence margin 6%).
cards.watchOut: A programme-scale cluster trial from the CD4-350 initiation era: mortality was high in both arms (about a fifth of cohort 1) because patients presented late — the equivalence finding is about who delivers care, and the authors note expanded nursing roles might not reduce time to ART or mortality itself.
cards.source: Fairall L et al. Task shifting of antiretroviral treatment from doctors to primary-care nurses in South Africa (STRETCH): a pragmatic, parallel, cluster-randomised trial. Lancet (London, England). 2012;380(9845):889-98. PMID: 22901955. Registry ID: ISRCTN46836853, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Group antenatal care (CenteringPregnancy): the Ickovics trials
shelves.question: Does group prenatal care improve perinatal outcomes versus individual care, in Ickovics's first randomised trial and in the New York City cluster-randomised trial in adolescents?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials of the same care model in different young populations each found a benefit — on different outcomes: the 2007 trial reduced preterm birth (9.8% vs 13.8%; relative odds ratio 0.67), stronger in African-American women (10.0% vs 15.8%), while the 2016 New York City cluster trial reduced small-for-gestational-age infants (11.0% vs 15.8%; relative odds ratio 0.66) without reporting a preterm-birth effect in its abstract. Each outcome rests on a single trial, and the model is unblindable by nature — POSSIBLE. Preterm-birth and process outcomes; no mortality claim is made. cards.headline: Ickovics 2007: group prenatal care reduced preterm birth — 9.8% vs 13.8% (relative odds ratio 0.67); in African-American women 10.0% vs 15.8%
cards.summary: Ickovics (2007): group prenatal care reduced preterm birth — 9.8% vs 13.8% (OR 0.67 relative).
cards.type: Multisite randomised controlled trial (two university-affiliated hospital prenatal clinics)
cards.people: 1,047 pregnant women aged 14-25 years (mean age 20.4 years; 80% African American), without medical conditions requiring individualised care, randomised to standard individual care or group care with women sharing an expected delivery month; 2-hour sessions from week 18 through delivery.
cards.result: Preterm birth occurred in 9.8% of the group-care women vs 13.8% with standard care (odds ratio 0.67; 95% CI 0.44 to 0.99; P=0.045) — a relative measure with absolute rates beside it, equivalent to 40 fewer preterm births per 1,000. The effect was stronger in African-American women: 10.0% vs 15.8% (odds ratio 0.59, 0.38 to 0.92; P=0.02). Group care also gave less suboptimal prenatal care (P<0.01), better prenatal knowledge (P<0.001), greater readiness and satisfaction (P<0.001), and higher breastfeeding initiation (66.5% vs 54.6%, P<0.001). There were no differences in birth weight or in prenatal/delivery costs.
cards.watchOut: Young, predominantly African-American women at two academic clinics, with the headline subgroup (African-American women) being the population the model was designed around: generalisation to older, low-risk, or rural populations is an extrapolation.

cards.headline: Ickovics 2016 (New York City): group care in adolescents reduced small-for-gestational-age infants — 11.0% vs 15.8% (relative odds ratio 0.66)
cards.summary: Ickovics (2016, New York City): group care in adolescents reduced small-for-gestational-age infants — 11.0% vs 15.8% (OR relative).
cards.type: Multisite cluster randomised controlled trial (14 New York City health centres, 2008-2012)
cards.people: 1,148 pregnant women aged 14 to 21 years, at less than 24 weeks' gestation and not at high obstetrical risk, analysed from intervention and control health centres (CenteringPregnancy Plus vs traditional individual care). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: In intention-to-treat analysis, women at intervention sites were significantly less likely to have a small-for-gestational-age infant (<10th percentile): 11.0% vs 15.8% (odds ratio 0.66; 95% confidence interval 0.44 to 0.99) — a relative measure with absolute rates beside it. In as-treated analyses, more group visits were associated with better outcomes across small-for-gestational-age, gestational age, birth weight, neonatal intensive care days, rapid repeat pregnancy, condom use and unprotected sex (P=0.030 to <0.001). No associated risks were found. A preterm-birth comparison is not reported in the abstract, so none is printed.
cards.watchOut: Cluster-randomised by health centre with the dose-response (as-treated) analyses vulnerable to self-selection — women who attend more group sessions differ from those who don't — so the causal claim rests on the intention-to-treat small-for-gestational-age result alone.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the format of antenatal care can move perinatal outcomes, modestly and inconsistently by outcome — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: the format of antenatal care can move perinatal outcomes, modestly and inconsistently by outcome — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Ickovics 2007 (1,047 women aged 14-25) and Ickovics 2016 (1,148 adolescents, 14 centres).
cards.result: Group prenatal care beat individual care on preterm birth in the first trial (9.8% vs 13.8%) and on small-for-gestational-age in the second (11.0% vs 15.8%), with better knowledge, satisfaction and breastfeeding initiation and no added cost in the trial that measured costs. No group-antenatal-care shelf existed in the library; the pregnancy shelves test drugs, supplements and screening, not the format of care.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are in young US urban populations: the model's peer-support mechanism may be doing the work, and effects in older or lower-risk populations are unproven.

shelves.title: GP referral to commercial and total-diet-replacement weight programmes (WRAP; DROPLET)
shelves.question: In adults with overweight or obesity in primary care, does referral to a commercial open-group weight-management programme produce more weight loss than brief GP intervention or written information, and does the benefit persist?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Obesity · Overweight · Referral and Consultation · Weight Loss · Weight Reduction Programs
shelves.balance: Two UK primary-care trials answer two strengths of the same idea. WRAP (1,267 adults with BMI ≥28) randomised patients to brief advice with self-help materials, a 12-week commercial open-group programme (Weight Watchers), or the same programme for 52 weeks: at 1 year the programmes beat brief intervention by an adjusted 2.71 kg, and 52 weeks beat 12 weeks by a further 2.14 kg. But the mature data discipline the claim — at 5 years mean losses were −0.46 kg (brief), −1.95 kg (12-week) and −2.67 kg (52-week), and the adjusted 52-week-versus-brief difference of −1.76 kg was no longer statistically significant (95% CI −3.68 to 0.17). DROPLET tested the intensive end of referral: GP referral to a total-diet-replacement programme (810 kcal/day for 8 weeks with behavioural support) produced −10.7 kg versus −3.1 kg with nurse-led usual care at 12 months, an adjusted difference of −7.2 kg. So referral beats brief advice at one year in both trials, longer beats shorter, intensity buys more loss — and most of the advantage attenuates by five years. Cost-effectiveness modelling in WRAP favours referral despite that fade. Both trials were necessarily open-label. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: WRAP at 1 year: referral to a commercial programme beat brief advice by 2.71 kg, and 52 weeks beat 12 weeks by a further 2.14 kg
cards.summary: WRAP at 1 year: referral to a commercial programme beat brief advice by 2.71 kg, and 52 weeks beat 12 weeks by a further 2.14 kg
cards.people: 1,267 eligible adults aged 18 or older with BMI of 28 kg/m² or higher, recruited from 23 primary care practices in England and assigned 2:5:5 to brief advice and self-help materials (n=211), a 12-week open-group Weight Watchers programme (n=528), or the same programme for 52 weeks (n=528). The primary outcome was weight at 1 year, analysed by intention to treat; 65% completed a 1-year assessment and 68% a 2-year assessment.
cards.result: Mean weight change at 1 year was −3.26 kg (brief intervention), −4.75 kg (12-week programme) and −6.76 kg (52-week programme). The combined behavioural-programme arms lost more than brief intervention (adjusted difference −2.71 kg, 95% CI −3.86 to −1.55; p<0.0001), and the 52-week programme beat the 12-week programme (−2.14 kg, 95% CI −3.05 to −1.22; p<0.0001); differences remained significant at 2 years. Over 2 years the incremental cost per kilogram lost versus brief intervention was £91 for the 12-week and £159 for the 52-week programme.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with about a third of participants missing measured weights at follow-up (handled by mixed-effects intention-to-treat models). This record's registration (ISRCTN82857232) differs from the 5-year follow-up report's (ISRCTN64986150); each card cites its own record.

cards.headline: WRAP at 5 years: the referral advantage shrank and lost significance (−2.67 kg vs −0.46 kg; adjusted difference −1.76 kg, CI crossing zero)
cards.summary: WRAP at 5 years: the referral advantage shrank and lost significance (−2.67 kg vs −0.46 kg; adjusted difference −1.76 kg, CI crossing zero)
cards.type: Randomized trial long-term follow-up (5-year report of WRAP)
cards.people: The same WRAP cohort followed for 5 years after randomisation using practice or research-centre measurements, primary-care record review and questionnaires; 82% consented to the extra follow-up, and the primary outcome (weight) was ascertained for 871 of 1,267 eligible participants (69%).
cards.result: Mean weight change from baseline to 5 years was −0.46 kg (SD 8.31) in the brief intervention group, −1.95 kg (9.55) in the 12-week programme group and −2.67 kg (9.81) in the 52-week group. The adjusted difference was −1.76 kg (95% CI −3.68 to 0.17) for 52-week versus brief intervention, −0.96 kg (−2.90 to 0.97) for 12-week versus brief, and −0.80 kg (−2.13 to 0.54) for 52-week versus 12-week — none statistically significant. Within the trial the 12-week programme incurred the lowest cost and produced the most QALYs; simulation beyond 5 years favoured the 52-week programme as most cost-effective. No intervention-related adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: This is the mature update and the shelf's stamp follows it: the honest claim is a real 1-year benefit that attenuates, not a durable 5-year weight difference. With 31% of 5-year weights missing, the long-term estimate is also the least precise of the WRAP reports.

cards.headline: DROPLET: GP referral to total diet replacement lost 7.2 kg more than nurse-led usual care at 12 months
cards.summary: DROPLET: GP referral to total diet replacement lost 7.2 kg more than nurse-led usual care at 12 months
cards.people: 278 obese adults seeking weight-loss support in 10 Oxfordshire primary care practices, assigned to a total-diet-replacement (TDR) programme (n=138) or usual care from a practice nurse (n=140). TDR comprised weekly behavioural support for 12 weeks then monthly support for 3 months, with formula products providing 810 kcal/day as sole food for the first 8 weeks, followed by food reintroduction; 73% were re-measured at 12 months.
cards.result: At 12 months the TDR group had lost −10.7 kg versus −3.1 kg in usual care (adjusted mean difference −7.2 kg, 95% CI −9.4 to −4.9). Weight loss of 10% or more was achieved by 45% of the TDR group versus 15% of usual care, with greater improvements in cardiometabolic risk biomarkers. Adverse events of moderate or greater severity occurred in 11% (TDR) and 12% (usual care).
cards.watchOut: DROPLET's intervention is far more intensive than an open-group commercial programme — it supports the referral mechanism at high intensity, not the same product as WRAP's — and it has no follow-up beyond 12 months, so WRAP's 5-year attenuation warning should be read across to it.

shelves.title: Screening and brief alcohol intervention in primary care (SIPS)
shelves.question: In primary-care patients who screen positive for hazardous or harmful drinking, does screening plus structured brief intervention reduce alcohol consumption more than screening with simple feedback and a leaflet?
shelves.mesh: Alcoholism · Cluster Analysis · Counseling · Early Diagnosis · Female · General Practice · Humans · London · Male · Middle Aged · Pamphlets · Patient Education as Topic · Risk Reduction Behavior · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SIPS was built to find the extra value of doing more: 3,562 primary-care patients were screened, 900 screened positive for hazardous or harmful drinking, and practices were cluster-randomised to hand over a patient information leaflet, add five minutes of structured brief advice, or add twenty minutes of brief lifestyle counselling — with every participant first receiving simple feedback on their screening result. At 6 months there were no significant differences in the proportion no longer drinking hazardously (AUDIT-negative): versus the leaflet group, the odds ratio was 0.85 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.39) for brief advice and 0.78 (0.48 to 1.25) for lifestyle counselling, with the same picture at 12 months and in per-protocol analysis. All three groups drank less than at baseline — screening and feedback happened to everyone, and that shared ingredient is the plausible active one. Smaller earlier brief-intervention trials sit behind SIPS, but a pragmatic cluster trial of this size, null on its own primary outcome with point estimates leaning the wrong way, sets the shelf: brief advice and counselling add nothing measurable on top of feedback plus a leaflet. The shelf says nothing about screening versus no screening, which SIPS did not test. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: SIPS: brief advice (OR 0.85) and lifestyle counselling (OR 0.78) added nothing to feedback plus a leaflet for hazardous drinking
cards.summary: SIPS: brief advice (OR 0.85) and lifestyle counselling (OR 0.78) added nothing to feedback plus a leaflet for hazardous drinking
cards.people: Primary care practices in the north east and south east of England and London. Of 3,562 patients aged 18 or over who were screened, 900 (30.1% of those eligible) screened positive for hazardous or harmful drinking and 756 (84.0%) received an intervention. Practices were randomised to one of three escalating strategies: patient information leaflet after screening feedback; five minutes of structured brief advice; or 20 minutes of brief lifestyle counselling at a subsequent consultation. The primary outcome was a negative AUDIT result (score <8, i.e., no longer hazardous or harmful drinking) at 6 months; follow-up was 83% at 6 months and 79% at 12 months.
cards.result: An intention-to-treat analysis found no significant differences in AUDIT-negative status between the three interventions at 6 or 12 months. Compared with the patient information leaflet group, the odds ratio of a negative AUDIT result was 0.85 (95% CI 0.52 to 1.39) for brief advice and 0.78 (0.48 to 1.25) for brief lifestyle counselling; a per-protocol analysis confirmed these findings. The authors concluded that beyond simple feedback on the screening outcome, evidence of important additional benefit from brief advice or lifestyle counselling was lacking.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was not 'nothing': every participant received screening with simple feedback plus a leaflet, so the null applies to the added advice and counselling, not to screening itself. Drinking outcomes were self-reported (AUDIT), and the confidence intervals cannot exclude a small benefit — but the point estimates favour the leaflet, so 'underpowered near-miss' is not an available reading.
cards.source: Kaner E et al. Effectiveness of screening and brief alcohol intervention in primary care (SIPS trial): pragmatic cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2013. PMID: 23303891. Registry ID: ISRCTN06145674, from the record. shelves.title: Amoxicillin for acute lower-respiratory-tract infection when pneumonia is not suspected (GRACE)
shelves.question: In adults presenting to primary care with acute cough and lower-respiratory-tract infection where pneumonia is not suspected, does amoxicillin speed recovery or reduce symptom severity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aged · Amoxicillin · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Confidence Intervals · Diarrhea · Double-Blind Method · Drug Eruptions · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea · Primary Health Care · Proportional Hazards Models · Respiratory Tract Infections · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors
shelves.balance: The GRACE trial randomised 2,061 adults with acute cough and lower-respiratory-tract infection — pneumonia not suspected — across 12 European countries to amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 7 days or placebo, double-blind. On the outcomes patients care about, the antibiotic did nothing significant: duration of 'moderately bad or worse' symptoms (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.18) and symptom severity on days 2–4 (difference −0.07 points, p=0.074). The one significant secondary result — fewer new or worsening symptoms, 15.9% versus 19.3% (number needed to treat 30) — is smaller than the harm flowing the other way: nausea, rash or diarrhoea significantly more common (number needed to harm 21), plus one anaphylaxis on amoxicillin. The prespecified older subgroup (age ≥60, n=595) showed no selective benefit either, answering the 'older patients are different' argument directly. Hospitalisations were 1 versus 2 and there were no study-related deaths. A large, blinded, placebo-controlled trial with a null primary endpoint and harms exceeding the one positive secondary: the stamp follows. The same research programme's prescriber-training question (GRACE INTRO) is a different shelf (pack #1698); this shelf is the drug question. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: GRACE: amoxicillin did not shorten symptoms (HR 1.06) or reduce severity in 2,061 adults with acute LRTI — and harms (NNH 21) outnumbered the one secondary benefit (NNT 30)
cards.summary: GRACE: amoxicillin did not shorten symptoms (HR 1.06) or reduce severity in 2,061 adults with acute LRTI — and harms (NNH 21) outnumbered the one secondary benefit (NNT 30)
cards.people: 2,061 adults older than 18 years with acute lower-respiratory-tract infection (cough of ≤28 days' duration) in whom pneumonia was not suspected, recruited in primary care in 12 European countries and randomly assigned to amoxicillin 1 g three times daily for 7 days (n=1,038) or placebo (n=1,023), with patients and investigators masked. The primary outcome was duration of symptoms rated 'moderately bad' or worse; secondary outcomes were symptom severity on days 2–4 and new or worsening symptoms.
cards.result: Neither the duration of moderately bad or worse symptoms (hazard ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.96–1.18; p=0.229) nor mean symptom severity (1.62 with amoxicillin vs 1.69 with placebo; difference −0.07, 95% CI −0.15 to 0.007; p=0.074) differed significantly between groups. New or worsening symptoms were less common with amoxicillin (162/1,021, 15.9%, vs 194/1,006, 19.3%; p=0.043; number needed to treat 30), while nausea, rash or diarrhoea were significantly more common (number needed to harm 21, 95% CI 11–174; p=0.025) and one case of anaphylaxis occurred with amoxicillin. Two placebo patients and one amoxicillin patient were admitted to hospital; there were no study-related deaths, and no selective benefit in patients aged 60 years or older (n=595).
cards.watchOut: The population is precisely defined: pneumonia was not suspected clinically. The trial does not speak to suspected pneumonia, to COPD exacerbations, or to patients the clinician judges need antibiotics. And the single significant secondary outcome should not be quoted without its NNT-versus-NNH context — that pairing is the trial's real clinical message.
cards.source: Little P et al. Amoxicillin for acute lower-respiratory-tract infection in primary care when pneumonia is not suspected: a 12-country, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Infect Dis. 2013. PMID: 23265995. Registry ID: ISRCTN52261229, from the record (the record also lists EudraCT 2007-001586-15). shelves.title: Oral prednisolone for acute lower-respiratory-tract infection in non-asthmatic adults (OSAC)
shelves.question: In non-asthmatic adults with acute lower-respiratory-tract infection, does a short course of oral prednisolone shorten the duration of moderately severe symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Cough · Female · Glucocorticoids · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prednisolone · Respiratory Tract Infections · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: OSAC randomised 401 adults with acute cough and at least one lower-respiratory symptom — no asthma, no chronic lung disease, no immediate need for antibiotics — in 54 English family practices to prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days or placebo. The primary outcome, duration of moderately bad or worse cough, was identical at the median: 5 days in both groups (adjusted hazard ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.89 to 1.39; P=.36). The co-primary symptom-severity score was 1.99 versus 2.16 points (adjusted difference −0.20, 95% CI −0.40 to 0.00), which at P=.05 against the trial's prespecified α of 0.001 is a null, not a near-miss. Nothing else moved either — not other symptom durations, peak flow, or antibiotic use — and there were no serious adverse events. Why only POSSIBLE where the companion antibiotic trial (GRACE, shelf #1932) earns LIKELY: OSAC is a single trial a fifth of GRACE's size, and its duration interval (0.89–1.39) cannot exclude a modest severity benefit. One good trial, a clean primary null, some residual imprecision. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: OSAC: prednisolone did not shorten cough (median 5 days in both groups; HR 1.11) in 401 non-asthmatic adults with acute LRTI
cards.summary: OSAC: prednisolone did not shorten cough (median 5 days in both groups; HR 1.11) in 401 non-asthmatic adults with acute LRTI
cards.people: 401 adults with acute cough and at least one lower respiratory tract symptom, not requiring immediate antibiotic treatment, with no history of chronic pulmonary disease and no asthma medication use in the past 5 years, recruited in 54 family practices in England and randomised to two 20-mg prednisolone tablets once daily for 5 days (n=199) or matched placebo (n=202); 398 patients had baseline data, 334 (84%) provided cough-duration data and 369 (93%) symptom-severity data. The co-primary outcomes were duration of moderately bad or worse cough (minimal clinically important difference 3.79 days) and mean symptom severity on days 2–4 (MCID 1.66 units, tested at α=.001).
cards.result: Median cough duration was 5 days (IQR 3–8) in the prednisolone group and 5 days (IQR 3–10) in the placebo group (adjusted hazard ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.89–1.39; P=.36). Mean symptom severity was 1.99 points with prednisolone and 2.16 with placebo (adjusted difference −0.20, 95% CI −0.40 to 0.00; P=.05 at an α of .001 — not significant). No significant treatment effects were observed for duration or severity of other symptoms, duration of abnormal peak flow, antibiotic use, or nonserious adverse events, and there were no serious adverse events. The authors concluded oral corticosteroids should not be used for acute lower respiratory tract infection symptoms in adults without asthma.
cards.watchOut: The severity P value of .05 invites misreading: the trial prespecified α=.001 for that outcome, so by its own design this is a negative result, and the observed −0.20 difference is an eighth of the 1.66-unit difference the trial defined as clinically important. Patients judged to need immediate antibiotics were excluded — the shelf covers uncomplicated presentations only, the same boundary as the GRACE shelf.

shelves.title: Fluvoxamine for early COVID-19 in high-risk outpatients (TOGETHER; ACTIV-6)
shelves.question: In symptomatic high-risk adults with early COVID-19 managed in the community, does fluvoxamine reduce emergency care retention or hospitalisation versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Brazil · Double-Blind Method · Emergency Medical Services · Female · Fluvoxamine · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · SARS-CoV-2 · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · COVID-19 Drug Treatment
shelves.balance: Two platform trials, two answers — and the disagreement is structured, not random. TOGETHER randomised high-risk, largely unvaccinated Brazilian outpatients early in the pandemic to fluvoxamine 100 mg twice daily for 10 days or placebo: the composite of retention in a COVID-19 emergency setting or transfer to hospital occurred in 11% versus 16% (relative risk 0.68, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.52 to 0.88; absolute difference 5.0 percentage points), and the arm was stopped for superiority. Deaths (17 versus 25; OR 0.68, 95% CI 0.36–1.27) were not significantly different and are not claimed. ACTIV-6, in the United States, used HALF the dose (50 mg twice daily) in a mostly vaccinated, lower-risk population with a recovery-time primary outcome and found nothing: median sustained recovery 12 versus 13 days (hazard ratio 0.96), with hospital-level events at 3.9% versus 3.8%. ACTIV-6 does not refute TOGETHER on TOGETHER's terms — different dose, population, era and endpoint — but it removes any presumption that the effect generalises, and a single positive platform result contradicted in a second setting is exactly what POSSIBLE is for. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: TOGETHER: fluvoxamine 100 mg twice daily cut emergency retention or hospitalisation in high-risk outpatients (11% vs 16%; relative risk 0.68)
cards.summary: TOGETHER: fluvoxamine 100 mg twice daily cut emergency retention or hospitalisation in high-risk outpatients (11% vs 16%; relative risk 0.68)
cards.people: High-risk symptomatic Brazilian adults with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 and at least one risk factor for progression, randomised on the TOGETHER adaptive platform between January and August 2021 to fluvoxamine 100 mg twice daily for 10 days (n=741) or placebo (n=756), with patients, site staff and the trial team masked. The primary outcome was a composite of retention in a COVID-19 emergency setting for more than 6 hours or transfer to a tertiary hospital due to COVID-19 within 28 days, analysed by intention to treat in a Bayesian framework.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 79 of 741 patients (11%) on fluvoxamine versus 119 of 756 (16%) on placebo (relative risk 0.68, 95% Bayesian credible interval 0.52 to 0.88; absolute risk difference 5.0%), with a 99.8% probability of superiority against a prespecified 97.6% threshold; 87% of primary-outcome events were hospitalisations. Results were similar in the modified intention-to-treat analysis (relative risk 0.69) and larger per-protocol (0.34). Deaths were 17 versus 25 (odds ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.36–1.27), not significantly different, and treatment-emergent adverse events did not differ.
cards.watchOut: The composite leans on emergency-department retention — a health-system outcome recorded during Brazilian surge conditions, in a pre-Omicron, essentially unvaccinated population. Mortality, the outcome readers most want, was not significantly reduced in this record and is not claimed on this shelf.

cards.headline: ACTIV-6: at half the dose in a vaccinated US population, fluvoxamine did not speed recovery (HR 0.96) and hospital-level events were identical (3.9% vs 3.8%)
cards.summary: ACTIV-6: at half the dose in a vaccinated US population, fluvoxamine did not speed recovery (HR 0.96) and hospital-level events were identical (3.9% vs 3.8%)
cards.people: 1,331 US outpatients aged 30 years or older with test-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 and two or more COVID-19 symptoms for 7 days or fewer (1,288 completed: 674 fluvoxamine, 614 placebo), randomised on the ACTIV-6 platform to fluvoxamine 50 mg twice daily for 10 days or placebo; 67% reported two or more vaccine doses. The primary outcome was time to sustained recovery (the third of 3 consecutive symptom-free days).
cards.result: Median time to sustained recovery was 12 days (IQR 11–14) with fluvoxamine and 13 days (IQR 12–13) with placebo (hazard ratio 0.96, 95% credible interval 0.86–1.06) — no improvement. The composite of hospitalisation, urgent care visit, emergency department visit or death occurred in 3.9% versus 3.8% (hazard ratio 1.1, 95% credible interval 0.5–1.8); hospitalisations were 1 versus 2 and there were no deaths in either group. The authors concluded the findings do not support fluvoxamine at this dose and duration in mild to moderate COVID-19.
cards.watchOut: ACTIV-6 differs from TOGETHER in dose (50 mg vs 100 mg twice daily), population risk, vaccination, era and primary endpoint — it is a failed generalisation test, not a head-on replication. The shelf holds both facts at once: the TOGETHER effect estimate stands unretracted, and the ACTIV-6 null stands beside it.
