shelves.title: Metformin for early COVID-19 and post-COVID condition (COVID-OUT)
shelves.question: In adults with overweight or obesity and early COVID-19, does immediate metformin reduce severe acute outcomes — and does it reduce the incidence of post-COVID condition over 10 months?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Pregnancy · Humans · Male · Female · Middle Aged · COVID-19 · Incidence · Ivermectin · Post-Acute COVID-19 Syndrome · COVID-19 Drug Treatment · Fluvoxamine · Outpatients · SARS-CoV-2 · Metformin · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: COVID-OUT randomised 1,431 adults aged 30–85 with overweight or obesity, within days of a positive test, in a quadruple-blind 2×3 factorial of metformin, ivermectin and fluvoxamine against concurrent controls. The acute story is a null: the primary composite (hypoxaemia, emergency visit, hospitalisation or death) gave an adjusted odds ratio of 0.84 for metformin (95% CI 0.66 to 1.09; P=0.19), and the hospitalisation-or-death composite also crossed 1 (OR 0.47, 0.20–1.11); only a prespecified secondary composite of ED visit, hospitalisation or death was nominally positive (OR 0.58, 0.35–0.94). The long-term story is the interesting one: over 10 months, in the 1,126 participants followed for it, provider-diagnosed post-COVID condition occurred in 6.3% on metformin versus 10.4% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.39–0.89; p=0.012) — a 4.1-percentage-point absolute reduction, about 41% in relative terms, with a stronger estimate when treatment started within 3 days of symptoms (HR 0.37). Ivermectin (HR 0.99) and fluvoxamine (HR 1.36) showed no long-COVID effect. One trial, and the positive outcome is a prespecified but secondary endpoint ascertained by survey report of a provider diagnosis: that combination is POSSIBLE, and this shelf makes no acute-treatment claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: COVID-OUT acute outcomes: metformin's primary composite was not significant (adjusted OR 0.84; P=0.19)
cards.summary: COVID-OUT acute outcomes: metformin's primary composite was not significant (adjusted OR 0.84; P=0.19)
cards.people: 1,431 nonhospitalised adults aged 30–85 years, all with overweight or obesity, enrolled within 3 days of a confirmed SARS-CoV-2 diagnosis and fewer than 7 days after symptom onset, randomised in a 2-by-3 factorial design to metformin, ivermectin or fluvoxamine versus concurrent controls; 1,323 were included in the primary analysis (median age 46; 56% female; 52% vaccinated). The primary composite endpoint was hypoxaemia (≤93% on home oximetry), emergency department visit, hospitalisation, or death.
cards.result: The adjusted odds ratio for a primary event was 0.84 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.09; P=0.19) with metformin, 1.05 (0.76–1.45) with ivermectin and 0.94 (0.66–1.36) with fluvoxamine — none significant. In prespecified secondary analyses, the adjusted odds ratio for emergency department visit, hospitalisation or death was 0.58 (95% CI 0.35–0.94) with metformin, while for hospitalisation or death it was 0.47 (0.20–1.11), not significant. The authors concluded that none of the three medications prevented the primary composite.
cards.watchOut: Lead with the primary: it is negative. The significant secondary composite (ED visit, hospitalisation or death) coexists with a non-significant hospitalisation-or-death composite — quoting the 0.58 without that context overstates the acute evidence, and this card does not.

cards.headline: COVID-OUT at 10 months: metformin reduced post-COVID condition from 10.4% to 6.3% (HR 0.59) — a 4.1-point absolute, ~41% relative reduction
cards.summary: COVID-OUT at 10 months: metformin reduced post-COVID condition from 10.4% to 6.3% (HR 0.59) — a 4.1-point absolute, ~41% relative reduction
cards.type: Randomized trial long-term follow-up (prespecified secondary outcome)
cards.people: The COVID-OUT cohort's long-term follow-up: of 1,323 participants who received study treatment, 1,126 (564 metformin, 562 metformin-placebo) consented to long-term follow-up and completed at least one survey from day 180; 95% completed at least 9 months. The outcome was a long COVID diagnosis made by a medical provider, reported on survey, assessed to day 300 — a prespecified long-term secondary outcome of the trial.
cards.result: Overall, 93 of 1,126 participants (8.3%) reported a long COVID diagnosis by day 300. Cumulative incidence was 6.3% (95% CI 4.2–8.2) with metformin versus 10.4% (7.8–12.9) with placebo (hazard ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.39–0.89; p=0.012), an absolute reduction of 4.1 percentage points and a relative reduction of about 41%. The effect was consistent across prespecified subgroups and larger when metformin was started within 3 days of symptom onset (hazard ratio 0.37, 95% CI 0.15–0.95). Ivermectin (HR 0.99, 0.59–1.64) and fluvoxamine (HR 1.36, 0.78–2.34) showed no effect on long COVID incidence.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a survey-reported provider diagnosis, not an adjudicated or criteria-based assessment, and it is a secondary outcome of a single trial whose primary outcome was negative. Unreplicated — which is why this shelf is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, despite the clean confidence interval.

shelves.title: N-of-1 statin rechallenge for muscle symptoms (StatinWISE; SAMSON)
shelves.question: In patients who stopped or are considering stopping a statin because of muscle symptoms, do symptom scores differ between statin and placebo periods in a series of randomised double-blind n-of-1 trials?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Atorvastatin · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Male · Middle Aged · Muscular Diseases · Primary Health Care · Symptom Assessment · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: Two independent research groups asked patients who blamed a statin for their muscle symptoms to test themselves, blinded. StatinWISE ran 200 patients through six randomised 2-month periods of atorvastatin 20 mg or placebo: symptom scores did not differ (mean difference −0.11 on a 0–10 scale, 95% CI −0.36 to 0.14; P=0.40), withdrawals for intolerable symptoms were 9% in statin periods and 7% in placebo periods, and two thirds of completers planned to restart statins. SAMSON was smaller and more granular — 60 patients, monthly bottles of statin, placebo or nothing, daily symptom scores by app: symptoms were 8.0 in no-tablet months, 16.3 in statin months and 15.4 in placebo months, with no statin-versus-placebo difference (P=0.388) and a nocebo ratio of 0.90, meaning 90% of the symptom burden provoked by a statin tablet was also provoked by an identical dummy tablet; half the participants were back on statins 6 months later. Same drug, same dose, same design family, same answer: in this population the symptoms are real, but they are not, in aggregate, pharmacologically caused by atorvastatin 20 mg — they are triggered by taking a tablet believed to cause them. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: StatinWISE: muscle symptom scores were identical on statin and placebo (mean difference −0.11; P=0.40), and two thirds of completers restarted statins
cards.summary: StatinWISE: muscle symptom scores were identical on statin and placebo (mean difference −0.11; P=0.40), and two thirds of completers restarted statins
cards.type: Series of randomized double-blind n-of-1 trials
cards.people: 200 primary-care patients across 50 UK sites who had recently stopped, or were considering stopping, statins because of muscle symptoms. Each participant was randomised to a sequence of six double-blind 2-month treatment periods of atorvastatin 20 mg daily or placebo, rating muscle symptoms on a 0–10 visual analogue scale at the end of each period; 151 participants provided scores for at least one statin and one placebo period and entered the primary analysis.
cards.result: Overall there was no difference in muscle symptom scores between statin and placebo periods (mean difference, statin minus placebo, −0.11; 95% CI −0.36 to 0.14; P=0.40). Withdrawals because of intolerable muscle symptoms occurred in 18 participants (9%) during a statin period and 13 (7%) during a placebo period. Two thirds of those completing the trial reported that they planned to restart long-term statin treatment.

shelves.title: Gabapentin for chronic pelvic pain in women (GaPP2)
shelves.question: In women with chronic pelvic pain and no identified pathology, does gabapentin reduce pelvic pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Analgesics · Chronic Pain · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gabapentin · Humans · Off-Label Use · Pelvic Pain · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: GaPP2 was designed to settle a widespread off-label habit: 306 women with chronic pelvic pain of at least 3 months and no obvious pathology at laparoscopy, in 39 UK centres, randomised double-blind to gabapentin titrated to a maximum of 2,700 mg daily or placebo for 16 weeks. Both co-primary outcomes were null. Worst pain scores at weeks 13–16 were 7.1 versus 7.4 (adjusted mean difference −0.20, 97.5% CI −0.81 to 0.42; p=0.47) and average pain 4.3 versus 4.5 (adjusted difference −0.18, −0.71 to 0.35; p=0.45), with intervals that exclude a one-point benefit on a 0–10 scale. The harm side was not symmetrical: serious adverse events occurred in 10 women (7%) on gabapentin versus 3 (2%) on placebo (p=0.04), and dizziness, drowsiness and visual disturbances were all more common on the drug. An adequately powered, double-blind, single trial with a null primary and a significant harm excess earns the definitive-negative stamp; the population boundary — pain without identified pathology — is on the card's face. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: GaPP2: gabapentin was no better than placebo for pelvic pain (worst pain adjusted difference −0.20) and caused more serious adverse events (7% vs 2%)
cards.summary: GaPP2: gabapentin was no better than placebo for pelvic pain (worst pain adjusted difference −0.20) and caused more serious adverse events (7% vs 2%)
cards.people: 306 women aged 18–50 with chronic pelvic pain (with or without dysmenorrhoea or dyspareunia) of at least 3 months' duration and no obvious pelvic pathology at laparoscopy performed 2 weeks to 36 months before consent, recruited in 39 UK hospital centres and randomised 1:1 to gabapentin titrated to a maximum tolerated dose up to 2,700 mg daily (n=153) or matching placebo (n=153) for 16 weeks, with patients, clinicians and research staff masked. The dual primary outcomes were worst and average pain scores (0–10 numerical rating scale) in weeks 13–16, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: There were no significant between-group differences in either primary outcome. Mean worst pain score was 7.1 (SD 2.6) on gabapentin versus 7.4 (2.2) on placebo, a change from baseline of −1.4 versus −1.2 (adjusted mean difference −0.20, 97.5% CI −0.81 to 0.42; p=0.47). Mean average pain was 4.3 (2.3) versus 4.5 (2.2), change −1.1 versus −0.9 (adjusted difference −0.18, 97.5% CI −0.71 to 0.35; p=0.45). Serious adverse events occurred in 10 of 153 women (7%) in the gabapentin group versus 3 of 153 (2%) in the placebo group (p=0.04), and dizziness, drowsiness and visual disturbances were more common with gabapentin. The authors concluded gabapentin did not lower pain scores and was associated with higher rates of side effects.
cards.watchOut: The eligibility gate matters: women had a laparoscopy showing no obvious pathology, so this shelf does not cover pelvic pain with identified causes such as endometriosis. Within its population, though, the trial was adequately powered and its intervals exclude the benefit sizes clinicians usually hope for from this drug.

shelves.title: Haemorrhoidal artery ligation versus rubber band ligation (HubBLe)
shelves.question: In symptomatic grade II–III haemorrhoids, does haemorrhoidal artery ligation (HAL) reduce recurrence at one year versus rubber band ligation (RBL)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Ambulatory Surgical Procedures · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Care Costs · Hemorrhoids · Humans · Ligation · Male · Middle Aged · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Recurrence · Reoperation · Rubber · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Correction first, because the topic draft had the headline backwards: the fetched record shows recurrence at 1 year was LOWER after haemorrhoidal artery ligation than after rubber band ligation — 30% (48/161) versus 49% (87/176), adjusted odds ratio 2.23 (95% CI 1.42–3.51; p=0.0005) for recurrence with banding versus ligation. What complicates the verdict is everything around that number. The difference was driven by repeat procedures: 32% of banded patients needed a subsequent haemorrhoid procedure versus 14% after ligation — and repeat banding is an accepted part of an RBL course, so HubBLe effectively compared one operation against one banding, not against a banding strategy. Ligation also hurt more (day-1 pain 4.6 versus 3.4; day-7 pain 3.1 versus 1.6) and produced more serious adverse events requiring admission (12 events, ~7%, versus 2, ~1%), which is why the trialists themselves concluded that patients and commissioners might prefer a course of RBL despite the recurrence figures. A single open-label trial whose own conclusion cuts against its primary outcome, with the comparison structurally favouring the operation: POSSIBLE for the narrow claim that HAL reduces 1-year recurrence after a single procedure, at a pain and safety cost. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: HubBLe: recurrence at 1 year was lower after artery ligation (30%) than after banding (49%) — but ligation hurt more and caused more serious adverse events
cards.summary: HubBLe: recurrence at 1 year was lower after artery ligation (30%) than after banding (49%) — but ligation hurt more and caused more serious adverse events
cards.people: 372 patients aged 18 or older with grade II–III haemorrhoids, recruited from 17 UK NHS trusts and randomised 1:1 to haemorrhoidal artery ligation with Doppler guidance (n=185) or rubber band ligation (n=187); 337 patients (176 RBL, 161 HAL) had primary outcome data. The trial was open-label — no masking of participants, clinicians or research staff. The primary outcome was recurrence at 1 year, derived from patient self-report combined with GP and hospital records of resource use.
cards.result: At 1 year, haemorrhoid recurrence occurred in 48 of 161 patients (30%) in the HAL group and 87 of 176 (49%) in the RBL group (adjusted odds ratio 2.23, 95% CI 1.42–3.51; p=0.0005, for recurrence with RBL versus HAL). The main reason for the difference was repeat procedures: 57 RBL patients (32%) versus 23 HAL patients (14%) had a subsequent procedure for haemorrhoids. Pain favoured RBL: mean pain at day 1 was 3.4 (SD 2.8) after RBL versus 4.6 (2.8) after HAL (difference −1.2, 95% CI −1.8 to −0.5; p=0.0002) and at day 7 was 1.6 versus 3.1 (p<0.0001), with no difference by 21 days. Serious adverse events requiring hospital admission numbered 12 (7%) among HAL-treated participants versus 2 (1%) with RBL, including bleeding, urinary retention and possible sepsis after HAL.
cards.watchOut: Read the primary outcome carefully: it counts needing another procedure as recurrence, and repeat banding is routine RBL care — so the trial compares one HAL operation with a single banding session, not with an RBL treatment course. The authors' own interpretation — that patients and commissioners might prefer such a course of RBL to the more invasive HAL — is part of this trial's result and is carried here in full. (An earlier draft of this shelf's topic file reversed the recurrence direction; the record controls, and it favours HAL on recurrence.)

shelves.title: Behavioural weight-loss treatment delivered in primary care practice (POWER)
shelves.question: In obese adults with cardiovascular risk factors, do remote (telephone/web) or in-person behavioural weight-loss interventions delivered through primary care produce more weight loss at two years than a self-directed control?
shelves.mesh: Behavior Therapy · Cardiovascular Diseases · Counseling · Diet, Reducing · Exercise · Female · Health Behavior · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity · Physicians, Primary Care · Risk Factors · Telemedicine · Weight Loss
shelves.balance: POWER randomised 415 obese adults (mean BMI 36.6) with at least one cardiovascular risk factor, recruited from six primary care practices, to self-directed weight loss or to a behavioural programme delivered remotely (telephone, website, email) or in person (group and individual sessions plus the remote tools), with primary care providers reinforcing participation at routine visits. At 24 months both supported programmes clearly beat control: −4.6 kg (remote) and −5.1 kg (in-person) versus −0.8 kg, both P<0.001 against control, with 38.2% and 41.4% losing at least 5% of body weight versus 18.8% of controls. The comparison that gives this shelf its practical payload — remote versus in-person — showed no significant difference: travelling to sessions bought nothing measurable over the phone and the website. A single trial, and unblinded as behavioural trials must be; it is flagged as such. Its direction agrees with the referral trials on shelf #1930, but this shelf stands on POWER alone: supported behavioural treatment, however delivered, produces ~4–5 kg more loss than going it alone, sustained to two years. PROPOSED LIKELY (single trial).

cards.headline: POWER: at 24 months, remote support (−4.6 kg) and in-person support (−5.1 kg) both beat self-directed control (−0.8 kg) — and matched each other
cards.summary: POWER: at 24 months, remote support (−4.6 kg) and in-person support (−5.1 kg) both beat self-directed control (−0.8 kg) — and matched each other
cards.people: 415 obese patients with at least one cardiovascular risk factor, recruited from six primary care practices (mean age 54.0 years; mean BMI 36.6; mean weight 103.8 kg; 63.6% women). One group received weight-loss support remotely — telephone, a study website and email, with no face-to-face contact with coaches; another received in-person group and individual sessions plus the same remote tools; the control group pursued self-directed weight loss. In both intervention arms, primary care providers reinforced participation at routinely scheduled visits. Trial duration was 24 months.
cards.result: At 24 months, mean weight change was −0.8 kg in the control group, −4.6 kg in the remote-support group (P<0.001 versus control) and −5.1 kg in the in-person group (P<0.001 versus control). The proportion losing 5% or more of initial weight was 18.8% (control), 38.2% (remote) and 41.4% (in-person). Weight change did not differ significantly between the two intervention groups. The authors concluded that obese patients achieved and sustained clinically significant weight loss over 24 months with either delivery mode.
cards.watchOut: Single trial, US practices, study-funded coaches — effects in routine services typically shrink (compare the community-programme results on shelf #1930). Participants could not be blinded, and weight was the endpoint: the shelf claims weight loss, not cardiovascular-event reduction, which POWER was not powered to show.

shelves.title: A re-engineered hospital discharge programme (Project RED)
shelves.question: In medical inpatients, does a re-engineered discharge — nurse discharge advocate, tailored after-hospital care plan, and pharmacist follow-up call — reduce hospital utilisation (readmission plus emergency visits) at 30 days versus usual discharge?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Boston · Cost Savings · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Hospitalization · Hospitals, University · Hospitals, Urban · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Patient Care Team · Patient Discharge · Patient Education as Topic
shelves.balance: Project RED tested a package, not a pill: a nurse discharge advocate who arranged follow-up appointments, confirmed medication reconciliation and taught from an individualised instruction booklet (copied to the primary care provider), plus a clinical pharmacist telephone call 2–4 days after discharge to reinforce the plan and review medications. In 749 medical inpatients at a single urban US safety-net hospital, the intervention group used significantly less hospital care in the 30 days after discharge — 0.314 versus 0.451 visits per person per month, an incidence rate ratio of 0.695 (95% CI 0.515 to 0.937; P=0.009), roughly a 30% relative reduction — with the effect concentrated in patients who had used hospital care in the previous 6 months. The limits define the stamp: one centre, one trial, no blinding of participants or providers (follow-up assessors were blinded), outcome assessment partly by participant report, and adverse events were collected but not assessed in this report. A promising, widely imitated single-centre result that has not been re-run at this rigour on this card. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Project RED: a re-engineered discharge cut 30-day hospital utilisation by about 30% (0.314 vs 0.451 visits per person-month; IRR 0.695)
cards.summary: Project RED: a re-engineered discharge cut 30-day hospital utilisation by about 30% (0.314 vs 0.451 visits per person-month; IRR 0.695)
cards.people: 749 English-speaking hospitalised adults (mean age 49.9 years) on the general medical service of an urban academic safety-net hospital in Boston, randomised to the re-engineered discharge intervention (n=370 analysed) or usual care (n=368). The intervention comprised a nurse discharge advocate who worked with patients during the stay to arrange follow-up appointments, confirm medication reconciliation and deliver education using an individualised instruction booklet also sent to the primary care provider, plus a clinical pharmacist call 2–4 days after discharge to reinforce the plan and review medications. Primary outcomes were emergency department visits and hospitalisations within 30 days of discharge.
cards.result: Participants in the intervention group had a lower rate of hospital utilisation than those receiving usual care (0.314 vs 0.451 visits per person per month; incidence rate ratio 0.695, 95% CI 0.515 to 0.937; P=0.009). The intervention was most effective among participants with hospital utilisation in the 6 months before the index admission (P=0.014). The authors concluded that a package of discharge services reduced hospital utilisation within 30 days of discharge.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and unblinded (participants and providers knew the assignment; follow-up research staff did not). Not all eligible patients could be enrolled, some outcomes relied on participant report, and — stated plainly in the record — adverse events were not assessed in this report. The composite counts ED visits and readmissions together; the record does not break out a significant readmissions-only effect on this card.

shelves.title: Extended thromboprophylaxis after hospitalisation for medical illness (MARINER; EXCLAIM; APEX)
shelves.question: In medically ill patients discharged from hospital at raised VTE risk, does 45 days of rivaroxaban reduce symptomatic VTE and VTE-related death versus placebo without excess major bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Aftercare · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Factor Xa Inhibitors · Female · Hemorrhage · Hospitalization · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Discharge · Rivaroxaban · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thromboembolism · Venous Thrombosis
shelves.balance: Three large trials of extended post-discharge prophylaxis tell one consistent, uncomfortable story. MARINER — the only trial powered on symptomatic outcomes — randomised 12,024 discharged medically ill patients at raised VTE risk to rivaroxaban 10 mg daily or placebo for 45 days: its primary composite of symptomatic VTE or VTE-related death was NOT significantly reduced (0.83% vs 1.10%; hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.09; P=0.14), although the symptomatic nonfatal VTE component was lower (0.18% vs 0.42%; HR 0.44, 0.22–0.89), and major bleeding was numerically higher (0.28% vs 0.15%; HR 1.88, 0.84–4.23). EXCLAIM found extended enoxaparin cut a VTE endpoint dominated by screening-detected clots (2.5% vs 4.0%; absolute difference −1.53 points) at the cost of significantly more major bleeding (0.8% vs 0.3%), with benefit concentrated in women, patients over 75 and the most immobile. APEX missed its prespecified primary cohort analysis (6.9% vs 8.5%; relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.00; P=0.054); its positive broader-cohort results are formally exploratory under the trial's own gatekeeping plan. Net: extended prophylaxis prevents some, mostly asymptomatic, clots; a symptomatic or survival benefit is unproven where it was tested head-on, and bleeding tilts against treatment. Tier C because the question includes VTE-related death. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: MARINER: 45 days of rivaroxaban after discharge did not significantly reduce symptomatic VTE or VTE death (0.83% vs 1.10%; HR 0.76; P=0.14)
cards.summary: MARINER: 45 days of rivaroxaban after discharge did not significantly reduce symptomatic VTE or VTE death (0.83% vs 1.10%; HR 0.76; P=0.14)
cards.people: 12,024 medically ill patients randomised at hospital discharge (12,019 in the intention-to-treat analysis) who were at increased VTE risk — a modified IMPROVE score of 4 or higher, or 2–3 plus a D-dimer more than twice the upper limit of normal — assigned to once-daily rivaroxaban 10 mg (renally adjusted; n=6,007) or placebo (n=6,012) for 45 days. The primary efficacy outcome was the composite of symptomatic venous thromboembolism or death due to venous thromboembolism; the principal safety outcome was major bleeding.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 50 of 6,007 patients (0.83%) on rivaroxaban and 66 of 6,012 (1.10%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.09; P=0.14) — not significant. The prespecified secondary outcome of symptomatic nonfatal VTE occurred in 0.18% versus 0.42% (hazard ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.22 to 0.89). Major bleeding occurred in 17 of 5,982 patients (0.28%) on rivaroxaban versus 9 of 5,980 (0.15%) on placebo (hazard ratio 1.88, 95% CI 0.84 to 4.23). The authors concluded rivaroxaban was not associated with a significantly lower risk of symptomatic VTE and VTE-related death than placebo, with a low incidence of major bleeding.
cards.watchOut: The significant symptomatic-nonfatal-VTE result is a component of a primary composite that failed — it inherits that caution, and absolute event rates were low in both arms (a 0.27-percentage-point absolute difference on the primary). The topic draft's gloss ('symptomatic VTE events were fewer; bleeding not significantly increased') is literally true and materially incomplete; this card carries the primary outcome first, as the shelf requires.
cards.source: Spyropoulos AC et al. Rivaroxaban for Thromboprophylaxis after Hospitalization for Medical Illness. N Engl J Med. 2018. PMID: 30145946. Registry ID: NCT02111564, from the record. cards.headline: EXCLAIM: extended enoxaparin cut VTE (2.5% vs 4.0%) but significantly increased major bleeding (0.8% vs 0.3%)
cards.summary: EXCLAIM: extended enoxaparin cut VTE (2.5% vs 4.0%) but significantly increased major bleeding (0.8% vs 0.3%)
cards.people: 5,963 acutely ill medical patients aged 40 or older with recently reduced mobility, at 370 sites in 20 countries. After an initial open-label enoxaparin course of about 10 days, patients received enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily (n=2,975) or placebo (n=2,988) for a further 28±4 days, with patients, caregivers and outcome assessors blinded. Outcomes were VTE incidence to day 28 and major bleeding.
cards.result: Extended-duration enoxaparin reduced VTE incidence compared with placebo (2.5% vs 4.0%; absolute risk difference −1.53%, 95.8% CI −2.54 to −0.52) and increased major bleeding (0.8% vs 0.3%; absolute risk difference +0.51%, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.89). The benefit appeared restricted to women, patients older than 75 years, and those with level-1 immobility (bed rest or sedentary without bathroom privileges).
cards.watchOut: The VTE endpoint included asymptomatic, ultrasound-detected thrombosis — a softer currency than MARINER's symptomatic composite — and eligibility criteria were amended mid-trial after lower-than-expected event rates, which the authors themselves flag as complicating interpretation of the overall estimates.
cards.source: Hull RD et al. Extended-duration venous thromboembolism prophylaxis in acutely ill medical patients with recently reduced mobility: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2010. cards.headline: APEX: extended betrixaban missed its prespecified primary cohort analysis (P=0.054); the positive wider-cohort results are exploratory by the trial's own rules
cards.summary: APEX: extended betrixaban missed its prespecified primary cohort analysis (P=0.054); the positive wider-cohort results are exploratory by the trial's own rules
cards.people: 7,513 patients hospitalised for acute medical illnesses, randomised to extended-duration oral betrixaban 80 mg daily for 35–42 days (with enoxaparin placebo for the first 10±4 days) or standard subcutaneous enoxaparin 40 mg daily for 10±4 days (with betrixaban placebo thereafter). The primary efficacy outcome was a composite of asymptomatic proximal deep-vein thrombosis and symptomatic VTE, analysed in three prespecified, progressively inclusive cohorts under a sequential testing plan; the principal safety outcome was major bleeding.
cards.result: In cohort 1 (elevated D-dimer), the primary outcome occurred in 6.9% on betrixaban versus 8.5% on enoxaparin (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.00; P=0.054) — not significant. Rates in cohort 2 were 5.6% versus 7.1% (relative risk 0.80, 0.66–0.98; P=0.03) and in the overall population 5.3% versus 7.0% (relative risk 0.76, 0.63–0.92; P=0.006), but under the prespecified hierarchy those analyses are exploratory because cohort 1 did not reach significance. Major bleeding in the overall population was 0.7% versus 0.6% (relative risk 1.19, 95% CI 0.67 to 2.12; P=0.55).
cards.watchOut: Most events in the composite were asymptomatic ultrasound-detected DVTs. The statistical hierarchy is not pedantry: APEX is frequently cited as a positive trial, and on its own registered analysis plan it is not — this card records it as the trial reported it.
cards.source: Cohen AT et al. Extended Thromboprophylaxis with Betrixaban in Acutely Ill Medical Patients. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 27232649. Registry ID: NCT01583218, from the record. cards.result: Symptomatic VTE/VTE-death (MARINER primary): HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.52–1.09), not significant. Total VTE endpoints (EXCLAIM −1.53 points; APEX overall relative risk 0.76, exploratory): reduced. shelves.title: Oral midodrine to wean intravenous vasopressors in the ICU (MIDAS)
shelves.question: In ICU patients with persistent hypotension on a single intravenous vasopressor, does oral midodrine shorten time to vasopressor discontinuation versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Australia · Humans · Hypotension · Intensive Care Units · Midodrine · Vasoconstrictor Agents
shelves.balance: MIDAS asked a practical ICU question — can an oral α1-agonist get stable patients off the drip that is keeping them in the unit? In 132 analysed patients on a single intravenous vasopressor for at least 24 hours across three US and Australian tertiary centres, midodrine 20 mg every 8 hours did not shorten time to vasopressor discontinuation: median 23.5 hours versus 22.5 hours on placebo (difference 1 hour, 95% CI −10.4 to 12.3; p=0.62). No secondary endpoint moved — not ICU-discharge readiness, lengths of stay or readmission — and the trial's one clear between-group difference was harm-shaped: bradycardia in 5 patients (7.6%) on midodrine versus none on placebo (p=0.02). The stamp stops at POSSIBLE because a single 132-patient trial whose interval still admits roughly ten hours' faster weaning shows 'no demonstrated benefit', not proof of none. Midodrine's other common question — preventing vasovagal syncope — is a different shelf (pack #1557). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: MIDAS: midodrine did not accelerate vasopressor liberation (median 23.5 vs 22.5 hours; p=0.62) and caused more bradycardia (7.6% vs 0%)
cards.summary: MIDAS: midodrine did not accelerate vasopressor liberation (median 23.5 vs 22.5 hours; p=0.62) and caused more bradycardia (7.6% vs 0%)
cards.people: 136 ICU patients with hypotension requiring a single-agent intravenous vasopressor for at least 24 hours, randomised at three tertiary referral hospitals in the US and Australia; 132 received the allocated intervention and were analysed (modified intention to treat). Patients received oral midodrine 20 mg or placebo every 8 hours in addition to standard care until intravenous vasopressors stopped, ICU discharge, or an adverse event. The primary outcome was time to vasopressor discontinuation.
cards.result: Time to vasopressor discontinuation did not differ between groups (median [IQR] 23.5 [10–54] hours with midodrine vs 22.5 [10.4–40] hours with placebo; difference 1 hour, 95% CI −10.4 to 12.3; p=0.62). No differences were observed in time to ICU discharge readiness, ICU or hospital length of stay, or ICU readmission. Bradycardia occurred more often after midodrine (5 patients [7.6%] vs 0 [0%]; p=0.02). The authors concluded midodrine did not accelerate liberation from intravenous vasopressors and was not effective for treating hypotension in critically ill patients.
cards.watchOut: Recruitment ran from 2012 to 2019 for 136 patients — a slow, small trial, and its confidence interval cannot exclude a half-day benefit. What it does exclude is the large weaning effect that would justify routine use, and the bradycardia signal is a cost attached to a benefit not shown.
cards.source: Santer P et al. Effect of midodrine versus placebo on time to vasopressor discontinuation in patients with persistent hypotension in the intensive care unit (MIDAS): an international randomised clinical trial. shelves.title: Patient education to prevent falls among older hospital inpatients (Haines; Hill)
shelves.question: In older hospital inpatients, does individualised patient education (with written and video materials and follow-up) reduce falls and fall-related injuries versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Australia · Female · Humans · Inpatients · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Education as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two Australian trials converge on the same qualifier: education works in patients who can act on it. Haines (2011) randomised 1,206 older inpatients to usual care, multimedia materials alone, or materials plus trained-professional follow-up: overall fall rates did not differ significantly (9.27, 8.61 and 7.63 per 1,000 patient-days), but there was a significant interaction with cognitive status — among cognitively intact patients the complete programme nearly halved falls versus control (4.01 vs 8.72 per 1,000 patient-days; adjusted hazard ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.78) and beat materials alone (HR 0.51). Hill (2015) then tested individualised education plus staff training and feedback in eight rehabilitation units, enrolling only patients with MMSE above 23 — that is, the cognitively intact population Haines pointed to — and found falls cut from 13.78 to 7.80 per 1,000 patient-days (adjusted rate ratio 0.60, 95% CI 0.42–0.94) with injurious falls also reduced (rate ratio 0.65). The shelf's claim is therefore scoped: individualised education with professional follow-up reduces falls in cognitively intact older inpatients, best evidenced in rehabilitation settings. Materials alone did nothing measurable; the human follow-up is part of the treatment. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: Haines 2011: multimedia education alone did not cut falls overall, but with professional follow-up it halved falls in cognitively intact patients (HR 0.43)
cards.summary: Haines 2011: multimedia education alone did not cut falls overall, but with professional follow-up it halved falls in cognitively intact patients (HR 0.43)
cards.people: 1,206 older patients admitted to acute (orthopaedic, respiratory, medical) and subacute (geriatric, neurorehabilitation) wards at two Australian hospitals, randomised to usual care, a multimedia patient-education programme alone ('materials only'), or the same materials combined with follow-up by a trained health professional ('complete programme'). Falls were collected by blinded research assistants from incident reports, medical records and weekly patient interviews, and expressed per 1,000 patient-days.
cards.result: Overall fall rates did not differ significantly between groups (control 9.27; materials only 8.61; complete programme 7.63 per 1,000 patient-days). However, there was a significant interaction between intervention and cognitive impairment: among cognitively intact patients, falls were less frequent in the complete programme group (4.01 per 1,000 patient-days) than in the materials-only group (8.18; adjusted hazard ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.28–0.93) and the control group (8.72; adjusted hazard ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.24–0.78). The authors concluded that multimedia patient education with trained health professional follow-up reduced falls among patients with intact cognitive function.
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison is null and the benefit is an interaction with cognitive status — a subgroup structure that deserves one notch of caution even though the second trial on this shelf was designed around exactly that qualifier. The topic draft described the subgroup as a 'rehabilitation setting' effect; the record's interaction is with cognitive impairment, and this card follows the record.

cards.headline: Hill 2015: in rehabilitation units, individualised education plus staff training cut falls (rate ratio 0.60) and injurious falls (0.65) in cognitively intact patients
cards.summary: Hill 2015: in rehabilitation units, individualised education plus staff training cut falls (rate ratio 0.60) and injurious falls (0.65) in cognitively intact patients
cards.people: Eight rehabilitation units in Australian general hospitals participated in a 50-week stepped-wedge cluster-randomised study; 3,606 patients were admitted during control (n=1,983) and intervention (n=1,623) periods. Patients with a Mini-Mental State Examination score above 23/30 received individualised falls-prevention education from a trained health professional, based on health-behaviour-change principles, in addition to usual care; staff received patients' goals and environmental feedback and were trained to support the strategies. Coprimary outcomes were falls per 1,000 patient-days and the proportion of patients who fell.
cards.result: Falls were fewer during intervention periods (196 falls, 7.80 per 1,000 patient-days) than control periods (380 falls, 13.78 per 1,000 patient-days; adjusted rate ratio 0.60, robust 95% CI 0.42–0.94; p=0.003), as were injurious falls (2.63 vs 4.75 per 1,000 patient-days; rate ratio 0.65, 0.42–0.88; p=0.006) and the proportion of fallers (8.38% vs 12.51%; adjusted odds ratio 0.55, 0.38–0.81; p=0.003). Length of stay did not differ significantly. The authors concluded that individualised patient education combined with training and feedback to staff reduces falls and injurious falls in older patients in rehabilitation units.
cards.watchOut: A stepped-wedge cluster design in rehabilitation units only, and the intervention bundles staff training with patient education — the two cannot be separated on this evidence. Eligibility required MMSE >23, so the trial is silent, by design, on the cognitively impaired patients at highest falls risk.
cards.source: Hill AM et al. Fall rates in hospital rehabilitation units after individualised patient and staff education programmes: a pragmatic, stepped-wedge, cluster-randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2015. PMID: 25865864. Registry ID: ACTRN12612000877886, from the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, one population — education with human follow-up prevents falls in cognitively intact inpatients (HR 0.43; rate ratio 0.60), and print/video alone does not
cards.people: 1,206 patients in Haines 2011 and 3,606 admitted patients in Hill 2015.
cards.result: Haines, cognitively intact subgroup: complete programme 4.01 vs 8.72 falls per 1,000 patient-days (adjusted HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.24–0.78). shelves.title: Multifaceted clinical pharmacist intervention in hospital (OPTIMIST)
shelves.question: In acutely admitted medical patients, does a multifaceted clinical-pharmacist intervention (medication review, discharge planning, and post-discharge follow-up) reduce readmissions versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Drug Prescriptions · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Medication Reconciliation · Middle Aged · Patient Care Team · Patient Education as Topic · Patient Readmission · Pharmacy Service, Hospital
shelves.balance: The OPTIMIST trial (reported by Ravn-Nielsen and colleagues) randomised 1,499 acutely admitted Danish medical patients taking at least five medications to usual care, a basic intervention (medication review alone), or an extended intervention (medication review, three motivational interviews, and structured follow-up with the primary care physician, pharmacy and nursing home). The extended package worked on the outcomes it aimed at: versus usual care it reduced readmission within 30 days (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.84) and within 180 days (HR 0.75, 0.62–0.90), and the primary composite of readmission or emergency visit within 180 days (HR 0.77, 0.64–0.93), with a number needed to treat of 12. Drug-related readmissions and deaths were numerically lower but not significant (deaths HR 0.83, 0.22–3.11) — no mortality claim is made. Crucially, the record reports no significant effect for the basic review-only arm: the benefit belongs to the extended, follow-up-heavy package, not to 'a pharmacist looked at the chart'. Single trial, one country's system, and the stamp prices that in. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: OPTIMIST: the extended pharmacist intervention cut 180-day readmission or ED visits (HR 0.77; NNT 12); the basic review alone showed no significant effect
cards.summary: OPTIMIST: the extended pharmacist intervention cut 180-day readmission or ED visits (HR 0.77; NNT 12); the basic review alone showed no significant effect
cards.people: 1,499 acutely admitted medical patients aged 18 or older taking five or more medications, randomised in Danish acute admission wards (1,467 in the primary analysis; median age 72) to usual care (n=498), a basic intervention of medication review (n=493), or an extended intervention (n=476) comprising medication review, three motivational interviews with the patient, and follow-up after discharge in collaboration with the primary care physician, community pharmacy and nursing home. Follow-up was 6 months, analysed by intention to treat; the primary composite endpoint was readmission or an emergency department visit within 180 days.
cards.result: The extended intervention significantly reduced readmission within 30 days (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.46–0.84) and within 180 days (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.62–0.90), and the primary composite of readmission or ED visit within 180 days (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.64–0.93), with a number needed to treat of 12 for the composite. Reductions in drug-related readmissions were not significant at 30 days (HR 0.65, 0.39–1.09) or 180 days (HR 0.80, 0.59–1.08), nor were deaths (HR 0.83, 0.22–3.11). The authors concluded that a multifaceted clinical pharmacist intervention may reduce ED visits and hospital readmissions.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports effects for the extended arm only — no significant benefit is reported for the basic medication-review-only intervention, so this shelf must not be cited as evidence that medication review by itself prevents readmissions. One trial in one health system, with a labour-intensive intervention whose staffing model may not transfer.

shelves.title: Automated electronic alerts for acute kidney injury (Wilson 2015; Wilson 2021)
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients who develop acute kidney injury, does an automated electronic alert to the treating team improve kidney recovery and reduce dialysis or death versus usual care without alerts?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury · Adult · Aged · Automation · Biomarkers · Cell Phone · Creatinine · Early Diagnosis · Electronic Health Records · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Single-Blind Method · Young Adult
shelves.balance: The same investigative group tested AKI alerting twice, at two scales, and got the same answer with a warning attached. The 2015 single-centre trial randomised 2,393 inpatients with stage 1 or greater AKI to a text alert to the covering provider and unit pharmacist or usual care: the primary composite of creatinine change, dialysis and death at 7 days did not differ (p=0.88), with dialysis (7.2% vs 5.9%; OR 1.25) and death (5.9% vs 5.1%; OR 1.16) both numerically higher in the alert arm. The 2021 multicentre trial randomised 6,030 patients across six hospitals to an EHR pop-up alert with an AKI order set or usual care: the primary composite of AKI progression, dialysis or death within 14 days was 21.3% versus 20.9% (relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.13; P=0.67) — and at the two non-teaching hospitals alerts were associated with significantly WORSE outcomes (relative risk 1.49, 1.12–1.98), including more deaths (15.6% vs 8.6%). Alerts did increase some AKI care practices without those changes mediating outcomes. Two randomised trials, over 8,400 patients, no benefit on any primary outcome: telling clinicians louder that AKI has happened does not, by itself, change what happens next. (Correction: the topic draft cited the 2021 trial as N Engl J Med; the fetched record is BMJ 2021.) PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Wilson 2015: an electronic AKI alert did not improve the composite of creatinine change, dialysis or death at 7 days (p=0.88)
cards.summary: Wilson 2015: an electronic AKI alert did not improve the composite of creatinine change, dialysis or death at 7 days (p=0.88)
cards.people: 2,393 hospitalised adults with stage 1 or greater acute kidney injury by KDIGO creatinine criteria at the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, randomly assigned to an automated AKI alert (a text-based alert sent to the covering provider and unit pharmacist indicating new AKI; n=1,201) or usual care (n=1,192), stratified by medical versus surgical admission and ICU status. The primary outcome was a composite of relative maximum change in creatinine, dialysis, and death at 7 days after randomisation, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: The composite outcome did not differ between the alert and usual care groups (p=0.88), nor within any of the four randomisation strata. At 7 days, median maximum relative change in creatinine was 0.0% (IQR 0.0–18.4) in the alert group and 0.6% (0.0–17.5) in the usual care group (p=0.81); dialysis had been received by 87 patients (7.2%) in the alert group and 70 (5.9%) in usual care (odds ratio 1.25, 95% CI 0.90–1.74; p=0.18); and 71 patients (5.9%) in the alert group and 61 (5.1%) in usual care had died (odds ratio 1.16, 0.81–1.68; p=0.40). The authors concluded that an electronic alert system for AKI did not improve clinical outcomes among hospital inpatients.
cards.watchOut: A single hospital and a text-page intervention; the trial cannot exclude benefit from a differently designed response system (alert plus mandated actions, for example). But its point estimates for dialysis and death lean against the alert, which matters when read beside the multicentre trial.

cards.headline: Wilson 2021: across six hospitals, AKI alerts were null overall (RR 1.02) and associated with harm at non-teaching hospitals (RR 1.49; deaths 15.6% vs 8.6%)
cards.summary: Wilson 2021: across six hospitals, AKI alerts were null overall (RR 1.02) and associated with harm at non-teaching hospitals (RR 1.49; deaths 15.6% vs 8.6%)
cards.people: 6,030 adult inpatients with AKI by KDIGO creatinine criteria at six hospitals (four teaching, two non-teaching) in the Yale New Haven Health System, randomised to an electronic health record 'pop-up' alert for AKI with an associated AKI order set, triggered when a provider opened the chart (n=3,059), or usual care (n=2,971). The primary outcome was a composite of progression of AKI, receipt of dialysis, or death within 14 days of randomisation; effects at each hospital were prespecified secondary analyses.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 653 of 3,059 patients (21.3%) in the alert group and 622 of 2,971 (20.9%) in the usual care group (relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.13; P=0.67). Analysis by hospital showed heterogeneity: at the two non-teaching hospitals (n=765, 13% of the sample), alerts were associated with a higher risk of the primary outcome (relative risk 1.49, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.98; P=0.006), and more deaths occurred at these centres (15.6% in the alert group vs 8.6% in usual care; P=0.003). Certain AKI care practices were increased in the alert group but did not appear to mediate the outcomes. The authors concluded that alerts did not reduce the primary outcome and that the heterogeneity should lead to re-evaluation of existing AKI alerting systems.
cards.watchOut: The non-teaching-hospital harm signal is a subgroup finding in 13% of the sample — hypothesis-raising, not proof that alerts kill — and the correction to the topic draft belongs here: this trial was published in BMJ (2021), not the New England Journal of Medicine as drafted. Neither caveat rescues a benefit: the overall result is null with a tight interval.

shelves.title: Ramelteon and melatonin to prevent delirium in hospital (Hatta; Al-Aama)
shelves.question: In older hospitalised or ICU patients at risk of delirium, does nightly ramelteon (or melatonin) reduce incident delirium versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease · Delirium · Female · Hospitals, General · Hospitals, University · Humans · Indenes · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Risk · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: Two small placebo-controlled trials of melatonin-pathway agents point the same way, with effect sizes large enough to demand a discount. Hatta randomised just 67 patients aged 65–89 admitted with serious medical problems to ramelteon 8 mg nightly or placebo for 7 days: delirium occurred in 3% versus 32% (relative risk 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.69; adjusted odds ratio 0.07). Al-Aama randomised 145 patients aged 65 or over on a medical unit to melatonin 0.5 mg nightly or placebo: delirium in 12.0% versus 31.0% (adjusted odds ratio 0.19, 95% CI 0.06–0.62). Put together, that is about 210 patients, two different agents, two countries — and relative reductions of 70–90%, exactly the profile (tiny samples, huge effects) that most often shrinks on replication. Al-Aama also carries an honesty flag on its own record: loss to follow-up made an intention-to-treat analysis impossible. The signal is worth a larger trial and worth this shelf; it is not yet worth more than POSSIBLE. No mortality or length-of-stay claim is made. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Hatta 2014: ramelteon cut delirium from 32% to 3% in 67 elderly acute-care patients (relative risk 0.09)
cards.summary: Hatta 2014: ramelteon cut delirium from 32% to 3% in 67 elderly acute-care patients (relative risk 0.09)
cards.people: 67 patients aged 65 to 89 years, newly admitted because of serious medical problems to intensive care units and regular acute wards of four university hospitals and one general hospital in Japan, who could take oral medication and were expected to stay and live at least 48 hours. Patients were randomly assigned by sealed envelope to ramelteon 8 mg nightly (n=33) or placebo (n=34) for 7 days. The outcome was incidence of delirium as defined by DSM-IV criteria.
cards.result: Ramelteon was associated with a lower risk of delirium (3% vs 32%; P=.003), with a relative risk of 0.09 (95% CI 0.01–0.69). After adjustment for risk factors the association persisted (P=.01; odds ratio 0.07, 95% CI 0.008–0.54). Kaplan-Meier estimates of time to delirium were 6.94 days for ramelteon versus 5.74 days for placebo, with a significantly lower frequency of delirium in the ramelteon group by log-rank test (P=.002). The authors concluded that nightly ramelteon in elderly patients admitted for acute care may protect against delirium.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-three versus thirty-four patients: the headline effect rests on roughly one delirium case against eleven, and a fragility that small can evaporate with a handful of events. Rater-blinded rather than fully double-blind. This card reports the result; the shelf's stamp is where its size is priced in. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

shelves.title: Sustained care intervention for hospitalised smokers (Rigotti 2014; Helping HAND 2)
shelves.question: In smokers hospitalised for any cause who want to quit, does a sustained care intervention — free cessation medication plus automated calls and counsellor contact after discharge — increase biochemically confirmed abstinence versus standard post-discharge advice?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Automation · Counseling · Evidence-Based Practice · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Discharge · Smoking Cessation · Telephone · Time Factors · Tobacco Use Cessation Devices · Tobacco Use Disorder · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: This shelf's second card reverses its first impression, so the correction leads. The topic draft promised an earlier, concordant JAMA 2012 trial by the same group; no such trial exists in the record (the group's 2012 JAMA item is a clinical review, not a trial). The real second trial is the later, larger replication — Helping HAND 2 (2016) — and it failed on its primary outcome. The sequence in full: Rigotti 2014, a single-centre trial of 397 hospitalised smokers who wanted to quit, found sustained care (free cessation medication for up to 90 days plus automated interactive-voice-response calls with counsellor triage) beat standard care on biochemically confirmed 7-day abstinence at 6 months, 26% versus 15% (relative risk 1.71, 95% CI 1.14 to 2.56; NNT 9.4). HAND 2 then ran the same model across three hospitals in 1,357 smokers, with quitline linkage added for scalability: confirmed abstinence at 6 months was 17% versus 16% (p=0.58) — no difference — although self-reported abstinence was higher during the 3 treatment months (overall self-reported relative risk 1.25) and treatment use was greater. A positive single-centre result that its own scale-up could not confirm on the outcome that counts earns POSSIBLE, scoped to the original model and setting. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Rigotti 2014: sustained care raised biochemically confirmed abstinence at 6 months (26% vs 15%; relative risk 1.71; NNT 9.4)
cards.summary: Rigotti 2014: sustained care raised biochemically confirmed abstinence at 6 months (26% vs 15%; relative risk 1.71; NNT 9.4)
cards.people: 397 hospitalised daily smokers (mean age 53; 48% male) at Massachusetts General Hospital who had received a tobacco-dependence intervention in hospital, wanted to quit after discharge, and were randomised to sustained care (n=198) or standard care (n=199). Sustained care comprised automated interactive voice response telephone calls plus the patient's choice of free FDA-approved cessation medication for up to 90 days, with calls promoting cessation, managing medication and triaging to additional counselling; standard care participants received recommendations for post-discharge pharmacotherapy and counselling. The primary outcome was biochemically confirmed past-7-day tobacco abstinence at 6 months.
cards.result: Sustained care participants used more counselling and more pharmacotherapy at every follow-up. Biochemically validated 7-day abstinence at 6 months was higher with sustained care (26%) than standard care (15%) (relative risk 1.71, 95% CI 1.14–2.56; P=.009; number needed to treat 9.4, 95% CI 5.4–35.5); with multiple imputation for missing outcomes the relative risk was 1.55 (1.03–2.21; P=.04). Self-reported continuous abstinence over 6 months was also higher (27% vs 16%; relative risk 1.70, 1.15–2.51; P=.007).
cards.watchOut: Single centre, and 397 of the smokers screened — enrolment captured 92% of eligible patients but only 44% of those screened. The result is genuine on its own terms; the question this shelf must answer is whether it travels, which is what the second card tests.

cards.headline: Helping HAND 2 (2016): the three-hospital replication found no difference in confirmed abstinence (17% vs 16%; p=0.58)
cards.summary: Helping HAND 2 (2016): the three-hospital replication found no difference in confirmed abstinence (17% vs 16%; p=0.58)
cards.people: 1,357 daily smokers admitted to three US hospitals who wanted to quit and received in-hospital cessation counselling, randomised to sustained care (n=680) — automated interactive voice response calls plus choice of cessation medication for 3 months, with calls triaging smokers seeking more help directly to a telephone quitline — or standard care (n=677), consisting of medication and counselling recommendations at discharge. The primary outcome was again biochemically confirmed past-7-day abstinence 6 months after discharge.
cards.result: Sustained care did not increase biochemically confirmed abstinence at 6 months (17% vs 16%; p=0.58). The sustained care group reported more cessation counselling and medication use at each follow-up and higher self-reported past-7-day abstinence at 1 month (43% vs 32%; p<0.0001) and 3 months (37% vs 30%; p=0.008), narrowing by 6 months (31% vs 27%; p=0.09); overall, self-reported 7-day abstinence across the 6-month follow-up was higher (relative risk 1.25, 95% CI 1.10–1.40; p=0.0006). The authors concluded that real-time quitline linkage increased short-term self-reported abstinence but did not sustain long-term intervention effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: This is the correction card for the whole shelf: the topic draft described the second trial as an earlier (JAMA 2012) study with the same direction of effect. The fetched record shows the second trial is this 2016 replication, and on the primary, biochemically confirmed outcome it is null. Whether the quitline substitution or the multi-site setting explains the failure cannot be resolved from these records — but the unconfirmed status of the intervention can be, and is, stated.

shelves.title: Symptom-triggered versus fixed-schedule benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal (Saitz; Daeppen)
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients treated for alcohol withdrawal, does symptom-triggered dosing (CIWA-guided) achieve safe withdrawal with less benzodiazepine and shorter treatment than a fixed tapering schedule?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcohol Withdrawal Delirium · Alcoholism · Chlordiazepoxide · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Ethanol · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Psychoses, Alcoholic · Severity of Illness Index · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two double-blind randomised trials, on two continents, with two different benzodiazepines, found the same thing. Saitz (1994) randomised 101 patients on a VA detoxification unit to fixed-schedule chlordiazepoxide four times daily (plus as-needed doses) or to symptom-triggered dosing guided by a validated withdrawal-severity scale: the symptom-triggered group was treated for a median of 9 hours instead of 68, and received 100 mg of chlordiazepoxide instead of 425 mg (both P<.001), with no significant differences in withdrawal severity during treatment or in seizures or delirium tremens. Daeppen (2002) repeated the experiment in 117 patients at two Swiss university hospitals with oxazepam: only 39% of the symptom-triggered group needed any benzodiazepine at all (versus 100%), the mean dose was 37.5 mg versus 231.4 mg, mean duration 20.0 versus 62.7 hours (all P<.001), comfort did not differ, and complications were limited to a single seizure in the symptom-triggered group. Symptom-triggered dosing individualises treatment, cuts drug exposure roughly four- to six-fold and treatment time roughly three- to seven-fold, with no observed safety penalty — provided the structured scale and monitoring that both trials used are actually in place. Both trials predate routine registration. PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.headline: Saitz 1994: symptom-triggered chlordiazepoxide used a quarter of the drug (100 vs 425 mg) in a seventh of the time (9 vs 68 hours), with no more seizures or delirium
cards.summary: Saitz 1994: symptom-triggered chlordiazepoxide used a quarter of the drug (100 vs 425 mg) in a seventh of the time (9 vs 68 hours), with no more seizures or delirium
cards.people: 101 patients admitted to an inpatient detoxification unit at a Veterans Affairs medical centre for treatment of alcohol withdrawal, who could give informed consent and had no history of seizures or medication use that might alter the course of withdrawal. Patients were randomised to fixed-schedule chlordiazepoxide four times daily with additional medication as needed, or to symptom-triggered therapy in which chlordiazepoxide was given only in response to signs and symptoms of withdrawal, with the need for as-needed medication determined by a validated measure of withdrawal severity (the CIWA scale). Outcomes were duration of medication treatment and total chlordiazepoxide administered.
cards.result: The median duration of treatment in the symptom-triggered group was 9 hours compared with 68 hours in the fixed-schedule group (P<.001). Total chlordiazepoxide administered was 100 mg in the symptom-triggered group and 425 mg in the fixed-schedule group (P<.001). There were no significant differences between groups in the severity of withdrawal during treatment or in the incidence of seizures or delirium tremens. The authors concluded that symptom-triggered therapy individualises treatment, decreases treatment duration and benzodiazepine use, and is as efficacious as standard fixed-schedule therapy.
cards.watchOut: A 1994 trial predating registration — the record carries no registry ID, and none is claimed. The population excluded patients with a seizure history; and the intervention is inseparable from the validated scale and the monitoring cadence used to trigger doses — symptom-triggered dosing without them is not the tested intervention.
cards.source: Saitz R et al. Individualized treatment for alcohol withdrawal. A randomized double-blind controlled trial. JAMA. 1994. PMID: 8046805. Registry ID: none — this trial predates trial registration, and the record shows none. cards.headline: Daeppen 2002: with symptom-triggered oxazepam, 61% of patients needed no benzodiazepine at all; dose fell from 231.4 to 37.5 mg with equal comfort
cards.summary: Daeppen 2002: with symptom-triggered oxazepam, 61% of patients needed no benzodiazepine at all; dose fell from 231.4 to 37.5 mg with equal comfort
cards.people: 117 consecutive patients with alcohol dependence (DSM-IV) entering an alcohol treatment programme at the Lausanne and Geneva university hospitals, Switzerland, randomised to symptom-triggered oxazepam given in response to signs of withdrawal (n=56) or fixed-schedule oxazepam every 6 hours with additional doses as needed (n=61), with administration in both groups determined using a standardised measure of alcohol withdrawal. Main outcomes were total amount and duration of oxazepam treatment, incidence of complications, and comfort level.
cards.result: Only 22 patients (39%) in the symptom-triggered group were treated with oxazepam, versus 100% in the fixed-schedule group (P<.001). The mean oxazepam dose was 37.5 mg in the symptom-triggered group compared with 231.4 mg in the fixed-schedule group (P<.001), and mean treatment duration was 20.0 hours versus 62.7 hours (P<.001). Withdrawal complications were limited to a single episode of seizures in the symptom-triggered group, and there were no differences in comfort measures between the groups. The authors concluded symptom-triggered benzodiazepine treatment is safe, comfortable, and decreases medication quantity and treatment duration.
cards.watchOut: One seizure did occur in the symptom-triggered arm — with 117 patients, neither trial can compare rare complications, so this shelf claims no observed increase in complications, not proven equality for rare events. Like Saitz, the trial predates registration and shows no registry ID in the record.

shelves.title: Oral versus intravenous prednisolone for hospitalised COPD exacerbation (de Jong)
shelves.question: In patients hospitalised with an acute COPD exacerbation, is oral prednisolone non-inferior to intravenous prednisolone for treatment failure over 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Admission/statistics & numerical data · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Prednisolone/administration & dosage · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/drug therapy,mortality · Quality of Life · Respiratory Function Tests · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One double-blind, double-dummy randomised trial (210 patients hospitalised with COPD exacerbation) found oral prednisolone 60 mg daily for 5 days not inferior to the same dose intravenously: 90-day treatment failure was 56.3% on oral versus 61.7% on IV therapy, with the one-sided lower confidence bound (−5.8%) inside the non-inferiority margin, and no differences in early failure, length of stay, spirometry recovery, or quality of life. Treatment failure was common in both arms — this trial answers the route question, not whether steroids help (that is settled elsewhere). Single trial, modest size, so the stamp is POSSIBLE: the oral route is a reasonable default for patients who can swallow and absorb, sparing a cannula, but one 210-patient trial cannot exclude a small penalty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (single trial, THIN).

cards.headline: de Jong 2007: oral prednisolone was not inferior to IV — 90-day treatment failure 56.3% vs 61.7%
cards.summary: de Jong 2007: oral prednisolone was not inferior to IV — 90-day treatment failure 56.3% vs 61.7%
cards.people: 210 patients hospitalised for a COPD exacerbation (of 435 referred), randomised to 5 days of prednisolone 60 mg orally (n=103) or intravenously (n=107) in a double-blind, double-dummy design. The primary outcome was treatment failure — death, admission to the ICU, readmission to the ICU because of COPD, or intensification of pharmacologic therapy — over 90 days.
cards.result: Overall treatment failure within 90 days was 56.3% with oral prednisolone versus 61.7% with IV prednisolone (one-sided lower bound of the 95% CI for the difference, −5.8%), meeting the study's non-inferiority criterion. Early failure (within 2 weeks) was 18.4% versus 17.8% (lower bound −9.4%), late failure 47.0% versus 54.0% (lower bound −5.6%), and mean length of stay 11.2 versus 11.9 days. Spirometry and health-related quality of life improved clinically over one week in both groups without significant differences.
cards.watchOut: A single, modest-sized trial, and non-inferiority rests on the prespecified margin — the confidence bound excludes a large penalty but not a small one (up to about 6 percentage points more failures on oral therapy within the bound reported). Failure rates above 55% in both arms reflect how broadly failure was defined (any intensification of therapy counted). Patients unable to take or absorb oral medication were not the population studied, so IV remains the route when the gut is unavailable.
cards.source: de Jong YP et al. Oral or IV prednisolone in the treatment of COPD exacerbations: a randomized, controlled, double-blind study. Chest. 2007. PMID: 17646228. Registry ID: NCT00311961, from the record. shelves.title: Interdisciplinary palliative care in advanced heart failure (PAL-HF)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced heart failure, does an interdisciplinary palliative care intervention improve quality of life versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Failure · Humans · Male · Palliative Care · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One single-centre randomised trial (PAL-HF, 150 patients with advanced heart failure). Adding an interdisciplinary palliative care intervention to usual care improved both primary quality-of-life measures at 6 months by clinically significant margins: Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire by 9.49 points (95% CI 0.94–18.05, P=0.030) and FACIT-Pal by 11.77 points (CI 0.84–22.71, P=0.035). Depression, anxiety, and spiritual well-being also improved. Rehospitalisation and mortality were not affected. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single small single-centre trial with subjective endpoints and intervals that only just exclude no effect; the direction is consistent across every patient-reported measure, which keeps it above MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: PAL-HF: palliative care added to usual care improved quality of life at 6 months (KCCQ +9.49 points; FACIT-Pal +11.77 points)
cards.summary: PAL-HF: palliative care added to usual care improved quality of life at 6 months (KCCQ +9.49 points; FACIT-Pal +11.77 points)
cards.people: 150 patients with advanced heart failure at a single centre, randomised between August 2012 and June 2015 to usual care (n=75) or usual care plus an interdisciplinary palliative care intervention (n=75). Primary endpoints were two quality-of-life measures — the Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire (KCCQ) overall summary and the FACIT-Pal scale — at 6 months. Secondary endpoints included depression and anxiety (HADS), spiritual well-being (FACIT-Sp), hospitalisations, and mortality.
cards.result: From randomisation to 6 months, the palliative care group improved more on KCCQ (difference 9.49 points, 95% CI 0.94 to 18.05, P=0.030) and FACIT-Pal (difference 11.77 points, 95% CI 0.84 to 22.71, P=0.035) — both described by the authors as clinically significant. Depression improved (HADS-depression difference −1.94 points, P=0.020), as did anxiety (−1.83 points, P=0.048) and spiritual well-being (FACIT-Sp difference 3.98 points, P=0.027). Randomisation to palliative care did not affect rehospitalisation or mortality.
cards.watchOut: Single centre and unblinded, with self-reported endpoints — expectation effects cannot be excluded, and both primary confidence intervals only narrowly exclude zero. The trial was not powered for hospitalisation or mortality, and its null findings there should be read as absence of evidence, not proof of no effect.
cards.source: Rogers JG et al. Palliative Care in Heart Failure: The PAL-HF Randomized, Controlled Clinical Trial. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2017. PMID: 28705314. Registry ID: NCT01589601, from the record. shelves.title: Palliative oxygen versus room air for refractory breathlessness (Abernethy)
shelves.question: In patients with life-limiting illness and refractory dyspnoea who are not hypoxaemic, does oxygen relieve breathlessness more than room air delivered the same way?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Air · Anxiety · Australia · Double-Blind Method · Dyspnea · Epistaxis · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen · Palliative Care · Quality of Life · Sleep · Sleep Stages · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · United States
shelves.balance: One large double-blind randomised trial (Abernethy 2010, 239 patients with life-limiting illness, refractory dyspnoea, and PaO2 above 7.3 kPa — i.e., not qualifying for long-term oxygen therapy). Oxygen and room air were delivered identically by concentrator and nasal cannula at 2 L/min for 7 days. Both groups' breathlessness improved; oxygen was not better: morning breathlessness changed by −0.9 points on oxygen versus −0.7 on room air (P=0.504), and evening scores likewise did not differ (P=0.554). Side-effect frequency was similar. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the definitive double-blind trial for this exact question; smaller blinded trials in palliative and COPD populations exist but none approaches this rigour, and none is carded here.

cards.headline: Abernethy 2010: oxygen was no better than room air for refractory breathlessness (morning change −0.9 vs −0.7 points, P=0.504)
cards.summary: Abernethy 2010: oxygen was no better than room air for refractory breathlessness (morning change −0.9 vs −0.7 points, P=0.504)
cards.people: 239 adults at nine outpatient sites in Australia, the USA, and the UK with life-limiting illness, refractory dyspnoea, and arterial oxygen pressure (PaO2) above 7.3 kPa — patients ineligible for long-term oxygen therapy. Participants were randomised 1:1 to oxygen (n=120) or room air (n=119), each delivered by concentrator through a nasal cannula at 2 L/min for 7 days, at least 15 hours per day. The primary outcome was breathlessness on a 0–10 numerical rating scale, morning and evening. 112 (93%) of the oxygen group and 99 (83%) of the room-air group completed all 7 days of assessments.
cards.result: From baseline to day 6, mean morning breathlessness changed by −0.9 points (95% CI −1.3 to −0.5) on oxygen and −0.7 points (−1.2 to −0.2) on room air (P=0.504). Mean evening breathlessness changed by −0.3 points (−0.7 to 0.1) on oxygen and −0.5 (−0.9 to −0.1) on room air (P=0.554). Side-effect frequency did not differ between groups; extreme drowsiness was reported by 12 (10%) on oxygen versus 14 (13%) on room air.
cards.watchOut: Both arms improved — moving air itself, the ritual of treatment, or natural fluctuation may relieve breathlessness, so the finding is 'oxygen adds nothing over air', not 'nothing helps'. The trial excludes hypoxaemic patients: oxygen remains standard where blood oxygen is genuinely low, and long-term oxygen in severe resting hypoxaemia is a different shelf.

shelves.title: Parenteral hydration in advanced cancer at the end of life (Bruera)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced cancer receiving hospice care, does parenteral hydration (1 L/day) improve dehydration symptoms, quality of life, or survival versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Dehydration · Double-Blind Method · Fatigue · Female · Fluid Therapy · Follow-Up Studies · Hospice Care · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local · Neoplasms · Parenteral Nutrition · Prognosis · Quality of Life · Survival Rate · Symptom Assessment
shelves.balance: One multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (Bruera 2013, 129 patients with advanced cancer in six hospices): 1 L/day of normal saline versus 100 mL/day placebo, each over 4 hours daily. The primary outcome — change in the sum of four dehydration symptoms (fatigue, myoclonus, sedation, hallucinations) by day 4 — did not differ (−3.3 vs −2.8, P=.77), nor did symptom scales, delirium measures, or quality-of-life measures at day 4 or day 7. Overall survival did not differ either (median 21 vs 15 days, P=.83) — a null on survival in a small trial, not evidence of harm or benefit. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for symptoms and quality of life at this dose and duration; not Tier C, because no benefit on survival is claimed — the survival result is reported as the null it is.

cards.headline: Bruera 2013: 1 L/day hydration did not improve dehydration symptoms, quality of life, or survival versus placebo (primary outcome P=.77)
cards.summary: Bruera 2013: 1 L/day hydration did not improve dehydration symptoms, quality of life, or survival versus placebo (primary outcome P=.77)
cards.people: 129 patients with advanced cancer at six hospices, randomised to parenteral hydration (normal saline 1 L/day, n=63) or placebo (normal saline 100 mL/day, n=66), each infused over 4 hours daily. The primary outcome was change from baseline to day 4 in the sum of four dehydration symptoms — fatigue, myoclonus, sedation, and hallucinations (0 best, 40 worst). Secondary outcomes included the Edmonton Symptom Assessment Scale, delirium scales (MDAS, NuDESC), myoclonus rating, FACIT-Fatigue, creatinine and urea, and overall survival, with intention-to-treat analyses at day 4 and day 7.
cards.result: The change in the four-symptom sum by day 4 was −3.3 with hydration versus −2.8 with placebo (P=.77). All ESAS comparisons were nonsignificant, as were MDAS (1 vs 3.5, P=.084), NuDESC (0 vs 0, P=.13), and UMRS (0 vs 0, P=.54). Day 7 results, including FACIT-F, were similar. Overall survival did not differ between groups (median 21 vs 15 days, P=.83).
cards.watchOut: The trial tested one regimen — 1 L/day over 4 hours — in hospice patients close to death; it does not address hydration for specific indications such as opioid toxicity with a reversible cause, hypercalcaemia, or patients earlier in their disease. With 129 patients it cannot exclude small symptom effects, and the survival medians (21 vs 15 days) have wide uncertainty around a null P value.
