shelves.title: Dignity therapy at the end of life (Chochinov)
shelves.question: In terminally ill patients, does dignity therapy improve sense of dignity, quality of life, and end-of-life experience versus standard palliative care or client-centred care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Australia · Canada · Counseling · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms · Palliative Care · Psychotherapy, Brief · Quality of Life · Stress, Psychological · Surveys and Questionnaires · Terminally Ill · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: One randomised trial (Chochinov 2011, 441 patients with a life expectancy of 6 months or less in Canada, the USA, and Australia) comparing dignity therapy with client-centred care and standard palliative care. Read primary-first: the trial's primary outcomes — dimensions of distress measured on validated scales before and after the intervention — showed NO significant differences between the three groups. The positive findings are all in the secondary, self-reported end-of-life experience survey: patients who received dignity therapy were significantly more likely to say it had been helpful, improved their quality of life, increased their sense of dignity, and helped their family (all P≤.002). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — the experience outcomes are consistent and strongly significant, but they are unblinded self-reports in a trial whose prespecified distress outcomes were null; the topic draft's summary ('improved quality of life') repeats the secondary claim without the null primary, and the card corrects that order.

cards.headline: Chochinov 2011: dignity therapy did not reduce measured distress (primary outcomes null) but patients rated their end-of-life experience far better
cards.summary: Chochinov 2011: dignity therapy did not reduce measured distress (primary outcomes null) but patients rated their end-of-life experience far better
cards.people: 441 patients aged 18 or over with a terminal prognosis (life expectancy ≤6 months) receiving palliative care in hospital or the community (hospice or home) in Canada, the USA, and Australia, randomised 1:1:1 to dignity therapy (n=165), client-centred care (n=136), or standard palliative care (n=140); 108, 107, and 111 patients respectively were analysed. Primary outcomes were changes in dimensions of distress (spiritual well-being, Patient Dignity Inventory, anxiety and depression, symptom and quality-of-life scales). Secondary outcomes were self-reported end-of-life experiences in a post-study survey.
cards.result: No significant differences were found in distress levels before and after the intervention across the three groups. On the secondary survey, dignity therapy patients were significantly more likely than the other groups to report the intervention had been helpful (χ²=35.50, P<.0001), improved quality of life (χ²=14.52, P=.001), increased sense of dignity (χ²=12.66, P=.002), changed how their family saw and appreciated them (χ²=33.81, P<.0001), and been helpful to their family (χ²=33.86, P<.0001). Dignity therapy was also better than client-centred care for spiritual well-being (P=.006) and better than standard care for sadness or depression (P=.009) on individual scale comparisons.
cards.watchOut: The trial's prespecified primary outcomes were null; the strongly positive results come from a post-treatment self-report survey in an unblinded trial, where gratitude and expectation effects are plausible. The honest summary is the authors' own: dignity therapy's ability to mitigate outright distress 'has yet to be proven', while its benefits for self-reported end-of-life experience support its use.
cards.source: Chochinov HM et al. Effect of dignity therapy on distress and end-of-life experience in terminally ill patients: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet Oncol. 2011. PMID: 21741309. shelves.title: CALM therapy for depression in advanced cancer (Rodin)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced cancer, does CALM (Managing Cancer and Living Meaningfully), a brief individual psychotherapy, reduce depressive symptoms versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Attitude to Death · Depression · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms · Psychotherapy, Brief · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One randomised trial (Rodin 2018, 305 patients with advanced cancer at a single comprehensive cancer centre). CALM — a brief, manualised individual psychotherapy — reduced depressive symptoms (the primary outcome) versus usual care at 3 months (difference 1.09 points, P=.04, Cohen's d 0.23) and at 6 months (difference 1.29 points, P=.02, d 0.29), with greater end-of-life preparation at 6 months and no adverse effects identified. The effects are statistically significant but small — effect sizes of roughly a quarter of a standard deviation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single unblinded trial with a small effect on a self-reported outcome; consistent and prespecified, which keeps it above MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: CALM: depressive symptoms fell modestly versus usual care at 3 months (d=0.23) and 6 months (d=0.29)
cards.summary: CALM: depressive symptoms fell modestly versus usual care at 3 months (d=0.23) and 6 months (d=0.29)
cards.people: 305 patients with advanced cancer recruited from outpatient oncology clinics at a comprehensive cancer centre between February 2012 and March 2016, randomised to CALM plus usual care (n=151) or usual care alone (n=154), stratified by baseline PHQ-9 depression score. The trial was unblinded. Depressive symptoms were the primary outcome, assessed at baseline, 3 months (primary endpoint), and 6 months (trial endpoint), with death-related distress and other secondary outcomes; analyses were by intention to treat.
cards.result: CALM participants reported less severe depressive symptoms than usual care at 3 months (difference 1.09; P=.04; Cohen's d=0.23; 95% CI 0.04 to 2.13) and at 6 months (difference 1.29; P=.02; d=0.29; 95% CI 0.24 to 2.35). Greater end-of-life preparation at 6 months also favoured CALM. No adverse effects were identified.
cards.watchOut: The absolute differences are small (about 1.1–1.3 points) and the confidence interval at 3 months nearly touches zero (0.04). Usual care is a softer comparator than an attention-matched therapy, and participants knew their allocation — relevant for a self-reported depression outcome.
cards.source: Rodin G et al. Managing Cancer and Living Meaningfully (CALM): A Randomized Controlled Trial of a Psychological Intervention for Patients With Advanced Cancer. J Clin Oncol. 2018. shelves.title: Meaning-centred psychotherapy in advanced cancer (Breitbart)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced cancer, does meaning-centred psychotherapy (group or individual format) improve spiritual well-being and reduce depression versus supportive group therapy or therapeutic massage?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anxiety · Depression · Female · Hope · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms · Outpatients · Psychotherapy, Group · Quality of Life · Spirituality · Stress, Psychological · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials of meaning-centred psychotherapy from the same programme, in two formats. The group trial (Breitbart 2015, 253 patients) found meaning-centred group psychotherapy superior to supportive group psychotherapy on spiritual well-being and quality of life, with greater reductions in depression, hopelessness, desire for hastened death, and physical symptom distress; intention-to-treat analyses retained significant effects for quality of life, depression, and hopelessness. The individual-format trial (Breitbart 2018, 321 patients, published in Cancer — the topic draft's 'J Clin Oncol 2018' attribution is wrong) found small-to-medium effects versus enhanced usual care on five of seven outcomes, with a smaller margin over supportive psychotherapy (significant for quality of life and sense of meaning only). PROPOSED LIKELY — two concordant randomised trials against active comparators; the effects are modest and shrink against the strongest comparator, which the cards state.

cards.headline: Breitbart 2015: meaning-centred group psychotherapy beat supportive group therapy on spiritual well-being, quality of life, and depression
cards.summary: Breitbart 2015: meaning-centred group psychotherapy beat supportive group therapy on spiritual well-being, quality of life, and depression
cards.people: 253 patients with advanced cancer randomised to eight sessions of manualised meaning-centred group psychotherapy (MCGP) or supportive group psychotherapy (SGP). Primary outcomes were spiritual well-being and overall quality of life; secondary outcomes included depression, hopelessness, desire for hastened death, anxiety, and physical symptom distress. Assessments were made before and after treatment and 2 months later. The headline analyses used hierarchical linear models including participants who attended at least three sessions; intention-to-treat analyses were also reported.
cards.result: Patients receiving MCGP showed significantly greater improvement in spiritual well-being and quality of life and significantly greater reductions in depression, hopelessness, desire for hastened death, and physical symptom distress than SGP; no group difference was seen for anxiety. In intention-to-treat analyses including all randomised patients, significant treatment effects favouring MCGP remained for quality of life, depression, and hopelessness, but not for the other variables.
cards.watchOut: The strongest results come from the analysis restricted to patients attending ≥3 sessions; the intention-to-treat effects are a subset. Both arms were group therapies, so the comparison isolates the meaning-centred content rather than the effect of group support itself.
cards.source: Breitbart W et al. Meaning-centered group psychotherapy: an effective intervention for improving psychological well-being in patients with advanced cancer. J Clin Oncol. 2015. shelves.title: Prophylactic scopolamine butylbromide for death rattle (SILENCE)
shelves.question: In dying patients recognised as entering the dying phase, does prophylactic subcutaneous scopolamine butylbromide prevent death rattle versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Butylscopolammonium Bromide · Cholinergic Antagonists · Confidence Intervals · Death · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Hospice Care · Humans · Incidence · Informed Consent · Injections, Subcutaneous · Life Expectancy · Male · Middle Aged · Netherlands · Placebos · Proportional Hazards Models · Respiratory Sounds · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (SILENCE, van Esch 2021, six Dutch hospices). Among 157 patients analysed, a grade ≥2 death rattle occurred in 13% on prophylactic subcutaneous scopolamine butylbromide (20 mg four times daily, started when the dying phase was recognised) versus 27% on placebo — an absolute difference of 14 percentage points (95% CI 2%–27%, P=.02), i.e. about a halving in relative terms; time to death rattle also favoured scopolamine (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.44, CI 0.20–0.92). Anticholinergic adverse events (restlessness, dry mouth, urinary retention) were not clearly worse. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single well-designed trial of modest size for a prophylactic intervention given to all dying patients to prevent a sign that troubles witnesses more than patients; replication is lacking.

cards.headline: SILENCE: prophylactic scopolamine cut death rattle from 27% to 13% (absolute difference 14 points, P=.02)
cards.summary: SILENCE: prophylactic scopolamine cut death rattle from 27% to 13% (absolute difference 14 points, P=.02)
cards.people: Patients with a life expectancy of 3 or more days admitted to six hospices in the Netherlands gave advance informed consent (229 patients); when the dying phase was recognised, 162 eligible patients were randomised to subcutaneous scopolamine butylbromide 20 mg four times a day (n=79) or placebo (n=78). The primary outcome was occurrence of a grade 2 or higher death rattle (Back scale 0–3) at two consecutive time points 4 hours apart; 157 patients (97%) were included in the primary analyses. Secondary outcomes included time to death rattle and anticholinergic adverse events.
cards.result: Death rattle occurred in 10 patients (13%) in the scopolamine group versus 21 (27%) in the placebo group (difference 14%; 95% CI 2%–27%; P=.02) — the 13% vs 27% rates are absolute risks, a relative reduction of about half. Time to death rattle favoured scopolamine (subdistribution hazard ratio 0.44; 95% CI 0.20–0.92; P=.03; cumulative incidence at 48 hours 8% vs 17%). Restlessness occurred in 28% vs 23%, dry mouth in 10% vs 15%, and urinary retention in 23% vs 17% (smaller denominators), none clearly different.
cards.watchOut: Prophylaxis means treating every dying patient to prevent an outcome that would occur in about one in four; roughly seven patients are treated for one death rattle avoided (from the 14-point absolute difference). Death rattle is not known to distress the dying patient — the beneficiaries are family and staff — and the trial's advance-consent design means randomised patients were a selected subset of hospice admissions.

shelves.title: Regular low-dose extended-release morphine for chronic breathlessness in COPD (BEAMS)
shelves.question: In people with COPD and severe chronic breathlessness despite optimal treatment, does regular low-dose extended-release morphine improve worst breathlessness versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Delayed-Action Preparations · Double-Blind Method · Dyspnea · Morphine · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive · Respiratory System Agents · Chronic Disease · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The largest trial answers the question directly and negatively. BEAMS (Ekström 2022, 160 people with COPD and severe chronic breathlessness, double-blind) found no significant difference in worst breathlessness at 1 week for 8 mg/day (−0.3 points, 95% CI −0.9 to 0.4) or 16 mg/day (−0.3, CI −1.0 to 0.4) extended-release morphine versus placebo, and no difference in daily step count at week 3 at any dose. The smaller MORDYC trial (2020) complicates the picture only at the edges: its primary outcome was health status, which improved modestly (CAT score −2.18 points, P=.03), while breathlessness in the previous 24 hours was unchanged overall and worst breathlessness improved only in the prespecified severe (mMRC 3–4) subgroup. Read together: for worst breathlessness — the outcome this shelf asks about — the treatment made no difference at the doses tested (PROPOSED LIKELY, the treatment made no difference); a small health-status signal in MORDYC is a different question and is carded as such.

cards.headline: BEAMS: 8 or 16 mg/day extended-release morphine did not improve worst breathlessness at 1 week (both differences −0.3 points, CIs crossing zero)
cards.summary: BEAMS: 8 or 16 mg/day extended-release morphine did not improve worst breathlessness at 1 week (both differences −0.3 points, CIs crossing zero)
cards.type: Multicenter double-blind placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial
cards.people: 160 people with COPD and chronic breathlessness (modified Medical Research Council score 3–4) at 20 Australian centres, randomised 1:1:1 to 8 mg/day or 16 mg/day oral extended-release morphine or placebo during week 1, with further dose randomisation in weeks 2–3; 156 were included in the primary analyses. The primary outcome was change in intensity of worst breathlessness (0–10 numerical rating scale) from baseline to week 1. A secondary outcome was change in daily step count by actigraphy at week 3.
cards.result: Change in worst breathlessness at week 1 did not differ significantly between 8 mg/day morphine and placebo (mean difference −0.3; 95% CI −0.9 to 0.4) or between 16 mg/day and placebo (−0.3; 95% CI −1.0 to 0.4). At week 3, change in mean daily step count also did not differ at any dose (differences −1453 to −692 steps, all confidence intervals crossing zero). The authors conclude these findings do not support the use of these doses of extended-release morphine to relieve breathlessness.
cards.watchOut: BEAMS tested 8–32 mg/day over 1–3 weeks in mMRC 3–4 patients; it does not exclude benefit at other doses, over longer treatment, or for breathlessness outcomes other than 'worst' intensity. Earlier smaller dose-increment studies from the Currow programme reported responder benefits, but without placebo control at this size — BEAMS is the trial built to test them, and it was null on its primary outcome.
cards.source: Ekström M et al. Effect of Regular, Low-Dose, Extended-release Morphine on Chronic Breathlessness in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease: The BEAMS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2022. PMID: 36413230. Registry ID: NCT02720822, from the record. cards.headline: MORDYC: morphine improved COPD health status (CAT −2.18 points, P=.03) but not breathlessness overall — benefit only in the severe subgroup
cards.summary: MORDYC: morphine improved COPD health status (CAT −2.18 points, P=.03) but not breathlessness overall — benefit only in the severe subgroup
cards.people: Patients with COPD and moderate to very severe chronic breathlessness (mMRC grades 2–4) after pulmonary rehabilitation, randomised to regular oral sustained-release morphine 10 mg twice daily (titrable to three times daily) or placebo for 4 weeks; 111 of 124 included participants were analysed. Primary outcomes were COPD Assessment Test (CAT) health-status score and arterial PaCO2; breathlessness in the previous 24 hours was secondary.
cards.result: CAT score was 2.18 points lower (better) on morphine (95% CI −4.14 to −0.22; P=.03). PaCO2 did not differ (1.19 mm Hg higher; CI −2.70 to 5.07; P=.55). Five of 54 morphine patients (9%) versus 1 of 57 (2%) on placebo withdrew because of adverse effects; there were no morphine-related hospital admissions or deaths.
cards.watchOut: MORDYC's positive primary outcome is health status, not breathlessness; its breathlessness signal is confined to a subgroup and conflicts with BEAMS, which enrolled exactly that severe population and found nothing. The two trials also differ in duration (4 weeks vs 1 week for the primary endpoint).

shelves.title: The handheld fan for chronic breathlessness (Galbraith)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic breathlessness at rest, does directing a handheld fan at the face relieve breathlessness versus the fan directed at the legs?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cross-Over Studies · Dyspnea · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Palliative Care · Patient Selection · Self Care · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One small randomised crossover trial (Galbraith 2010, 50 patients with advanced disease and chronic breathlessness). Each participant used a handheld fan for five minutes directed at the face and five minutes at the legs, in randomised order. Breathlessness on a 10 cm visual analogue scale improved significantly more with the fan to the face (P=0.003); the trial's responder definition was a fall of more than 1 cm. The abstract does not report the size of the mean difference, so the card does not invent one. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single tiny unblinded crossover trial, but the intervention is free, harmless, and mechanistically plausible (facial cooling), and later fan studies are feasibility work pointing the same way rather than contradicting it.

cards.headline: Galbraith 2010: a fan to the face reduced breathlessness significantly more than a fan to the legs (P=0.003)
cards.summary: Galbraith 2010: a fan to the face reduced breathlessness significantly more than a fan to the legs (P=0.003)
cards.people: 50 participants with advanced disease and chronic breathlessness, each randomised to use a handheld fan for five minutes directed to the face (across the nose and mouth) or to the leg first, then crossing over to the other. The primary outcome was a decrease of more than 1 cm in breathlessness on a 10 cm visual analogue scale.
cards.result: There was a significant difference in visual analogue scale scores between the two treatments, with a reduction in breathlessness when the fan was directed to the face (P=0.003). The record reports the P value and the responder threshold but not the mean size of the difference, so no magnitude is claimed here. Participants found the fan acceptable; the authors note it is inexpensive, portable, and enhances self-efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Five minutes of fan use in a supervised session is not the same as sustained benefit at home over days; blinding is impossible for this comparison, and expectation effects are plausible. The evidence supports offering a fan as part of breathlessness management, not any claim about how large or durable the effect is.
cards.source: Galbraith S et al. Does the use of a handheld fan improve chronic dyspnea? A randomized, controlled, crossover trial. J Pain Symptom Manage. 2010. PMID: 20471544. Registry ID: ISRCTN44193804, from the record. shelves.title: Dexamethasone for cancer-related fatigue (Yennurajalingam)
shelves.question: In patients with advanced cancer, does dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily for 14 days improve cancer-related fatigue versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Dexamethasone · Double-Blind Method · Fatigue · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: One small double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (Yennurajalingam 2013, 84 evaluable patients with advanced cancer and multiple fatigue-related symptoms). Dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily for 14 days improved the FACIT-F fatigue subscale at day 15 significantly more than placebo (mean improvement 9 [SD 10.3] vs 3.1 [SD 9.59], P=.008), with better FACIT-F total quality-of-life scores (P=.03) and physical distress scores (P=.013), but no difference in overall symptom distress (P=.22) or psychological distress (P=.76), and no significant difference in adverse-effect frequency. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a single small trial with a short 14-day horizon; the fatigue-specific benefit is real on its own measure, but durability, and the balance against steroid harms beyond two weeks, are untested. The trial record carries no registry ID.

cards.headline: Yennurajalingam 2013: dexamethasone improved fatigue at day 15 (+9 vs +3.1 FACIT-F points, P=.008)
cards.summary: Yennurajalingam 2013: dexamethasone improved fatigue at day 15 (+9 vs +3.1 FACIT-F points, P=.008)
cards.people: Patients with advanced cancer who had at least three fatigue-related symptoms (fatigue, pain, nausea, appetite loss, depression, anxiety, or sleep disturbance) scored ≥4 of 10 on the Edmonton Symptom Assessment Scale, randomised to dexamethasone 4 mg or placebo orally twice daily for 14 days. 84 patients were evaluable (43 dexamethasone, 41 placebo). The primary endpoint was change in the FACIT-F fatigue subscale from baseline to day 15; secondary outcomes included anorexia, anxiety, depression, and symptom distress scores.
cards.result: Mean improvement in the FACIT-F subscale at day 15 was 9 (±10.3) on dexamethasone versus 3.1 (±9.59) on placebo (P=.008). FACIT-F total quality-of-life scores also improved more on dexamethasone (P=.03), as did ESAS physical distress scores (P=.013). There were no differences in ESAS overall symptom distress (P=.22) or psychological distress (P=.76). Adverse-effect frequency did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Only 84 of the randomised patients were evaluable, treatment lasted 14 days, and the record carries no registration ID. Nothing here addresses longer steroid courses, where hyperglycaemia, insomnia, myopathy, and mood effects accumulate — the trial's own horizon is the limit of the claim. Patients had a symptom cluster, not fatigue alone.
cards.source: Yennurajalingam S et al. Reduction of cancer-related fatigue with dexamethasone: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial in patients with advanced cancer. shelves.title: Multicomponent communication and pain intervention in nursing homes with dementia (COSMOS)
shelves.question: In nursing-home residents with dementia, does a multicomponent intervention (staff education in communication, pain assessment and treatment, medication review, and activities) reduce neuropsychiatric symptoms and psychotropic use versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Dementia · Humans · Nursing Homes · Pain · Psychotic Disorders · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: The anchored report of the COSMOS cluster-randomised trial (Habiger 2021; 67 units in 33 Norwegian nursing homes, 723 residents) does not show what the topic draft claims. Read from the record: pain was associated with psychosis symptoms over time (odds ratio 2.03 for psychosis symptoms as a group, P=.009; delusion OR 2.12, P=.007), but NO significant intervention effect on psychosis symptoms was observed, analgesic prescription was not affected, and the one positive intervention finding was less musculoskeletal pain in residents with dementia (β −0.47, P=.047). Psychotropic use as such is not reported as improved in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the neuropsychiatric-symptom and medication questions as asked, with the pain signal carded honestly. This card follows the anchored 2021 report; other COSMOS reports (e.g. on quality of life) are not adjudicated here. The trial record carries no registry ID.

cards.headline: COSMOS (Habiger 2021): no intervention effect on psychosis symptoms and no change in analgesic prescribing; musculoskeletal pain improved in dementia
cards.summary: COSMOS (Habiger 2021): no intervention effect on psychosis symptoms and no change in analgesic prescribing; musculoskeletal pain improved in dementia
cards.people: 723 patients aged 65 or over in 67 units of 33 Norwegian nursing homes, randomised by unit to the COSMOS multicomponent intervention (staff training in communication, pain treatment, medication review, organisation of activities, and safety, over 4 months, with follow-up at month 9) or care as usual. Pain was measured with the MOBID pain scale and psychosis symptoms with the Neuropsychiatric Inventory–Nursing Home version, at baseline and months 4 and 9.
cards.result: Psychosis symptoms as a group were associated with pain over time (odds ratio 2.03, P=.009), as was delusion specifically (OR 2.12, P=.007). However, no significant intervention effect on psychosis symptoms was observed. Compared with control, residents with dementia in the intervention group had less musculoskeletal pain (β −0.47, P=.047). Analgesic prescription was not affected by the intervention.
cards.watchOut: Summaries sometimes describe COSMOS as reducing neuropsychiatric symptoms and psychotropic use; this anchored report — the trial's pain-and-psychosis report — shows neither. Its durable finding is observational within the trial: untreated pain and psychosis symptoms travel together, so pain assessment belongs in any decision about psychosis in a nursing-home resident.
cards.source: Habiger TF et al. Managing Pain and Psychosis Symptoms in Nursing Home Patients: Results from a Cluster-Randomized Controlled Trial (COSMOS). J Am Med Dir Assoc. 2021. PMID: 34087225. No registry ID in the record. MeSH: Dementia · Humans · Nursing Homes · Pain · Psychotic Disorders · Quality of Life

shelves.title: Guided Care teams for multimorbid older adults (Boult)
shelves.question: In multimorbid older adults at high risk of hospitalisation, does a nurse-led Guided Care team embedded in primary care reduce use of health services and improve quality of care versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Baltimore · Chronic Disease · Cluster Analysis · Delivery of Health Care · District of Columbia · Female · Health Services · Humans · Male · Patient Care · Patient Care Team · Patient Satisfaction · Primary Health Care · Skilled Nursing Facilities · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One cluster-randomised trial (Boult 2011, 850 older patients at high predicted risk of heavy health-care use, three systems in the Baltimore–Washington area, 20 months). Guided Care — a nurse embedded with primary care physicians providing assessment, care planning, monitoring, transitional care, coordination, self-management and caregiver support, and community-service access — produced exactly one statistically significant overall effect: fewer episodes of home health care (odds ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.53–0.93). Hospital admissions and other service use were not significantly reduced overall; in a preplanned subgroup analysis, Kaiser Permanente patients also had fewer skilled-nursing-facility admissions (OR 0.53, CI 0.31–0.89) and days (OR 0.48, CI 0.28–0.84). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — for the narrow home-health effect; the broader hope of cutting hospital use was not realised in the whole sample. Quality-of-care ratings were addressed in a companion report and are not carded here.

cards.headline: Guided Care: home health episodes fell (OR 0.70) but hospital and other service use did not change significantly overall
cards.summary: Guided Care: home health episodes fell (OR 0.70) but hospital and other service use did not change significantly overall
cards.people: 850 older patients at high risk of using health care heavily, from three health care systems in the Baltimore, Maryland–Washington, DC area, cluster-randomised to Guided Care or usual care for 20 months (November 2006 to June 2008). A Guided Care nurse working with patients' own primary care physicians provided eight services: comprehensive assessment, evidence-based care planning, monthly monitoring of symptoms and adherence, transitional care, coordination of professionals, self-management support, family-caregiver support, and enhanced access to community services. Outcomes were frequency of use of emergency departments, hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies, and primary and specialty physician services.
cards.result: The only statistically significant overall effect was a reduction in episodes of home health care (odds ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.53–0.93). In a preplanned analysis, Guided Care also reduced skilled nursing facility admissions (OR 0.53; 95% CI 0.31–0.89) and days (0.48; 0.28–0.84) among Kaiser Permanente patients. The authors' summary: Guided Care reduces use of home health care but has little effect on use of other health services in the short run.
cards.watchOut: The skilled-nursing finding is a within-system subgroup result, however preplanned — it may reflect Kaiser's integrated structure rather than the intervention itself. Twenty months may be short for a coordination intervention, and this card covers service use only; the programme's quality-of-care findings were published separately and are not adjudicated here.

shelves.title: Community health worker support in primary care: the IMPaCT model (Kangovi)
shelves.question: In low-income patients with chronic conditions, does a standardised community-health-worker intervention improve chronic disease control, mental health, and hospital use versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Chronic Disease · Community Health Workers · Delivery of Health Care · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Poverty · Primary Health Care · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: Split by outcome, because the trials split. In the multicentre primary-care trial (Kangovi 2018, 592 low-income patients with ≥2 chronic diseases), the PRIMARY outcome — change in self-rated physical health — did not differ (P=.89), and the record does not support the topic draft's claim of improved chronic disease control and mental health as headline findings. What did improve was patient-perceived quality of primary care (odds ratio 1.8, CI 1.4–2.4) and hospital use: total hospital days were 155 versus 345 at 6 months and 300 versus 471 at 9 months, with lower odds of repeat hospitalisation (OR 0.4, CI 0.2–0.9) and 30-day readmission (OR 0.3, CI 0.1–0.9). A pooled analysis of all three IMPaCT randomised trials (1,340 patients, including the programme's post-discharge trial) confirms the utilisation result: hospital days per patient were 66% of control (incidence rate ratio 0.66, P<.0001; 849 vs 1258 days), driven by fewer hospitalisations (0.27 vs 0.34 per patient) and shorter stays. PROPOSED SPLIT — LIKELY for fewer hospital days; POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for self-rated health.

cards.headline: IMPaCT 2018: self-rated physical health did not improve (P=.89), but hospital days fell sharply and perceived quality of care rose
cards.summary: IMPaCT 2018: self-rated physical health did not improve (P=.89), but hospital days fell sharply and perceived quality of care rose
cards.people: 592 patients from three primary care facilities in Philadelphia who lived in a high-poverty zip code, were uninsured or publicly insured, and had two or more chronic diseases; recruited January 2015 to March 2016 and randomised to six months of tailored community-health-worker support (IMPaCT) or a control arm of goal-setting only. The primary outcome was change in self-rated physical health; secondary outcomes included self-rated mental health, chronic disease control, patient activation, perceived quality of primary care, and all-cause hospitalisation, assessed at 6 and 9 months by intention to treat.
cards.result: Self-rated physical health improved similarly in both arms (mean change 1.8 vs 1.6; P=.89). Intervention patients were more likely to report the highest quality of care (odds ratio 1.8; 95% CI 1.4–2.4; P<.001) and spent fewer total days in hospital at 6 months (155 vs 345 days) and 9 months (300 vs 471 days), driven by shorter stays and fewer repeat admissions among those hospitalised; odds of repeat hospitalisation were lower (OR 0.4; 95% CI 0.2–0.9; P=.02), as were 30-day readmissions (OR 0.3; 95% CI 0.1–0.9; P=.04).
cards.watchOut: The trial's primary outcome was null, and the abstract reports no significant headline result for chronic disease control or mental health — summaries claiming those improved overstate this record. The hospital-day totals are group aggregates, not per-patient means, and the admission-count components were individually borderline (P=.06–.07) even though repeat-admission odds were significant.
cards.source: Kangovi S et al. Effect of Community Health Worker Support on Clinical Outcomes of Low-Income Patients Across Primary Care Facilities: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2018. PMID: 30422224. Registry ID: NCT02347787, from the record. cards.summary: IMPaCT pooled analysis (three RCTs, 1,340 patients): hospital days per patient were 66% of control (IRR 0.66, P<.0001)
cards.type: Pooled analysis of three randomized clinical trials
cards.people: Pooled data from the programme's three randomised trials (n=1,340) conducted 2011–2016 in high-poverty Philadelphia populations, predominantly Medicaid-insured: a 2-week post-discharge intervention in hospitalised general medical patients (n=446), six months of IMPaCT in two academic primary care clinics (n=302), and the six-month three-system primary care trial carded above (n=592). cards.result: Over 9,398 observed patient-months, total hospital days per patient in the intervention group were 66% of control (849 days in 674 intervention patients vs 1258 days in 660 control patients; incidence rate ratio 0.66, P<.0001). shelves.title: Person-centred care, activities, and antipsychotic review in dementia care homes (WHELD)
shelves.question: In people with dementia living in care homes, do person-centred care training, person-centred activities, and structured antipsychotic review improve quality of life and reduce antipsychotic use and agitation versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antipsychotic Agents · Cluster Analysis · Dementia · Exercise Therapy · Female · Health Status · Humans · Interpersonal Relations · Male · Nursing Homes · Person-Centered Psychotherapy · Quality of Life · Socioenvironmental Therapy
shelves.balance: Split by outcome inside one programme. The large WHELD trial (Ballard 2018, 69 UK nursing homes, 847 residents) found person-centred care training plus social interaction, with antipsychotic review built in, improved quality of life (DEMQOL-Proxy mean difference 2.54, P=.0042, effect size 0.24), agitation (effect size 0.23), and overall neuropsychiatric symptoms (effect size 0.30) — statistically significant but small effects. Antipsychotic use, however, was NOT reduced: it sat at a low stable level in both arms — the topic draft's claim that the 2018 report 'quantifies the antipsychotic reduction' is wrong; there was none. The programme's earlier factorial report (2017, 16 homes) adds a caution: antipsychotic review alone worsened two quality-of-life domains, social interaction improved quality of life, and the combination caused no deterioration. An independent earlier trial (Fossey 2006) shows staff training and support CAN cut neuroleptic use (23.0% vs 42.1% of residents) without worsening agitation — so the drug-reduction claim belongs to that design, not to WHELD. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — real but small quality-of-life and agitation benefits from one programme; the antipsychotic-sparing claim is not WHELD's to make.

cards.headline: WHELD 2018: quality of life, agitation, and neuropsychiatric symptoms improved modestly — antipsychotic use did not fall
cards.summary: WHELD 2018: quality of life, agitation, and neuropsychiatric symptoms improved modestly — antipsychotic use did not fall
cards.people: 847 people with dementia randomised across 69 UK nursing homes (553 completed the 9-month trial) to the WHELD intervention — staff training in person-centred care and social interaction plus education to trigger antipsychotic review, delivered through care-staff champions — or treatment as usual. The primary outcome was quality of life (DEMQOL-Proxy); secondary outcomes included agitation (CMAI), neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI-NH), antipsychotic use, mood, unmet needs, mortality, quality of interactions, pain, and cost.
cards.result: WHELD significantly improved quality of life (DEMQOL-Proxy mean difference 2.54; 95% CI 0.81–4.28; P=.0042; Cohen's D 0.24), agitation (mean difference −4.27 on the CMAI; P=.0076; D 0.23), and overall neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI-NH mean difference −4.55; P<.001; D 0.30), with the largest benefits in moderately severe dementia. Positive care interactions increased (QUIS, P=.03; D 0.55). There were no significant differences in the other outcomes, and antipsychotic drug use was at a low stable level in both groups — the intervention did not reduce use. The intervention cost less than usual care, so the benefits came with a cost saving.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes are small (D≈0.24–0.30), quality of life is proxy-rated, and 847 randomised fell to 553 completing. The antipsychotic-review component in this trial worked by prompting medical review rather than proactively educating prescribers — one plausible reason drug use did not move — but the result stands: WHELD did not demonstrate antipsychotic reduction.
cards.source: Ballard C et al. Impact of person-centred care training and person-centred activities on quality of life, agitation, and antipsychotic use in people with dementia living in nursing homes: A cluster-randomised controlled trial. PLoS Med. 2018. PMID: 29408901. Registry ID: ISRCTN62237498, stated in the record. cards.type: Factorial cluster randomised trial (analysis within the WHELD programme)
cards.people: Analysis within the WHELD cluster-randomised factorial study in 16 UK care homes, examining antipsychotic review, social interaction, and exercise interventions, alone and combined, on health-related quality of life (DEMQOL-Proxy); data were available for 187 participants.
cards.result: People receiving antipsychotic review showed significant worsening in two DEMQOL-Proxy domains (negative emotion, P=.02; appearance, P=.04), and a best-case-scenario analysis showed significant worsening of the total score. The social interaction intervention significantly benefited quality of life (P=.04). There was no deterioration in groups receiving both antipsychotic review and social interaction (P=.62). Its message cuts both ways for deprescribing: review without replacement support may make residents feel worse.

cards.headline: Fossey 2006: training and support for care staff cut neuroleptic use from 42.1% to 23.0% of residents, with no rise in agitation
cards.summary: Fossey 2006: training and support for care staff cut neuroleptic use from 42.1% to 23.0% of residents, with no rise in agitation
cards.people: 12 specialist nursing homes for people with dementia in London, Newcastle, and Oxford, randomised to a 10-month training and support intervention for staff — focused on alternatives to drugs for managing agitated behaviour, i.e. promotion of person-centred care — or control, with blinded outcome assessment. Outcomes at 12 months were the proportion of residents prescribed neuroleptics and mean agitation levels (Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory).
cards.result: At 12 months, 23.0% of residents in intervention homes were taking neuroleptics versus 42.1% in control homes — an average reduction in neuroleptic use of 19.1 percentage points (95% CI 0.5% to 37.7%). No significant differences were found in levels of agitated or disruptive behaviour between intervention and control homes.
cards.watchOut: Twelve homes only, in specialist dementia units, with a wide confidence interval on the reduction (0.5% to 37.7%). Fossey's intervention was sustained staff training and support without a formal medication-review protocol — the mirror image of WHELD's null drug result, and the two together suggest the active ingredient for drug reduction is staff capability, not review paperwork.

shelves.title: Case management after wrist fracture to start osteoporosis care (Majumdar)
shelves.question: In patients who have had a fragility (wrist) fracture, does a case-manager or multifaceted intervention increase osteoporosis assessment and treatment initiation versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alberta · Bone Density · Bone Density Conservation Agents · Delivery of Health Care · Diphosphonates · Epidemiologic Methods · Female · Health Care Costs · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nurse Administrators · Osteoporosis · Osteoporotic Fractures · Quality Improvement · Wrist Injuries
shelves.balance: Process outcomes, dramatically improved, in small Alberta trials from one research group. The anchored pilot (Majumdar 2011) randomised 46 patients still untreated a year after a wrist fracture: a nurse case-manager (counselling, arranging bone-density tests, prescribing treatment) versus the group's multifaceted intervention (patient education plus physician guidelines and reminders). At 6 months, bisphosphonate treatment was 43% versus 12% (relative risk 3.6, 95% CI 1.1–11.5 — a relative measure; the absolute rates are 43% and 12%), bone-density testing 81% versus 52%, and appropriate care 57% versus 28%. The same record reports the group's earlier controlled trial, in which the multifaceted intervention itself tripled treatment versus controls in relative terms (22% vs 7% absolute). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — pilot-scale numbers (46 patients) and process outcomes only; nothing here shows fracture prevention, only that the care gap after fracture can be closed, best by a case-manager. Case management cost $44 (Canadian) per patient versus $12 for the multifaceted intervention.

cards.headline: Majumdar 2011 pilot: a nurse case-manager tripled bisphosphonate treatment versus the multifaceted intervention (43% vs 12%; RR 3.6 relative)
cards.summary: Majumdar 2011 pilot: a nurse case-manager tripled bisphosphonate treatment versus the multifaceted intervention (43% vs 12%; RR 3.6 relative)
cards.people: 46 patients who remained untreated for osteoporosis one year after a wrist fracture (median age 60 years, 68% women), randomised to a nurse case-manager (n=21), who counselled patients, arranged bone mineral density tests, and prescribed treatments, or to a multifaceted intervention (n=25) of patient education plus physician guidelines and reminders. The primary outcome was bisphosphonate treatment at 6 months; secondary outcomes were BMD testing, appropriate care (BMD test plus treatment if bone mass was low), and costs.
cards.result: At 6 months, 9 of 21 case-managed patients (43%) were treated with bisphosphonates versus 3 of 25 (12%) with the multifaceted intervention (relative risk 3.6; 95% CI 1.1–11.5; P=.019). Case-managed patients were more likely to undergo BMD testing (81% vs 52%; RR 1.6 relative; 95% CI 1.1–2.4; P=.042) and to receive appropriate care (57% vs 28%; RR 2.0 relative; 95% CI 1.0–4.2; P=.048). Case management cost $44 (Canadian) per patient versus $12 for the multifaceted intervention. Even with case management, nearly half of patients did not receive appropriate care.
cards.watchOut: A pilot: 46 patients, one health system, and a comparison against an already-active intervention rather than usual care. All the striking ratios are relative measures on small absolute numbers (9 vs 3 treated patients); the absolute rates are printed beside them on this card deliberately.

shelves.title: GRACE geriatric care management for low-income seniors (Counsell)
shelves.question: In low-income older adults, does GRACE team care (geriatrician-led interdisciplinary team with an advanced practice nurse and social worker) improve quality of care and reduce acute service use versus usual primary care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Acute Disease · Aged · Family Practice · Female · Geriatrics · Health Services · Health Status · Home Care Services · Humans · Male · Patient Care Team · Poverty · Quality of Health Care · United States
shelves.balance: One randomised trial (GRACE, Counsell 2007, 951 low-income adults aged 65+, income below 200% of the federal poverty level, two years of home-based care management by a nurse practitioner and social worker working with the primary care physician and a geriatrics team under 12 condition protocols). Quality-of-life results were mixed: at 24 months, four of eight SF-36 scales (general health, vitality, social functioning, mental health) and the Mental Component Summary improved significantly, but physical function and ADLs did not differ, and neither did death. Emergency department visits not resulting in admission were lower over two years (1,445 vs 1,748 per 1,000; P=.03), while hospital admissions overall were not (700 vs 740 per 1,000; P=.66); in the predefined high-risk subgroup, both ED visits and admissions were lower in the second year. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — a large, long trial with genuine but partial gains: mental-health-related quality and emergency use improved; physical function and overall admissions did not.

cards.headline: GRACE: mental-component quality of life and ED visits improved; admissions and physical function did not (overall)
cards.summary: GRACE: mental-component quality of life and ED visits improved; admissions and physical function did not (overall)
cards.people: 951 adults aged 65 or older with annual income below 200% of the federal poverty level, whose primary care physicians in community health centres were randomised (January 2002 to August 2004) to GRACE intervention (474 patients) or usual care (477). Intervention patients received two years of home-based care management by a nurse practitioner and social worker collaborating with the primary care physician and a geriatrics interdisciplinary team, guided by 12 care protocols for common geriatric conditions. Outcomes included SF-36 scales, ADLs, emergency department visits not resulting in hospitalisation, and hospitalisations.
cards.result: At 24 months, intervention patients improved significantly more on four of eight SF-36 scales — general health (0.2 vs −2.3, P=.045), vitality (2.6 vs −2.6, P<.001), social functioning (3.0 vs −2.3, P=.008), and mental health (3.6 vs −0.3, P=.001) — and on the Mental Component Summary (2.1 vs −0.3, P<.001). No group differences were found for ADLs or death. The cumulative 2-year ED visit rate was lower with GRACE (1,445 vs 1,748 per 1,000; P=.03), but hospital admission rates were not significantly different (700 vs 740 per 1,000; P=.66). In a predefined high-risk group, ED visits and admissions were both lower in the second year (848 vs 1,314 per 1,000, P=.03; and 396 vs 705 per 1,000, P=.03).
cards.watchOut: The admission benefit lives entirely in the predefined high-risk subgroup's second year; the whole-population admission result is null, and the quality-of-life gains are concentrated in mental and social domains, not physical function. Effects of this size need the programme's full interdisciplinary staffing — they are not a promise for a lighter-touch version.
cards.source: Counsell SR et al. Geriatric care management for low-income seniors: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2007. PMID: 18073358. Registry ID: NCT00182962, from the record. MeSH: Activities of Daily Living · Acute Disease · Aged · Family Practice · Female · Geriatrics · Health Services · Health Status · Home Care Services · Humans · Male · Patient Care Team · Poverty · Quality of Health Care · United States

shelves.title: Advance care planning in dialysis: the SPIRIT intervention (Song)
shelves.question: In adults receiving dialysis and their surrogates, does a structured advance-care-planning intervention improve surrogate readiness, patient–surrogate congruence, and bereavement outcomes versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Middle Aged · Renal Dialysis · Pandemics · Advance Care Planning · Death · Ambulatory Care Facilities · COVID-19
shelves.balance: One cluster-randomised trial (SPIRIT, Song 2024, 42 dialysis clinics in five US states, 426 patient–surrogate dyads). Trained clinic staff held a 45–60 minute structured discussion with each dyad (remote after March 2020), with a summary in the record. The two-week preparedness outcomes improved: dyad congruence on goals of care (odds ratio 1.61, 95% CI 1.12–2.31, P=.001), decisional conflict (β −0.10, P<.001), and the congruence-plus-confidence composite (OR 1.57, CI 1.06–2.34, P=.03); surrogate decision-making confidence alone did not differ (P=.12). Bereavement outcomes, in only 77 bereaved surrogates, were mixed: anxiety was lower (β −1.55, CI −3.08 to −0.01, P=.05 — a borderline result whose interval nearly touches zero), while depression (P=.84) and posttraumatic distress (P=.75) were similar. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — preparation for decision-making clearly improved; the bereavement claim rests on a small subsample and one borderline outcome, and the topic draft's broader 'surrogate outcomes improved' needs that qualification.

cards.headline: SPIRIT: dyad congruence on goals of care improved (OR 1.61) and decisional conflict fell; bereavement anxiety lower, depression and PTSD unchanged
cards.summary: SPIRIT: dyad congruence on goals of care improved (OR 1.61) and decisional conflict fell; bereavement anxiety lower, depression and PTSD unchanged
cards.people: 426 patient–surrogate dyads in 42 dialysis clinics across five US states (Georgia, New Mexico, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Virginia), clinics randomised to the SPIRIT intervention (231 dyads) or usual care (195), recruited February 2018 to January 2022 and followed for 21 months or until the patient's death. Each intervention clinic designated one or two health care workers to conduct a 45- to 60-minute structured advance-care-planning discussion with the dyad — in clinic, or remotely after the March 2020 COVID-19 emergency declaration — with an ACP summary placed in the patient's record. Primary outcomes at 2 weeks were dyad congruence on end-of-life goals, patient decisional conflict, surrogate decision-making confidence, and a composite of congruence and confidence; secondary bereavement outcomes (anxiety, depression, posttraumatic distress) were assessed 3 months after death.
cards.result: At 2 weeks, adjusted for baseline, dyad congruence was higher in the intervention group (odds ratio 1.61; 95% CI 1.12–2.31; P=.001), decisional conflict scores were lower (β −0.10; 95% CI −0.13 to −0.07; P<.001), and the composite was higher (OR 1.57; 95% CI 1.06–2.34; P=.03); surrogate decision-making confidence alone was similar (β 0.06; P=.12). Among 77 bereaved surrogates, intervention-group anxiety was lower (β −1.55; 95% CI −3.08 to −0.01; P=.05), while depression (β −0.18; P=.84) and posttraumatic distress (β −0.96; P=.75) were similar.
cards.watchOut: The bereavement analysis rests on 77 surrogates and a P value of exactly .05 for the single positive outcome. The trial ran through the COVID-19 pandemic, which forced remote delivery partway and may have altered both the intervention and bereavement itself (the analysis adjusted for assessment timing). This shelf is dialysis-specific; the general advance-care-planning evidence (PREPARE, Detering) lives on its own shelf.
cards.source: Song MK et al. Effectiveness of an Advance Care Planning Intervention in Adults Receiving Dialysis and Their Families: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open. 2024. shelves.title: Quinine for night leg cramps: it does work, modestly, in two small blinded trials — its problem is safety and licensing, not efficacy
shelves.question: In adults with nocturnal leg cramps, does quinine (or its relative hydroquinine) reduce cramp frequency compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Double-Blind Method · Humans · Leg · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Cramp/*drug therapy · Quinine/*therapeutic use · Sleep Wake Disorders/prevention & control · Vitamin E/*therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Quinine for night cramps is an old remedy that regulators have pushed off the market in several countries over rare but serious blood side effects — which makes the actual efficacy evidence worth stating precisely. Two small double-blind trials found a real effect. In a crossover trial of 27 men, quinine cut cramp frequency and the sleep disturbance cramps cause (13 of 27 had at least half their cramps abolished), while vitamin E, the comparison remedy, did nothing. In a Dutch trial (112 enrolled, 102 analysed), hydroquinine — quinine's close chemical relative — reduced cramps by a median of 8 attacks over the treatment period versus 3 on placebo, with 65% of the hydroquinine group achieving at least a 50% reduction in cramp frequency. So the efficacy answer is yes, modestly; the reason quinine is nonetheless hard to obtain is safety, not inefficacy, and this shelf grades the efficacy question only. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two small blinded trials agree that quinine-class drugs reduce nocturnal cramps.

cards.headline: Crossover trial: quinine cut cramp frequency and sleep disturbance in 27 men; vitamin E did not (13/27 had ≥50% fewer cramps)
cards.summary: Crossover trial: quinine cut cramp frequency and sleep disturbance in 27 men; vitamin E did not (13/27 had ≥50% fewer cramps)
cards.people: 27 men with nocturnal leg cramps completed a randomised double-blind crossover trial of quinine versus vitamin E.
cards.result: Quinine reduced the frequency of nocturnal cramps and of cramp-disturbed sleep; 13 of 27 men had at least 50% fewer cramps on quinine. Vitamin E showed no effect. Side effects were mildly more frequent on quinine.
cards.watchOut: Men only, and small. This is an efficacy result only: quinine's rare serious haematological toxicity (immune thrombocytopenia) is why regulators in several countries do not license it for cramps, whatever the efficacy.
cards.source: Connolly PS et al.. Treatment of nocturnal leg cramps. A crossover trial of quinine vs vitamin E. Archives of Internal Medicine. 1992. PMID: 1520054. shelves.title: Beta-sitosterol for prostate symptoms: two blinded trials show about a 5-point IPSS advantage and better flow — symptoms improve, the gland does not shrink
shelves.question: In men with benign prostatic hyperplasia, does beta-sitosterol improve urinary symptoms and flow compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Placebos · Prostate/pathology · Prostatic Hyperplasia/complications/*drug therapy/pathology · Quality of Life · Sitosterols/administration & dosage/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Retention/etiology/physiopathology · Urodynamics
shelves.balance: Beta-sitosterol, the plant sterol sold for prostate symptoms, is a useful contrast with its food-spread cousins on shelf #2481: there, sterols lower cholesterol; here, the question is urinary symptoms. Two German double-blind trials from the 1990s found genuine symptom benefit. In Berges (200 patients, 20 mg three times daily, 6 months), the modified Boyarsky symptom score fell 6.7 points against 2.1 on placebo (p<0.01), IPSS fell 7.4 versus 2.1 points, peak flow rose from 9.9 to 15.2 mL/s, and residual urine volume halved — with no change in prostate volume. In Klippel (177 men, the named preparation Azuprostat, 130 mg/day), the adjusted IPSS advantage over placebo was 5.4 points (p<0.01), with quality of life, flow rate and residual volume all moving the same way. Symptom relief without shrinkage is a coherent profile — think of it as a mild symptomatic drug, not a disease modifier — but both trials are old, short, and predate modern reporting standards. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Berges 1995: symptom scores fell 6.7 versus 2.1 points on placebo; peak flow rose 9.9→15.2 mL/s; prostate volume unchanged
cards.summary: Berges 1995: symptom scores fell 6.7 versus 2.1 points on placebo; peak flow rose 9.9→15.2 mL/s; prostate volume unchanged
cards.people: 200 men with symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia randomised double-blind to beta-sitosterol 20 mg three times daily or placebo for 6 months in a multicentre trial; primary endpoint the modified Boyarsky score, with IPSS, flow rates and prostate volume secondary.
cards.result: Boyarsky score fell −6.7 (SD 4.0) on beta-sitosterol versus −2.1 (3.2) on placebo (p<0.01); IPSS fell −7.4 versus −2.1 points; peak urinary flow rose from 9.9 to 15.2 mL/s and mean residual volume fell from 65.8 to 30.4 mL on treatment, with no significant change on placebo and no reduction in prostate volume in either group. The publication describes the preparation by dose and content and names no retail brand.
cards.watchOut: Six months is short for a lifelong condition, and 1990s phytotherapy trials predate modern registration and reporting norms — the effect is plausible but the literature has not been re-tested since.
cards.source: Berges RR et al.. Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trial of beta-sitosterol in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia. Beta-sitosterol Study Group. cards.headline: Klippel 1997: the named preparation Azuprostat beat placebo by 5.4 IPSS points, with flow and residual volume improved
cards.summary: Klippel 1997: the named preparation Azuprostat beat placebo by 5.4 IPSS points, with flow and residual volume improved
cards.people: 177 men with BPH randomised double-blind in 13 German centres to the beta-sitosterol preparation Azuprostat (130 mg/day of free beta-sitosterol, a chemically defined phytosterol extract) or placebo for 6 months; IPSS was the primary outcome.
cards.result: Improvements over placebo were significant (p<0.01): the adjusted mean IPSS difference was 5.4 points and the quality-of-life index difference 0.9, both favouring beta-sitosterol, with peak flow up 4.5 mL/s and post-void residual down 33.5 mL after adjustment for placebo changes. cards.watchOut: One of the two trials names its product (Azuprostat) and the other does not — beta-sitosterol content varies between modern supplements, so the trial doses (60–130 mg/day) are the anchor, not any particular shelf product.

shelves.title: Hospitalist vs traditional attending care: stay about half a day shorter and cheaper — a mortality benefit showed only in one trial's second year
shelves.question: For general medical inpatients, does care led by a hospitalist rather than a traditional attending physician or the patient's own primary care physician improve mortality, length of stay and cost?
shelves.mesh: Chicago · Cohort Studies · Female · Hospital Costs · Hospital Mortality · Hospitalists/*economics/*standards · Hospitals, University/*economics/*standards · Humans · Length of Stay/economics · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · *Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Physicians/*economics/*standards
shelves.balance: Hospitalist care reliably shortens the stay and cuts hospital cost; whether it saves lives is unproven. In the one allocated comparison (Meltzer 2002, 6,511 patients), the hospitalist advantage appeared only in the service's second year: stay 0.49 day shorter, costs $782 lower, and 30-day mortality 4.2% versus 6.0% (adjusted relative risk 0.65 — a relative measure from a single centre's second year; with years 1 and 2 combined, mortality was not significantly different). The two systematic reviews agree on efficiency and not on outcomes: Peterson 2009 (33 reports) found general agreement on shorter stay and lower cost, with outcome gains only in pockets — orthopaedic co-management, pneumonia and heart-failure quality markers; White & Glazier 2011 (65 evaluations) found stay reduced in 69% of studies and costs in 70%, clinical quality comparable to traditional attendings, and the underlying studies methodologically weak. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the efficiency benefit is consistent; the mortality signal rests on one centre's experienced second year — which is why the experience question gets its own shelf (#2544). Tier C: this shelf carries a mortality claim.

cards.headline: Meltzer 2002: no difference in year 1; in year 2, 30-day mortality 4.2% vs 6.0% (adjusted relative risk 0.65), stay 0.49 day shorter, costs $782 lower
cards.summary: Meltzer 2002: no difference in year 1; in year 2, 30-day mortality 4.2% vs 6.0% (adjusted relative risk 0.65), stay 0.49 day shorter, costs $782 lower
cards.type: Cohort study with systematic (every-fourth-day) allocation — the 'trial of hospitalists' (Meltzer 2002)
cards.people: 6,511 patients admitted to an academic general medicine service (July 1997 to June 1999). Patients admitted every fourth day were assigned to 1 of 2 hospitalists caring for inpatients 6 months each year, or 1 of 58 nonhospitalists caring for inpatients 1 to 2 months each year. Hospitalist patients were 24.8% of the cohort; the groups did not differ in age, race, sex, diagnosis mix or Charlson index score.
cards.result: Year 1: adjusted length of stay 0.29 day shorter for hospitalists (95% CI −0.66 to 0.06 day; P = 0.06), with no significant cost or mortality difference. Year 2: stay 0.49 day shorter (CI −0.79 to −0.15 day; P = 0.01), costs $782 lower (CI −$1,313 to −$187; P = 0.01), and 30-day mortality 4.2% for hospitalists versus 6.0% for nonhospitalists (absolute difference 1.8 percentage points; adjusted relative risk 0.65, CI 0.44 to 0.96; P = 0.03). When years 1 and 2 were combined, 30-day mortality was not significantly different. Resource use fell — and mortality showed a similar pattern — as the physician's cumulative experience with a patient's primary diagnosis grew. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: Allocation was by admission day in a single academic centre, and the mortality finding is a second-year result: the honest headline is 'no overall mortality difference, with a benefit appearing as the hospitalists gained disease-specific experience' — not 'hospitalists save lives'. The experience pattern behind it is examined on shelf #2544.
cards.source: Meltzer D et al. Effects of physician experience on costs and outcomes on an academic general medicine service: results of a trial of hospitalists. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2002. PMID: 12458986. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Peterson 2009: 33 reports agree hospitalists shorten stay and lower cost; outcome gains only in pockets
cards.summary: Peterson 2009: 33 reports agree hospitalists shorten stay and lower cost; outcome gains only in pockets
cards.people: Systematic review of 33 English-language reports comparing inpatient medical care of adults by hospitalists versus nonhospitalists, included on the basis of quality and relevance after a computerised and hand search.
cards.result: The included reports showed general agreement that hospitalist care leads to shorter length of stay and lower cost per stay. Improvements beyond efficiency were confined to pockets: 3 reports showed better outcomes for orthopaedic surgery patients who had hospitalist consultation or co-management, 3 showed improvement in markers of quality of care for pneumonia, and 2 showed improvement in aspects of heart-failure management. No pooled mortality estimate is reported. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative synthesis without pooled effect sizes, so it cannot size the efficiency gain or any outcome effect. Some of this record's PubMed MeSH indexing is plainly noisy (drug-class terms unrelated to the paper); the MeSH are copied verbatim from the record, as indexed, and flagged here rather than corrected.
cards.source: Peterson MC. A systematic review of outcomes and quality measures in adult patients cared for by hospitalists vs nonhospitalists. Mayo Clinic Proceedings. 2009. PMID: 19252112. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: White & Glazier 2011: stay down in 69% of 65 evaluations, costs in 70% — clinical quality comparable, study quality poor
cards.summary: White & Glazier 2011: stay down in 69% of 65 evaluations, costs in 70% — clinical quality comparable, study quality poor
cards.type: Systematic review of 65 comparative evaluations (White & Glazier 2011)
cards.people: Systematic review of 65 comparative evaluations published 1996–2010 comparing hospitalists with community-based physicians and traditional academic attending physicians on process, efficiency and clinical outcome measures.
cards.result: The majority of evaluations found hospitalists efficient: average length of stay was reduced in 69% of articles and total hospital costs in 70%. The clinical quality of hospitalist care appeared comparable to that provided by their colleagues. Methodological quality had not improved over time: 37 evaluations failed to adjust for established confounders, 42 did not account for patients lost to follow-up, and 55 used inappropriate statistical tests. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: The 69% and 70% figures are vote counts across heterogeneous studies, not pooled effect sizes; and 'comparable quality' drawn from mostly weak observational studies is weaker reassurance than it sounds.
cards.source: White HL et al. Do hospitalist physicians improve the quality of inpatient care delivery? A systematic review of process, efficiency and outcome measures. BMC Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21592322. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: efficiency benefit consistent across two decades of studies; a mortality benefit is not established — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: efficiency benefit consistent across two decades of studies; a mortality benefit is not established — POSSIBLE
cards.people: One allocated comparison (6,511 patients), one systematic review of 33 reports, and one systematic review of 65 comparative evaluations, spanning 1996–2010.
cards.result: Length of stay fell by about half a day and hospital costs by several hundred dollars per stay in the best single study, and the efficiency direction is consistent across both reviews. Mortality was not significantly different overall in the allocated study (both years combined) and was not shown to differ in the reviews; the one positive mortality result is confined to the second year of a single service, as its two hospitalists accumulated experience. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C for the mortality content.
cards.watchOut: Almost all of this literature is observational and vulnerable to confounding by which patients are assigned to hospitalists. What happens after the shorter stay ends is a separate question, on shelf #2545.
cards.source: Synthesis of Meltzer D et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2002 (PMID: 12458986); Peterson MC. Mayo Clinic Proceedings. 2009 (PMID: 19252112); White HL et al. BMC Medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21592322).

shelves.title: Hospitalist experience and continuity: first-year hospitalists' patients die more often, and fragmented schedules track with more deaths and readmissions
shelves.question: Among hospitalists, do years of experience and more continuous work schedules change their patients' mortality, readmission and discharge outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · *Hospital Costs · Hospital Mortality/trends · Hospitalists/*standards · Hospitalization/*trends · Humans · Male · Medicare/*statistics & numerical data · Middle Aged · Retrospective Studies · Survival Rate/trends · United States/epidemiology
shelves.balance: Within hospitalist care, who the hospitalist is and how they work appears to matter. In national Medicare data (Goodwin 2018; 21,612 hospitalists), patients of first-year hospitalists had higher mortality than patients of hospitalists a year further on: observed 30-day mortality 10.50% in a hospitalist's first year versus 9.97% in the second year (mortality odds ratio 0.90 for year 2 versus year 1 — a relative measure), with hospital mortality 3.33% versus 2.96% (odds ratio 0.84) and little further change after year 2. In Texas Medicare data (Goodwin 2020; 114,777 admissions), care from hospitalists in the most continuous schedule quartile was associated with lower mortality in the 30 days after discharge (adjusted odds ratio 0.88), fewer readmissions (0.94), more discharges home (1.08) and $223 lower 30-day post-discharge costs than the least continuous quartile. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two large observational datasets with coherent dose patterns — but every ratio sits between 0.5 and 2.0, inside the library's weak-association band, and no trial has randomised experience or rosters. Tier C: this shelf carries mortality associations.

cards.headline: Goodwin 2018: first-year hospitalists' patients died more — 30-day mortality 10.50% vs 9.97% by the second year (odds ratio 0.90)
cards.summary: Goodwin 2018: first-year hospitalists' patients died more — 30-day mortality 10.50% vs 9.97% by the second year (odds ratio 0.90)
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study (5% national Medicare sample; Goodwin 2018)
cards.people: A 5% sample of national Medicare data. Cross-sectional cohort of 21,612 hospitalists working July 2013 to June 2014 (5,445, or 25%, had 1 year of experience or less; 11,596, or 54%, had 4 years or more), plus a longitudinal cohort of 3,860 hospitalists followed from their first year of practice for at least 4 years. Mortality was modelled with hospitalist experience as the exposure, adjusted for patient and hospital characteristics.
cards.result: Observed 30-day mortality was 10.50% for patients of first-year hospitalists versus 9.97% for patients of hospitalists in their second year; the mortality odds ratio for second-year versus first-year hospitalists was 0.90 (95% CI 0.84–0.96 — a relative measure). Observed hospital mortality was 3.33% versus 2.96% (odds ratio 0.84, CI 0.75–0.95). For both outcomes there was little change in odds between the second year and subsequent years. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: Observational: first-year hospitalists may work in different hospitals, with different support, or be assigned different patients than experienced colleagues, and claims data cannot capture all of that. The association is consistent and plateaus plausibly after year 2, but the mechanism — growing skill versus sorting — is not proven.
cards.source: Goodwin JS et al. Association of Hospitalist Years of Experience With Mortality in the Hospitalized Medicare Population. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29279886. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Goodwin 2020: most continuous hospitalist schedules — 30-day mortality adjusted odds ratio 0.88, readmissions 0.94, discharge home 1.08
cards.summary: Goodwin 2020: most continuous hospitalist schedules — 30-day mortality adjusted odds ratio 0.88, readmissions 0.94, discharge home 1.08
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study (Texas Medicare claims; Goodwin 2020)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort study of 114,777 Medicare medical admissions with a 3- to 6-day length of stay (229 hospitals in Texas, January 2014 to November 2016) in which all general medical care was provided by hospitalists. Schedule continuity was the percentage of a hospitalist's working days that were part of a block of 7 or more consecutive working days: 0–30% in the lowest quartile versus 67–100% in the highest. Mean patient age was 79.9 years; 61.0% were women.
cards.result: Highest versus lowest continuity quartile: lower patient mortality in the 30 days after discharge (adjusted odds ratio 0.88, 95% CI 0.81–0.95 — a relative measure; the abstract reports no absolute mortality rates), lower readmission rates (aOR 0.94, CI 0.90–0.99), higher rates of discharge to the home (aOR 1.08, CI 1.03–1.13), and lower Medicare costs in the 30 days after discharge (−$223, CI −$441 to −$7). Patient characteristics were not associated with the continuity of the treating hospitalists' schedules, and results were similar across alternative definitions of continuity. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: One state's Medicare data and an observational design: hospitals that roster hospitalists in long blocks may differ from other hospitals in ways claims cannot capture. All the ratios are modest and inside the 0.5–2.0 weak-association band.
cards.source: Goodwin JS et al. Association of the Work Schedules of Hospitalists With Patient Outcomes of Hospitalization. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2020. PMID: 31764937. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: experience and continuity both track with lower mortality, in observational data only — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: experience and continuity both track with lower mortality, in observational data only — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Two large Medicare cohort studies: 21,612 hospitalists nationally (experience and mortality, 2018) and 114,777 admissions in Texas (schedule continuity and outcomes, 2020).
cards.result: The pattern coheres with the trial finding on shelf #2543, where the hospitalist mortality advantage appeared only in the service's second, experienced year: mortality is highest in a hospitalist's first year and plateaus after the second, and fragmented schedules are associated with more deaths and readmissions after discharge than block schedules. All measures are relative (odds ratios 0.84 to 0.94), so the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Neither study randomised anything. Read these as reasons to support early-career hospitalists and to prefer block scheduling — not as proof that either change saves lives.
cards.source: Synthesis of Goodwin JS et al. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29279886); Goodwin JS et al. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 31764937).

shelves.title: Hospitalist care after discharge: the in-hospital saving reverses — more ED visits, readmissions and Medicare cost in the 30 days after going home
shelves.question: After discharge, how do medical utilization, readmissions and total Medicare costs compare for medical inpatients cared for by hospitalists versus by their own primary care physicians?
shelves.mesh: Continuity of Patient Care · Cost Allocation · Emergency Service, Hospital/economics/*statistics & numerical data · *Hospital Costs · Hospitalists/*economics · Humans · Length of Stay/economics · Medicare/economics/*statistics & numerical data · Nursing Homes/statistics & numerical data · Patient Discharge/*economics · *Patient Readmission/economics · Primary Health Care/economics/*statistics & numerical data · Propensity Score · United States
shelves.balance: The hospitalist saving is partly a cost shift. In a national 5% Medicare sample (Kuo & Goodwin 2011), enrollees who had a primary care physician were compared according to who actually cared for them in hospital: those cared for by hospitalists stayed 0.64 day less and generated $282 lower hospital charges — but Medicare costs in the 30 days after discharge were $332 higher (P < 0.001 for both differences), more than wiping out the in-hospital saving. Hospitalist patients were also less likely to be discharged home (odds ratio 0.82) and more likely to have an emergency department visit (odds ratio 1.18) or a readmission (odds ratio 1.08) after discharge — relative measures, all inside the library's weak-association band — and they had fewer visits with their own primary care physician and more nursing facility visits. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): the post-discharge pattern comes from a single large propensity-analysed observational study, so it is credible but not proven. The abstract reports no mortality outcome, so this shelf makes no mortality claim and is not Tier C.

cards.headline: Kuo & Goodwin 2011: stay 0.64 day shorter and charges $282 lower in hospital — then $332 higher Medicare costs in the 30 days after discharge
cards.summary: Kuo & Goodwin 2011: stay 0.64 day shorter and charges $282 lower in hospital — then $332 higher Medicare costs in the 30 days after discharge
cards.type: Population-based cohort study with propensity-score analysis (5% Medicare sample; Kuo & Goodwin 2011)
cards.people: Population-based national cohort study of a 5% sample of Medicare Parts A and B enrollees with a primary care physician, hospitalised for medical conditions from 2001 to 2006 and cared for by either their primary care physician or a hospitalist; the two groups were compared by propensity-score analysis. Outcomes included length of stay, hospital charges, discharge location, and physician visits, emergency department visits, rehospitalisation and Medicare spending within 30 days after discharge.
cards.result: Hospital length of stay was 0.64 day less and hospital charges were $282 lower among patients receiving hospitalist care, whereas Medicare costs in the 30 days after discharge were $332 higher (P < 0.001 for both). Patients cared for by hospitalists were less likely to be discharged to home (odds ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.86) and were more likely to have emergency department visits (odds ratio 1.18, CI 1.12 to 1.24) and readmissions (odds ratio 1.08, CI 1.02 to 1.14) after discharge — all relative measures. They also had fewer visits with their primary care physician and more nursing facility visits after discharge. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: Observational, and from 2001–2006 practice: patients handed to hospitalists may be more complex in ways propensity scores cannot fully capture, and discharge practice has changed since — the abstract itself flags selection bias as the limitation. The abstract reports no mortality outcome, so nothing on this shelf speaks to survival.
cards.source: Kuo YF et al. Association of hospitalist care with medical utilization after discharge: evidence of cost shift from a cohort study. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21810708. Registry ID: none in the record.
