cards.headline: Synthesis: the in-hospital saving is offset after discharge — a cost shift, from one large observational study — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: the in-hospital saving is offset after discharge — a cost shift, from one large observational study — POSSIBLE
cards.people: One national Medicare cohort study with propensity-score analysis (Kuo & Goodwin 2011). No second general-medical study of post-discharge utilisation was carded for this shelf; the reasons are set out in the build report.
cards.result: Shorter stay and lower hospital charges under hospitalist care were fully offset within 30 days by higher post-discharge Medicare spending, alongside more emergency department visits and readmissions and fewer discharges home. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) for the post-discharge pattern: the associations are modest (odds ratios 0.82 to 1.18) and observational, so the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.watchOut: Do not read this as 'hospitalists harm patients': the in-hospital efficiency on shelf #2543 is real. The claim here is narrower — the model should be judged on the whole 30-day episode, not the hospital bill alone. Whether structured transitional care repairs the post-discharge gap is a different question (shelf #790).
cards.source: Synthesis of Kuo YF et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21810708).

shelves.title: Hospitalist co-management of surgical patients: fewer minor complications in the one trial — pooled stay and mortality gains only for team-based models
shelves.question: For surgical patients — older patients with hip fracture and patients having joint replacement in particular — does hospitalist (internal medicine) co-management improve complications, length of stay and mortality compared with surgeon-led care with consultation on request?
shelves.mesh: Aged · *Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip/adverse effects/economics/standards · *Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee/adverse effects/economics/standards · Attitude of Health Personnel · Female · Hospital Costs · *Hospitalists · Humans · Internal Medicine · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · *Orthopedics · *Outcome Assessment, Health Care · *Patient Care Team · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: Co-management works best as a team sport. The one randomised trial (Huddleston 2004; 526 higher-risk patients having elective hip or knee replacement) found a hospitalist–orthopaedic team discharged more patients with no complications (61.6% versus 49.8%) and fewer minor complications (30.2% versus 44.3%), with no significant difference in observed length of stay or total cost; adjusted for discharge delays, stay was 0.5 day shorter. In hip fracture specifically, a before-and-after cohort (Phy 2005; 466 patients aged 65 and over) found a hospitalist service cut time to surgery (38 to 25 hours), time from surgery to dismissal (9 to 7 days) and stay (10.6 to 8.4 days), with no difference in inpatient deaths or 30-day readmission rates. The meta-analysis (Shaw 2020; 14 studies, 35,800 patients, only one a randomised trial) found no significant overall association with stay (mean difference −1.02 days, 95% CI −2.09 to 0.04) or mortality (odds ratio 0.79, CI 0.56 to 1.11 — a relative measure), but multidisciplinary-team co-management was associated with shorter stay (−2.03 days) and lower mortality (odds ratio 0.67, CI 0.51 to 0.88); risk of bias was serious in 10 of the 14 studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real complication benefit in one trial, process gains in hip fracture, and pooled hard-outcome signals only for team-based models in low-quality evidence. Tier C: this shelf carries mortality content.

cards.headline: Huddleston 2004 (randomised trial): co-management after hip or knee replacement — discharged with no complications 61.6% vs 49.8%, minor complications 30.2% vs 44.3%
cards.summary: Huddleston 2004 (randomised trial): co-management after hip or knee replacement — discharged with no complications 61.6% vs 49.8%, minor complications 30.2% vs 44.3%
cards.people: Randomised, controlled trial of 526 patients having elective hip or knee arthroplasty who were at elevated risk for postoperative morbidity, at one academic medical centre. The intervention was a collaborative hospitalist-led Hospitalist-Orthopedic Team; the comparison was standard postoperative care by orthopaedic surgeons with medical consultation on request.
cards.result: More patients in the hospitalist group were discharged with no complications (61.6% vs 49.8%; difference 11.8 percentage points, 95% CI 2.8 to 20.7) and fewer had minor complications (30.2% vs 44.3%; difference −14.1 percentage points, CI −22.7 to −5.3). Observed length of stay was not statistically different; adjusted for discharge delays, mean stay was 0.5 day shorter with the hospitalist model (5.1 vs 5.6 days; CI for the difference −0.8 to −0.1 day). Total costs did not differ between groups. Orthopaedic surgeons and nurses preferred the hospitalist model. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: Elective joint replacement, not hip fracture, at a single centre, with patients and providers aware of the assignment. The gains were in minor complications and smoother discharge; major complications and mortality were not outcomes that moved.
cards.source: Huddleston JM et al. Medical and surgical comanagement after elective hip and knee arthroplasty: a randomized, controlled trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15238368. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Phy 2005: in hip fracture, a hospitalist service cut time to surgery (38 to 25 hours) and stay (10.6 to 8.4 days); deaths and readmissions unchanged
cards.summary: Phy 2005: in hip fracture, a hospitalist service cut time to surgery (38 to 25 hours) and stay (10.6 to 8.4 days); deaths and readmissions unchanged
cards.people: Retrospective historical cohort study of 466 patients aged 65 years or older admitted for surgical repair of hip fracture at one centre over 2 years, comparing the year before and the year after care changed from the standard model to a hospitalist service created to manage these patients medically.
cards.result: Mean time to surgery was shorter under the hospitalist model (25 vs 38 hours; P < .001), as were time from surgery to dismissal (7 vs 9 days; P = .04) and length of stay (8.4 vs 10.6 days; P < .001). Delirium was diagnosed more often in the hospitalist group (32.2%, 74 of 230, vs 17.8%, 42 of 236; P < .001). There were no differences in inpatient deaths or 30-day readmission rates. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: A before-and-after design bundles everything that changed with the new service — protocols, staffing, attention — into the 'hospitalist' effect, and secular trends cannot be excluded. The higher delirium rate most plausibly reflects detection by a service looking for it, not harm.
cards.source: Phy MP et al. Effects of a hospitalist model on elderly patients with hip fracture. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2005. PMID: 15824300. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Shaw 2020: pooled stay and mortality show no significant association overall — but team-based co-management: stay −2.03 days, mortality odds ratio 0.67
cards.summary: Shaw 2020: pooled stay and mortality show no significant association overall — but team-based co-management: stay −2.03 days, mortality odds ratio 0.67
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies (Shaw 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 prospective studies (1 randomised clinical trial) involving 35,800 adults who underwent surgery, comparing internal medicine physician consultation or co-management with usual surgical care. Most interventions were co-management by a hospitalist or internist; 7 of 14 (50%) included a multidisciplinary team, and 9 (64%) studied predominantly elective procedures.
cards.result: Meta-analysis showed no significant association of co-management with length of stay (mean difference −1.02 days, 95% CI −2.09 to 0.04; P = .06) or mortality (odds ratio 0.79, CI 0.56 to 1.11; P = .18 — a relative measure), and no difference in 30-day readmissions (odds ratio 0.89, CI 0.68 to 1.16). Multidisciplinary-team involvement, however, was associated with significant reductions in length of stay (mean difference −2.03 days, CI −4.05 to −0.01; P = .05) and mortality (odds ratio 0.67, CI 0.51 to 0.88; P = .004). Risk of bias was serious in 10 of 14 studies (71%), data could not be pooled for complications or costs, and the authors characterise the evidence as low quality. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: The team-subgroup mortality result rests mostly on non-randomised studies at serious risk of bias — it is a hypothesis about how to organise co-management, not proof. Geriatrician-led orthogeriatric co-management after hip fracture is a different model with its own home (shelves #793 and #342); this shelf covers internist/hospitalist co-management.
cards.source: Shaw M et al. Evaluation of Internal Medicine Physician or Multidisciplinary Team Comanagement of Surgical Patients and Clinical Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Network Open. 2020. PMID: 32369179. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: fewer complications in the one trial, faster hip-fracture care in the cohort, pooled benefits only for team models — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: fewer complications in the one trial, faster hip-fracture care in the cohort, pooled benefits only for team models — POSSIBLE
cards.people: One randomised trial (526 elective arthroplasty patients), one before-and-after hip-fracture cohort (466 patients aged 65+), and one systematic review and meta-analysis (14 studies, 35,800 surgical patients).

shelves.title: Hospitalist burnout: over half report high depersonalisation or lost accomplishment in the quantifying survey — workload is the recurring driver
shelves.question: How common is burnout among hospitalists, and which features of the hospitalist job — workload, hours, control, support — drive it or protect against it?
shelves.mesh: Humans · *Burnout, Professional/epidemiology/psychology · Republic of Korea/epidemiology · Male · Female · *Hospitalists/psychology · Adult · Risk Factors · Cross-Sectional Studies · Middle Aged · Prevalence · Protective Factors · Surveys and Questionnaires · Workload/psychology
shelves.balance: Burnout is common among hospitalists in every survey that has looked, and workload is the driver that recurs in all of them. The only survey here reporting percentages (Park 2025, Korea) found high-grade depersonalisation in 50.6% of respondents and reduced personal accomplishment in 57%, with excessive workload, long working hours and conflicts with caregivers as the shared risk factors — and a cap on daily inpatient load, the availability of a research mentor, and satisfaction with nonclinical work as the protective factors. A British Columbia workforce survey (Yousefi 2025) likewise found high rates of burnout, with workload the important associated factor in regression and many hospitalists planning to reduce or stop their acute-care work, though its abstract reports no prevalence figure and no respondent count. A small US survey (Warner 2025, 88 hospitalists) ties burnout to how safe the workload feels, frustration at work, and lack of control over the working day. All three are cross-sectional surveys: they show association, not causation, and none of them tested an intervention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: prevalence and the workload story point the same way in three countries, but the hard percentages rest on one small survey with a 24.1% response rate. Tier C: survey-based workforce topic, taken to the developer personally.

cards.headline: Park 2025: high depersonalisation in 50.6% of Korean hospitalists and reduced personal accomplishment in 57% — workload, hours and caregiver conflict drive it
cards.summary: Park 2025: high depersonalisation in 50.6% of Korean hospitalists and reduced personal accomplishment in 57% — workload, hours and caregiver conflict drive it
cards.type: Cross-sectional survey of a national hospitalist workforce (Park 2025)
cards.people: Cross-sectional online survey of the whole Korean hospitalist workforce: 303 hospitalists invited, 79 completed it (24.1%). Burnout measured with the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey; psychiatric symptoms and insomnia measured with standard scales; risk and protective factors rated on 5-point Likert scales.
cards.result: More than half of respondents reported high-grade burnout in two domains: depersonalisation 50.6% and reduced personal accomplishment 57%. Conflicts with caregivers, excessive workload and long working hours were common risk factors for both domains. Satisfaction with nonclinical work protected against depersonalisation; availability of a research mentor and a cap on daily inpatient load per hospitalist protected against reduced personal accomplishment. In correlation analysis, the maximum number of inpatients and of hospitalists per hospital was a significant factor in reducing burnout. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: A 24.1% response rate means the percentages describe the hospitalists who chose to answer, who may be more burned out than those who did not; the sample is small (79) and from a single country's young hospitalist system. The abstract headlines depersonalisation and personal accomplishment; it does not give a single overall burnout prevalence.
cards.source: Park KM et al. Prevalence, risk and protective factors of burnout among Korean hospitalists. PLoS One. 2025. PMID: 40294062. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yousefi 2025: high burnout among British Columbia hospitalists, workload the associated factor, many planning to cut back — no prevalence figure in the abstract
cards.summary: Yousefi 2025: high burnout among British Columbia hospitalists, workload the associated factor, many planning to cut back — no prevalence figure in the abstract
cards.people: Cross-sectional survey of physicians participating in hospitalist programmes across British Columbia's 21 acute care facilities. The abstract reports neither the number invited nor the number responding.
cards.result: The abstract states that high rates of burnout were demonstrated among hospitalists and that a large number of providers were planning to significantly reduce or stop their involvement in acute care. Regression analysis identified workload as an important factor associated with burnout. Older physicians, those practising longer, and those with a moderate to high number of shifts were more likely to consider reducing their involvement with their programmes. Almost all respondents (96%) had been involved in the care of patients with COVID-19 in 2021. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: The abstract is qualitative: it asserts 'high rates of burnout' without a percentage, a denominator, or a response rate, so this card can corroborate the workload association and the intention to cut back but cannot size burnout in this workforce. Single-author report of a provincial programme survey.
cards.source: Yousefi V. Prevalence of burnout and impact of workload on physician wellness: A cross-sectional survey of hospitalists in British Columbia, Canada. Journal of Hospital Medicine. 2025. cards.headline: Warner 2025: in 88 US hospitalists, burnout tracked workload safety, frustration at work, and lack of control over the day
cards.summary: Warner 2025: in 88 US hospitalists, burnout tracked workload safety, frustration at work, and lack of control over the day
cards.people: Online cross-sectional survey of 88 US hospitalists, completed July–October 2020. Burnout assessed with the Mini-Z burnout scale and the Abbreviated Maslach Burnout Inventory; work well-being with the Work Well-Being Scale; work-structure variables included hours worked, frustration at work, perceived safety of clinical workload, and control over schedule and daily work.
cards.result: The presence of burnout was significantly associated with safety of workload (χ² = 8.167; P = .017), frustration at work (χ² = 15.29; P = .005), control over daily work (χ² = 12.48; P = .002) and current desire to practise medicine (χ² = 7.12; P = .03). Work well-being was positively associated with years as a hospitalist (r = .249; P = .02) and differed significantly by workload safety, frustration, and control over schedule and daily work. The abstract reports no burnout prevalence percentage. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: Small (88 respondents), single cross-sectional survey fielded during the COVID-19 period in 2020, and the abstract reports associations rather than a prevalence; cross-sectional links between frustration, control and burnout cannot show which causes which. (The abstract prints the sample size as 'Eight-eight', read as 88.)
cards.source: Warner ME et al. The work environment and hospitalist work well-being and burnout. Journal of Hospital Medicine. 2025. PMID: 39344938. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: hospitalist burnout is common wherever it is surveyed and workload is the recurring driver — but the percentages rest on one small survey — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: hospitalist burnout is common wherever it is surveyed and workload is the recurring driver — but the percentages rest on one small survey — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Three cross-sectional surveys of hospitalist workforces: Korea (79 respondents of 303 invited), British Columbia, Canada (21 facilities; abstract reports no denominator), and the United States (88 respondents).
cards.result: The direction is consistent across three countries: burnout at levels that prompt plans to reduce acute-care work, with workload, long hours, perceived unsafe census, frustration and loss of control over the working day as the associated features, and census caps, mentorship and satisfying nonclinical work on the protective side. Only the Korean survey quantifies prevalence from its abstract (high depersonalisation 50.6%, reduced personal accomplishment 57%), so no worldwide hospitalist burnout rate can honestly be stated. No card here is a trial and none tested an intervention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Survey non-response can inflate burnout estimates in either direction, and instruments and cut-offs differ between the three surveys; the percentages are not pooled anywhere on this shelf because the underlying reports do not support a pooled figure. Whether hospitalists burn out more than the physicians they replaced is a different question — the national all-physician surveys are on shelf #2548.
cards.source: Synthesis of Park KM et al. PLoS One. 2025 (PMID: 40294062); Yousefi V. Journal of Hospital Medicine. 2025 (PMID: 39741466); Warner ME et al. Journal of Hospital Medicine. 2025 (PMID: 39344938).

shelves.title: Emergency physician burnout: front-line specialties rank highest in US national surveys, and 43% of ED staff meet burnout criteria across 29 studies
shelves.question: Is emergency medicine the highest-burnout specialty — how do emergency physicians compare with other physicians and with the wider emergency department workforce?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Burnout, Professional/*epidemiology · Female · Humans · *Job Satisfaction · Male · Middle Aged · Physicians/*psychology · Surveys and Questionnaires · United States/epidemiology · Workload · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Emergency physicians sit in the highest-burnout group in every source here, though no abstract publishes an emergency-medicine-only percentage or a numeric league table of specialties. In the US national survey (Shanafelt 2012), 45.8% of all physicians reported at least one burnout symptom, with the highest rates among the front-line specialties — family medicine, general internal medicine and emergency medicine; by 2014 the all-physician figure had risen to 54.4% (Shanafelt 2015). Pooling 29 studies of emergency department staff (Alanazy 2023), 43% met overall burnout criteria, with nurses the most affected group and physicians next. The emergency-physician-specific review (Somville 2024, 35 papers) found emergency physicians scoring higher than other healthcare professions on every burnout dimension, with critical incidents, aggression from patients, and organisational factors as the determinants. A caution the developer should see plainly: the often-quoted 'about 65% of emergency physicians' figure is NOT in the Shanafelt 2012 abstract and is not carded anywhere on this shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: 'highest-burnout specialty' is supported as a front-line grouping, not as a proven solo ranking. Tier C: survey-based workforce topic, taken to the developer personally.

cards.headline: Shanafelt 2012: 45.8% of US physicians had a burnout symptom; the highest rates were in front-line specialties — family medicine, general internal medicine, emergency medicine
cards.summary: Shanafelt 2012: 45.8% of US physicians had a burnout symptom; the highest rates were in front-line specialties — family medicine, general internal medicine, emergency medicine
cards.type: National cross-sectional survey of US physicians (Shanafelt 2012)
cards.people: National survey of US physicians from all specialties drawn from the AMA Physician Masterfile: 27,276 invited, 7,288 (26.7%) completed surveys; burnout measured with the Maslach Burnout Inventory. A probability-based sample of 3,442 working US adults provided the non-physician comparison.
cards.result: 45.8% of physicians reported at least 1 symptom of burnout. Substantial differences were observed by specialty, with the highest rates among physicians at the front line of care access (family medicine, general internal medicine, and emergency medicine). On the single-item measures used for the population comparison, physicians were more likely than working US adults to have symptoms of burnout (37.9% vs 27.8%) and to be dissatisfied with work-life balance (40.2% vs 23.2%; P < .001 for both); these are relative contrasts between two large survey samples, with the absolute rates stated. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: The abstract names the front-line specialties as the highest group but does not publish an emergency-medicine-specific percentage; the frequently repeated figure of roughly 65% burnout among emergency physicians comes from the paper's full-text specialty table, not its abstract, and is deliberately not used on this shelf. Response rate 26.7%.
cards.source: Shanafelt TD et al. Burnout and satisfaction with work-life balance among US physicians relative to the general US population. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22911330. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Shanafelt 2015: physician burnout worsened to 54.4% by 2014 while the general workforce barely changed
cards.summary: Shanafelt 2015: physician burnout worsened to 54.4% by 2014 while the general workforce barely changed
cards.people: Repeat of the 2011 national survey using the same methods and measures: 35,922 US physicians invited in 2014, 6,880 (19.2%) completed surveys, with a probability-based sample of the general US working population for comparison.
cards.result: 54.4% (n = 3,680) of physicians reported at least 1 symptom of burnout in 2014, compared with 45.5% (n = 3,310) in 2011 (P < .001) — an absolute rise of about 9 percentage points. Satisfaction with work-life balance fell over the same period (48.5% vs 40.9%; P < .001), and substantial differences by specialty persisted. Burnout and work-life balance in the general working population changed minimally, so the gap widened: in pooled adjusted analysis physicians were at increased risk of burnout relative to other workers (odds ratio 1.97, 95% CI 1.80 to 2.16 — a relative measure). Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: Again the abstract reports specialty differences without an emergency-medicine figure, so this card supports 'burnout rose across medicine, front-line specialties worst' rather than any emergency-specific rate. Response rate fell to 19.2% in the 2014 wave.
cards.source: Shanafelt TD et al. Changes in Burnout and Satisfaction With Work-Life Balance in Physicians and the General US Working Population Between 2011 and 2014. Mayo Clinic Proceedings. 2015. PMID: 26653297. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Alanazy 2023: pooled burnout prevalence 43% across 29 studies of emergency department staff (16,619 workers) — nurses most affected, physicians next
cards.summary: Alanazy 2023: pooled burnout prevalence 43% across 29 studies of emergency department staff (16,619 workers) — nurses most affected, physicians next
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 studies (Alanazy 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 articles reporting burnout or its domains in emergency medicine healthcare workers (16,619 participants: nurses, physicians, residents and other ED staff), searched across six databases to February 2023.
cards.result: The pooled prevalence of overall burnout was 43%, and 35% of ED healthcare workers were at high risk of burnout. By domain: 39% reported high emotional exhaustion, 43% high depersonalisation, and 36% low personal accomplishment. Rates of high burnout and of each domain were higher during the COVID-19 pandemic than before it. Profession modified the rates — nurses were most affected, followed by physicians — and residents' likelihood of burnout rose with training year; gender was not a significant determinant. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: The population is the whole ED workforce, not emergency physicians alone, and the pooled 43% mixes countries, instruments and cut-offs (random-effects models used where heterogeneity was present); the physician-specific rate is described only as second to nurses'. This record carries no MeSH headings in PubMed, which is why the card says so.
cards.source: Alanazy ARM et al. The Global Prevalence and Associated Factors of Burnout among Emergency Department Healthcare Workers and the Impact of the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Healthcare (Basel). 2023. PMID: 37570460. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record.

cards.headline: Somville 2024: emergency physicians score higher than other healthcare professions on every burnout dimension; critical incidents and aggression are key determinants
cards.summary: Somville 2024: emergency physicians score higher than other healthcare professions on every burnout dimension; critical incidents and aggression are key determinants
cards.people: Systematic review of the 2011–2022 literature on work stress and burnout in emergency physicians: 35 papers retained from PubMed and Embase, including comparative primary studies quantifying burnout in emergency physicians.
cards.result: Emergency physicians scored significantly higher for all dimensions of burnout compared with other healthcare professions, with higher emotional exhaustion and depersonalisation in particular. Significant correlations were found with work characteristics and organisational factors; critical incidents and aggression were identified as the most important acute work characteristics affecting emergency physicians' mental wellbeing, including post-traumatic stress disorder. Personal factors — age, type D personality, previous experiences and coping strategies — also contributed. The review reports no single pooled prevalence. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: The comparison here is with other healthcare professions, not with other physician specialties, and the synthesis is narrative — it cannot by itself crown emergency medicine the highest-burnout specialty among doctors. That ranking claim rests on the Shanafelt surveys' front-line grouping (cards 1–2).
cards.source: Somville F et al. Work stress and burnout among emergency physicians: a systematic review of last 10 years of research. Acta Clinica Belgica. 2024. PMID: 37889050. cards.headline: Synthesis: emergency physicians are in the highest-burnout group by every measure here — a solo numeric ranking is not in the abstract-level evidence — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: emergency physicians are in the highest-burnout group by every measure here — a solo numeric ranking is not in the abstract-level evidence — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Two US national physician surveys (7,288 respondents in 2011; 6,880 in 2014), one meta-analysis of 29 ED-workforce studies (16,619 staff), and one systematic review of 35 emergency-physician studies.
cards.result: Three independent angles agree: US surveys place emergency medicine in the highest-burnout front-line group while overall physician burnout rose from 45.8% to 54.4% between 2011 and 2014; ED staff pooled across studies meet burnout criteria at 43%; and emergency physicians outscore other healthcare professions on all burnout dimensions, driven by critical incidents, aggression and organisational factors. What the abstract-level evidence does not contain is an emergency-physician-only prevalence or a numeric specialty league table, so the shelf claims 'among the highest, in the front-line group' and no more. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Burnout percentages move with the instrument and cut-off used, and survey response rates of 19–27% leave room for non-response bias in both directions; cross-survey comparisons should be read as direction, not decimal places. The hospitalist-specific surveys are on shelf #2547.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shanafelt TD et al. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22911330); Shanafelt TD et al. Mayo Clinic Proceedings. 2015 (PMID: 26653297); Alanazy ARM et al. Healthcare (Basel). 2023 (PMID: 37570460); Somville F et al. Acta Clinica Belgica. 2024 (PMID: 37889050).

shelves.title: Geriatric care in hospital: the proven benefit sits in dedicated wards and units — the mobile consult team is the unproven model
shelves.question: For older hospital inpatients, does it matter how geriatric expertise is delivered — on a dedicated geriatric ward or Acute Care for Elders unit, or by a mobile consultation team visiting general wards?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Emergencies · *Geriatric Assessment · *Hospitalization · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Whether geriatric assessment helps older inpatients at all is answered on shelf #605 (the Cochrane review: more patients alive and at home, risk ratio 1.06 — a relative measure; fewer nursing-home admissions, 0.80; no mortality difference, 1.00). This shelf asks the delivery question the Cochrane review left open: ward or team? The earlier meta-analysis of the same trial programme (Ellis 2011, 22 trials) found the same overall pattern — alive and at home, odds ratio 1.16 at a median 12 months — and a subgroup interaction suggesting the benefit belongs to designated wards rather than mobile teams; its abstract reports no subgroup effect sizes, and the 2017 Cochrane update judged the ward-versus-team analysis underpowered and uncertain. The named unit model has its own randomised trial: the Acute Care for Elders unit (Counsell 2000) did not improve its primary functional outcome but did reduce the composite of functional decline or nursing-home placement (34% vs 40% at discharge, sustained over the following year) at no extra length of stay or cost. No card on this shelf supports a roving consultation team improving outcomes — the one randomised proactive geriatrics consultation trial (hip fracture, Marcantonio 2001) and the Hospital Elder Life Program delirium-prevention evidence live on shelf #340. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the benefit concentrates in ward- and unit-based models; the consult-team model is the unproven one. Tier C: care-model topic with a composite touching death, taken to the developer personally. This shelf makes no mortality claim of its own.

cards.headline: Ellis 2011: CGA raised the odds of being alive at home (OR 1.16 at 12 months) — and a subgroup interaction favoured designated wards over mobile teams
cards.summary: Ellis 2011: CGA raised the odds of being alive at home (OR 1.16 at 12 months) — and a subgroup interaction favoured designated wards over mobile teams
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 22 randomised controlled trials (10,315 participants in six countries) of comprehensive geriatric assessment for older adults admitted to hospital as an emergency, whether delivered by mobile teams or on designated wards, compared with general medical care.
cards.result: Patients who underwent comprehensive geriatric assessment were more likely to be alive and in their own homes at the end of follow-up (odds ratio 1.16, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.28; P = 0.003; number needed to treat 33, at a median follow-up of 12 months; odds ratio 1.25, 1.11 to 1.42, at a median of six months) and less likely to be living in residential care (odds ratio 0.78, 0.69 to 0.88; P < 0.001). They were also less likely to die or experience deterioration (odds ratio 0.76, 0.64 to 0.90; P = 0.001 — a composite, not a mortality result) and had slightly better cognition (standardised mean difference 0.08, 0.01 to 0.15). All odds ratios are relative measures; the abstract gives no absolute event rates for these contrasts. Critically for this shelf: a subgroup interaction suggested differences between the subgroups 'wards' and 'teams' in favour of wards. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports the ward-versus-team interaction only as a suggestion of difference — it does not print separate effect sizes for wards and for teams, so the stronger numbers sometimes quoted for that split come from the full text and are not carded here. This 2011 analysis is the predecessor of the 2017 Cochrane update carded on shelf #605, whose authors were uncertain whether wards and teams differ because that analysis was underpowered; the two shelves are deliberately complementary, not duplicates.

cards.headline: Counsell 2000 (ACE unit): no gain on the primary functional outcome, but functional decline or nursing-home placement fell (34% vs 40%) at no extra stay or cost
cards.summary: Counsell 2000 (ACE unit): no gain on the primary functional outcome, but functional decline or nursing-home placement fell (34% vs 40%) at no extra stay or cost
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of an Acute Care for Elders unit (Counsell 2000)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial of 1,531 community-dwelling patients aged 70 or older admitted with an acute medical illness to a community teaching hospital (November 1994 to May 1997). The Acute Care for Elders (ACE) intervention combined a specially designed environment, patient-centred nursing care plans to prevent disability and promote rehabilitation, discharge-to-home planning, and medical-care review to prevent iatrogenic illness.
cards.result: The primary outcome — change in the number of independent activities of daily living from baseline to discharge — did not differ between groups on self-reported measures by intention-to-treat. The composite outcome of ADL decline from baseline or nursing home placement was less frequent in the intervention group at discharge (34% vs 40%; P = .027; absolute difference 6 percentage points) and remained less frequent during the year following hospitalisation (P = .022). There were no significant differences in length of stay, costs, home healthcare visits or readmissions. Process of care improved: nursing care plans to promote independent function implemented in 79% vs 50% (P = .001), physical therapy consults obtained in 42% vs 36% (P = .027), restraints applied to 2% vs 6% (P = .001), and satisfaction was higher among patients, caregivers, physicians and nurses. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: A single hospital in the mid-1990s, and the honest headline is double-sided: the trial's own primary functional outcome was null, and the positive result is a composite (decline or placement) driven at least partly by where patients were discharged to. ACE is a unit-plus-process package, so the trial cannot separate the ward environment from the nursing and discharge-planning components.
cards.source: Counsell SR et al. Effects of a multicomponent intervention on functional outcomes and process of care in hospitalized older patients: a randomized controlled trial of Acute Care for Elders (ACE) in a community hospital. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2000. PMID: 11129745. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the geriatric benefit lives in wards and units; a mobile consult team's benefit is unproven at abstract level — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the geriatric benefit lives in wards and units; a mobile consult team's benefit is unproven at abstract level — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: One meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (10,315 patients) spanning both delivery models, and one randomised trial (1,531 patients) of a named unit model, read alongside the 2017 Cochrane update carded on shelf #605.
cards.result: The evidence points the same way from both directions: pooled geriatric assessment helps (alive at home odds ratio 1.16; residential care 0.78), the one signal about how it is delivered favours designated wards over mobile teams, and the purpose-built unit trial shows less functional decline-or-placement without longer stays or higher costs. Set against that, the 2017 Cochrane authors — on the larger, updated dataset — were explicitly uncertain whether wards and teams differ, because the comparison was underpowered. This shelf therefore claims the unit/ward model as the supported one and the roving consultation team as unproven, and makes no mortality claim: the Cochrane mortality estimate is 1.00 and lives on shelf #605. The delirium-specific consult-model evidence (proactive geriatrics consultation in hip fracture; the Hospital Elder Life Program) is on shelf #340, and orthogeriatric co-management of hip fracture is on shelves #793 and #342. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: If the developer prefers one consolidated geriatric-assessment shelf, this material could fold into #605 as additional cards; it is built separately here because #605 asks whether CGA works while this shelf asks how it should be delivered — the same keep-both-with-cross-points pattern as the hospitalist shelves. The ward-versus-team contrast has never been tested head-to-head in a trial of its own; it rests on subgroup interaction plus one unit trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ellis G et al. BMJ. 2011 (PMID: 22034146); Counsell SR et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2000 (PMID: 11129745); with the Cochrane update of Ellis G et al. 2017 (PMID: 28898390) cross-pointed to shelf #605, not re-carded.

shelves.title: Inpatient palliative care: quality of life improves modestly (the pooled effect halves in low-bias trials), symptoms ease, survival unchanged
shelves.question: For hospital inpatients with life-limiting illness, does involving a palliative care team improve quality of life and symptom burden — and does it change survival or cost?
shelves.mesh: Advance Care Planning · Aged · Caregivers/*psychology · Humans · *Palliative Care · Patient Satisfaction · *Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: Yes for quality of life — with the size of the benefit honestly in doubt. Across 43 randomised trials in life-limiting illness (Kavalieratos 2016), palliative care improved quality of life at 1–3 months by a standardised mean difference of 0.46, translating to 11.36 points on the FACIT-Pal scale against a minimal clinically important difference of 9; but restricted to the five trials at low risk of bias the effect more than halved (0.20; 4.94 points, below the clinically important threshold) and the symptom-burden benefit (−0.66 overall) lost significance (−0.21, confidence interval reaching 0.00). There was no association with survival (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.17 — a relative measure whose interval spans no effect). The inpatient model specifically has two randomised trials in stem-cell transplant patients (El-Jawahri 2016 and the 2025 multisite replication): quality of life fell less at the week-2 nadir, with less depression, anxiety and symptom burden, and a post-traumatic stress benefit still separating the groups at six months in 2025. An observational cost study (Morrison 2008) found palliative consultation associated with lower hospital costs, but it is propensity-matched administrative data, not a trial. The early-outpatient palliative care question (Temel 2010 and successors) is a different model and lives on shelf #367. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): direction consistent, magnitude bias-sensitive, no survival claim. Tier C: quality-of-life benefit claim in serious illness, taken to the developer personally.

cards.headline: Kavalieratos 2016: palliative care improved quality of life (SMD 0.46) across 43 trials — but the effect halved in low-bias trials and survival was unchanged
cards.summary: Kavalieratos 2016: palliative care improved quality of life (SMD 0.46) across 43 trials — but the effect halved in low-bias trials and survival was unchanged
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 43 randomised trials (Kavalieratos 2016)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 43 randomised clinical trials of palliative care interventions in adults with life-limiting illness (12,731 patients, mean age 67 years, and 2,479 caregivers). Thirty-five trials used usual care as control; 14 took place in the ambulatory setting, so the pooled estimate mixes inpatient and outpatient models.
cards.result: At 1- to 3-month follow-up, palliative care was associated with improved patient quality of life (standardised mean difference 0.46, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.83; FACIT-Pal mean difference 11.36 points, against a minimal clinically important difference of 9 points on the 0–184 scale) and lower symptom burden (standardised mean difference −0.66, 95% CI −1.25 to −0.07; Edmonton Symptom Assessment Scale mean difference −10.30, against a clinically important difference of 5.7). When analyses were limited to the five trials at low risk of bias, the quality-of-life association was attenuated but remained significant (SMD 0.20, 0.06 to 0.34; FACIT-Pal 4.94 points — below the clinically important difference), while the symptom-burden association was no longer significant (SMD −0.21, −0.42 to 0.00). There was no association between palliative care and survival (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.17 — a relative measure). Palliative care was consistently associated with better advance care planning, patient and caregiver satisfaction, and lower healthcare utilisation. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: The gap between the all-trials estimate and the low-bias estimate is the story of this card: unblinded trials with subjective outcomes inflate effects, and on the stricter reading the average quality-of-life gain sits below the threshold patients can feel. The pooled trials also mix settings — the inpatient-specific randomised evidence is cards 2 and 3.
cards.source: Kavalieratos D et al. Association Between Palliative Care and Patient and Caregiver Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27893131. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: El-Jawahri 2016: inpatient palliative care during stem-cell transplant — quality of life fell less at week 2 (−14.7 vs −21.5 points), with less depression, anxiety and symptom burden
cards.summary: El-Jawahri 2016: inpatient palliative care during stem-cell transplant — quality of life fell less at week 2 (−14.7 vs −21.5 points), with less depression, anxiety and symptom burden
cards.people: Nonblinded randomised clinical trial at a single Boston hospital: 160 adults with haematologic malignancies undergoing autologous or allogeneic stem cell transplantation, and 94 caregivers. Intervention patients (81) were seen by palliative care clinicians at least twice a week during the transplant admission; standard-care patients (79) could request palliative care. Median hospital stay 21 days.
cards.result: The primary outcome — change in quality of life (FACT-BMT) from baseline to week 2 — favoured the intervention: quality of life fell by 14.72 points with inpatient palliative care versus 21.54 points with standard care (between-group difference in change 6.82 points in favour of the intervention; the abstract reports the difference as −6.82, 95% CI −13.48 to −0.16; P = .045). At week 2 the intervention group also had less increase in depression (P = .02), lower anxiety (P < .001) and less increase in symptom burden (P = .03), with no difference in fatigue (P = .09). At 3 months, quality of life remained higher (112.00 vs 106.66; P = .048) and depression lower (P = .002). Caregivers of intervention patients had a smaller increase in depression at week 2 (P = .03), with no difference in caregiver quality of life or anxiety. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02207322, from the record's databank fields.
cards.watchOut: Nonblinded, single-centre, and in one highly specialised population enduring an unusually toxic admission; the week-2 quality-of-life difference is statistically real but modest beside the size of the transplant-related decline itself, and usual-care patients could still request palliative care, which biases the contrast toward no effect.
cards.source: El-Jawahri A et al. Effect of Inpatient Palliative Care on Quality of Life 2 Weeks After Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27893130. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02207322, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: El-Jawahri 2025: the multisite replication — better week-2 quality of life, less depression and fewer PTSD symptoms, with the PTSD benefit sustained to 6 months
cards.summary: El-Jawahri 2025: the multisite replication — better week-2 quality of life, less depression and fewer PTSD symptoms, with the PTSD benefit sustained to 6 months
cards.people: Multisite randomised trial at three academic institutions: 360 adults undergoing autologous or allogeneic stem cell transplantation (68.7% of 524 eligible patients enrolled, October 2018 to July 2022) and their caregivers. Intervention patients met palliative care clinicians twice weekly during the transplant hospitalisation; usual-care patients could be referred to palliative care as standard.
cards.result: At week 2 — the quality-of-life nadir of transplant — the intervention group reported better quality of life (adjusted mean difference 6.3 points; P < .001), lower depression (adjusted difference −1.0; P = .026) and fewer post-traumatic stress symptoms (adjusted difference −1.9; P = .046); patient-reported anxiety did not differ significantly. In longitudinal analysis, intervention patients showed a steeper decline in PTSD symptoms over the 6 months after transplant (slope difference −0.9; P = .012); all other longitudinal outcomes, including quality of life, did not differ between groups. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03641378, from the record's databank fields.
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints the standard error for the week-2 quality-of-life difference as 0.1, implausibly small beside the effect size and the P value; the card relies on the difference and P value as printed and flags the standard error rather than correcting it. Otherwise: the durable benefit is narrow — PTSD symptoms only — and the population is again transplant patients, whose prolonged, symptom-dense admission may be unusually receptive to twice-weekly specialist visits.

usual-care patients could be referred to palliative care as standard. at week 2 — the quality-of-life nadir of transplant — the intervention group reported better quality of life (adjusted mean difference 6.3 points; p < .001), lower depression (adjusted difference −1.0; p = .026) and fewer post-traumatic stress symptoms (adjusted difference −1.9; p = .046); patient-reported anxiety did not differ significantly. in longitudinal analysis, intervention patients showed a steeper decline in ptsd symptoms over the 6 months after transplant (slope difference −0.9; p = .012); all other longitudinal outcomes, including quality of life, did not differ between groups. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct03641378, from the record's databank fields. the abstract prints the standard error for the week-2 quality-of-life difference as 0.1, implausibly small beside the effect size and the p value; cards.headline: Morrison 2008 (observational): palliative care consultation was associated with lower hospital costs — $1,696 saved per admission for patients discharged alive, $4,908 for those who died
cards.summary: Morrison 2008 (observational): palliative care consultation was associated with lower hospital costs — $1,696 saved per admission for patients discharged alive, $4,908 for those who died
cards.type: Propensity-matched observational study of hospital costs (Morrison 2008)
cards.people: Propensity-score-matched analysis of administrative data from 8 US hospitals with established palliative care consultation programmes, 2002–2004: 2,630 palliative care patients discharged alive matched to 18,427 usual care patients, and 2,278 palliative care patients who died matched to 2,124 usual care patients. This is an observational study, not a trial.
cards.result: Palliative care patients discharged alive had an adjusted net saving of $1,696 in direct costs per admission (P = .004) and $279 per day (P < .001), including significant reductions in laboratory and intensive care unit costs. Patients who died had an adjusted net saving of $4,908 per admission (P = .003) and $374 per day (P < .001), including reductions in pharmacy, laboratory and intensive care costs. Two confirmatory analyses — adding pre-consultation costs to the matching model, and projecting palliative care patients' costs as if unconsulted — gave similar or non-significantly different results. Registry ID: none in the record.
cards.watchOut: Propensity matching on administrative data cannot remove confounding by why a team was consulted — clinicians may consult palliative care precisely when they judge further intensive treatment unhelpful — so the savings are an association, plausibly overstated, and are a cost outcome, not evidence about quality of life. Data are from 2002–2004 at hospitals that already ran established programmes.
cards.source: Morrison RS et al. Cost savings associated with US hospital palliative care consultation programs. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2008. PMID: 18779466. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: inpatient palliative care improves quality of life modestly and reproducibly, with no survival effect — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: inpatient palliative care improves quality of life modestly and reproducibly, with no survival effect — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: One meta-analysis of 43 randomised trials (12,731 patients, mixed inpatient and outpatient settings), two randomised trials of twice-weekly inpatient palliative care in stem cell transplant patients (160 and 360 patients), and one propensity-matched cost study (8 hospitals).
cards.result: The quality-of-life direction is consistent across the meta-analysis and both inpatient trials, and the transplant trials show it at the hardest point of the admission; but the trustworthy size of the effect is the low-bias pooled estimate (standardised mean difference 0.20, below the clinically important difference on the FACIT-Pal scale), not the headline 0.46. Symptom-burden benefit is present in the full pool and not significant in low-bias trials. Survival shows no association (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.17), and this shelf makes no survival or mortality claim. Costs appear lower in observational data only. Early outpatient palliative care integrated with oncology (Temel 2010) is a separate model, carded on shelf #367; palliative care in advanced heart failure (PAL-HF) is on shelf #1990. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: Palliative care cannot be blinded, and its outcomes are patient-reported, so every estimate here carries performance and reporting bias risk; the shelf's calibration deliberately follows the low-bias subset of the meta-analysis rather than the pooled headline.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kavalieratos D et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 27893131); El-Jawahri A et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 27893130); El-Jawahri A et al. Journal of Clinical Oncology. 2025 (PMID: 40549982); Morrison RS et al. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2008 (PMID: 18779466).

shelves.title: I-PASS: a structured handoff bundle cut medical errors by about a quarter and preventable adverse events by about a third in its first multicentre test — and the harm reduction held up when the programme spread and when families were brought into it
shelves.question: Does implementing the I-PASS structured handoff programme — a standardised mnemonic, training, and faculty observation — reduce medical errors and preventable adverse events in hospital care?
shelves.mesh: Child · Child, Preschool · *Communication · Female · Humans · Internship and Residency/*organization & administration · Length of Stay · Male · Medical Errors/prevention & control/*statistics & numerical data · Organizational Case Studies · Patient Handoff/*standards · *Patient Safety · Pediatrics/education/organization & administration · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Workflow
shelves.balance: I-PASS is a named programme (like the MENOS CBT protocol, it is identified by its programme name because that is what was tested): a mnemonic structuring oral and written handoffs — Illness severity, Patient summary, Action list, Situation awareness and contingency planning, Synthesis by receiver — bundled with communication training, faculty development and observation, and a sustainability campaign. In the original nine-hospital study (Starmer 2014, PMID: 25372088), across 10,740 admissions the medical-error rate fell from 24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions (a 23% relative reduction) and preventable adverse events from 4.7 to 3.3 per 100 admissions (a 30% relative reduction), while nonpreventable adverse events did not change — the internal control that makes the before–after design believable — and handoffs took no longer (2.4 vs 2.5 minutes per patient). When the programme was implemented across 32 hospitals in multiple specialties (Starmer 2023, PMID: 36326255), resident-reported major handoff-related adverse events fell from 1.7 to 0.9 per person-year (47% relative) and minor events from 17.5 to 9.3. The family-centred version (Khan 2018, PMID: 30518517) is the honest complication: overall medical errors did not fall significantly (41.2 vs 35.8 per 1,000 patient-days, P=0.21), though harmful errors fell 37.9% in relative terms (20.7 to 12.9 per 1,000 patient-days, P=0.01) — and non-preventable events fell too, which warns that some of the improvement may be secular trend rather than programme. No study randomised hospitals. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (Tier C: all evidence is before–after).

cards.headline: Starmer 2014: across 10,740 admissions in nine hospitals, medical errors fell 23% in relative terms (24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions) and preventable adverse events 30% (4.7 to 3.3), with nonpreventable events unchanged
cards.summary: Starmer 2014: across 10,740 admissions in nine hospitals, medical errors fell 23% in relative terms (24.5 to 18.8 per 100 admissions) and preventable adverse events 30% (4.7 to 3.3), with nonpreventable events unchanged
cards.type: Prospective multicentre before–after intervention study (Starmer 2014, I-PASS)
cards.people: Prospective intervention study of a resident handoff-improvement programme in nine hospitals (paediatric residency programmes). The intervention combined the I-PASS mnemonic to standardise oral and written handoffs, handoff and communication training, a faculty development and observation programme, and a sustainability campaign. Errors were measured by active surveillance in 10,740 patient admissions; handoffs were assessed from printed documents and audio recordings; workflow by time-motion observation.
cards.result: The medical-error rate decreased by 23% in relative terms from the preintervention to the postintervention period (24.5 vs 18.8 per 100 admissions, P<0.001), and the rate of preventable adverse events decreased by 30% in relative terms (4.7 vs 3.3 events per 100 admissions, P<0.001). The rate of nonpreventable adverse events did not change significantly (3.0 and 2.8 per 100 admissions, P=0.79). Six of nine sites showed significant error reductions. Inclusion of all prespecified key elements in written and oral handoffs increased significantly, while oral handoff duration (2.4 vs 2.5 minutes per patient, P=0.55) and resident workflow did not change.
cards.watchOut: Before–after, not randomised: the unchanged rate of nonpreventable adverse events is the study's own best argument that the fall in preventable events is real rather than a drift in detection, but concurrent safety initiatives cannot be excluded. The setting is paediatric residency programmes; the error rates (roughly one error per four admissions) reflect intensive surveillance, not the rates a hospital's incident-report system would show.
cards.source: Starmer AJ et al. Changes in medical errors after implementation of a handoff program. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2014. PMID: 25372088. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Starmer 2023: in 32 hospitals across specialties, reported major handoff-related adverse events fell from 1.7 to 0.9 per person-year (47% relative) after I-PASS implementation, with handoff content transformed
cards.summary: Starmer 2023: in 32 hospitals across specialties, reported major handoff-related adverse events fell from 1.7 to 0.9 per person-year (47% relative) after I-PASS implementation, with handoff content transformed
cards.people: Prospective type 2 hybrid effectiveness–implementation study in 32 hospitals (12 community, 20 academic); 2,735 resident physicians and 760 faculty champions across internal medicine (16 programmes), paediatrics (13) and other specialties (3). External teams coached implementation of an enhanced I-PASS programme over 18 months. Outcomes: 1,942 resident error-surveillance reports and direct observation of 4,812 verbal and 1,787 written handoffs.
cards.result: Major handoff-related reported adverse events decreased 47% in relative terms after implementation (1.7 to 0.9 major events per person-year, p<0.05) and minor events fell from 17.5 to 9.3 per person-year (p<0.001). Inclusion of all five key handoff elements rose from 20% to 66% in verbal handoffs and from 10% to 74% in written handoffs (both p<0.001); high-quality verbal patient summaries rose from 39% to 81% and receiver synthesis from 31% to 83%. Improvement was similar in adult and paediatric settings and in community and academic hospitals.
cards.watchOut: The safety outcome here is resident-reported events — a softer measure than the 2014 study's active surveillance, and reporting itself can change when a programme teaches people what a handoff error is. The process measures (element inclusion, summary quality) are dramatic and directly observed; the harm reduction rests on the reports.
cards.source: Starmer AJ et al. Implementation of the I-PASS handoff program in diverse clinical environments: A multicenter prospective effectiveness implementation study. Journal of Hospital Medicine. 2023. PMID: 36326255. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Khan 2018 (Family-Centered I-PASS): overall medical errors did not fall significantly, but harmful errors fell 37.9% in relative terms (20.7 to 12.9 per 1,000 patient-days, P=0.01)
cards.summary: Khan 2018 (Family-Centered I-PASS): overall medical errors did not fall significantly, but harmful errors fell 37.9% in relative terms (20.7 to 12.9 per 1,000 patient-days, P=0.01)
cards.type: Prospective multicentre before–after study (Khan 2018, Family-Centered I-PASS)
cards.people: Prospective multicentre before–after study on paediatric inpatient units in seven North American hospitals: 3,106 admissions (13,171 patient-days), with 2,148 parents or caregivers, 435 nurses, 203 medical students and 586 residents. Families, nurses and physicians coproduced a structured family-centred rounds programme — high-reliability communication on bedside rounds, written real-time summaries, provider training — built on the I-PASS framework.
cards.result: The overall rate of medical errors was unchanged (41.2 (95% CI 31.2 to 54.5) pre-intervention vs 35.8 (26.9 to 47.7) per 1,000 patient-days post-intervention, P=0.21), but harmful errors (preventable adverse events) decreased by 37.9% in relative terms (20.7 (15.3 to 28.1) vs 12.9 (8.9 to 18.6), P=0.01). Non-preventable adverse events also decreased (12.6 vs 5.2, P=0.003). Family experience ratings improved on six of 25 components and worsened on none; family-centred rounds, family engagement and nurse engagement all increased; trainee teaching and rounds duration did not change significantly.
cards.watchOut: The fall in non-preventable adverse events — events the intervention should not be able to prevent — is the tell that some of the improvement may be temporal trend or surveillance drift rather than programme effect; the authors' own primary outcome (all medical errors) was null. This card tempers the shelf: the family-centred variant improved experience and communication clearly, and harmful errors on paper, but its causal claim is the weakest of the three.
cards.source: Khan A et al. Patient safety after implementation of a coproduced family centered communication programme: multicenter before and after intervention study. BMJ. 2018. PMID: 30518517. cards.headline: Synthesis: structured handoffs reduce errors in every test so far, by roughly a quarter to a third where harm is measured by surveillance — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: structured handoffs reduce errors in every test so far, by roughly a quarter to a third where harm is measured by surveillance — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Three multicentre before–after evaluations: the original programme (9 hospitals, 10,740 admissions, active surveillance), the spread study (32 hospitals, resident-reported events), and the family-centred variant (7 hospitals, 3,106 admissions).
cards.result: Medical errors −23% relative and preventable adverse events −30% relative in the original study, with nonpreventable events flat; reported major handoff-related events −47% relative on spread; harmful errors −37.9% relative in the family-centred study, whose overall error rate was unchanged (P=0.21). Handoff content and completeness improved by large, directly observed margins in all three, at no measured cost in time. No randomised comparison exists anywhere in this literature.
cards.watchOut: Every number on this shelf is a relative reduction from a before–after design in motivated academic centres with external coaching — the true effect in an average hospital implementing from a toolkit is likely smaller. What is actually being bought is a bundle (mnemonic plus training plus observation plus campaign); the mnemonic alone, laminated on a wall, has never been tested.
cards.source: Synthesis of Starmer AJ et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2014 (PMID: 25372088); Starmer AJ et al. Journal of Hospital Medicine. 2023 (PMID: 36326255); Khan A et al. BMJ. 2018 (PMID: 30518517).

shelves.title: FIRST and iCOMPARE: letting residency programmes flex shift-length rules did not worsen patient outcomes — death and serious complications in surgery, 30-day mortality in internal medicine — and interns slept no less
shelves.question: For resident physicians, do flexible duty-hour policies — no limits on shift length or on time off between shifts, within the 80-hour week — worsen patient outcomes or resident sleep, compared with the standard ACGME duty-hour rules?
shelves.mesh: Accreditation · Continuity of Patient Care · Education, Medical, Graduate/standards · Fatigue · General Surgery/*education · Hospital Administration · Humans · Internship and Residency/*organization & administration · *Job Satisfaction · Patient Safety · Personnel Staffing and Scheduling · Postoperative Complications/*epidemiology/mortality · Surgical Procedures, Operative/mortality · United States · Work Schedule Tolerance · Workload/*standards
shelves.balance: Two national cluster-randomised noninferiority trials asked whether the specific 2011 ACGME limits on shift length and time between shifts are load-bearing for safety. In surgery (FIRST; Bilimoria 2016, PMID: 26836220), 117 programmes were randomised to standard or flexible policies; among 138,691 patients, the 30-day rate of death or serious complications was 9.1% under flexible policies versus 9.0% under standard policies (P=0.92), with noninferiority satisfied, and residents in flexible programmes reported leaving operations (7.0% vs 13.2%) and handing off active issues (32.0% vs 46.3%) less often, with no significant difference in satisfaction with education or well-being. In internal medicine (iCOMPARE; Silber 2019, PMID: 30855740), 63 programmes were randomised; the change in 30-day mortality was noninferior under flexible rules (the upper limit of the one-sided 95% CI for the difference in change, 0.93 percentage points, sat below the 1-point margin), though noninferiority was not met for 30-day readmissions or prolonged stay. The companion sleep study (Basner 2019, PMID: 30855741) measured what the rules are supposed to protect: interns in flexible programmes slept 6.85 versus 7.03 hours per 24 hours — noninferior, as was morning sleepiness — but noninferiority was not established for objective alertness on psychomotor vigilance testing. The fair reading: the shift-length rules, specifically, are not what stands between patients and harm in these systems; the trials do not test abolishing the 80-hour week, which both kept. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference to patient outcomes) (Tier C: mortality is a primary outcome of both trials).

cards.headline: Bilimoria 2016 (FIRST): death or serious complications in 9.1% of surgical patients under flexible duty-hour policies versus 9.0% under standard policies — noninferior, across 138,691 patients
cards.summary: Bilimoria 2016 (FIRST): death or serious complications in 9.1% of surgical patients under flexible duty-hour policies versus 9.0% under standard policies — noninferior, across 138,691 patients
cards.people: National cluster-randomised pragmatic noninferiority trial: 117 US general surgery residency programmes (2014–15 academic year) assigned to current ACGME duty-hour policies or to flexible policies waiving maximum shift length and time-off-between-shifts rules. Patient outcomes in 138,691 patients; perceptions surveyed in 4,330 residents.
cards.result: Flexible policies were not associated with an increased rate of death or serious complications within 30 days (9.1% flexible vs 9.0% standard, P=0.92; unadjusted odds ratio 0.96, 92% CI 0.87 to 1.06; P=0.44; noninferiority criteria satisfied), nor with any secondary postoperative outcome. Residents in flexible programmes did not report significantly greater dissatisfaction with overall education quality (11.0% vs 10.7%, P=0.86) or well-being (14.9% vs 12.0%, P=0.10); they were less likely to report leaving during an operation (7.0% vs 13.2%, P<0.001) or handing off active patient issues (32.0% vs 46.3%, P<0.001), and perceived fewer negative effects on continuity and professionalism, but more negative effects on personal activities.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority within a prespecified margin is not proof of identity — the confidence interval (odds ratio up to 1.06) admits a small harm. Programmes volunteered for a trial about flexibility, the intervention kept the 80-hour cap and all other rules, and resident well-being is self-reported perception, not measured health.
cards.source: Bilimoria KY et al. National Cluster-Randomized Trial of Duty-Hour Flexibility in Surgical Training. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2016. PMID: 26836220. Registry ID: NCT02050789. cards.headline: Silber 2019 (iCOMPARE): the change in 30-day mortality under flexible internal-medicine duty hours was noninferior to standard rules — but noninferiority was not met for 30-day readmissions or prolonged stay
cards.summary: Silber 2019 (iCOMPARE): the change in 30-day mortality under flexible internal-medicine duty hours was noninferior to standard rules — but noninferiority was not met for 30-day readmissions or prolonged stay
cards.people: Cluster-randomised noninferiority trial in 63 US internal-medicine residency programmes (2015–16 academic year), randomised to standard 2011 ACGME duty hours or flexible rules with no specified limits on shift length or mandatory time off between shifts. Primary outcome: change in unadjusted 30-day mortality from the pretrial year to the trial year (Medicare claims), analysed as a difference-in-differences against a 1-percentage-point noninferiority margin.
cards.result: Thirty-day mortality in flexible programmes moved from 12.6% (pretrial year) to 12.5% (trial year), versus 12.7% to 12.2% in standard programmes; the test for noninferiority was significant (P=0.03), with the upper limit of the one-sided 95% CI for the between-group difference in change (0.93%) below the 1-percentage-point margin. Differences in change for 7-day readmission, patient safety indicators and Medicare payments were also below 1 percentage point, but the noninferiority criterion was not met for 30-day readmissions or prolonged length of stay. Risk-adjusted measures generally showed similar findings.
cards.watchOut: The headline is a difference-in-differences against a 1-point margin on a ~12.5% mortality base — the trial excludes a large mortality penalty, not a small one, and two secondary outcomes (30-day readmission, prolonged stay) failed their noninferiority tests, which the conclusions do not hide. Medicare claims capture older patients; outcomes for younger inpatients are outside the primary analysis.
cards.source: Silber JH et al. Patient Safety Outcomes under Flexible and Standard Resident Duty-Hour Rules. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30855740. Registry ID: NCT02274818. cards.headline: Basner 2019 (iCOMPARE sleep study): interns in flexible programmes slept 6.85 versus 7.03 hours per 24 hours (noninferior) and were no sleepier — but noninferiority was not established for objective alertness
cards.summary: Basner 2019 (iCOMPARE sleep study): interns in flexible programmes slept 6.85 versus 7.03 hours per 24 hours (noninferior) and were no sleepier — but noninferiority was not established for objective alertness
cards.type: Randomised trial sleep and alertness substudy (Basner 2019, iCOMPARE)
cards.people: Sleep substudy of the iCOMPARE trial: actigraphy, sleepiness scores and brief psychomotor vigilance testing over 14 days in 205 interns at six flexible-policy programmes and 193 interns at six standard-policy programmes. Noninferiority margins: −0.5 hours for sleep duration, 1 point on the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (1–9), 1 lapse on the PVT-B.
cards.result: Average sleep per 24 hours was 6.85 hours (95% CI 6.61 to 7.10) in flexible programmes versus 7.03 hours (6.78 to 7.27) in standard programmes — a between-group difference of −0.17 hours, with the one-sided lower 95% confidence limit (−0.45) inside the −0.5-hour margin (P=0.02 for noninferiority). Morning sleepiness was also noninferior (difference 0.12 points; upper limit 0.31; margin 1 point; P<0.001). Noninferiority was not established for alertness on the PVT-B (difference −0.3 lapses; one-sided upper limit 1.6 lapses; margin 1 lapse; P=0.10).
cards.watchOut: This is a second report of the same trial as the Silber card (same registry number, NCT02274818), not an independent replication. Both groups slept under 7.1 hours — the trial shows flexibility did not make a short-sleep reality worse, not that either schedule delivers enough sleep; and the one objective performance measure, vigilance lapses, is exactly where noninferiority failed.
cards.source: Basner M et al. Sleep and Alertness in a Duty-Hour Flexibility Trial in Internal Medicine. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 30855741. Registry ID: NCT02274818. cards.headline: Synthesis: two national cluster trials agree — shift-length flexibility within the 80-hour week did not worsen patient outcomes — LIKELY (no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two national cluster trials agree — shift-length flexibility within the 80-hour week did not worsen patient outcomes — LIKELY (no difference)
cards.people: FIRST: 117 surgical programmes, 138,691 patients, 4,330 residents surveyed. iCOMPARE: 63 internal-medicine programmes, Medicare 30-day mortality as primary outcome, with a 398-intern actigraphy substudy.
cards.result: Death or serious complications after surgery: 9.1% versus 9.0%. Change in 30-day mortality in internal medicine: noninferior within a 1-percentage-point margin (upper CI 0.93%). Intern sleep: 6.85 versus 7.03 hours per 24 hours, noninferior; sleepiness noninferior; psychomotor vigilance noninferiority not established. Residents under flexibility handed off less and left operations less. The evidence supports programme-level flexibility about shift length; it is silent on total hours, which neither trial changed.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are noninferiority designs run in programmes that volunteered, in one country's training system, over single academic years; 'no worse within the margin' is the claim, and the margins (especially iCOMPARE's 1 point on mortality) are wide enough to matter at national scale. Longer-horizon outcomes — resident burnout careers, education depth, rare catastrophic fatigue events — are outside both trials' reach.

shelves.title: Two weeks versus four after the washout: 99% cured on the short course in native joint arthritis — but two-thirds of the joints were hands and wrists
shelves.question: In adults with native joint bacterial arthritis treated with surgical drainage, are 2 weeks of antibiotics as effective as 4 weeks for remission?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage*/pharmacology · Arthritis, Infectious/drug therapy*/microbiology/surgery* · Databases, Factual · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drainage/methods* · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Hand Joints/drug effects/physiopathology · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Hospitals, University · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Wrist Joint/drug effects/physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one prospective randomised non-inferiority trial (Gjika E et al., PMID: 30992295) asked the duration question after surgical drainage of native joint bacterial arthritis and found almost nothing separating the courses: among 154 cases (77 per arm), recurrence occurred in 3 patients in total — cure 99% on 2 weeks versus 97% on 4 weeks — with no difference in adverse events or sequelae, and a significantly shorter hospital stay on the shorter course. The catch is the case mix: 99 of the 154 cases were hand and wrist infections, where the per-protocol subgroup analysis likewise found cure of 97% versus 96% but sequelae in about half of patients either way (50% vs 55%). No systematic review of antibiotic duration in native joint arthritis was found to corroborate the trial, so the shelf stands on this single study: after adequate surgical lavage, two weeks of targeted therapy looks sufficient for hand and wrist septic arthritis, and is unproven — not disproven — for large joints. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the shorter course halves antibiotic exposure without a measured cure cost, within the population actually studied.

cards.headline: Gjika 2019: 2 weeks cured 99% versus 97% on 4 weeks after surgical drainage — three recurrences in 154 cases, and a shorter hospital stay
cards.summary: Gjika 2019: 2 weeks cured 99% versus 97% on 4 weeks after surgical drainage — three recurrences in 154 cases, and a shorter hospital stay
cards.people: 154 adult cases of native joint bacterial arthritis treated with surgical drainage at a university hospital, randomised prospectively (77 per arm) to 2 or 4 weeks of antibiotic therapy after drainage; implant-related infections, episodes without surgical lavage, and follow-up under 2 months were excluded. Median intravenous treatment was 1 day in the 2-week arm and 2 days in the 4-week arm; the median number of surgical lavages was 1 in both arms. Of the 154 cases, 99 concerned the hand and wrist.
cards.result: Recurrence of infection occurred in 3 patients (2%) overall: 1 in the 2-week arm (99% cure rate) and 2 in the 4-week arm (97% cure rate). There was no difference in adverse events or sequelae between arms, and the 2-week arm had a significantly shorter hospital stay. In the hand-and-wrist per-protocol subgroup, the same three recurrences appeared (cure 97% on 2 weeks, 96% on 4 weeks), with sequelae in 50% versus 55% of patients, of which 13% in each arm needed further interventions. The authors conclude 2 weeks of targeted therapy after initial surgical lavage is not inferior to 4 weeks, at least for hand and wrist arthritis.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, single-centre, and dominated by hand and wrist infections (99 of 154) — small joints that are drained early and thoroughly. Three recurrences in total means the trial cannot exclude a clinically important difference in either direction for knees, hips or shoulders, and it says nothing about joints that were not surgically lavaged, implant infections (excluded), or patients whose organism or immune state makes relapse likelier. Sequelae affected about half of patients regardless of duration — duration was not the lever for function.
cards.source: Gjika E et al. Two weeks versus four weeks of antibiotic therapy after surgical drainage for native joint bacterial arthritis: a prospective, randomised, non-inferiority trial. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2019. PMID: 30992295. Registry ID: NCT03615781.
