cards.headline: Synthesis: after good surgical drainage, two weeks matched four on cure in the only randomised test — a hand-and-wrist answer that large joints have not yet been given
cards.summary: Synthesis: after good surgical drainage, two weeks matched four on cure in the only randomised test — a hand-and-wrist answer that large joints have not yet been given
cards.people: One prospective randomised non-inferiority trial: 154 drained native joint infections in adults (77 per arm), 99 of them hand or wrist, with a median of one surgical lavage and only 1–2 days of intravenous therapy.
cards.result: Cure 99% (2 weeks) vs 97% (4 weeks); recurrences 1 vs 2; adverse events and sequelae not different; hospital stay significantly shorter on 2 weeks. Hand/wrist subgroup: cure 97% vs 96%, sequelae 50% vs 55%. No corroborating systematic review of duration in native joint arthritis was found. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The honest boundary of this shelf is anatomical: it is a small-joint result. Extending 'two weeks is enough' to a drained knee or hip is an extrapolation the trial's numbers (three recurrences, mostly fingers) cannot carry, and prosthetic joint infection is a different question entirely (shelf #2223 covers duration there). Tier C is set because the evidence is one unblinded single-centre trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gjika E et al. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2019 (PMID: 30992295).

shelves.title: Five days was not enough for the under-twos: clinical failure 34% on the short course versus 16% on ten days of amoxicillin-clavulanate
shelves.question: In young children with acute otitis media, does a shortened 5-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate produce worse outcomes than the standard 10-day course?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Amoxicillin-Potassium Clavulanate Combination/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Anti-Infective Agents/administration & dosage*/adverse effects · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Resistance, Bacterial · Female · Haemophilus influenzae/isolation & purification · Humans · Infant · Male · Nasopharynx/microbiology · Otitis Media/drug therapy* · Prognosis · Streptococcus pneumoniae/isolation & purification · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — in the youngest children, the short course lost. Hoberman A et al. (PMID: 28002709) randomised 520 children aged 6 to 23 months with rigorously diagnosed acute otitis media to 5 days of amoxicillin-clavulanate (then 5 days of placebo) or the standard 10 days, and clinical failure was twice as common on the short course: 34% (77/229) versus 16% (39/238), a difference of 17 percentage points (95% CI 9 to 25). The shorter regimen bought nothing in exchange — no significant difference in recurrence, adverse events, or nasopharyngeal colonisation with penicillin-nonsusceptible pathogens. The older meta-analysis (Kozyrskyj AL et al., PMID: 9624028) had found 5-day courses broadly comparable by 20 to 30 days in children aged 4 weeks to 18 years (odds ratio 1.22, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.54) — but its children were older, its diagnoses less strict, and even it found more early failures on short courses (OR 1.52 at 8 to 19 days). The two records reconcile by age and diagnostic certainty: shortening is a gamble that the under-twos, diagnosed strictly, demonstrably lose. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): in children 6 to 23 months old with certain acute otitis media, cutting amoxicillin-clavulanate to 5 days worsens outcomes without reducing resistance or side effects.

cards.headline: Hoberman 2016: 5 days failed twice as often as 10 days in children 6–23 months — clinical failure 34% vs 16% (difference 17 points)
cards.summary: Hoberman 2016: 5 days failed twice as often as 10 days in children 6–23 months — clinical failure 34% vs 16% (difference 17 points)
cards.people: 520 children aged 6 to 23 months with acute otitis media diagnosed by strict criteria, randomised to amoxicillin-clavulanate for the standard 10 days or a reduced 5 days followed by 5 days of placebo; clinical response was measured systematically from signs and symptom scores (0 to 14), with recurrence and nasopharyngeal colonisation also assessed, analysed on a non-inferiority approach. Outcome data: 229 children in the 5-day group and 238 in the 10-day group.
cards.result: Clinical failure occurred in 34% (77/229) on 5 days versus 16% (39/238) on 10 days (difference 17 percentage points, 95% CI 9 to 25) — non-inferiority was not approached. Mean symptom scores from day 6 to 14 were 1.61 versus 1.34 (P=0.07), and at the day-12-to-14 assessment 1.89 versus 1.20 (P=0.001); the share whose symptom scores fell by more than 50% was 80% (181/227) versus 91% (211/233) (P=0.003). There were no significant differences in recurrence, adverse events, or nasopharyngeal colonisation with penicillin-nonsusceptible pathogens. Failure was more likely with exposure to three or more children for 10 or more hours weekly (P=0.02) and with infection in both ears (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The population is the narrow, high-risk end of otitis media: under-twos with stringently diagnosed, often bilateral disease, treated with amoxicillin-clavulanate. The result does not settle duration for older children, for milder or uncertain diagnoses, or for other antibiotics — and it does not reopen whether antibiotics are needed at all in such children (shelf #253, Hoberman 2011, answers that: they are, in this age group). Funded by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases.

cards.headline: Kozyrskyj 1998 meta-analysis: 5-day courses looked comparable by 20–30 days in older, broadly diagnosed children (OR 1.22) — but worse early (OR 1.52 at 8–19 days)
cards.summary: Kozyrskyj 1998 meta-analysis: 5-day courses looked comparable by 20–30 days in older, broadly diagnosed children (OR 1.22) — but worse early (OR 1.52 at 8–19 days)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 30 randomised trials of antibiotic duration in acute otitis media in children aged 4 weeks to 18 years, grouped by the short-course drug: 15 trials of short-acting oral antibiotics (including amoxicillin with or without clavulanate), 4 of intramuscular ceftriaxone, and 11 of oral azithromycin; short courses were under 7 days versus 7 days or more.
cards.result: For 5 days versus 8 to 10 days of short-acting antibiotics, the summary odds ratio for treatment failure, relapse or reinfection was 1.52 (95% CI 1.17 to 1.98) at 8 to 19 days, but 1.22 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.54) at 20 to 30 days; the risk difference at 20 to 30 days was 2.3% (95% CI −0.2% to 4.9%), implying 44 children treated with the long course to avoid one failure, and comparability held to 3 months (OR 1.16, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.50). Ceftriaxone and azithromycin short courses were comparable to at least 7 days of other antibiotics. The authors concluded 5 days of short-acting antibiotics is effective for uncomplicated acute otitis media in children.
cards.watchOut: Published in 1998, before pneumococcal conjugate vaccination reshaped otitis media, and pooling children up to 18 years old with variably strict diagnoses — its reassuring average can hide exactly the subgroup Hoberman later isolated: the under-twos with certain, severe disease. Its own early-outcome signal (OR 1.52) already pointed the way Hoberman's trial confirmed.
cards.source: Kozyrskyj AL et al. Treatment of acute otitis media with a shortened course of antibiotics: a meta-analysis. JAMA. 1998. PMID: 9624028. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: shortening failed its strictest test — in under-twos with certain otitis media, 5 days doubled failure and bought no resistance or safety advantage
cards.summary: Synthesis: shortening failed its strictest test — in under-twos with certain otitis media, 5 days doubled failure and bought no resistance or safety advantage
cards.people: One randomised trial in 520 children aged 6 to 23 months with strictly diagnosed acute otitis media (amoxicillin-clavulanate 5 vs 10 days), read against a 30-trial meta-analysis spanning ages 4 weeks to 18 years.
cards.result: Strict trial: clinical failure 34% vs 16% (difference 17 points, 95% CI 9 to 25); symptom resolution slower; recurrence, adverse events and resistant colonisation not different. Older pooled evidence: early failure OR 1.52 (1.17 to 1.98), settling to OR 1.22 (0.98 to 1.54) by 20–30 days in a broader, older population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) for the 5-day course in this age group.
cards.watchOut: Do not generalise the harm stamp beyond its ground: it belongs to children under two with rigorously diagnosed acute otitis media on amoxicillin-clavulanate. For older children with uncomplicated disease, the older pooled evidence remains the best available and is far more forgiving of 5 days. Tier C is set because the modern direct evidence is a single trial in one age band.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hoberman A et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2016 (PMID: 28002709); Kozyrskyj AL et al. JAMA. 1998 (PMID: 9624028).

shelves.title: Switching suppressed HIV patients to the doravirine single tablet: suppression held in the one DRIVE-SHIFT trial, with better lipids for those leaving a boosted protease inhibitor
shelves.question: In virologically suppressed adults with HIV-1, does switching to doravirine/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil maintain suppression versus continuing the current regimen?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Retroviral Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use* · Equivalence Trials as Topic · Female · HIV-1/drug effects* · Humans · Lamivudine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use* · Male · Middle Aged · Protease Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Pyridones/administration & dosage/therapeutic use* · Quinolones/therapeutic use · Ritonavir/therapeutic use · Tenofovir/administration & dosage/therapeutic use* · Treatment Outcome · Triazoles/administration & dosage/therapeutic use* · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the single DRIVE-SHIFT trial, switching suppressed adults to once-daily doravirine/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate maintained suppression: 93.7% versus 94.6% still below 50 copies/mL at week 24 against continuing the baseline regimen (difference −0.9, 95% CI −4.7 to 3.0), and 90.8% at week 48 met non-inferiority against the baseline regimen's week-24 result. In participants switching from a boosted protease inhibitor, fasting lipids fell significantly more. The costs: adverse events were more frequent after switching by week 24 (68.9% vs 52.5%) and discontinuation for adverse events was 2.5% versus 0.4%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): switching maintains suppression in this one trial, with a lipid gain for protease-inhibitor switchers and a small early tolerability price. Tier C is set because this is a single trial.

cards.headline: Johnson 2019 (DRIVE-SHIFT): switching to doravirine combination maintained suppression — 93.7% vs 94.6% at week 24, 90.8% at week 48
cards.summary: Johnson 2019 (DRIVE-SHIFT): switching to doravirine combination maintained suppression — 93.7% vs 94.6% at week 24, 90.8% at week 48
cards.type: Randomised open-label non-inferiority switch trial (DRIVE-SHIFT, Johnson 2019)
cards.people: 670 adults with HIV-1 virologically suppressed for at least 6 months on two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors plus a boosted protease inhibitor, boosted elvitegravir, or a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, randomised 2:1 (447 switch, 223 continue) in an open-label, active-controlled non-inferiority trial.
cards.result: At week 24, 93.7% on doravirine/lamivudine/tenofovir disoproxil fumarate versus 94.6% on the baseline regimen had HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL [difference −0.9 (95% CI −4.7 to 3.0)]. At week 48, 90.8% on the doravirine combination had HIV-1 RNA below 50 copies/mL, demonstrating non-inferiority versus the baseline regimen at week 24 [difference −3.8 (−7.9 to 0.3); margin −8%]. In participants on a ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitor at entry, mean reductions in fasting LDL cholesterol and non-HDL cholesterol at week 24 were significantly greater after switching (P < 0.0001). Adverse events occurred in 68.9% (switch) and 52.5% (continue) by week 24, leading to discontinuation in 2.5% and 0.4% respectively.
cards.watchOut: The primary week-48 comparison is against the control group's week-24 result — a design that flatters the switch arm — and the trial was open-label, so the higher adverse-event rate after switching (68.9% vs 52.5%) may partly reflect expectation. Participants were stably suppressed volunteers, the easiest switch population there is.
cards.source: Johnson M et al. Switching to Doravirine/Lamivudine/Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (DOR/3TC/TDF) Maintains HIV-1 Virologic Suppression Through 48 Weeks: Results of the DRIVE-SHIFT Trial. Journal of acquired immune deficiency syndromes (1999). 2019. PMID: 30985556. Registry ID: NCT02397096. cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, suppression maintained after switch, lipids better for protease-inhibitor switchers, slightly more adverse events early

shelves.title: Hepatitis C treatment with almost no monitoring: 95% cured in the single-arm MINMON study — feasibility demonstrated, equivalence to monitored care untested
shelves.question: In adults with chronic hepatitis C, does a minimal-monitoring direct-acting antiviral approach (no scheduled on-treatment visits or labs) achieve cure rates comparable to standard monitored care?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Antiviral Agents/adverse effects · Genotype · Hepacivirus/genetics · Hepatitis C*/drug therapy · Hepatitis C, Chronic*/drug therapy · Humans · RNA/therapeutic use · Sofosbuvir/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — MINMON was a single-arm phase 4 study: 399 people with hepatitis C across five countries took 12 weeks of sofosbuvir-velpatasvir with no pre-treatment genotyping, the whole course dispensed at entry, no scheduled on-treatment visits or laboratory monitoring, and only remote contacts at weeks 4 and 22. Overall 379 of 399 (95.0%, 95% CI 92.4 to 96.7) achieved sustained virological response, 89% of those assessed reported taking 100% of the medication, serious adverse events occurred in 4% (none treatment-related), and only 4% had unplanned visits (none treatment-related). Those cure figures resemble standard monitored care in real-world data — but resemblance is not a comparison: with no control arm, the study cannot show minimal monitoring costs nothing, only that high cure is achievable under it in trial-supported conditions. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): minimal monitoring is feasible and achieved 95% cure in this cohort; equivalence to monitored care is unproven. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single-arm study.

cards.headline: Solomon 2022 (MINMON): 95.0% cured with no genotyping, no scheduled visits, and no on-treatment labs — in a single-arm study of 399 people
cards.summary: Solomon 2022 (MINMON): 95.0% cured with no genotyping, no scheduled visits, and no on-treatment labs — in a single-arm study of 399 people
cards.type: Phase 4 open-label single-arm trial (MINMON / ACTG A5360, Solomon 2022)
cards.people: 400 adults enrolled (399 initiated treatment) with active hepatitis C virus infection (HCV RNA above 1000 IU/mL), treatment-naive, at 38 sites in Brazil, South Africa, Thailand, Uganda, and the USA; people with compensated cirrhosis and HIV/HCV co-infection were included with capped enrolment. All received oral sofosbuvir 400 mg and velpatasvir 100 mg once daily for 12 weeks under the minimal-monitoring approach: no pre-treatment genotyping, all 84 tablets dispensed at entry, no scheduled visits or laboratory monitoring, and remote contact at week 4 (adherence) and week 22 (to schedule outcome assessment).
cards.result: Sustained virological response was achieved by 379 of 399 participants who initiated treatment (95.0%, 95% CI 92.4 to 96.7), using a missing-equals-failure analysis. At the outcome visit, 355 (89%) of 397 participants reported taking 100% of the trial medication. Serious adverse events were reported by 14 (4%) of 397 participants between treatment initiation and week 28; none were treatment-related or led to discontinuation or death. Unplanned visits occurred in 15 (4%) of 399 participants; none were treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: No comparator arm: the 95% cure rate is set against historical and real-world expectations, not against monitored care in the same population. Trial entry still involved screening, a dispensing visit, and a study team reachable for unplanned visits — a thinner safety net than 'no care at all', and decompensated cirrhosis was outside the studied population.
cards.source: Solomon SS et al. A minimal monitoring approach for the treatment of hepatitis C virus infection (ACTG A5360 [MINMON]): a phase 4, open-label, single-arm trial. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022. PMID: 35026142. Registry ID: NCT03512210. cards.headline: Synthesis: minimal monitoring achieved standard-looking cure rates (95.0%) in one single-arm study — feasibility shown, equivalence not tested
cards.summary: Synthesis: minimal monitoring achieved standard-looking cure rates (95.0%) in one single-arm study — feasibility shown, equivalence not tested
cards.people: 399 treated adults with hepatitis C across 38 sites in five countries, all under the minimal-monitoring approach (MINMON).
cards.result: Sustained virological response 95.0% (95% CI 92.4 to 96.7); 89% reported complete adherence; serious adverse events 4%, none treatment-related; unplanned visits 4%, none treatment-related. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The patients most likely to need monitoring — advanced liver disease, interacting medicines, adherence difficulty — are exactly those a single-arm average can hide. Programmes adopting minimal monitoring still need a route back into care for the minority who fail or deteriorate unseen. Tier C is set because the evidence is a single-arm study without a monitored comparison group.
cards.source: Synthesis of Solomon SS et al. The lancet. Gastroenterology & hepatology. 2022 (PMID: 35026142).

shelves.balance: MI FREEE (Choudhry NK et al., PMID: 22080794) randomised insurance-plan sponsors — 1,494 sponsors with 2,845 patients to full coverage and 1,486 with 3,010 patients to usual coverage — so that after myocardial infarction, statins, beta-blockers, and ACE inhibitors or ARBs cost patients nothing. Adherence, poor at baseline (35.9–49.0% under usual coverage), rose by 4 to 6 percentage points with full coverage (P < 0.001 for all comparisons). The event record splits: the primary outcome — first major vascular event or revascularisation — did not significantly differ (17.6 vs 18.8 per 100 person-years; HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.04; P = 0.21), yet total major vascular events or revascularisation were significantly reduced (21.5 vs 23.3 per 100 person-years; HR 0.89; P = 0.03), as was the rate of first major vascular events alone (11.0 vs 12.8; HR 0.86, 0.74 to 0.99; P = 0.03), and total spending did not rise ($66,008 vs $71,778; P = 0.68) while patient costs fell. A systematic review of cost-sharing interventions (Sensharma A et al., PMID: 30628493) generalises the adherence half of that story: across 28 studies, removing or reducing out-of-pocket costs usually improved adherence modestly, with higher plan drug spending generally offset by lower non-drug medical spending. PROPOSED SPLIT: free medicines after a heart attack are an adherence intervention with a real but modest clinical dividend — significant on several event measures, null on the one the trial named primary — and they pay for themselves in this record mainly by shifting, not shrinking, costs.

cards.headline: Choudhry 2011 (MI FREEE): adherence up 4–6 points and first major vascular events down (HR 0.86) — but the primary outcome was null (HR 0.93, P = 0.21) and total spending unchanged
cards.summary: Choudhry 2011 (MI FREEE): adherence up 4–6 points and first major vascular events down (HR 0.86) — but the primary outcome was null (HR 0.93, P = 0.21) and total spending unchanged
cards.people: 5,855 patients discharged after myocardial infarction, randomised by insurance-plan sponsor (1,494 sponsors / 2,845 patients to full prescription coverage; 1,486 sponsors / 3,010 patients to usual coverage) for all statins, beta-blockers, angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors, or angiotensin-receptor blockers; primary outcome was the first major vascular event or revascularisation.
cards.result: Adherence rates were 35.9–49.0% in the usual-coverage group and 4 to 6 percentage points higher in the full-coverage group (P < 0.001 for all comparisons). The primary outcome did not significantly differ: 17.6 per 100 person-years with full coverage versus 18.8 with usual coverage (HR 0.93, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.04; P = 0.21). Total major vascular events or revascularisation were significantly reduced (21.5 vs 23.3 per 100 person-years; HR 0.89; P = 0.03), as was the first major vascular event (11.0 vs 12.8 per 100 person-years; HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.99; P = 0.03). Total spending was not increased ($66,008 full coverage vs $71,778 usual; relative spending 0.89, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.56; P = 0.68), and patient costs fell (relative spending 0.74, 0.68 to 0.80; P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Randomisation was by plan sponsor, not patient, in one US insurer's population, and even with medicines free, adherence stayed below half for some drug classes — cost is only one of the reasons people stop. The significant secondary event results sit beside a null primary outcome and multiple comparisons; the trial's own conclusion is the careful one, that the primary outcome was not significantly reduced. One confidence interval in the record's abstract is internally inconsistent and is not quoted on this card.
cards.source: Choudhry NK et al. Full coverage for preventive medications after myocardial infarction. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2011. PMID: 22080794. Registry ID: NCT00566774. cards.headline: Sensharma 2019 (28 studies of cost-sharing interventions): adherence usually improved, but modestly and unevenly — patient costs fell, plan drug costs rose, and medical savings generally compensated
cards.summary: Sensharma 2019 (28 studies of cost-sharing interventions): adherence usually improved, but modestly and unevenly — patient costs fell, plan drug costs rose, and medical savings generally compensated
cards.people: 28 published studies covering 22 distinct interventions that addressed patient cost-sharing for prescription drugs in the United States, most published in or after 2010, reviewed for effects on medication adherence and on drug and non-drug health-care costs.
cards.result: Many interventions were associated with improved adherence compared with controls, but effects were modest and varied across drug classes; in some studies adherence merely held stable in the intervention group while declining in controls. Patient out-of-pocket costs generally declined (usually by the design of the intervention, such as eliminating copayments), health-plan prescription-drug costs increased accordingly, and in studies reporting both, lower non-drug medical spending generally compensated for the increased drug spending. The authors frame value-based financial-incentive models as promising but in need of continued evaluation.
cards.watchOut: This is a narrative systematic review without a pooled effect size in the record, spanning many drug classes and benefit designs — it supports the direction of the adherence effect, not its size in any one disease. 'Generally compensated' on costs is a qualitative summary across heterogeneous studies, not a guarantee for a given plan.
cards.source: Sensharma A et al. Do interventions that address patient cost-sharing improve adherence to prescription drugs? A systematic review of recently published studies. Expert Review of Pharmacoeconomics & Outcomes Research. 2019. PMID: 30628493. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: free post-MI medicines buy a modest adherence gain and a split event record — better adherence and fewer first events, a null primary outcome, and no net spending increase
cards.summary: Synthesis: free post-MI medicines buy a modest adherence gain and a split event record — better adherence and fewer first events, a null primary outcome, and no net spending increase
cards.people: One 5,855-patient cluster-randomised trial of full coverage after myocardial infarction, plus a 28-study systematic review of cost-sharing interventions for prescription-drug adherence.
cards.result: Adherence: +4 to 6 percentage points from a 35.9–49.0% base (MI FREEE); 'modest and varied' gains across the wider literature (Sensharma 2019). Events: primary outcome HR 0.93 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.04), null; first major vascular event HR 0.86 (0.74 to 0.99); total events HR 0.89, P = 0.03. Costs: total spending unchanged (P = 0.68), patient spending down. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit on adherence and several event measures, no significant effect on the primary outcome.
cards.watchOut: A SPLIT stamp here is about outcomes within one trial, not about subgroups: the same patients got the adherence gain and the null primary result. Policy readers should also note what free coverage did not do — it left adherence below 50% for some classes, so copayment elimination is a floor-raiser for access, not a solution to post-MI non-adherence on its own. Tier C is set because the event evidence is a single trial programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Choudhry NK et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2011 (PMID: 22080794); Sensharma A et al. Expert Review of Pharmacoeconomics & Outcomes Research. 2019 (PMID: 30628493).

shelves.title: Video-observed tuberculosis therapy: 70% versus 31% of patients hit the observation target by phone video — superior on being watched, with treatment-outcome equivalence resting on the wider review, not this trial
shelves.question: In adults with drug-sensitive tuberculosis, does smartphone video-observed therapy achieve treatment observation and completion non-inferior or superior to clinic-based directly observed therapy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Clinical Protocols · Directly Observed Therapy/standards* · England/epidemiology · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis/methods · London/epidemiology · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Self Administration/methods, statistics & numerical data · Smartphone/instrumentation*, statistics & numerical data · Tuberculosis/drug therapy*, epidemiology · Video Recording/methods* · Young Adult
shelves.balance: The head-to-head trial (Story A et al., PMID: 30799062) randomised 226 tuberculosis patients in 22 English clinics — a population in which 58% had a history of homelessness, imprisonment, drug use, alcohol problems, or mental-health problems — to daily smartphone video observation or to directly observed therapy three to five times a week. In intention-to-treat, 70% of the video group (78/112) achieved at least 80% of scheduled observations in the first two months versus 31% (35/114) on direct observation (adjusted OR 5.48, 95% CI 3.10 to 9.68; p < 0.0001); the restricted analysis was closer (77% vs 63%; adjusted OR 2.52, 1.17 to 5.54). A systematic review restricted to randomised trials (Areas Lisboa Netto T et al., PMID: 39405342) found video observation non-inferior for treatment adherence in every included trial, with lower observation costs, less professional supervision time, and higher patient satisfaction where those were measured. The gap in the record is the endpoint itself: what is proven is observation — doses seen taken — while cure, completion of the full course, and relapse were not the powered outcomes of the anchor trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for the job of supervising daily doses, video observation is at least the equal of in-person observation and reaches far more of them; calling it better tuberculosis treatment, rather than better treatment observation, would go past the evidence.

cards.headline: Story 2019: video observation hit the ≥80% observations target in 70% versus 31% on direct observation (adjusted OR 5.48) over the first two months
cards.summary: Story 2019: video observation hit the ≥80% observations target in 70% versus 31% on direct observation (adjusted OR 5.48) over the first two months
cards.people: 226 patients aged 16 or older with active pulmonary or non-pulmonary tuberculosis, eligible for directly observed therapy under local guidance, at 22 clinics in England; 112 randomised to smartphone video-observed therapy (daily videos of every dose, viewed by a centralised London service; phones and data plans provided free) and 114 to directly observed therapy (observation three to five times weekly at home, in the community, or in clinic, remaining doses self-administered). Overall 131 patients (58%) had a history of homelessness, imprisonment, drug use, alcohol problems, or mental-health problems.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, 78 of 112 video-observation patients (70%) achieved ≥80% of scheduled treatment observations in the first 2 months versus 35 of 114 direct-observation patients (31%) — adjusted OR 5.48 (95% CI 3.10 to 9.68; p < 0.0001), against a superiority target of a 15-percentage-point difference. In the restricted analysis (patients completing at least 1 week on the allocated arm), the figures were 78 of 101 (77%) versus 35 of 56 (63%) — adjusted OR 2.52 (1.17 to 5.54; p = 0.017). The most common adverse events, stomach pain, nausea, and vomiting, were reported in 16 of 112 (14%) on video observation and 9 of 114 (8%) on direct observation. The authors conclude video observation was more effective for treatment observation and is likely cheaper and more acceptable.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is observations completed, and the comparison is structurally uneven: video patients were scheduled for observation seven days a week while direct-observation patients were scheduled three to five times, with the rest self-administered — part of the gap is the design of the two services, not only the technology. Patients without access to charging a smartphone were excluded, phones and data were free (a cost real programmes must carry), and the trial does not report cure or relapse as powered outcomes. Distinct from shelf #2158, which tested medication-monitor boxes with reminders in China, not video observation.
cards.source: Story A et al. Smartphone-enabled video-observed versus directly observed treatment for tuberculosis: a multicentre, analyst-blinded, randomised, controlled superiority trial. The Lancet. 2019. PMID: 30799062. Registry ID: ISRCTN26184967. cards.headline: Areas Lisboa Netto 2024 (systematic review of RCTs): video observation was non-inferior to direct observation for adherence in every trial — and cheaper, quicker to supervise, and better liked where measured
cards.summary: Areas Lisboa Netto 2024 (systematic review of RCTs): video observation was non-inferior to direct observation for adherence in every trial — and cheaper, quicker to supervise, and better liked where measured
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Areas Lisboa Netto 2024)
cards.people: Randomised trials only, comparing video-observed therapy with directly observed therapy in patients with pulmonary or extrapulmonary tuberculosis, reporting adherence, cost of treatment observation, time spent observing treatment, or patient satisfaction; searched in MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane sources.
cards.result: In all included randomised trials, video-observed therapy demonstrated non-inferiority to directly observed therapy for treatment adherence. Where costs were assessed, video observation reduced them; where supervision time was evaluated, video observation reduced the time health professionals spent supervising treatment; and where satisfaction was measured, video observation contributed to higher treatment satisfaction. The review reports these findings qualitatively, without a pooled effect estimate in the record. The authors conclude video observation is comparable to direct observation on adherence but cost-effective, more satisfying, and less time-consuming, for patients with internet access.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative synthesis: 'non-inferior in all trials' is only as strong as each small trial's margin and sample, and cost, time, and satisfaction were each measured in subsets of the trials, not all of them. The review's population is patients with internet access — the digital-exclusion caveat runs through every favourable finding.
cards.source: Areas Lisboa Netto T et al. Video-observed therapy (VOT) vs directly observed therapy (DOT) for tuberculosis treatment: A systematic review on adherence, cost of treatment observation, time spent observing treatment and patient satisfaction. cards.headline: Synthesis: video observation supervises more doses, at less cost and bother, with adherence non-inferior in the randomised record — the unproven step is from observed doses to cured patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: video observation supervises more doses, at less cost and bother, with adherence non-inferior in the randomised record — the unproven step is from observed doses to cured patients
cards.people: One 226-patient multicentre randomised trial of smartphone video versus in-person observation, plus a systematic review restricted to randomised VOT-versus-DOT comparisons.
cards.result: Observation completion (≥80% of scheduled observations, 2 months): 70% vs 31%, adjusted OR 5.48 (95% CI 3.10 to 9.68) intention-to-treat; 77% vs 63% in the restricted analysis (Story 2019). Adherence across trials: non-inferior in all included RCTs; costs and supervision time lower, satisfaction higher, where measured (Areas Lisboa Netto 2024). Adverse events in the anchor trial were the drugs' own (nausea, vomiting, stomach pain: 14% vs 8%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Observation is a process outcome standing in for adherence, which itself stands in for cure — two inferential steps separate this shelf's proven result from the outcome programmes ultimately report. Settings without reliable connectivity, or patients for whom the in-person visit itself carries clinical value, are outside what these trials tested. Tier C is set because the anchor is a single trial programme and the endpoint is observational completion rather than treatment outcome.
cards.source: Synthesis of Story A et al. The Lancet. 2019 (PMID: 30799062); Areas Lisboa Netto T et al. PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. 2024 (PMID: 39405342).

shelves.title: Spacer versus nebuliser in acute asthma: across 39 trials and 2,626 patients, admissions and lung function were the same — and children using spacers left the emergency department 33 minutes sooner, with less tremor
shelves.question: In children and adults with acute asthma, does beta-agonist delivery by metered-dose inhaler with a holding chamber (spacer) work as well as delivery by nebuliser?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adrenergic beta-Agonists/administration & dosage* · Adult · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage* · Asthma/drug therapy* · Child · Child, Preschool · Emergency Service, Hospital/statistics & numerical data · Equipment Design · Humans · Inhalation Spacers/statistics & numerical data · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Nebulizers and Vaporizers* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: The Cochrane review by Cates CJ et al. (PMID: 24037768) pools 39 trials — 1,897 children and 729 adults, 33 of them in emergency or equivalent community settings — in which beta-agonist treatment was repeated and titrated to response. The delivery method made no significant difference to hospital admission: risk ratio 0.94 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.43) in adults and 0.71 (0.47 to 1.08, moderate quality evidence) in children, and peak flow and forced expiratory volume were similar between methods in both age groups. Where the spacer did win was around the edges that matter to families and departments: children given spacer treatment spent 33 minutes less in the emergency department (95% CI −43 to −24; mean nebuliser stay 103 minutes), had a lower pulse rate (mean difference −5% of baseline, −8% to −2%), and developed tremor less often (RR 0.64, 0.44 to 0.95); adult length of stay was similar by either method. Nebulisers need power, maintenance, and cost more in the community; spacers need neither. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): not a stronger bronchodilator effect — the review's own conclusion is that nebuliser delivery produced outcomes not significantly better than a metered-dose inhaler with spacer — but equal efficacy with practical and small clinical advantages, on a moderate-quality paediatric evidence base, earns the benefit stamp for the device choice rather than for the drug.

cards.headline: Cates 2013 (Cochrane, 39 trials, 2,626 patients): no difference in admissions or lung function — children on spacers left the ED 33 minutes sooner, with less tremor and a lower pulse
cards.summary: Cates 2013 (Cochrane, 39 trials, 2,626 patients): no difference in admissions or lung function — children on spacers left the ED 33 minutes sooner, with less tremor and a lower pulse
cards.people: 39 randomised trials totalling 1,897 children (from age 2) and 729 adults with acute asthma, comparing beta-agonist delivery by metered-dose inhaler with a holding chamber (spacer) against wet nebulisation; 33 trials ran in emergency-room or equivalent community settings and six in inpatients (207 children, 28 adults), with treatments repeated and titrated to the participant's response.
cards.result: Hospital admission did not differ significantly by delivery method: risk ratio for spacer versus nebuliser 0.94 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.43) in adults and 0.71 (95% CI 0.47 to 1.08, moderate quality evidence) in children. In children, emergency-department length of stay was significantly shorter with the spacer — the mean stay on nebulised treatment was 103 minutes, and spacer treatment was 33 minutes less (95% CI −43 to −24, moderate quality evidence); adult length of stay was similar between methods. Peak flow and forced expiratory volume were similar for the two methods. In children, pulse rate was lower with the spacer (mean difference −5% of baseline, 95% CI −8% to −2%, moderate quality evidence), as was the risk of tremor (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.95, moderate quality evidence). The reviewers conclude nebuliser delivery produced outcomes not significantly better than metered-dose inhalers delivered by spacer, and spacers may have some advantages for children.
cards.watchOut: 'No significant difference' in admissions is not a formal equivalence proof — the adult interval (0.61 to 1.43) is wide, the adult evidence is thinner than the paediatric, and most trials titrated repeated doses to response, which compresses differences between devices; a single fixed dose comparison could look different. The review's search closed in February 2013, and life-threatening asthma with poor inspiratory effort is barely represented in trials like these — the spacer conclusion belongs to the mild-to-severe-but-breathing trial population, not to the peri-arrest patient.
cards.source: Cates CJ et al. Holding chambers (spacers) versus nebulisers for beta-agonist treatment of acute asthma. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013. PMID: 24037768. shelves.title: Home blood-pressure telemonitoring with pharmacist case management: control in 57.2% versus 30.0% at 12 months — and the advantage persisted 6 months after the intervention stopped
shelves.question: In adults with uncontrolled hypertension, does home blood-pressure telemonitoring combined with pharmacist case management improve blood-pressure control versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Pressure · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Case Management · Combined Modality Therapy · Diastole · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Hypertension/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Satisfaction · Pharmacists · Systole · Telemedicine/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two randomised trials of the same model, a decade apart, agree. In the HyperLink cluster trial (Margolis KL et al., PMID: 23821088), 450 adults with uncontrolled blood pressure in 16 Minnesota clinics received home telemonitoring with pharmacist case management or usual care: blood pressure was controlled at both 6 and 12 months in 57.2% versus 30.0% (P=0.001), systolic pressure fell 9.7 mmHg more than usual care at 12 months (P<0.001), and at 18 months — six months after the intervention stopped — control remained higher at 71.8% versus 57.1% (P=0.003). In the earlier e-BP trial (Green BB et al., PMID: 18577730), 778 patients randomised to home monitoring plus web-based pharmacist care achieved control in 56% versus 31% on usual care (P<0.001), while home monitoring with web training but no pharmacist did not significantly improve control (36% versus 31%; P=0.21). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): the pharmacist acting on transmitted home readings is the ingredient that doubles control rates.

cards.headline: Margolis 2013 (HyperLink): control at both 6 and 12 months in 57.2% versus 30.0% (P=0.001); still ahead at 18 months, 71.8% versus 57.1%
cards.summary: Margolis 2013 (HyperLink): control at both 6 and 12 months in 57.2% versus 30.0% (P=0.001); still ahead at 18 months, 71.8% versus 57.1%
cards.people: 450 adults with uncontrolled blood pressure (mean age 61.1 years; 45% women; mean systolic 148 mmHg, diastolic 85 mmHg) recruited from 16 primary care clinics in an integrated Minnesota health system (8 clinics telemonitoring, 228 patients; 8 clinics usual care, 222 patients); intervention patients transmitted home readings to pharmacists who adjusted therapy; 12 months of intervention plus 6 months of post-intervention follow-up.
cards.result: Blood pressure was controlled at both 6 and 12 months in 57.2% (95% CI 44.8–68.7) of the telemonitoring group versus 30.0% (95% CI 23.2–37.8) of usual care (P=0.001). Systolic pressure fell more with the intervention at 6 months (−10.7 mmHg; 95% CI −14.3 to −7.3), 12 months (−9.7 mmHg; 95% CI −13.4 to −6.0), and 18 months (−6.6 mmHg; 95% CI −10.7 to −2.5). At 18 months control was 71.8% versus 57.1% (P=0.003).
cards.watchOut: Cluster-randomised by clinic in one integrated US health system with pharmacists empowered to adjust therapy — systems where pharmacists cannot titrate, or patients lack coverage for home monitors, may not reproduce it. Control targets included a lower goal (<130/80) for patients with diabetes or chronic kidney disease.
cards.source: Margolis KL et al. Effect of home blood pressure telemonitoring and pharmacist management on blood pressure control: a cluster randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2013. PMID: 23821088. cards.headline: Green 2008 (e-BP): control in 56% with home monitoring plus web pharmacist care versus 31% usual care (P<0.001) — monitoring plus web training alone, 36%, was not significant
cards.summary: Green 2008 (e-BP): control in 56% with home monitoring plus web pharmacist care versus 31% usual care (P<0.001) — monitoring plus web training alone, 36%, was not significant
cards.people: 778 patients aged 25–75 with uncontrolled essential hypertension and internet access at an integrated Washington-state group practice, randomised to usual care, home BP monitoring with secure-website training only, or home monitoring plus pharmacist care management delivered through web communications; 730 (94%) completed the 1-year follow-up.
cards.result: Controlled blood pressure (<140/90 mmHg) at 12 months was achieved by 31% (95% CI 25–37) on usual care, 36% (95% CI 30–42) with home monitoring and web training only (P=0.21 versus usual care), and 56% (95% CI 49–62) with added pharmacist care (P<0.001 versus both other groups). In patients with baseline systolic pressure ≥160 mmHg, pharmacist care gave a net systolic reduction of −13.2 mmHg (95% CI −19.2 to −7.1) versus usual care and improved control (relative risk 3.32; 95% CI 1.86–5.94).
cards.watchOut: Required internet access and an integrated practice's secure web platform in 2005–2007 — the technology is dated even though the care model is the point. The trial isolates the pharmacist, not the monitor, as the active ingredient, which is exactly what services buying monitors alone should note.
cards.source: Green BB et al. Effectiveness of home blood pressure monitoring, Web communication, and pharmacist care on hypertension control: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2008. shelves.title: The Diabetes Prevention Program in the real world: about 4% of body weight lost at 12 months survives translation — roughly half the trial's punch, and more with every session attended
shelves.question: When the Diabetes Prevention Program lifestyle intervention is translated into community and primary-care settings, how much weight loss and diabetes prevention survives the move?
shelves.mesh: Diabetes Mellitus/prevention & control · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Program Evaluation · Risk Reduction Behavior · United States · Weight Reduction Programs
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — attenuated but real. Ali MK et al. (PMID: 22232096) pooled 28 US studies translating the Diabetes Prevention Program lifestyle intervention into real-world settings: average weight change at 12 months was a loss of about 4% of baseline weight, similar whether programmes were delivered by clinically trained professionals or lay educators, and each additional lifestyle session attended added 0.26 percentage points of weight loss. Dunkley AJ et al. (PMID: 24652723) pooled 25 translational studies (22 in the primary weight analysis) and found a mean weight loss of 2.12 kg at 12 months (95% CI −2.61 to −1.63; I²=91.4%), with greater weight loss where programmes adhered more closely to international guideline recommendations (0.3 kg more per point on a 12-point adherence scale). Neither meta-analysis could pool diabetes incidence the way the original trial reported it, so the 'prevention survives' half of the question rests on weight loss as the standing surrogate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): translated programmes deliver roughly half the original trial's weight loss, reliably, and fidelity plus attendance are the levers that protect it.

cards.headline: Ali 2012: 28 US translation studies averaged about 4% weight loss at 12 months; each extra session attended added 0.26 percentage points
cards.summary: Ali 2012: 28 US translation studies averaged about 4% weight loss at 12 months; each extra session attended added 0.26 percentage points
cards.people: 28 US-based studies applying the Diabetes Prevention Program lifestyle intervention in real-world settings for people at high risk of diabetes; analyses of weight change at 12 months, with a 17-study subset followed for 9 months or longer.
cards.result: Average weight change 12 months after the intervention was a loss of about 4% from baseline weight, similar regardless of whether the intervention was delivered by clinically trained professionals or lay educators. With every additional lifestyle session attended, weight loss increased by 0.26 percentage point. The authors conclude costs can be lowered without sacrificing effectiveness by using non-medical personnel and motivating higher attendance.
cards.watchOut: Most included studies were single-group pre–post evaluations rather than randomised comparisons, so regression to the mean and self-selection inflate the estimate; the journal of record for this meta-analysis is Health Affairs, not the American Journal of Preventive Medicine named in the candidate list — the substitution is declared in the part summary.
cards.source: Ali MK et al. How effective were lifestyle interventions in real-world settings that were modeled on the Diabetes Prevention Program? Health Affairs. 2012. PMID: 22232096. cards.headline: Dunkley 2014: pooled weight loss 2.12 kg at 12 months (I²=91.4%); guideline-adherent programmes lost 0.3 kg more per adherence point
cards.summary: Dunkley 2014: pooled weight loss 2.12 kg at 12 months (I²=91.4%); guideline-adherent programmes lost 0.3 kg more per adherence point
cards.people: 25 studies of pragmatic lifestyle interventions translating diabetes-prevention efficacy trials into real-world settings, with follow-up of at least 12 months; 22 studies (24 groups) contributed 12-month weight data to the primary meta-analysis (search to July 2012).
cards.result: Pooled mean weight loss at 12 months was 2.12 kg (95% CI −2.61 to −1.63; I²=91.4%). Adherence to international guideline recommendations was significantly associated with greater weight loss — an increase of 0.3 kg per point increase on a 12-point guideline-adherence scale. The authors conclude pragmatic programmes are effective but effectiveness varies substantially and improves with guideline adherence.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is very high (I²=91.4%), so the pooled 2.12 kg is an average of widely differing programmes, not a promise; outcomes on progression to diabetes were too inconsistently reported to pool, leaving weight as the operative endpoint.

shelves.title: Reciprocal peer support beat nurse care management on HbA1c by 0.58 points at 6 months in veterans — but the wider peer-support literature improves control in only a minority of trials
shelves.question: In veterans with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, does reciprocal peer support — patients paired to support each other — improve glycaemic control versus nurse care management?
shelves.mesh: Blood Pressure · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 1/blood/nursing/psychology/therapy · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Insulin/therapeutic use · Male · Medication Adherence · Motivation · Psychotherapy, Group/methods · Self Efficacy · Social Support · Stress, Psychological · Telephone · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — proven in one well-run trial against an active comparator, unproven as a class. Heisler M et al. (PMID: 20956707) randomised 244 male veterans with HbA1c above 7.5% to reciprocal peer support (paired peers, weekly telephone contact, optional group sessions) or nurse care management: at 6 months HbA1c fell by 0.29 points in the peer group and rose by 0.29 points under nurse management — a between-group difference of 0.58 points (P=0.004) — and among those starting above 8.0% the peer group fell 0.88 points versus 0.07 (difference 0.81; P<0.001); blood pressure, self-reported adherence, and distress did not differ. The systematic review by Dale JR et al. (PMID: 22804713; 25 studies, 14 randomised or comparative trials) found peer support improved glycaemic control in only 3 of 14 trials, with no consistent pattern by model of support. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the reciprocal, paired model worked in its trial; generic 'peer support' should not inherit the claim.

cards.headline: Heisler 2010: HbA1c −0.29 points on peer support versus +0.29 on nurse care management (difference 0.58; P=0.004); 0.81 points in those starting above 8.0%
cards.summary: Heisler 2010: HbA1c −0.29 points on peer support versus +0.29 on nurse care management (difference 0.58; P=0.004); 0.81 points in those starting above 8.0%
cards.people: 244 men with HbA1c above 7.5% at 2 US Veterans Affairs facilities, randomised to reciprocal peer support (initial group goal-setting and communication-skills session, age-matched peer pairing, weekly telephone contact via a monitored platform, optional group sessions at 1, 3, and 6 months) or nurse care management (1.5-hour education session plus an assigned nurse care manager); 216 (89%) completed HbA1c assessment at 6 months.
cards.result: Mean HbA1c decreased from 8.02% to 7.73% (change −0.29%) with peer support and increased from 7.93% to 8.22% (change +0.29%) with nurse care management — a difference in change of 0.58% (P=0.004). Among patients with baseline HbA1c above 8.0%, peer support fell 0.88% versus 0.07% (difference 0.81%; P<0.001). Eight peer-group patients started insulin versus 1 in the nurse group (P=0.020). Groups did not differ in blood pressure, self-reported medication adherence, or diabetes-specific distress, though the peer group reported improved diabetes social support.
cards.watchOut: All-male veterans, 6 months, and the comparator arm actually worsened — half the headline difference is nurse-management drift, not peer gain. The insulin-start difference may reflect peers prompting treatment intensification rather than behaviour change alone.
cards.source: Heisler M et al. Diabetes control with reciprocal peer support versus nurse care management: a randomized trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20956707. cards.headline: Dale 2012 review: glycaemic control improved in 3 of 14 peer-support trials; no model of peer support consistently worked
cards.summary: Dale 2012 review: glycaemic control improved in 3 of 14 peer-support trials; no model of peer support consistently worked
cards.people: 25 studies of peer support in adults with diabetes, including 14 randomised, controlled, or comparative trials, across varied designs, settings, and outcome measures (search 1966–2011).
cards.result: Peer support was associated with statistically significant improvements in glycaemic control in 3 of 14 trials, blood pressure in 1 of 4, cholesterol in 1 of 6, BMI/weight in 2 of 7, physical activity in 2 of 5, self-efficacy in 2 of 3, depression in 4 of 6, and perceived social support in 2 of 2. No consistent pattern of effect related to any model of peer support emerged; the authors judge the evidence too limited and inconsistent for firm recommendations.
cards.watchOut: A narrative synthesis of heterogeneous small studies — it cannot identify which ingredients (reciprocity, pairing, telephone platform, group sessions) carried the Heisler result, and publication bias toward positive pilot studies is likely.
cards.source: Dale JR et al. What is the effect of peer support on diabetes outcomes in adults? A systematic review. Diabetic Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22804713. cards.summary: Synthesis: one strong reciprocal-model trial inside an inconsistent field — claim the model, not the category

shelves.title: Reminder packaging works on the pill count: 11% more pills taken in the Cochrane pooling — with diastolic pressure and HbA1c gains in the few trials that measured them, and huge heterogeneity throughout
shelves.question: Does reminder packaging for medicines — calendar blister packs and pill organisers with date cues — improve adherence versus ordinary bottles?
shelves.mesh: Drug Packaging/methods · Humans · Medication Adherence · Pharmaceutical Preparations/administration & dosage · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Reminder Systems · Self Administration
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for adherence itself; clinical spillovers are thinner. Mahtani KR et al. (PMID: 21901694), in the Cochrane review of reminder packaging (12 studies, 2,196 participants), found reminder packaging increased the percentage of pills taken by a mean difference of 11% (95% CI 6–17) across six intervention groups in four trials — with notable heterogeneity (I²=96.3%) — while self-reported adherent-patient proportions did not significantly change (odds ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.56–1.40). In the two trials measuring each clinical outcome, diastolic blood pressure fell by 5.89 mmHg (95% CI −6.70 to −5.09) and HbA1c by 0.72 points (95% CI −0.83 to −0.60), with no effect on systolic pressure. The wider Cochrane adherence review by Nieuwlaat R et al. (PMID: 25412402; 182 randomised trials) is the cautionary frame: even the most effective adherence interventions did not lead to large improvements, and only 5 of the 17 lowest-bias trials improved both adherence and clinical outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dated packaging makes people take measurably more of their medicine; expect modest, not transformative, clinical gains.

cards.headline: Mahtani 2011 Cochrane: percentage of pills taken up by a mean 11% (95% CI 6–17); diastolic BP −5.89 mmHg and HbA1c −0.72 in two-trial poolings
cards.summary: Mahtani 2011 Cochrane: percentage of pills taken up by a mean 11% (95% CI 6–17); diastolic BP −5.89 mmHg and HbA1c −0.72 in two-trial poolings
cards.people: 12 randomised trials with 2,196 participants taking self-administered medication for at least one month, comparing reminder packaging (packaging incorporating a date or time cue) with no device; searches to September 2010.
cards.result: Reminder packaging increased the percentage of pills taken (mean difference 11%; 95% CI 6% to 17%; six intervention groups in four trials), with notable heterogeneity (I²=96.3%). Self-reported adherent patients did not significantly increase (odds ratio 0.89; 95% CI 0.56 to 1.40; two trials). Meta-analysis of two trials each found diastolic blood pressure decreased by 5.89 mmHg (95% CI −6.70 to −5.09; P<0.00001) and HbA1c by 0.72 points (95% CI −0.83 to −0.60; P<0.00001), with no effect on systolic blood pressure (mean change −1.01; 95% CI −2.22 to 0.20).
cards.watchOut: The clinical-outcome poolings rest on two trials apiece, the adherence pooling is extremely heterogeneous (I²=96.3%), and pill counts are a process measure — taking more pills out of a pack is not identical to taking them correctly or benefiting from them.
cards.source: Mahtani KR et al. Reminder packaging for improving adherence to self-administered long-term medications. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2011. PMID: 21901694. cards.headline: Nieuwlaat 2014 Cochrane: across 182 adherence-intervention trials, effects were inconsistent and even the best interventions were not large
cards.summary: Nieuwlaat 2014 Cochrane: across 182 adherence-intervention trials, effects were inconsistent and even the best interventions were not large
cards.people: 182 randomised trials of interventions to enhance adherence to prescribed medications (109 new in this update), spanning many conditions, regimens, and intervention types, each measuring both adherence and a clinical outcome with at least 80% follow-up.
cards.result: Studies were too heterogeneous to pool. Of the 17 trials at lowest risk of bias, only 5 reported improvements in both adherence and clinical outcomes, with no common intervention characteristics apparent; the effective ones generally involved complex, multicomponent support from allied health professionals. The authors conclude that even the most effective interventions did not lead to large improvements in adherence or clinical outcomes and that effects were inconsistent across the body of evidence.
cards.watchOut: This is the background rate for all adherence interventions, not a trial of packaging — it disciplines the packaging claim rather than refuting it: packaging is one of the simplest interventions in a field where simple interventions usually disappoint.
cards.source: Nieuwlaat R et al. Interventions for enhancing medication adherence. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 25412402. MeSH: Drug Therapy · Humans · Medication Adherence · Patient Education as Topic · Publication Bias · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Self Administration

cards.headline: Synthesis: the pack reminds, the count rises — keep expectations for downstream outcomes modest
cards.summary: Synthesis: the pack reminds, the count rises — keep expectations for downstream outcomes modest
cards.people: The Cochrane reminder-packaging review (Mahtani 2011: 12 trials, 2,196 participants) read against the Cochrane adherence-interventions review (Nieuwlaat 2014: 182 trials).
cards.result: Pills taken +11% (95% CI 6–17) with reminder packaging; diastolic BP −5.89 mmHg and HbA1c −0.72 points in two-trial subsets; self-reported adherence unchanged (OR 0.89). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for adherence, with clinical benefits possible but resting on few trials.
cards.watchOut: Reminder packaging shifts cost and effort to pharmacies and patients filling organisers; errors in filling a pill organiser are themselves a recognised harm this literature barely measures. Tier C is not set: Cochrane syntheses carry the shelf.

shelves.title: The New Medicine Service: adherence 71% versus 61% at 10 weeks with a pharmacist follow-up — an advantage that faded to non-significance by 26 weeks
shelves.question: In people starting a new medicine for a long-term condition, does a community-pharmacist follow-up service (the New Medicine Service) improve adherence versus usual pharmacy care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Chronic Disease/drug therapy · Community Pharmacy Services/economics/organization & administration · Cost-Benefit Analysis · England · Female · Health Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice · Health Status · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pharmacists · Professional Role · State Medicine/economics · Drug Monitoring
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — early, with fading. Elliott RA et al. (PMID: 26647412) randomised 504 people starting a new medicine for asthma/COPD, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or anticoagulation/antiplatelet therapy in 46 English community pharmacies to the New Medicine Service (pharmacist consultations 7–14 days and 14–21 days after starting) or normal practice: at 10 weeks, self-reported adherence was 71% with the service versus 61% without (adjusted odds ratio 1.67; 95% CI 1.06–2.62; P=0.027), with a non-significant NHS cost saving of £21 per patient. At the 26-week follow-up (Elliott RA et al., PMID: 31732700), adherence was 65.6% versus 57.1% unadjusted, but the adjusted odds ratio of 1.50 (95% CI 0.93–2.44; P=0.095) was no longer significant, with attrition a stated concern; modelling suggested an 89% probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000 per quality-adjusted life-year, with high uncertainty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real early adherence gain from two brief pharmacist consultations, durability unproven.

cards.headline: Elliott 2016: adherence at 10 weeks 71% with the New Medicine Service versus 61% with normal practice (adjusted OR 1.67; P=0.027)
cards.summary: Elliott 2016: adherence at 10 weeks 71% with the New Medicine Service versus 61% with normal practice (adjusted OR 1.67; P=0.027)
cards.people: 504 participants aged 14 and over starting a new medicine for asthma/COPD, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or an anticoagulant/antiplatelet agent, in 46 community pharmacies in England, randomised to the New Medicine Service (251) — consultations 7–14 and 14–21 days after presentation of the prescription — or normal practice; 443 patients (85%) were contacted at 10 weeks and 378 still taking the initial medicine were analysed unadjusted.
cards.result: Self-reported adherence (no missed doses without medical advice in the previous 7 days) at 10 weeks was 71% (95% CI 64–77) in the New Medicine Service arm versus 61% (95% CI 54–67) in normal practice (P=0.04 unadjusted); the adjusted intention-to-treat odds ratio for adherence was 1.67 (95% CI 1.06–2.62; P=0.027). NHS costs trended lower with the service (saving £21; 95% CI −£59 to £100; P=0.128).
cards.watchOut: Self-reported adherence over a 7-day recall window, unblinded, in patients who knew they were in a medicines study — the measured gap (10 points) is exactly the size social-desirability bias can manufacture, though the randomised design protects the comparison itself. Conditions were limited to the four eligible groups.
cards.source: Elliott RA et al. Supporting adherence for people starting a new medication for a long-term condition through community pharmacies: a pragmatic randomised controlled trial of the New Medicine Service. BMJ Quality & Safety. 2016. PMID: 26647412. Registry ID: NCT01635361. cards.headline: Elliott 2020 (26-week follow-up): adherence 65.6% versus 57.1% unadjusted, adjusted OR 1.50 — no longer significant (P=0.095); cost-effectiveness probability 89% with high uncertainty
cards.summary: Elliott 2020 (26-week follow-up): adherence 65.6% versus 57.1% unadjusted, adjusted OR 1.50 — no longer significant (P=0.095); cost-effectiveness probability 89% with high uncertainty
cards.people: The same 504-participant trial cohort (251 New Medicine Service, 253 normal practice) in 46 English community pharmacies, followed to 26 weeks; 327 patients still taking the initial medicine contributed to the unadjusted adherence analysis.
cards.result: Unadjusted adherence at 26 weeks was 65.6% (103/157) with the service versus 57.1% (97/170) with normal practice (P=0.113); the adjusted intention-to-treat odds ratio was 1.50 (95% CI 0.93–2.44; P=0.095). NHS costs were non-significantly lower (−£104; 95% CI −£37 to £257 per the record's figures; P=0.168), and long-term modelling gave 0.04 more quality-adjusted life-years per patient with an 89% probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000 per QALY, with high uncertainty.
cards.watchOut: Attrition by 26 weeks was substantial (327 of 504 still taking the initial medicine in the unadjusted analysis), and the economic case rests on modelled lifetime consequences of an adherence difference that was itself no longer significant — treat the cost-effectiveness figure as suggestive, not established.
cards.source: Elliott RA et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: two pharmacist conversations buy about 10 points of early adherence; whether anything remains at six months is unresolved
cards.summary: Synthesis: two pharmacist conversations buy about 10 points of early adherence; whether anything remains at six months is unresolved
cards.people: One pragmatic RCT programme: Elliott 2016 (504 participants, 10-week outcome) and Elliott 2020 (26-week follow-up of the same trial).
cards.result: Adherence odds ratio 1.67 (95% CI 1.06–2.62) at 10 weeks and 1.50 (95% CI 0.93–2.44) at 26 weeks; absolute adherence 71% versus 61% early, 65.6% versus 57.1% later. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single trial programme carries the claim, so the developer reviews this shelf personally.

shelves.title: Medication reconciliation finds discrepancies — most of them harmless: the systematic review and the big pharmacist RCT agree it does not, by itself, cut errors that hurt patients or post-discharge utilisation
shelves.question: Does structured medication reconciliation at admission, transfer, and discharge reduce medication errors and adverse drug events versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Emergency Service, Hospital/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Medical History Taking · Medication Reconciliation/economics · Patient Discharge · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Patient Safety/economics/standards · Pharmacists · Professional Role · Risk Assessment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for patient-level outcomes, on the evidence as it stands. Kwan JL et al. (PMID: 23460096) reviewed 18 studies of 20 hospital-based medication-reconciliation interventions (pharmacist-led in 17 of 20) and concluded that most unintentional discrepancies identified had no clinical significance, and that medication reconciliation alone probably does not reduce post-discharge hospital utilisation, though it may do so when bundled with broader care-transition interventions. In the PILL-CVD randomised trial (Kripalani S et al., PMID: 22751755), 851 patients discharged after acute coronary syndromes or heart failure received pharmacist-assisted reconciliation plus counselling and follow-up or usual care: 50.8% had at least one clinically important medication error within 30 days regardless, and the intervention did not significantly change errors per patient (incidence rate ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.77–1.10) or adverse drug events (1.09; 95% CI 0.86–1.39), with only a trend toward fewer potential adverse drug events (0.80; 95% CI 0.61–1.04). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): reconciliation reliably finds discrepancies, but most are trivial, and no reduction in clinically important errors or utilisation has been shown for reconciliation alone.

cards.headline: Kwan 2013: 18 studies — most discrepancies found by reconciliation had no clinical significance; utilisation probably unchanged unless reconciliation is bundled
cards.summary: Kwan 2013: 18 studies — most discrepancies found by reconciliation had no clinical significance; utilisation probably unchanged unless reconciliation is bundled
cards.people: 18 studies evaluating 20 hospital-based medication-reconciliation interventions at care transitions, with pharmacists performing reconciliation in 17 of the 20 interventions; outcomes were unintentional discrepancies with nontrivial harm risk and 30-day post-discharge emergency visits and readmission (searches to 2012).
cards.result: Most unintentional discrepancies identified by medication reconciliation had no clinical significance. The reviewers conclude that medication reconciliation alone probably does not reduce post-discharge hospital utilisation, but may do so when bundled with other interventions aimed at improving care transitions.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative synthesis of heterogeneous, mostly non-randomised studies — 'probably does not reduce' is a judgement over weak primary evidence, not a pooled null; interventions bundled with counselling, follow-up, and discharge planning were not separable from reconciliation alone in most studies.
cards.source: Kwan JL et al. Medication reconciliation during transitions of care as a patient safety strategy: a systematic review. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2013. PMID: 23460096. cards.headline: Kripalani 2012 (PILL-CVD): 50.8% of patients had a clinically important medication error after discharge; the pharmacist intervention did not significantly reduce them (IRR 0.92)
cards.summary: Kripalani 2012 (PILL-CVD): 50.8% of patients had a clinically important medication error after discharge; the pharmacist intervention did not significantly reduce them (IRR 0.92)
cards.people: 851 adults hospitalised with acute coronary syndromes or acute decompensated heart failure at 2 US academic hospitals, randomised to a pharmacist intervention (assisted medication reconciliation, inpatient counselling, low-literacy adherence aids, post-discharge telephone follow-up) or usual care, with blinded outcome assessment over 30 days after discharge.
cards.result: 432 participants (50.8%) had 1 or more clinically important medication errors; 22.9% of errors were judged serious and 1.8% life-threatening. Adverse drug events occurred in 30.3% and potential adverse drug events in 29.7% of patients. The intervention did not significantly alter clinically important medication errors per patient (unadjusted incidence rate ratio 0.92; 95% CI 0.77–1.10) or adverse drug events (1.09; 95% CI 0.86–1.39), with a trend toward fewer potential adverse drug events (0.80; 95% CI 0.61–1.04).
cards.watchOut: The intervention bundled reconciliation with counselling and follow-up and still missed — which strengthens the null for reconciliation alone, but the two academic hospitals' usual care may already have included substantial pharmacist activity, compressing the contrast.

cards.summary: Synthesis: an accurate list is necessary housekeeping, not a proven safety intervention on its own
cards.people: A systematic review of hospital reconciliation interventions (Kwan 2013, 18 studies) and a randomised trial of a pharmacist reconciliation bundle (Kripalani 2012, 851 patients).
cards.result: Discrepancies found are mostly without clinical significance; clinically important errors occurred in 50.8% of discharged cardiac patients and were not significantly reduced (IRR 0.92; 95% CI 0.77–1.10); post-discharge utilisation probably unchanged by reconciliation alone. shelves.title: Teach-back discharge education: 30-day readmission odds nearly halved in a five-study review (OR 0.55) — but the studies were few, small, and at high risk of selection bias
shelves.question: In patients discharged with heart failure, does discharge education using the teach-back method reduce 30-day readmission versus standard discharge education?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Patient Discharge · Patient Readmission
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a large-looking effect on a thin base. Oh EG et al. (PMID: 30882616) reviewed experimental studies of discharge education with the teach-back method (5 studies: 3 in heart failure, 1 in total joint replacement, 1 in coronary artery bypass grafting): across the 3 studies pooled, the odds ratio for 30-day readmission with teach-back versus usual care was 0.55 (95% CI 0.34–0.91; P=0.02), described by the authors as a 45% relative reduction in readmission odds — but the included studies were few and showed a high risk of selection bias. The earlier systematic review by Ha Dinh TT et al. (PMID: 26878928) of teach-back in chronic-disease education (12 studies) found improved disease-specific knowledge in 4 studies and significant self-efficacy gains in 2 (P=0.0026 and P<0.001), while 5 studies found reductions in readmission or hospitalisation that were not always statistically significant, and the single heart-failure quality-of-life study was null (P=0.59). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): teach-back is cheap, safe, and plausibly reduces readmissions — the heart-failure-specific claim awaits a proper randomised trial.

cards.headline: Oh 2021: teach-back discharge education — 30-day readmission OR 0.55 (95% CI 0.34–0.91) in a 3-study meta-analysis; 3 of the 5 reviewed studies were in heart failure
cards.summary: Oh 2021: teach-back discharge education — 30-day readmission OR 0.55 (95% CI 0.34–0.91) in a 3-study meta-analysis; 3 of the 5 reviewed studies were in heart failure
cards.people: 5 experimental studies of discharge education using the teach-back method (3 on heart failure, 1 on total joint replacement, 1 on coronary artery bypass grafting), identified from searches to July 2017; 3 studies contributed to the readmission meta-analysis.
cards.result: The odds ratio for 30-day readmission with teach-back discharge education versus usual care was 0.55 (95% CI 0.34–0.91; P=0.02), with I²=0% — reported by the authors as a 45% relative reduction in readmission. The main content of the education was confirming and reinforcing patients' comprehension of health-related information.
cards.watchOut: Only a few studies, appraised by the reviewers themselves as showing a high risk of selection bias, and the designs were non-randomised — an odds ratio of 0.55 from such a base should be read as an upper bound. The reviewers explicitly call for well-designed randomised trials.
cards.source: Oh EG et al. Effectiveness of Discharge Education With the Teach-Back Method on 30-Day Readmission: A Systematic Review. Journal of Patient Safety. 2021. PMID: 30882616. MeSH: Humans · Patient Discharge · Patient Readmission

cards.headline: Ha Dinh 2016: across 12 teach-back studies, knowledge improved in 4, self-efficacy in 2 — readmission fell in 5 but not always significantly; heart-failure quality of life was null (P=0.59)
cards.summary: Ha Dinh 2016: across 12 teach-back studies, knowledge improved in 4, self-efficacy in 2 — readmission fell in 5 but not always significantly; heart-failure quality of life was null (P=0.59)
cards.people: 12 studies of health education using the teach-back method in adults with chronic disease (randomised and non-randomised trials, cohort, before–after, and case–control designs), covering heart failure, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic conditions.
cards.result: Four studies confirmed improved disease-specific knowledge; one showed significantly improved adherence to medication and diet in type 2 diabetes (P<0.001); two showed significant self-efficacy improvements (P=0.0026 and P<0.001). Five studies found reductions in readmission rates and hospitalisation, not always statistically significant; two showed improved daily weighing in heart failure; one heart-failure quality-of-life study did not improve (P=0.59). Heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis.
cards.watchOut: Narrative synthesis over mixed designs, with several included studies at meaningful risk of bias; 'positive but inconsistent' is the reviewers' own summary, and publication bias in a fashionable education method is a live concern.
cards.source: Ha Dinh TT et al. The effectiveness of the teach-back method on adherence and self-management in health education for people with chronic disease: a systematic review. JBI Database of Systematic Reviews and Implementation Reports. 2016. PMID: 26878928.
