shelves.title: Automatic referral plus a liaison conversation: cardiac-rehab enrolment in 73.5% versus 29.0% with usual referral — the referral system, not the patient, was the barrier
shelves.question: After a cardiac event, do systematic referral strategies — automatic referral plus a liaison visit — increase cardiac-rehabilitation enrolment versus usual physician referral?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/rehabilitation · Aged · Angioplasty, Balloon, Coronary/rehabilitation · Cooperative Behavior · Female · Health Services Accessibility/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Interdisciplinary Communication · Male · Medical Records Systems, Computerized/statistics & numerical data · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Ontario · Patient Acceptance of Health Care/statistics & numerical data · Patient Care Team · Patient Discharge/statistics & numerical data · Pilot Projects · Prospective Studies · Referral and Consultation/statistics & numerical data · Rehabilitation Centers/statistics & numerical data · Telephone · Utilization Review/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for enrolment, from a large prospective controlled comparison. Grace SL et al. (PMID: 21325114) followed 2,635 inpatients with coronary artery disease at 11 Ontario hospitals using four referral strategies: combined automatic referral (discharge order or electronic record) plus a liaison discussion achieved 85.8% referral and 73.5% enrolment (odds ratio 8.41 versus usual care), ahead of automatic only (70.2% referral, 60.0% enrolment; OR 3.27) and liaison only (59.0%, 50.6%; OR 3.35), versus usual referral at 32.2% and 29.0%; among referred patients, attendance did not differ by strategy (mean 82.87% of classes). The Cochrane review by Karmali KN et al. (PMID: 24963623) of interventions to promote cardiac-rehabilitation uptake (10 studies, 1,338 participants) found 8 of 10 studies increased uptake, with successful interventions including structured nurse- or therapist-led contacts, early appointments, and motivational letters. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): systematising referral roughly doubles-to-triples enrolment; the mortality benefit of rehabilitation itself is claimed on rehabilitation's own shelves, not this one.

cards.headline: Grace 2011: enrolment 73.5% (combined), 60.0% (automatic), 50.6% (liaison) versus 29.0% (usual referral); combined-strategy OR 8.41
cards.summary: Grace 2011: enrolment 73.5% (combined), 60.0% (automatic), 50.6% (liaison) versus 29.0% (usual referral); combined-strategy OR 8.41
cards.people: 2,635 inpatients with coronary artery disease at 11 Ontario hospitals, each hospital using one of four referral strategies — automatic only (via discharge order or electronic record), healthcare-provider liaison only, combined automatic plus liaison, or usual referral; 1,809 participants completed the 1-year follow-up survey assessing rehabilitation utilisation, with analyses adjusted for hospital clustering.
cards.result: Combined automatic and liaison referral produced the greatest use (odds ratio 8.41; 85.8% referred, 73.5% enrolled), followed by automatic only (OR 3.27; 70.2% referred, 60.0% enrolled) and liaison only (OR 3.35; 59.0% referred, 50.6% enrolled), versus usual referral (32.2% referred, 29.0% enrolled); referral strategy was significantly related to referral and enrolment (P<0.001). Among referred participants, the percentage of classes attended did not differ by strategy (mean 82.87%; P=0.88).
cards.watchOut: Not randomised — hospitals chose or already used their strategies, so hospital culture and resources are entangled with the strategy effect despite adjusted analyses; enrolment was self-reported at one year in the 1,809 of 2,635 who responded.
cards.source: Grace SL et al. Effect of cardiac rehabilitation referral strategies on utilization rates: a prospective, controlled study. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21325114. cards.headline: Karmali 2014 Cochrane: 8 of 10 uptake interventions increased cardiac-rehab uptake; structured contacts, early appointments, and motivational letters worked
cards.summary: Karmali 2014 Cochrane: 8 of 10 uptake interventions increased cardiac-rehab uptake; structured contacts, early appointments, and motivational letters worked
cards.people: 18 studies (2,505 participants) of interventions to increase uptake of or adherence to cardiac rehabilitation in adults with myocardial infarction, bypass surgery, angioplasty, heart failure, angina, or coronary disease — 10 studies (1,338 participants) addressed uptake and 8 (1,167) adherence; most studies were at high or unclear risk of bias.
cards.result: Eight of 10 studies demonstrated increased uptake of cardiac rehabilitation; successful interventions included structured nurse- or therapist-led contacts, early appointments after discharge, motivational letters, gender-specific programmes, and intermediate-phase programmes for older patients. Three of 8 adherence studies showed improvement. Data on mortality and morbidity were limited and showed no difference in cardiovascular events or mortality, except one study noting increased revascularisation in the intervention group.
cards.watchOut: Meta-analysis was impossible because of heterogeneity, and most studies carried high or unclear risk of bias — this card establishes that referral interventions commonly work, not the size of any one strategy's effect.
cards.source: Karmali KN et al. Promoting patient uptake and adherence in cardiac rehabilitation. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 24963623. cochrane systematic review (karmali 2014) 18 studies (2,505 participants) of interventions to increase uptake of or adherence to cardiac rehabilitation in adults with myocardial infarction, bypass surgery, angioplasty, heart failure, angina, or coronary disease — 10 studies (1,338 participants) addressed uptake and 8 (1,167) adherence; most studies were at high or unclear risk of bias. eight of 10 studies demonstrated increased uptake of cardiac rehabilitation; successful interventions included structured nurse- or therapist-led contacts, early appointments after discharge, motivational letters, gender-specific programmes, and intermediate-phase programmes for older patients. three of 8 adherence studies showed improvement. data on mortality and morbidity were limited and showed no difference in cardiovascular events or mortality, except one study noting increased revascularisation in the intervention group. meta-analysis was impossible because of heterogeneity, and most studies carried high or unclear risk of bias — this card establishes that referral interventions commonly work, not the size of any one strategy's effect. karmali kn et al. promoting patient uptake and adherence in cardiac rehabilitation. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. pmid: 24963623. mesh: adult · angina pectoris/rehabilitation · angioplasty, balloon, coronary/rehabilitation · coronary artery bypass/rehabilitation · coronary disease/rehabilitation · exercise · heart failure/rehabilitation · humans · middle aged · myocardial infarction/rehabilitation · patient acceptance of health care/statistics & numerical data · patient compliance/statistics & numerical data · randomized controlled trials as topic

shelves.title: Home-based pulmonary rehabilitation matched centre-based rehabilitation at programme end in two randomised trials — and by 12 months neither model had held its gains
shelves.question: In adults with COPD, is a home-based pulmonary rehabilitation programme non-inferior to centre-based rehabilitation for dyspnoea and exercise capacity?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Dyspnea/etiology · Female · Home Care Services · House Calls · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/complications/economics/physiopathology/rehabilitation · Quality of Life · Rehabilitation Centers · Single-Blind Method · Telephone · Therapeutic Equivalency · Walk Test
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — equivalence at the end of the programme, honestly time-limited. Holland AE et al. (PMID: 27672116) randomised 166 people with stable COPD to 8 weeks of centre-based rehabilitation or a minimal-resource home model (one home visit plus seven weekly physiotherapist telephone calls): the between-group difference in 6-minute walk distance at programme end favoured home by 18.6 m (95% CI −3.3 to 40.7), meeting non-inferiority without excluding superiority, and dyspnoea-related quality of life was equivalent at 12 months (difference 0.05 points; 95% CI −2.0 to 2.1) — but at 12 months the walk-distance interval (−5.1 m; 95% CI −29.2 to 18.9) did not exclude inferiority, and neither group maintained its gains. Maltais F et al. (PMID: 19075206) randomised 252 patients with moderate-to-severe COPD to self-monitored home rehabilitation or hospital outpatient rehabilitation after a shared 4-week education programme: at 1 year, dyspnoea improved by 0.62 units (95% CI 0.43–0.80) at home and 0.46 (95% CI 0.28–0.64) in outpatients, a difference of 0.16 (95% CI −0.08 to 0.40) inside the 0.5-unit non-inferiority margin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): home-based rehabilitation is a genuine equivalent for patients who cannot reach a centre — for as long as either model works.

cards.headline: Holland 2016: 6-minute walk difference +18.6 m favouring home at programme end (non-inferior); at 12 months the interval (−29.2 to 18.9) no longer excluded inferiority
cards.summary: Holland 2016: 6-minute walk difference +18.6 m favouring home at programme end (non-inferior); at 12 months the interval (−29.2 to 18.9) no longer excluded inferiority
cards.people: 166 participants with stable COPD randomised to 8 weeks of standard outpatient centre-based pulmonary rehabilitation (n=86) or a home-based model with minimal resources — one home visit and seven once-weekly physiotherapist telephone calls (n=80) — with 12 months of follow-up; primary outcome was change in 6-minute walk distance.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat analysis confirmed non-inferiority of home-based rehabilitation for 6-minute walk distance at end-rehabilitation, with the confidence interval not ruling out superiority (mean difference favouring home 18.6 m; 95% CI −3.3 to 40.7). At 12 months the interval did not exclude inferiority (−5.1 m; 95% CI −29.2 to 18.9). Dyspnoea-related quality-of-life differences did not rule out superiority of home rehabilitation at programme completion (1.6 points; 95% CI −0.3 to 3.5) and groups were equivalent at 12 months (0.05 points; 95% CI −2.0 to 2.1). Neither group maintained post-rehabilitation gains at 12 months.
cards.watchOut: The home model still included a home visit and weekly professional telephone contact — it is a staffed programme, not a leaflet — and the 12-month walk result means long-term equivalence is unproven, a caveat the title of this shelf carries.
cards.source: Holland AE et al. Home-based rehabilitation for COPD using minimal resources: a randomised, controlled equivalence trial. Thorax. 2017. PMID: 27672116. Registry ID: NCT01423227. cards.headline: Maltais 2008: dyspnoea improved 0.62 units at home versus 0.46 in outpatients at 1 year — difference 0.16, inside the 0.5 non-inferiority margin
cards.summary: Maltais 2008: dyspnoea improved 0.62 units at home versus 0.46 in outpatients at 1 year — difference 0.16, inside the 0.5 non-inferiority margin
cards.people: 252 patients with moderate-to-severe COPD at 10 Canadian academic and community centres; after a shared 4-week education programme, patients completed 8 weeks of self-monitored home-based rehabilitation or outpatient hospital-based rehabilitation and were followed to 1 year; the primary outcome was change in the Chronic Respiratory Questionnaire dyspnoea subscale, analysed in 107 home and 109 outpatient patients.
cards.result: Dyspnoea improved by 0.62 units (95% CI 0.43–0.80) in the home group and 0.46 units (95% CI 0.28–0.64) in the outpatient group at 1 year; the between-group difference of 0.16 units (95% CI −0.08 to 0.40) did not exceed the prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.5. Most adverse events were COPD exacerbations, and no serious adverse event was considered related to the intervention.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received the same 4-week education programme first, whose contribution to improvement cannot be separated from the rehabilitation itself; the analysis was a modified intention-to-treat using patients with data at each time point, which can flatter equivalence.
cards.source: Maltais F et al. Effects of home-based pulmonary rehabilitation in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a randomized trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2008. cards.headline: Synthesis: home rehabilitation is a real alternative for access — with the same 12-month fade as centre-based care
cards.summary: Synthesis: home rehabilitation is a real alternative for access — with the same 12-month fade as centre-based care
cards.people: Two randomised trials in COPD: Holland 2016 (n=166, minimal-resource home model) and Maltais 2008 (n=252, self-monitored home model).
cards.result: End-of-programme equivalence in both trials (walk +18.6 m favouring home; dyspnoea difference 0.16 units within a 0.5 margin); at 12 months, dyspnoea equivalence held in Holland (0.05 points) while walk-distance equivalence did not. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): non-inferior delivery of a beneficial intervention, claimed as equivalence rather than superiority.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial compared home rehabilitation with no rehabilitation, so this shelf borrows the efficacy of pulmonary rehabilitation from its own shelves and claims only the delivery equivalence. Tier C is not set: two randomised trials carry the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Holland AE et al. Thorax. 2017 (PMID: 27672116); Maltais F et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2008 (PMID: 19075206).

shelves.title: COPD telemonitoring: admissions unchanged in the large pragmatic TELESCOT trial (HR 0.98) — the earlier Cochrane pooling of telehealthcare packages had found fewer admissions (OR 0.46); the split is the service around the monitor
shelves.question: In adults with COPD already under specialist services, does adding home telemonitoring reduce hospital admissions for exacerbations versus usual care alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Algorithms · Decision Support Systems, Clinical · Disease Progression · Female · Health Knowledge, Attitudes, Practice · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Male · Medication Adherence · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Primary Health Care · Program Evaluation · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/epidemiology/physiopathology/psychology/therapy · Quality of Life · Scotland/epidemiology · Self Care/psychology · Single-Blind Method · Surveys and Questionnaires · Telemedicine
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the biggest, cleanest trial is null; the older pooled literature is positive. Pinnock H et al. (PMID: 24136634; TELESCOT) randomised 256 adults with a previous COPD admission in Lothian, Scotland, to telemonitoring (daily symptom questionnaire and oxygen saturation with algorithm-generated alerts) or conventional self-monitoring, with both groups receiving the same existing clinical services: time to hospital admission for exacerbation did not differ (adjusted hazard ratio 0.98; 95% CI 0.66–1.44), mean admissions were 1.2 versus 1.1 per person over a year (P=0.59), and quality of life did not improve (St George's Respiratory Questionnaire 68.2 versus 67.3). The earlier Cochrane review by McLean S et al. (PMID: 21735417; 10 trials) found telehealthcare associated with fewer patients having one or more hospital admissions over 12 months (odds ratio 0.46; 95% CI 0.33–0.65; 6 trials, 604 participants) and fewer emergency attendances (odds ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.11–0.66), with no difference in deaths (odds ratio 1.05; 95% CI 0.63–1.75) — but telehealthcare there was embedded in complex packages including nurse case management. PROPOSED SPLIT: telemonitoring bolted onto an already-good service adds nothing; the positive trials bundled monitoring with an enhanced clinical service, which is the likelier active ingredient.

cards.headline: Pinnock 2013 (TELESCOT): time to COPD admission HR 0.98; admissions 1.2 versus 1.1 per person; no quality-of-life gain
cards.summary: Pinnock 2013 (TELESCOT): time to COPD admission HR 0.98; admissions 1.2 versus 1.1 per person; no quality-of-life gain
cards.people: 256 adults in Lothian, Scotland, with at least one hospital admission for COPD exacerbation in the previous year, randomised to telemonitoring (128) — daily touch-screen symptom and treatment questionnaire plus oxygen-saturation monitoring with algorithm-generated alerts — or conventional self-monitoring (128), with both groups receiving similar care from existing clinical services; researcher-blind, multicentre, 1-year follow-up.
cards.result: Days to admission did not differ significantly (adjusted hazard ratio 0.98; 95% CI 0.66–1.44). Mean COPD admissions over one year were 1.2 per person (SD 1.9) on telemonitoring versus 1.1 (SD 1.6) on control (P=0.59), and mean admission duration was 9.5 versus 8.8 days (P=0.88). St George's Respiratory Questionnaire scores were 68.2 (SD 16.3) versus 67.3 (SD 17.3) (adjusted mean difference 1.39; 95% CI −1.57 to 4.35), with no significant effects on anxiety, depression, self-efficacy, knowledge, or adherence.
cards.watchOut: A null in patients already admitted once and already served by the same clinical teams — it does not test telemonitoring where usual care is thin. The authors' own interpretation, that earlier positive trials may have credited the monitor for the effect of the enhanced service beneath it, is the reading this shelf adopts.
cards.source: Pinnock H et al. Effectiveness of telemonitoring integrated into existing clinical services on hospital admission for exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: researcher blind, multicentre, randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2013. PMID: 24136634. Registry ID: ISRCTN96634935. cards.headline: McLean 2011 Cochrane: admissions OR 0.46 and emergency attendances OR 0.27 with telehealthcare — delivered as part of complex packages with nurse case management; deaths OR 1.05
cards.summary: McLean 2011 Cochrane: admissions OR 0.46 and emergency attendances OR 0.27 with telehealthcare — delivered as part of complex packages with nurse case management; deaths OR 1.05
cards.people: 10 randomised trials of telehealthcare for COPD versus usual face-to-face care (searches to January 2010), in which telehealthcare was assessed as part of complex interventions including nurse case management and other components.
cards.result: Telehealthcare was associated with fewer patients having one or more hospital admissions over 12 months (odds ratio 0.46; 95% CI 0.33–0.65; 6 trials, 604 participants) and one or more emergency department attendances (odds ratio 0.27; 95% CI 0.11–0.66; 3 trials, 449 participants). There was no significant difference in deaths over 12 months (odds ratio 1.05; 95% CI 0.63–1.75; 3 trials, 503 participants). Quality of life improved by a mean difference of −6.57 (95% CI −13.62 to 0.48) in 2 trials with 253 participants — a wide interval spanning the −4.0 minimum clinically important difference and no effect.
cards.watchOut: Small, older trials where monitoring was inseparable from intensified nursing care — the comparison TELESCOT was designed to clean up. Pooling used fixed effects on low-heterogeneity data, but small-study effects in a fashionable technology area remain a concern.
cards.source: McLean S et al. Telehealthcare for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2011. PMID: 21735417. cards.summary: Synthesis: the monitor is not the medicine — the service wrapped around it is what the positive trials were testing
cards.people: One large pragmatic RCT (Pinnock 2013, n=256) and the Cochrane review of 10 earlier trials (McLean 2011).
cards.result: Admissions: hazard ratio 0.98 (95% CI 0.66–1.44) when telemonitoring was added to an unchanged service; odds ratio 0.46 (95% CI 0.33–0.65) for telehealthcare bundled with case management. Deaths: odds ratio 1.05, no difference. PROPOSED SPLIT, split by what the monitoring is attached to.

shelves.title: CPAP telemonitoring: automated feedback raised use by about an hour a night in a 556-patient trial — clinician-contact telemonitoring in a smaller trial did not
shelves.question: In adults starting CPAP for obstructive sleep apnoea, does telemonitoring with feedback improve CPAP adherence versus usual follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Automation · California · Confidence Intervals · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure/methods · Feedback · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Monitoring, Physiologic/methods · Patient Compliance/statistics & numerical data · Patient Education as Topic/methods · Polysomnography/methods · Quality Improvement · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/diagnosis/therapy · Telemedicine/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the kind of telemonitoring decides it. In the large Tele-OSA factorial trial (Hwang D et al., PMID: 28858567), CPAP telemonitoring with automated patient feedback raised 90-day use to 4.4 hours a night and telemonitoring plus web education to 4.8 hours, versus 3.8 hours with usual care (P=0.0002 for both); Medicare adherence criteria were met by 65.6% and 73.2% versus 53.5%. Education alone did not significantly raise use (4.0 hours, P=0.10). In the smaller European trial (PMID: 28179438), telemonitoring that triggered clinician contact changed nothing: use was 5.1±2.1 versus 4.9±2.2 hours a night, although telemonitoring cost less (€123.65 versus €170.97, P=0.022) and satisfaction was lower (74% versus 96% rating it high or very high, P=0.034). PROPOSED SPLIT: automated feedback messaging improves early CPAP use by roughly an hour a night; telemonitoring as surveillance plus clinician contact does not, and may satisfy patients less.

cards.headline: Hwang 2018 (Tele-OSA): telemonitoring with automated feedback 4.4 h/night and telemonitoring plus education 4.8 h versus 3.8 h usual care at 90 days; Medicare adherence 73.2% versus 53.5%
cards.summary: Hwang 2018 (Tele-OSA): telemonitoring with automated feedback 4.4 h/night and telemonitoring plus education 4.8 h versus 3.8 h usual care at 90 days; Medicare adherence 73.2% versus 53.5%
cards.people: 1,455 patients referred for suspected obstructive sleep apnoea at a US centre (51.0% women, mean age 49.1 years); 956 had home sleep testing and 556 were prescribed CPAP and randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to usual care, web-based education (Tel-Ed), CPAP telemonitoring with automated feedback (Tel-TM), or both, with 90-day CPAP use as the primary endpoint.
cards.result: Average daily CPAP use at 90 days was 3.8±2.5 hours (usual care), 4.0±2.4 (Tel-Ed), 4.4±2.2 (Tel-TM) and 4.8±2.3 hours (Tel-both); Tel-TM and Tel-both were significantly higher than usual care (P=0.0002 for both), Tel-Ed was not (P=0.10). Medicare adherence rates were 53.5%, 61.0%, 65.6% and 73.2% respectively (Tel-both vs usual care P=0.001; Tel-TM vs usual care P=0.003). Telemedicine education also improved clinic attendance (show rate 68.5% vs 62.7%, P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: Ninety days is early adherence, not the years-long use that determines benefit, and the trial tested one automated messaging system in one US sleep programme; whether the extra hour persists, or changes sleepiness or cardiovascular outcomes, is not shown here.
cards.source: Hwang D et al. Effect of Telemedicine Education and Telemonitoring on Continuous Positive Airway Pressure Adherence. The Tele-OSA Randomized Trial. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2018. PMID: 28858567. Registry ID: NCT02279901. cards.headline: Turino 2017: telemonitoring with clinician contact did not improve compliance (5.1 vs 4.9 h/night) — cheaper, but patients were less satisfied
cards.summary: Turino 2017: telemonitoring with clinician contact did not improve compliance (5.1 vs 4.9 h/night) — cheaper, but patients were less satisfied
cards.people: 100 newly diagnosed patients with obstructive sleep apnoea (apnoea–hypopnoea index >15 events/hour) requiring CPAP, randomised to standard management or a telemonitoring programme collecting daily compliance, leak and residual-event data and prompting staff contact to resolve problems, followed for 3 months.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in CPAP compliance (5.1±2.1 telemedicine vs 4.9±2.2 hours/night standard), symptoms, quality of life or unwanted effects. Telemedicine cost less (€123.65 vs €170.97; P=0.022) and was cost-effective in the trial's analysis, but significantly fewer telemedicine patients rated satisfaction high or very high (74% vs 96%, P=0.034).
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 100 patients over 3 months cannot exclude a modest effect, and its telemonitoring relied on human follow-up rather than the automated feedback that worked in Tele-OSA — the contrast between the two trials is about the feedback loop, not monitoring itself.
cards.source: Turino C et al. Management of continuous positive airway pressure treatment compliance using telemonitoring in obstructive sleep apnoea. The European respiratory journal. 2017. PMID: 28179438. Registry ID: NCT02517346. cards.headline: Synthesis: monitoring alone is inert — automated feedback to the patient is the active ingredient found so far
cards.summary: Synthesis: monitoring alone is inert — automated feedback to the patient is the active ingredient found so far
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 656 patients prescribed CPAP (Tele-OSA, US, n=556 prescribed; Turino, Europe, n=100), each comparing a telemonitoring model with usual follow-up over about 3 months.
cards.result: Automated-feedback telemonitoring: 4.4–4.8 vs 3.8 hours/night and Medicare adherence up to 73.2% vs 53.5% (Tele-OSA). Clinician-contact telemonitoring: 5.1 vs 4.9 hours/night, no significant difference, at lower cost and lower satisfaction (Turino). PROPOSED SPLIT, as in the balance above.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are short; neither measures whether better early adherence survives a year or improves patient-important outcomes. Programmes buying telemonitoring should buy the feedback messaging, not just the dashboard.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hwang D et al. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2018 (PMID: 28858567); Turino C et al. The European respiratory journal. 2017 (PMID: 28179438).

shelves.title: Supported asthma self-management: 270 trials say unscheduled care falls and control improves — the support, not the plan alone, is what works
shelves.question: In adults with asthma, does supported self-management — a personalised action plan plus regular professional review — reduce hospitalisations and emergency attendances versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Asthma/economics/epidemiology/therapy · Delivery of Health Care/economics/methods · Health Care Costs · Hospitalization/economics/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Quality of Life · Self Care/economics/methods
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two independent syntheses of the randomised literature agree. The PRISMS meta-review (Pinnock H et al., PMID: 28302126) combined 27 systematic reviews (244 randomised trials) with 13 update trials and found supported self-management reduces hospitalisations, accident and emergency attendances and unscheduled consultations, and improves markers of control and quality of life across cultural, demographic and healthcare settings, with total costs offset by reduced hospital and emergency care (standard mean difference 0.13, 95% CI -0.09 to 0.34). The 2020 network meta-analysis (PMID: 32816816; 105 trials, 27,767 participants) found regularly supported self-management beat usual care on healthcare use (standardised mean difference -0.30, 95% credible interval -0.46 to -0.15) and quality of life (0.54, 0.11 to 0.96). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a written action plan plus regular professional review — totalling at least two hours of support — reduces unscheduled asthma care and improves quality of life.

cards.headline: Pinnock 2017 (PRISMS meta-review): 27 systematic reviews and 13 update trials — fewer hospitalisations and emergency visits, better control, costs offset
cards.summary: Pinnock 2017 (PRISMS meta-review): 27 systematic reviews and 13 update trials — fewer hospitalisations and emergency visits, better control, costs offset
cards.people: People with asthma across a range of cultural, demographic and healthcare settings, in 27 systematic reviews covering 244 randomised trials of supported self-management, plus 13 randomised trials published after the reviews' search dates, and a health-economic meta-analysis of 24 trials.
cards.result: Supported self-management reduced hospitalisations, accident and emergency attendances and unscheduled consultations, and improved markers of asthma control and quality of life. Core components were patient education, provision of an action plan and regular professional review. The total cost of providing support was offset by reduced hospitalisations and emergency visits (standard mean difference 0.13, 95% confidence interval -0.09 to 0.34).
cards.watchOut: A meta-review inherits the heterogeneity of its reviews: effects are reported as consistent directions rather than one pooled event rate, so the size of the hospitalisation benefit for any single service cannot be read off precisely; unsupported or plan-only self-management is not what was tested.
cards.source: Pinnock H et al. Systematic meta-review of supported self-management for asthma: a healthcare perspective. BMC medicine. 2017. PMID: 28302126. cards.headline: Hodkinson 2020: regularly supported self-management beat usual care on healthcare use (SMD -0.30) and quality of life (SMD 0.54) in 105 trials
cards.summary: Hodkinson 2020: regularly supported self-management beat usual care on healthcare use (SMD -0.30) and quality of life (SMD 0.54) in 105 trials
cards.people: 105 randomised trials with 27,767 participants comparing multidisciplinary case management, regularly supported self-management, minimally supported self-management and self-monitoring models against usual care or education in asthma, searched to April 2019.
cards.result: For healthcare use, multidisciplinary case management (standardised mean difference -0.18, 95% credible interval -0.32 to -0.05) and regularly supported self-management (-0.30, -0.46 to -0.15) were significantly better than usual care. For quality of life, only regularly supported self-management showed a significant benefit (0.54, 0.11 to 0.96). In children and adolescents, regularly supported self-management improved healthcare use (-0.21, -0.40 to -0.03) and quality of life (0.23, 0.03 to 0.48).
cards.watchOut: Effects are standardised mean differences across differently-scaled outcomes, not event counts; minimally supported models did not show the same benefits, so the regular professional review is part of the treatment, not an optional extra.
cards.source: Hodkinson A et al. Self-management interventions to reduce healthcare use and improve quality of life among patients with asthma: systematic review and network meta-analysis. BMJ. 2020. PMID: 32816816. MeSH: Asthma/therapy · Humans · Patient Acceptance of Health Care/statistics & numerical data · Quality of Life · Self-Management

cards.headline: Synthesis: the plan plus scheduled review is the intervention; either alone is a lesser treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: the plan plus scheduled review is the intervention; either alone is a lesser treatment
cards.people: A meta-review of 27 systematic reviews (244 randomised trials) with 13 update trials, and a network meta-analysis of 105 trials with 27,767 participants, spanning adults and children with asthma in many health systems.
cards.result: Healthcare use: regularly supported self-management standardised mean difference -0.30 (95% credible interval -0.46 to -0.15) versus usual care; quality of life 0.54 (0.11 to 0.96). Costs of support offset by fewer hospital and emergency attendances (standard mean difference 0.13, -0.09 to 0.34). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), as in the balance above.
cards.watchOut: Neither synthesis can name a single best action-plan format, and most trials predate current inhaler therapy; the consistent finding is about supported self-management as a service model, not about any one leaflet or app.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pinnock H et al. BMC medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28302126); Hodkinson A et al. BMJ. 2020 (PMID: 32816816).

shelves.title: Pharmacist inhaler-technique training works — and reminder labels stop the skill fading: correct technique retained by 67% versus 12% at 3 months in one trial
shelves.question: In adults with asthma, does pharmacist-led inhaler-technique training and follow-up improve asthma control versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Analysis of Variance · Anti-Asthmatic Agents · Asthma/drug therapy/psychology · Attitude of Health Personnel · Attitude to Health · Chi-Square Distribution · Drug Labeling/methods · Education, Pharmacy, Continuing · Feasibility Studies · Humans · Nebulizers and Vaporizers · New South Wales · Patient Education as Topic/methods · Pharmacies · Qualitative Research · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Reminder Systems · Self Administration · Severity of Illness Index · Single-Blind Method · Statistics, Nonparametric
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — pharmacist training corrects technique, and a personalised reminder label protects the gain. In the Australian cluster study (Basheti IA et al., PMID: 18314294), patients of trained pharmacists improved their inhaler technique score (of 9) by 2.8±1.6 points versus 0.9±1.4 with control pharmacists over 6 months (P<0.001), with asthma severity also significantly improved (P=0.015). In the Jordanian single-blind randomised trial (PMID: 28184045), every patient reached a perfect 9/9 after training, but at 3 months technique had declined significantly less in patients whose inhalers carried labels flagging their own errors (mean difference -1.04 points for Accuhaler, -1.61 for Turbuhaler), and label patients used less reliever medication (2.19 versus 3.42 puffs/day, P=0.002). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): brief pharmacist show-and-tell training improves inhaler technique and short-term control; labels extend the benefit, but the trials are small and from one research group.

cards.headline: Basheti 2008: technique score improved 2.8 versus 0.9 points (of 9) over 6 months with trained community pharmacists
cards.summary: Basheti 2008: technique score improved 2.8 versus 0.9 points (of 9) over 6 months with trained community pharmacists
cards.people: 31 community pharmacists in New South Wales, Australia (16 active, 15 control) and their asthma patients (53 active, 44 control) using dry-powder inhalers; active pharmacists were trained to assess and teach technique with patient-centred tools including inhaler technique labels, over four visits in 6 months.
cards.result: Baseline technique was poor (mean 5.7±1.6 of 9). At 6 months, improvement in inhaler technique score was significantly greater in active than control patients (2.8±1.6 vs 0.9±1.4, P<0.001), and asthma severity was significantly improved (P=0.015). Patients and pharmacists reported high satisfaction with the intervention.
cards.watchOut: Pharmacists, not patients, were the randomised unit, numbers are small, and asthma severity was a secondary outcome; the study shows a training service can work in motivated pharmacies, not that routine brief dispensing advice does.
cards.source: Basheti IA et al. Evaluation of a novel educational strategy, including inhaler-based reminder labels, to improve asthma inhaler technique. Patient education and counseling. 2008. PMID: 18314294. cards.headline: Basheti 2017: after training everyone scored 9/9 — labels limited the 3-month decline and cut reliever use (2.19 vs 3.42 puffs/day)
cards.summary: Basheti 2017: after training everyone scored 9/9 — labels limited the 3-month decline and cut reliever use (2.19 vs 3.42 puffs/day)
cards.people: 95 asthma patients in Jordan using Accuhaler or Turbuhaler controller medication (68% female, mean age 44.9 years), all given pharmacist show-and-tell technique counselling, then randomised to personalised inhaler reminder labels highlighting their initial errors, or no labels, for 3 months.
cards.result: All patients had correct technique (9/9) immediately after training. At 3 months, decline in technique score was significantly smaller with labels (Accuhaler mean difference -1.04, 95% CI -1.92 to -0.16, P=0.022; Turbuhaler -1.61, -2.63 to -0.59, P=0.003); the journal's summary reports 67% of label patients retained correct technique versus 12% of controls. Symptom control improved in both groups without a significant between-group difference, but label patients used less reliever medication (2.19 (SD 1.78) vs 3.42 (1.83) puffs/day, P=0.002).
cards.watchOut: Asthma was poorly controlled at baseline (mean Asthma Control Test scores 12.1–14.3) and the trial is small and single-group-led; technique is a skill surrogate — exacerbations and admissions were not measured.
cards.source: Basheti IA et al. Effect of novel inhaler technique reminder labels on the retention of inhaler technique skills in asthma: a single-blind randomized controlled trial. NPJ primary care respiratory medicine. 2017. PMID: 28184045. cards.headline: Synthesis: teach it properly once, then remind — technique, not control, is the proven endpoint
cards.summary: Synthesis: teach it properly once, then remind — technique, not control, is the proven endpoint
cards.people: Two small studies from the Basheti group (Australia, 97 patients via 31 pharmacists; Jordan, 95 patients) of pharmacist-delivered inhaler-technique training with or without personalised reminder labels.
cards.result: Technique improvement 2.8 vs 0.9 points of 9 at 6 months (2008); at 3 months after universal retraining, labels reduced skill decay by about 1.0–1.6 points and reliever use by about 1.2 puffs/day (2017). Asthma severity/control signals favoured intervention but were secondary and inconsistent between trials. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C for small single-group evidence on a skill outcome.
cards.watchOut: No trial here measures exacerbations, admissions or quality of life, and independent replication outside this research group is lacking; a larger pragmatic trial could still shrink the effect.
cards.source: Synthesis of Basheti IA et al. Patient education and counseling. 2008 (PMID: 18314294); Basheti IA et al. NPJ primary care respiratory medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28184045).

shelves.title: Once a day beats four times a day for taking medicines — 79% versus 51% of doses taken — but once versus twice daily is a small step, not a leap
shelves.question: Does simplifying dosing frequency — once-daily instead of multiple daily doses — improve medication adherence across chronic conditions?
shelves.mesh: Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Monitoring · Humans · Patient Compliance · Pharmaceutical Preparations/administration & dosage · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — adherence falls as daily doses multiply, with the cliff beyond twice daily. The electronic-monitoring systematic review (Claxton AJ et al., PMID: 11558866; 76 studies) found mean dose-taking compliance of 79%±14% for once-daily, 69%±15% for twice-daily, 65%±16% for three-times-daily and 51%±20% for four-times-daily regimens (P<0.001 across schedules); once-daily beat three-times (P=0.008) and four-times daily (P<0.001), but once-daily versus twice-daily was not significantly different. In cardiovascular medicines specifically (PMID: 27144286; 26 studies), regimen adherence was 83.1% once-daily versus 73.8% twice-daily, with adjusted adherence 14.2% worse (95% CI 6.8 to 21.7) on twice-daily dosing. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cutting doses per day improves adherence — decisively when regimens drop from three or four doses to one or two, modestly from two to one. Tier C: the comparisons are pooled across studies, not randomised head-to-head.

cards.headline: Claxton 2001: dose-taking compliance 79% once-daily, 69% twice, 65% three-times, 51% four-times daily across 76 electronically monitored studies
cards.summary: Claxton 2001: dose-taking compliance 79% once-daily, 69% twice, 65% three-times, 51% four-times daily across 76 electronically monitored studies
cards.people: 76 studies (1986–2000) across therapeutic classes in which compliance was measured with electronic monitoring (medication event monitoring systems), pooled to calculate mean dose-taking and dose-timing compliance by prescribed doses per day.
cards.result: Mean dose-taking compliance was 71%±17% overall and fell with dose frequency: 1 dose 79%±14%, 2 doses 69%±15%, 3 doses 65%±16%, 4 doses 51%±20% (P<0.001 among schedules). Once-daily was significantly better than three-times-daily (P=0.008) and four-times-daily (P<0.001), and twice-daily better than four-times-daily (P=0.001); once- versus twice-daily and twice- versus three-times-daily differences were not significant. Dose-timing compliance averaged 59%±24% in 14 studies.
cards.watchOut: Studies were not randomised by dose frequency — different drugs, diseases and eras contribute different schedules, so part of the gradient may be confounding by regimen and population rather than frequency itself; electronic monitoring itself can change behaviour.
cards.source: Claxton AJ et al. A systematic review of the associations between dose regimens and medication compliance. Clinical therapeutics. 2001. PMID: 11558866. cards.headline: Weeda 2016: cardiovascular medicines — regimen adherence 83.1% once-daily versus 73.8% twice-daily; adjusted gap 14.2%
cards.summary: Weeda 2016: cardiovascular medicines — regimen adherence 83.1% once-daily versus 73.8% twice-daily; adjusted gap 14.2%
cards.people: 26 prospective studies electronically measuring adherence for at least 4 weeks to oral chronic cardiovascular disease medicines: 40 once-daily arms (1,834 patients) and 18 twice-daily arms (451 patients).
cards.result: Unadjusted regimen adherence was 83.1% for once-daily versus 73.8% for twice-daily dosing, and timing adherence 74.2% versus 50.4% (P≤0.02 for both). On meta-regression, adjusted mean regimen adherence was 14.2% worse (95% CI 6.8 to 21.7) and timing adherence 22.9% worse (13.0 to 32.8) with twice-daily dosing (P≤0.002 for both).
cards.watchOut: Arms come from different studies rather than within-trial randomisation, twice-daily arms were much smaller, and cardiovascular medicines are a favourable case (many true once-daily equivalents exist); the result supports choosing once-daily options where they exist, not switching stable patients blindly.
cards.source: Weeda ER et al. Impact of once- or twice-daily dosing frequency on adherence to chronic cardiovascular disease medications: A meta-regression analysis. International journal of cardiology. 2016. PMID: 27144286. cards.headline: Synthesis: simplify to once or twice daily where the pharmacology allows — expect roughly 10–28 points of adherence, not miracles
cards.summary: Synthesis: simplify to once or twice daily where the pharmacology allows — expect roughly 10–28 points of adherence, not miracles
cards.people: Two pooled analyses of electronically monitored adherence (76 studies across conditions; 26 cardiovascular studies with 2,285 patients in analysed arms), spanning 1986–2015.
cards.result: Dose-taking adherence by frequency: 79% / 69% / 65% / 51% for one to four daily doses (Claxton). Once- versus twice-daily cardiovascular adherence: 83.1% vs 73.8% unadjusted; adjusted regimen gap 14.2% (6.8 to 21.7) (Weeda). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C for non-randomised comparisons.
cards.watchOut: Adherence is a behaviour surrogate: neither synthesis shows that simplifying frequency by itself improves clinical outcomes, and long-acting formulations can cost more or suit some drugs poorly.

shelves.title: Showing patients their own dosing history lifts adherence by about 9–20 points — the largest single component effect in the electronic-monitoring literature
shelves.question: Does electronically compiled dosing-history feedback — showing patients and clinicians their actual dosing pattern — improve medication adherence versus monitoring without feedback?
shelves.mesh: Drug Prescriptions · Electronic Health Records/trends · Humans · Medication Adherence · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/methods/trends
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — feedback is the best-supported single adherence component, on process outcomes. The meta-analysis of 79 randomised trials with electronically compiled dosing histories (Demonceau J et al., PMID: 23588595) found intervention groups averaged 74.3% adherence versus 60.2% in controls, and that adding feedback of the patient's own dosing history (EM-feedback) was associated with a 19.8% adherence improvement (95% CI 10.7 to 28.9) versus 10.3% (7.5 to 13.1) for interventions without it (P<0.01); meta-regression attributed an independent 8.8% increase to feedback (P<0.01). The later focused systematic review (PMID: 28991903) of 10 randomised trials found significant positive effects on full adherence in all five studies reporting it, but a significant clinical-outcome benefit in only one of seven studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dosing-history feedback improves measured adherence; whether it improves health outcomes is unproven.

cards.headline: Demonceau 2013: 79 RCTs — adherence 74.3% with intervention versus 60.2% control; feedback interventions improved adherence 19.8% versus 10.3% without feedback
cards.summary: Demonceau 2013: 79 RCTs — adherence 74.3% with intervention versus 60.2% control; feedback interventions improved adherence 19.8% versus 10.3% without feedback
cards.people: 79 randomised trials (1995–2011) of adherence-enhancing strategies for self-administered medicines in ambulatory patients, all measuring adherence by electronically compiled drug dosing histories; 48 trials contributed to the random-effects meta-analysis and 57 measured clinical outcomes.
cards.result: Patients randomised to intervention averaged a combined adherence outcome of 74.3%, 14.1 points above controls (60.2%). Improvement was 19.8% (95% CI 10.7 to 28.9) in studies with EM-feedback versus 10.3% (7.5 to 13.1) without (P<0.01); meta-regression estimated an 8.8% adherence increase attributable to feedback (P<0.01) and 5.0% to a cognitive-educational component (P=0.02), with intervention effects decaying 1.1% per month. Only 8 of 57 studies measuring clinical outcomes reported a significant improvement.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity was substantial and the funnel plot suggested possible publication bias; feedback was usually bundled with education or counselling, so the isolated effect of showing the graph alone is estimated by modelling, not by clean head-to-head trials.
cards.source: Demonceau J et al. Identification and assessment of adherence-enhancing interventions in studies assessing medication adherence through electronically compiled drug dosing histories: a systematic literature review and meta-analysis. Drugs. 2013. PMID: 23588595. MeSH: Drug Prescriptions · Electronic Health Records/trends · Humans · Medication Adherence · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/methods/trends

cards.headline: van Heuckelum 2017: 10 feedback RCTs — full adherence improved in 5 of 5 studies reporting it; clinical outcomes positive in only 1 of 7
cards.summary: van Heuckelum 2017: 10 feedback RCTs — full adherence improved in 5 of 5 studies reporting it; clinical outcomes positive in only 1 of 7
cards.people: 10 randomised trials (sample sizes 18–205 patients) comparing electronic monitoring feedback with usual care in adults, identified from 9,993 screened records, with dose adherence, full adherence and clinical outcomes extracted and GRADE-assessed.
cards.result: Four of six studies (66.7%) reported a significant positive effect on mean dose adherence, and all five studies reporting mean full adherence (100%) found a significant positive effect. A significant positive effect on clinical outcomes was reported in only one of the seven studies assessing them. The overall effect on adherence was judged positive and on clinical outcomes inconclusive.
cards.watchOut: The trials are small and half were low quality, with co-interventions common; the review supports feedback as an adherence tool while underlining that better adherence on a monitor has not yet been shown to translate into better health.
cards.source: van Heuckelum M et al. The effect of electronic monitoring feedback on medication adherence and clinical outcomes: A systematic review. PloS one. 2017. PMID: 28991903. cards.headline: Synthesis: feedback works on the behaviour it displays — prescribe it for adherence problems, not as proven outcome therapy
cards.summary: Synthesis: feedback works on the behaviour it displays — prescribe it for adherence problems, not as proven outcome therapy
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 79 electronically monitored randomised trials and a focused systematic review of 10 feedback-specific randomised trials.
cards.result: Adherence: 74.3% vs 60.2% for interventions overall; feedback-containing interventions improved adherence 19.8% vs 10.3% for non-feedback interventions; independent feedback contribution 8.8 points. Clinical outcomes: significant in 8 of 57 trials in the meta-analysis and 1 of 7 in the focused review. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for adherence, with the outcome gap on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Monitoring itself changes behaviour (a Hawthorne-type effect), effects decay about 1.1% per month in the meta-regression, and device cost and clinic time are real; long-term persistence after feedback stops is largely unmeasured.
cards.source: Synthesis of Demonceau J et al. Drugs. 2013 (PMID: 23588595); van Heuckelum M et al. PloS one. 2017 (PMID: 28991903).

shelves.title: Paying for viral suppression worked modestly in the big US trial — suppression up 3.8 points, continuity up 8.7 — but paying for linkage to care did nothing
shelves.question: In people with HIV attending clinics, do financial incentives for viral suppression increase the proportion virally suppressed versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-HIV Agents/economics/therapeutic use · Continuity of Patient Care/economics/organization & administration/statistics & numerical data · Female · HIV Infections/diagnosis/economics/psychology/therapy · Humans · Male · Medication Adherence/psychology · Motivation · Patient Care Planning/organization & administration/standards · Quality Improvement · United States · Viral Load/methods/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but small effect, confined to people already in care. In HPTN 065 (El-Sadr WM et al., PMID: 28628702), a site-randomised trial in the Bronx and Washington DC, $70 gift cards paid quarterly for viral suppression raised the proportion suppressed by 3.8 percentage points overall (95% CI 0.7 to 6.8, P=0.01) and by 4.9 points (1.4 to 8.5, P=0.007) among patients not previously consistently suppressed, and raised continuity of care by 8.7 points (4.2 to 13.2, P<0.001); $125 linkage coupons did not increase linkage to care (adjusted odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.67, P=0.65). The meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials (PMID: 32968885; 38,119 participants) found incentives improved ART adherence (risk ratio 1.30, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.50) and continuity (1.24, 1.09 to 1.41), with viral-suppression benefit clearest in high-income-country studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the suppression claim rests mainly on one large trial.

cards.headline: El-Sadr 2017 (HPTN 065): suppression +3.8 points and continuity +8.7 points with $70 quarterly gift cards; linkage coupons null (aOR 1.10)
cards.summary: El-Sadr 2017 (HPTN 065): suppression +3.8 points and continuity +8.7 points with $70 quarterly gift cards; linkage coupons null (aOR 1.10)
cards.people: 37 HIV test sites and 39 HIV care sites in the Bronx, New York and Washington DC, randomised to financial incentives or standard care; 9,641 HIV-positive patients on antiretroviral therapy were eligible for gift cards at 17 incentive care sites (39,359 cards dispensed), and 1,061 linkage coupons were dispensed at 18 incentive test sites.
cards.result: Financial incentives did not increase linkage to care (adjusted odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.67, P=0.65). Viral suppression (<400 copies/mL) was 3.8 percentage points higher at incentive sites (95% CI 0.7 to 6.8, P=0.01), and 4.9 points higher (1.4 to 8.5, P=0.007) among patients not previously consistently suppressed. Continuity in care was 8.7 points higher (4.2 to 13.2, P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Randomisation was by site, not patient, in two US cities with established care systems; the absolute gains are small, cost per extra suppressed patient is not the headline, and durability after payments stop was not the trial's question.
cards.source: El-Sadr WM et al. Financial Incentives for Linkage to Care and Viral Suppression Among HIV-Positive Patients: A Randomized Clinical Trial (HPTN 065). JAMA internal medicine. 2017. PMID: 28628702. Registry ID: NCT01152918. cards.headline: Krishnamoorthy 2021: 22 RCTs, 38,119 participants — adherence RR 1.30 and continuity RR 1.24 with incentives; suppression benefit concentrated in high-income studies
cards.summary: Krishnamoorthy 2021: 22 RCTs, 38,119 participants — adherence RR 1.30 and continuity RR 1.24 with incentives; suppression benefit concentrated in high-income studies
cards.people: 22 studies with 38,119 participants evaluating financial incentives across the HIV care continuum, searched to July 2019, pooled with random-effects models.
cards.result: All six outcomes favoured incentives, significantly for HIV testing uptake (pooled risk ratio 2.42, 95% CI 1.06 to 5.54, I²=100%), ART adherence (1.30, 1.13 to 1.50, I²=44%) and continuity in care (1.24, 1.09 to 1.41, I²=86%). For viral load suppression, benefit was reported among studies conducted in high-income countries rather than as a consistent overall effect.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is extreme for some outcomes (I² up to 100%), incentive sizes and schedules vary widely, and most component trials are small — the pooled adherence effect is more secure than any claim about suppression worldwide.
cards.source: Krishnamoorthy Y et al. Effectiveness of Financial Incentives in Achieving UNAID Fast-Track 90-90-90 and 95-95-95 Target of HIV Care Continuum: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. AIDS and behavior. 2021. PMID: 32968885. cards.headline: Synthesis: pay for the behaviour in care, not for showing up once — expect single-digit percentage gains
cards.summary: Synthesis: pay for the behaviour in care, not for showing up once — expect single-digit percentage gains
cards.people: One large site-randomised US trial (39 care/test sites; 9,641 patients eligible for suppression incentives) and a meta-analysis of 22 randomised trials with 38,119 participants.
cards.result: Viral suppression: +3.8 points (0.7 to 6.8) in HPTN 065; adherence risk ratio 1.30 (1.13 to 1.50) and continuity 1.24 (1.09 to 1.41) in meta-analysis; linkage to care: no effect (adjusted odds ratio 1.10, 0.73 to 1.67). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C as flagged in the balance.

shelves.title: Adherence clubs at city scale: 95.2% retained at a year and 97.2% suppressed among those tested — reassuring numbers, but from selected stable patients with no comparison group
shelves.question: For stable patients on antiretroviral therapy, do adherence clubs and other differentiated service-delivery models maintain viral suppression with fewer clinic visits versus standard clinic care?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anti-HIV Agents/therapeutic use · Cohort Studies · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · HIV Infections/drug therapy/virology · Humans · Male · Medication Adherence · Middle Aged · Proportional Hazards Models · Retrospective Studies · South Africa · Viral Load · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the outcomes inside clubs look excellent; the comparison the question asks for was never randomised. In the Cape Town scale-up sample (Tsondai PR et al., PMID: 28770595), 3,216 adults in adherence clubs had retention of 95.2% (95% CI 94.0 to 96.4) at 12 months and 89.3% (87.1 to 91.4) at 24 months, and 97.2% (96.5 to 97.8) of those with a viral load in the prior 13 months were suppressed (≤400 copies/mL). The implementation report (PMID: 27097834) shows the model reached 32,425 patients in 1,308 clubs at 55 facilities by March 2015 — 25.2% of the district's ART cohort — offsetting 51% of the cohort's doubling. But club members are chosen for being stable and adherent, and neither report compares them with matched clinic patients. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): clubs demonstrably sustain high retention and suppression in selected stable patients at scale; superiority or equivalence to clinic care is not established by these data.

cards.headline: Tsondai 2017: 3,216 club patients — retention 95.2% at 12 months, 89.3% at 24 months; 97.2% of tested viral loads suppressed
cards.summary: Tsondai 2017: 3,216 club patients — retention 95.2% at 12 months, 89.3% at 24 months; 97.2% of tested viral loads suppressed
cards.people: 3,216 adults (70% women) enrolled in antiretroviral therapy adherence clubs at non-research-supported sites in Cape Town between 2011 and 2014, sampled from 100 clubs (10% sample) and linked to city-wide laboratory and service data, contributing 4,019 person-years (median 1.1 years in a club).
cards.result: Retention was 95.2% (95% CI 94.0 to 96.4) at 12 months and 89.3% (87.1 to 91.4) at 24 months after club enrolment. In the 13 months before analysis closure, 88.1% of patients had viral load assessments and 97.2% (96.5 to 97.8) of those were ≤400 copies/mL. Loss to follow-up was higher in younger patients and at facilities with larger ART cohorts; viral rebound was higher in younger patients and those longer on ART.
cards.watchOut: There is no clinic-care comparison group, and clubs enrol patients already stable and suppressed — high absolute rates are expected from selection alone and cannot show the model causes them; 11.9% had no recent viral load, so suppression among all enrolled is lower than the tested figure.
cards.source: Tsondai PR et al. High rates of retention and viral suppression in the scale-up of antiretroviral therapy adherence clubs in Cape Town, South Africa. Journal of the International AIDS Society. 2017. PMID: 28770595. cards.headline: Wilkinson 2016: clubs scaled to 32,425 patients in 1,308 clubs — 25.2% of the Cape Metro ART cohort by March 2015
cards.summary: Wilkinson 2016: clubs scaled to 32,425 patients in 1,308 clubs — 25.2% of the Cape Metro ART cohort by March 2015
cards.people: The Cape Metro health district, Cape Town, South Africa, January 2011 to March 2015: monthly aggregate adherence-club monitoring reports and district electronic monitoring data covering the whole ART cohort, which grew from 66,616 to 128,697 patients.
cards.result: The programme expanded to 32,425 patients in 1,308 clubs at 55 facilities; the proportion of the total ART cohort retained in a club rose from 7.3% at the end of 2011 to 25.2% by March 2015, and 92.3% of patients were receiving ART at a facility offering clubs. The authors estimate implementation offset the cohort's doubling by 51%.
cards.watchOut: This is a feasibility and reach report without patient-level outcome comparison; it proves a health system can run clubs at scale, not that outcomes equal clinic care — that inference needs the comparative and randomised literature carded on the companion multi-month dispensing shelf.

shelves.title: A GP's signature on the screening invitation is worth about 6 points of uptake — 11.8 points combined with a better leaflet in the English factorial trial
shelves.question: Does adding a GP endorsement letter and a patient leaflet to a colorectal screening invitation raise screening participation versus the standard invitation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Colorectal Neoplasms/diagnosis/prevention & control · Confounding Factors, Epidemiologic · Correspondence as Topic · Early Detection of Cancer · England · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Mass Screening/methods · Middle Aged · Occult Blood · Pamphlets · Persuasive Communication · Primary Health Care/methods/standards/statistics & numerical data/trends · Reagent Kits, Diagnostic/statistics & numerical data · Research Design
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted factorial trial, consistent with the wider screening-intervention literature. In the English Bowel Cancer Screening Programme trial (Hewitson P et al., PMID: 21829202; 1,288 invitees of 20 GPs), a GP endorsement letter raised participation by 5.8 percentage points (95% CI 4.1 to 7.8) and an enhanced procedural leaflet by 6.0 points (4.3 to 8.1), with no important interaction — adjusted rate ratios 1.11 (P=0.038) and 1.12 (P=0.029) — so receiving both added 11.8 points (8.5 to 16). The US systematic review of 73 screening trials (PMID: 30326005) confirms invitation-side interventions work, with larger effects for mailed test outreach (risk ratio 2.26; risk difference 22%) and navigation (2.01; 18%) than for education (1.20; 4%) or reminders (1.20; 3%) alone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the endorsement estimate itself rests on a single trial.

cards.headline: Hewitson 2011: GP letter +5.8% and leaflet +6.0% participation; both together +11.8% — rate ratios 1.11 and 1.12
cards.summary: Hewitson 2011: GP letter +5.8% and leaflet +6.0% participation; both together +11.8% — rate ratios 1.11 and 1.12
cards.people: 1,288 patients registered with 20 GPs in the south of England, invited to the English Bowel Cancer Screening Programme in October 2009, randomised 2×2 to a GP endorsement letter and/or an enhanced leaflet explaining how to complete the faecal occult blood test, with kit return within 20 weeks as the primary outcome.
cards.result: The GP endorsement letter increased participation by 5.8 percentage points (95% CI 4.1 to 7.8) and the enhanced leaflet by 6.0 points (4.3 to 8.1); the random-effects logistic model found no important interaction, with adjusted rate ratios of 1.11 (P=0.038) for the letter and 1.12 (P=0.029) for the leaflet, and an additive combined effect of 11.8 points (8.5 to 16). An electronic GP signature on the letter was associated with higher participation in per-protocol analysis (P=0.039).
cards.watchOut: One programme, one test (guaiac faecal occult blood), one country and era; absolute gains depend on baseline uptake, and the trial cannot say whether endorsement works as well for colonoscopy-based or FIT-based programmes, though the mechanism — a trusted sender — plausibly transfers.
cards.source: Hewitson P et al. Primary care endorsement letter and a patient leaflet to improve participation in colorectal cancer screening: results of a factorial randomised trial. British journal of cancer. 2011. PMID: 21829202. cards.headline: Dougherty 2018: across 73 US trials, outreach (RR 2.26) and navigation (RR 2.01) beat education (1.20) and reminders (1.20) for screening completion
cards.summary: Dougherty 2018: across 73 US trials, outreach (RR 2.26) and navigation (RR 2.01) beat education (1.20) and reminders (1.20) for screening completion
cards.people: 73 randomised trials with 366,766 average-risk adults in US clinical settings, evaluating interventions to increase colorectal cancer screening completion, searched 1996–2017.
cards.result: Interventions associated with increased completion included faecal blood test outreach (risk ratio 2.26, 95% CI 1.81 to 2.81; risk difference 22%, 17 to 27), patient navigation (2.01, 1.64 to 2.46; 18%, 13 to 23), patient education (1.20, 1.06 to 1.36; 4%, 1 to 6), patient reminders (1.20, 1.02 to 1.41; 3%, 0 to 5), clinician reminders (risk difference 13%, 8 to 19) and academic detailing (10%, 3 to 17). Multicomponent combinations beat single components (risk ratio 1.18, 1.09 to 1.29).
cards.watchOut: GP endorsement is not pooled as its own category in this review, so it corroborates the class of invitation interventions rather than the Hewitson estimate directly; US settings and tests differ from the English programme.
cards.source: Dougherty MK et al. Evaluation of Interventions Intended to Increase Colorectal Cancer Screening Rates in the United States: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: cheap paper interventions buy real, single-digit uptake — endorsement is among the cheapest
cards.summary: Synthesis: cheap paper interventions buy real, single-digit uptake — endorsement is among the cheapest
cards.people: One English factorial randomised trial (1,288 invitees) testing GP endorsement and an enhanced leaflet, set against a 73-trial US meta-analysis (366,766 patients) of screening-completion interventions.
cards.result: Endorsement letter +5.8 points, leaflet +6.0 points, both +11.8 points (Hewitson). Class context: outreach +22 points, navigation +18 points, education +4 points, reminders +3 points (Dougherty). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C for the single-trial endorsement estimate.
cards.watchOut: Participation is not cancer mortality: extra invitees who complete screening are likely lower-risk than spontaneous attenders, and programmes should expect smaller absolute gains where baseline uptake is already high.

shelves.title: Targeted lung-screening invitations did not raise uptake — 52.3% versus 52.9% — but the stepped Lung Health Check invitation itself drew over half of deprived smokers in
shelves.question: In deprived heavy smokers, do targeted, stepped invitation materials increase uptake of lung cancer screening versus standard invitations?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Breath Tests · Carbon Monoxide · Early Detection of Cancer/methods · Ex-Smokers · Female · Humans · Lung Neoplasms/diagnostic imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Patient Selection · Smokers · Socioeconomic Factors · Spirometry · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — for the targeted leaflet, in the only randomised test. In the Lung Screen Uptake Trial (Quaife SL et al., PMID: 31825647; 2,012 people aged 60–75 recorded as current smokers, from 16 primary care practices), uptake of a Lung Health Check appointment was 52.6% overall with no difference between the targeted low-burden leaflet and the control leaflet (52.3% versus 52.9%; odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.16). Current smokers attended less than former smokers (adjusted odds ratio 0.70, 0.56 to 0.86). The screening-round report (PMID: 32759387) records what that uptake yielded: 768 of 996 analysed attendees scanned, 36 lung cancers (4.7%), 72.2% at stage I/II. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): psychologically targeted materials added nothing over a well-designed stepped invitation; the high uptake in both arms is the service finding, not a leaflet effect.

cards.headline: Quaife 2020 (LSUT): uptake 52.3% targeted versus 52.9% control — OR 0.98 (0.82 to 1.16); current smokers less likely to attend (aOR 0.70)
cards.summary: Quaife 2020 (LSUT): uptake 52.3% targeted versus 52.9% control — OR 0.98 (0.82 to 1.16); current smokers less likely to attend (aOR 0.70)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Quaife 2020, Lung Screen Uptake Trial)
cards.people: 2,012 participants aged 60–75, recorded as current smokers within the previous 7 years, selected from 16 UK primary care practices (predominantly lower socioeconomic position); both arms received a stepped pre-invitation, invitation and reminder sequence from their own practice offering pre-scheduled Lung Health Check appointments, differing only in the accompanying leaflet (targeted low-burden 'M.O.T. For Your Lungs' versus control).
cards.result: Uptake was 52.6% overall, with no difference between intervention (52.3%) and control (52.9%) groups in unadjusted (odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.16) or adjusted (0.98, 0.82 to 1.17) analyses. Current smokers were less likely to attend than former smokers (adjusted odds ratio 0.70, 0.56 to 0.86); socioeconomic deprivation was associated with lower uptake in the control group only (P<0.01).
cards.watchOut: The control was itself a carefully designed stepped invitation, so the trial tests the extra targeting, not invitation versus nothing; uptake far above earlier real-world studies in both arms suggests the shared Lung Health Check format did the work — a hypothesis this design cannot confirm.
cards.source: Quaife SL et al. Lung Screen Uptake Trial (LSUT): Randomized Controlled Clinical Trial Testing Targeted Invitation Materials. American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine. 2020. PMID: 31825647. Registry ID: NCT02558101. cards.headline: Ruparel 2020: what LSUT uptake delivered — 768 scanned, 36 cancers (4.7%), 72.2% stage I/II
cards.summary: Ruparel 2020: what LSUT uptake delivered — 768 scanned, 36 cancers (4.7%), 72.2% stage I/II
cards.type: Screening-round cohort report of the LSUT population (Ruparel 2020)
cards.people: The 2,012 LSUT invitees: 1,058 (52.6%) attended a Lung Health Check; 996 were included in the screening-round analysis, of whom 768 (77.1%) underwent low-dose CT, with median follow-up of 1,044 days for cancer outcomes.
cards.result: Of those scanned, 92 (11.9%) had indeterminate nodules needing 3-month and 33 (4.3%) 12-month surveillance; 36 lung cancers (4.7% of those scanned) were diagnosed, 72.2% at stage I/II, and 79.4% of non-small-cell lung cancers received curative-intent treatment.
cards.watchOut: This card describes yield in attenders, not an invitation comparison — it is included so the shelf shows what the (equal) uptake in both arms produced; cancer yield in self-selected attenders cannot be credited to either leaflet.

shelves.title: Diabetes medication conversation aids: patients know more and join in more — adherence and HbA1c unmoved in both randomised trials, and once better in usual care
shelves.question: In primary-care consultations for type 2 diabetes, does an encounter decision aid for glucose-lowering medicines improve knowledge, decisional comfort, and adherence versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Decision Making · Decision Support Techniques · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/drug therapy · Humans · Medication Adherence · Patient Participation
shelves.balance: SPLIT — decision quality improves; the downstream outcomes do not. In the multicentre cluster trial of the Diabetes Medication Choice conversation aid (Kunneman M et al., PMID: 34499328; 350 patients, 99 clinicians, 20 practices), knowledge rose (52% versus 45% correct answers, P=0.02) and observed patient involvement rose (OPTION12 difference 7.3, 95% CI 3 to 12, P=0.003), with no between-arm differences in treatment choice, satisfaction, encounter length, medication adherence or glycaemic control. The earlier pilot trial (PMID: 19786674) found the same pattern — knowledge +1.10 of 10 questions (95% CI 0.11 to 2.09) and involvement +21.8 of 100 (13.0 to 30.5) — but adherence at 6 months was better in usual care (9% more days covered, 4 to 14) and HbA1c identical (difference 0.01, -0.49 to 0.50). PROPOSED SPLIT: conversation aids do what they are built to do — inform and involve — and should not be sold as adherence or glycaemic interventions.

cards.headline: Kunneman 2022: knowledge 52% versus 45% and involvement +7.3 OPTION12 points — no difference in adherence, glycaemic control or encounter length
cards.summary: Kunneman 2022: knowledge 52% versus 45% and involvement +7.3 OPTION12 points — no difference in adherence, glycaemic control or encounter length
cards.people: 350 patients with type 2 diabetes and 99 primary care clinicians from 20 practices, cluster-randomised to consultations with or without the Diabetes Medication Choice conversation aid (shared decision-making tool), with participant-reported decision quality, observed involvement (OPTION12), adherence and glycaemic outcomes, plus interviews with 26 patients.
cards.result: The conversation aid increased post-encounter patient knowledge (correct answers 52% vs 45%, P=0.02) and clinician involvement of patients (OPTION12 mean difference 7.3, 95% CI 3 to 12, P=0.003). There were no between-arm differences in treatment choice, patient or clinician satisfaction, encounter length, medication adherence, or glycaemic control.
cards.watchOut: Clinicians and practices volunteering for a shared-decision-making trial may already involve patients more than average, compressing the measurable gain; adherence was not the tool's design target, and follow-up was not powered for HbA1c differences.
cards.source: Kunneman M et al. Making sense of diabetes medication decisions: a mixed methods cluster randomized trial using a conversation aid intervention. Endocrine. 2022. PMID: 34499328. cards.headline: Mullan 2009: knowledge +1.10/10 and involvement +21.8/100 — but 6-month adherence favoured usual care by 9% of days covered; HbA1c difference 0.01
cards.summary: Mullan 2009: knowledge +1.10/10 and involvement +21.8/100 — but 6-month adherence favoured usual care by 9% of days covered; HbA1c difference 0.01
cards.people: 85 patients with type 2 diabetes of 40 clinicians (21 randomised to the Diabetes Medication Choice decision aid describing 5 antihyperglycaemic drugs, 19 to usual care plus an educational pamphlet), with post-visit decisional outcomes and 6-month pharmacy-record adherence and HbA1c.
cards.result: Decision-aid patients (n=48) versus usual care (n=37) found the tool more helpful (+0.38 on a 7-point scale, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.72), had better knowledge (+1.10 of 10 questions, 0.11 to 2.09) and more involvement (+21.8 of 100, 13.0 to 30.5). At 6 months both groups had near-perfect median medication use (100% of days covered), but adherence (9% more days covered, 4 to 14) and persistence (12 more days, 3 to 21) were better in usual care, with no HbA1c impact (0.01, -0.49 to 0.50).
cards.watchOut: A small pilot (85 patients) with ceiling-level adherence in both arms — the usual-care adherence advantage may be chance or case-mix; the durable finding across both trials is the knowledge/involvement gain with glycaemic neutrality.
cards.source: Mullan RJ et al. The diabetes mellitus medication choice decision aid: a randomized trial. Archives of internal medicine. 2009. PMID: 19786674. Registry ID: NCT00388050. cards.summary: Synthesis: judge decision aids by decision quality — on that outcome two trials agree; on adherence and HbA1c they agree the other way
cards.people: Two cluster randomised trials of the same decision-aid family in primary care type 2 diabetes (85 patients pilot; 350 patients multicentre).

shelves.title: Midwife-led continuity of care: preterm birth down by about a quarter (RR 0.76) and fetal loss/neonatal death down (RR 0.84) across 15 trials — with fewer interventions and no caesarean penalty
shelves.question: In pregnant women and new mothers, does midwife-led continuity of care — the same midwife or team throughout — reduce preterm birth and interventions versus other models of care?
shelves.mesh: Amnion/surgery · Analgesia, Obstetrical/statistics & numerical data · Cesarean Section/statistics & numerical data · Continuity of Patient Care/organization & administration · Episiotomy/statistics & numerical data · Female · Humans · Infant · Infant Mortality · Infant, Newborn · Midwifery/economics/methods/organization & administration · Models, Organizational · Patient Satisfaction · Perinatal Care/methods/organization & administration · Postnatal Care/methods/organization & administration · Pregnancy · Prenatal Care/methods/organization & administration · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a high-quality Cochrane synthesis, with a mortality-adjacent outcome that puts this shelf in Tier C for personal review. Across 15 trials with 17,674 women (Sandall J et al., PMID: 27121907), midwife-led continuity models reduced preterm birth before 37 weeks (average risk ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.91; 13,238 women, 8 trials), all fetal loss plus neonatal death (0.84, 0.71 to 0.99; 17,561 women, 13 trials), regional analgesia (0.85, 0.78 to 0.92) and instrumental vaginal birth (0.90, 0.83 to 0.97), and increased spontaneous vaginal birth (1.05, 1.03 to 1.07) — all graded high-quality evidence — with no difference in caesarean birth. The largest single caseload trial (PMID: 22830446; 2,314 low-risk women) did find fewer caesareans (19.4% versus 24.9%; risk ratio 0.78, 0.67 to 0.91), a setting-specific result the pooled analysis does not reproduce overall. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): continuity models reduce preterm birth and interventions with at least comparable safety.

cards.headline: Sandall 2016 (Cochrane): 15 trials, 17,674 women — preterm birth RR 0.76, fetal loss + neonatal death RR 0.84, epidural RR 0.85, caesarean unchanged
cards.summary: Sandall 2016 (Cochrane): 15 trials, 17,674 women — preterm birth RR 0.76, fetal loss + neonatal death RR 0.84, epidural RR 0.85, caesarean unchanged
cards.people: 15 published and unpublished randomised trials involving 17,674 childbearing women allocated to midwife-led continuity models (caseload or team midwifery providing care across pregnancy, birth and postnatally) versus other models of care; primary outcomes GRADE-assessed as high quality.
cards.result: Women with midwife-led continuity were less likely to have regional analgesia (average risk ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.78 to 0.92), instrumental vaginal birth (0.90, 0.83 to 0.97), preterm birth <37 weeks (0.76, 0.64 to 0.91) and all fetal loss before/after 24 weeks plus neonatal death (0.84, 0.71 to 0.99), and more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth (1.05, 1.03 to 1.07). There were no differences in caesarean birth or intact perineum. Secondary outcomes included less episiotomy (0.84, 0.77 to 0.92) and amniotomy (0.80, 0.66 to 0.98).
cards.watchOut: Models varied (caseload versus team), most trials were in high-income settings with midwifery already established, and the fetal-loss finding combines losses before and after 24 weeks; the review authors call for more work on why preterm birth and early fetal loss fall.
cards.source: Sandall J et al. Midwife-led continuity models versus other models of care for childbearing women. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 27121907.
