cards.headline: McLachlan 2012 (COSMOS): caseload midwifery cut caesareans in low-risk women — 19.4% versus 24.9% (RR 0.78) — and neonatal unit admissions (RR 0.63)
cards.summary: McLachlan 2012 (COSMOS): caseload midwifery cut caesareans in low-risk women — 19.4% versus 24.9% (RR 0.78) — and neonatal unit admissions (RR 0.63)
cards.people: 2,314 women at low obstetric risk at a Melbourne tertiary women's hospital, randomised to caseload midwifery (antenatal, intrapartum and postpartum care from a primary midwife with back-up midwives; n=1,156) or standard care (n=1,158) with varying continuity.
cards.result: Caseload women were less likely to have a caesarean (19.4% vs 24.9%; risk ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.91, P=0.001), more likely to have a spontaneous vaginal birth (63.0% vs 55.7%; 1.13, 1.06 to 1.21), less likely to have epidural analgesia (30.5% vs 34.6%; 0.88, 0.79 to 0.996) or episiotomy (23.1% vs 29.4%; 0.79, 0.67 to 0.92). Their infants were less likely to be admitted to special or neonatal intensive care (4.0% vs 6.4%; 0.63, 0.44 to 0.90). No infant outcome favoured standard care.
cards.watchOut: Low-risk women at one hospital with a high baseline caesarean rate (24.9%) — the caesarean reduction was not seen in the pooled Cochrane analysis across all risk groups and settings, so it should be read as what caseload care can do in this context, not a guaranteed class effect.

cards.headline: Synthesis: continuity is one of the few maternity service models with high-grade randomised evidence of benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: continuity is one of the few maternity service models with high-grade randomised evidence of benefit
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 15 trials (17,674 women) plus the 2,314-woman COSMOS caseload trial, spanning team and caseload continuity models in several countries.
cards.result: Pooled: preterm birth risk ratio 0.76 (0.64 to 0.91); fetal loss plus neonatal death 0.84 (0.71 to 0.99); spontaneous vaginal birth 1.05 (1.03 to 1.07); caesarean no overall difference. COSMOS alone: caesarean 0.78 (0.67 to 0.91) in low-risk women. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C because of the fetal/neonatal mortality component.
cards.watchOut: Satisfaction and cost outcomes could not be pooled consistently (both trended favourable); workforce feasibility — midwives carrying caseloads with on-call commitments — is the main implementation constraint and is not measured by these trials.

shelves.title: Telephone triage splits by setting: out-of-hours nurse consultation halved GP workload safely — in-hours triage raised total contacts by a third to a half at no cost saving
shelves.question: In general practice, does telephone triage by GPs or nurses change same-day consultation demand, safety, and costs versus usual appointment booking?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Child · Child, Preschool · Cluster Analysis · Cost Savings · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Female · General Practice/methods · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Referral and Consultation/economics/statistics & numerical data · State Medicine/economics · Telephone/economics/statistics & numerical data · Time Factors · Triage/economics/methods · United Kingdom · Workload · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two big randomised tests answer different questions and point opposite ways on workload. For same-day requests in UK general practice (Campbell JL et al., PMID: 25098487; ESTEEM, 42 practices, 20,990 patients), GP telephone triage increased contacts over 28 days by 33% (2.65 versus 1.91 per person; rate ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.30 to 1.36) and nurse triage by 48% (2.81; 1.48, 1.44 to 1.52), with similar costs (about £75 per patient) and eight deaths within 7 days across arms that were not associated with trial group. For out-of-hours care (PMID: 9774295; 14,492 calls), nurse telephone consultation let nurses manage 49.8% of calls without a GP, cut GP telephone advice by 69%, primary-care-centre attendance by 38% and home visits by 23% — about a 50% workload reduction — with statistical equivalence in deaths, emergency admissions and A&E attendances. PROPOSED SPLIT: triage reorganises demand rather than abolishing it; out-of-hours nurse consultation substitutes safely, in-hours triage adds contacts.

cards.headline: Campbell 2014 (ESTEEM): GP triage +33% contacts and nurse triage +48% over 28 days; costs similar (~£75/patient); no safety signal
cards.summary: Campbell 2014 (ESTEEM): GP triage +33% contacts and nurse triage +48% over 28 days; costs similar (~£75/patient); no safety signal
cards.people: 42 UK general practices (13 GP triage, 15 nurse triage with computer support, 14 usual care) and 20,990 patients telephoning for a same-day GP consultation between 2011 and 2013; primary outcome was total primary care contacts (including A&E) in the 28 days after the request; 16,211 patients (77%) provided primary outcome data.
cards.result: GP triage was associated with a 33% increase in mean contacts per person over 28 days versus usual care (2.65 (SD 1.74) vs 1.91 (1.43); rate ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.30 to 1.36) and nurse triage with a 48% increase (2.81 (1.68); 1.48, 1.44 to 1.52). Estimated 28-day costs were similar across groups (roughly £75 per patient). Eight patients died within 7 days of the index request (five GP triage, two nurse triage, one usual care); the deaths were not associated with trial group or procedures.

cards.headline: Lattimer 1998 (SWOOP): nurses managed 49.8% of out-of-hours calls alone; GP workload fell ~50% with equivalence in deaths and admissions
cards.summary: Lattimer 1998 (SWOOP): nurses managed 49.8% of out-of-hours calls alone; GP workload fell ~50% with equivalence in deaths and admissions
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Lattimer 1998, South Wiltshire Out of Hours Project)
cards.people: A 55-member GP cooperative serving 97,000 patients in Wiltshire, England: 156 matched pairs of days/weekends over one year randomised to nurse telephone consultation (trained nurses with decision-support software) or usual GP-managed out-of-hours care; 14,492 calls concerning 10,134 patients.
cards.result: Nurses managed 49.8% of calls during intervention periods without referral to a GP. GP telephone advice fell 69%, patient attendance at primary care centres fell 38% and home visits fell 23% — an overall GP workload reduction of about 50%. Statistical equivalence was observed for deaths within 7 days, emergency hospital admissions within 24 hours and 3 days, and A&E attendances within 3 days.
cards.watchOut: A 1990s out-of-hours cooperative is a different service from modern in-hours access systems, and equivalence testing of that era was less formal; the result supports nurse consultation as a substitute where GPs are the bottleneck, not as an in-hours demand filter.
cards.source: Lattimer V et al. Safety and effectiveness of nurse telephone consultation in out of hours primary care: randomised controlled trial. The South Wiltshire Out of Hours Project (SWOOP) Group. BMJ. 1998. PMID: 9774295. cards.headline: Synthesis: ask what triage is for — substitution out of hours, addition in hours
cards.summary: Synthesis: ask what triage is for — substitution out of hours, addition in hours
cards.people: Two large UK randomised evaluations: ESTEEM (42 practices, 20,990 same-day requesters, in-hours) and SWOOP (14,492 out-of-hours calls, one cooperative).
cards.result: In-hours triage: contacts +33% (GP) and +48% (nurse), costs unchanged, no safety signal. Out-of-hours nurse consultation: ~50% GP workload reduction, equivalence on deaths/admissions/A&E. PROPOSED SPLIT, as in the balance.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial measures patient satisfaction or diagnostic accuracy for specific conditions at scale, and both predate app-based triage; digital-first systems should be evaluated as new interventions, not assumed to inherit either result.
cards.source: Synthesis of Campbell JL et al. Lancet. 2014 (PMID: 25098487); Lattimer V et al. BMJ. 1998 (PMID: 9774295).

shelves.title: Community paramedics in social housing: blood pressure and quality of life improved in both trial reports — the ambulance-call reduction was clear in the first, not significant in the full trial
shelves.question: In older adults living in social housing, does a community paramedicine wellness programme (CP@clinic) improve blood pressure and diabetes risk versus usual access to care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Allied Health Personnel · Canada · Cluster Analysis · Community Health Services/organization & administration/standards · Delivery of Health Care, Integrated/organization & administration/standards · Emergency Medical Services/statistics & numerical data · Emergency Medical Technicians/organization & administration · Female · Health Promotion · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Program Evaluation · Risk Assessment
shelves.balance: SPLIT — health measures improve; the headline service outcome is unstable across reports of the same trial programme. In the first cluster-randomised report (Agarwal G et al., PMID: 29807936; 6 buildings, 1,092 residents), CP@clinic lowered mean monthly ambulance calls (3.11 versus 3.99 per 100 units/month; adjusted difference -0.88, 95% CI -0.45 to -1.30 as printed), systolic blood pressure (mean change 5.0, 1.0 to 9.0) and diastolic pressure (4.8, 1.9 to 7.6), and improved quality-adjusted life years (difference 0.09, 0.01 to 0.17). In the larger multi-site report (PMID: 30624150; 30 buildings), the primary intention-to-treat analysis found no significant difference in EMS calls (-0.37 per 100 units/month, -0.98 to 0.24), though a sensitivity analysis excluding two ineligible building pairs did (-0.90, -1.54 to -0.26), and blood pressure and quality-of-life gains persisted (systolic -3.65, quality-adjusted life years +0.06); the cost analysis put the programme at about $C2,933 per quality-adjusted life year (PMID: 33109643, cited in synthesis). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: a single trial programme with successive reports.

cards.headline: Agarwal 2018: 6 buildings — ambulance calls 3.11 versus 3.99 per 100 units/month, systolic BP down 5.0, QALYs +0.09
cards.summary: Agarwal 2018: 6 buildings — ambulance calls 3.11 versus 3.99 per 100 units/month, systolic BP down 5.0, QALYs +0.09
cards.people: Six subsidised apartment buildings for older adults in Ontario, Canada (3 intervention with 455 residents, 3 control with 637), randomised to one year of CP@clinic — a weekly paramedic-led health promotion, risk assessment and referral programme for residents aged 55+ — or usual care; primary outcome building-level mean monthly ambulance calls.
cards.result: Mean monthly ambulance calls were significantly lower in intervention buildings (3.11 (SD 1.30) vs 3.99 (1.17) calls per 100 units/month; adjusted difference -0.88, 95% CI -0.45 to -1.30 as printed in the record). Surveyed residents (28.4% intervention, 20.3% control) showed improved quality-adjusted life years (mean difference 0.09, 0.01 to 0.17), better ability to perform usual activities (odds ratio 2.6, 1.2 to 5.8), and significant decreases in systolic (mean change 5.0, 1.0 to 9.0) and diastolic (4.8, 1.9 to 7.6) blood pressure.
cards.watchOut: Only six buildings — the effective sample for the primary outcome is tiny, survey response was low and self-selected, and residents could not be blinded; a single enthusiastic paramedic service could drive the result.
cards.source: Agarwal G et al. Evaluation of a community paramedicine health promotion and lifestyle risk assessment program for older adults who live in social housing: a cluster randomized trial. CMAJ : Canadian Medical Association journal = journal de l'Association medicale canadienne. 2018. PMID: 29807936. Registry ID: NCT02152891. cards.headline: Agarwal 2019: 30 buildings — EMS calls not significant intention-to-treat (-0.37, -0.98 to 0.24); BP and QALY gains persisted
cards.summary: Agarwal 2019: 30 buildings — EMS calls not significant intention-to-treat (-0.37, -0.98 to 0.24); BP and QALY gains persisted
cards.type: Multi-site cluster-randomised controlled trial report (Agarwal 2019, CP@clinic)
cards.people: 30 eligible subsidised public-housing buildings across five Ontario paramedic services, pair-randomised to one year of CP@clinic or usual care; residents aged 55+ analysed; primary outcome building-level EMS calls from paramedic service databases (same trial registration as the 2018 report, NCT02152891).
cards.result: Intention-to-treat analysis showed no significant difference in EMS calls (mean difference -0.37 per 100 apartment units/month, 95% CI -0.98 to 0.24). A sensitivity analysis excluding two building pairs with post-randomisation eligibility changes found a significant difference favouring intervention (-0.90, -1.54 to -0.26). At individual level there was a significant quality-adjusted life year increase (mean difference 0.06, 0.02 to 0.10) and blood pressure decrease (systolic mean change 3.65 mmHg, 2.37 to 4.94; diastolic 2.03, 1.00 to 3.06).
cards.watchOut: The discrepancy between the 2018 and 2019 primary results is the central caution on this shelf: both are reports of one programme under one registration, and the larger, fuller analysis is the one whose primary outcome is null; blood-pressure analyses rest on the surveyed minority.
cards.source: Agarwal G et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: a promising, cheap programme whose service-use claim awaits an independent trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: a promising, cheap programme whose service-use claim awaits an independent trial
cards.people: Successive reports of the CP@clinic cluster trial programme in Ontario subsidised housing (6 buildings in 2018; 30 buildings in 2019; cost-utility analysis of 1,461 residents in 32 buildings, PMID: 33109643).
cards.result: Ambulance/EMS calls: -0.88 per 100 units/month (2018 report) versus -0.37 and non-significant intention-to-treat (2019 report). Blood pressure: systolic about -3.7 to -5.0 across reports. Quality-adjusted life years: +0.03 to +0.09; cost-utility about $C2,933 per quality-adjusted life year, below the $C50,000 threshold cited by the authors. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C, as in the balance.
cards.watchOut: All evidence comes from the programme's own investigators in one province; replication by an independent group, with individual-level clinical outcomes, is the missing step before scale-up claims harden.

shelves.title: Text reminders get people through the door: attendance 78.6% versus 67.8% in the Cochrane review — matching phone calls at roughly half the cost
shelves.question: Do mobile-phone text-message reminders improve attendance at healthcare appointments versus no reminders or other reminder types?
shelves.mesh: Appointments and Schedules · Cell Phone · Humans · Patient Compliance · Reminder Systems
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two concordant syntheses, on attendance rather than health outcomes. The meta-analysis by Guy R et al. (PMID: 22091980) pooled eight randomised trials and found a summary effect of 1.48 (95% CI 1.23 to 1.72) for SMS reminders on attendance, with heterogeneity (I²=90%) driven by the ten included observational studies rather than the trials. The Cochrane update (PMID: 24310741; 8 randomised trials, 6,615 participants) found moderate-quality evidence that text reminders improved attendance versus no reminder (risk ratio 1.14, 1.03 to 1.26; attendance 78.6% versus 67.8%), matched phone-call reminders (risk ratio 0.99, 0.95 to 1.02; 80.3% attended after calls), and cost 55% and 65% less per attendance than calls in the two costing studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a cheap, reliable nudge for attendance — distinct from the adherence-texting shelf, which asks a different question.

cards.headline: Guy 2012: eight RCTs give a summary effect of 1.48 (1.23 to 1.72) for SMS reminders on clinic attendance
cards.summary: Guy 2012: eight RCTs give a summary effect of 1.48 (1.23 to 1.72) for SMS reminders on clinic attendance
cards.people: 18 reports meeting review criteria (8 randomised trials and 10 controlled observational studies) comparing appointment attendance with versus without SMS reminders, published before June 2010, across primary care and hospital outpatient clinics and paediatric and older populations.
cards.result: Across all studies, heterogeneity was significant (I²=90%, P<0.01), so no overall summary was calculated; stratification showed the heterogeneity came from the observational studies. The summary effect from the randomised trials was 1.48 (95% CI 1.23 to 1.72), with no significant subgroup differences by clinic type, message timing (24, 48 or 72+ hours ahead) or target age group.
cards.watchOut: The 1.48 figure is reported by the record as a summary effect across differently-reported trial measures and should not be quoted as a risk ratio; the cleaner absolute estimate comes from the Cochrane review carded next.
cards.source: Guy R et al. How effective are short message service reminders at increasing clinic attendance? A meta-analysis and systematic review. Health services research. 2012. PMID: 22091980. MeSH: Appointments and Schedules · Cell Phone · Humans · Patient Compliance · Reminder Systems

cards.headline: Gurol-Urganci 2013 (Cochrane): attendance 78.6% with texts versus 67.8% with no reminder (RR 1.14); 80.3% with phone calls (RR 0.99 vs texts)
cards.summary: Gurol-Urganci 2013 (Cochrane): attendance 78.6% with texts versus 67.8% with no reminder (RR 1.14); 80.3% with phone calls (RR 0.99 vs texts)
cards.people: 8 randomised trials with 6,615 participants assessing mobile phone messaging reminders for healthcare appointments, in which the messaging effect could be isolated from other interventions; searches to August 2012.
cards.result: Moderate-quality evidence from seven studies (5,841 participants) showed improved attendance versus no reminders (risk ratio 1.14, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.26). Moderate-quality evidence from three studies (2,509 participants) showed text reminders matched phone-call reminders (0.99, 0.95 to 1.02). Overall attendance rates were 67.8% (no reminder), 78.6% (text) and 80.3% (phone call). Two studies reported cost per attendance 55% and 65% lower for texts than calls. No included study reported health outcomes in detail.
cards.watchOut: Evidence quality was low to moderate and studies were heterogeneous; the trials predate smartphone messaging, and none measured whether attending the extra appointments improved health — attendance is an efficiency outcome.
cards.source: Gurol-Urganci I et al. Mobile phone messaging reminders for attendance at healthcare appointments. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 24310741. cards.headline: Synthesis: send the text — expect about 11 more attendances per 100 appointments than silence, the same as phoning for more money
cards.summary: Synthesis: send the text — expect about 11 more attendances per 100 appointments than silence, the same as phoning for more money
cards.people: Two syntheses of the randomised literature (Guy: 8 trials within 18 reports; Cochrane update: 8 trials, 6,615 participants).
cards.result: Attendance: 78.6% text versus 67.8% none (risk ratio 1.14, 1.03 to 1.26); text versus phone call 0.99 (0.95 to 1.02); trial summary effect 1.48 (1.23 to 1.72) in the earlier meta-analysis. Costs per attendance 55–65% lower than calls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), as in the balance.

shelves.title: OpenNotes: most patients who read their notes said they felt more in control and took medicines more reliably — self-reported, from volunteers, with almost no doctors quitting
shelves.question: Does giving patients open access to their clinicians' visit notes (OpenNotes) improve engagement, understanding, and medication adherence versus usual record access?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Boston · Communication · Confidentiality · Electronic Health Records · Female · Humans · Internet · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Access to Records · Pennsylvania · Physician-Patient Relations · Physicians, Primary Care · Pilot Projects · Surveys and Questionnaires · Washington · Workload · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — large, consistent patient-reported gains; objectively weak designs, hence Tier C. In the original quasi-experimental study (Delbanco T et al., PMID: 23027317; 105 primary care physicians, 13,564 patients at three US systems), 11,155 patients opened at least one note; of 5,219 survey respondents who opened a note, 59–77% across sites said open notes helped them feel more in control of their care and 60–78% of those taking medications reported increased medication adherence, while 26–36% had privacy concerns and only 1–8% reported confusion, worry or offence; 99% of patients wanted open notes to continue and no doctor elected to stop. The later mixed-methods evaluation (PMID: 26826154; 576 free-text responses, 13 interviews) found the same themes — improved understanding, relationships, self-care and perceived adherence — with fewer concerns among experienced note-readers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): patients value and report benefiting from open notes; measured adherence or outcome effects have not been demonstrated.

cards.headline: Delbanco 2012: 11,155 of 13,564 patients opened a note; 60–78% of medication users reported better adherence; 99% wanted it to continue
cards.summary: Delbanco 2012: 11,155 of 13,564 patients opened a note; 60–78% of medication users reported better adherence; 99% wanted it to continue
cards.people: 105 volunteering primary care physicians and 13,564 of their patients with at least one available note during a year-long programme at Beth Israel Deaconess (Massachusetts), Geisinger (Pennsylvania) and Harborview (Washington); portal use, messaging volume and pre/post surveys of patients and doctors (5,219 patients who opened a note completed the post-intervention survey; patient survey response rate 41%).
cards.result: Across sites, 77% to 59% of respondents reported open notes helped them feel more in control of their care; 60% to 78% of those taking medications reported increased medication adherence; 26% to 36% had privacy concerns; 1% to 8% reported confusion, worry or offence; 20% to 42% shared notes with others. Patient message volume did not change; 0–5% of doctors reported longer visits and 3–36% changed documentation content. At the end, 99% of patients wanted open notes to continue and no doctor elected to stop.
cards.watchOut: Volunteer doctors and portal-using patients, a 41% survey response rate, and self-reported adherence with no pharmacy or clinical outcome data — the study measures experience and perception, not verified adherence; the adherence percentages cannot be read as effect sizes.
cards.source: Delbanco T et al. Inviting patients to read their doctors' notes: a quasi-experimental study and a look ahead. Annals of internal medicine. 2012. PMID: 23027317. cards.headline: Esch 2016: experienced note-readers report better understanding, relationships and self-care — concerns fade with repeated reading
cards.summary: Esch 2016: experienced note-readers report better understanding, relationships and self-care — concerns fade with repeated reading
cards.people: Primary care patients at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center with electronic access to visit notes: 576 free-text survey answers analysed (414 from female patients, 162 from male; ages 23–88) plus semi-structured interviews with 13 patients (ages 58–87), with patient activation measures.
cards.result: Patient experiences indicated improved understanding of health information, better relationships with doctors, better perceived quality (including adherence and keeping track) and improved self-care, patient-centredness and empowerment. cards.watchOut: Qualitative and self-selected: it explains how open notes may help engaged patients, but provides no comparative effect estimate and cannot rescue the adherence claim from its self-reported status.

shelves.title: Organised anticoagulation care keeps INRs in range about 12 points more of the time than community practice — event-rate benefits come from observational comparisons, not trials
shelves.question: In patients on warfarin, does management through a dedicated anticoagulation clinic or management service improve time in therapeutic range and reduce bleeding and thrombosis versus usual physician care?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants/therapeutic use · Blood Coagulation/drug effects · Confidence Intervals · Humans · Pulmonary Embolism/blood/prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic/methods · Treatment Outcome · Venous Thrombosis/blood/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the control advantage is consistent; the clinical-event advantage is observational. The systematic review and metaregression (van Walraven C et al., PMID: 16685005; 67 studies, 50,208 patients, 57,154.7 patient-years) found patients were in therapeutic range 63.6% of the time overall (95% CI 61.6 to 65.6), with community-practice care significantly worse than anticoagulation clinics or trials (-12.2%, -19.5 to -4.8, P<0.0001) and self-management better (+7.0%, 0.7 to 13.3, P=0.03). The pharmacist-led service review (PMID: 26100092; 24 studies, 11,607 patients) found, in non-randomised studies, time in range of 72.1% versus 56.7% (P=0.013) with less major bleeding (0.6% versus 1.7%), thromboembolism (0.6% versus 2.9%) and hospitalisation (3% versus 10%) — while its four randomised trials showed only comparability with usual care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: dedicated services improve INR control; claims of fewer bleeds and clots rest on non-randomised data.

cards.headline: van Walraven 2006: time in range 63.6% overall — community practice 12.2 points below clinics/trials; self-management +7.0 points
cards.summary: van Walraven 2006: time in range 63.6% overall — community practice 12.2 points below clinics/trials; self-management +7.0 points
cards.people: 67 published randomised or cohort studies with 123 patient groups (50,208 patients, 57,154.7 patient-years) reporting serial INRs on oral anticoagulants; 68.3% of groups were from anticoagulation clinics, 7.3% from clinical trials and 24.4% from community practices.
cards.result: Patients were in the therapeutic range 63.6% of the time (95% CI 61.6 to 65.6). In metaregression, study setting had the greatest effect: community-practice groups had significantly lower control than anticoagulation clinics or clinical trials (-12.2%, -19.5 to -4.8, P<0.0001). Self-management was associated with significantly better time in range (+7.0%, 0.7 to 13.3, P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: This compares settings across studies, not randomised services within them — clinic populations, indications and INR targets differ, and the analysis is at study level; it shows where good control is achieved, not a randomised effect of referring a given patient.
cards.source: van Walraven C et al. Effect of study setting on anticoagulation control: a systematic review and metaregression. Chest. 2006. PMID: 16685005. cards.headline: Entezari-Maleki 2016: pharmacist-led care — time in range 72.1% versus 56.7% and fewer events in observational studies; RCTs showed comparability only
cards.summary: Entezari-Maleki 2016: pharmacist-led care — time in range 72.1% versus 56.7% and fewer events in observational studies; RCTs showed comparability only
cards.people: 24 studies (4 randomised trials, 20 non-randomised) with 11,607 patients comparing pharmacist-managed warfarin therapy with usual medical care on anticoagulation control, bleeding and thromboembolic events, mortality, hospitalisation, emergency visits, cost and satisfaction, searched to January 2014.
cards.result: Among non-randomised studies, pharmacist-led care favoured time in therapeutic range (72.1% vs 56.7%, P=0.013), major bleeding (0.6% vs 1.7%, P<0.001), thromboembolic events (0.6% vs 2.9%, P<0.001), hospitalisation (3% vs 10%, P<0.001) and emergency department visits (7.9% vs 23.9%, P<0.0001), with cost saving and better satisfaction. The authors conclude pharmacist-led care is superior on observational evidence and comparable on randomised evidence.
cards.watchOut: Twenty of 24 studies are non-randomised and prone to selection and era effects; event-rate gaps of this size from such designs should be treated as upper bounds. The randomised subset supports safety and equivalence, not superiority.
cards.source: Entezari-Maleki T et al. A systematic review on comparing 2 common models for management of warfarin therapy; pharmacist-led service versus usual medical care. shelves.title: Virtual wards split by diagnosis: no effect in the large mixed high-risk trial — fewer deaths and readmissions only in heart-failure trials
shelves.question: After hospital discharge, does a virtual ward — daily interdisciplinary rounds on patients monitored at home — reduce readmission or death versus usual post-discharge care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Ambulatory Care/methods · Community Health Services · Continuity of Patient Care · Female · House Calls · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Telemedicine
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by diagnosis, and the largest single trial is null. In the Toronto randomised trial (Dhalla IA et al., PMID: 25268437; 1,923 high-risk patients), a post-discharge virtual ward did not significantly change the composite of readmission or death at 30 days (21.2% (203/959) versus 24.6% (235/956); absolute difference 3.4%, 95% CI -0.3 to 7.2, P=0.09) or at 90 days, 6 months or 1 year. The meta-analysis of 24 randomised trials (PMID: 35763296; 10,876 patients) found virtual wards associated with fewer deaths (risk ratio 0.86, 0.76 to 0.97) and readmissions (0.84, 0.74 to 0.96) only in heart-failure trials, with no such associations in other diagnoses (mortality 0.93, 0.83 to 1.04; readmissions 0.96, 0.88 to 1.05), though emergency department visits fell overall (0.83, 0.70 to 0.98). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C for the heart-failure mortality component: build virtual wards for heart failure if at all; the generic high-risk model failed its test.

cards.headline: Dhalla 2014: virtual ward 21.2% versus usual care 24.6% readmission-or-death at 30 days (P=0.09) — null at every timepoint to 1 year
cards.summary: Dhalla 2014: virtual ward 21.2% versus usual care 24.6% readmission-or-death at 30 days (P=0.09) — null at every timepoint to 1 year
cards.people: 1,923 high-risk adult patients discharged from Toronto hospitals (963 virtual ward, 960 usual care), enrolled 2010–2014; the virtual ward provided care coordination plus direct care by an interprofessional team (telephone, home and clinic visits, daily central rounds) for several weeks after discharge, versus structured discharge summary and usual follow-up arrangements.
cards.result: There were no statistically significant between-group differences in primary or secondary outcomes at 30 or 90 days, 6 months or 1 year. The primary outcome (readmission or death within 30 days) occurred in 203 of 959 virtual ward patients (21.2%) and 235 of 956 usual care patients (24.6%) — absolute difference 3.4% (95% CI -0.3 to 7.2, P=0.09). No prespecified subgroup showed a significant interaction.
cards.watchOut: A single-city trial in a system with comparatively good usual discharge care; the confidence interval excludes large benefit but not a small one, and the intervention's intensity may have been diluted across a very heterogeneous high-risk population — the heart-failure signal in the meta-analysis is the plausible exception.
cards.source: Dhalla IA et al. Effect of a postdischarge virtual ward on readmission or death for high-risk patients: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 25268437. Registry ID: NCT01108172. cards.headline: Chauhan 2022: 24 RCTs — heart failure deaths RR 0.86 and readmissions RR 0.84 with virtual wards; other diagnoses null
cards.summary: Chauhan 2022: 24 RCTs — heart failure deaths RR 0.86 and readmissions RR 0.84 with virtual wards; other diagnoses null
cards.people: 24 randomised trials with 10,876 patients comparing virtual ward transitional care with usual post-discharge care (11 heart failure, 3 COPD, 4 high-risk, 6 mixed populations), published 2000–2021.
cards.result: In heart failure, virtual wards were associated with fewer deaths (risk ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.97) and fewer readmissions (0.84, 0.74 to 0.96). In other diagnoses, associations were absent (mortality 0.93, 0.83 to 1.04; readmissions 0.96, 0.88 to 1.05). Across all studies, virtual wards were associated with fewer emergency department visits (0.83, 0.70 to 0.98) and shorter readmission stays (mean difference -1.94 days, -3.28 to -0.60); three of seven cost studies reported significantly lower costs.
cards.watchOut: Virtual ward definitions vary and earlier reviews conflated telemonitoring with ward models; the heart-failure subgroup result, while pre-stratified by diagnosis, pools smaller older trials and should be confirmed rather than assumed for modern heart-failure pathways.
cards.source: Chauhan U et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: one model, two answers — diagnosis is the effect modifier
cards.summary: Synthesis: one model, two answers — diagnosis is the effect modifier
cards.people: One large pragmatic randomised trial in mixed high-risk discharges (1,923 patients) and a meta-analysis of 24 randomised trials (10,876 patients) stratified by diagnosis.
cards.result: Mixed high-risk: readmission-or-death 21.2% vs 24.6% at 30 days, non-significant, null to 1 year. shelves.title: Barcode medication administration: non-timing errors fell 41% relative and potential harm events halved — provided every dose is scanned; scanning one dose of many made harm events rise
shelves.question: In hospital inpatients, does barcode medication administration reduce medication administration errors and potential adverse drug events versus manual checking?
shelves.mesh: Academic Medical Centers/organization & administration · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Electronic Data Processing · Humans · Medical Order Entry Systems · Medication Errors/prevention & control/statistics & numerical data · Medication Systems, Hospital · Organizational Case Studies · Organizational Innovation · Pharmaceutical Preparations/administration & dosage · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — large, directly observed before-and-after evidence with a crucial configuration warning; Tier C because nothing here is randomised. In the academic-centre study (Poon EG et al., PMID: 20445181; 14,041 observed administrations, 3,082 transcriptions), barcode eMAR cut non-timing administration errors from 11.5% to 6.8% (41.4% relative reduction, P<0.001) and potential adverse drug events from 3.1% to 1.6% (50.8% relative reduction, P<0.001), and eliminated transcription errors (6.1% to 0%). In the same group's pharmacy study (PMID: 16983130; 369,148 observed doses), target potential adverse drug events fell 74% relative overall — but in the configuration that scanned only one dose of a multi-dose fill, target potential adverse events rose 2.4-fold (P=0.014), while scan-every-dose configurations cut target errors 93–96% relative. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): barcode verification works when the workflow forces a scan of every dose, every time.

cards.headline: Poon 2010: non-timing errors 11.5% to 6.8% (41.4% relative reduction); potential ADEs 3.1% to 1.6% (50.8% relative); transcription errors eliminated
cards.summary: Poon 2010: non-timing errors 11.5% to 6.8% (41.4% relative reduction); potential ADEs 3.1% to 1.6% (50.8% relative); transcription errors eliminated
cards.people: One US academic medical centre implementing barcode electronic medication administration records (bar-code eMAR): 14,041 directly observed medication administrations and 3,082 reviewed order transcriptions on units before and after implementation; two clinicians classified errors' potential to harm.
cards.result: Observers recorded 776 non-timing administration errors without bar-code eMAR (11.5% error rate) versus 495 with it (6.8%) — a 41.4% relative reduction (P<0.001). Potential adverse drug events (non-timing) fell from 3.1% to 1.6% (50.8% relative reduction, P<0.001); timing errors fell 27.3% relative (P<0.001) without a significant change in timing-related potential adverse events. Transcription errors occurred at 6.1% without the system and were completely eliminated with it.
cards.watchOut: Before-and-after designs cannot exclude secular safety trends, assessors were not masked, and outcomes are errors and potential — not actual — adverse drug events; one centre's implementation quality may not travel.
cards.source: Poon EG et al. Effect of bar-code technology on the safety of medication administration. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20445181. Registry ID: NCT00243373. cards.headline: Poon 2006: pharmacy barcode dispensing cut target potential ADEs 74% relative — but the scan-one-dose configuration increased them 2.4-fold
cards.summary: Poon 2006: pharmacy barcode dispensing cut target potential ADEs 74% relative — but the scan-one-dose configuration increased them 2.4-fold
cards.people: Hospital pharmacy of a 735-bed US academic centre: 115,164 dispensed doses observed before and 253,984 after barcode implementation in three configurations — two requiring every dose to be scanned, one scanning a single dose when several of the same medication were dispensed.
cards.result: Overall rates of target potential adverse drug events and all potential adverse drug events fell 74% and 63% relative respectively. The two scan-every-dose configurations achieved 93–96% relative reductions in target dispensing errors and 86–97% relative reductions in potential adverse events (P<0.001). The configuration not requiring every dose to be scanned achieved only a 60% relative reduction in target errors and a 2.4-fold increase in target potential adverse events (P=0.014), including potentially life-threatening intravenous dopamine and heparin events.
cards.watchOut: Surrogate outcomes, unmasked assessors, and exclusion of the controlled-substance fill process (low baseline errors) may inflate the combined benefit; the configuration contrast, however, is an internal comparison and the most actionable finding in either study.
cards.source: Poon EG et al. Medication dispensing errors and potential adverse drug events before and after implementing bar code technology in the pharmacy. Annals of internal medicine. 2006. PMID: 16983130. cards.summary: Synthesis: the technology is only as good as the scanning discipline it enforces
cards.people: Two large directly-observed before-and-after studies from one academic centre (14,041 administrations; 369,148 dispensed doses), covering ward administration and pharmacy dispensing.
cards.result: Administration: non-timing errors -41.4% relative, potential adverse events -50.8% relative, transcription errors 6.1% to 0%. shelves.title: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist: deaths 1.5% to 0.8% and complications 11.0% to 7.0% in the eight-hospital study — consistent in meta-analysis, but never randomised
shelves.question: Across hospitals, does implementing the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist reduce surgical complications and death versus care without the checklist?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care · Postoperative Complications/mortality/prevention & control · Prospective Studies · Safety Management/methods/standards · Surgical Procedures, Operative/mortality/standards
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large consistent signal from non-randomised evidence; Tier C for the mortality claim and design. In the Safe Surgery Saves Lives study (Haynes AB et al., PMID: 19144931; eight hospitals in eight cities, 3,733 patients before and 3,955 after checklist introduction), inpatient death fell from 1.5% to 0.8% (P=0.003) and complications from 11.0% to 7.0% (P<0.001) in patients aged 16+ undergoing noncardiac surgery. The systematic review and meta-analysis (PMID: 24469615; seven studies) found risk ratios of 0.59 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.74) for any complication, 0.77 (0.60 to 0.98) for mortality and 0.57 (0.41 to 0.79) for surgical-site infection, with effectiveness correlated with adherence to the checklist's embedded care processes (Q=0.82, P=0.042) — while cautioning the evidence 'cannot be regarded as definitive' without higher-quality studies. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the checklist probably reduces complications and deaths when actually used as designed; the size of the true effect is uncertain.

cards.headline: Haynes 2009: death 1.5% to 0.8% (P=0.003) and complications 11.0% to 7.0% (P<0.001) across eight hospitals after checklist introduction
cards.summary: Haynes 2009: death 1.5% to 0.8% (P=0.003) and complications 11.0% to 7.0% (P<0.001) across eight hospitals after checklist introduction
cards.type: Prospective before-and-after study (Haynes 2009, Safe Surgery Saves Lives)
cards.people: Eight hospitals in eight cities (Toronto, New Delhi, Amman, Auckland, Manila, Ifakara, London, Seattle) in varied economic settings: 3,733 consecutively enrolled patients aged 16+ undergoing noncardiac surgery before, and 3,955 after, introduction of the 19-item WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, October 2007 to September 2008; primary endpoint complications including death within 30 days/in hospital.
cards.result: The rate of death was 1.5% before the checklist and 0.8% afterwards (P=0.003). Inpatient complications occurred in 11.0% of patients at baseline and 7.0% after introduction (P<0.001). Improvements were seen across the diverse sites.
cards.watchOut: No concurrent controls: concurrent safety initiatives, case-mix drift and Hawthorne effects could each contribute, and sites volunteered for a WHO programme; the true checklist-attributable share of the improvement cannot be separated in this design.
cards.source: Haynes AB et al. A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population. The New England journal of medicine. 2009. PMID: 19144931. cards.headline: Bergs 2014: meta-analysis RR 0.59 for any complication, 0.77 for mortality, 0.57 for surgical-site infection — 'highly suggestive', not definitive
cards.summary: Bergs 2014: meta-analysis RR 0.59 for any complication, 0.77 for mortality, 0.57 for surgical-site infection — 'highly suggestive', not definitive
cards.people: Seven studies (of 723 identified) reporting quantitative effects of the WHO surgical safety checklist on postoperative complications, with meta-analysis of any complication, mortality and surgical-site infection, and an adherence analysis using Yule's Q.
cards.result: Risk ratios with the checklist were 0.59 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.74) for any complication, 0.77 (0.60 to 0.98) for mortality and 0.57 (0.41 to 0.79) for surgical-site infection. There was a strong correlation between significant complication reductions and adherence to aspects of care embedded in the checklist (Q=0.82, P=0.042). The authors conclude the evidence is highly suggestive of benefit but cannot be regarded as definitive in the absence of higher-quality studies, given marked methodological heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: Seven heterogeneous before-and-after studies, mostly in motivated early-adopter hospitals; publication bias toward successful implementations is plausible, and adherence — the apparent active ingredient — is the least standardised part of the intervention.
cards.source: Bergs J et al. Systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of the World Health Organization surgical safety checklist on postoperative complications. The British journal of surgery. 2014. PMID: 24469615. shelves.title: X-PERT structured diabetes education: HbA1c -0.6% versus +0.1% at 14 months in its trial, with one medication increase prevented for every four participants
shelves.question: In people with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, does the X-PERT structured education programme improve glycaemic control versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Body Constitution · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/blood/psychology/therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Glycated Hemoglobin/metabolism · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents/administration & dosage · Life Style · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care/methods · Patient Education as Topic/methods · Patient-Centered Care/methods · Primary Health Care/methods · Program Evaluation · Self Care/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one good trial of the named programme, backed by a consistent meta-analysis of its class; Tier C because the X-PERT claim itself is single-trial. In the X-PERT randomised trial (Deakin TA et al., PMID: 16922700; 314 adults with type 2 diabetes in Lancashire), six 2-hour group sessions produced an HbA1c change of -0.6% versus +0.1% in individual-appointment controls at 14 months (P<0.001), with a number needed to treat of 4 (95% CI 3 to 7) to prevent a diabetes medication increase and 7 (5 to 11) for medication reduction, plus significant improvements in weight, waist circumference, total cholesterol, knowledge, empowerment and treatment satisfaction; 95% attended and 82% attended at least four sessions. The meta-analysis of group-based education generally (PMID: 22824531; 21 studies, 2,833 participants) found HbA1c reductions of 0.44 points at 6 months, 0.46 at 12 months and 0.87 at 2 years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): X-PERT improves glycaemic control at about a year; durability beyond the trial and in newly diagnosed-only populations is less certain.

cards.headline: Deakin 2006 (X-PERT): HbA1c -0.6% versus +0.1% at 14 months (P<0.001); NNT 4 to prevent a medication increase
cards.summary: Deakin 2006 (X-PERT): HbA1c -0.6% versus +0.1% at 14 months (P<0.001); NNT 4 to prevent a medication increase
cards.people: 314 adults with type 2 diabetes in Burnley, Pendle and Rossendale, UK, randomised to the X-PERT Programme (six 2-hour group self-management sessions based on empowerment and discovery learning; n=157) or individual appointments (n=157), with outcomes at baseline, 4 and 14 months; 149 (95%) attended X-PERT and 128 (82%) attended four or more sessions.
cards.result: At 14 months the X-PERT group improved HbA1c significantly more than controls (-0.6% vs +0.1%, repeated measures ANOVA, P<0.001). The number needed to treat was 4 (95% CI 3 to 7) for preventing a diabetes medication increase and 7 (5 to 11) for reducing diabetes medication. Weight, body mass index, waist circumference, total cholesterol, self-empowerment, diabetes knowledge, physical activity, foot care, fruit and vegetable intake, enjoyment of food and treatment satisfaction also improved significantly.
cards.watchOut: Participants had established diabetes (the candidate question says newly diagnosed — the trial population was broader), controls received individual appointments rather than no education, and a single UK trial in motivated attenders may overstate routine-programme effects; medication outcomes were clinician-managed, not blinded.
cards.source: Deakin TA et al. Structured patient education: the diabetes X-PERT Programme makes a difference. Diabetic medicine : a journal of the British Diabetic Association. 2006. PMID: 16922700. cards.headline: Steinsbekk 2012: group-based diabetes education meta-analysis — HbA1c -0.44 at 6 months, -0.46 at 12 months, -0.87 at 2 years across 21 trials
cards.summary: Steinsbekk 2012: group-based diabetes education meta-analysis — HbA1c -0.44 at 6 months, -0.46 at 12 months, -0.87 at 2 years across 21 trials
cards.people: 21 randomised trials (26 publications, 2,833 participants) of group-based diabetes self-management education versus routine treatment in adults with type 2 diabetes, with at least one session and at least 6 months' follow-up; participants averaged 60 years, body mass index 31.6, HbA1c 8.23% and 8 years' diabetes duration.
cards.result: HbA1c was significantly reduced at 6 months (0.44 percentage points, P=0.0006; 13 studies, 1,883 participants), 12 months (0.46, P=0.001; 11 studies, 1,503) and 2 years (0.87, P<0.00001; 3 studies, 397). Fasting glucose fell at 12 months (1.26 mmol/L (≈23 mg/dL), P<0.00001). Diabetes knowledge and self-management skills improved significantly at 6, 12 and (for knowledge) 2 years, and empowerment/self-efficacy at 6 months. There were no differences in mortality, body mass index, blood pressure or lipids.
cards.watchOut: Programmes were heterogeneous and the 2-year estimate rests on three small studies; this card supports the class of group education, of which X-PERT is one branded example — it does not independently verify X-PERT itself.
cards.source: Steinsbekk A et al. Group based diabetes self-management education compared to routine treatment for people with type 2 diabetes mellitus. A systematic review with meta-analysis. BMC health services research. 2012. PMID: 22824531. systematic review with meta-analysis (steinsbekk 2012) 21 randomised trials (26 publications, 2,833 participants) of group-based diabetes self-management education versus routine treatment in adults with type 2 diabetes, with at least one session and at least 6 months' follow-up; participants averaged 60 years, body mass index 31.6, hba1c 8.23% and 8 years' diabetes duration. hba1c was significantly reduced at 6 months (0.44 percentage points, p=0.0006; 13 studies, 1,883 participants), 12 months (0.46, p=0.001; 11 studies, 1,503) and 2 years (0.87, p<0.00001; 3 studies, 397). fasting glucose fell at 12 months (1.26 mmol/l (≈23 mg/dl), p<0.00001). diabetes knowledge and self-management skills improved significantly at 6, 12 and (for knowledge) 2 years, and empowerment/self-efficacy at 6 months. there were no differences in mortality, body mass index, blood pressure or lipids. programmes were heterogeneous and the 2-year estimate rests on three small studies; this card supports the class of group education, of which x-pert is one branded example — it does not independently verify x-pert itself. steinsbekk a et al. group based diabetes self-management education compared to routine treatment for people with type 2 diabetes mellitus. a systematic review with meta-analysis. bmc health services research. 2012. pmid: 22824531. mesh: adult · diabetes mellitus, type 2/prevention & control/psychology/therapy · diagnostic tests, routine · female · group processes · health knowledge, attitudes, practice · humans · male · outcome assessment, health care · patient education as topic · power, psychological · quality of life · randomized controlled trials as topic · self care/methods

cards.people: The X-PERT randomised trial (314 participants, 14 months) and a 21-trial meta-analysis of group-based diabetes self-management education (2,833 participants).
cards.result: X-PERT: HbA1c -0.6% vs +0.1% (between-group difference about 0.7 points) at 14 months; medication-increase NNT 4. Class: HbA1c -0.44 to -0.46 points at 6–12 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C, as in the balance.

shelves.title: Intensive case management (the ACT family): about 0.86 fewer hospital days a month versus standard care — and the benefit concentrates where hospital use is high and teams follow the ACT model
shelves.question: In adults with severe mental illness living in the community, does assertive community treatment reduce hospital use and improve engagement versus standard community care?
shelves.mesh: Case Management · Community Mental Health Services/methods · Employment/statistics & numerical data · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Mental Disorders/therapy · Outcome and Process Assessment, Health Care/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Regression Analysis · Suicide/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large randomised literature with honestly low-grade certainty. The Cochrane review of intensive case management (Dieterich M et al., PMID: 28067944; 40 randomised trials, 7,524 participants — the successor to the withdrawn Marshall & Lockwood review) found, versus standard care, slightly fewer hospital days per month (mean difference -0.86, 95% CI -1.37 to -0.34; 24 trials, 3,595 participants, low-quality evidence) and fewer people leaving care early (risk ratio 0.68, 0.58 to 0.79), with little or no difference in suicide (0.68, 0.31 to 1.51); versus less-intensive case management, hospital days did not differ (-0.08, -0.37 to 0.21, moderate-quality evidence). The meta-regression (PMID: 17631513) explains the inconsistency across trials: effects grow with baseline hospital use (coefficient -0.23, -0.36 to -0.09) and with fidelity to the assertive community treatment team model (-0.31, -0.59 to -0.03). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): deploy intensive, ACT-faithful teams for high hospital users; expect little where bed use is already low.

cards.headline: Dieterich 2017 (Cochrane): 40 RCTs, 7,524 participants — hospital days MD -0.86/month versus standard care; versus non-intensive case management, no difference
cards.summary: Dieterich 2017 (Cochrane): 40 RCTs, 7,524 participants — hospital days MD -0.86/month versus standard care; versus non-intensive case management, no difference
cards.people: 40 randomised trials with 7,524 participants aged 18–65 with severe mental illness treated in community settings, comparing intensive case management (caseloads under 20, high-intensity input, encompassing assertive community treatment) with standard care or with non-intensive case management; searches to April 2015.
cards.result: Versus standard care, intensive case management slightly reduced days in hospital per month (mean difference -0.86, 95% CI -1.37 to -0.34; 24 trials, 3,595 participants, low-quality evidence) and reduced leaving the trial early (risk ratio 0.68, 0.58 to 0.79; 13 trials, 1,798, low-quality). Suicide showed little or no difference (0.68, 0.31 to 1.51). Versus non-intensive case management, hospital days probably did not differ (-0.08, -0.37 to 0.21; 21 trials, 2,220, moderate-quality evidence). Greater fidelity to the ACT model and higher baseline hospital use predicted larger hospital-day reductions.
cards.watchOut: Most studies had high risk of selective reporting, evidence quality is low to moderate, and no studies reported relapse or important improvement in mental state — the proven gains are service-use and engagement, not symptoms.
cards.source: Dieterich M et al. Intensive case management for severe mental illness. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28067944. cards.headline: Burns 2007: why trials disagree — intensive case management cuts hospital use where baseline use is high (coefficient -0.23) and in ACT-organised teams (-0.31)
cards.summary: Burns 2007: why trials disagree — intensive case management cuts hospital use where baseline use is high (coefficient -0.23) and in ACT-organised teams (-0.31)
cards.people: Randomised trials of intensive case management versus standard or low-intensity care in severe mental illness: 1,335 abstracts screened, 5,961 participants, 49 trials eligible and 29 providing analysable data on mean days per month in hospital, with a fidelity scale for assertive community treatment organisation.
cards.result: Trials with high hospital use at baseline were more likely to find intensive case management reduced hospital care (coefficient -0.23, 95% CI -0.36 to -0.09), as were trials with high control-group hospital use (-0.44, -0.57 to -0.31). Teams organised on the assertive community treatment model were more likely to reduce hospital care (-0.31, -0.59 to -0.03), though this was less robust in sensitivity analyses and recommended staffing levels alone did not predict benefit.
cards.watchOut: Meta-regression across trials is observational reasoning about trial-level averages; the ACT-fidelity finding weakened in sensitivity analyses, so 'organisation matters more than staffing ratios' is a guide for service design, not a proven recipe.
cards.source: Burns T et al. Use of intensive case management to reduce time in hospital in people with severe mental illness: systematic review and meta-regression. BMJ. 2007. PMID: 17631513. cards.headline: Synthesis: a service for high users, delivered as a team — not a universal community-care upgrade
cards.summary: Synthesis: a service for high users, delivered as a team — not a universal community-care upgrade
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 40 randomised trials (7,524 participants) and a BMJ meta-regression of 29 analysable trials (5,961 participants) of intensive case management/assertive community treatment in severe mental illness.
cards.result: Versus standard care: hospital days -0.86 per month (-1.37 to -0.34); leaving care early risk ratio 0.68 (0.58 to 0.79). Versus non-intensive case management: no hospital-day difference. Effect modifiers: baseline hospital use and ACT fidelity. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), as in the balance. Note for the record: the candidate anchor (Marshall & Lockwood Cochrane) is a withdrawn record; this shelf rests on its Dieterich 2017 successor, on which Marshall is a co-author.
cards.watchOut: Mental state, quality of life and social functioning effects remain unclear or very low quality; commissioning intensive teams for low-using populations is the specific mistake this literature warns against.

shelves.title: Pharmacist-led care splits by outcome: blood pressure falls clearly (-7.6/-3.9 mmHg across 39 trials) — but broad medication therapy management evidence is 'insufficient' for most health outcomes
shelves.question: In adults with chronic conditions managed in primary care, does pharmacist-led medication therapy management improve disease control and reduce hospital use versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease/drug therapy · Humans · Medication Therapy Management · Outpatients · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by outcome and by how tightly the intervention is defined. The AHRQ systematic review of medication therapy management in outpatients (Viswanathan M et al., PMID: 25401788; 44 studies) graded evidence insufficient for most outcomes — drug therapy problems, adverse drug events, morbidity, mortality and harms — while finding low-strength evidence of improved medication appropriateness (4.9 versus 0.9 points on the medication appropriateness index, P<0.001), adherence (about +4.6%) and lower odds of hospitalisation in diabetes (odds ratio 0.91 to 0.93) and heart failure (adjusted hazard ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.77). The focused meta-analysis of pharmacist interventions for hypertension (PMID: 24721801; 39 randomised trials, 14,224 patients) found systolic pressure 7.6 mmHg lower (95% CI -9.0 to -6.3) and diastolic 3.9 lower (-5.1 to -2.8) than usual care, albeit with wide prediction intervals. PROPOSED SPLIT: pharmacist care is a proven blood-pressure intervention and a plausible medication-safety one; it is not yet a proven general outcome intervention.

cards.headline: Viswanathan 2015: 44 MTM studies — evidence insufficient for most outcomes; appropriateness and adherence improved; HF hospitalisation HR 0.55 in one analysis
cards.summary: Viswanathan 2015: 44 MTM studies — evidence insufficient for most outcomes; appropriateness and adherence improved; HF hospitalisation HR 0.55 in one analysis
cards.people: 44 studies of medication therapy management interventions (comprehensive medication review and related clinical pharmacy services) in ambulatory adults with chronic illness, with comparators, searched to January 2014; outcomes included medication-related problems, morbidity, mortality, quality of life, health care use, costs and harms, with strength-of-evidence grading.
cards.result: Evidence was insufficient for most evaluated outcomes. With low strength of evidence, interventions improved medication appropriateness (4.9 vs 0.9 points on the medication appropriateness index, P<0.001), adherence (approximately 4.6%, and odds ratios 0.99 to 5.98 for achieving threshold adherence) and reduced dosing (mean difference -2.2 doses, -3.738 to -0.662). For diabetes or heart failure, interventions lowered odds of hospitalisation (diabetes odds ratio 0.91 to 0.93 by insurance type; heart failure adjusted hazard rate 0.55, 0.39 to 0.77) and hospitalisation costs (-$363.45 to -$398.98). There was no benefit for satisfaction and most quality-of-life measures.
cards.watchOut: 'MTM' bundles very different interventions and populations, which is exactly why the evidence grades as inconsistent and imprecise; single favourable subgroups (heart failure hospitalisation) come from few studies and should not be generalised to all chronic disease.
cards.source: Viswanathan M et al. Medication therapy management interventions in outpatient settings: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA internal medicine. 2015. PMID: 25401788. MeSH: Chronic Disease/drug therapy · Humans · Medication Therapy Management · Outpatients · Quality of Life

cards.headline: Santschi 2014: pharmacist interventions cut systolic BP by 7.6 mmHg and diastolic by 3.9 across 39 RCTs (14,224 patients)
cards.summary: Santschi 2014: pharmacist interventions cut systolic BP by 7.6 mmHg and diastolic by 3.9 across 39 RCTs (14,224 patients)
cards.people: 39 randomised trials with 14,224 outpatients with or without diabetes, testing pharmacist interventions (patient education, feedback to physicians, medication management), alone or with other professionals, against usual care for blood pressure control.
cards.result: Pharmacist interventions reduced systolic blood pressure by 7.6 mmHg more than usual care (weighted mean difference -7.6, 95% CI -9.0 to -6.3, I²=67%) and diastolic by 3.9 mmHg (-3.9, -5.1 to -2.8, I²=83%). The 95% prediction intervals were wide (-13.9 to -1.4 systolic; -9.9 to +2.0 diastolic), and effects tended to be larger when interventions were pharmacist-led and at least monthly.
cards.watchOut: High heterogeneity with a diastolic prediction interval crossing zero means some real-world implementations will see little effect; blood pressure is a surrogate, and this meta-analysis does not itself show fewer strokes or admissions.
cards.source: Santschi V et al. Improving blood pressure control through pharmacist interventions: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of the American Heart Association. 2014. PMID: 24721801. shelves.title: Six-monthly ART refills hold the line: retention 92.6% versus 93.6% and suppression actually higher (+4.6 points) at 24 months in the adherence-club trial — with far fewer visits
shelves.question: In people with HIV established on antiretroviral therapy, does multi-month (three- to six-monthly) dispensing maintain viral suppression and retention in care versus monthly dispensing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-HIV Agents/therapeutic use · Female · HIV Infections/drug therapy/virology · Humans · Male · Medication Adherence · Middle Aged · Time Factors · Viral Load
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — maintained outcomes on far fewer visits, shown in randomised programmes. In the Khayelitsha cluster trial (Cassidy T et al., PMID: 33340284; 2,150 adherence-club patients, 88 clubs), six-monthly refills gave 24-month retention of 92.6% (905/977) versus 93.6% (1,098/1,173) with standard club refills (risk difference -1.0%, 95% CI -3.2 to 1.3; non-inferior), with higher viral load completion (90.8% (887/977) versus 85.1% (999/1,173); +5.5%, 1.5 to 9.5) and suppression (87.3% (853/977) versus 82.6% (969/1,173); +4.6%, 0.2 to 9.0). The pooled analysis of two cluster trials in Zimbabwe and Lesotho (PMID: 34713614; 599 newly stable adults) found six-monthly community dispensing non-inferior for retention (95.8% versus 93.4%; adjusted risk difference +1.7%, -2.5 to 5.9) with suppression of 98.1–99.3% across arms. The meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (PMID: 37655428; 13,886 participants) found differentiated models at least comparable (retention risk ratio 1.09, 1.08 to 1.11; suppression 1.01, 1.00 to 1.02). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for stable patients, multi-month dispensing maintains suppression and retention while cutting visit burden.

cards.headline: Cassidy 2020: 2,150 club patients — retention -1.0% (non-inferior), viral load completion +5.5% and suppression +4.6% with six-monthly refills at 24 months
cards.summary: Cassidy 2020: 2,150 club patients — retention -1.0% (non-inferior), viral load completion +5.5% and suppression +4.6% with six-monthly refills at 24 months
cards.people: 2,150 clinically stable ART patients in 88 existing adherence clubs at a large Khayelitsha, South Africa primary care facility (40 clubs/977 patients randomised to six-monthly refills meeting twice yearly; 48 clubs/1,173 to standard clubs meeting five times yearly with two-month refills), followed 24 months; registry PACTR201810631281009 (the results report of the Wilkinson protocol).
cards.result: Retention in care at 24 months was 92.6% (905/977) in the intervention arm and 93.6% (1,098/1,173) in standard care (risk difference -1.0%, 95% CI -3.2 to 1.3), meeting non-inferiority. Viral load completion was higher with six-monthly refills (90.8% (887/977) vs 85.1% (999/1,173); risk difference +5.5%, 1.5 to 9.5), as was viral suppression <400 copies/mL (87.3% (853/977) vs 82.6% (969/1,173); +4.6%, 0.2 to 9.0). (Percentages are given as computed from the record's fractions; the abstract's parenthetical ordering is transposed.)
cards.watchOut: Participants were already stable club members in one high-volume facility with strong systems; results do not cover unstable patients, children, or settings without reliable viral-load monitoring and drug supply for six-month fills.
cards.source: Cassidy T et al. Twenty-four-month outcomes from a cluster-randomized controlled trial of extending antiretroviral therapy refills in ART adherence clubs. cards.headline: Fatti 2021: pooled two cluster trials (599 newly stable adults) — six-monthly community dispensing non-inferior for retention (+1.7%); suppression 98–99% in all arms
cards.summary: Fatti 2021: pooled two cluster trials (599 newly stable adults) — six-monthly community dispensing non-inferior for retention (+1.7%); suppression 98–99% in all arms
cards.type: Pooled analysis of two cluster-randomised trials (Fatti 2021)
cards.people: 599 adults in Zimbabwe and Lesotho who became stable 6–12 months after starting ART, pooled from two three-arm cluster trials (2017–2019): standard three-monthly facility care (n=212), three-monthly community ART groups (n=128), and six-monthly community dispensing (n=259), with annual clinical visits in the community arms; registries NCT03438370 and NCT03238846.
cards.result: At 12 months, retention was 93.4% (standard), 96.1% (three-monthly community) and 95.8% (six-monthly): three-monthly community was superior (adjusted risk difference +4.6%, 0.7 to 8.5) and six-monthly was non-inferior (+1.7%, -2.5 to 5.9, against a -3.25% margin). Viral suppression was similar (99.3%, 98.6% and 98.1%; adjusted risk ratios 0.98 for both community arms). Unscheduled clinic visits were not increased (incidence rate ratios 0.53 and 0.82, both non-significant).
cards.watchOut: Few participants were under 25 (n=32), follow-up is 12 months, and both trials ran in well-supported programmes (including during early COVID-19); newly stable patients are still a selected group, though less selected than long-term club members.
cards.source: Fatti G et al. cards.headline: Bwire 2023: 16 RCTs, 13,886 participants — differentiated delivery retention RR 1.09 and suppression RR 1.01 versus standard care
cards.summary: Bwire 2023: 16 RCTs, 13,886 participants — differentiated delivery retention RR 1.09 and suppression RR 1.01 versus standard care
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Bwire 2023)
cards.people: 16 randomised trials with 13,886 people living with HIV in sub-Saharan Africa evaluating differentiated service delivery models (including adherence clubs and multi-month dispensing) versus standard care, searched to May 2023.
cards.result: Across differentiated models, retention in care favoured the models (risk ratio 1.09, 95% CI 1.08 to 1.11, I²=0%) and viral suppression was comparable (1.01, 1.00 to 1.02, I²=0%). For adherence clubs specifically, retention (1.01, 0.96 to 1.07, I²=84%) and suppression (1.02, 0.98 to 1.07, I²=77%) were comparable to standard care.
cards.watchOut: The headline retention risk ratio pools different model types with suspicious precision given clinical diversity, and club-specific estimates are heterogeneous; the safe conclusion is comparability-to-modest-benefit for stable patients, not superiority for every model.
cards.source: Bwire GM et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: for stable patients the evidence supports fewer, bigger collections — the constraint is the system, not the patient
cards.summary: Synthesis: for stable patients the evidence supports fewer, bigger collections — the constraint is the system, not the patient
cards.people: Two cluster-randomised programmes (2,150 patients in South African clubs; 599 newly stable adults pooled from Zimbabwe/Lesotho trials) and a 16-trial meta-analysis (13,886 participants) of differentiated HIV delivery in sub-Saharan Africa.
cards.result: Retention: 92.6% vs 93.6% at 24 months (six-monthly vs standard clubs); 95.8% vs 93.4% at 12 months (six-monthly community vs facility). Suppression: 87.3% vs 82.6% (Cassidy); 98.1% vs 99.3% (Fatti); pooled risk ratio 1.01 (Bwire). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), as in the balance.
cards.watchOut: All trials enrol stable, suppressed patients and require functioning supply chains and viral-load monitoring; extending multi-month dispensing to unstable patients or fragile supply settings is an extrapolation these data do not cover.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cassidy T et al. Journal of the International AIDS Society. 2020 (PMID: 33340284); Fatti G et al. Journal of the International AIDS Society. 2021 (PMID: 34713614); Bwire GM et al. Reviews in medical virology. 2023 (PMID: 37655428).

shelves.title: INR self-testing and self-management: pooled trials show thromboembolism halved and mortality cut by a third — but the benefit sits in self-management, and the largest trial of self-testing alone found nothing
shelves.question: In patients on warfarin, does self-testing or self-management of the INR reduce thromboembolism, bleeding, and death compared with clinic management?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Anticoagulants/administration & dosage · Cause of Death · Child · Hemorrhage/mortality/prevention & control · Humans · International Normalized Ratio · Point-of-Care Systems · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Assessment · Self Care/methods · Thromboembolism/mortality/prevention & control
shelves.balance: SPLIT — who adjusts the dose decides whether this works. The Cochrane review (Garcia-Alamino JM et al., PMID: 20393937) pooled 18 randomised trials with 4,723 participants: self-monitoring or self-management reduced thromboembolic events (risk ratio 0.50; 95% CI 0.36–0.69) and all-cause mortality (risk ratio 0.64; 95% CI 0.46–0.89) versus standard monitoring, with no increase in harm. Split by mode, self-management alone reduced thromboembolism (risk ratio 0.47) and mortality (risk ratio 0.55), while self-testing alone — phoning the result to a clinic — did not significantly reduce either, though it did reduce major haemorrhage (risk ratio 0.56). The individual-patient meta-analysis (Heneghan C et al., PMID: 22137798; 11 trials, 6,417 participants) likewise found thromboembolism halved (hazard ratio 0.51; 95% CI 0.31–0.85) but mortality (hazard ratio 0.82) and major haemorrhage (hazard ratio 0.88) not significantly reduced. And the largest single trial, THINRS (Matchar DB et al., PMID: 20961244; 2,922 patients), found weekly home self-testing no better than monthly high-quality clinic testing for stroke, major bleeding, or death (hazard ratio 0.88; p=0.14). PROPOSED SPLIT: teach suitable patients to manage their own dose and events fall; hand them a meter and a phone number and the advantage evaporates. Tier C: mortality benefit claim.

cards.headline: Garcia-Alamino 2010 (Cochrane): thromboembolic events RR 0.50 and mortality RR 0.64 pooled — self-management RR 0.47 and 0.55; self-monitoring alone not significant for either
cards.summary: Garcia-Alamino 2010 (Cochrane): thromboembolic events RR 0.50 and mortality RR 0.64 pooled — self-management RR 0.47 and 0.55; self-monitoring alone not significant for either
cards.people: 18 randomised trials with 4,723 participants on oral anticoagulation, comparing patient self-testing with dose adjustment by a predetermined schedule (self-management) or with clinic-advised adjustment (self-monitoring) against standard clinic monitoring; trials searched to November 2007.
cards.result: Pooled across both modes, self-testing strategies reduced thromboembolic events (risk ratio 0.50; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.69) and all-cause mortality (risk ratio 0.64; 95% CI 0.46 to 0.89; 0.65 after removing low-quality studies). Self-management alone reduced thromboembolic events (risk ratio 0.47; 95% CI 0.31 to 0.70) and mortality (risk ratio 0.55; 95% CI 0.36 to 0.84); self-monitoring alone did not (thrombotic events risk ratio 0.57; 95% CI 0.32 to 1.00; mortality risk ratio 0.84; 95% CI 0.50 to 1.41) but did reduce major haemorrhage (risk ratio 0.56; 95% CI 0.35 to 0.91), while self-management did not (risk ratio 1.12). Twelve trials reported improved percentage of INR measurements in range. Up to half of patients needing anticoagulation could not self-monitor — refusal, GP exclusion, or inability to complete training.
cards.watchOut: The trials are small, mostly older, and enrolled the motivated minority who could be trained — the pooled mortality benefit may partly be a selection effect of who can self-manage at all. 'Standard monitoring' in the comparator arms was often less intensive than a modern anticoagulation clinic, which is exactly the comparison THINRS then tested.
cards.source: Garcia-Alamino JM et al. Self-monitoring and self-management of oral anticoagulation. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010. PMID: 20393937. cards.headline: Heneghan 2012 (individual-patient meta-analysis): thromboembolism HR 0.51, but death HR 0.82 and major haemorrhage HR 0.88 — neither significant
cards.summary: Heneghan 2012 (individual-patient meta-analysis): thromboembolism HR 0.51, but death HR 0.82 and major haemorrhage HR 0.88 — neither significant
cards.people: 11 randomised trials with individual data for 6,417 participants (12,800 person-years) on oral anticoagulation, comparing self-monitoring or self-management with clinic or primary-care control; prespecified subgroups by age, control type, self-testing alone versus self-management, sex, and by mechanical valve versus atrial fibrillation.
cards.result: Self-monitoring significantly reduced thromboembolic events (hazard ratio 0.51; 95% CI 0.31–0.85) but not major haemorrhage (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.74–1.06) or death (hazard ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.62–1.09). The thrombotic reduction was largest in patients younger than 55 (hazard ratio 0.33; 95% CI 0.17–0.66) and in those with a mechanical heart valve (hazard ratio 0.52; 95% CI 0.35–0.77); in the very elderly (≥85 years, n=99) no outcome showed significant adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: With individual data and time-to-event analysis, the mortality claim from the aggregate Cochrane pool shrinks to a non-significant 0.82 — the two analyses differ mainly in method, and the more rigorous one is the more sober. Subgroup findings (under-55s, mechanical valves) are hypothesis-grade despite prespecification.
cards.source: Heneghan C et al. Self-monitoring of oral anticoagulation: systematic review and meta-analysis of individual patient data. The Lancet. 2012. PMID: 22137798. cards.headline: Matchar 2010 (THINRS): weekly home self-testing versus monthly high-quality clinic testing — time to stroke, major bleeding, or death HR 0.88 (p=0.14); time in range better by only 3.8 points
cards.summary: Matchar 2010 (THINRS): weekly home self-testing versus monthly high-quality clinic testing — time to stroke, major bleeding, or death HR 0.88 (p=0.14); time in range better by only 3.8 points
cards.people: 2,922 patients taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation or mechanical heart valves, all competent with point-of-care INR devices, randomised in the US Veterans Affairs system to weekly home self-testing or monthly high-quality clinic testing; follow-up 2.0–4.75 years (8,730 patient-years).
cards.result: Time to a first major event (stroke, major bleeding episode, or death) was not significantly longer with self-testing (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.04; p=0.14). Clinical outcome rates were similar except for more minor bleeding episodes reported in the self-testing group. Time in therapeutic range was better by an absolute 3.8 percentage points (p<0.001), and at 2 years satisfaction (p=0.002) and quality of life (p<0.001) were modestly better with self-testing.
cards.watchOut: THINRS tested self-testing only — patients reported results and the clinic dosed — against an unusually good clinic comparator (monthly, high-quality), in a VA population; it does not refute self-management, and its null is the strongest single-trial evidence on the testing-only model. More minor bleeding was reported by self-testers, plausibly an ascertainment effect of weekly contact with one's own numbers.
cards.source: Matchar DB et al. Effect of home testing of international normalized ratio on clinical events. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20961244. Registry ID: NCT00032591. cards.headline: Synthesis: the meter is not the intervention — the dosing decision is
cards.summary: Synthesis: the meter is not the intervention — the dosing decision is
cards.people: Two meta-analyses (18 aggregate trials, 4,723 participants; 11 individual-data trials, 6,417 participants) and one large randomised trial (THINRS, 2,922 patients) of INR self-testing and self-management versus clinic care.
cards.result: Thromboembolism: consistently reduced where patients adjust their own dose (RR 0.47–0.50; HR 0.51). Mortality: RR 0.64 in the aggregate pool, HR 0.82 (not significant) with individual data, HR 0.88 (not significant) for self-testing in THINRS. Major haemorrhage: no increase anywhere; reduced with self-monitoring in the Cochrane pool (RR 0.56). PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: the mortality claim earns personal review.
cards.watchOut: Direct oral anticoagulants have since removed the INR question for most atrial-fibrillation patients; this evidence now matters chiefly for mechanical-valve and antiphospholipid patients who must stay on warfarin — a population the trials included but did not isolate, mechanical valves excepted in the Heneghan subgroup.
