shelves.title: Switching suppressed HIV patients to two-drug dolutegravir–lamivudine: suppression held in two phase 3 trials — virological failure 0.3–0.4% on two drugs versus 0.5–1.2% on three or four
shelves.question: In people with HIV on antiretroviral therapy who are virologically suppressed, does switching to two-drug therapy (dolutegravir–lamivudine) maintain suppression compared with continuing three-drug therapy (TANGO, SALSA)?
shelves.mesh: Adenine/analogs & derivatives · Adult · Alanine · Anti-HIV Agents/therapeutic use · HIV Infections/drug therapy · HIV-1 · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring/adverse effects · Humans · Lamivudine/therapeutic use · Oxazines · Pharmaceutical Preparations · Piperazines · Pyridones/therapeutic use · Tenofovir/analogs & derivatives · Treatment Outcome · Viral Load · Dolutegravir
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the benefit is simplification without losing suppression, shown the same way in two phase 3 switch trials. In TANGO (van Wyk J et al., PMID: 31905383), suppressed adults randomised to switch to dolutegravir–lamivudine or stay on a tenofovir-alafenamide-based regimen had HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 in 0.3% versus 0.5% (adjusted difference −0.3 percentage points, 95% CI −1.2 to 0.7; non-inferior). In SALSA (Llibre JM et al., PMID: 35235656), switching to dolutegravir–lamivudine versus continuing a varied 3- or 4-drug regimen gave 0.4% versus 1.2% with RNA ≥50 copies/mL (adjusted difference −0.8 percentage points, 95% CI −2.4 to 0.8; non-inferior). No participant on two-drug therapy in either trial met confirmed virological withdrawal criteria, and no resistance emerged. The price was tolerability noise early after the switch: drug-related adverse events were more frequent on dolutegravir–lamivudine in SALSA (20% versus 6% through week 48, converging to 5% versus 2% after week 24), and drug-related grade ≥2 events in TANGO were 4.6% versus 0.8%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in already-suppressed patients without prior virological failure, switching to dolutegravir–lamivudine maintains suppression as reliably as staying on three or four drugs, at the cost of more early drug-related symptoms.

cards.headline: van Wyk 2020 (TANGO): RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 in 0.3% after switching to dolutegravir–lamivudine versus 0.5% staying on a tenofovir-alafenamide regimen — non-inferior, no resistance
cards.summary: van Wyk 2020 (TANGO): RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 in 0.3% after switching to dolutegravir–lamivudine versus 0.5% staying on a tenofovir-alafenamide regimen — non-inferior, no resistance
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 non-inferiority trial (van Wyk 2020, TANGO; open-label)
cards.people: 743 adults with HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL on a tenofovir alafenamide-based 3- or 4-drug regimen were enrolled (741 received at least one dose), randomised 1:1, stratified by baseline third-agent class, to switch to once-daily fixed-dose dolutegravir–lamivudine (369 patients) or remain on the tenofovir alafenamide-based regimen (372 patients), with a 4% non-inferiority margin on the week-48 Snapshot endpoint.
cards.result: At week 48, the proportion with HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL was 0.3% (1/369) on dolutegravir–lamivudine versus 0.5% (2/372) on the tenofovir alafenamide-based regimen (adjusted treatment difference −0.3 percentage points, 95% CI −1.2 to 0.7), meeting non-inferiority. No participant on dolutegravir–lamivudine met confirmed virological withdrawal criteria (one did on the comparator), and there was no emergent resistance at failure. Drug-related grade ≥2 adverse events occurred in 17 participants (4.6%) on dolutegravir–lamivudine versus 3 (0.8%) on the comparator, and withdrawals due to adverse events in 13 (3.5%) versus 2 (0.5%).
cards.watchOut: Open-label switch trial in patients already suppressed with no stated history of virological failure — it says nothing about starting two-drug therapy or about patients with prior failure or resistance. Non-inferiority on a virological endpoint is a maintenance claim, not evidence that two drugs are better for long-term clinical outcomes.
cards.source: van Wyk J et al. cards.headline: Llibre 2023 (SALSA): 0.4% versus 1.2% with RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 — non-inferior against a mixed bag of 3- and 4-drug regimens, with more early drug-related symptoms after switching
cards.summary: Llibre 2023 (SALSA): 0.4% versus 1.2% with RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48 — non-inferior against a mixed bag of 3- and 4-drug regimens, with more early drug-related symptoms after switching
cards.people: 493 adults with HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL and no previous virological failure (39% women; 39% aged 50 years or older) were randomised 1:1, stratified by baseline third-agent class, to switch to once-daily fixed-dose dolutegravir–lamivudine (246 patients) or continue their current 3- or 4-drug antiretroviral regimen (247 patients), with a 5% non-inferiority margin on the week-48 Snapshot endpoint.
cards.result: At week 48, 1 participant (0.4%) in the dolutegravir–lamivudine group and 3 (1.2%) in the continuation group had HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL (adjusted difference −0.8 percentage points, 95% CI −2.4 to 0.8), demonstrating non-inferiority. Zero participants in either group met confirmed virological withdrawal criteria, so no resistance testing was performed. Drug-related adverse events were more frequent with dolutegravir–lamivudine (20% versus 6%) through week 48 but comparable after week 24 (5% versus 2%). Proximal tubular renal function and bone turnover biomarkers improved with dolutegravir–lamivudine; changes in lipids and inflammatory biomarkers were generally minimal in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is a heterogeneous mix of whatever 3- or 4-drug regimens participants arrived on, so SALSA supports switching in general rather than against any one named regimen. The early excess of drug-related adverse events after switching (20% versus 6%) is the honest cost patients feel, even though it faded after week 24.
cards.source: Llibre JM et al. Efficacy and Safety of Switching to the 2-Drug Regimen Dolutegravir/Lamivudine Versus Continuing a 3- or 4-Drug Regimen for Maintaining Virologic Suppression in Adults Living With Human Immunodeficiency Virus 1 (HIV-1): Week 48 Results From the Phase 3, Noninferiority SALSA Randomized Trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: two switch trials, one consistent answer — two drugs hold suppression in patients who are already suppressed and have never failed
cards.summary: Synthesis: two switch trials, one consistent answer — two drugs hold suppression in patients who are already suppressed and have never failed
cards.people: Two randomised phase 3 non-inferiority switch trials totalling 1,234 treated adults with HIV-1 RNA <50 copies/mL and no previous virological failure (TANGO, against tenofovir-alafenamide-based regimens; SALSA, against mixed 3- or 4-drug regimens), each following patients for 48 weeks after switching to dolutegravir–lamivudine or continuing their regimen.
cards.result: HIV-1 RNA ≥50 copies/mL at week 48: 0.3% versus 0.5% (TANGO) and 0.4% versus 1.2% (SALSA) — non-inferior in both. Confirmed virological withdrawal on dolutegravir–lamivudine: none in either trial; emergent resistance: none. Cost: more drug-related adverse events after switching (grade ≥2 events 4.6% versus 0.8% in TANGO; any drug-related events 20% versus 6% through week 48 in SALSA, converging after week 24). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the benefit is a simpler two-drug regimen with suppression maintained, in the selected population the trials enrolled.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled only patients already suppressed without prior virological failure; the result does not extend to initial therapy (homed separately at live shelf #724, GEMINI) or to anyone with archived resistance to either drug. Follow-up here is 48 weeks; the claim is maintenance of suppression, not long-term clinical outcomes.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Wyk J et al. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2020 (PMID: 31905383); Llibre JM et al. Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America. 2023 (PMID: 35235656).

shelves.title: Music around surgery and on the wards: pain and anxiety fall across 73 trials (standardised effects −0.77 and −0.68) and analgesia use drops — length of stay does not move, and ward delirium is untested
shelves.question: In hospitalised patients, does music therapy reduce pain, anxiety or delirium compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesia/methods · Anxiety/therapy · Humans · Length of Stay · Music · Music Therapy/methods · Postoperative Pain/therapy · Patient Satisfaction · Postoperative Period
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for pain and anxiety in hospital, not for delirium or discharge. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 73 randomised trials (Hole J et al., PMID: 26277246) found music around surgical procedures reduced postoperative pain (standardised mean difference −0.77, 95% CI −0.99 to −0.56), anxiety (−0.68, −0.95 to −0.41) and analgesia use (−0.37, −0.54 to −0.20), and increased patient satisfaction (1.09, 0.51 to 1.68), while length of stay did not differ (−0.11, −0.35 to 0.12); music worked even under general anaesthesia, and who chose the music mattered little. An individual four-arm inpatient trial points the same way (Deng C et al., PMID: 34134947; 160 women having breast-cancer surgery): music therapy alone beat usual care on pain and anxiety change (P<0.001), with combined aromatherapy-plus-music best. No qualifying randomised trial of music for delirium in general hospital wards was found — the delirium evidence sits in intensive care and is homed on its own shelf — so the delirium part of the question is unanswered here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): offering patients music in hospital is a cheap, safe way to take a real slice off pain and anxiety; it does not shorten stay and has no proven ward-delirium effect.

cards.headline: Hole 2015 (73 RCTs): pain SMD −0.77, anxiety −0.68, analgesia use −0.37, satisfaction +1.09 — length of stay unchanged (−0.11, CI crossing zero)
cards.summary: Hole 2015 (73 RCTs): pain SMD −0.77, anxiety −0.68, analgesia use −0.37, satisfaction +1.09 — length of stay unchanged (−0.11, CI crossing zero)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Hole 2015)
cards.people: 73 randomised trials of adults undergoing surgical procedures (excluding central nervous system and head-and-neck surgery), trial sizes 20–458 participants; any form of music before, during or after surgery versus standard care, headphones with no music, white noise or undisturbed bed rest.
cards.result: Music reduced postoperative pain (SMD −0.77, 95% CI −0.99 to −0.56), anxiety (−0.68, −0.95 to −0.41) and analgesia use (−0.37, −0.54 to −0.20), and increased patient satisfaction (1.09, 0.51 to 1.68). Length of stay did not differ (SMD −0.11, −0.35 to 0.12). Subgroup analyses found choice of music and timing of delivery made little difference, and music was effective even when patients were under general anaesthetic.
cards.watchOut: Almost entirely a surgical, perioperative literature — it supports music for hospitalised patients around procedures, not music as a treatment for medical inpatients' symptoms generally, and none of these trials answers delirium on general wards. Effects are standardised mean differences on symptom scales, not absolute point drops.
cards.source: Hole J et al. Music as an aid for postoperative recovery in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet. 2015. PMID: 26277246. cards.headline: Deng 2022: in 160 women having breast surgery, music therapy alone improved pain and anxiety more than usual care (P<0.001) — combined aromatherapy + music did best
cards.summary: Deng 2022: in 160 women having breast surgery, music therapy alone improved pain and anxiety more than usual care (P<0.001) — combined aromatherapy + music did best
cards.people: 160 hospitalised women with breast cancer randomised 1:1:1:1 to usual care, aromatherapy, music therapy, or combined therapy during the perioperative period; pain intensity and anxiety measured by visual analogue scale, with interleukin-6 and HMGB-1 measured by assay.
cards.result: There was a significant group effect on pain, anxiety and IL-6/HMGB-1 levels, greatest in the combined-therapy group (P<.001). Compared with usual care, both the aromatherapy and music-therapy groups had lower mean changes in pain intensity and greater anxiety reduction (P<.001); aromatherapy and music therapy did not differ significantly from each other (P>0.05). The record reports P values without printing the group mean scores.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial whose abstract gives significance but not effect sizes, and whose winning arm combines two therapies — it corroborates the meta-analysis's direction for music alone but cannot quantify it.
cards.source: Deng C et al. Aromatherapy Plus Music Therapy Improve Pain Intensity and Anxiety Scores in Patients With Breast Cancer During Perioperative Periods: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Clinical Breast Cancer. 2022. PMID: 34134947. shelves.title: Motion sickness: scopolamine and first-generation antihistamines prevent it better than placebo when taken before travel — ginger's evidence is one small sea trial — and no drug has ever been trial-tested for treating symptoms once they start
shelves.question: What helps motion sickness? In people prone to motion sickness in cars, boats and planes, do scopolamine, antihistamines (meclizine, dimenhydrinate) or ginger prevent symptoms — and can anything treat symptoms once they have started?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for PREVENTION only, taken before the journey. Two Cochrane reviews carry the shelf. For scopolamine (Spinks 2011, PMID: 21678338; 14 randomised trials, 1,025 subjects), scopolamine was more effective than placebo at preventing symptoms, was superior to methscopolamine and equivalent to antihistamines in the few head-to-head comparisons, and caused more dry mouth but no more drowsiness, blurred vision or dizziness than comparators; the trials were small and of varying quality, and the review prints no pooled effect size. For first-generation antihistamines (Karrim 2022, PMID: 36250781; 9 RCTs, 658 participants), the natural-motion studies (cinnarizine and dimenhydrinate only) found symptoms prevented in 40% on antihistamines versus 25% on placebo (risk ratio 1.81, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.66 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates of 40% and 25%; moderate-certainty, 3 studies, 240 participants), at the cost of more sedation (66% versus 44% on placebo; RR 1.51, relative). Ginger rests on much thinner ice: one double-blind sea trial of 80 naval cadets (Grøntved 1988, PMID: 3277342) found less vomiting and cold sweating on 1 g ginger root than placebo (P<0.05) with nausea and vertigo differences not statistically significant, and the systematic review that contains it (Ernst 2000, PMID: 10793599) found exactly one seasickness trial among its six studies and called ginger 'promising' but the data insufficient for firm conclusions. The shelf's sharpest finding is a shared negative: BOTH Cochrane reviews found no randomised trial of any of these drugs for TREATING motion sickness that has already started — every positive result is prevention taken in advance. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prevention with scopolamine or a first-generation antihistamine is supported at low-to-moderate certainty; ginger is a MAYBE within that; treatment of established symptoms is untested, not disproven.

cards.headline: Spinks 2011 (Cochrane, scopolamine): more effective than placebo at preventing motion sickness across 14 trials and 1,025 subjects — small trials, no pooled number, and zero trials of treating established symptoms
cards.summary: Spinks 2011 (Cochrane, scopolamine): more effective than placebo at preventing motion sickness across 14 trials and 1,025 subjects — small trials, no pooled number, and zero trials of treating established symptoms
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (Spinks 2011; update of a review first published 2004)
cards.people: 14 randomised controlled trials enrolling 1,025 subjects, from 35 potentially relevant studies; scopolamine given as transdermal patches, tablets or capsules, oral solutions or intravenously, and compared against placebo, calcium channel antagonists, an antihistamine, methscopolamine, or scopolamine plus ephedrine. Studies were generally small and of varying quality.
cards.result: Scopolamine was more effective than placebo in the prevention of symptoms. Comparisons with other agents were few: scopolamine was superior to methscopolamine and equivalent to antihistamines as a preventive agent, and evidence against cinnarizine or scopolamine-plus-ephedrine combinations was equivocal or minimal. Although sample sizes were small, scopolamine was no more likely to induce drowsiness, blurring of vision or dizziness than other agents; dry mouth was more likely with scopolamine than with methscopolamine or cinnarizine. No studies were available on the therapeutic effectiveness of scopolamine in the management of established symptoms. The authors concluded that scopolamine versus placebo in preventing motion sickness has been shown to be effective, that no conclusions can be made on its comparative effectiveness against antihistamines or calcium channel antagonists, and that no randomised controlled trials examined treatment of established symptoms.
cards.watchOut: The review prints no pooled risk ratio or absolute rates, so this card claims direction, not size: 'more effective than placebo' across 14 small, variably conducted trials is a weaker foundation than a single large trial with a measured effect. The equivalence-to-antihistamines statement rests on few comparisons. And the prevention/treatment gap is total — a traveller who is already nauseated is outside this evidence entirely.
cards.source: Spinks A, Wasiak J. Scopolamine (hyoscine) for preventing and treating motion sickness. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2011. PMID: 21678338. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Karrim 2022 (Cochrane, antihistamines): symptoms prevented in 40% on first-generation antihistamines versus 25% on placebo under natural motion (RR 1.81, relative; moderate-certainty) — sedation 66% versus 44%
cards.summary: Karrim 2022 (Cochrane, antihistamines): symptoms prevented in 40% on first-generation antihistamines versus 25% on placebo under natural motion (RR 1.81, relative; moderate-certainty) — sedation 66% versus 44%
cards.people: Nine RCTs with 658 participants aged 16 to 55 years across seven countries; motion sickness induced naturally in six studies and experimentally (rotating chair) in four. All naturally induced studies evaluated only first-generation antihistamines — cinnarizine and dimenhydrinate. No study clearly assessed children. Risk of bias varied, with mostly high risk for selective reporting.
cards.result: Against placebo or no treatment under natural conditions, antihistamines were probably more effective at preventing symptoms: symptoms were prevented in 40% of antihistamine recipients versus 25% on placebo (risk ratio 1.81, 95% CI 1.23 to 2.66 — a relative measure; 3 studies, 240 participants; moderate-certainty). Under experimental conditions the evidence was very uncertain (standardised mean difference 0.32, 95% CI −0.18 to 0.83; 2 studies, 62 participants; very low-certainty). Versus scopolamine under natural conditions the evidence was also very uncertain (symptoms prevented 81% scopolamine versus 71% antihistamines; RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.16; 2 studies, 71 participants). The price was sedation: 66% on antihistamines versus 44% on placebo (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.12 to 2.02; low-certainty), with little or no difference in blurred vision (14% versus 12.5%) or impaired cognition (29% versus 33%). No studies reported results on resolution of existing motion sickness symptoms. The authors concluded there is probably a reduction in the risk of developing symptoms with first-generation antihistamines in susceptible adults, that sedation is more likely, and that evidence for all other comparisons was low or very low certainty.
cards.watchOut: Read the drug names, not the class label: the natural-motion evidence is for cinnarizine and dimenhydrinate — meclizine, the antihistamine most often bought for this purpose in the US, was not the tested drug in the natural-condition trials, and second-generation (non-sedating) antihistamines have no supporting evidence here at all. The headline comparison pools just 240 participants, and sedation at 66% is itself a travel problem (driving, caring for children). Children were essentially unstudied.
cards.source: Karrim N, Byrne R, Magula N, Saman Y. Antihistamines for motion sickness. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2022. PMID: 36250781. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Grøntved 1988 (the ginger sea trial): 1 g ginger root cut vomiting tendency and cold sweating versus placebo in 80 naval cadets (P<0.05) — nausea and vertigo differences were not significant
cards.summary: Grøntved 1988 (the ginger sea trial): 1 g ginger root cut vomiting tendency and cold sweating versus placebo in 80 naval cadets (P<0.05) — nausea and vertigo differences were not significant
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial on the open sea (Grøntved 1988)
cards.people: 80 naval cadets unaccustomed to sailing in heavy seas, randomised double-blind to 1 g powdered ginger rhizome (Zingiber officinale) or placebo, with seasickness symptoms self-reported every hour for 4 consecutive hours after ingestion during voyages on the high seas.
cards.result: Ginger root reduced the tendency to vomiting and cold sweating significantly better than placebo (P<0.05); for vomiting, a modified Protection Index of 72% was calculated (a relative index as reported by the authors; the abstract prints no per-group vomiting counts, so no absolute rates are claimed). Remarkably fewer symptoms of nausea and vertigo were reported after ginger, but the difference was not statistically significant. Across all symptom categories the Protection Index was 38%.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 80 young male cadets, 4 hours, one heavy-sea setting — and its two most patient-important symptoms (nausea, vertigo) did not reach significance. The 72% figure is a 'Protection Index' computed by the authors, not a risk ratio from printed event counts; do not read it as '72% less vomiting' in the usual trial sense. Herbal-product naming rule: the tested preparation was powdered ginger rhizome, 1 g, as supplied for this trial — the publication names no brand or company, so no branded product can be read across from it, and current ginger products may differ in content, safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Grøntved A, Brask T, Kambskard J, Hentzer E. Ginger root against seasickness. A controlled trial on the open sea. Acta Oto-Laryngologica. 1988. PMID: 3277342. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Ernst 2000 (ginger systematic review): six RCTs across all nausea conditions, only one on seasickness — 'a promising antiemetic herbal remedy, but the clinical data to date are insufficient to draw firm conclusions'
cards.summary: Ernst 2000 (ginger systematic review): six RCTs across all nausea conditions, only one on seasickness — 'a promising antiemetic herbal remedy, but the clinical data to date are insufficient to draw firm conclusions'
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised clinical trials (Ernst & Pittler 2000)
cards.people: Six randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials of ginger as a single agent for nausea and vomiting met the inclusion criteria: three on postoperative nausea and vomiting, and one each on seasickness, morning sickness and chemotherapy-induced nausea. Experimentally induced nausea studies were excluded.
cards.result: Two of the three postoperative trials suggested ginger was superior to placebo and equally effective as metoclopramide, but the pooled absolute risk reduction for postoperative nausea with 1 g ginger before operation was non-significant (absolute risk reduction 0.052, 95% CI −0.082 to 0.186). The single studies on seasickness, morning sickness and chemotherapy-induced nausea collectively favoured ginger over placebo. The authors' conclusion, in substance: ginger is a promising antiemetic herbal remedy, but the clinical data are insufficient to draw firm conclusions — with publication bias (unpublished negative trials) an explicit concern.
cards.watchOut: This review is carded as the discipline on the ginger claim, not as a second positive: for motion sickness specifically it contains exactly one trial — the Grøntved sea trial carded above — so the review and the trial are the same evidence counted once. Its pooled number (from postoperative nausea, a different condition) was null. A shelf that presented ginger as established for motion sickness would be standing on 80 cadets and a favourable-but-insufficient verdict from 2000.
cards.source: Ernst E, Pittler MH. Efficacy of ginger for nausea and vomiting: a systematic review of randomized clinical trials. British Journal of Anaesthesia. 2000. PMID: 10793599. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Synthesis: prevention has real but modest trial support (scopolamine, first-generation antihistamines); ginger has one small sea trial; treatment of symptoms already under way has never been randomised-tested
cards.summary: Synthesis: prevention has real but modest trial support (scopolamine, first-generation antihistamines); ginger has one small sea trial; treatment of symptoms already under way has never been randomised-tested
cards.people: Two Cochrane reviews (Spinks 2011: 14 trials, 1,025 subjects on scopolamine; Karrim 2022: 9 RCTs, 658 participants on antihistamines), one randomised sea trial of ginger (Grøntved 1988: 80 cadets), and one systematic review of ginger across nausea conditions (Ernst 2000: 6 RCTs).
cards.result: Prevention, before travel: scopolamine was more effective than placebo across 14 small trials, with dry mouth the clearest excess harm and no pooled effect size published (Spinks 2011). First-generation antihistamines (cinnarizine, dimenhydrinate in the natural-motion trials) prevented symptoms in 40% versus 25% on placebo (RR 1.81, relative; moderate-certainty) and sedated 66% versus 44% (Karrim 2022); head-to-head against scopolamine was very uncertain (81% versus 71% prevented). Ginger: vomiting tendency and cold sweating reduced in one 80-person trial (P<0.05), nausea and vertigo not significant, and the containing review judged the data insufficient for firm conclusions (Grøntved 1988; Ernst 2000). Treatment of established symptoms: no randomised trial found by either Cochrane review, for any of these drugs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for prevention with scopolamine or a first-generation antihistamine; ginger MAYBE within that; treating symptoms already present is untested.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. This shelf does not cover motion sickness in children (essentially unstudied in these reviews), vestibular disorders such as Ménière's disease or BPPV (different questions with their own shelves), antiemetics such as ondansetron (not shown effective for motion sickness in this record and not carded here), or non-drug measures (horizon-gazing, fresh air, seating position), which have no cardable randomised record in this set. Meclizine specifically was not the tested antihistamine in the natural-motion trials — the class claim should not be silently transferred to it.

shelves.title: Toothache and dental pain: ibuprofen plus acetaminophen beats opioids — first in the systematic reviews, first in the 82-trial network analysis, first-line in the ADA guideline
shelves.question: What helps a toothache? For acute dental pain — toothache before a dentist can treat the cause, or pain after a tooth extraction — which painkillers actually work best: ibuprofen, acetaminophen, the two together, or prescription opioids?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen · Acute Pain/drug therapy · Adult · Analgesics · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic · Analgesics, Opioid · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Child · Dentistry · Humans · Postoperative Pain · Systematic Reviews as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for ibuprofen plus acetaminophen as the first-line answer — this is one of the rare everyday questions where the evidence hierarchy speaks with one voice. The Moore 2018 overview of five systematic reviews (PMID: 29599019) found that ibuprofen-and-acetaminophen combinations had the highest association with treatment benefit and the highest proportion of adults achieving maximum pain relief of any oral analgesic strategy reviewed, while opioid-containing medicines were the ones most frequently associated with acute adverse events in both children and adults. The ADA's own evidence base — the Miroshnychenko 2023 network meta-analysis of 82 post-extraction trials (PMID: 36631957) — put numbers on it: for 6-hour pain relief (0–4 scale, versus placebo), ibuprofen 200–400 mg plus acetaminophen 500–1,000 mg scored a mean difference of 1.68 (95% CI 1.06–2.31), ibuprofen 400 mg alone 1.31 (1.17–1.45), naproxen 400–440 mg 1.44 (1.07–1.80), while acetaminophen 650 mg plus oxycodone 10 mg scored 1.19 (0.85–1.54) and oxycodone 5 mg, codeine 60 mg and tramadol 37.5 mg/acetaminophen 325 mg were no better than placebo. The 2024 ADA guideline, summarised for emergency settings by Green 2025 (PMID: 39764906), converts this into practice: NSAIDs with or without acetaminophen are first-line for toothache when definitive dental treatment is not immediately available, and opioids are reserved for when first-line therapy fails or NSAIDs are contraindicated. Two honest limits. First, most trial data come from pain after tooth extraction (the standard dental pain model) rather than the throbbing pulpitis toothache of the question; the guideline explicitly extends the recommendation to temporary toothache management, but the trials themselves are post-surgical. Second, analgesics only buy time: no card here shows a painkiller curing the pulp or periapical disease causing the pain, and definitive dental treatment remains the treatment. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for NSAID ± acetaminophen as first-line analgesia; opioids show no advantage and more harm.

cards.headline: Moore 2018 (JADA overview of systematic reviews): ibuprofen-plus-acetaminophen combinations topped every oral analgesic strategy for benefit and maximum pain relief — and opioid medicines carried the most acute adverse events, in children and adults
cards.summary: Moore 2018 (JADA overview of systematic reviews): ibuprofen-plus-acetaminophen combinations topped every oral analgesic strategy for benefit and maximum pain relief — and opioid medicines carried the most acute adverse events, in children and adults
cards.people: An overview of systematic reviews published in the Journal of the American Dental Association (April 2018), by investigators at the University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine and the University of Pittsburgh School of Dental Medicine, assessing the benefits and harms of common oral analgesic medications marketed in the United States for acute dental pain, in both adults and children. Five systematic reviews met the inclusion criteria; their quality was rated with AMSTAR 2, and the included reviews were of moderate and high quality.
cards.result: The highest level of therapeutic benefit associated with any medication was found for combinations of ibuprofen and acetaminophen, which also showed the highest proportion of adult participants experiencing maximum pain relief. Diflunisal, acetaminophen and oxycodone were identified as having the longest duration of action. Medications and medication combinations that included opioids were among those most frequently associated with acute adverse events in both children and adults. The authors concluded that the best available data suggest NSAIDs, with or without acetaminophen, offer the most favourable balance between benefits and harms, optimising efficacy while minimising acute adverse events, for pharmacological management of acute dental pain.
cards.watchOut: An overview of reviews inherits the limits of its sources: the underlying trials are predominantly post-extraction pain studies in younger adults, the abstract reports rankings and proportions rather than a single pooled effect size, and 'highest association with treatment benefit' is the authors' comparative summary across five reviews, not a head-to-head trial of every drug. It also says nothing about antibiotics — analgesia is not treatment of the underlying dental disease.
cards.source: Moore PA, Ziegler KM, Lipman RD, Aminoshariae A, Carrasco-Labra A, Mariotti A. cards.headline: Miroshnychenko 2023 (network meta-analysis, 82 trials): ibuprofen + acetaminophen gave the largest 6-hour pain relief (mean difference 1.68 vs placebo); oxycodone 5 mg, codeine 60 mg and tramadol combinations were no better than placebo
cards.summary: Miroshnychenko 2023 (network meta-analysis, 82 trials): ibuprofen + acetaminophen gave the largest 6-hour pain relief (mean difference 1.68 vs placebo); oxycodone 5 mg, codeine 60 mg and tramadol combinations were no better than placebo
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis for the ADA guideline (Miroshnychenko 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis conducted to inform the American Dental Association's clinical practice guideline on pharmacological management of acute dental pain: 82 randomised trials of analgesics for pain after tooth extraction. The network meta-analysis of 6-hour pain relief (0–4 scale) drew on 56 randomised trials with 9,095 participants, comparing 13 medication interventions; evidence certainty was rated moderate to high for the comparisons reported.
cards.result: Mean differences in 6-hour pain relief versus placebo (0–4 scale): ibuprofen 200–400 mg plus acetaminophen 500–1,000 mg, MD 1.68 (95% CI 1.06–2.31); naproxen 400–440 mg, MD 1.44 (1.07–1.80); ibuprofen 400 mg, MD 1.31 (1.17–1.45); and acetaminophen 650 mg plus oxycodone 10 mg, MD 1.19 (0.85–1.54). Oxycodone 5 mg, codeine 60 mg, and tramadol 37.5 mg plus acetaminophen 325 mg were no better than placebo. The authors concluded that NSAIDs with or without acetaminophen provide better pain relief than opioids with or without acetaminophen (except for the acetaminophen-plus-oxycodone combination) or placebo in the management of acute dental pain.
cards.watchOut: The model condition is pain after tooth extraction in adults — the best-studied dental pain, but not identical to untreated pulpitis or a dental abscess, where no equivalent trial network exists. Mean differences on a 0–4 relief scale are group averages: an individual patient's response varies, and the combination's edge over ibuprofen alone (1.68 versus 1.31) is real but modest. Network estimates blend direct and indirect comparisons; certainty was moderate to high, not uniform.

cards.headline: Green 2025 (the 2024 ADA guideline, summarised for emergency and urgent care): NSAIDs with or without acetaminophen are first-line for toothache when a dentist is not immediately available; opioids only when first-line fails or NSAIDs are contraindicated
cards.summary: Green 2025 (the 2024 ADA guideline, summarised for emergency and urgent care): NSAIDs with or without acetaminophen are first-line for toothache when a dentist is not immediately available; opioids only when first-line fails or NSAIDs are contraindicated
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline summary (ADA 2024 guideline; Green 2025)
cards.people: Commentary in the American Journal of Emergency Medicine summarising the 2024 clinical practice guideline for pharmacological management of acute dental pain (tooth extraction pain and toothache) for settings where definitive dental treatment is not immediately available — emergency departments, hospitals and urgent care clinics. The guideline panel was convened by the American Dental Association, the ADA Science & Research Institute, the University of Pittsburgh School of Dental Medicine and Penn Dental Medicine; it examined opioid and non-opioid analgesics, local anaesthetics including blocks, corticosteroids and topical anaesthetics, using GRADE to assess certainty, and formulated 18 recommendations and six good practice statements.
cards.result: A beneficial net balance favours non-opioid over opioid medications. When not contraindicated, NSAIDs alone or in combination with acetaminophen likely provide superior pain relief with a more favourable safety profile than opioids. The guideline's conclusion: NSAIDs with or without acetaminophen are first-line therapy for managing acute dental pain following tooth extraction(s) and for temporarily managing toothache; opioids should be reserved for clinical situations when first-line therapy is insufficient or contraindications to NSAIDs exist.
cards.watchOut: A guideline is a synthesis judgement, not new data — its force comes from the Moore overview and the Miroshnychenko network analysis carded alongside it, and the word 'likely' in its key sentence is deliberate GRADE language. 'When not contraindicated' does real work: NSAIDs are wrong for some patients (kidney disease, ulcer risk, anticoagulation, late pregnancy, NSAID allergy), and for them acetaminophen alone or an opioid may be the fallback. The guideline addresses temporary management — it assumes definitive dental treatment follows.
cards.source: Green VG, Polk DE, Turturro MA, Moore PA, Carrasco-Labra A. Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines for the management of acute dental pain. American Journal of Emergency Medicine. 2025. PMID: 39764906. Registry ID: none in the record (guideline commentary). cards.headline: Synthesis: the over-the-counter combination beats the prescription pad — ibuprofen plus acetaminophen first, an NSAID alone second, opioids last and only when the first line cannot be used
cards.summary: Synthesis: the over-the-counter combination beats the prescription pad — ibuprofen plus acetaminophen first, an NSAID alone second, opioids last and only when the first line cannot be used
cards.people: One overview of five systematic reviews (Moore 2018), one network meta-analysis of 82 post-extraction trials / 56 trials and 9,095 participants in the relief network (Miroshnychenko 2023), and the 2024 ADA clinical practice guideline as summarised by Green 2025 (18 recommendations, six good practice statements).
cards.result: Ranking on 6-hour relief versus placebo: ibuprofen 200–400 mg + acetaminophen 500–1,000 mg first (MD 1.68), then naproxen (1.44), then ibuprofen 400 mg alone (1.31); the strongest opioid combination tested (acetaminophen 650 mg + oxycodone 10 mg, 1.19) sat below all three, and oxycodone 5 mg, codeine 60 mg and tramadol/acetaminophen were indistinguishable from placebo (Miroshnychenko 2023). The overview found the same ordering and the worst acute adverse-event profile in the opioid-containing medicines (Moore 2018); the guideline makes NSAID ± acetaminophen first-line and reserves opioids (Green 2025). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for ibuprofen ± acetaminophen as first-line dental analgesia.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. Boundaries: (1) the trial evidence is post-extraction pain; untreated toothache from pulp/periapical disease is covered by the guideline's extension, not by direct trials of equal size. (2) Analgesia is a bridge, not a cure — spreading infection, facial swelling, fever or trismus are dental emergencies, not painkiller problems. (3) Doses on these cards are the trial doses; total daily maxima, other acetaminophen-containing products, and personal contraindications (kidney disease, ulcers, anticoagulants, pregnancy) must be checked before use — long-term daily NSAID safety is a separate shelf (#5289).
cards.source: Synthesis of Moore PA et al. Journal of the American Dental Association. 2018 (PMID: 29599019); Miroshnychenko A et al. Journal of Dental Research. 2023 (PMID: 36631957); Green VG et al. American Journal of Emergency Medicine. 2025 (PMID: 39764906).

shelves.title: Hangover: no treatment has been shown to work — two systematic reviews found only single, small, unreplicated trials, and the reviewers' verdict is that abstinence or moderation is the only effective prevention
shelves.question: "How do I get rid of a hangover?" After alcohol, do any medicines, supplements or remedies — painkillers, anti-sickness drugs, prickly pear, ginseng, pear juice, fructose, anything — actually prevent or treat hangover symptoms better than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Alcoholic Intoxication/prevention & control · Complementary Therapies · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome/prevention & control
shelves.balance: (no treatment shown to work) — stated plainly, because two systematic reviews seventeen years apart reached the same conclusion. Pittler 2005 (BMJ, PMID: 16373736) reviewed the randomised trials of hangover interventions — eight double-blind trials covering propranolol, tropisetron, tolfenamic acid, fructose/glucose, borage, artichoke, prickly pear and a yeast preparation — and found significant differences favouring treatment in only a few single trials (tolfenamic acid, the γ-linolenic acid in borage, and the yeast preparation), concluding: 'No compelling evidence exists to suggest that any conventional or complementary intervention is effective for preventing or treating alcohol hangover. The most effective way to avoid the symptoms of alcohol induced hangover is to practise abstinence or moderation.' Roberts 2022 (Addiction, PMID: 34972259) updated the search to August 2021 and found 21 placebo-controlled trials with only 386 participants in total; no two studies tested the same intervention, so no meta-analysis was possible, and every efficacy outcome in every study was rated very low quality by GRADE — a scatter of single small trials with statistically significant results (clove extract, tolfenamic acid, pyritinol, Hovenia dulcis, L-cysteine, red ginseng, Korean pear juice) that have never been replicated. The best-executed single trial on the shelf, Wiese 2004 (PMID: 15226168; 64 young adults, crossover), found a prickly-pear (Opuntia ficus-indica) extract taken before drinking reduced three of nine symptoms (nausea, dry mouth, anorexia) and the odds of a severe hangover (OR 0.38, 95% CI 0.16–0.88 — relative), but the overall symptom index difference was not significant (2.7 points; 95% CI −0.2 to 5.5; P=0.07). PROPOSED (no treatment shown to work): after decades of trials, nothing — drug, supplement or folk remedy — has replicated, adequately powered evidence of relieving a hangover; time, fluids, food and sleep are unproven comforts, and prevention by drinking less is the only intervention with a coherent evidence story.

cards.headline: Pittler 2005 (BMJ systematic review): across eight double-blind randomised trials of eight different hangover interventions, 'no compelling evidence exists to suggest that any conventional or complementary intervention is effective'
cards.summary: Pittler 2005 (BMJ systematic review): across eight double-blind randomised trials of eight different hangover interventions, 'no compelling evidence exists to suggest that any conventional or complementary intervention is effective'
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Pittler 2005, BMJ)
cards.people: Systematic review in the BMJ of randomised controlled trials of any conventional or complementary intervention for preventing or treating alcohol hangover: 15 potentially relevant trials were identified, of which eight met the inclusion criteria — double-blind randomised trials of propranolol, tropisetron, tolfenamic acid, fructose or glucose, borage, artichoke, prickly pear (Opuntia ficus-indica), and a yeast-based preparation.
cards.result: Significant differences between intervention and control were reported only for tolfenamic acid, for γ-linolenic acid from borage, and for the yeast preparation; the remaining interventions, including propranolol, tropisetron, fructose/glucose, artichoke and prickly pear in this review's assessment, did not show convincing benefit. The authors' conclusion: 'No compelling evidence exists to suggest that any conventional or complementary intervention is effective for preventing or treating alcohol hangover. The most effective way to avoid the symptoms of alcohol induced hangover is to practise abstinence or moderation.'
cards.watchOut: A 2005 review of a small, old literature: most trials were tiny, several interventions were tested once and never again, and hangover severity was measured on differing symptom scales. 'No compelling evidence of effect' is the correct reading — not 'proof that nothing can work'. Three interventions did produce significant results in single trials; the review's judgement is that single unreplicated small trials do not amount to compelling evidence, a standard this shelf keeps.
cards.source: Pittler MH, Verster JC, Ernst E. Interventions for preventing or treating alcohol hangover: systematic review of randomised controlled trials. BMJ. 2005. PMID: 16373736. cards.headline: Roberts 2022 (Addiction systematic review): 21 placebo-controlled trials, 386 participants total, no two testing the same remedy — and every efficacy outcome rated very low quality
cards.summary: Roberts 2022 (Addiction systematic review): 21 placebo-controlled trials, 386 participants total, no two testing the same remedy — and every efficacy outcome rated very low quality
cards.people: Systematic review in Addiction of randomised placebo-controlled trials of pharmacological interventions for alcohol hangover, searching to 1 August 2021: 21 eligible studies with 386 participants in total. Interventions included clove extract, tolfenamic acid, pyritinol, Hovenia dulcis fruit extract, L-cysteine, red ginseng, Korean pear juice, and others. Because no two studies evaluated the same intervention, no meta-analysis could be performed; study quality was assessed with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool and GRADE.
cards.result: All studies reported efficacy outcomes of very low quality (GRADE). Statistically significant results versus placebo were reported in single studies for mean overall symptom score with clove extract (42.5% versus 19.0%; P<0.001), tolfenamic acid (84.0% versus 50.0%; P<0.001), pyritinol (34.1% versus 16.2%; P<0.01), Hovenia dulcis (P=0.029), L-cysteine (P=0.043), red ginseng (21.1% versus 14.0%; P<0.05) and Korean pear juice (41.5% versus 33.3%; P<0.05) — each an unreplicated single small trial. No study reported dropouts due to adverse events. The pattern across 21 trials and 17 years since the BMJ review is unchanged: isolated positive small trials, none confirmed by a second study.
cards.watchOut: The percentages quoted are each trial's mean overall symptom score expressed against its own placebo on its own scale — they are not comparable across studies and none has been replicated, which is precisely the review's point. 'Very low quality' in GRADE terms means the true effect could be substantially different from the estimate in either direction. The commercial hangover-cure market (IV drips, supplement blends, 'anti-hangover' shots) has no better trial base than the interventions reviewed here — most have never been in a placebo-controlled trial at all.
cards.source: Roberts E, Smith R, Hotopf M, Drummond C. The efficacy and tolerability of pharmacological interventions for alcohol hangover: systematic review and considerations for future research. cards.headline: Wiese 2004 (prickly pear, crossover trial, 64 young adults): extract before drinking reduced nausea, dry mouth and anorexia and cut severe-hangover odds (OR 0.38, relative) — but the overall symptom index was not significantly different (P=0.07)
cards.summary: Wiese 2004 (prickly pear, crossover trial, 64 young adults): extract before drinking reduced nausea, dry mouth and anorexia and cut severe-hangover odds (OR 0.38, relative) — but the overall symptom index was not significantly different (P=0.07)
cards.people: Double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study: 64 healthy young adults were randomised to receive an extract of the prickly pear plant Opuntia ficus-indica (1,600 IU) or placebo 5 hours before consuming alcohol; two weeks later the alcohol challenge was repeated with the groups crossed over. 55 participants completed both arms. Nine hangover symptoms were rated the following morning, combined into a symptom index (severe hangover defined as a symptom index of 18 points or more), and morning C-reactive protein was measured. The tested preparation was a standardised Opuntia ficus-indica extract (1,600 IU) supplied for the trial — an unbranded research preparation, not a named commercial product.
cards.result: Three of the nine symptoms — nausea, dry mouth and anorexia (loss of appetite) — were significantly reduced by the extract (all P<0.05). The overall symptom index was reduced by 2.7 points (95% CI −0.2 to 5.5; P=0.07), which did not reach significance. The odds of a severe hangover (symptom index ≥18) were lower with the extract (odds ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.16–0.88; P=0.02 — a relative measure). C-reactive protein levels were 40% higher in the placebo period than in the extract period, and participants with higher morning C-reactive protein had a symptom index 4.1 points higher (95% CI 1.2 to 7.1; P=0.007) than those with lower levels, consistent with hangover severity tracking inflammation.
cards.watchOut: This is a PREVENTION trial — the extract was taken 5 hours before drinking — so it says nothing about treating a hangover already in progress, the question most readers bring. The headline symptom index missed significance (P=0.07); the significant findings are three individual symptoms and a dichotomised severe-hangover endpoint in 55 completers, never replicated since 2004. Product discipline: the trial used a standardised research extract at 1,600 IU; commercial prickly-pear supplements are unregulated and may differ in composition, dose and effect — the publication does not name a brand, and none should be inferred.
cards.source: Wiese J, McPherson S, Odden MC, Shlipak MG. Effect of Opuntia ficus indica on symptoms of the alcohol hangover. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15226168. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Synthesis: two systematic reviews, 17 years apart, one conclusion — no hangover treatment has replicated evidence; the only supported intervention is drinking less in the first place
cards.summary: Synthesis: two systematic reviews, 17 years apart, one conclusion — no hangover treatment has replicated evidence; the only supported intervention is drinking less in the first place
cards.people: Pittler 2005 (8 double-blind randomised trials of 8 interventions), Roberts 2022 (21 placebo-controlled trials, 386 participants, all outcomes very low quality by GRADE), and the largest single prevention trial on the shelf, Wiese 2004 (64 randomised, 55 completing a crossover).
cards.result: No intervention — conventional drug, supplement or food-based remedy — has been shown effective for preventing or treating alcohol hangover in more than a single small trial (Pittler 2005; Roberts 2022). The scattered positives (tolfenamic acid in both reviews; clove extract, pyritinol, Hovenia dulcis, L-cysteine, red ginseng, Korean pear juice in Roberts 2022; prickly-pear extract for 3 of 9 symptoms in Wiese 2004) are unreplicated, very-low-quality signals. The reviews' own bottom line stands: abstinence or moderation is the only effective prevention. PROPOSED (no treatment shown to work).
cards.watchOut: Tier C. What this shelf does not cover: (1) Symptomatic self-care — fluids, food, sleep, and an analgesic for headache are reasonable comforts, but no card here shows they shorten a hangover, and acetaminophen after heavy drinking and NSAIDs on an alcohol-irritated stomach each carry their own cautions. (2) 'Hair of the dog' has no trial support and delays recovery. (3) A 'hangover' with confusion, vomiting that will not stop, slow breathing, seizures or inability to wake is alcohol poisoning, not a hangover — an emergency, not a remedies question. (4) Absence of evidence is partly a research-funding artefact: hangover is self-limiting and commercially unglamorous, so adequately powered replication trials may simply never be run.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pittler MH et al. BMJ. 2005 (PMID: 16373736); Roberts E et al. Addiction. 2022 (PMID: 34972259); Wiese J et al. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2004 (PMID: 15226168).

shelves.title: Treatment for optic nerve atrophy: none has been shown to work for optic atrophy in general — idebenone's only randomised trial is in Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (Shelf #4253), and its dominant-optic-atrophy data are uncontrolled (an 87-patient cohort and a 16-patient open-label phase 2 trial)
shelves.question: 'Is there a treatment for optic nerve atrophy?' — For optic atrophy in general, and for its commonest inherited forms (dominant optic atrophy and Leber hereditary optic neuropathy), has any treatment been shown to preserve or restore vision?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers · Disease Progression · Humans · Optic Atrophy, Autosomal Dominant/diagnosis · Optic Atrophy, Autosomal Dominant/physiopathology · Visual Acuity/physiology
shelves.balance: No treatment has been shown to work for optic atrophy in general, and the fetched record supports that scoping exactly. For dominant optic atrophy (DOA), the commonest inherited form, the 2025 systematic review of its natural history states plainly that there is currently no disease-modifying treatment for DOA, and it quantifies why weak studies mislead here: untreated visual acuity declines at only 0.022 LogMAR per year, a rate not significantly different from zero (95% CI −0.008 to 0.052; p=0.155) (Ovens 2025, PMID: 40329928). The only treatment signal in DOA comes from idebenone used off-label: a non-randomised historical cohort of 87 OPA1 patients found stabilisation or recovery of acuity in 92% of treated versus 75.7% of untreated patients (adjusted OR 4.37; 95% CI 1.01–18.9 — a relative measure whose confidence interval nearly touches 1) (Romagnoli 2020, PMID: 32243103), and a 16-patient open-label phase 2 trial reported improved best recovery of visual acuity over 12 months but, being uncontrolled, cannot separate drug effect from placebo effect or natural history (Valentin 2023, PMID: 38130806). The one randomised placebo-controlled idebenone trial in any optic atrophy is in a different disease — Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (RHODOS) — and it is homed on Shelf #4253 (Klopstock 2011, PMID: 21788663); it is cross-pointed here, not re-carded, under the one-home rule. PROPOSED (the treatment made no difference): for optic atrophy as a whole, no therapy has beaten control or natural history in a fetched record; idebenone in DOA remains an uncontrolled, off-label hypothesis, and idebenone's trial and licensing history belongs to LHON.

cards.headline: Ovens 2025: dominant optic atrophy progresses at only 0.022 LogMAR per year (not significant) — and the review states there is currently no disease-modifying treatment for it
cards.summary: Ovens 2025: dominant optic atrophy progresses at only 0.022 LogMAR per year (not significant) — and the review states there is currently no disease-modifying treatment for it
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal biomarkers in dominant optic atrophy (Ovens 2025)
cards.people: Patients with genetically proven dominant optic atrophy (DOA) in the longitudinal literature: 7 studies met the systematic review's criteria and 4 entered the meta-analysis of visual change over time.
cards.result: Visual acuity declined at a pooled rate of 0.022 LogMAR per year (95% CI −0.008 to 0.052), which was not statistically significant (Z=1.4; p=0.155); visual acuity was the only biomarker with longitudinal data to pool. The review frames DOA as causing slowly progressive bilateral visual decline beginning in childhood, and its introduction states that there is currently no disease-modifying treatment for DOA — the position this shelf's question turns on.
cards.watchOut: This is a natural-history review, not a treatment trial; it is carded because it is the fetched record that both states the field's position (no disease-modifying treatment) and measures the untreated course. That course is so slow and variable that almost any small uncontrolled treatment series will appear to 'stabilise' most patients — the trap the next two cards sit in.
cards.source: Ovens CA, Grigg JR, Fraser CL. Longitudinal Visual Biomarkers in Dominant Optic Atrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology. 2025. PMID: 40329928. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42024548499 (protocol registered, per the record). cards.headline: Romagnoli 2020: idebenone-treated DOA patients stabilised or recovered acuity more often than untreated (92% versus 75.7%) — but the comparison was never randomised
cards.summary: Romagnoli 2020: idebenone-treated DOA patients stabilised or recovered acuity more often than untreated (92% versus 75.7%) — but the comparison was never randomised
cards.type: Historical cohort study of off-label idebenone in OPA1-dominant optic atrophy (Romagnoli 2020)
cards.people: 87 patients with genetically confirmed OPA1-dominant optic atrophy from 69 pedigrees at a single centre: 50 had taken off-label idebenone for at least 7 months (doses 135–675 mg/day) and 37 had never taken it; mean observation was 4.2 years in the treated group and 3.4 years in the untreated group.
cards.result: Stabilisation or recovery of visual acuity in the best-seeing eye occurred in 92% (46 of 50) of idebenone-treated patients versus 75.7% (28 of 37) of untreated patients (P=0.03). The adjusted odds ratio for stabilisation/recovery with idebenone was 4.37 (95% CI 1.01–18.9; P=0.049) — a relative measure from a non-randomised comparison, with a confidence interval that nearly reaches 1 — while the median change in visual acuity was 0.00 logMAR in both groups. The authors concluded that idebenone increased the chance of stabilisation or recovery of visual acuity in OPA1-dominant optic atrophy.
cards.watchOut: Patients were not randomised: who received a decade of off-label idebenone, at doses varying five-fold, was decided in clinic, and untreated patients were followed for less time. Against a natural history in which acuity may not measurably decline at all over years (Ovens 2025), a 92% versus 76% 'stabilisation' gap can arise from selection and measurement alone. This is a hypothesis, not proof of benefit.
cards.source: Romagnoli M, La Morgia C, Carbonelli M, Di Vito L, Amore G, Zenesini C, Cascavilla ML, Barboni P, Carelli V. Idebenone increases chance of stabilization/recovery of visual acuity in OPA1-dominant optic atrophy. Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology. 2020. PMID: 32243103. Registry ID: none in the record (observational cohort). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Valentin 2023: in 16 DOA patients on idebenone 900 mg/day for 12 months, best recovery of visual acuity improved — with no control group to credit the drug (n=16 printed on the face)
cards.summary: Valentin 2023: in 16 DOA patients on idebenone 900 mg/day for 12 months, best recovery of visual acuity improved — with no control group to credit the drug (n=16 printed on the face)
cards.type: Prospective open-label phase 2 trial of idebenone in OPA1-dominant optic atrophy, n=16 (Valentin 2023)
cards.people: 16 patients with genetically confirmed OPA1-dominant optic atrophy (n=16) treated prospectively with idebenone 900 mg/day for 12 months in an open-label phase 2 trial; there was no placebo or untreated comparison group.
cards.result: Best recovery of visual acuity improved over the 12 months of treatment, as reported by the investigators and summarised in subsequent reviews of the trial. Because the trial was open-label and uncontrolled, the improvement cannot be attributed to idebenone rather than to placebo effect, measurement variability, or the natural history of the disease — which the natural-history review on this shelf (Ovens 2025) shows is slow enough to look flat or improving over a single year.
cards.watchOut: n=16, open-label, no control arm — the weakest design that still counts as a trial, carded with its size on the face under the n-reporting rule. The card reports only the qualitative finding that fetched records support; the trial's precise effect sizes were not carded because they could not be verified from a fetched primary record this session. A positive uncontrolled result in a slowly progressive disease is the expected appearance of no effect.
cards.source: Valentin K, Georgi T, Riedl R, Aminfar H, Singer C, Klopstock T, Wedrich A, Schneider M. Idebenone Treatment in Patients with OPA1-Dominant Optic Atrophy: A Prospective Phase 2 Trial. Neuro-Ophthalmology. 2023. PMID: 38130806. Registry ID: none in the record as fetched. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: no proven treatment for optic atrophy — idebenone's randomised evidence and licence belong to Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (Shelf #4253), and its dominant-optic-atrophy data are uncontrolled
cards.summary: Synthesis: no proven treatment for optic atrophy — idebenone's randomised evidence and licence belong to Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (Shelf #4253), and its dominant-optic-atrophy data are uncontrolled
cards.people: The fetched record for this question: a natural-history systematic review of dominant optic atrophy (Ovens 2025), a non-randomised 87-patient idebenone cohort (Romagnoli 2020), and a 16-patient open-label idebenone trial (Valentin 2023). The randomised idebenone evidence in Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (RHODOS, Klopstock 2011) is homed on Shelf #4253 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: For optic atrophy in general, no fetched record shows any treatment preserving or restoring vision against a control: the DOA literature's own systematic review states there is no disease-modifying treatment, and untreated acuity declines at a non-significant 0.022 LogMAR/year. Idebenone in DOA rests on a non-randomised cohort (stabilisation/recovery 92% versus 75.7%; adjusted OR 4.37, 95% CI 1.01–18.9, relative) and an uncontrolled 16-patient trial — designs that cannot exclude natural history. The exception that proves the scoping: idebenone does have a randomised placebo-controlled trial, RHODOS, but in Leber hereditary optic neuropathy, a different disease — see Shelf #4253 (PMID: 21788663) — and idebenone is licensed for LHON in Europe, not for dominant optic atrophy or optic atrophy generally. PROPOSED (the treatment made no difference): as the evidence stands, optic atrophy has no treatment shown to work; management is diagnosis of the cause, low-vision support, and genetic counselling for the inherited forms.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. 'No treatment shown to work' is a statement about the fetched evidence, not a claim that nothing can ever work: gene-therapy and other trials in the inherited optic atrophies are in progress, and optic atrophy from a treatable cause (compression, inflammation, nutritional deficiency, raised intracranial pressure) is treated by treating that cause — a different question from restoring an already-atrophied nerve, for which no fetched record shows benefit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ovens CA et al. Clinical and Experimental Ophthalmology. 2025 (PMID: 40329928); Romagnoli M et al. Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology. 2020 (PMID: 32243103); Valentin K et al. Neuro-Ophthalmology. 2023 (PMID: 38130806). Cross-reference, not carded: Klopstock T et al. Brain. 2011 (PMID: 21788663), homed on Shelf #4253.

shelves.title: Knock knees (genu valgum) at 23: no trials — realignment osteotomy is the adult treatment in the published series, correcting the mechanical axis accurately (96.1% in a 31-procedure series) with osteotomy survival of roughly 74–90% at 10 years in valgus knees with lateral arthritis
shelves.question: 'I am 23 with knock knees — what treatment is there?' — In a skeletally mature young adult with genu valgum, what do the published series show for realignment osteotomy (femoral or tibial): correction achieved, durability, and complications? (Guided growth is a children's treatment and does not apply at 23.)
shelves.mesh: Femur/surgery · Humans · Knee Joint/surgery · Osteoarthritis, Knee/surgery · Osteotomy/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: There are no trials for a 23-year-old with knock knees — the entire fetched record is retrospective series and systematic reviews of series, and most of it concerns older patients whose valgus deformity comes with lateral compartment arthritis. What the record does show: realignment osteotomy corrects the deformity accurately — in a consecutive series of 31 procedures (23 patients, mean age 41.2 years), the mechanical axis deviation moved from 32.5 mm lateral to 2.44 mm medial with 96.1% correction accuracy, one stable hinge fracture and one chronic regional pain syndrome, and no non-union or revision (Sheridan 2024, PMID: 39359363). For durability, the distal femoral osteotomy reviews report mean survival of 80% at 10 years in one synthesis (Chahla 2016, PMID: 27331074) and survival of 74–90% at 10 years in a 2025 synthesis of 18 studies, with conversion to knee replacement reaching 48.4% in the longest series (Yazdi 2025, PMID: 41082590) — survival figures that mean 'not yet converted to arthroplasty' in arthritic knees, a different endpoint from what a 23-year-old without arthritis needs. Guided growth (hemiepiphysiodesis), the low-morbidity option in children, requires open growth plates and is not available at 23. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: osteotomy is a real, mechanically effective treatment for adult genu valgum on consistent case-series evidence — but for a young adult without arthritis there is no comparative evidence at all, and the durability numbers are borrowed from an older, arthritic population.

cards.headline: Sheridan 2024: 31 consecutive realignment procedures corrected genu valgum accurately — mechanical axis deviation from 32.5 mm lateral to 2.44 mm medial, 96.1% correction accuracy (23 patients, n printed on the face)
cards.summary: Sheridan 2024: 31 consecutive realignment procedures corrected genu valgum accurately — mechanical axis deviation from 32.5 mm lateral to 2.44 mm medial, 96.1% correction accuracy (23 patients, n printed on the face)
cards.type: Retrospective consecutive case series of osteotomy for genu valgum, 31 procedures in 23 patients (Sheridan 2024)
cards.people: 23 patients undergoing 31 consecutive procedures (February 2018–October 2022) for genu valgum: 18 medial closing-wedge high tibial osteotomies alone and 13 combined with lateral opening-wedge distal femoral osteotomy; mean age 41.2 years (SD 14.99), approximately 70% female.
cards.result: The medial proximal tibial angle improved from 92.9° to 86.0° (p<0.0001) and mechanical axis deviation from 32.5 mm lateral to 2.44 mm medial (p<0.0001), a mean correction of 38.16 mm with 96.1% accuracy against the planned target. Unassisted weight-bearing was achieved at a mean of 75 days. Complications were one stable hinge fracture and one case of chronic regional pain syndrome; there was no non-union and no revision surgery over a mean follow-up of 309 days.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre retrospective series with a mean age of 41 — nearly two decades older than the person asking — and follow-up under a year (mean 309 days): it proves the deformity can be corrected precisely and safely in expert hands, not that correction at 23 prevents arthritis or symptoms decades later. No comparison group, no untreated controls, and patient-reported outcomes were not the focus.
cards.source: Sheridan GA, Hatzantonakis T, Kooner SS, Somerville L, Willing R, Vasarhelyi EM, Howard JL, Lanting BA. Medial Closing Wedge High Tibial Osteotomy Accurately Corrects Genu Valgum without Iatrogenic Deformity or Complications: A Consecutive Series of Thirty-one Procedures. cards.headline: Chahla 2016: across 14 retrospective studies of distal femoral osteotomy for genu valgum with lateral arthritis, all reported good-to-excellent outcomes and mean survival was 80% at 10 years
cards.summary: Chahla 2016: across 14 retrospective studies of distal femoral osteotomy for genu valgum with lateral arthritis, all reported good-to-excellent outcomes and mean survival was 80% at 10 years
cards.type: Systematic review of distal femoral osteotomy outcomes for genu valgum with lateral compartment osteoarthritis (Chahla 2016)
cards.people: Patients with genu valgum and isolated lateral compartment osteoarthritis treated by distal femoral osteotomy in 14 retrospective studies (9 closing-wedge, 5 opening-wedge), each with a minimum of 2 years' follow-up.
cards.result: All 14 studies reported good-to-excellent patient-reported outcomes after osteotomy. Mean survival of the osteotomy was 80% at 10 years, but the range across studies was wide — from 100% at 6.5 years in one study to 21.5% at 20 years in another. Symptomatic hardware requiring removal was the most prevalent complication. The reviewers emphasised that the literature is highly heterogeneous and consists of Level 4 evidence (case series).
cards.watchOut: 'Survival' here means the knee had not yet been converted to a total knee replacement — an endpoint defined for arthritic knees in mostly middle-aged patients. It does not translate into a prognosis for a 23-year-old with (presumably) healthy cartilage, whose relevant questions — pain, function, arthritis prevention over 40+ years — no included study was designed to answer.
cards.source: Chahla J, Mitchell JJ, Liechti DJ, Moatshe G, Menge TJ, Dean CS, LaPrade RF. Opening- and Closing-Wedge Distal Femoral Osteotomy: A Systematic Review of Outcomes for Isolated Lateral Compartment Osteoarthritis. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2016. PMID: 27331074. cards.headline: Yazdi 2025: 18 studies of distal femoral varus osteotomy for valgus knees with lateral arthritis — survival 74–90% at 10 years, conversion to knee replacement up to 48.4%
cards.summary: Yazdi 2025: 18 studies of distal femoral varus osteotomy for valgus knees with lateral arthritis — survival 74–90% at 10 years, conversion to knee replacement up to 48.4%
cards.type: Systematic review of distal femoral varus osteotomy for valgus knee with lateral compartment osteoarthritis (Yazdi 2025)
cards.people: Patients with valgus knee deformity and lateral compartment osteoarthritis treated by distal femoral varus osteotomy in 18 studies (6 closing-wedge, 12 opening-wedge), each with a minimum of 2 years' follow-up.
cards.result: Reported osteotomy survival was 74–88% at 5 years, 74–90% at 10 years, and 45–79% at 15 years. The highest rate of conversion to total knee arthroplasty among the included studies was 48.4%. Lateral cortex injury (hinge fracture) was the most common complication. Both opening-wedge and closing-wedge techniques showed satisfactory long-term outcomes in these arthritic valgus knees.
cards.watchOut: Same population caveat as the 2016 review, a decade on: every included study treats valgus WITH lateral compartment osteoarthritis. The 48.4% conversion figure comes from the longest-followed arthritic series — it describes arthritic knees eventually needing replacement despite osteotomy, not failure of deformity correction in a young non-arthritic knee. No study in the review enrolled patients like the 23-year-old asking this question.
cards.source: Yazdi H, Torkaman A, Sahrai R, Raygani MJ, Makhmalbaf AR, Fathi M. Distal Femoral Varus Osteotomy in Valgus Knee With Lateral Compartment Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review. JAAOS Global Research & Reviews. 2025. PMID: 41082590. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Synthesis: for a skeletally mature 23-year-old, osteotomy is the only corrective treatment in the record — it corrects accurately (96.1%) but its evidence base is older, arthritic knees, with no trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: for a skeletally mature 23-year-old, osteotomy is the only corrective treatment in the record — it corrects accurately (96.1%) but its evidence base is older, arthritic knees, with no trials
cards.people: The fetched record: one consecutive case series of 31 osteotomy procedures in 23 patients (mean age 41.2 years; Sheridan 2024) and two systematic reviews of distal femoral osteotomy for valgus knees with lateral compartment osteoarthritis (Chahla 2016 — 14 retrospective studies; Yazdi 2025 — 18 studies). No randomised or comparative study of any treatment for adult genu valgum was found in the fetched record.
cards.result: Correction is achievable and precise: mechanical axis deviation normalised from 32.5 mm lateral to 2.44 mm medial with 96.1% accuracy, full unassisted weight-bearing at a mean of 75 days, and few complications in the consecutive series. Durability in arthritic valgus knees: survival (freedom from knee replacement) of roughly 74–90% at 10 years across reviews, falling to 45–79% at 15 years, with symptomatic hardware and lateral cortex injury the commonest problems. What the record does not contain: any study of osteotomy in young adults without arthritis, any comparison against physiotherapy, orthotics or watchful waiting, and any evidence that correcting alignment at 23 prevents later arthritis. Guided growth surgery is not an option at 23 — it requires open growth plates. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: realignment osteotomy probably achieves its mechanical goal safely in adults with genu valgum; whether a 23-year-old without arthritis benefits over a lifetime is unstudied, so the decision rests on symptoms, deformity severity and progression, not on trial evidence.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. The stamp is POSSIBLE and cannot be higher: the evidence is entirely retrospective case series (Level 4), mostly in a different population (valgus with established lateral arthritis) from the person asking. Mild, asymptomatic genu valgum at 23 is often simply observed — the fetched record contains no study of non-operative management in adults, so this shelf makes no claim for or against it; severity grading, leg-length and rotational assessment, and the state of the lateral cartilage all change the surgical decision and are clinical assessments, not literature questions.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sheridan GA et al. Strategies in Trauma and Limb Reconstruction. 2024 (PMID: 39359363); Chahla J et al. Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2016 (PMID: 27331074); Yazdi H et al. JAAOS Global Research & Reviews. 2025 (PMID: 41082590).
