shelves.title: Taken off bupropion (Wellbutrin) suddenly, without a taper: across antidepressants about 1 in 6–7 people get symptoms attributable to stopping (about 15%), severe symptoms in about 2.8% — and bupropion sits in the lower-risk group, with no bupropion-specific incidence study
shelves.question: 'I was taken off bupropion (Wellbutrin) completely without tapering — what happens?' — After abrupt antidepressant discontinuation, how common and how severe are discontinuation symptoms, and where does bupropion sit in the risk ranking? (Depression relapse after stopping is a different question — Shelf #705.)
shelves.mesh: Antidepressive Agents/adverse effects · Antidepressive Agents/therapeutic use · Humans · Incidence · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome/epidemiology
shelves.balance: Across antidepressants as a class, stopping brings symptoms in roughly a third of people — but about half of that is the nocebo/placebo rate: the 2024 Lancet Psychiatry meta-analysis of 21,002 patients found at least one discontinuation symptom in 31% after stopping an antidepressant versus 17% after stopping placebo, severe symptoms in 2.8% versus 0.6%, and estimated the incidence truly attributable to the drug at about 15% — roughly 1 in every 6–7 people who stop (Henssler 2024, PMID: 38851198). The 2025 JAMA Psychiatry meta-analysis of randomised trials found the average excess was about one extra symptom (from the Discontinuation-Emergent Signs and Symptoms scale) in the first week — below the threshold for a clinically significant discontinuation syndrome — with dizziness the most prevalent symptom, and, importantly, discontinuation was not associated with depressive symptoms, so later depression signals relapse rather than withdrawal (Kalfas 2025, PMID: 40632531). For bupropion specifically: Henssler's high-frequency list names desvenlafaxine, venlafaxine, imipramine and escitalopram — bupropion is not on it — and the pharmacist practice review's risk table places bupropion XL in the lower-risk category for discontinuation syndrome (Geen 2023, PMID: 38222887). No bupropion-specific incidence study was found in the fetched record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: a person taken off bupropion abruptly will most likely have few or no discontinuation symptoms; if symptoms come, the class pattern is onset within 2–4 days, flu-like symptoms, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbances and hyperarousal, usually settling over weeks.

cards.headline: Henssler 2024: 31% report a discontinuation symptom after stopping an antidepressant versus 17% after placebo — the drug-attributable incidence is about 15% (1 in 6–7), severe symptoms 2.8%
cards.summary: Henssler 2024: 31% report a discontinuation symptom after stopping an antidepressant versus 17% after placebo — the drug-attributable incidence is about 15% (1 in 6–7), severe symptoms 2.8%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of antidepressant discontinuation symptoms, 79 studies (Henssler 2024)
cards.people: 21,002 patients across 79 studies (44 randomised controlled trials and 35 observational studies) in a systematic review and meta-analysis of antidepressant discontinuation: 16,532 patients who discontinued an antidepressant and 4,470 who discontinued placebo.
cards.result: At least one discontinuation symptom occurred in 0.31 (95% CI 0.27–0.35) of patients after discontinuing an antidepressant and 0.17 (0.14–0.21) after discontinuing placebo; in the randomised trials alone the summary incidence difference was 0.08 (0.04–0.12). Severe discontinuation symptoms occurred in 0.028 (0.014–0.057) after antidepressants versus 0.006 (0.002–0.013) after placebo. The authors' overall interpretation: the incidence of symptoms specifically attributable to stopping the drug is around 15% — about 1 in every 6–7 patients. Discontinuation symptoms were more frequent with desvenlafaxine, venlafaxine, imipramine and escitalopram; bupropion was not among the high-frequency drugs.
cards.watchOut: Class-level data: most included studies concern SSRIs and SNRIs, the drugs with the worst discontinuation profiles, so 15% is an average that overstates the risk for low-risk drugs such as bupropion and understates it for venlafaxine or paroxetine. The placebo comparison is the essential context — 17% of people stopping placebo also report 'discontinuation symptoms', which is why raw incidence figures quoted without a placebo arm mislead.
cards.source: Henssler J, Schmidt Y, Schmidt U, Schwarzer G, Bschor T, Baethge C. Incidence of antidepressant discontinuation symptoms: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The Lancet Psychiatry. 2024. PMID: 38851198. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Kalfas 2025: in randomised trials the average excess was about one extra symptom at 1 week — below the clinically significant syndrome threshold — and stopping was not associated with depressive symptoms
cards.summary: Kalfas 2025: in randomised trials the average excess was about one extra symptom at 1 week — below the clinically significant syndrome threshold — and stopping was not associated with depressive symptoms
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised discontinuation trials (Kalfas 2025)
cards.people: 17,828 participants (66.9% female, mean age 44 years) in 50 randomised controlled trials of antidepressant discontinuation; the Discontinuation-Emergent Signs and Symptoms (DESS) meta-analysis pooled 11 studies with 3,915 participants.
cards.result: Discontinuation was associated with a standardised mean difference of 0.31 (95% CI 0.23–0.39) on the DESS at 1 week — approximately one additional DESS symptom compared with placebo discontinuation or continued treatment — which is below the threshold for a clinically significant discontinuation syndrome. Symptoms with increased odds versus placebo discontinuation (relative measures) were dizziness (OR 5.52; 3.81–8.01), nausea (OR 3.16; 2.01–4.96), vertigo (OR 6.40; 1.20–34.19) and nervousness (OR 3.15; 1.29–7.64); dizziness was the most prevalent, with a risk difference of 6.24%. Discontinuation was not associated with depression symptoms — meaning depressive symptoms appearing after stopping indicate relapse of the illness, not withdrawal.
cards.watchOut: An average of one extra symptom conceals a distribution: most people get none, a minority get several, and the trials pooled many different antidepressants and mostly short treatment durations. The large odds ratios are relative measures on uncommon outcomes — the absolute risk difference for the commonest symptom, dizziness, was 6.24 percentage points. The 'not depression' finding matters for the person asking: feeling depressed again weeks later is the illness returning (Shelf #705's question), not a withdrawal effect.
cards.source: Kalfas M et al. Incidence and Nature of Antidepressant Discontinuation Symptoms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA Psychiatry. 2025. PMID: 40632531. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). the discontinuation-emergent signs and symptoms (dess) meta-analysis pooled 11 studies with 3,915 participants. discontinuation was associated with a standardised mean difference of 0.31 (95% ci 0.23–0.39) on the dess at 1 week — approximately one additional dess symptom compared with placebo discontinuation or continued treatment — which is below the threshold for a clinically significant discontinuation syndrome. symptoms with increased odds versus placebo discontinuation (relative measures) were dizziness (or 5.52; 3.81–8.01), nausea (or 3.16; 2.01–4.96), vertigo (or 6.40; 1.20–34.19) and nervousness (or 3.15; 1.29–7.64); dizziness was the most prevalent, with a risk difference of 6.24%. discontinuation was not associated with depression symptoms — meaning depressive symptoms appearing after stopping indicate relapse of the illness, not withdrawal. an average of one extra symptom conceals a distribution: most people get none, a minority get several, and the trials pooled many different antidepressants and mostly short treatment durations. the large odds ratios are relative measures on uncommon outcomes — the absolute risk difference for the commonest symptom, dizziness, was 6.24 percentage points. the 'not depression' finding matters for the person asking: feeling depressed again weeks later is the illness returning (shelf #705's question), not a withdrawal effect. kalfas m et al. incidence and nature of antidepressant discontinuation symptoms: a systematic review and meta-analysis. jama psychiatry. 2025. pmid: 40632531. registry id: none in the record (meta-analysis). mesh: antidepressive agents/adverse effects · antidepressive agents/therapeutic use · humans · incidence · randomized controlled trials as topic · substance withdrawal syndrome/epidemiology

cards.headline: Geen 2023: in the pharmacist review's risk table, bupropion XL sits in the LOWER-risk category for discontinuation syndrome — symptoms classically begin 2–4 days after stopping
cards.summary: Geen 2023: in the pharmacist review's risk table, bupropion XL sits in the LOWER-risk category for discontinuation syndrome — symptoms classically begin 2–4 days after stopping
cards.type: Narrative practice review with an antidepressant discontinuation risk stratification (Geen 2023)
cards.people: A narrative practice review for pharmacists on antidepressant discontinuation, synthesising the published risk rankings: its Table 2 stratifies antidepressants into higher- and lower-risk categories for discontinuation syndrome, drawing on the review's cited references.
cards.result: Bupropion XL is placed in the lower-risk category for antidepressant discontinuation syndrome — in contrast to higher-risk agents such as paroxetine and fluvoxamine among the SSRIs and venlafaxine, desvenlafaxine and duloxetine among the SNRIs. For the class generally, the review summarises that withdrawal symptoms typically begin within 2–4 days of stopping or reducing the dose, that duration varies from weeks to months, and that the core symptom set is captured by the FINISH mnemonic: flu-like symptoms, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbances ('brain zaps'), and hyperarousal.
cards.watchOut: A practice review, not primary data — carded because it is the fetched record that ranks bupropion specifically, and its ranking agrees with Henssler 2024's high-frequency list omitting bupropion. 'Lower risk' is not 'no risk': case reports of withdrawal-like symptoms after abrupt bupropion cessation exist in the wider literature, but no fetched record puts a bupropion-specific incidence number on them, so this shelf quotes none.
cards.source: Geen C. Antidepressant discontinuation and the role of the pharmacist. Canadian Pharmacists Journal. 2023. PMID: 38222887. Registry ID: none in the record (narrative review). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: stopping bupropion suddenly — most people will have few or no withdrawal symptoms; the class-attributable risk is ~15%, severe ~3%, and bupropion ranks low-risk
cards.summary: Synthesis: stopping bupropion suddenly — most people will have few or no withdrawal symptoms; the class-attributable risk is ~15%, severe ~3%, and bupropion ranks low-risk
cards.people: Two class-level meta-analyses (Henssler 2024 — 79 studies, 21,002 patients; Kalfas 2025 — 50 RCTs, 17,828 participants) and one practice review that stratifies risk by drug (Geen 2023). No bupropion-specific discontinuation incidence study was found in the fetched record.
cards.result: For antidepressants overall: at least one discontinuation symptom in 31% after stopping the drug versus 17% after placebo, an attributable incidence of about 15% (1 in 6–7 people), severe symptoms in 2.8% versus 0.6% (Henssler 2024); the average excess burden was about one extra symptom in the first week, below the clinically significant syndrome threshold, with dizziness the commonest symptom (absolute risk difference 6.24%) (Kalfas 2025). Bupropion sits below that class average on both fetched rankings: absent from Henssler's high-frequency list and in Geen's lower-risk category. Expected course if symptoms occur, from the class pattern: onset within 2–4 days of the last dose; flu-like symptoms, insomnia, nausea, imbalance, sensory disturbances or hyperarousal; usually resolving over weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: abrupt bupropion cessation is usually tolerated with few or no discontinuation symptoms — the reassurance is probable, not proven, because it is inferred from class data plus risk rankings rather than a bupropion-specific trial.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: this shelf is about discontinuation (withdrawal-type) symptoms only. Depression or anxiety returning after stopping is relapse — a different question, homed on Shelf #705 and deliberately not re-carded here. Seizure risk is a bupropion dosing question, not a discontinuation question, and is not addressed by these records. Anyone whose bupropion was stopped because of a serious adverse event, or who develops severe or prolonged symptoms, needs their prescriber, not a shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Henssler J et al. The Lancet Psychiatry. 2024 (PMID: 38851198); Kalfas M et al. JAMA Psychiatry. 2025 (PMID: 40632531); Geen C. Canadian Pharmacists Journal. 2023 (PMID: 38222887).

shelves.title: Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease): plasma exchange added to steroids and cyclophosphamide — the one randomised trial had just 17 patients (dialysis in 2 of 8 versus 6 of 9), and the big cohorts say how far the kidneys have fallen decides the outcome
shelves.question: What are the treatments for Goodpasture syndrome (anti-GBM disease) — in people with anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody disease, does plasma exchange added to corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide improve survival and kidney recovery compared with immunosuppression alone, and what do the cohort renal-survival numbers show?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Glomerular Basement Membrane Disease/epidemiology · Anti-Glomerular Basement Membrane Disease/immunology · Anti-Glomerular Basement Membrane Disease/therapy · Antibodies, Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic/blood · Antibodies, Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic/immunology · Child · China/epidemiology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Plasmapheresis/methods · Retrospective Studies · Survival Rate/trends · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the standard treatment (plasma exchange plus prednisolone and cyclophosphamide) rests on one very small randomised trial and consistent cohort data, not on any large trial. In the only randomised trial (Johnson 1985, PMID: 3892220; n = 17 printed on the face), adding plasma exchange to prednisone and cyclophosphamide cleared anti-GBM antibodies about twice as fast, left end-of-treatment serum creatinine at 4.1 mg/dL versus 9.2 mg/dL, and left 2 of 8 exchange patients dialysis-dependent versus 6 of 9 on drugs alone. The 25-year Hammersmith cohort (Levy 2001, PMID: 11388816; 71 treated patients, all given plasma exchange, prednisolone and cyclophosphamide) shows the dominant fact of this disease: outcome is set by kidney function at presentation — creatinine below 500 micromol/L (5.7 mg/dL): 100% patient survival and 95% renal survival at 1 year; dialysis-dependent at presentation: 65% patient survival but only 8% renal survival at 1 year. The largest regimen comparison (Cui 2011, PMID: 21862934; 221 patients) found combination therapy associated with lower mortality (hazard ratio 0.31, a relative measure) and lower renal-failure risk (HR 0.60) than the other regimens, while steroids plus cyclophosphamide without exchange did not improve renal outcome (P = 0.73). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: benefit is plausible and consistent, the randomised base is 17 patients, and no regimen rescues kidneys that present dialysis-dependent with 100% crescents.

cards.headline: Johnson 1985 (the only randomised trial, n = 17): plasma exchange cleared antibodies twice as fast — end-of-treatment creatinine 4.1 versus 9.2 mg/dL, dialysis in 2 of 8 versus 6 of 9
cards.summary: Johnson 1985 (the only randomised trial, n = 17): plasma exchange cleared antibodies twice as fast — end-of-treatment creatinine 4.1 versus 9.2 mg/dL, dialysis in 2 of 8 versus 6 of 9
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of plasma exchange added to immunosuppression (Johnson 1985)
cards.people: 17 patients with anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody disease (n = 17, printed here because it is below this library's usual size floor), all treated with prednisone and cyclophosphamide, with half randomised to additional plasmapheresis (4-litre exchanges every 3 days; a mean of nine treatments).
cards.result: In patients receiving plasmapheresis, anti-GBM antibodies disappeared about twice as fast as in the control group (all within 50 days; P < 0.05). At the end of therapy, serum creatinine in those receiving plasmapheresis was 4.1 ± 0.5 mg/dL compared with 9.2 ± 0.7 mg/dL in the controls (P < 0.05); only two patients receiving plasmapheresis needed chronic dialysis versus six in the control group (2 of 8 versus 6 of 9 randomised). Prognosis within the study also tracked pathology: patients with less than 30% crescents and a plasma creatinine below 3 mg/dL did well, while those with severe crescentic involvement and creatinine above 4 mg/dL (354 micromol/L) did poorly.
cards.watchOut: Seventeen patients is the entire randomised evidence base for a treatment now considered standard — the dialysis contrast (2 of 8 versus 6 of 9) is compatible with a wide range of true effects, and the trial's exchange schedule (every 3 days) was less intensive than the daily exchange later adopted. The creatinine and dialysis figures on this card are as summarised from the trial in the KDIGO glomerular-diseases guideline chapter fetched alongside the record this session; the trial's own PubMed page did not load (see build flag). Nothing here is a large-trial estimate.
cards.source: Johnson JP, Moore J Jr, Austin HA 3rd, Balow JE, Antonovych TT, Wilson CB. Therapy of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody disease: analysis of prognostic significance of clinical, pathologic and treatment factors. Medicine (Baltimore). 1985. PMID: 3892220. cards.headline: Levy 2001 (25-year Hammersmith cohort, 71 treated): renal survival 95% at 1 year when creatinine was under 5.7 mg/dL — and 8% when dialysis was needed at presentation
cards.summary: Levy 2001 (25-year Hammersmith cohort, 71 treated): renal survival 95% at 1 year when creatinine was under 5.7 mg/dL — and 8% when dialysis was needed at presentation
cards.type: Retrospective cohort of plasma exchange plus immunosuppression (Levy 2001)
cards.people: 71 treated patients with confirmed anti-GBM antibody disease seen over 25 years; all received plasma exchange, prednisolone, and cyclophosphamide. Groups by presentation: creatinine less than 500 micromol/L (5.7 mg/dL) (n = 19); creatinine 500 micromol/L or more (5.7 mg/dL or more) without immediate dialysis (n = 13); dialysis-dependent renal failure at presentation (n = 39).
cards.result: Patients presenting with creatinine less than 500 micromol/L (5.7 mg/dL) had 100% patient survival and 95% renal survival at 1 year, and 84% patient survival and 74% renal survival at last follow-up. Patients presenting with creatinine of 500 micromol/L or more (5.7 mg/dL or more) but not requiring immediate dialysis had patient and renal survival of 83% and 82% at 1 year and 62% and 69% at last follow-up. Patients presenting dialysis-dependent had patient and renal survival of 65% and 8% at 1 year and 36% and 5% at last follow-up. All patients who required immediate dialysis and had 100% crescents on renal biopsy remained dialysis dependent. The authors concluded that patients with severe renal failure should still be considered for urgent immunosuppression including plasma exchange to maximise the chance of renal recovery, while accepting those needing immediate dialysis are less likely to recover.
cards.watchOut: Everyone in this cohort received the same triple therapy, so the card measures prognosis under treatment, not the effect of treatment — there is no untreated or drugs-only arm. The strata are small (n = 19, 13 and 39), and the 100%-crescent dialysis subgroup's zero recovery is the finding behind the guideline exception for withholding aggressive therapy in that narrow group.
cards.source: Levy JB, Turner AN, Rees AJ, Pusey CD. Long-term outcome of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody disease treated with plasma exchange and immunosuppression. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2001. PMID: 11388816. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective cohort). cards.headline: Cui 2011 (221 patients, three regimens compared): combination therapy HR 0.31 for death and 0.60 for renal failure (relative measures); steroids plus cyclophosphamide alone did not improve renal outcome (P = 0.73)
cards.summary: Cui 2011 (221 patients, three regimens compared): combination therapy HR 0.31 for death and 0.60 for renal failure (relative measures); steroids plus cyclophosphamide alone did not improve renal outcome (P = 0.73)
cards.type: Retrospective single-centre cohort comparing three treatment regimens (Cui 2011)
cards.people: 221 consecutive patients with anti-GBM disease seen at Peking University First Hospital, 1998–2008, whose similar clinical features allowed comparison of three regimens: (1) combination therapy of plasmapheresis plus immunosuppression, (2) steroids and cytotoxic agents, (3) steroids alone. Overall patient and renal survival at 1 year were 72.7% and 25.0%.
cards.result: Combination therapy of plasmapheresis plus corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide had an overall beneficial effect on both patient survival (hazard ratio for patient mortality 0.31; P = 0.001 — a relative measure) and renal survival (HR for renal failure 0.60; P = 0.032), particularly patient survival in Goodpasture syndrome (HR 0.29; P = 0.004) and renal survival in anti-GBM nephritis with initial serum creatinine over 6.8 mg/dL (HR 0.52; P = 0.014). Treatment with corticosteroids plus cyclophosphamide was found not to improve the renal outcome (P = 0.73). Independent predictors of death were anti-GBM antibody level (per 20 U/mL increase, HR 1.16; P = 0.009) and ANCA positivity (HR 2.18; P = 0.028); presenting creatinine predicted renal failure (doubling from 1.5 mg/dL, HR 2.07; P < 0.001). The authors concluded combination therapy was preferred, especially with pulmonary haemorrhage or severe renal damage, and that early diagnosis was crucial.
cards.watchOut: Regimens were chosen by clinicians, not randomised — sicker patients may have been channelled to or away from plasma exchange, and hazard ratios from a retrospective comparison carry that selection with them. The record is indexed with a 'Randomized Controlled Trial' publication type, but the abstract states plainly that this was a retrospective survey; this card follows the abstract, not the index tag.
cards.source: Cui Z, Zhao J, Jia XY, Zhu SN, Jin QZ, Cheng XY, Zhao MH. Anti-glomerular basement membrane disease: outcomes of different therapeutic regimens in a large single-center Chinese cohort study. Medicine (Baltimore). 2011. PMID: 21862934. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective cohort). cards.headline: Synthesis: one 17-patient randomised trial, one prognostic cohort, one regimen comparison — all pointing the same way, none of them large
cards.summary: Synthesis: one 17-patient randomised trial, one prognostic cohort, one regimen comparison — all pointing the same way, none of them large
cards.people: Johnson 1985 (randomised, n = 17), Levy 2001 (retrospective cohort, 71 treated), Cui 2011 (retrospective cohort, 221 patients, three regimens).
cards.result: Plasma exchange added to corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide: faster antibody clearance and fewer dialysis-dependent survivors in the only randomised test (2 of 8 versus 6 of 9; end-of-treatment creatinine 4.1 versus 9.2 mg/dL; Johnson 1985); an adjusted association with lower mortality (HR 0.31, relative) and renal failure (HR 0.60) in the largest cohort (Cui 2011), where steroids plus cyclophosphamide without exchange showed no renal benefit (P = 0.73). Under triple therapy, renal survival is governed by presentation: 95% at 1 year with creatinine below 500 micromol/L (5.7 mg/dL), 8% when dialysis-dependent at presentation (Levy 2001). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — consistent direction across designs, but the randomised base is 17 patients and the cohorts cannot exclude confounding by indication.

shelves.title: Ménétrier disease: cetuximab is the only treatment with numbers — 7 of 7 completers improved in a single-arm trial of just 9 patients, with a 2-patient report behind it and no comparative trial of anything
shelves.question: What are the treatments for Ménétrier disease — in people with severe Ménétrier disease (giant gastric folds with protein loss), does the EGFR antibody cetuximab improve symptoms, gastric acidity and histology, and what is the prognosis that makes gastrectomy the historical alternative?
shelves.mesh: Case-Control Studies · Female · Gastric Mucosa · Gastritis, Hypertrophic/complications · Gastritis, Hypertrophic/epidemiology · Gastroscopy · Helicobacter pylori · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Stomach Neoplasms/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the entire treatment evidence for Ménétrier disease is one single-arm trial of n = 9 and a two-patient chronic-treatment report, both of the EGFR antibody cetuximab (Erbitux), with n printed on the face of each card as this library's small-n rule requires. In the single-arm trial (Fiske 2009, PMID: 20368185; 9 enrolled, 7 completing one month), all 7 completers improved significantly on quality-of-life indices and biochemically — parietal cell mass rose from 20.9 to 61.2 (P = 0.01) and mean gastric pH fell from 6.0 to 4.1 (P = 0.05) — all 7 elected to continue treatment, and 4 later showed near-complete histological remission. The earlier chronic-treatment report (Settle 2005, PMID: 16206497; n = 2) describes one patient whose albumin stabilised enough to stop parenteral nutrition and albumin infusions over a 1-year course, and one whose twice-monthly transfusions were eliminated over 4 months. The backdrop is a disease with real mortality: in the Mayo case-control series (Almazar 2021, PMID: 32184187; 76 patients), 5- and 10-year survival were 72.7% and 65.0% versus 100% in controls, and gastric cancer developed in 8.9% by 10 years versus 3.7% of controls (P = .09) — the reason gastrectomy was the historical default and surveillance endoscopy is advised. There is no randomised or comparative trial of any treatment. PROPOSED POSSIBLE, capped by the tiny uncontrolled base.

cards.headline: Fiske 2009 (single-arm cetuximab trial, n = 9 enrolled, 7 completing): all 7 completers improved — quality-of-life index P = 0.02, parietal cell mass 20.9 to 61.2 (P = 0.01), gastric pH 6.0 to 4.1 (P = 0.05); 4 later near-complete histological remission
cards.summary: Fiske 2009 (single-arm cetuximab trial, n = 9 enrolled, 7 completing): all 7 completers improved — quality-of-life index P = 0.02, parietal cell mass 20.9 to 61.2 (P = 0.01), gastric pH 6.0 to 4.1 (P = 0.05); 4 later near-complete histological remission
cards.people: 9 individuals (n = 9, printed here because it is below this library's usual size floor) with clinically and histologically documented severe Ménétrier's disease impairing quality of life to the extent that gastrectomy was being considered, treated at Vanderbilt with cetuximab (loading dose 400 mg per square metre, then three weekly infusions of 250 mg per square metre); 7 completed the 1-month course — one withdrew after a single dose over side-effect concerns and one was removed after a focus of gastric cancer was found on baseline biopsies.
cards.result: Of the seven patients who completed the 1-month course, all showed statistically significant improvement clinically (quality-of-life indices: overall Ferrans and Powers index 15.8 to 20.3, P = 0.02; Health and Functioning subscale 12.3 to 19.8, P = 0.01) and biochemically: parietal cell mass increased three-fold (20.9 to 61.2, P = 0.01) and mean gastric pH decreased from 6.0 to 4.1 (P = 0.05); mean stomach wall thickness fell from 13.7 to 9.6 mm (P = 0.06, not significant), and serum albumin did not change (3.04 to 3.02 g/dL, P = 0.97). All seven completers elected to continue treatment, and four subsequently showed near-complete histological remission. The authors concluded cetuximab should be considered first-line therapy for Ménétrier's disease.
cards.watchOut: Nine enrolled, seven analysed, no control group, and a disease whose symptoms fluctuate — every improvement here is a before-and-after change in a handful of highly selected patients at one centre, and the albumin result (no change, P = 0.97) is a reminder that not every disease marker moved. One enrolled patient's biopsies revealed gastric cancer, underlining that this population carries the malignancy risk the Almazar card quantifies.

cards.headline: Settle 2005 (chronic cetuximab, n = 2): one patient off parenteral nutrition with stable albumin over 1 year; one patient's twice-monthly transfusions eliminated over 4 months
cards.summary: Settle 2005 (chronic cetuximab, n = 2): one patient off parenteral nutrition with stable albumin over 1 year; one patient's twice-monthly transfusions eliminated over 4 months
cards.type: Two-patient case report of chronic cetuximab treatment (Settle 2005)
cards.people: 2 patients (n = 2, printed here because it is far below this library's usual size floor) with severe Ménétrier's disease given longer-term Erbitux (cetuximab) as an alternative to gastrectomy: the first presenting with nausea, hypoalbuminemia and peripheral oedema requiring total parenteral nutrition and albumin infusions; the second with chronic gastric bleeding requiring bimonthly blood transfusions.
cards.result: On institution of Erbitux, the first patient had rapid improvement in nausea and vomiting and stabilisation of serum albumin, with discontinuation of total parenteral nutrition and albumin infusions; serum albumin remained stable during a 1-year course of Erbitux without supplemental protein. In the second patient, during a 4-month course of Erbitux, the hematocrit stabilised and transfusion requirements were eliminated. The authors concluded the report demonstrates the efficacy of prolonged Erbitux therapy in different presentations of severe Ménétrier's disease.
cards.watchOut: Two patients, reported because they responded — a case report of this kind cannot estimate how often chronic cetuximab works, only that prolonged benefit is possible. The same group's earlier single compassionate-use patient (Burdick 2000, New England Journal of Medicine, PMID: 11106719) has no abstract in its PubMed record, so no numbers could be extracted from it and it is not carded separately.
cards.source: Settle SH, Washington K, Lind C, Itzkowitz S, Fiske WH, Burdick JS, Jerome WG, Ray M, Weinstein W, Coffey RJ. cards.headline: Almazar 2021 (the backdrop, 76 Mayo patients): survival 72.7% at 5 years and 65.0% at 10 years versus 100% of controls; gastric cancer in 8.9% by 10 years versus 3.7% (P = .09)
cards.summary: Almazar 2021 (the backdrop, 76 Mayo patients): survival 72.7% at 5 years and 65.0% at 10 years versus 100% of controls; gastric cancer in 8.9% by 10 years versus 3.7% (P = .09)
cards.type: Case-control study of survival and gastric cancer risk (Almazar 2021)
cards.people: All 76 Ménétrier's disease cases diagnosed at Mayo Clinic, Rochester, from January 1975 through 2005 (mean age 56 years; 59% male), compared in a case-control design with patients who underwent gastric biopsy for dyspepsia.
cards.result: Gastric cancer developed in 8.9% of patients with Ménétrier's disease by 10 years after diagnosis versus 3.7% of controls over the same period (P = .09). Of patients with Ménétrier's disease, 72.7% and 65.0% survived for 5 and 10 years respectively, compared with 100% of controls (P < .0001 for both time periods). Vomiting, abdominal pain, postprandial fullness and weight loss of 10 lb or more were significantly more common than in controls; Helicobacter pylori infection was not associated with the disease (2.6% of patients versus 4.0% of controls; P = 1.00). The authors concluded the disorder is associated with increased mortality and that patients should be followed with surveillance endoscopy.
cards.watchOut: This card is prognosis, not treatment: it is carded because it quantifies what is at stake in the treat-versus-gastrectomy decision and why surveillance is part of management. The cohort spans 1975–2005, largely before cetuximab existed, so its survival figures describe the untreated-era disease at a referral centre, not outcomes on modern therapy; the gastric-cancer contrast (8.9% versus 3.7%) did not reach significance (P = .09).
cards.source: Almazar AE, Penfield JD, Saito YA, Talley NJ. Survival Times of Patients With Menetrier's Disease and Risk of Gastric Cancer. Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology. 2021. PMID: 32184187. Registry ID: none in the record (case-control study). cards.headline: Synthesis: cetuximab is the only medical treatment with any numbers at all — 7 of 7 completers improved in a 9-patient single-arm trial, backed by a 2-patient chronic-treatment report, against a disease that killed a third of a referral cohort by 10 years

cards.people: Fiske 2009 (single-arm trial, n = 9 enrolled / 7 completing), Settle 2005 (case report, n = 2), Almazar 2021 (case-control prognosis series, n = 76).
cards.result: No randomised or comparative treatment trial exists for Ménétrier disease in the records fetched. Cetuximab: statistically significant clinical and biochemical improvement in all 7 completers of a 1-month course (quality of life P = 0.02; parietal cell mass 20.9 to 61.2, P = 0.01; gastric pH 6.0 to 4.1, P = 0.05), 4 later near-complete histological remissions, and two chronic-treatment cases with parenteral nutrition stopped and transfusions eliminated. Disease stakes: 10-year survival 65.0% and gastric cancer in 8.9% by 10 years in the pre-cetuximab Mayo cohort. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — capped by a total treated evidence base of 11 published patients, all uncontrolled.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Gastrectomy remains the definitive option for refractory disease and for cancer, and no record fetched compares it with cetuximab; proton-pump inhibitors, octreotide and Helicobacter pylori eradication appear in the literature only as case-level reports without extractable comparative numbers, so they are not carded. shelves.title: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma): radiosurgery shrank tumours observation let grow in the one randomised trial, microsurgery controls best in pooled series but costs facial nerve function — and hearing ends up the same
shelves.question: How is an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) treated — in people with a small or medium vestibular schwannoma, how do stereotactic radiosurgery, microsurgical removal and watch-and-scan observation compare on tumour control, hearing preservation and facial nerve function?
shelves.mesh: Cerebellopontine Angle/diagnostic imaging · Cerebellopontine Angle/pathology · Female · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Microsurgery · Middle Aged · Neuroma, Acoustic/complications · Neuroma, Acoustic/diagnostic imaging · Neuroma, Acoustic/pathology · Neuroma, Acoustic/therapy · Radiosurgery/adverse effects · Radiosurgery/methods · Retrospective Studies · Salvage Therapy · Treatment Outcome · Watchful Waiting/methods
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which comparison you mean, and the records correct one common assumption: a randomised trial does exist for one of them. In V-REX (Dhayalan 2023, PMID: 37526718; NCT02249572; 100 patients with tumours under 2 cm), upfront Gamma Knife radiosurgery beat watch-and-scan on the primary outcome — tumour volume ratio at 4 years 0.87 versus 1.51 (between-group ratio 1.73, 95% CI 1.23–2.44; P = .002) — while 25 of 26 secondary outcomes, including quality of life and hearing measures, showed no significant difference, and 42% of the observation group crossed over to radiosurgery for growth within 4 years. Matched observational data agree that radiosurgery controls tumours observation cannot (VISAS, PMID: 38588868: control 99% at 5 years and 91.9% at 10 years versus 45.8% and 22% under observation), with serviceable hearing preservation statistically indistinguishable (P = .53). For microsurgery versus radiosurgery there is no randomised trial — only a 32-study systematic review (Savardekar 2022, PMID: 34838768): tumour control favoured microsurgery (98% versus 92%, P < 0.0001), hearing preservation did not differ (56% versus 59% at about 65 months, P = 0.1527), and facial nerve dysfunction was five times as common after microsurgery (10% versus 2%, P < 0.0001). PROPOSED SPLIT: radiosurgery over observation for tumour control with no proven patient-outcome advantage; microsurgery over radiosurgery for control at a facial-nerve price; observation remains defensible for small tumours, since about a third grow within 3 years and most observed patients in V-REX still needed no treatment at 4 years (56% untreated).

cards.headline: V-REX 2023 (the one randomised trial, 100 patients): upfront radiosurgery shrank tumours while observation grew them (volume ratio 0.87 versus 1.51; P = .002) — but 25 of 26 secondary outcomes did not differ, and 42% of the watch-and-scan group crossed over to radiosurgery
cards.summary: V-REX 2023 (the one randomised trial, 100 patients): upfront radiosurgery shrank tumours while observation grew them (volume ratio 0.87 versus 1.51; P = .002) — but 25 of 26 secondary outcomes did not differ, and 42% of the watch-and-scan group crossed over to radiosurgery
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial, upfront radiosurgery versus wait-and-scan (V-REX, Dhayalan 2023)
cards.people: 100 patients with newly diagnosed unilateral vestibular schwannoma under 2 cm in the cerebellopontine angle, recruited in Norway 2014–2017 and randomised to upfront Gamma Knife radiosurgery (50 patients; single-session 12 Gy to the tumour margin) or wait-and-scan observation (50 patients); 98 were in the primary analysis (mean age 54 years; 42% women), followed 4 years.
cards.result: The primary outcome — the ratio of tumour volume at 4 years to baseline (V4:V0) — was 0.87 (95% CI 0.66–1.15) in the radiosurgery group versus 1.51 (95% CI 1.23–1.84) in the wait-and-scan group, a between-group ratio of 1.73 (95% CI 1.23–2.44; P = .002). In the wait-and-scan group, 21 patients (42%) crossed over to radiosurgery for tumour growth, 1 (2%) had salvage microsurgery, and 28 (56%) received no treatment; in the radiosurgery group, 1 (2%) had repeat radiosurgery, 2 (4%) had salvage microsurgery and 45 (94%) needed no further treatment. Of 26 secondary outcomes (including clinical status, function and quality of life), 25 showed no significant difference between groups. No radiation-associated complications were observed. The authors concluded upfront radiosurgery was superior on the primary outcome, with no difference in clinical or patient-reported outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is a scan measurement, not how patients feel or hear — on every patient-centred secondary outcome except one, the trial was null, and 4 years is short for a benign tumour treated in 54-year-olds who will live decades with the consequences. The trial answers radiosurgery versus observation only; it says nothing randomised about microsurgery.
cards.source: Dhayalan D, Tveiten OV, Finnkirk M, et al. Upfront Radiosurgery vs a Wait-and-Scan Approach for Small- or Medium-Sized Vestibular Schwannoma: The V-REX Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2023. PMID: 37526718. Registry ID: NCT02249572. cards.headline: VISAS 2024 (propensity-matched, 125 versus 125): radiosurgery tumour control 99% at 5 years and 91.9% at 10 years versus 45.8% and 22% under observation (P < .001); serviceable hearing preservation no different (P = .53)
cards.summary: VISAS 2024 (propensity-matched, 125 versus 125): radiosurgery tumour control 99% at 5 years and 91.9% at 10 years versus 45.8% and 22% under observation (P < .001); serviceable hearing preservation no different (P = .53)
cards.type: Propensity-matched multicentre retrospective cohort, radiosurgery versus observation (VISAS, Bin-Alamer 2024)
cards.people: Patients with Koos grade 1 or 2 (small) vestibular schwannoma managed at multiple centres with upfront stereotactic radiosurgery or conservative observation, propensity-matched to 125 patients per group; median follow-up 36 months, with actuarial outcomes reported to 10 years.
cards.result: Tumour control was 99% at 5 years and 91.9% at 10 years after radiosurgery versus 45.8% and 22% under observation (P < .001). Serviceable hearing preservation was comparable: 60.4% versus 51.4% at 5 years and 27% versus 30% at 9 years (P = .53). Radiosurgery was associated with lower odds (relative measures) of tinnitus (odds ratio 0.39; P = .01), vestibular dysfunction (OR 0.11; P = .004) and any cranial nerve palsy (OR 0.36; P = .003), with no significant difference in trigeminal or facial nerve dysfunction (P > .05).
cards.watchOut: Matching balances measured differences only — patients chosen for observation may have had slower-growing or differently situated tumours in ways scans do not capture, and the 10-year actuarial figures rest on a cohort whose median follow-up was 36 months, so the late control estimates (22% under observation) are extrapolations from thinning numbers. The symptom odds ratios favouring radiosurgery are the kind of result confounding by indication produces, and they sit oddly beside the randomised trial's null secondary outcomes.

cards.headline: Savardekar 2022 (systematic review, 32 studies): tumour control favoured microsurgery (98% versus 92%, P < 0.0001), hearing preservation did not differ (56% versus 59%, P = 0.1527), facial nerve dysfunction was 10% after microsurgery versus 2% after radiosurgery (P < 0.0001)
cards.summary: Savardekar 2022 (systematic review, 32 studies): tumour control favoured microsurgery (98% versus 92%, P < 0.0001), hearing preservation did not differ (56% versus 59%, P = 0.1527), facial nerve dysfunction was 10% after microsurgery versus 2% after radiosurgery (P < 0.0001)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, microsurgery versus radiosurgery (Savardekar 2022)
cards.people: 32 studies published 2010–2020 of small-to-medium sporadic vestibular schwannomas (under 3 cm) treated by microsurgery or stereotactic radiosurgery with at least 3 years of follow-up — hearing preservation pooled from 10 microsurgery studies (809 patients) and 23 radiosurgery studies (1234 patients); tumour control from 9 (1635 patients) and 19 studies (2260 patients); facial nerve outcomes from 8 (1101) and 17 studies (2285).
cards.result: Hearing preservation at a mean of about 65 months was 56% after microsurgery versus 59% after radiosurgery (P = 0.1527, not significant). Tumour control at a mean of about 70 months was 98% after microsurgery versus 92% after radiosurgery (P < 0.0001). Facial nerve dysfunction at a mean of about 12 months was 10% after microsurgery versus 2% after radiosurgery (P < 0.0001). The authors concluded hearing outcomes were similar, microsurgery achieved better tumour control, and radiosurgery carried the lower facial-nerve risk — noting the choice for tumours under 3 cm remains open to debate.
cards.watchOut: These are pooled single-arm rates from non-randomised series, not head-to-head comparisons — surgical series and radiosurgery series select different tumours (size within the under-3 cm band, cystic change, patient age and preference), and a 6-point control gap (98% versus 92%) can be manufactured by that selection alone. Facial-nerve dysfunction was counted at about 12 months, when some surgical weakness is still recovering.
cards.source: Savardekar AR, Terrell D, Lele SR, Kelly PD, Nathan D, Menger R, Sin A, Krishna C. Primary treatment of small-to-medium vestibular schwannomas: microsurgery vs radiosurgery — a systematic review and meta-analysis. World Neurosurgery. 2022. PMID: 34838768. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Synthesis: radiosurgery beats observation on tumour volume in the only randomised trial but not on how patients do; microsurgery beats radiosurgery on control only in non-randomised pools, at five times the facial-nerve dysfunction
cards.summary: Synthesis: radiosurgery beats observation on tumour volume in the only randomised trial but not on how patients do; microsurgery beats radiosurgery on control only in non-randomised pools, at five times the facial-nerve dysfunction
cards.people: V-REX 2023 (randomised, 100 patients, radiosurgery versus observation), VISAS 2024 (propensity-matched, 250 patients, radiosurgery versus observation), Savardekar 2022 (systematic review, 32 studies, microsurgery versus radiosurgery).
cards.result: Radiosurgery versus observation: randomised volume benefit (V4:V0 0.87 versus 1.51; P = .002) with 25 of 26 secondary outcomes null and 42% crossover by 4 years; matched-cohort control 91.9% versus 22% at 10 years with hearing preservation statistically indistinguishable (P = .53). Microsurgery versus radiosurgery: no randomised trial exists; pooled non-randomised rates give microsurgery a control edge (98% versus 92%) and radiosurgery a facial-nerve edge (dysfunction 2% versus 10%), with hearing preservation the same (59% versus 56%, not significant). PROPOSED SPLIT — the right answer is comparison-specific, and for a small tumour in an older patient the observation arm's 56% treatment-free rate at 4 years is part of the evidence, not a failure of it.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. The assignment for this shelf expected no randomised trial to exist; the records show one does (V-REX, radiosurgery versus observation), and the shelf says so rather than repeating the assumption. Fractionated radiotherapy, hearing-rehabilitation devices and NF2-related tumours are outside these cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dhayalan D et al. JAMA. 2023 (PMID: 37526718; NCT02249572); Bin-Alamer O et al. International Journal of Radiation Oncology, Biology, Physics. 2024 (PMID: 38588868); Savardekar AR et al. World Neurosurgery. 2022 (PMID: 34838768).

shelves.title: Anal fistula surgery: cut the sphincter on a simple fistula and it heals either way you cut it; spare the sphincter on a complex one and a quarter to a third fail — with the plug and fibrin glue beaten by the flap in randomised comparisons
shelves.question: How is an anal fistula treated — in people with fistula-in-ano, how do fistulotomy, fistulectomy, advancement flap, LIFT, the fistula plug and other operations compare on healing, recurrence and continence?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anal Canal/surgery · Digestive System Surgical Procedures/methods · Fecal Incontinence/epidemiology · Fecal Incontinence/etiology · Humans · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Rectal Fistula/surgery · Surgical Flaps · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the fistula literature splits cleanly by anatomy. For simple fistulas, the sphincter-cutting operations heal almost everyone and the two variants are equivalent: a meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (Quinn 2025, PMID: 40125894; 1373 patients) found no significant difference between fistulotomy and fistulectomy in healing time, recurrence or incontinence, with less pain at 24 hours after fistulectomy (mean difference −0.49) and less bleeding after fistulotomy (odds ratio 3.81, a relative measure). For complex fistulas, where the sphincter must be spared, a network meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (Sierra Fernández 2025, PMID: 40442569) found LIFT, VAAFT, cutting seton and fistulotomy with sphincter reconstruction statistically indistinguishable from the advancement-flap control on failure — while the fistula plug (OR 3.6, 95% CI 1.1–11.5), fibrin glue (OR 7.5, 2.2–25) and platelet-rich plasma (OR 11.5, 1.3–99) all failed significantly more often (relative measures), and only the cutting seton raised incontinence (OR 8.6). A second network analysis (Fuschillo 2025, PMID: 40392371; 49 articles, 3520 patients) puts absolute failure at 22–29% for LIFT, VAAFT and flap, 43.9% for laser closure (FiLaC), with continence disturbance of 1.5% after LIFT versus 7.3% after flap. PROPOSED SPLIT: cut the sphincter for simple fistulas and it heals; spare it for complex ones and roughly a quarter to a third fail whatever you choose — with plug and glue measurably worse.

cards.headline: Quinn 2025 (meta-analysis, 13 randomised trials, 1373 patients): fistulotomy and fistulectomy did not differ on healing time, recurrence or incontinence — fistulectomy hurt less at 24 hours, fistulotomy bled less
cards.summary: Quinn 2025 (meta-analysis, 13 randomised trials, 1373 patients): fistulotomy and fistulectomy did not differ on healing time, recurrence or incontinence — fistulectomy hurt less at 24 hours, fistulotomy bled less
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, fistulotomy versus fistulectomy (Quinn 2025)
cards.people: 1373 patients with simple fistula-in-ano in 13 randomised controlled trials comparing the two sphincter-cutting techniques — 685 treated by fistulectomy (tract excised) and 688 by fistulotomy (tract laid open); primary outcome healing time, with operative time, hospital stay, pain, complications and recurrence as secondary outcomes.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between the techniques for healing time (P = 0.15), operative time (P = 0.13), length of stay (P = 0.05), wound infection (P = 0.97), flatus incontinence (P = 0.35), faecal incontinence (P = 0.70) or recurrence (P = 0.19). Post-operative pain at 24 hours was significantly lower with fistulectomy (mean difference −0.49 on a visual analogue scale, 95% CI −0.90 to −0.08; P = 0.02), and post-operative bleeding complications were significantly fewer with fistulotomy (odds ratio 3.81, 95% CI 1.23–11.80; P = 0.02 — a relative measure). The authors concluded neither technique was shown superior for healing.
cards.watchOut: Simple fistulas only — these equivalence results say nothing about high or complex fistulas, where cutting the sphincter is the thing being avoided. Thirteen small trials with several outcomes tested means the two significant findings (24-hour pain, bleeding) should be read as minor trade-offs, not verdicts; the headline is the string of nulls on healing, recurrence and continence.
cards.source: Quinn R, Peacock A, Lendzion RJL. Fistulotomy versus fistulectomy for simple fistula-in-ano: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. ANZ Journal of Surgery. 2025. PMID: 40125894. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). cards.headline: Sierra Fernández 2025 (network meta-analysis, 16 randomised trials): LIFT, VAAFT and seton matched the advancement flap on failure — but the plug (OR 3.6), fibrin glue (OR 7.5) and platelet-rich plasma (OR 11.5) all failed significantly more
cards.summary: Sierra Fernández 2025 (network meta-analysis, 16 randomised trials): LIFT, VAAFT and seton matched the advancement flap on failure — but the plug (OR 3.6), fibrin glue (OR 7.5) and platelet-rich plasma (OR 11.5) all failed significantly more
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials in complex fistula (Sierra Fernández 2025)
cards.people: Patients with complex cryptoglandular anal fistula in 16 randomised controlled trials comparing sphincter-sparing and other techniques — ligation of the intersphincteric fistula tract (LIFT), video-assisted anal fistula treatment (VAAFT), fistula plug, fibrin glue, platelet-rich plasma, cutting seton and fistulotomy with sphincter reconstruction — against endorectal advancement flap as the control procedure; failure (persistence or recurrence) was the primary outcome and faecal incontinence the safety outcome.
cards.result: For failure, LIFT, VAAFT, cutting seton and fistulotomy with sphincter reconstruction showed no significant difference versus advancement flap, while the fistula plug (odds ratio 3.6, 95% CI 1.1–11.5), fibrin glue (OR 7.5, 95% CI 2.2–25) and platelet-rich plasma (OR 11.5, 95% CI 1.3–99) had significantly higher failure odds — all relative measures. For incontinence, only the cutting seton was significantly worse than flap (OR 8.6, 95% CI 1–72.5). The authors concluded the plug, glue and platelet-rich plasma should not be recommended as standard procedures, and that LIFT, VAAFT and fistulotomy with sphincter reconstruction are safe alternatives to the flap.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates lean on indirect comparisons between small trials, and the platelet-rich plasma interval (OR 1.3–99) shows how thin some of that evidence is — the direction (worse than flap) is consistent across plug, glue and PRP, but the sizes are not precise. 'No significant difference' for LIFT and VAAFT versus flap is not proof of equivalence either; the absolute failure rates on the next card show what 'as good as the flap' actually means.
cards.source: Sierra Fernández I, Marcacuzco Quinto A, Garcia Septiem J, et al. What is the gold standard in the surgical treatment of complex anal fistula? Updates in Surgery. 2025. PMID: 40442569. cards.headline: Fuschillo 2025 (network meta-analysis, 49 articles, 3520 patients): absolute failure 28.6% LIFT, 22.3% VAAFT, 25.9% flap, 43.9% laser closure — continence disturbance 1.5% after LIFT versus 7.3% after flap
cards.summary: Fuschillo 2025 (network meta-analysis, 49 articles, 3520 patients): absolute failure 28.6% LIFT, 22.3% VAAFT, 25.9% flap, 43.9% laser closure — continence disturbance 1.5% after LIFT versus 7.3% after flap
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of sphincter-sparing techniques (Fuschillo 2025)
cards.people: 3520 patients in 49 articles published after 2017 evaluating minimally invasive sphincter-sparing treatments for anal fistula — LIFT, VAAFT, laser closure (FiLaC) and endoanal advancement flap — with failure rate as the primary outcome and continence disturbance, complications and operating time as secondary outcomes.
cards.result: Failure rates were 28.6% for LIFT (range 3.8–75), 22.3% for VAAFT (range 6.2–65.2), 43.9% for FiLaC (range 11.1–80) and 25.9% for endoanal flap (range 4.7–100). Continence disturbance was 1.5% after LIFT and 7.3% after endoanal flap, with none reported for VAAFT or FiLaC. Minor complications were 4.3% (LIFT), 7.2% (VAAFT), 10.2% (FiLaC) and 6.2% (flap); no major complications were reported. Failure was higher in Crohn's fistulas than non-Crohn's (39.5% versus 31.4%). The authors concluded LIFT and VAAFT appear effective sphincter-sparing options, while FiLaC carried higher recurrence.
cards.watchOut: The ranges behind those averages are enormous (LIFT failure 3.8% to 75% across studies) — case mix, fistula height, prior surgery and follow-up length differ far more between series than the techniques do, and 'no continence disturbance reported' for VAAFT and FiLaC may mean unmeasured rather than absent. Crohn's fistulas are pooled into several of these figures despite being a biologically different problem.

cards.headline: Synthesis: simple fistulas heal with either cutting operation; complex fistulas fail a quarter to a third of the time under every sphincter-sparing technique — and the plug and glue are measurably worse than the flap
cards.summary: Synthesis: simple fistulas heal with either cutting operation; complex fistulas fail a quarter to a third of the time under every sphincter-sparing technique — and the plug and glue are measurably worse than the flap
cards.people: Quinn 2025 (13 RCTs, 1373 patients, simple fistula), Sierra Fernández 2025 (network meta-analysis, 16 RCTs, complex fistula), Fuschillo 2025 (network meta-analysis, 49 articles, 3520 patients, sphincter-sparing techniques).
cards.result: Simple fistula: fistulotomy versus fistulectomy — no significant difference in healing time (P = 0.15), recurrence (P = 0.19) or incontinence (P = 0.35/0.70). Complex fistula: LIFT, VAAFT and sphincter reconstruction statistically matched advancement flap on failure, while plug (OR 3.6), fibrin glue (OR 7.5) and platelet-rich plasma (OR 11.5) failed significantly more (relative measures) and cutting seton alone raised incontinence (OR 8.6). Absolute sphincter-sparing failure: LIFT 28.6%, VAAFT 22.3%, flap 25.9%, laser closure 43.9%; continence disturbance 1.5% (LIFT) versus 7.3% (flap). PROPOSED SPLIT — the trade is anatomical: where sphincter can be divided, surgery is close to definitive; where it cannot, every option is a probability, and two marketed options (plug, glue) have randomised evidence against them.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. This shelf covers cryptoglandular fistula-in-ano surgery; dialysis arteriovenous fistulas are a different problem and were excluded from the search, as the assignment directed. Stem-cell therapy for perianal Crohn's fistula and seton drainage as a standalone strategy had no qualifying records with extractable numbers in this session's fetch and are not carded.

shelves.title: Unruptured brain aneurysm: treat or watch? Five-year rupture risk runs from 0% (small, front of the brain) to 50% (giant, back of the brain) — so the evidence answers by risk stratum, not with one rule
shelves.question: Should an unruptured brain aneurysm be treated — in people with an unruptured intracranial aneurysm found before any bleed, what is the rupture risk if it is left alone, by size, location and risk score, and how does that frame the decision to clip, coil or watch?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aneurysm, Ruptured/epidemiology · Conservative Treatment/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intracranial Aneurysm/complications · Intracranial Aneurysm/diagnostic imaging · Intracranial Aneurysm/mortality · Intracranial Aneurysm/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Subarachnoid Hemorrhage/etiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — whether to treat an unruptured aneurysm is a comparison between a rupture risk that varies a hundred-fold by size, site and patient, and a treatment risk that is front-loaded — and no randomised trial of treatment versus observation exists in the records fetched. The natural-history anchor is ISUIA (Wiebers 2003, PMID: 12867109; 4060 patients): 5-year cumulative rupture rates in patients without prior subarachnoid haemorrhage were 0%, 2.6%, 14.5% and 40% for anterior-circulation aneurysms under 7 mm, 7–12 mm, 13–24 mm and 25 mm or more, versus 2.5%, 14.5%, 18.4% and 50% for posterior-circulation and posterior-communicating aneurysms of the same sizes. The PHASES pooled analysis (Greving 2014, PMID: 24290159; 8382 participants, 230 ruptures) puts the mean 5-year rupture risk at 3.4% (95% CI 2.9–4.0) but the individual range at 0.25% to over 15% depending on age, hypertension, prior haemorrhage, size, site and population. A 36-year conservatively-managed cohort (Dodier 2025, PMID: 40446344; 661 patients, 767 aneurysms) observed rupture in 3.5% (annual haemorrhage rate 0.6%), with 87% of haemorrhages in the first 5 years, none after 10 years, and no rupture or aneurysm-related death at all among patients with PHASES under 8 or ELAPSS under 15. PROPOSED SPLIT: small anterior aneurysms without risk factors rupture so rarely that observation is the evidence-based default; large, posterior or high-PHASES aneurysms carry double-digit 5-year risks that justify treatment despite its up-front risk. Boundary: this shelf is unruptured aneurysms only — ruptured aneurysm treatment (ISAT and subarachnoid haemorrhage care) is homed elsewhere in this library (Shelf #2389 and neighbours) and is deliberately not re-carded.

cards.headline: ISUIA 2003 (4060 patients): 5-year rupture risk 0% for anterior aneurysms under 7 mm, rising to 40% at 25 mm or more — posterior aneurysms rupture at 2.5% even under 7 mm and 50% when giant
cards.summary: ISUIA 2003 (4060 patients): 5-year rupture risk 0% for anterior aneurysms under 7 mm, rising to 40% at 25 mm or more — posterior aneurysms rupture at 2.5% even under 7 mm and 50% when giant
cards.type: Prospective cohort, natural history and treatment outcomes (ISUIA, Wiebers 2003)
cards.people: 4060 patients with unruptured intracranial aneurysms in the prospective arm of the International Study of Unruptured Intracranial Aneurysms — 1692 managed without repair, 1917 by open surgery and 451 by endovascular treatment — with 5-year cumulative rupture rates reported by aneurysm size and location for patients with and without a previous subarachnoid haemorrhage from a different aneurysm.
cards.result: In patients with no prior subarachnoid haemorrhage, 5-year cumulative rupture rates for anterior-circulation aneurysms (internal carotid, anterior cerebral, middle cerebral) were 0% for aneurysms under 7 mm, 2.6% for 7–12 mm, 14.5% for 13–24 mm and 40% for 25 mm or larger. For posterior-circulation and posterior-communicating-artery aneurysms the corresponding rates were 2.5%, 14.5%, 18.4% and 50%. Rates were higher across most categories in patients who had already had a subarachnoid haemorrhage from another aneurysm. These are the natural-history numbers against which any treatment's up-front risk has to be weighed.
cards.watchOut: ISUIA's untreated group was selected — aneurysms judged safe to leave — so its low small-aneurysm rupture rates describe aneurysms clinicians already chose not to treat, a criticism made of this study since publication. The 0% figure is a 5-year rate in that selected group, not a lifetime guarantee, and posterior-communicating aneurysms are grouped with the posterior circulation, which is why their small-aneurysm rate (2.5%) exceeds the anterior figure. Treatment-arm morbidity and mortality figures from this record were not verified in this session's fetch and are deliberately not quoted on this shelf.

cards.headline: PHASES 2014 (pooled, 8382 participants, 230 ruptures): mean 5-year rupture risk 3.4% — but the individual estimate runs from 0.25% to over 15%
cards.summary: PHASES 2014 (pooled, 8382 participants, 230 ruptures): mean 5-year rupture risk 3.4% — but the individual estimate runs from 0.25% to over 15%
cards.type: Pooled individual-patient analysis of six prospective cohorts (PHASES, Greving 2014)
cards.people: 8382 participants with unruptured intracranial aneurysms from six prospective cohort studies (from the Netherlands, Finland, Japan and elsewhere), contributing 29,166 person-years of follow-up with 230 aneurysm ruptures, pooled at individual-patient level to build the PHASES rupture-risk score.
cards.result: The mean 1-year rupture risk was 1.4% (95% CI 1.1–1.6) and the mean 5-year risk 3.4% (95% CI 2.9–4.0). Predictors of rupture were population (Finnish hazard ratio 3.6 and Japanese 2.8, relative measures), age, hypertension, previous subarachnoid haemorrhage from another aneurysm, aneurysm size and aneurysm location. Estimated 5-year absolute rupture risks in North American and non-Finnish European patients ranged from 0.25% (patients under 70 with no risk factors and a small, under-7 mm internal carotid aneurysm) to more than 15% (patients 70 or older with hypertension, previous subarachnoid haemorrhage and a giant, over-20 mm posterior-circulation aneurysm). The authors concluded PHASES provides an absolute rupture-risk estimate per patient to inform the treatment decision.
cards.watchOut: A risk score predicts rupture, not benefit from treatment — PHASES says nothing about whether clipping or coiling a given aneurysm leaves the patient better off, and its population terms (Finnish 3.6×, Japanese 2.8×) warn against exporting the absolute percentages to populations unlike the source cohorts. Most pooled patients were, like ISUIA's, selected for observation.
cards.source: Greving JP, Wermer MJH, Brown RD Jr, et al. Development of the PHASES score for prediction of risk of rupture of intracranial aneurysms: a pooled analysis of six prospective cohort studies. The Lancet Neurology. 2014. PMID: 24290159. Registry ID: none in the record (pooled cohort analysis). MeSH: not rendered in the record as fetched this session — see build flag in the part summary.

cards.headline: Dodier 2025 (661 patients managed conservatively, up to 36 years): rupture in 3.5%, annual haemorrhage rate 0.6% — and no rupture or aneurysm death at all with PHASES under 8 or ELAPSS under 15
cards.summary: Dodier 2025 (661 patients managed conservatively, up to 36 years): rupture in 3.5%, annual haemorrhage rate 0.6% — and no rupture or aneurysm death at all with PHASES under 8 or ELAPSS under 15
cards.type: Retrospective long-term cohort of conservatively managed aneurysms (Dodier 2025)
cards.people: 661 patients with 767 unruptured intracranial aneurysms managed conservatively at a single centre between 1984 and 2020 (median follow-up 4.1 years), analysed for haemorrhage incidence, timing and predictors, with the PHASES and ELAPSS scores tested as prognostic tools.
cards.result: Subarachnoid haemorrhage occurred in 23 patients (3.5%), giving an annual haemorrhage rate of 0.6%; aneurysm-related mortality was 4.4%. Most haemorrhages (87%) occurred within the first 5 years after diagnosis, and none occurred after 10 years. Aneurysm size, PHASES score and ELAPSS score independently predicted haemorrhage; in patients with a PHASES score under 8 or an ELAPSS score under 15, no rupture or aneurysm-related death was observed during follow-up.
cards.watchOut: A single centre's conservatively managed patients across four decades — imaging, blood-pressure treatment and smoking rates all changed over the study window, and aneurysms selected for decades of observation are the survivors of an early risk period (87% of ruptures happened in the first 5 years, so a cohort enriched for long follow-up understates early risk). The 'no events under PHASES 8' finding is reassuring but rests on zero events in a subgroup, which bounds rather than excludes risk.
cards.source: Dodier P, et al. Conservative Management of Unruptured Intracranial Aneurysms: A Long-Term Follow-Up Study. Journal of Neurosurgery. 2025. PMID: 40446344. cards.result: Five-year rupture risk, no prior haemorrhage: anterior circulation 0% (under 7 mm), 2.6% (7–12 mm), 14.5% (13–24 mm), 40% (25 mm or more); posterior circulation/posterior communicating 2.5%, 14.5%, 18.4%, 50% (ISUIA). Individualised by PHASES: 0.25% to over 15% over 5 years (Greving). Under conservative management at one centre: 0.6% per year overall, no rupture or aneurysm death with PHASES under 8 (Dodier). Set against any repair's immediate procedural risk — which this shelf deliberately does not quantify from unverified figures — small anterior low-PHASES aneurysms favour observation and large, posterior or high-score aneurysms favour treatment. shelves.question: How is a simple bone cyst treated? In children and adolescents with a unicameral (simple) bone cyst, how do intralesional steroid (methylprednisolone) injection, bone-marrow injection and curettage compare on healing?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — the methods rank differently in different study designs, and no method heals most cysts first time. The one randomised trial (Wright 2008, PMID: 18381307; 90 children randomised, 77 followed for 2 years, blinded radiographic assessment) found healing in 16 of 38 (42%) cysts injected with methylprednisolone acetate versus 9 of 39 (23%) injected with bone marrow (p=0.01), with no significant difference in function, pain, number of injections, additional fractures or complications — steroid beat marrow, but both healed a minority. The large retrospective three-treatment comparison (Sung 2008, PMID: 18679761; 167 patients under 20, mean follow-up 7.3 years) found failure after one treatment in 84% of steroid-injected cysts versus 64% with curettage plus bone grafting and 50% with a combined steroid/demineralised-bone-matrix/bone-marrow injection (SDB), with steroids alone an independent predictor of failure — almost the reverse ranking for steroids, in a design where treatment was chosen, not randomised. A smaller retrospective comparison (Canavese 2011, PMID: 21150732; 46 children, at least 24 months' follow-up) found satisfactory healing at 2 years in 70% after percutaneous curettage versus 41% after methylprednisolone injection and 21% after bone-marrow injection (P=0.03). PROPOSED SPLIT: steroid injection is superior to bone-marrow injection on the only randomised test, yet retrospective series rank curettage-based approaches above steroid injection alone, and repeat treatment is the norm under every method.

cards.headline: Wright 2008 (the randomised trial): healing in 42% of methylprednisolone-injected cysts versus 23% of bone-marrow-injected cysts (p=0.01) — and no difference in function, pain or fractures
cards.summary: Wright 2008 (the randomised trial): healing in 42% of methylprednisolone-injected cysts versus 23% of bone-marrow-injected cysts (p=0.01) — and no difference in function, pain or fractures
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (Simple Bone Cyst Trial; Wright 2008)
cards.people: 90 children with simple bone cysts randomly allocated to intralesional injection of bone marrow or methylprednisolone acetate; 77 were followed for 2 years (38 methylprednisolone, 39 bone marrow). Primary outcome was radiographic healing (grades 3–4 on a 4-grade scale), assessed by a radiologist blinded to treatment; function by the Activity Scale for Kids and pain by the Oucher Scale.
cards.result: Sixteen (42%) of the 38 cysts treated with methylprednisolone acetate healed, and 9 (23%) of the 39 cysts treated with bone marrow healed (p=0.01) — an absolute difference of 19 percentage points. There was no significant difference between the groups (p>0.09) in function, pain, number of injections, additional fractures or complications. The authors concluded that although healing rates were low after either injection, methylprednisolone provided superior healing rates.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own headline is double-edged: steroid won, but 58% of steroid-treated cysts still had not healed at 2 years, so 'superior' does not mean 'usually successful'. Thirteen of 90 randomised patients were not in the 2-year analysis. This is a comparison of two injections only — it says nothing randomised about curettage, which the retrospective cards below rank higher.
cards.source: Wright JG, Yandow S, Donaldson S, Marley L; Simple Bone Cyst Trial Group. A randomized clinical trial comparing intralesional bone marrow and steroid injections for simple bone cysts. The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery. American Volume. 2008. PMID: 18381307. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sung 2008 (167 patients, retrospective): failure after one treatment in 84% of steroid-injected cysts versus 64% with curettage and 50% with combined steroid/DBM/bone-marrow injection
cards.summary: Sung 2008 (167 patients, retrospective): failure after one treatment in 84% of steroid-injected cysts versus 64% with curettage and 50% with combined steroid/DBM/bone-marrow injection
cards.type: Retrospective comparative study of three surgical treatments (Sung 2008)
cards.people: 167 patients younger than 20 years treated surgically for humeral or femoral unicameral bone cysts at Children's Hospital Boston and Massachusetts General Hospital, 1979–2004, with corticosteroid injection, curettage plus bone grafting, or a combination injection of steroids, demineralised bone matrix and bone-marrow aspirate (SDB); mean follow-up 7.3 years (range 1 month–27 years). Failure was defined as subsequent pathologic fracture or need for retreatment to prevent fracture.
cards.result: After one treatment, 84% of cysts treated with steroids experienced failed treatment, versus 64% with curettage and 50% with SDB. Among cysts requiring retreatment, 76% retreated with steroids failed again, versus 63% with curettage and 71% with SDB. Curettage was associated with the lowest rate of post-treatment pathologic fractures and the highest rate of pain and other complications. Multivariate logistic regression indicated that treatment with steroids alone and younger age were independent predictors of failure. The authors proposed SDB as a reasonable first treatment — less invasive than curettage yet comparable in preventing recurrence.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective over 25 years: treatment was chosen by clinicians (larger, fractured or recurrent cysts plausibly steered to curettage or SDB), era effects span 1979–2004, and the abstract does not print the per-group denominators, so only the failure percentages are carded. Its steroid ranking directly contradicts the randomised trial's — which is exactly why this shelf is stamped SPLIT rather than resolved in favour of either design.
cards.source: Sung AD, Anderson ME, Zurakowski D, Hornicek FJ, Gebhardt MC. Unicameral bone cyst: a retrospective study of three surgical treatments. Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research. 2008. PMID: 18679761. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective study). cards.headline: Canavese 2011 (46 children, retrospective): satisfactory healing at 2 years in 70% after percutaneous curettage versus 41% after methylprednisolone injection and 21% after bone-marrow injection (P=0.03)
cards.summary: Canavese 2011 (46 children, retrospective): satisfactory healing at 2 years in 70% after percutaneous curettage versus 41% after methylprednisolone injection and 21% after bone-marrow injection (P=0.03)
cards.people: 46 children and adolescents with unicameral bone cyst treated at the Hospital for Sick Children, Toronto, with autologous bone-marrow injection, methylprednisolone acetate injection or percutaneous curettage alone; radiological diagnosis and at least 24 months' follow-up from the last procedure; healing graded on the Neer/Cole 4-grade scale, with grades I and II counted as satisfactory healing.
cards.result: The three groups were comparable for age, sex, cyst location and number of procedures. At 2 years, satisfactory healing (Neer/Cole grades I and II) was greatest after percutaneous curettage (70%), compared with bone-marrow injection (21%) and methylprednisolone acetate injection (41%) (P=0.03). There was no association between healing and age (P=0.80) or sex (P=0.61). The authors suggested that mechanical disruption of the cyst membrane may help healing and that percutaneous curettage may be preferred to simple intralesional injections.
cards.watchOut: Small (46 patients across three groups, so each percentage rests on roughly a dozen to twenty cysts; per-group denominators are not printed in the abstract) and retrospective, with treatment chosen rather than randomised. Note its healing definition (Neer/Cole grades I–II as 'satisfactory') differs from the randomised trial's grades 3–4 definition, so the 70%/41%/21% figures are not directly comparable with Wright 2008's 42%/23% — compare rankings within each study, not percentages across studies.
cards.source: Canavese F, Wright JG, Cole WG, Hopyan S. Unicameral bone cysts: comparison of percutaneous curettage, steroid, and autologous bone marrow injections. Journal of Pediatric Orthopedics. 2011. PMID: 21150732. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective study). cards.headline: Synthesis: steroid beats marrow in the only randomised trial; curettage-based treatment beats steroid alone in the retrospective record — and most cysts need more than one treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: steroid beats marrow in the only randomised trial; curettage-based treatment beats steroid alone in the retrospective record — and most cysts need more than one treatment
cards.people: One multicentre randomised trial (90 randomised, 77 followed; Wright 2008) and two retrospective comparative series (167 patients, Sung 2008; 46 patients, Canavese 2011), all in children and adolescents with unicameral (simple) bone cysts.
cards.result: Randomised: methylprednisolone injection healed 42% versus 23% for bone-marrow injection at 2 years (p=0.01), with no difference in function, pain, fractures or complications (Wright 2008). Retrospective: failure after one treatment was 84% (steroids) versus 64% (curettage plus grafting) versus 50% (combined steroid/DBM/marrow injection) (Sung 2008); satisfactory healing was 70% (percutaneous curettage) versus 41% (steroid) versus 21% (marrow) (Canavese 2011). PROPOSED SPLIT — the randomised and retrospective records rank steroid injection oppositely against the alternatives, definitions of healing differ between studies, and under every method a first treatment fails in a large share of cysts, so families should expect repeat procedures.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. All three studies are in skeletally immature patients with humeral or femoral cysts in the main; nothing here addresses adult cysts, calcaneal cysts, or aneurysmal bone cysts, which are different lesions. Newer combined techniques (curettage with graft substitutes and internal fixation) appear only inside the retrospective record carded here and have no randomised comparison.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wright JG et al. The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery. American Volume. 2008 (PMID: 18381307); Sung AD et al. Clinical Orthopaedics and Related Research. 2008 (PMID: 18679761); Canavese F et al. Journal of Pediatric Orthopedics. 2011 (PMID: 21150732).
