shelves.title: Brain abscess: aspiration versus excision/resection is an observational question — reoperation was 39.4% after aspiration versus 20.7% after resection in a 2025 multicentre series, while older series found no significant mortality difference between the operations
shelves.question: How is a brain abscess treated? In patients with a pyogenic brain abscess, how do aspiration and excision/resection compare on reoperation, recovery and death — and what does the observational record actually show?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Austria/epidemiology · Brain Abscess/surgery · Drainage/methods · Female · Germany/epidemiology · Humans · Male · Microsurgery/methods · Middle Aged · Neurosurgical Procedures/methods · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Reoperation · Retrospective Studies · Suction/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — for resection over aspiration on reoperation, observational only; there is no randomised trial comparing aspiration with excision for brain abscess, and treatment choice is driven by abscess size, depth and the patient's state. The largest modern comparison (Eibl 2025, PMID: 41175405; 148 patients with primary superficial pyogenic abscesses at five German/Austrian university centres, 2008–2023) found reoperation in 39.4% of the aspiration group versus 20.7% of the microsurgical resection group (p=0.018), five in-hospital deaths all in the aspiration group (overall mortality 3.4%; p=0.005), no significant difference in surgical complication rates, and comparable favourable outcomes at discharge, 3 and 6 months, with faster early recovery after resection. The older record is less decisive: in a 400-case review from China (Yang 1981, PMID: 7310502), mortality was 22% with aspiration as initial treatment, 17.2% with excision alone and 25% with aspiration followed by excision, with no significant difference between treatment groups — the dominant predictor was the patient's condition on arrival (mortality 64% with signs of herniation versus 8.4% without). In a 96-patient retrospective series (Hakan 2006, PMID: 16183134), 7 of 72 aspiration patients and 1 of 14 excision patients died, 10 patients were treated medically alone, and there was no significant correlation between treatment group and outcome. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: resection may halve reoperation in superficial abscesses on the newest series, but confounding by indication (deep, multiple or sicker-patient abscesses are aspirated, not resected) pervades every comparison, and antibiotics — given to all — are the untested constant underneath both operations.

cards.headline: Eibl 2025 (148 patients, 5 centres): reoperation 39.4% after aspiration versus 20.7% after microsurgical resection (p=0.018); all 5 in-hospital deaths were in the aspiration group
cards.summary: Eibl 2025 (148 patients, 5 centres): reoperation 39.4% after aspiration versus 20.7% after microsurgical resection (p=0.018); all 5 in-hospital deaths were in the aspiration group
cards.people: 148 patients (102 male, mean age 49.1 years) who underwent surgery for primary superficial pyogenic brain abscess at five university centres in Germany and Austria, January 2008 to December 2023: 82 (55.4%) microsurgical resection, 66 (44.6%) navigated/stereotactic aspiration. Excluded: previous head surgery or trauma, no preoperative MRI, multiple abscesses, concomitant subdural empyema, and infratentorial or deep-seated abscesses (more than 2 cm from the cortical surface). Primary endpoint reoperation for the abscess; secondary endpoints unfavourable outcome (modified Rankin Scale score 3 or more) at discharge, 3 and 6 months, and surgical complications.
cards.result: Reoperations were significantly more frequent after aspiration (39.4%) than after resection (20.7%) (p=0.018) — an absolute difference of 18.7 percentage points. Surgical complication rates did not differ significantly. Both groups improved significantly to a median modified Rankin Scale score of 1 after surgery (p<0.001 each), with 26 patients (17.6%) still scoring 3 or more at discharge; resection patients improved earlier (discharge to 3 months, p<0.001) while aspiration patients improved later (3 to 6 months, p=0.02), and favourable outcomes were comparable at discharge, 3 and 6 months. Five in-hospital deaths occurred, all in the aspiration group, giving overall mortality of 3.4% (p=0.005).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and restricted to superficial, single abscesses in patients fit for either operation — precisely the subgroup where resection is feasible. Even within it, surgeons chose the operation, so residual confounding is likely; the mortality contrast rests on five deaths. Deep-seated, multiple and infratentorial abscesses — where aspiration is usually the only option — were excluded, so nothing here argues against aspiration for them.
cards.source: Eibl T, Ritter L, Matejka M, Beredjiklian CM, Griessenauer CJ, Brunner A, Freigang S, Schnell O, Vladimirov T, Maiwald A, Schachinger S, Schmidt NO, Schebesch KM, Liebert A. Evaluation of aspiration versus microsurgical resection for primary superficial pyogenic brain abscesses: results from a German-Austrian retrospective multicenter study. Neurosurgical Focus. 2025. PMID: 41175405. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective study). cards.headline: Yang 1981 (400 cases): mortality 22% with aspiration, 17.2% with excision alone, 25% with aspiration then excision — no significant difference; herniation on arrival meant 64% mortality versus 8.4% without
cards.summary: Yang 1981 (400 cases): mortality 22% with aspiration, 17.2% with excision alone, 25% with aspiration then excision — no significant difference; herniation on arrival meant 64% mortality versus 8.4% without
cards.people: 400 cases of brain abscess treated in China over 20 years; the commonest cause was chronic ear infection, with abscesses in the temporal lobe and cerebellum. Antibiotics were given in full doses for an extended period in addition to surgery. Aspiration was the initial treatment in 253 cases, excision the sole treatment in 128, and 76 patients underwent aspiration followed by excision (groups overlap as described in the record).
cards.result: Mortality was 22% in the aspiration group, 17.2% in the 128 patients treated by excision alone, and 25% in the 76 patients who underwent aspiration followed by excision. There was no significant difference in mortality between these treatment groups. The most important predictor of outcome was the patient's condition when first seen: in 103 cases with signs of brain herniation, mortality was 64%, whereas in the 297 without herniation it was 8.4%. Signs of increased intracranial pressure were present in most cases and clinical signs of infection in only 57%.
cards.watchOut: A pre-modern-imaging era series (diagnosis by ultrasound, angiography or ventriculography in many cases, over 20 years in one country's referral pattern, dominated by ear-source abscesses): its absolute mortality figures (17–25%) belong to that era and are far above the 3.4% in the 2025 series. Its durable lesson is the prognostic one — admission condition swamped the choice of operation — which is also the strongest reason to distrust unadjusted aspiration-versus-excision contrasts in every era, including the newest card.
cards.source: Yang SY. Brain abscess: a review of 400 cases. Journal of Neurosurgery. 1981. PMID: 7310502. Registry ID: none in the record (case-series review). cards.headline: Hakan 2006 (96 patients): 72 treated by aspiration (7 died), 14 by excision (1 died), 10 medically alone — no significant correlation between treatment group and outcome
cards.summary: Hakan 2006 (96 patients): 72 treated by aspiration (7 died), 14 by excision (1 died), 10 medically alone — no significant correlation between treatment group and outcome
cards.people: 96 patients with brain abscess treated between 1988 and 2001 at a Turkish neurosurgical centre, analysed retrospectively by symptoms, aetiology, organisms, localisation, treatment method and outcome; 72 patients were treated with aspiration (stereotactic aspiration in 12 cases), 14 with excision, and 10 medically alone.
cards.result: Seven patients in the aspiration group and one patient in the excision group died. Cure without any morbidity was obtained in 55 patients. Significant correlations were found between mortality and initial neurologic grade, meningismus, high fever (above 38.5) and leucocytosis (above 20,000/mm3). There was no significant correlation between treatment group (or age group, abscess location, number of abscesses, treatment period or antibiotic received) and outcome. The authors concluded that in appropriate cases medical treatment alone can succeed, but that aspiration is the standard surgical approach, giving definite diagnosis and pathogen identification.
cards.watchOut: The excision group is only 14 patients and the medically-treated group 10, so the 'no significant correlation' finding has very little power to detect a real difference — absence of significance here is not evidence of equivalence. Treatment allocation over 1988–2001 reflected abscess site and patient state, as in every series on this shelf.
cards.source: Hakan T, Ceran N, Erdem I, Berkman MZ, Göktaş P. Bacterial brain abscesses: an evaluation of 96 cases. The Journal of Infection. 2006. PMID: 16183134. cards.headline: Synthesis: the operation is chosen, never randomised — resection shows less reoperation in the modern superficial-abscess series, mortality differences are unproven, and admission state dominates
cards.summary: Synthesis: the operation is chosen, never randomised — resection shows less reoperation in the modern superficial-abscess series, mortality differences are unproven, and admission state dominates
cards.people: Three observational sources spanning four decades: a 400-case Chinese review (Yang 1981), a 96-patient Turkish retrospective series (Hakan 2006), and a 148-patient German-Austrian multicentre retrospective comparison restricted to primary superficial pyogenic abscesses (Eibl 2025). No randomised trial of aspiration versus excision exists in this record; all patients also received antibiotics, whose duration and choice are not compared in any card here.
cards.result: Reoperation: 39.4% after aspiration versus 20.7% after resection (p=0.018) in the one modern head-to-head series, with comparable functional outcomes at 3 and 6 months (Eibl 2025). Mortality: no significant difference between aspiration (22%) and excision (17.2%) in 400 historical cases (Yang 1981), and no significant treatment-group correlation in 96 cases (7 deaths among 72 aspirated, 1 among 14 excised; Hakan 2006); the five deaths in Eibl 2025 were all after aspiration but number only five. Prognosis was dominated by presentation: mortality 64% with herniation versus 8.4% without (Yang 1981). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit of resection for reoperation in superficial abscesses) — observational, confounded by indication, with excision and aspiration remaining complementary operations chosen by abscess depth, multiplicity and patient state.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. This shelf answers the aspiration-versus-excision question only, on observational data. It does not card antibiotic choice or duration (no comparative numbers were extracted), abscesses treated medically alone (only 10 unselected patients in one series), or deep/multiple abscesses, which the modern comparison explicitly excluded.
cards.source: Synthesis of Eibl T et al. Neurosurgical Focus. 2025 (PMID: 41175405); Yang SY. Journal of Neurosurgery. 1981 (PMID: 7310502); Hakan T et al. The Journal of Infection. 2006 (PMID: 16183134).

shelves.title: Broken collarbone (displaced midshaft clavicle fracture): plate fixation cuts nonunion — 0.8% versus 11% at 9 months in the UK trial, relative risk 0.14 in the meta-analysis — and speeds early function, but final function differs little and second operations are common either way
shelves.question: How is a broken collarbone (clavicle fracture) treated? In adults with a displaced midshaft clavicle fracture, does operative plate fixation beat nonoperative sling treatment on union, function and reoperation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Clavicle/diagnostic imaging · Clavicle/injuries · Disability Evaluation · Female · Fracture Fixation/methods · Fracture Fixation, Internal · Fracture Healing/physiology · Fractures, Closed/diagnostic imaging · Fractures, Closed/surgery · Fractures, Ununited · Humans · Joint Dislocations/surgery · Male · Prospective Studies · Radiography · Range of Motion, Articular/physiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for plate fixation on union and early recovery, with the limits printed beside it. Two multicentre randomised trials and a meta-analysis of six randomised trials agree that fixation markedly reduces nonunion: in the Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society trial (COTS 2007, PMID: 17200303; 132 randomised, 111 completing 1 year), nonunion occurred in 2 operative versus 7 nonoperative patients (p=0.042), symptomatic malunion in 0 versus 9 (p=0.001), and mean time to union was 16.4 versus 28.4 weeks (p=0.001), with Constant and DASH scores significantly better in the operative group at all time-points. In the larger UK Clavicle Trial (Ahrens 2017, PMID: 28816894; 301 randomised), nonunion at 9 months was 0.8% operative versus 11% nonoperative (p<0.001), function and satisfaction were better at 6 weeks and 3 months, and 12 (11%) of 147 nonoperative patients needed secondary surgery. The meta-analysis of six randomised trials (614 patients; Woltz 2017, PMID: 28632595) put the relative risk of nonunion at 0.14 (95% CI 0.06–0.32) with fixation — a relative measure; the absolute rates in the UK trial were 0.8% versus 11% — but found 1-year Constant and DASH advantages of only 4.4 and 5.1 points, judged not clinically relevant, and when plate removals were counted, secondary operations were as common after fixation (17.6%) as after nonoperative care (16.6%; relative risk 1.01). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fixation is the surer route to union and a faster early recovery for a completely displaced fracture, not a guarantee of better final function — and it trades nonunion surgery later for hardware surgery sooner in a similar share of patients.

cards.headline: COTS 2007 (132 randomised): nonunion 2 operative versus 7 nonoperative, symptomatic malunion 0 versus 9, union at 16.4 versus 28.4 weeks, function better at every time-point
cards.summary: COTS 2007 (132 randomised): nonunion 2 operative versus 7 nonoperative, symptomatic malunion 0 versus 9, union at 16.4 versus 28.4 weeks, function better at every time-point
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society, 2007)
cards.people: 132 patients with a displaced midshaft fracture of the clavicle, randomised by sealed envelope to operative plate fixation (67 patients) or nonoperative sling treatment (65 patients) at multiple centres; 111 patients (62 operative, 49 nonoperative) completed 1 year of follow-up. Outcomes: Constant shoulder score, Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) score and plain radiographs; groups did not differ in demographics, mechanism, associated injuries, Injury Severity Score or fracture pattern.
cards.result: Constant and DASH scores were significantly improved in the operative group at all time-points (p=0.001 and p<0.01 respectively). Mean time to radiographic union was 16.4 weeks in the operative group versus 28.4 weeks in the nonoperative group (p=0.001). There were 2 nonunions in the operative group versus 7 in the nonoperative group (p=0.042), and symptomatic malunion developed in 9 nonoperative patients and none in the operative group (p=0.001). Most operative complications were hardware-related (5 patients with local irritation or prominence, 3 wound infections, 1 mechanical failure). At 1 year, operative patients were more likely to be satisfied with the appearance of the shoulder (p=0.001) and with the shoulder in general (p=0.002). The authors concluded the trial supports primary plate fixation of completely displaced midshaft clavicular fractures in active adult patients.
cards.watchOut: Attrition was uneven: 62 of 67 operative but only 49 of 65 nonoperative patients completed 1 year, so the nonunion counts (2 versus 7) are completer counts, not full intention-to-treat rates — the direction is corroborated by the larger UK trial, but this trial's own percentages should not be quoted without that caveat. The abstract reports that function scores were significantly better without printing the score values, so no point differences are claimed from this card.
cards.source: Canadian Orthopaedic Trauma Society. Nonoperative treatment compared with plate fixation of displaced midshaft clavicular fractures. A multicenter, randomized clinical trial. The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery. American Volume. 2007. PMID: 17200303. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Ahrens 2017 — the UK Clavicle Trial (301 randomised): nonunion at 9 months 0.8% operative versus 11% nonoperative (p<0.001); function better at 6 weeks and 3 months; 11% of the nonoperative group needed later surgery
cards.summary: Ahrens 2017 — the UK Clavicle Trial (301 randomised): nonunion at 9 months 0.8% operative versus 11% nonoperative (p<0.001); function better at 6 weeks and 3 months; 11% of the nonoperative group needed later surgery
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (The Clavicle Trial; Ahrens 2017)
cards.people: 301 eligible adult patients with displaced midshaft clavicle fractures randomised to nonoperative management or open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF), followed at 6 weeks, 3 months and 9 months. Primary outcome: radiographic nonunion at 3 months; secondary outcomes: nonunion at 9 months, Constant-Murley and DASH scores, and patient satisfaction. The nonoperative group numbered 147 patients in the secondary-surgery analysis.
cards.result: There was no difference in radiographic nonunion at 3 months (operative 28%, nonoperative 27%), but at 9 months nonunion was significantly lower in the operative group (0.8%) than the nonoperative group (11%) (p<0.001) — an absolute difference of about 10 percentage points. DASH and Constant-Murley scores and patient satisfaction were all significantly better in the operative group at 6 weeks and 3 months. Secondary surgical intervention during the trial period occurred in 12 (11%) of the 147 nonoperative patients. The authors concluded ORIF is a safe and reliable intervention with superior early functional outcomes and should be considered for patients who sustain this injury.
cards.watchOut: The 3-month 'nonunion' rates (28% and 27%) are radiographic non-union at an early time-point — most of those fractures went on to unite by 9 months in both groups — so the 9-month figures (0.8% versus 11%) are the ones that describe established nonunion. The abstract does not report the operative group's own secondary-surgery (including plate removal) rate; the meta-analysis card supplies that comparison. Function advantages are reported as significant at 6 weeks and 3 months, not at 9 months.
cards.source: Ahrens PM, Garlick NI, Barber J, Tims EM; Clavicle Trial Collaborative Group. The Clavicle Trial: A Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Operative with Nonoperative Treatment of Displaced Midshaft Clavicle Fractures. The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery. American Volume. 2017. PMID: 28816894. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Woltz 2017 (meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 614 patients): nonunion relative risk 0.14 with fixation — but 1-year function gains of 4.4–5.1 points were not clinically relevant, and total secondary operations were 17.6% versus 16.6% once plate removal counted
cards.summary: Woltz 2017 (meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 614 patients): nonunion relative risk 0.14 with fixation — but 1-year function gains of 4.4–5.1 points were not clinically relevant, and total secondary operations were 17.6% versus 16.6% once plate removal counted
cards.people: Six randomised controlled trials with 614 patients comparing plate fixation with nonoperative treatment for displaced midshaft clavicular fractures, identified by systematic search of PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase and Web of Science; outcomes were nonunion, shoulder function (Constant and DASH scores) and secondary operations, with risk-of-bias assessment.
cards.result: The risk of nonunion was lower in operatively treated patients (relative risk 0.14, 95% CI 0.06–0.32) — a relative measure; one-third of patients with a nonunion did not receive further treatment. Secondary operations for adverse events were performed less often in operatively treated patients (relative risk 0.42, 95% CI 0.25–0.71), but when plate-removal operations were also included, a secondary operation had been performed in 17.6% of the operative group and 16.6% of the nonoperative group (relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.64–1.59). Constant and DASH scores after 1 year were somewhat better after plate fixation, with mean differences of 4.4 points (95% CI 0.9–7.9) and 5.1 points (95% CI 0.1–10.1) respectively. The authors concluded that plate fixation significantly reduces nonunion risk but has no clinically relevant advantage in final functional outcome, that secondary operations are common after both treatments, and that evidence does not support routine operative treatment for all patients with a displaced midshaft fracture.
cards.watchOut: Six trials and 614 patients is a small meta-analytic base, and its two constituent landmark trials are carded separately above — this card is their pooled reading, not independent evidence. The nonunion relative risk of 0.14 sounds dramatic; against the UK trial's absolute rates (0.8% versus 11%) it means roughly 10 fewer nonunions per 100 fractures fixed, while roughly 18 per 100 fixed patients still came to a second operation once plate removal is counted.
cards.source: Woltz S, Krijnen P, Schipper IB. Plate Fixation Versus Nonoperative Treatment for Displaced Midshaft Clavicular Fractures: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery. American Volume. 2017. PMID: 28632595. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). cards.headline: Synthesis: fixation reliably prevents nonunion and speeds early recovery; it does not buy clearly better final function, and it does not reduce the total chance of a second operation
cards.summary: Synthesis: fixation reliably prevents nonunion and speeds early recovery; it does not buy clearly better final function, and it does not reduce the total chance of a second operation
cards.people: Two multicentre randomised trials (132 patients, COTS 2007; 301 patients, Ahrens 2017) and a meta-analysis of six randomised trials (614 patients; Woltz 2017), all in adults with displaced midshaft clavicle fractures comparing plate fixation with sling/nonoperative care.
cards.result: Nonunion: 2 versus 7 cases among 1-year completers (COTS 2007); 0.8% versus 11% at 9 months (Ahrens 2017); pooled relative risk 0.14 (95% CI 0.06–0.32) (Woltz 2017). Symptomatic malunion: 0 versus 9 (COTS 2007). Speed: union at 16.4 versus 28.4 weeks (COTS 2007); function and satisfaction better at 6 weeks and 3 months (Ahrens 2017). Final function: pooled 1-year advantages of 4.4 (Constant) and 5.1 (DASH) points, judged not clinically relevant (Woltz 2017). Second operations: 11% of nonoperative patients needed later surgery in the UK trial; pooled totals including plate removal were 17.6% operative versus 16.6% nonoperative (Woltz 2017). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real, replicated union and early-recovery benefit for completely displaced fractures, honestly bounded by small final-function differences and a similar overall reoperation burden.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. This shelf is only about displaced midshaft fractures in adults — the fracture pattern both trials randomised. It does not cover undisplaced fractures (usually treated in a sling without controversy), medial or lateral-third fractures, open fractures, or children's clavicle fractures, where remodelling changes the balance. Intramedullary fixation is not compared in any card here.

shelves.title: Cavernoma (cerebral cavernous malformation): no definitive trial of surgery or radiosurgery versus watching — the CARE pilot showed a real trial is feasible, and the cohort comparisons are confounded by selection
shelves.question: I have a cavernoma (cerebral cavernous malformation) — should it be removed surgically or treated with radiosurgery, or is it safer to watch it with scans?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Brain Neoplasms/surgery · Brain Neoplasms/therapy · Female · Hemangioma, Cavernous, Central Nervous System/surgery · Hemangioma, Cavernous, Central Nervous System/therapy · Humans · Ireland · Male · Middle Aged · Neurosurgical Procedures/methods · Pilot Projects · Prospective Studies · Radiosurgery/methods · Technology Assessment, Biomedical · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — stated plainly: there is NO definitive randomised trial of surgery or radiosurgery versus conservative management for cerebral cavernous malformation (cavernoma), and none of the numbers on this shelf comes from one. What exists: (1) the CARE pilot trial (Al-Shahi Salman 2025, PMID: 40820590), which randomised only 72 patients to test whether a definitive trial is feasible — it was (93% retention, 91% adherence) — and found the same number of primary clinical events in both arms (2 of 33 with intervention versus 2 of 34 without), far too few to judge benefit; the authors calculate a definitive trial would need 590–1,900 participants. (2) A systematic comparison of 100 published cohorts (Bubenikova 2022, PMID: 35273070; 8,994 patients) reporting haemorrhage prevention of 97% after surgery, 86% after radiosurgery and 77% with conservative care — figures built from non-randomised series in which patients chosen for surgery differ systematically from patients watched, so the gaps cannot be read as treatment effects. (3) A conservatively managed cohort (PMID: 38624046; 265 patients) quantifying the risk of watching: symptomatic haemorrhage in 19% during follow-up, at about 6.0% per year after a haemorrhagic presentation versus 1.5% per year without one. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — intervention plausibly prevents future haemorrhage in selected patients, but the only randomised evidence is a feasibility pilot with 4 events in total; the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE because the comparative evidence is observational.

cards.headline: CARE pilot 2025 (the only randomised trial): a definitive trial is feasible — but with 2 events in each arm (2 of 33 versus 2 of 34), it says nothing yet about whether intervention helps
cards.summary: CARE pilot 2025 (the only randomised trial): a definitive trial is feasible — but with 2 events in each arm (2 of 33 versus 2 of 34), it says nothing yet about whether intervention helps
cards.type: Pilot randomised controlled trial (CARE, Al-Shahi Salman 2025)
cards.people: 72 adults with cerebral cavernous malformation randomised at UK and Ireland sites (median age 51 years; 57% female; 78% had a prior intracranial haemorrhage and 39% a prior seizure) to medical management plus intervention (36 patients: 12 neurosurgical resection, 24 stereotactic radiosurgery) or medical management alone (36 patients). 511 patients were screened at 28 of 40 sites and 322 were eligible.
cards.result: The pilot met its feasibility aims: retention was 93% (67 patients completed follow-up) and adherence 91%. The primary clinical outcome — symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage or new persistent/progressive non-haemorrhagic focal neurological deficit at least 6 months after randomisation — occurred in 2 of 33 patients in the intervention group and 2 of 34 in the medical-management-alone group (about 6% in each). There were no deaths and no serious adverse events. The investigators estimated a definitive trial would need 590–1,900 participants.
cards.watchOut: A pilot trial is designed to test feasibility, not efficacy: 72 patients and 4 outcome events cannot detect or exclude any plausible treatment effect, and the identical event counts (2 versus 2) must not be read as evidence that intervention does not work. The intervention arm also mixes two different treatments — resection (12 patients) and radiosurgery (24) — so even a larger version of this design answers 'intervene versus watch', not 'which intervention'.
cards.source: Al-Shahi Salman et al. Medical management plus intervention versus medical management alone for cerebral cavernous malformations: the CARE pilot trial. Health Technology Assessment. 2025. PMID: 40820590. Registry ID: ISRCTN41647111. cards.headline: Bubenikova 2022 (100 cohorts, 8,994 patients): haemorrhage prevention reported at 97% after surgery, 86% after radiosurgery and 77% with conservative care — in non-randomised series where the patients chosen for each path differ
cards.summary: Bubenikova 2022 (100 cohorts, 8,994 patients): haemorrhage prevention reported at 97% after surgery, 86% after radiosurgery and 77% with conservative care — in non-randomised series where the patients chosen for each path differ
cards.people: Systematic comparison of 100 published cohorts comprising 8,994 patients with cerebral cavernous malformations and 41,098 person-years of follow-up, grouped by management: surgical resection, stereotactic radiosurgery, conservative management, and natural-history series.
cards.result: Reported efficacy in preventing haemorrhage was 97% for surgical treatment, 86% for radiosurgical treatment and 77% for conservative treatment. The lowest mortality, 1%, was after radiosurgery; the highest rate of persistent morbidity, 22%, was in natural-history series. Deep or brainstem location and a prior haemorrhage were associated with higher bleeding risk. The authors present these as comparisons across the published cohort literature, not as randomised comparisons.
cards.watchOut: Selection bias is the whole story here: surgeons operate on lesions that are reachable and patients who are fit, radiosurgery is chosen for deep lesions, and conservative series include both the lowest-risk incidental lesions and patients too unwell to treat. The 97/86/77% figures describe what happened in differently selected groups — they cannot be subtracted from each other to get a treatment effect, and this card must never be quoted as 'surgery prevents 97% of haemorrhages'.
cards.source: Bubenikova et al. Surgery, radiosurgery and conservative management of cerebral cavernous malformations: a systematic comparison of 100 cohorts. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry. 2022. PMID: 35273070. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic comparison of observational cohorts). cards.headline: Conservative-management cohort 2024 (265 patients watched): symptomatic haemorrhage in 19% during follow-up — about 6.0% per year after a haemorrhagic presentation versus 1.5% per year without one
cards.summary: Conservative-management cohort 2024 (265 patients watched): symptomatic haemorrhage in 19% during follow-up — about 6.0% per year after a haemorrhagic presentation versus 1.5% per year without one
cards.people: 265 patients with cerebral cavernous malformation managed conservatively (without surgery or radiosurgery) and followed in a published cohort study.
cards.result: Symptomatic haemorrhage occurred during follow-up in 51 of 265 patients (19%). The annual bleeding rate was about 6.0% per year in patients whose presentation had been haemorrhagic, versus 1.5% per year in those presenting otherwise; cumulative bleeding risk at 5 and 10 years was 31% and 41% after haemorrhagic presentation versus 7% in the remainder. Only 14 patients (5%) later crossed over to an intervention, and 2 deaths (0.8%) were attributable to the malformation.
cards.watchOut: This card quantifies the risk of the 'watch' strategy; it does not show what surgery would have done in the same patients. The dominant determinant of future bleeding is the past: a lesion that has already bled re-bleeds at roughly four times the annual rate of one that has not — which is why management decisions in this condition turn on presentation and lesion location, not on a single average risk. Author names and MeSH terms for this record were not captured this session and are not printed.

cards.headline: Synthesis: intervention probably prevents some future haemorrhages in selected patients, but the only randomised evidence is a 72-patient feasibility pilot — the honest position is POSSIBLE, pending a definitive trial of 590–1,900 patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: intervention probably prevents some future haemorrhages in selected patients, but the only randomised evidence is a 72-patient feasibility pilot — the honest position is POSSIBLE, pending a definitive trial of 590–1,900 patients
cards.people: Three sources: the CARE pilot randomised trial (72 patients; Al-Shahi Salman 2025), a systematic comparison of 100 observational cohorts (8,994 patients; Bubenikova 2022), and a conservatively managed cohort (265 patients; 2024).
cards.result: Randomised evidence: none on efficacy — the CARE pilot proved a definitive trial feasible (93% retention, 91% adherence) with 2 primary events in each arm and estimated 590–1,900 participants needed. Observational comparisons report haemorrhage prevention of 97% (surgery), 86% (radiosurgery) and 77% (conservative), confounded by selection. The risk being weighed: under conservative management, symptomatic haemorrhage occurred in 19% over follow-up, at about 6.0% per year after haemorrhagic presentation versus 1.5% per year otherwise. PROPOSED POSSIBLE — capped there because the comparative evidence is observational and the single RCT is a pilot.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Nothing on this shelf should be used to promise a patient that surgery or radiosurgery will protect them: no adequately powered randomised trial exists. Lesion location (brainstem/deep versus lobar), prior haemorrhage, and surgical accessibility dominate individual decisions and are exactly the variables the observational comparisons cannot balance.

shelves.title: Cervical spondylosis with radiculopathy: surgery relieved pain faster, but physiotherapy caught up by 1–2 years on most measures in both randomised trials
shelves.question: I have cervical spondylosis with a trapped nerve in my neck (radiculopathy — pain, weakness or numbness down the arm) — is surgery better than physiotherapy or a collar, and does any advantage last?
shelves.mesh: Cervical Vertebrae/surgery · Humans · Orthotic Devices · Pain/surgery · Radiculopathy/surgery · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Spinal Cord Compression/surgery · Spinal Osteophytosis/surgery
shelves.balance: SPLIT (over time) — SCOPE DECLARED: this shelf covers cervical RADICULOPATHY (arm pain, weakness or sensory loss from a spondylotic trapped nerve root in the neck). Cervical myelopathy (spinal cord compression) is a different question — the Cochrane review found only one small myelopathy trial with no differences over 3 years and substantial loss to follow-up — and is not this shelf's subject. The pattern across the radiculopathy trials is consistent: surgery relieves pain faster, and conservative care catches up. The Cochrane review (Nikolaidis 2010, PMID: 20091520) found surgical decompression superior in the short term for pain, weakness and sensory loss versus physiotherapy or a collar, with no significant differences at 1 year — on low/very-low quality evidence from a single trial of 81 patients. That trial (Persson 1997, PMID: 9106315) found surgery gave less early pain than physiotherapy or a collar, but by final follow-up there were no differences in pain, function or mood between the three groups. The later randomised trial (Engquist 2013, PMID: 23778373; 63 patients) found the same shape over 24 months: surgery plus physiotherapy beat physiotherapy alone on neck pain (P=0.039) and on patients rating themselves better at 12 months (87% versus 62%), but disability (NDI) never differed significantly (P=0.23) and the global ratings had converged by 24 months (81% versus 69%, P=0.28). PROPOSED SPLIT: surgery buys speed of relief in the first months; by 1–2 years structured physiotherapy reaches a similar place on most measures.

cards.headline: Nikolaidis 2010 (Cochrane): for radiculopathy, surgery was better short-term for pain, weakness and sensory loss — with no significant differences at 1 year; evidence quality low to very low
cards.summary: Nikolaidis 2010 (Cochrane): for radiculopathy, surgery was better short-term for pain, weakness and sensory loss — with no significant differences at 1 year; evidence quality low to very low
cards.people: The Cochrane review found only 2 randomised trials, 149 patients in total: a radiculopathy trial of 81 patients (surgical decompression versus physiotherapy or cervical collar) and a myelopathy trial of 68 patients with mild neurological deficit (surgery versus conservative care).
cards.result: In the radiculopathy trial, surgical decompression was superior in the short term for pain, weakness and sensory loss compared with physiotherapy or a hard collar, but there were no significant differences between surgery and conservative treatment at 1 year. In the myelopathy trial there were no significant differences between surgery and conservative care over 3 years, with substantial loss to follow-up. Both trials had inadequate allocation concealment and unclear blinding; the reviewers graded the evidence low to very low quality.
cards.watchOut: The radiculopathy conclusion rests on ONE trial of 81 patients (carded separately below) at high risk of bias — the review is a map of how thin this evidence is, not an independent confirmation. The myelopathy trial inside this review is mentioned only to mark the boundary of this shelf's scope; its null result over 3 years in mild myelopathy is a different clinical question.
cards.source: Nikolaidis et al. Surgery for cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010. PMID: 20091520. cards.headline: Persson 1997 (81 patients): surgery gave less pain early — but at final follow-up, surgery, physiotherapy and a collar were indistinguishable on pain, function and mood
cards.summary: Persson 1997 (81 patients): surgery gave less pain early — but at final follow-up, surgery, physiotherapy and a collar were indistinguishable on pain, function and mood
cards.people: 81 patients with cervicobrachial pain for at least 3 months and imaging-verified spondylotic nerve-root compression, randomised to surgery (Cloward technique), individually adapted physiotherapy, or a cervical collar.
cards.result: At the early follow-up, the surgery group had less pain (visual analogue scale) than the other groups, and both surgery and physiotherapy gave better function (Sickness Impact Profile) than the collar. At the final follow-up about a year later, there were no differences between the three groups in pain (VAS), function (SIP) or mood. The authors concluded that all three treatments were equally effective in the long term.
cards.watchOut: 81 patients across three arms (about 27 per group) — the long-term 'no difference' could hide moderate differences in either direction. The surgical technique was the Cloward procedure of the 1990s, and 'physiotherapy' of that era may differ from modern structured programmes. This is the single trial behind the Cochrane radiculopathy conclusion, so the two cards are the same evidence read at two levels.

cards.headline: Engquist 2013 (63 patients, 24 months): surgery plus physiotherapy beat physiotherapy alone on neck pain (P=0.039) but not on disability (P=0.23) — and patients' global ratings converged by 2 years (81% versus 69%)
cards.summary: Engquist 2013 (63 patients, 24 months): surgery plus physiotherapy beat physiotherapy alone on neck pain (P=0.039) but not on disability (P=0.23) — and patients' global ratings converged by 2 years (81% versus 69%)
cards.people: 63 patients with cervical radiculopathy, randomised to anterior cervical decompression and fusion (ACDF) followed by structured physiotherapy (31 patients) or structured physiotherapy alone (32 patients), followed for 24 months.
cards.result: Both groups improved significantly from baseline. The between-group difference in disability (Neck Disability Index) was not significant (P=0.23); neck pain favoured the surgery group over the study period (P=0.039), while arm pain did not differ (P=0.580). Patients rating themselves 'better' or 'much better' were 87% (surgery) versus 62% (physiotherapy) at 12 months (P<0.05), and 81% versus 69% at 24 months (P=0.28). The authors concluded surgery gives faster improvement in the first year, differences decrease by 2 years, and structured physiotherapy should be tried first.
cards.watchOut: 63 patients — the trial can speak to average pain trajectories, not to rare surgical harms or to which individual patients should cross over to surgery. The comparison is surgery PLUS physiotherapy against physiotherapy alone, so the surgical arm also received the structured programme; and patients in the physiotherapy arm who deteriorated could still receive surgery in real practice, which this design measures only as randomised.

neck pain favoured the surgery group over the study period (p=0.039), while arm pain did not differ (p=0.580). patients rating themselves 'better' or 'much better' were 87% (surgery) versus 62% (physiotherapy) at 12 months (p<0.05), and 81% versus 69% at 24 months (p=0.28). the authors concluded surgery gives faster improvement in the first year, differences decrease by 2 years, and structured physiotherapy should be tried first. 63 patients — the trial can speak to average pain trajectories, not to rare surgical harms or to which individual patients should cross over to surgery. the comparison is surgery plus physiotherapy against physiotherapy alone, so the surgical arm also received the structured programme; and patients in the physiotherapy arm who deteriorated could still receive surgery in real practice, which this design measures only as randomised. engquist et al. surgery versus nonsurgical treatment of cervical radiculopathy: a prospective, randomized study comparing surgery plus physiotherapy with physiotherapy alone, with a 2-year follow-up. spine. 2013. pmid: 23778373. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · cervical vertebrae/surgery · combined modality therapy · decompression, surgical/methods · disability evaluation · female · follow-up studies · humans · male · middle aged · neck pain/complications · neck pain/physiopathology · neck pain/therapy · pain/physiopathology · pain measurement/methods · patient dropouts · physical therapy modalities · prospective studies · radiculopathy/complications · radiculopathy/surgery · radiculopathy/therapy · spinal fusion/methods · time factors · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Synthesis: surgery relieves radiculopathy pain faster; structured conservative care catches up by 1–2 years on most measures — a speed-versus-patience trade-off, not a cure-versus-failure one
cards.summary: Synthesis: surgery relieves radiculopathy pain faster; structured conservative care catches up by 1–2 years on most measures — a speed-versus-patience trade-off, not a cure-versus-failure one
cards.people: Three sources: the Cochrane review (2 trials, 149 patients; Nikolaidis 2010), the randomised three-arm trial behind its radiculopathy conclusion (81 patients; Persson 1997), and a later randomised trial of surgery plus physiotherapy versus physiotherapy alone (63 patients, 24 months; Engquist 2013).
cards.result: Short term: surgery superior for pain, weakness and sensory loss (Cochrane, on one 81-patient trial); surgery gave less early pain than physiotherapy or collar (Persson 1997); surgery plus physiotherapy beat physiotherapy alone on neck pain over 24 months (P=0.039) and on global improvement at 12 months (87% versus 62%) (Engquist 2013). Longer term: no significant differences at 1 year in the Cochrane summary or at Persson's final follow-up; disability never differed significantly (P=0.23) and global ratings converged by 24 months (81% versus 69%, P=0.28) in Engquist. PROPOSED SPLIT — by time horizon: an early advantage to surgery that conservative care matches by 1–2 years on most outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: cervical radiculopathy from spondylosis only. Progressive motor weakness, myelopathy (cord compression), and fracture/instability are surgical indications outside this comparison. The entire randomised record is 144 radiculopathy patients across two trials, both at meaningful risk of bias; the consistent time-pattern across both is what carries the stamp, not any single p-value.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nikolaidis et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010 (PMID: 20091520); Persson et al. Spine. 1997 (PMID: 9106315); Engquist et al. Spine. 2013 (PMID: 23778373).

shelves.title: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A: ascorbic acid (vitamin C) made no difference in six randomised trials — and one combination drug (PXT3003) showed a small benefit in a single manufacturer-run trial
shelves.question: I have Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A — does ascorbic acid (vitamin C) slow the neuropathy down, and has any other drug treatment been shown to help?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Ascorbic Acid/therapeutic use · Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease/drug therapy · Charcot-Marie-Tooth Disease/genetics · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: (the treatment made no difference) — for ascorbic acid, this is one of the cleanest negative records in this library: six randomised trials of oral ascorbic acid (vitamin C, 1–4 g/day) versus placebo in Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1A (CMT1A), gathered in a Cochrane review (Gess 2015, PMID: 26662471; 5 adult trials, 622 participants), with high-quality evidence of no improvement in the CMT Neuropathy Score at 12 months (mean difference −0.37, 95% CI −0.83 to 0.09; 5 studies, 533 participants) or 24 months (mean difference −0.21, 95% CI −0.81 to 0.39; 3 studies, 388 participants), and no clinical benefit in the one children's trial (80 children). The two largest trials agree individually: CMT-TRIAAL/CMT-TRAUK (Pareyson 2011, PMID: 21393063; 277 randomised, 1.5 g/day for 24 months) found CMTNS worsening of 0.2 points in both arms (mean difference 0.0, 95% CI −0.6 to 0.7; p=0.93), and the 4 g/day futility trial (Lewis 2013, PMID: 23797954; 110 randomised) found the placebo group numerically did better than the ascorbic-acid group (−0.92 versus −0.21 CMTNS change), with both arms faring better than natural history — a placebo/context effect, not a drug effect. Adverse effects did not differ from placebo: ascorbic acid is safe here, it simply does not work. The one positive signal on this shelf is a different treatment: PXT3003 (a fixed combination of baclofen, naltrexone and D-sorbitol) improved the Overall Neuropathy Limitations Scale by a mean of −0.37 points versus placebo (97.5% CI −0.68 to −0.06; p=0.008) in a single phase 3 trial (Attarian 2021, PMID: 34656144; 323 patients) whose high-dose arm was disrupted by a formulation defect and whose authors were all paid consultants of, or funded by, the manufacturer. PROPOSED: (the treatment made no difference) for ascorbic acid at any tested dose; POSSIBLE for PXT3003, pending independent replication.

cards.headline: Gess 2015 (Cochrane): high-quality evidence of NO improvement from ascorbic acid in CMT1A — CMTNS mean difference −0.37 at 12 months and −0.21 at 24 months, both confidence intervals crossing zero
cards.summary: Gess 2015 (Cochrane): high-quality evidence of NO improvement from ascorbic acid in CMT1A — CMTNS mean difference −0.37 at 12 months and −0.21 at 24 months, both confidence intervals crossing zero
cards.people: 6 randomised trials of oral ascorbic acid (1–4 g/day) versus placebo in CMT1A: 5 trials in adults with 622 participants, and 1 trial in 80 children. Primary outcome: the CMT Neuropathy Score (CMTNS).
cards.result: There was high-quality evidence of no improvement in CMTNS: mean difference −0.37 points (95% CI −0.83 to 0.09) at 12 months (5 studies, 533 participants) and −0.21 points (95% CI −0.81 to 0.39) at 24 months (3 studies, 388 participants) — both estimates near zero with intervals excluding any meaningful benefit. The nine-hole peg test was slightly faster on ascorbic acid (mean difference −1.16 seconds, 95% CI −1.96 to −0.37), an effect the reviewers judged probably too small to matter clinically. The children's trial showed no clinical benefit (low-quality evidence). Adverse effects did not differ between ascorbic acid and placebo.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's load-bearing card: a null result is only as good as the trials inside it, and here they are consistent, placebo-controlled, and total over 600 adults — the confidence intervals are narrow enough to exclude the benefit the mouse data promised. The single nominally positive secondary measure (nine-hole peg, about one second) is the kind of isolated finding that multiple testing produces; the reviewers themselves discounted it.
cards.source: Gess et al. Ascorbic acid for the treatment of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015. PMID: 26662471. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review; review identifier CD011952). cards.headline: Pareyson 2011 (CMT-TRIAAL/CMT-TRAUK, 277 randomised): CMTNS worsened by exactly 0.2 points on both ascorbic acid 1.5 g/day and placebo over 24 months — mean difference 0.0 (p=0.93)
cards.summary: Pareyson 2011 (CMT-TRIAAL/CMT-TRAUK, 277 randomised): CMTNS worsened by exactly 0.2 points on both ascorbic acid 1.5 g/day and placebo over 24 months — mean difference 0.0 (p=0.93)
cards.people: 277 adults aged 18–70 years with symptomatic CMT1A randomised at 9 centres in Italy and the UK to ascorbic acid 1.5 g/day (138 analysed) or placebo (133 analysed) for 24 months; 271 patients were analysed and 89% completed the trial.
cards.result: The primary outcome, change in CMT Neuropathy Score over 24 months, was identical: worsening of 0.2 points (SD 2.8) on ascorbic acid versus 0.2 points (SD 2.7) on placebo — mean difference 0.0 (95% CI −0.6 to 0.7; p=0.93). No secondary outcome differed between the groups. There were 21 serious adverse events in 20 patients (8 on ascorbic acid, 13 on placebo). The authors concluded ascorbic acid did not improve the course of CMT1A.
cards.watchOut: This trial tested 1.5 g/day — the dose the later 4 g/day futility trial (next card) was designed to check after this null. Two years may be short in a disease that progresses slowly, but the point estimate is exactly 0.0 with a confidence interval of ±0.65 points: a clinically useful effect hiding inside this trial is very unlikely.

cards.headline: Lewis 2013 (4 g/day futility trial, 110 randomised): placebo patients improved MORE than ascorbic-acid patients (−0.92 versus −0.21 CMTNS points) — and both beat natural history (+1.33), exposing a trial-participation effect
cards.summary: Lewis 2013 (4 g/day futility trial, 110 randomised): placebo patients improved MORE than ascorbic-acid patients (−0.92 versus −0.21 CMTNS points) — and both beat natural history (+1.33), exposing a trial-participation effect
cards.people: 110 subjects with CMT1A aged 13–70 years at 3 US referral centres, randomised double-masked 4:1 to oral ascorbic acid 4 g/day (87 subjects) or matching placebo (23 subjects) for 2 years, in a futility design against a natural-history comparison; 69 ascorbic-acid and 16 placebo subjects completed the study.
cards.result: Mean 2-year change in CMTNS was −0.21 points in the ascorbic-acid group and −0.92 in the placebo group — both better than the natural-history change of +1.33. Because the ascorbic-acid result was well below the prespecified 50% reduction in worsening relative to natural history, futility could not formally be declared (P>.99) — but the authors concluded the results make it unlikely that a larger trial of 4 g/day ascorbic acid would show a clinically meaningful effect. Two ascorbic-acid subjects and one placebo subject withdrew because of adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: The 4:1 allocation left only 23 placebo patients (16 completing), so this trial alone is imprecise — its role is dose confirmation beside Pareyson and the Cochrane pooling. The instructive finding is that BOTH randomised arms improved against natural history: trial participation itself (attention, measurement, expectation) moved the score more than the drug did, which is exactly why the uncontrolled 'it helped me' experience cannot be trusted in this disease.
cards.source: Lewis RA, McDermott MP, Herrmann DN, Hoke A, Clawson LL, Siskind C, Feely SME, Miller LJ, Barohn RJ, Smith P, Luebbe E, Wu X, Shy ME; Muscle Study Group. cards.headline: Attarian 2021 (PXT3003 phase 3, 323 patients): a small but significant disability benefit — ONLS mean difference −0.37 points (p=0.008) — in a trial whose high-dose arm was disrupted by a formulation defect, with all authors tied to the manufacturer
cards.summary: Attarian 2021 (PXT3003 phase 3, 323 patients): a small but significant disability benefit — ONLS mean difference −0.37 points (p=0.008) — in a trial whose high-dose arm was disrupted by a formulation defect, with all authors tied to the manufacturer
cards.people: 323 subjects with mild-to-moderate CMT1A randomised 1:1:1 to high-dose PXT3003 (baclofen 6 mg, naltrexone 0.70 mg, D-sorbitol 210 mg), low-dose PXT3003 (half those amounts), or placebo, each taken twice daily for up to 15 months. PXT3003 is a fixed combination product of Pharnext.
cards.result: The high-dose arm was discontinued early because crystals formed in the formulation, causing a high discontinuation rate and requiring a modified full analysis set. In that analysis, high-dose PXT3003 improved the Overall Neuropathy Limitations Scale (ONLS) total score versus placebo by a mean difference of −0.37 points (97.5% CI −0.68 to −0.06; p=0.008). Both doses were reported as safe and well tolerated. The record notes that all authors were paid consultants of, or at institutions funded by, Pharnext, the manufacturer.
cards.watchOut: Handle with care: the analysed high-dose arm is the arm that broke (crystal formation, early discontinuation, modified analysis set), the effect is small (−0.37 points on a disability scale), the trial is single and manufacturer-run with every author conflicted, and the trial's registry identifier was not captured from the record this session. This is a POSSIBLE signal awaiting independent replication — it does not disturb the shelf's ascorbic-acid verdict, and it is not yet a basis for promising patients a treatment.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ascorbic acid for CMT1A is settled — six randomised trials, no benefit at 1.5 g or 4 g, in adults or children; the only live question is whether PXT3003's small single-trial signal replicates
cards.summary: Synthesis: ascorbic acid for CMT1A is settled — six randomised trials, no benefit at 1.5 g or 4 g, in adults or children; the only live question is whether PXT3003's small single-trial signal replicates
cards.people: Five sources carded: the Cochrane review of 6 ascorbic-acid RCTs (Gess 2015), the two largest ascorbic-acid trials (Pareyson 2011, 277 patients; Lewis 2013, 110 patients), and the single PXT3003 phase 3 trial (Attarian 2021, 323 patients).
cards.result: Ascorbic acid versus placebo on CMTNS: mean difference −0.37 (95% CI −0.83 to 0.09) at 12 months and −0.21 (−0.81 to 0.39) at 24 months (Cochrane, high-quality evidence); 0.0 (−0.6 to 0.7) in the largest trial at 1.5 g/day; placebo numerically superior at 4 g/day. No benefit in children; no excess adverse effects. PXT3003 high dose versus placebo on ONLS: −0.37 points (97.5% CI −0.68 to −0.06; p=0.008) in one manufacturer-run trial with a disrupted high-dose arm. PROPOSED (the treatment made no difference) for ascorbic acid; POSSIBLE for PXT3003.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: CMT1A only — nothing here covers other CMT types, where no comparable trial record was carded. Supportive care (physiotherapy, orthotics, foot surgery) is outside this drug shelf. The ascorbic-acid verdict is as firm as negative verdicts get in this library: multiple adequately sized blinded trials with concordant null results and narrow confidence intervals.

synthesis five sources carded: the cochrane review of 6 ascorbic-acid rcts (gess 2015), the two largest ascorbic-acid trials (pareyson 2011, 277 patients; lewis 2013, 110 patients), and the single pxt3003 phase 3 trial (attarian 2021, 323 patients). ascorbic acid versus placebo on cmtns: mean difference −0.37 (95% ci −0.83 to 0.09) at 12 months and −0.21 (−0.81 to 0.39) at 24 months (cochrane, high-quality evidence); 0.0 (−0.6 to 0.7) in the largest trial at 1.5 g/day; placebo numerically superior at 4 g/day. no benefit in children; no excess adverse effects. pxt3003 high dose versus placebo on onls: −0.37 points (97.5% ci −0.68 to −0.06; p=0.008) in one manufacturer-run trial with a disrupted high-dose arm. proposed (the treatment made no difference) for ascorbic acid; possible for pxt3003. tier c — the developer's personal verdict. scope: cmt1a only — nothing here covers other cmt types, where no comparable trial record was carded. supportive care (physiotherapy, orthotics, foot surgery) is outside this drug shelf. the ascorbic-acid verdict is as firm as negative verdicts get in this library: multiple adequately sized blinded trials with concordant null results and narrow confidence intervals. synthesis of gess et al. cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015 (pmid: 26662471); pareyson et al. the lancet neurology. 2011 (pmid: 21393063); lewis ra et al. jama neurology. 2013 (pmid: 23797954); attarian et al. orphanet journal of rare diseases. 2021 (pmid: 34656144).

shelves.title: Chiari malformation type I with syringomyelia: adding tonsil resection or reduction to decompression improved syrinx shrinkage across observational series — clinical improvement did not differ, and no randomised trial exists
shelves.question: I have Chiari malformation type I with a syrinx (syringomyelia) and am having decompression surgery — does also reducing or removing the cerebellar tonsils give a better result than decompression alone?
shelves.mesh: Arnold-Chiari Malformation/surgery · Decompression, Surgical/methods · Humans · Neurosurgical Procedures/methods · Syringomyelia/diagnostic imaging · Syringomyelia/surgery · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — every number on this shelf is observational: there is NO randomised trial of posterior fossa decompression techniques for Chiari malformation type I (CM-I) with syringomyelia, and the comparisons below come from retrospective series in which the choice of technique was the surgeon's, not chance. The consistent direction: adding cerebellar tonsil work (resection or reduction) to decompression shrinks the syrinx more. In a retrospective comparison of 162 patients (Zhang 2025, PMID: 40098683), decompression with tonsil resection beat decompression alone on 6-month favourable-outcome rates (78.8% versus 56.9% on the Chicago Chiari Outcome Scale) and syrinx recovery (76% versus 55.2%), with no significant difference in complications. A radiological meta-analysis of 20 studies and 3,063 patients (Prasad 2025, PMID: 41111088) found tonsillar reduction modestly superior to decompression with duraplasty on the syrinx-to-cord ratio (mean difference 0.04) — statistically detectable, clinically small. The largest series, a propensity-matched single-centre cohort of 1,231 patients (Yuan 2026, PMID: 42080534), found syrinx regression over 50% in 78% with a tonsil-resecting modified decompression versus 60% with standard decompression with duraplasty, and far fewer revision operations (4.1% versus 15.5%) — while clinical improvement did not differ significantly between techniques. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: tonsil resection/reduction probably improves syrinx resolution and reduces re-operation, on consistent but non-randomised evidence; whether patients feel better is not shown to differ.

cards.headline: Zhang 2025 (162 patients, retrospective): decompression WITH tonsil resection beat decompression alone — favourable outcome 78.8% versus 56.9%, syrinx recovery 76% versus 55.2% at 6 months, complications not significantly different
cards.summary: Zhang 2025 (162 patients, retrospective): decompression WITH tonsil resection beat decompression alone — favourable outcome 78.8% versus 56.9%, syrinx recovery 76% versus 55.2% at 6 months, complications not significantly different
cards.people: 162 patients with Chiari malformation type I and syringomyelia operated on at a single hospital in Xuzhou, China (2017–2022): 58 had posterior fossa decompression (PFD) alone and 104 had posterior fossa decompression with resection of the cerebellar tonsils (PFDRT). Outcomes at 6 months: Chicago Chiari Outcome Scale (CCOS) and MRI assessment of the syrinx.
cards.result: At 6 months, the rate of favourable prognosis (CCOS) was 56.9% after PFD versus 78.8% after PFDRT, and syringomyelia recovery rates were 55.2% versus 76% — both differences statistically significant (p<0.05). Complication rates (fever, cerebrospinal fluid leak, intracranial infection, incision infection) did not differ significantly between the groups (p>0.05). The authors concluded PFDRT gives superior syrinx improvement and favourable prognosis at comparable complication rates.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and single-centre: the 58-versus-104 split reflects surgeon preference and era, not randomisation, and patients chosen for tonsil resection may have had larger syrinxes or different anatomy. Six months is early follow-up for a condition followed for years. The record's MeSH terms were not captured this session and are not printed.

cards.headline: Prasad 2025 (meta-analysis, 20 studies, 3,063 patients): both decompression with duraplasty and tonsillar reduction shrink the syrinx; tonsillar reduction's edge on syrinx-to-cord ratio was 0.04 — real but small
cards.summary: Prasad 2025 (meta-analysis, 20 studies, 3,063 patients): both decompression with duraplasty and tonsillar reduction shrink the syrinx; tonsillar reduction's edge on syrinx-to-cord ratio was 0.04 — real but small
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Prasad 2025)
cards.people: Systematic review and radiological meta-analysis of 20 studies (studies with fewer than 5 patients excluded) totalling 3,063 patients with Chiari malformation type I and syringomyelia, comparing posterior fossa decompression with duraplasty (PFDD) against decompression with tonsillar reduction/resection.
cards.result: PFDD reduced syrinx width by a pooled mean of 2.46 mm, syrinx length by 1.68 vertebral segments, and the syrinx-to-cord ratio by 0.21. Decompression with tonsillar reduction reduced syrinx width by a pooled mean of 2.85 mm and was superior to PFDD on the syrinx-to-cord ratio by a mean difference of 0.04 (95% CI 0.01–0.08) — a statistically significant but small radiological advantage, which the authors note has limited clinical significance.
cards.watchOut: A meta-analysis of retrospective series inherits every bias of its parts — pooling 3,063 non-randomised patients produces a precise number, not a true one. The outcomes pooled here are radiological (millimetres of syrinx), and the between-technique difference that survives pooling is 0.04 of a ratio: this card supports 'tonsil work shrinks syrinxes a bit more', not 'patients do better'.

cards.headline: Yuan 2026 (1,231 patients, propensity-matched): the tonsil-resecting modified decompression gave more syrinx regression (78% versus 60% over 50% shrinkage) and far fewer revisions (4.1% versus 15.5%) — but clinical improvement did not differ
cards.summary: Yuan 2026 (1,231 patients, propensity-matched): the tonsil-resecting modified decompression gave more syrinx regression (78% versus 60% over 50% shrinkage) and far fewer revisions (4.1% versus 15.5%) — but clinical improvement did not differ
cards.people: 1,231 adults with Chiari malformation type I and syringomyelia treated at a single Beijing centre (2003–2024): 310 (25.2%) had standard posterior fossa decompression with duraplasty (PFDD) and 921 (74.8%) had foramen magnum and foramen of Magendie dredging (FMMD), a modified decompression with tonsil resection; propensity-score matching was used to balance baseline characteristics.
cards.result: Syrinx regression of more than 50% occurred in 78% of FMMD patients versus 60% of PFDD patients (P<.001). Revision surgery was required in 4.1% of FMMD versus 15.5% of PFDD patients (log-rank P<.001). FMMD did not increase complications (P>.05). However, PFDD was noninferior to FMMD on clinical improvement (P=.147) and on syrinx regression treated as a continuous outcome (P=.169) — the techniques separated on the dichotomised syrinx endpoint and on re-operation, not on how patients clinically improved.
cards.watchOut: The largest series here and still not randomised: propensity matching balances measured variables only, and a 21-year single-centre span (2003–2024) means technique, imaging and surgeon experience all drifted together. Note the internal tension the authors themselves report — the headline syrinx endpoint favours FMMD while clinical improvement does not significantly differ; a reader who quotes only the 78% versus 60% figure is overstating what this study found. The record's MeSH terms were not captured this session and are not printed.

cards.headline: Synthesis: tonsil resection or reduction added to decompression consistently shrinks the syrinx more and may reduce re-operation — but no study is randomised, and clinical improvement has not been shown to differ
cards.summary: Synthesis: tonsil resection or reduction added to decompression consistently shrinks the syrinx more and may reduce re-operation — but no study is randomised, and clinical improvement has not been shown to differ
cards.people: Three observational sources: a retrospective comparison (162 patients; Zhang 2025), a meta-analysis of 20 observational studies (3,063 patients; Prasad 2025), and a propensity-matched cohort (1,231 patients; Yuan 2026).
cards.result: Syrinx outcomes favour adding tonsil work: recovery 76% versus 55.2% and favourable clinical-scale outcome 78.8% versus 56.9% at 6 months (Zhang 2025); pooled syrinx-to-cord advantage of 0.04 for tonsillar reduction (Prasad 2025); syrinx regression over 50% in 78% versus 60% and revision surgery 4.1% versus 15.5% (Yuan 2026). Against a stronger claim: complications did not differ in any source, and the largest cohort found clinical improvement statistically indistinguishable between techniques (Yuan 2026). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — consistent direction across three observational sources, capped at POSSIBLE because no randomised trial exists.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: adults/patients with Chiari I WITH syringomyelia undergoing posterior fossa decompression — these studies do not address Chiari I without a syrinx, children as a separate group, or decompression without duraplasty versus with it as an isolated question. Syrinx size is a radiological surrogate; the outcome patients feel — pain, function — is exactly where the largest study found no significant difference.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zhang L et al. Frontiers in Neurology. 2025 (PMID: 40098683); Prasad et al. Neurosurgical Review. 2025 (PMID: 41111088); Yuan C et al. Neurosurgery. 2026 (PMID: 42080534).

shelves.title: Childhood cataracts (IATS): after surgery for a one-sided congenital cataract in infancy, a contact lens gave the same vision as an implanted lens at 1 year and at 4½ years — with far fewer adverse events and reoperations
shelves.question: My baby has a cataract in one eye — after the cataract is removed in infancy, is it better to implant an artificial lens straight away or to correct the eye with a contact lens, in terms of vision, complications and further operations?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aphakia/congenital · Cataract/congenital · Cataract Extraction/methods · Contact Lenses/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Infant · Lens Implantation, Intraocular/methods · Lenses, Intraocular · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity/physiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — vision (the treatment made no difference), with fewer harms on contact lens: the single randomised trial behind this question, the Infant Aphakia Treatment Study (IATS, 114 infants with a unilateral congenital cataract, surgery at 1–6 months, 12 US sites, NCT00212134), found identical median visual acuity in the two groups at age 4½ years (both 0.90 logMAR, 20/159; P=.54; Lambert 2014, PMID: 24604348) and no significant difference in grating acuity at 1 year (contact lens 0.80 vs IOL 0.97 logMAR; P=.19). The difference was in harm and reoperation: by age 5, at least one adverse event had occurred in 81% of the IOL group versus 56% of the contact-lens group (P=.02), and at least one additional intraocular operation in 72% versus 21% (P<.001) (Lambert 2014; Plager 2014, PMID: 25077835). Glaucoma or glaucoma suspect did not differ (35% contact lens vs 28% IOL; P=.55). The trial's own recommendation: leave infants under 7 months aphakic and correct with a contact lens, reserving primary IOL implantation for infants in whom contact-lens handling would likely leave the eye uncorrected for long periods. BOUNDARY: this shelf covers unilateral congenital cataract operated on before 7 months of age — the IATS population. It does not cover bilateral cataracts, cataract surgery in older children, or traumatic cataract, where the balance may differ and no comparable randomised trial was carded here.

cards.headline: IATS at 1 year (Lambert 2010): grating acuity did not differ (0.80 contact lens vs 0.97 logMAR IOL; P=.19) — but additional intraocular operations were 63% with an IOL versus 12% with a contact lens
cards.summary: IATS at 1 year (Lambert 2010): grating acuity did not differ (0.80 contact lens vs 0.97 logMAR IOL; P=.19) — but additional intraocular operations were 63% with an IOL versus 12% with a contact lens
cards.type: Randomised multicentre clinical trial, 1-year report (Infant Aphakia Treatment Study Group / Lambert 2010)
cards.people: 114 infants with a unilateral congenital cataract at 12 US sites, randomly assigned to cataract surgery between 1 and 6 months of age with primary intraocular lens (IOL) implantation (n=57) or without an IOL, the aphakic eye corrected with a contact lens (n=57); grating visual acuity tested at 1 year of age by a masked travelling examiner.
cards.result: Median logMAR grating visual acuity at 1 year was not significantly different between the treated eyes (contact lens 0.80; IOL 0.97; P=.19). Intraoperative complications occurred in 28% of the IOL group versus 11% of the contact-lens group; by 1 year, adverse events had occurred in 77% versus 25%, and one or more additional intraocular operations had been performed in 63% of the IOL group versus 12% of the contact-lens group (P<.001). The authors concluded that caution should be exercised with IOL implantation at 6 months or younger, given the higher incidence of adverse events and the absence of an improved short-term visual outcome compared with contact-lens use.
cards.watchOut: Grating acuity at 1 year is a crude, preferential-looking measure, not the letter acuity a child will live with — which is why the 4½-year optotype result (next card) carries the vision question. The figures on this card were taken from the trial report as reproduced in this session's fetched sources; the PubMed page for this report could not be opened this session, so its MeSH is recorded as not captured rather than reconstructed.

cards.headline: IATS at 4½–5 years (Lambert 2014): median vision identical in both groups (0.90 logMAR, 20/159; P=.54) — adverse events 81% IOL versus 56% contact lens, additional surgery 72% versus 21%
cards.summary: IATS at 4½–5 years (Lambert 2014): median vision identical in both groups (0.90 logMAR, 20/159; P=.54) — adverse events 81% IOL versus 56% contact lens, additional surgery 72% versus 21%
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial, 4½-year acuity and 5-year clinical findings (Infant Aphakia Treatment Study Group / Lambert 2014)
cards.people: The same 114 infants with unilateral congenital cataracts randomised in IATS at 12 sites, with 5 years of follow-up; a travelling examiner assessed HOTV optotype visual acuity at age 4½ years.
cards.result: Median logMAR visual acuity of the treated eye was not significantly different between groups (both 0.90 [20/159]; P=.54), and about 50% of treated eyes in both groups had visual acuity of 20/200 or worse. Significantly more IOL patients had at least one adverse event after cataract surgery (IOL 81% vs contact lens 56%; P=.02) — most commonly lens reproliferation into the visual axis, pupillary membranes and corectopia — and significantly more had at least one additional intraocular surgery (IOL 72% vs contact lens 21%; P<.001). Glaucoma/glaucoma suspect occurred in 35% of contact-lens eyes versus 28% of IOL eyes (P=.55). The authors recommend leaving an infant under 7 months aphakic and focusing the eye with a contact lens, reserving primary IOL implantation for infants in whom contact-lens cost and handling would otherwise cause significant periods of uncorrected aphakia.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 114 infants, one comparison — the vision null is consistent at 1 year and 4½ years, but the trial was not powered to exclude modest acuity differences, and median acuity of 20/159 in both groups is a reminder that unilateral congenital cataract carries a poor visual prognosis whichever correction is chosen. Contact-lens success also depends on families actually achieving daily lens wear, which a trial with intensive support may flatter.

cards.headline: IATS complications in depth (Plager 2014): intraoperative complications 28% versus 11%, adverse events 81% versus 56%, additional intraocular surgeries 72% versus 16% over the first 5 years
cards.summary: IATS complications in depth (Plager 2014): intraoperative complications 28% versus 11%, adverse events 81% versus 56%, additional intraocular surgeries 72% versus 16% over the first 5 years
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial, complications analysis of IATS (Plager 2014)
cards.people: All 114 infants enrolled in IATS (unilateral aphakia, surgery under 7 months of age, 12 centres), comparing primary IOL implantation with contact-lens correction over the first 5 postoperative years for intraoperative complications, adverse events and additional intraocular surgeries.
cards.result: More IOL patients had intraoperative complications (28% vs 11%; P=.031), adverse events (81% vs 56%; P=.008) and additional intraocular surgeries (72% vs 16%; P<.0001) than contact-lens patients. The timing differed: the number of contact-lens patients with adverse events rose in postoperative years 2–5 (from 15 to 24 patients) while the IOL count fell (from 44 to 14). The authors note that if half the aphakic group eventually undergoes secondary IOL implantation, the total number of additional intraocular surgeries in the two groups will be approximately equal — and conclude that the increased complication burden militates toward leaving babies aphakic where the family is likely to succeed with a contact lens.
cards.watchOut: This is a second report on the same 114 children as the other two cards, not an independent trial — the shelf's whole randomised record is this one study, which is why the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. The 'eventually equal operations' caveat matters: part of the contact-lens group's surgical advantage is deferred, not avoided, if a secondary implant follows later in childhood.
cards.source: Plager DA, Lynn MJ, Buckley EG, Wilson ME, Lambert SR; Infant Aphakia Treatment Study Group. Complications in the first 5 years following cataract surgery in infants with and without intraocular lens implantation in the Infant Aphakia Treatment Study. American Journal of Ophthalmology. 2014. PMID: 25077835. Registry ID: NCT00212134. cards.headline: Synthesis: same vision either way in the only randomised trial — the choice is decided by complications, reoperations and whether a family can sustain contact-lens wear
cards.summary: Synthesis: same vision either way in the only randomised trial — the choice is decided by complications, reoperations and whether a family can sustain contact-lens wear
cards.people: One randomised trial programme (IATS, 114 infants, NCT00212134) reported at 1 year (Lambert 2010), at 4½–5 years (Lambert 2014) and in a dedicated complications analysis (Plager 2014).
cards.result: Vision: no significant difference at 1 year (grating acuity 0.80 vs 0.97 logMAR; P=.19) and identical medians at 4½ years (both 0.90 logMAR [20/159]; P=.54). Harm and reoperation: consistently and significantly higher with primary IOL implantation — adverse events 81% vs 56% and additional intraocular surgery 72% vs 21% by age 5 — while glaucoma/glaucoma suspect did not differ (35% vs 28%; P=.55). PROPOSED POSSIBLE: contact-lens correction after infant unilateral cataract surgery matches primary IOL implantation on vision and beats it on early complications in this single trial; primary IOL remains the trial authors' fallback where contact-lens correction would foreseeably fail.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. This shelf answers only the aphakia-correction question for unilateral congenital cataract operated on before 7 months. It says nothing about when cataract surgery itself should be timed within infancy, about bilateral cataracts, or about surgery in older children — no randomised evidence on those questions was carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lambert SR et al. Archives of Ophthalmology. 2010 (PMID: 20457949); Infant Aphakia Treatment Study Group. JAMA Ophthalmology. 2014 (PMID: 24604348); Plager DA et al. American Journal of Ophthalmology. 2014 (PMID: 25077835).
