shelves.title: Chipped, broken or cracked tooth: cracked teeth restored without covering the cusps failed more (pulpal complications relative risk 3.2, extraction relative risk 8.1 versus full crowns in pooled observational data) — and repairing a defective filling performed no worse than replacing it over seven years
shelves.question: I have chipped, broken or cracked a tooth — should it be repaired, crowned or replaced, and if the pulp is exposed can it be capped rather than having root canal treatment?
shelves.mesh: Cracked Tooth Syndrome · Crowns · Dental Restoration, Permanent · Humans · Root Canal Therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the comparative record is mostly observational, with one modern randomised pulp-therapy trial. For cracked teeth keeping a vital pulp, the systematic review and meta-analysis of 27 studies (Zhang 2024, PMID: 38272437) found tooth survival of 92.8–97.8% at 1–6 years, but direct restorations without cuspal coverage carried a relative risk of pulpal complications of 3.2 (95% CI 1.51–6.82) and of tooth extraction of 8.1 (95% CI 1.05–62.5) compared with full-crown restorations — relative measures from observational studies, with wide intervals. For a defective existing restoration, a prospective comparative study of 113 restorations followed for seven years (Gordan 2011, PMID: 21719808) found degradation in every group including full replacement, with no significant difference in failure rate — supporting repair over replacement for localised defects. For pulp exposure (studied in carious, not traumatic, exposures), a double-blind randomised trial of 140 teeth (Taha 2025, PMID: 40617285) found 1-year success of 91.5% for partial pulpotomy versus 81.3% for direct pulp capping, a difference that was not significant (P=.08). BOUNDARY: toothache pain relief itself is homed on Shelf #5287 and is not re-carded here; this shelf is about restoring and keeping the tooth.

cards.headline: Cracked teeth meta-analysis (Zhang 2024): vital cracked teeth survived 92.8–97.8% — but a direct filling without cuspal coverage carried relative risk 3.2 for pulpal complications and 8.1 for extraction versus a full crown
cards.summary: Cracked teeth meta-analysis (Zhang 2024): vital cracked teeth survived 92.8–97.8% — but a direct filling without cuspal coverage carried relative risk 3.2 for pulpal complications and 8.1 for extraction versus a full crown
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cracked-tooth treatment outcomes (Zhang 2024)
cards.people: 27 studies (26 in the meta-analysis) of cracked teeth retaining vital pulp (CT-VDP) or undergoing root canal treatment (CT-RCT), each with at least one year of follow-up, reporting tooth survival rate (TSR), pulp survival rate (PSR) and success rate (SR); risk of bias assessed with the Newcastle-Ottawa scale (observational studies).
cards.result: Success of monitoring without restorative treatment was 80% at three years. For vital cracked teeth, TSR was 92.8–97.8% at 1–6 years, PSR 85.6–90.4% at 1–3 years and SR 80.6–89.9% at 1–3 years; for root-treated cracked teeth, TSR was 90.5–91.1% at 1–2 years and SR 83.0–91.2% at 1–4 years. Direct restorations without cuspal coverage increased the relative risk of pulpal complications (RR 3.2, 95% CI 1.51–6.82; P=0.002) and of tooth extraction (RR 8.1, 95% CI 1.05–62.5; P=0.045) compared with full-crown restorations in vital cracked teeth; root-treated cracked teeth without full-crown restorations had an 11.3-fold higher risk of extraction than crowned ones (P<0.001). The authors recommend full-crown restorations for symptomatic cracked teeth and for root-treated cracked teeth.
cards.watchOut: Every number here comes from observational cohorts, not randomised trials: dentists choose crowns for worse cracks and fillings for milder ones (and sometimes the reverse), so the relative risks are confounded by case selection, and the extraction interval (1.05–62.5) is extremely wide. The relative measures are printed with the review's own survival ranges beside them; no absolute per-group complication rates were reported in the record.
cards.source: Zhang S, Xu Y, Ma Y, Zhao W, Jin X, Fu B. The treatment outcomes of cracked teeth: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Dentistry. 2024. PMID: 38272437. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). MeSH: Cracked Tooth Syndrome · Crowns · Dental Restoration, Permanent · Humans · Root Canal Therapy · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Repair versus replacement (Gordan 2011): over seven years every group degraded, including replacement — with no significant difference in failure rate, supporting repair of a defective restoration
cards.summary: Repair versus replacement (Gordan 2011): over seven years every group degraded, including replacement — with no significant difference in failure rate, supporting repair of a defective restoration
cards.type: Prospective comparative clinical study with partial random assignment, 7-year follow-up (Gordan 2011)
cards.people: 50 patients aged 21–77 (mean 56 years) with 113 defective amalgam restorations, each tooth assigned to repair with amalgam (n=20), sealing of defective margins (n=23), refinishing (n=23), replacement (n=22) or no treatment (n=25); the replacement and no-treatment groups were randomly assigned (47 teeth) and served as comparisons; restorations scored on modified US Public Health Service criteria.
cards.result: 94 restorations (83%) were examined at one year, 74 (65%) at two years and 54 (48%) at seven years. Some degree of degradation occurred in all treatment groups, including the replacement group, by the seven-year recall, with no significant failure rate difference between groups; most downgraded and failed restorations appeared after the first two years of service. The authors concluded the results support repair of defective amalgam restorations as an alternative to replacement, while noting that randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings.
cards.watchOut: Only the replacement and no-treatment arms were randomised; the repair, sealing and refinishing arms were clinician-assigned, and by seven years only 48% of restorations were still being examined, so attrition could hide a real difference. The restorations were amalgam with localised defects — the finding does not automatically transfer to a structurally broken or cracked tooth, which is the Zhang card's territory.
cards.source: Gordan VV, Riley JL 3rd, Blaser PK, Mondragon E, Garvan CW, Mjör IA. Alternative treatments to replacement of defective amalgam restorations: results of a seven-year clinical study. Journal of the American Dental Association. 2011. PMID: 21719808. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pulp capping versus partial pulpotomy (Taha 2025): in a double-blind randomised trial of 140 exposed pulps, 1-year success was 91.5% for partial pulpotomy versus 81.3% for direct pulp capping — not significant (P=.08)
cards.summary: Pulp capping versus partial pulpotomy (Taha 2025): in a double-blind randomised trial of 140 exposed pulps, 1-year success was 91.5% for partial pulpotomy versus 81.3% for direct pulp capping — not significant (P=.08)
cards.people: 140 mature permanent teeth with carious pulp exposure, asymptomatic or with reversible pulpitis, randomised to direct pulp capping (n=67) or partial pulpotomy (n=73); after intraoperative assessment under magnification and haemostasis, NeoPUTTY (Avalon Biomed, Bradenton, FL, USA) — the capping material named in the publication — was placed in both groups; clinical and radiographic follow-up at 6 and 12 months. The tested product and company are named here for clarification, as this shelf's naming rule requires for a specific tested preparation.
cards.result: About half the teeth (74/140) were symptomatic, with no significant difference in preoperative pain between groups (P=.75), and both treatments significantly reduced pain by one week (P<.001). By 6 months, 4 partial-pulpotomy and 10 direct-capping cases had failed (success 94.4% vs 84.4%; P=.057); by 1 year, two further failures in each group gave success rates of 91.5% for partial pulpotomy and 81.3% for direct pulp capping (P=.08) — a 10.2 percentage point absolute difference that did not reach significance. No prognostic factors or interactions were significant on multivariate analysis. The authors concluded either procedure can manage carious pulp exposure with reversible pulpitis successfully, chosen on the intraoperative assessment of the pulp.
cards.watchOut: These were carious exposures in teeth with reversible pulpitis — not the traumatic exposure of a chipped or broken tooth, and not irreversible pulpitis, where success would be expected to be lower. The consistent ~10-point gap favouring pulpotomy at both time points, just short of significance in a 140-tooth trial, should be read as 'unresolved, leaning pulpotomy', not as proof the two are equal.
cards.source: Taha NA, Jaradat HB, DkmaK A, Zainal Abidin I. Carious Pulp Exposure in Mature Teeth With Reversible Pulpitis: A Randomized Clinical Trial of Direct Pulp Capping and Partial Pulpotomy. Journal of Endodontics. 2025. PMID: 40617285. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: cover the cusps of a cracked tooth, repair rather than replace a locally defective filling, and an exposed vital pulp can often be capped — all on observational or single-trial evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: cover the cusps of a cracked tooth, repair rather than replace a locally defective filling, and an exposed vital pulp can often be capped — all on observational or single-trial evidence
cards.people: A 27-study observational meta-analysis of cracked teeth (Zhang 2024), a 113-restoration prospective comparative study with 7-year follow-up (Gordan 2011), and a 140-tooth double-blind randomised trial of vital pulp therapy (Taha 2025).
cards.result: Cracked vital teeth: survival 92.8–97.8% at 1–6 years, but uncovered direct restorations carried relative risk 3.2 for pulpal complications and 8.1 for extraction versus full crowns (observational). Defective restorations: repair, sealing and refinishing degraded no faster than full replacement over seven years, with no significant failure-rate difference. Exposed pulp (carious, reversible pulpitis): partial pulpotomy 91.5% versus direct pulp capping 81.3% success at one year (P=.08). PROPOSED POSSIBLE — the directions agree with minimally invasive, cusp-protecting practice, but only the pulp-therapy comparison is randomised, and it studied carious rather than traumatic exposures.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. This shelf does not cover toothache analgesia (Shelf #5287), root-canal-versus-extraction decisions for non-vital teeth, or replantation of knocked-out teeth. No randomised trial comparing crown, onlay and direct restoration for cracked teeth was found in this session's search — the crown recommendation rests on observational data alone.

synthesis a 27-study observational meta-analysis of cracked teeth (zhang 2024), a 113-restoration prospective comparative study with 7-year follow-up (gordan 2011), and a 140-tooth double-blind randomised trial of vital pulp therapy (taha 2025). cracked vital teeth: survival 92.8–97.8% at 1–6 years, but uncovered direct restorations carried relative risk 3.2 for pulpal complications and 8.1 for extraction versus full crowns (observational). defective restorations: repair, sealing and refinishing degraded no faster than full replacement over seven years, with no significant failure-rate difference. exposed pulp (carious, reversible pulpitis): partial pulpotomy 91.5% versus direct pulp capping 81.3% success at one year (p=.08). proposed possible — the directions agree with minimally invasive, cusp-protecting practice, but only the pulp-therapy comparison is randomised, and it studied carious rather than traumatic exposures. tier c. this shelf does not cover toothache analgesia (shelf #5287), root-canal-versus-extraction decisions for non-vital teeth, or replantation of knocked-out teeth. no randomised trial comparing crown, onlay and direct restoration for cracked teeth was found in this session's search — the crown recommendation rests on observational data alone. synthesis of zhang s et al. journal of dentistry. 2024 (pmid: 38272437); gordan vv et al. journal of the american dental association. 2011 (pmid: 21719808); taha na et al. journal of endodontics. 2025 (pmid: 40617285).

shelves.title: Cleft lip and palate: in the Scandcleft randomised trials of 431 children, no primary-surgery protocol beat the others — speech proficiency was 86–92% across all four protocols at 10 years and dental arches did not differ at 5, 8 or 10 years
shelves.question: My child has a cleft lip and palate — treatment is staged surgery, but does the timing or technique of the primary repairs (including vomer flap closure or delaying hard-palate closure), or the timing of alveolar bone grafting, change speech, dental and growth outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Child · Cleft Lip/surgery · Cleft Palate/surgery · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Speech · Treatment Outcome · Velopharyngeal Insufficiency/surgery
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) between the tested primary-surgery protocols — cleft lip and palate care is staged surgery, and the one large randomised programme, Scandcleft (three parallel randomised trials, 431 children with non-syndromic unilateral cleft lip and palate, nine teams in five countries, ISRCTN29932826), tested four sequences of lip and palate closure — including hard-palate closure delayed to 36 months, simultaneous hard and soft palate closure at 12 months, and a vomer-flap single-layer hard-palate closure at 3–4 months — against a common protocol. It found no winner: dental arch relationships did not differ within any trial at 5, 8 or 10 years (Heliövaara 2022, PMID: 34476476), and at 10 years consonant proficiency ranged only 86–92% across arms with contradictory velopharyngeal patterns, the authors concluding there is 'no obvious evidence to recommend any of the protocols as superior' (Willadsen 2023, PMID: 36541222). Maxillary growth likewise did not differ within trials. For the later staged step, alveolar bone grafting, there are no randomised timing trials in the fetched record: a systematic review of 15 studies (Mundra 2022, PMID: 34967522) reports grafting with pre- and post-operative orthodontics as standard care and recommends the early mixed dentition phase, typically 6–8 years, without consensus on how graft success should even be measured.

cards.headline: Scandcleft speech at 10 years (Willadsen 2023): consonant proficiency 86–92% across all four surgical protocols — 'no obvious evidence to recommend any of the protocols as superior'
cards.summary: Scandcleft speech at 10 years (Willadsen 2023): consonant proficiency 86–92% across all four surgical protocols — 'no obvious evidence to recommend any of the protocols as superior'
cards.type: Three parallel randomised multicentre trials, speech outcomes at 10 years (Scandcleft; Willadsen 2023)
cards.people: 431 children born with non-syndromic unilateral cleft lip and palate, randomised across three parallel multicentre trials by nine cleft teams in five countries to one of four primary-surgery protocols: Arm A (common) — lip and soft palate closure at 3–4 months, hard palate closure at 12 months; Arm B — lip and soft palate at 3–4 months, hard palate delayed to 36 months; Arm C — lip at 3–4 months, hard and soft palate together at 12 months; Arm D — lip at 3–4 months with single-layer vomer-flap closure of the hard palate, soft palate at 12 months. Speech recordings of 399 children were perceptually analysed at 10 years (percentage of consonants correct, PCC; velopharyngeal competence, VPC).
cards.result: Mean PCC scores were 86–92% across trial arms, and 58–83% of children had velopharyngeal competence (VPC-Sum); only 50–73% had consonant proficiency at peer level. The protocols traded advantages: long-delayed hard-palate repair (Arm B) indicated lower PCC but the highest proportion with primary VPC (68%), while simultaneous hard and soft palate closure (Arm C) indicated higher PCC but the lowest primary VPC (47%). Girls performed better throughout. The authors concluded speech outcomes were low across the trials, the protocols had pros and cons, and there is no obvious evidence to recommend any protocol as superior — surgical experience, hearing, language difficulties and speech therapy may matter more than the sequence itself.
cards.watchOut: These are unilateral cleft lip and palate protocols in Scandinavian and UK centres — the null applies to the four sequences tested, not to cleft care in general, to isolated cleft palate, or to bilateral clefts. Centre effects were visible in the wider Scandcleft reports: the same protocol performed differently in different centres, so 'no protocol won' is not the same as 'technique and team do not matter'.
cards.source: Willadsen E, Jørgensen LD, Alaluusua S, Pedersen NH, Nielsen JB, Hölttä E, Hide Ø, Hayden C, Havstam C, Hammarström IL, Davies J, Boers M, Andersen HS, Aukner R, Jackson Morris D, Nielsen SF, Semb G, Lohmander A, Persson C. Scandcleft randomized trials of primary surgery for unilateral cleft lip and palate: Speech proficiency at 10 years of age. International Journal of Language & Communication Disorders. 2023. PMID: 36541222. Registry ID: ISRCTN29932826. cards.headline: Scandcleft dental arches at 5, 8 and 10 years (Heliövaara 2022): no differences in index scores within any surgical trial — no evidence one surgical method is superior
cards.summary: Scandcleft dental arches at 5, 8 and 10 years (Heliövaara 2022): no differences in index scores within any surgical trial — no evidence one surgical method is superior
cards.type: Randomised trials, dental arch relationships at 5, 8 and 10 years (Scandcleft; Heliövaara 2022)
cards.people: Children with unilateral cleft lip and palate from the same three Scandcleft randomised trials (four protocols, Arms A–D); study models at ages 5 (n=418), 8 (n=411) and 10 years (n=410) scored by a blinded panel of orthodontists using the Eurocran index, the 5-year-olds' index and the GOSLON Yardstick.
cards.result: No differences were found in mean 5-, 8- or 10-year index scores or their distributions within the surgical trials. Mean Eurocran dental index scores for the whole material were 2.50 at 5 years, 2.60 at 8 years and 2.26 at 10 years (5YO index and GOSLON: 2.77, 2.90 and 2.54 respectively); by age 10, 75.8% of the children had had orthodontic treatment. Between-trial comparisons (which compare centres as well as protocols) found better scores in Trial 2 Arm C at all ages and Trial 1 Arm B at 5 and 10 years than in Trial 3 Arm D. The authors concluded the three trials do not provide evidence that one surgical method is superior to the others.
cards.watchOut: Dental arch indices are intermediate orthodontic outcomes scored from models, and three-quarters of the children had already had orthodontics by age 10, which compresses any protocol differences. The between-trial contrasts (Arm C and Arm B better than Arm D) are not randomised comparisons — each trial was run in different centres, so centre and protocol are confounded there.
cards.source: Heliövaara A, Küseler A, Skaare P, Bellardie H, Mølsted K, Karsten A, Marcusson A, Rizell S, Brinck E, Sæle P, Najar Chalien M, Mooney J, Eyres P, Shaw W, Semb G. cards.headline: Alveolar bone grafting timing (Mundra 2022): 15 studies, no randomised timing comparison — review recommends grafting in early mixed dentition, typically 6–8 years, with orthodontics before and after
cards.summary: Alveolar bone grafting timing (Mundra 2022): 15 studies, no randomised timing comparison — review recommends grafting in early mixed dentition, typically 6–8 years, with orthodontics before and after
cards.type: Systematic review of alveolar bone graft timing (Mundra 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review (PubMed, MEDLINE and EMBASE searched to PRISMA guidelines) of 15 studies of alveolar bone grafting for alveolar clefts in unilateral or bilateral cleft lip and palate, examining timing and orthodontic preparation.
cards.result: Most studies classified patients by chronological rather than dental age. Orthodontic treatment accompanied surgery in 12 of 15 studies (80.0%), and orthodontics was used before grafting in 8 of 12 (66.7%). There was no consensus on the best method to evaluate graft success. The authors state that alveolar bone grafting with pre- and post-operative orthodontics is currently the standard of care for alveolar defects in cleft lip and palate, and recommend grafting during the early mixed dentition phase, just before eruption of the permanent central incisors, typically between 6 and 8 years old, with preoperative orthodontics for incisor alignment and resumption about 6 months postoperatively.
cards.watchOut: A recommendation inside a narrative-systematic review is not a trial result: the 6–8-year timing rests on observational series with inconsistent success measures, and other cleft traditions graft later (before canine eruption, around 9–11 years). This card records what the review recommends and how thin the comparative base is — it does not settle graft timing.
cards.source: Mundra LS, Lowe KM, Khechoyan DY. Alveolar Bone Graft Timing in Patients With Cleft Lip & Palate. Journal of Craniofacial Surgery. 2022. PMID: 34967522. Registry ID: none in the record (review). MeSH: Alveolar Bone Grafting · Bone Transplantation · Child · Cleft Lip/surgery · Cleft Palate/surgery · Humans · Tooth Eruption

cards.headline: Synthesis: the staged operations are necessary, but among the sequences actually randomised, none beat the others on speech, dental arches or growth — and graft timing has never been randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: the staged operations are necessary, but among the sequences actually randomised, none beat the others on speech, dental arches or growth — and graft timing has never been randomised
cards.people: The Scandcleft randomised programme (431 children; speech in 399 at 10 years, dental models in 410–418 at 5–10 years; ISRCTN29932826) and a 15-study systematic review of alveolar bone graft timing (Mundra 2022).
cards.result: Primary surgery: no protocol — early two-stage, delayed hard palate to 36 months, simultaneous palate closure at 12 months, or vomer-flap hard-palate closure — was superior on speech proficiency (PCC 86–92% in all arms) or dental arch relationships (no within-trial differences at 5, 8 or 10 years). Alveolar bone grafting: standard care with orthodontics, recommended at 6–8 years by review consensus, with no randomised timing evidence and no agreed success measure. PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference) for the randomised primary-protocol comparison; graft timing remains an unrandomised convention.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. Nothing here questions whether cleft lip and palate should be repaired — surgery is the treatment; the evidence compares sequences and timings of that surgery in unilateral cleft lip and palate. Speech therapy, hearing care, orthodontics and secondary operations (fistula closure, velopharyngeal surgery, orthognathic surgery) are separate questions not carded on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Willadsen E et al. International Journal of Language & Communication Disorders. 2023 (PMID: 36541222); Heliövaara A et al. European Journal of Orthodontics. 2022 (PMID: 34476476); Mundra LS et al. Journal of Craniofacial Surgery. 2022 (PMID: 34967522).

shelves.title: Acute compartment syndrome: the diastolic-minus-compartment (delta-P) threshold under 30 mmHg missed no case in 116 monitored fractures — while cohorts disagree on how much fasciotomy timing itself changes death and amputation
shelves.question: I have acute compartment syndrome — how quickly must the fasciotomy be done, does pressure monitoring change outcomes, and which pressure threshold (absolute or diastolic-minus-compartment) should trigger decompression?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Anterior Compartment Syndrome/diagnosis · Anterior Compartment Syndrome/surgery · Compartment Syndromes/surgery · Fasciotomy · Humans · Monitoring, Physiologic · Pressure · Tibial Fractures/complications
shelves.balance: SPLIT / POSSIBLE — there are no randomised trials of fasciotomy (withholding decompression cannot be randomised), so everything here is cohort evidence, capped at POSSIBLE. Two findings are consistent. First, the diagnostic threshold: in 116 tibial fractures monitored continuously, using a differential pressure (diastolic minus compartment pressure) under 30 mmHg as the fasciotomy trigger produced no missed compartment syndromes, while an absolute 30 mmHg threshold would have flagged 43% for fasciotomy (McQueen 1996, PMID: 8898137). Second, monitored patients reached fasciotomy sooner (16 vs 32 hours) and 0 of 12 survivors had sequelae versus 10 of 11 unmonitored survivors with weakness and contractures (McQueen 1996, PMID: 8898136) — a tiny, non-randomised comparison. On timing itself the cohorts disagree: in earthquake crush injuries, amputation was 0% with fasciotomy within 24 hours, 11.5% at 24–48 hours and 31.4% after 48 hours (Demir 2025, PMID: 39853473), yet in the largest series — 546 patients at two Level I trauma centres — neither death (6.6%) nor amputation (9.5%) was associated with time from injury to fasciotomy at all; patient and injury-severity factors were (Zhang 2020, PMID: 31560102). Fasciotomy remains the emergency standard of care; this shelf cards what the comparative cohorts can and cannot show about timing and pressure thresholds, and does not question decompressing a clinically evident compartment syndrome.

cards.headline: Monitored versus unmonitored (McQueen 1996): continuous pressure monitoring halved the delay to fasciotomy (16 vs 32 hours) — sequelae in 0 of 12 monitored survivors versus 10 of 11 unmonitored
cards.summary: Monitored versus unmonitored (McQueen 1996): continuous pressure monitoring halved the delay to fasciotomy (16 vs 32 hours) — sequelae in 0 of 12 monitored survivors versus 10 of 11 unmonitored
cards.type: Comparative cohort study, monitored versus unmonitored (McQueen 1996)
cards.people: 25 patients with tibial diaphyseal fractures complicated by acute compartment syndrome at the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh; 13 had continuous monitoring of compartment pressure and 12 did not; outcomes reviewed at an average of 10.5 months.
cards.result: Average delay from injury to fasciotomy was 16 hours in the monitored group and 32 hours in the non-monitored group (P<0.05). Of the 12 surviving monitored patients, none had any sequelae of acute compartment syndrome at final review; of the 11 surviving non-monitored patients, ten had definite sequelae with muscle weakness and contractures (P<0.01). Tibial union was also significantly delayed in the non-monitored group (P<0.05). The authors recommend continuous compartment monitoring, where equipment is available, for patients with tibial fractures.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-five patients, not randomised: monitored and unmonitored patients may have differed in injury severity, era or vigilance of care, and a 0-of-12 versus 10-of-11 contrast in such small groups is fragile — one or two patients reclassified would change it materially. It is carded because it is the classic direct comparison behind monitoring practice, not because it can carry a strong stamp.
cards.source: McQueen MM, Christie J, Court-Brown CM. Acute compartment syndrome in tibial diaphyseal fractures. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (British Volume). 1996. PMID: 8898136. cards.headline: The pressure threshold (McQueen & Court-Brown 1996): a differential pressure under 30 mmHg missed no compartment syndrome in 116 monitored fractures — an absolute 30 mmHg rule would have sent 43% to fasciotomy
cards.summary: The pressure threshold (McQueen & Court-Brown 1996): a differential pressure under 30 mmHg missed no compartment syndrome in 116 monitored fractures — an absolute 30 mmHg rule would have sent 43% to fasciotomy
cards.people: 116 patients with tibial diaphyseal fractures who had continuous monitoring of anterior compartment pressure for 24 hours (prospective study).
cards.result: Three patients (2.6%) had acute compartment syndrome. In the first 12 hours, 53 patients had absolute compartment pressures over 30 mmHg and 30 over 40 mmHg, yet only one had a differential pressure (diastolic minus compartment pressure) under 30 mmHg — he had a fasciotomy; in the second 12 hours, two more patients crossed the differential threshold and had fasciotomies. No patient had sequelae of compartment syndrome at review at least six months after injury. A decompression threshold of 30 mmHg absolute would have indicated fasciotomy in 50 patients (43%), and a 40 mmHg threshold in 27 (23%) — unnecessary operations the differential rule avoided. The authors recommend decompression when the differential pressure drops under 30 mmHg.
cards.watchOut: Only three true compartment syndromes occurred, so 'no missed cases' rests on a very small numerator, and the study monitored the anterior compartment of tibial fractures only — it does not validate the threshold for the forearm, thigh or foot, or for non-fracture causes. A single differential reading under 30 mmHg in a hypotensive patient can also mislead; the card reports the study's rule, not a licence to delay fasciotomy in a clinically obvious case.
cards.source: McQueen MM, Court-Brown CM. Compartment monitoring in tibial fractures. The pressure threshold for decompression. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (British Volume). 1996. cards.headline: Earthquake crush cohort (Demir 2025): no amputations when fasciotomy was within 24 hours — 11.5% at 24–48 hours and 31.4% after 48 hours
cards.summary: Earthquake crush cohort (Demir 2025): no amputations when fasciotomy was within 24 hours — 11.5% at 24–48 hours and 31.4% after 48 hours
cards.type: Retrospective cohort by fasciotomy timing, crush injuries (Demir 2025)
cards.people: 129 extremities of 84 patients (mean age 34.5 years) who underwent fasciotomy for crush-induced compartment syndrome after the February 2023 Turkey earthquakes, analysed retrospectively at a single centre; 39 upper and 90 lower extremities.
cards.result: Amputations were performed in 25 extremities (19.4%) in 20 patients (23.8%). No patient fasciotomised within 24 hours required amputation; amputation occurred in 9 of 78 extremities (11.5%) fasciotomised at 24–48 hours and 16 of 51 (31.4%) after 48 hours (P=0.005), driven by lower extremities (P=0.002) rather than upper (P=0.661). Muscle compartment excision was required in 27 extremities (26%), and 19 patients (22.6%) received haemodialysis, significantly more often with late fasciotomy. The authors conclude fasciotomy earlier than 24 hours prevented amputation in this crush setting.
cards.watchOut: Earthquake crush injury is the extreme end of compartment syndrome: time trapped under rubble determines both the delay and the muscle damage, so timing and injury severity are inseparable here — the gradient cannot be read as the effect of hospital delay in an ordinary fracture patient. Single centre, retrospective, and the within-24-hours group size is not separately reported in the record.
cards.source: Demir EB, Barça F, Atilla HA, Çevik K, Tam E, Atlı OY, Yüksel S, Emet A, Çatma MF, Duman E, Fırat A, Akdoğan M. The effects of timing on fasciotomy outcomes in compartment syndrome — experience from crush-induced trauma following 2023 Turkey earthquakes. European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery. 2025. cards.headline: The counterweight (Zhang 2020): in 546 patients, neither death (6.6%) nor amputation (9.5%) was associated with time from injury to fasciotomy
cards.summary: The counterweight (Zhang 2020): in 546 patients, neither death (6.6%) nor amputation (9.5%) was associated with time from injury to fasciotomy
cards.people: 546 patients with acute compartment syndrome of 558 legs treated with fasciotomy from 2000 to 2015 at two Level I trauma centres (retrospective study); primary outcomes were in-hospital death and limb amputation.
cards.result: In-hospital death occurred in 6.6% and limb amputation in 9.5% of patients. Neither death nor limb amputation was associated with time from injury to fasciotomy. On multivariable analysis, death was associated with older age (P=0.03), higher modified Charlson Comorbidity Index (P=0.009), higher potassium (P=0.02), lower haemoglobin (P=0.002) and higher lactate (P<0.001); amputation was associated with diabetes mellitus (P=0.05), no compartment pressure measurement (P=0.009), higher PTT (P=0.03) and lower albumin (P=0.01). The authors conclude death and amputation track patient factors and injury severity rather than fasciotomy timing.
cards.watchOut: A null association with timing in a retrospective series can be manufactured by confounding in both directions — the sickest limbs are rushed to theatre (making early fasciotomy look bad) and unsalvageable limbs are sometimes decompressed late or not at all. 'Time not associated with amputation' must not be read as 'delay is safe': the functional outcomes that dominate the Edinburgh data (weakness, contracture in survivors) were not this study's endpoints.
cards.source: Zhang D, Janssen SJ, Tarabochia M, von Keudell A, Chen N. Risk factors for death and amputation in acute leg compartment syndrome. European Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery & Traumatology. 2020. PMID: 31560102. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: monitor with the differential-pressure rule and decompress promptly — but the timing evidence is observational and internally inconsistent
cards.summary: Synthesis: monitor with the differential-pressure rule and decompress promptly — but the timing evidence is observational and internally inconsistent
cards.people: Two small Edinburgh studies from 1996 (25 compartment-syndrome patients; 116 monitored fractures), a 129-extremity earthquake crush cohort (Demir 2025) and a 546-patient two-centre retrospective series (Zhang 2020). No randomised evidence exists.
cards.result: Diagnostic threshold: differential pressure (diastolic minus compartment) under 30 mmHg identified all cases in 116 monitored fractures, where an absolute 30 mmHg threshold would have indicated fasciotomy in 43%. Monitoring: associated with fasciotomy at 16 rather than 32 hours and with no sequelae in 12 survivors versus sequelae in 10 of 11 unmonitored survivors (small, non-randomised). Timing and hard outcomes: amputation rose steeply with delay in crush injuries (0% within 24 h; 31.4% after 48 h), but the largest general series found no association between time to fasciotomy and death or amputation (6.6% and 9.5% overall). PROPOSED POSSIBLE, split by question: the delta-P threshold and prompt decompression are supported; a precise hour-by-hour timing effect on survival or amputation is not established.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. This shelf must never be used to justify delaying fasciotomy in a clinically evident acute compartment syndrome — decompression is the emergency standard, and the cohorts carded here compare monitoring strategies, thresholds and observed timings, not treatment versus no treatment. Chronic exertional compartment syndrome is a different condition and is not covered.
cards.source: Synthesis of McQueen MM et al. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (British Volume). 1996 (PMID: 8898136); McQueen MM & Court-Brown CM. Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery (British Volume). 1996 (PMID: 8898137); Demir EB et al. European Journal of Trauma and Emergency Surgery. 2025 (PMID: 39853473); Zhang D et al. European Journal of Orthopaedic Surgery & Traumatology. 2020 (PMID: 31560102).

shelves.title: Corns and calluses: salicylic acid plasters resolved more corns than scalpel debridement (34% versus 21% at 3 months) — but for callus pain the scalpel beat a sham procedure by only 2–7 mm, not significantly
shelves.question: I have corns and calluses — do salicylic acid corn plasters work better than having them cut out (scalpel debridement), and does debridement itself relieve callus pain?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Callosities/surgery · Callosities/therapy · Debridement · Humans · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer splits by lesion and by treatment. For corns, one randomised trial of 202 adults (Farndon 2013, PMID: 24063387) found 40% salicylic acid plasters beat usual scalpel debridement: complete resolution at 3 months in 34% (32/95) versus 21% (20/94), reduced size in 83% versus 56%, less pain at 3 months, and longer time to recurrence over 12 months. For painful plantar callus in older people, the scalpel itself barely beat doing nothing real: against sham debridement, real debridement's pain advantage was only 2–7 mm on a 100-mm scale, never significant and never clinically worthwhile (Landorf 2013, PMID: 23915078; 80 participants), and a 300-person trial found full and partial debridement indistinguishable, both only marginally better than simulated debridement (Garcia 2020, PMID: 32997761). A small three-arm trial found podiatry (scalpel) treatment changed callus skin measures and pain immediately, with lesser, slower changes from two home keratolytics (Hashmi 2016, PMID: 27189190). Safety boundary: salicylic acid plasters in the corn trial were applied under podiatrist supervision in selected patients — corns that were infected or neurovascular were excluded — and keratolytics are generally avoided on broken skin and in people with diabetes or poor circulation, who were not the studied population.

cards.headline: Farndon 2013: salicylic acid plasters beat scalpel debridement for corns — resolution 34% versus 21% at 3 months, size reduced in 83% versus 56%, and recurrence took longer
cards.summary: Farndon 2013: salicylic acid plasters beat scalpel debridement for corns — resolution 34% versus 21% at 3 months, size reduced in 83% versus 56%, and recurrence took longer
cards.people: 202 adults presenting with one or more corns at two UK centres, randomised to 'usual' scalpel debridement (enucleation, n=101) or 40% salicylic acid corn plasters (n=101; the tested product named in the publication was Carnation corn plasters, Cuxson Gerrard & Co — named here under this library's rule for specific tested products), applied by the podiatrist; corn size, pain (100-mm VAS) and EQ-5D measured by a blinded independent podiatrist at baseline, 3, 6, 9 and 12 months.
cards.result: At 3 months, 34% (32/95) of plasters-group corns had completely resolved versus 21% (20/94) in the scalpel group (P=0.044) — an absolute difference of 13 percentage points — and 83% (79/95) had reduced in size versus 56% (53/94) (P<0.001). Pain was significantly lower in the plaster group at 3 months (P<0.001), time to corn recurrence over 12 months was longer in the plaster group (P<0.001), and EQ-5D change favoured plasters by month 12 (+0.12 vs −0.05; P=0.005). The economic analysis found corn plasters cost-effective. The authors concluded plasters, used under podiatrist supervision in appropriate patients, are an effective alternative to scalpel debridement.
cards.watchOut: One trial, and its protocol was a single plaster application course — participants who later needed follow-up treatment received scalpel care, so the 12-month recurrence advantage belongs to the initial strategy, not to repeated plastering. Patients could not be blinded to having a plaster versus a scalpel, and the trial excluded infected or neurovascular corns and people unable to reach their feet; it does not license unsupervised salicylic acid use in diabetes or poor circulation.
cards.source: Farndon LJ, Vernon W, Walters SJ, Dixon S, Bradburn M, Concannon M, Potter J. The effectiveness of salicylic acid plasters compared with 'usual' scalpel debridement of corns: a randomised controlled trial. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2013. PMID: 24063387. cards.headline: Landorf 2013: for painful plantar callus in older people, real scalpel debridement beat sham by only 2–7 mm of pain — never significant, never clinically worthwhile
cards.summary: Landorf 2013: for painful plantar callus in older people, real scalpel debridement beat sham by only 2–7 mm of pain — never significant, never clinically worthwhile
cards.type: Participant- and assessor-blinded randomised sham-controlled trial (Landorf 2013)
cards.people: 80 participants aged 65 years and older with painful forefoot plantar calluses, in a parallel-group participant- and assessor-blinded randomised trial of real versus sham scalpel debridement, followed for six weeks; pain measured on a 100-mm visual analogue scale immediately after treatment and at 1, 3 and 6 weeks.
cards.result: Both groups' pain fell from baseline (the wider trial report records decreases of up to 41.9 mm). Between-group differences at every time point were small and systematic — between 2 and 7 mm favouring real debridement — but none was statistically significant and none reached a level considered clinically worthwhile. Scalpel debridement caused no adverse events. The authors concluded that, used alone, scalpel debridement has a limited short-term effect on callus pain, without excluding cumulative benefit over longer periods or additive effects combined with other interventions.
cards.watchOut: Callus is not corn: this trial's lesion is the diffuse plantar callus of older forefoot skin, and its outcome is pain over six weeks after a single debridement — it does not contradict the Farndon corn result, which measured resolution and recurrence of a different lesion over a year. The sham procedure itself (attention, handling, expectation) produced most of the pain relief, which is the point of the card: much of debridement's short-term pain benefit is not the scalpel.
cards.source: Landorf KB, Morrow A, Spink MJ, Nash CL, Novak A, Potter J, Menz HB. Effectiveness of scalpel debridement for painful plantar calluses in older people: a randomized trial. Trials. 2013. PMID: 23915078. Registry ID: ACTRN012606000176561 (as printed in the PubMed record). cards.headline: Garcia 2020: full versus partial debridement made no difference to pain in 300 older people — both beat simulated debridement only marginally (P=.03–.05)
cards.summary: Garcia 2020: full versus partial debridement made no difference to pain in 300 older people — both beat simulated debridement only marginally (P=.03–.05)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, three debridement techniques (Garcia & Soler 2020)
cards.people: 300 older participants (mean age 76.3 ± 7.4 years) with plantar hyperkeratoses of the forefoot, randomly allocated to full debridement, partial debridement, or debridement simulation (control); pain on a visual analogue scale before treatment, just after, at 24 hours and at 7 days.
cards.result: Full and partial debridement produced similar pain levels at every time point (just after: P=.32; 24 hours: P=.15; 7 days: P=.22). Both scalpel groups differed significantly from the simulation control at each time point, but marginally (just after: P=.04 for full, P=.05 for partial; 24 hours: P=.03 and P=.04; 7 days: P=.04 for both). The authors concluded there are no significant differences in pain reduction between partial and full debridement of forefoot plantar hyperkeratoses in older people.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up was seven days and the outcome was self-perceived pain only — the trial says nothing about callus resolution, recurrence or function, and its scalpel-versus-simulation P values (.03–.05) sit at the edge of significance in a 300-person trial, consistent with Landorf's conclusion that the specific scalpel effect on pain is small.
cards.source: Garcia CA, Soler FC. Effectiveness of Three Scalpel Debridement Techniques on Painful Callus in Older People. Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association. 2020. cards.headline: Hashmi 2016: podiatry scalpel treatment changed callus skin and pain immediately (P<0.01); home potassium hydroxide and trichloroacetic acid changed less, over 21 days
cards.summary: Hashmi 2016: podiatry scalpel treatment changed callus skin and pain immediately (P<0.01); home potassium hydroxide and trichloroacetic acid changed less, over 21 days
cards.people: 46 participants (61 feet) with plantar calluses in a randomised three-armed parallel trial of potassium hydroxide 40% (home treatment), trichloroacetic acid (home treatment), or podiatry treatment (scalpel debridement), followed at days 7, 14 and 21 with objective skin measures (hydration, elasticity, texture, size), quality of life and pain/function.
cards.result: The podiatry treatment showed immediate and significant changes in all objective outcomes and in associated foot pain and function (P<0.01). Lesser changes in skin quality and perceived pain and functional benefits occurred with trichloroacetic acid and potassium hydroxide over 21 days — in the authors' words, lesser but sometimes comparable. The authors note this was the first study to use objective biophysical measures for callus treatment response.
cards.watchOut: Small (46 participants) and short (21 days), with a co-author from a consumer-products company and outcomes centred on skin biophysics rather than resolution or recurrence — it supports 'scalpel acts fastest, keratolytics act slowly' and little more. It studied callus, not corns, and home caustics at these strengths are not the supervised salicylic-acid plaster protocol of the Farndon trial.
cards.source: Hashmi F, Nester CJ, Wright CRF, Lam S. The evaluation of three treatments for plantar callus: a three-armed randomised, comparative trial using biophysical outcome measures. Trials. 2016. PMID: 27189190. Registry ID: ISRCTN14751843. cards.headline: Synthesis: plasters won the only corn trial; the scalpel's specific effect on callus pain is small — most short-term pain relief follows any attentive treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: plasters won the only corn trial; the scalpel's specific effect on callus pain is small — most short-term pain relief follows any attentive treatment
cards.people: Four randomised trials: salicylic acid plasters versus scalpel for corns (202 adults; Farndon 2013), real versus sham scalpel debridement for plantar callus (80 older people; Landorf 2013), full versus partial versus simulated debridement (300 older people; Garcia 2020), and podiatry versus two home keratolytics for callus (46 participants; Hashmi 2016).
cards.result: Corns: 40% salicylic acid plasters resolved more corns than scalpel debridement at 3 months (34% vs 21%; absolute difference 13 points), shrank more (83% vs 56%), hurt less and recurred later. Callus pain: real debridement's advantage over sham was 2–7 mm on a 100-mm scale, non-significant (Landorf); full and partial debridement were indistinguishable and only marginally better than simulation (Garcia); scalpel treatment changed skin measures immediately, keratolytics more slowly (Hashmi). PROPOSED SPLIT: plasters over scalpel for corns in supervised, selected patients; for callus pain, debridement helps some, but its specific contribution beyond the treatment encounter is small and short-term in the sham-controlled record.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. Corns and calluses are different lesions and this shelf keeps their evidence separate on purpose. Nothing here covers diabetic foot lesions, where debridement and keratolytics follow different, specialist rules, or the offloading and footwear changes that address why corns and calluses form.
cards.source: Synthesis of Farndon LJ et al. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. 2013 (PMID: 24063387); Landorf KB et al. Trials. 2013 (PMID: 23915078); Garcia CA & Soler FC. Journal of the American Podiatric Medical Association. 2020 (PMID: 32997761); Hashmi F et al. Trials. 2016 (PMID: 27189190).

shelves.title: Detached retina: the best operation depends on the eye — buckling won on vision in phakic eyes and vitrectomy on first-time reattachment in pseudophakic eyes (SPR), while a gas bubble beat vitrectomy on vision but not first-time success in selected detachments (PIVOT)
shelves.question: I have a detached retina — which operation is best: vitrectomy, scleral buckling, or pneumatic retinopexy (a gas-bubble procedure), for vision and for getting the retina back in place?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Humans · Prospective Studies · Retinal Detachment/surgery · Scleral Buckling/methods · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity · Vitrectomy/methods
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the randomised answer depends on the eye's lens status and on which detachments are eligible for the least invasive operation. In the SPR study (681 patients; Heimann 2007, PMID: 18054633), the largest randomised comparison of scleral buckling (SB) versus primary vitrectomy (PPV): in phakic eyes, vision improved more with buckling (mean BCVA change −0.71 vs −0.56 logMAR; P=0.0005) and cataract progressed more after vitrectomy; in pseudophakic eyes, vision did not differ, but primary anatomical success was significantly better with vitrectomy (72.0% [95/132] vs 53.4% [71/133]; P=0.0020) with fewer secondary operations — the authors recommend PPV in pseudophakic eyes. In PIVOT (176 patients; Hillier 2019, PMID: 30468761), restricted to detachments with breaks in the upper retina within one clock hour, pneumatic retinopexy (PnR) gave better 12-month vision than vitrectomy (79.9 vs 75.0 ETDRS letters, a 4.9-letter difference; P=0.024) and less vertical metamorphopsia, but lower primary anatomical success (80.8% vs 93.2%; P=0.045), with final (secondary) success equal at about 99% in both groups — and cataract surgery by 12 months in 65% of phakic PPV eyes versus 16% of PnR eyes. One-home note: retinal-detachment surgery was checked against the existing library before building; no prior shelf homes this SPR/PIVOT comparison.

cards.headline: SPR study, phakic eyes (Heimann 2007): buckling improved vision more than vitrectomy (−0.71 vs −0.56 logMAR; P=0.0005), with less cataract progression — redetachment was the same (26.3% vs 25.1%)
cards.summary: SPR study, phakic eyes (Heimann 2007): buckling improved vision more than vitrectomy (−0.71 vs −0.56 logMAR; P=0.0005), with less cataract progression — redetachment was the same (26.3% vs 25.1%)
cards.type: Prospective randomised multicentre trial, phakic stratum (SPR study; Heimann 2007)
cards.people: 416 phakic patients within the SPR study — a prospective randomised multicentre trial (45 surgeons, 25 centres, 5 European countries, enrolment over 5 years) of scleral buckling versus primary pars plana vitrectomy for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment of medium complexity, with 1-year follow-up completed in 93% of phakic patients; primary endpoint was change in best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) at 1 year.
cards.result: Mean BCVA change was significantly greater in the scleral buckling group (−0.71 logMAR, SD 0.68) than in the vitrectomy group (−0.56 logMAR, SD 0.76) (P=0.0005) — a 0.15 logMAR difference, roughly 1½ lines of acuity. Cataract progression was significantly greater in the vitrectomy group (P<0.00005). Redetachment rates did not differ: 26.3% (55/209) with buckling versus 25.1% (52/207) with vitrectomy. The authors concluded the study shows a benefit of scleral buckling in phakic eyes with respect to BCVA improvement.
cards.watchOut: 'Medium complexity' detachments only — eyes with more than grade A proliferative vitreoretinopathy and eyes suitable for a single small sponge were outside this trial, and surgeons in the vitrectomy arm could add a buckle at their discretion, which blurs the pure technique comparison. The vision advantage is partly a cataract story: vitrectomy accelerates cataract in a phakic eye, and later cataract surgery can recover some of the lost ground after the trial's 1-year endpoint.
cards.source: Heimann H, Bartz-Schmidt KU, Bornfeld N, Weiss C, Hilgers RD, Foerster MH; Scleral Buckling versus Primary Vitrectomy in Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment Study Group. Scleral buckling versus primary vitrectomy in rhegmatogenous retinal detachment: a prospective randomized multicenter clinical study. Ophthalmology. 2007. PMID: 18054633. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: SPR study, pseudophakic eyes (Heimann 2007): vision did not differ, but vitrectomy reattached the retina first time in 72.0% versus 53.4% (P=0.0020) and needed fewer reoperations
cards.summary: SPR study, pseudophakic eyes (Heimann 2007): vision did not differ, but vitrectomy reattached the retina first time in 72.0% versus 53.4% (P=0.0020) and needed fewer reoperations
cards.type: Prospective randomised multicentre trial, pseudophakic stratum (SPR study; Heimann 2007)
cards.people: 265 aphakic/pseudophakic patients within the same SPR randomised trial, with 1-year follow-up completed in 89%; scleral buckling versus primary pars plana vitrectomy for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment of medium complexity.
cards.result: Change in BCVA showed a non-significant difference of 0.09 logMAR between the groups. Primary anatomical success (retinal reattachment without any secondary retina-affecting surgery) was significantly better with vitrectomy: 72.0% (95/132) versus 53.4% (71/133) with buckling (P=0.0020) — an absolute difference of 18.6 percentage points — and the mean number of retina-affecting secondary surgeries was lower with vitrectomy (0.43, SD 0.85, vs 0.77, SD 1.08; P=0.0032). Redetachment occurred in 20.4% (27/132) of vitrectomy eyes versus 39.8% (53/133) of buckled eyes. On the better anatomical outcome, the authors recommend primary vitrectomy in pseudophakic patients.
cards.watchOut: The two SPR cards are strata of one trial, not two trials — together they enrolled 681 patients. 'Primary success' penalises buckling for needing a second procedure even when the retina ends attached; final anatomical success converged between techniques in the wider report. Pseudophakic detachments also differ anatomically (small, anterior breaks that are hard to find from outside the eye), which is the mechanism the authors invoke for vitrectomy's advantage here.
cards.source: Heimann H, Bartz-Schmidt KU, Bornfeld N, Weiss C, Hilgers RD, Foerster MH; Scleral Buckling versus Primary Vitrectomy in Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment Study Group. cards.headline: PIVOT (Hillier 2019): pneumatic retinopexy beat vitrectomy on 12-month vision by 4.9 letters (79.9 vs 75.0; P=0.024) — but first-time reattachment was lower (80.8% vs 93.2%)
cards.summary: PIVOT (Hillier 2019): pneumatic retinopexy beat vitrectomy on 12-month vision by 4.9 letters (79.9 vs 75.0; P=0.024) — but first-time reattachment was lower (80.8% vs 93.2%)
cards.people: 176 patients with primary rhegmatogenous retinal detachment demonstrating a single retinal break or a group of breaks within 1 clock hour above the 8- and 4-o'clock meridians (breaks or lattice in attached retina unrestricted), randomised at a single Toronto centre to pneumatic retinopexy or pars plana vitrectomy, treated within 24 hours (macula-on) or 72 hours (macula-off); primary outcome was 1-year ETDRS visual acuity.
cards.result: ETDRS acuity after pneumatic retinopexy exceeded vitrectomy by 4.9 letters at 12 months (79.9 ± 10.4 vs 75.0 ± 15.2 letters; P=0.024), and was also superior at 3 months (78.4 vs 68.5) and 6 months (79.2 vs 68.6). Vertical metamorphopsia scores were better after retinopexy at 12 months (0.14 ± 0.29 vs 0.28 ± 0.42; P=0.026). Primary anatomic success at 12 months was 80.8% for retinopexy versus 93.2% for vitrectomy (P=0.045) — an absolute difference of 12.4 percentage points the other way — while secondary anatomic success was 98.7% versus 98.6%. Cataract surgery in the study eye by 12 months occurred in 65% of phakic vitrectomy patients versus 16% of retinopexy patients (P<0.001). The authors conclude pneumatic retinopexy should be considered first-line for detachments fulfilling the PIVOT criteria.
cards.watchOut: PIVOT's eligibility is the catch: only detachments whose detached-retina breaks sit in the upper retina within one clock hour — a minority of all detachments — and retinopexy demands a patient who can hold strict head positioning and attend close follow-up, with about one in five needing a second, bigger operation. Single centre, 176 patients; the vision advantage partly reflects vitrectomy-induced cataract (65% vs 16% cataract surgery by 12 months).
cards.source: Hillier RJ, Felfeli T, Berger AR, Wong DT, Altomare F, Dai D, Giavedoni LR, Kertes PJ, Kohly RP, Muni RH. The Pneumatic Retinopexy versus Vitrectomy for the Management of Primary Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment Outcomes Randomized Trial (PIVOT). Ophthalmology. 2019. PMID: 30468761. Registry ID: NCT01639209. cards.headline: Synthesis: lens status and break position decide — buckling for phakic medium-complexity detachments, vitrectomy for pseudophakic ones, and retinopexy first for the PIVOT-eligible minority
cards.summary: Synthesis: lens status and break position decide — buckling for phakic medium-complexity detachments, vitrectomy for pseudophakic ones, and retinopexy first for the PIVOT-eligible minority
cards.people: Two randomised trials: the SPR study (681 patients in phakic and pseudophakic strata; Heimann 2007) and PIVOT (176 patients with upper-retina breaks; Hillier 2019).
cards.result: Phakic, medium complexity (SPR): buckling improved vision more (−0.71 vs −0.56 logMAR) with similar redetachment (26.3% vs 25.1%). Pseudophakic (SPR): vision equal; vitrectomy's primary reattachment was 72.0% versus 53.4%. PIVOT-eligible detachments: retinopexy gave 4.9 more ETDRS letters at 12 months and far less cataract surgery, at the cost of primary success 80.8% versus 93.2%, with final success ~99% either way. PROPOSED SPLIT — no single operation wins across eyes; the trials support matching the operation to the eye, not a universal technique.
cards.watchOut: Tier C. Both trials concern rhegmatogenous detachment; tractional (diabetic) and exudative detachments, giant tears, and detachments with advanced proliferative vitreoretinopathy are outside them. Surgical technique and instrumentation have moved since SPR enrolled (small-gauge vitrectomy), which may narrow — but has not been shown in a new trial to erase — the phakic buckling advantage.
cards.source: Synthesis of Heimann H et al. Ophthalmology. 2007 (PMID: 18054633); Hillier RJ et al. Ophthalmology. 2019 (PMID: 30468761).

shelves.title: Donepezil for cognition in Down syndrome: both large randomised trials were null on their primary measures (n=129 children; n=123 young adults) — only post-hoc and small-study signals remain
shelves.question: In people with Down syndrome, does donepezil improve cognition, adaptive behaviour or daily functioning compared with placebo — in children and young adults without dementia, and in adults with Alzheimer's dementia?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Cholinesterase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Cognition Disorders/drug therapy · Donepezil · Double-Blind Method · Down Syndrome/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Neuropsychological Tests
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — scoped exactly to donepezil for cognition in Down syndrome, the tested question. Two large multicentre randomised double-blind trials anchor the shelf, and both missed: in children aged 10–17 (Kishnani PS et al., PMID: 21108390; 129 participants, 10 weeks, donepezil 2.5–10 mg/day), Vineland-II v-scores improved significantly in BOTH groups (P < 0.0001) with no significant between-group difference — the trial 'failed to demonstrate any benefit'. In young adults aged 18–35 without Alzheimer's disease (Kishnani PS et al., PMID: 19606472; 123 participants, 12 weeks, 5–10 mg/day), Severe Impairment Battery scores likewise improved in both groups with no significant between-group difference on the primary measure; the encouraging findings were post hoc (Vineland scores in observed cases, P = 0.03 but P = 0.07 by last-observation-carried-forward; responder analyses significant on three of five definitions). The Cochrane review of all pharmacological interventions for cognitive decline in adults with Down syndrome (Livingstone N et al., PMID: 26513128; 9 RCTs, 427 participants; 4 donepezil studies, 192 participants) found donepezil's cognitive scores similar to placebo (standardised mean difference 0.52, 95% CI −0.27 to 1.13 — an interval spanning no effect) and behaviour likewise (SMD 0.42, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.89), with significantly more adverse events on donepezil and the body of evidence rated low quality. The one small trial in Down syndrome with Alzheimer's dementia (n=30, inside the Cochrane review) showed at best a non-significant trend. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): where it has been properly tested, donepezil has not beaten placebo on any pre-specified primary outcome in Down syndrome. BOUNDARY: memantine in Down syndrome is homed separately on Shelf #1399 (MEADOWS, also null) and is not re-carded here; this shelf is donepezil only.

cards.headline: Kishnani 2010 (children 10–17): both groups improved significantly on the Vineland-II (P < 0.0001) with no between-group difference — 'this trial failed to demonstrate any benefit for donepezil'
cards.summary: Kishnani 2010 (children 10–17): both groups improved significantly on the Vineland-II (P < 0.0001) with no between-group difference — 'this trial failed to demonstrate any benefit for donepezil'
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial, phase II (Kishnani 2010)
cards.people: 129 children and adolescents aged 10–17 years with Down syndrome of mild-to-moderate severity, assigned to donepezil (2.5–10 mg/day) or placebo for 10 weeks. Primary measure: Vineland-II Adaptive Behavior Scales Parent/Caregiver Rating Form — the sum of nine subdomain standardised scores (v-scores); secondary measures included the individual communication, daily-living and socialisation domains and the Test of Verbal Expression and Reasoning.
cards.result: During the double-blind phase, the VABS-II/PCRF sum of v-scores improved significantly from baseline in both groups (P < 0.0001), with no significant between-group differences. The authors state the conclusion plainly: this trial failed to demonstrate any benefit for donepezil versus placebo in children and adolescents with Down syndrome, although donepezil appeared to be well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The both-groups improvement is the classic practice/expectation pattern in caregiver-rated outcomes: parents re-rate a child after 10 weeks of trial attention and scores rise on placebo too. That is precisely why the between-group comparison is the result, and it is null. Ten weeks is also short for a cognitive claim — but a null at 10 weeks in the largest children's trial is the evidence that exists, not a gap to be filled by smaller open studies.

cards.headline: Kishnani 2009 (young adults 18–35, no dementia): primary Severe Impairment Battery outcome null between groups; the positive findings were post hoc (Vineland P = 0.03 observed cases, P = 0.07 LOCF)
cards.summary: Kishnani 2009 (young adults 18–35, no dementia): primary Severe Impairment Battery outcome null between groups; the positive findings were post hoc (Vineland P = 0.03 observed cases, P = 0.07 LOCF)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with open-label extension (Kishnani 2009)
cards.people: 123 young adults aged 18–35 years with Down syndrome but no evidence of Alzheimer disease, randomly assigned to donepezil (5–10 mg/day) or placebo for 12 weeks, followed by a 12-week open-label extension. Primary measure: Severe Impairment Battery (SIB); secondary: Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales, Rivermead Behavioral Memory Test for Children, Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals (3rd edition).
cards.result: During the double-blind phase, SIB scores improved significantly from baseline in both groups, with no significant between-group differences. In the open-label phase, SIB scores in the original donepezil group remained stable while the original placebo group improved similarly to its double-blind-phase pattern. Vineland scores improved for donepezil but not placebo during the double-blind phase (observed cases P = 0.03; last observation carried forward P = 0.07), and post hoc responder analyses were significant for donepezil on three of five response definitions (P ≤ 0.045). Adverse event rates were comparable to Alzheimer-disease studies. The authors note efficacy interpretation was limited by apparent learning/practice and ceiling effects on the primary measure.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc responder definitions chosen after seeing the data, and an observed-cases analysis that loses significance under the pre-specified-style LOCF analysis (P = 0.07), are hypothesis-generating at best — the same dataset's primary outcome is null. The open-label extension, in which everyone knows they are on the drug, cannot rescue a blinded null. Read this card as 'safe, primary-null, with exploratory signals', which is also how its own authors frame it.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2015 (all drug treatments for cognitive decline in adults with Down syndrome): donepezil cognition SMD 0.52 (95% CI −0.27 to 1.13) and behaviour SMD 0.42 (−0.06 to 0.89) — both similar to placebo, with significantly more adverse events; evidence low quality
cards.summary: Cochrane 2015 (all drug treatments for cognitive decline in adults with Down syndrome): donepezil cognition SMD 0.52 (95% CI −0.27 to 1.13) and behaviour SMD 0.42 (−0.06 to 0.89) — both similar to placebo, with significantly more adverse events; evidence low quality
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Livingstone 2015)
cards.people: Nine randomised controlled trials with 427 adults (aged 18+) with Down syndrome: four donepezil studies (192 participants), two memantine (139), one simvastatin (21), one antioxidants (35), one acetyl-L-carnitine (40); follow-up from four weeks to two years. This card reports the review's donepezil analyses, the subject of this shelf.
cards.result: For donepezil versus placebo, scores on measures of cognitive functioning (SMD 0.52, 95% CI −0.27 to 1.13) and measures of behaviour (SMD 0.42, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.89) were similar to placebo — both intervals include no effect. Participants who received donepezil were significantly more likely to experience an adverse event (reported in the review with headache, dizziness and nausea prominent). The quality of this body of evidence was low, and the reviewers conclude it is difficult to draw conclusions about the effectiveness of any pharmacological intervention for cognitive decline in people with Down syndrome. The single included trial of donepezil in Down syndrome with Alzheimer's dementia (n=30, 24 weeks) found no significant differences on any of its four validated outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A standardised mean difference whose confidence interval runs from −0.27 to 1.13 is compatible with anything from slight harm to large benefit — the pooling is imprecise because the constituent trials are small and use different scales. The shelf's stamp does not rest on this interval alone: it rests on the two large trials above, each null on its own pre-specified primary measure, with this review showing the smaller adult literature does not overturn them. Memantine's results inside this same review are homed on Shelf #1399 and are not re-judged here.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large trials, two primary-outcome nulls, one imprecise pooling — donepezil's benefit in Down syndrome is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: two large trials, two primary-outcome nulls, one imprecise pooling — donepezil's benefit in Down syndrome is unproven
cards.people: Two multicentre randomised double-blind trials (Kishnani 2010, 129 children aged 10–17; Kishnani 2009, 123 young adults aged 18–35) and the Cochrane review of nine RCTs in adults (427 participants; Livingstone 2015).
cards.result: Children: no between-group difference on the Vineland-II primary measure (both groups P < 0.0001 from baseline). Young adults without dementia: no between-group difference on the Severe Impairment Battery primary measure; secondary/post-hoc signals only (Vineland P = 0.03 observed cases, P = 0.07 LOCF). Adults pooled: cognition SMD 0.52 (95% CI −0.27 to 1.13), behaviour SMD 0.42 (−0.06 to 0.89), more adverse events on donepezil, evidence low quality. The n=30 trial in Down syndrome with Alzheimer's dementia: no significant difference on any outcome. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: This shelf is donepezil only, for cognition/function in Down syndrome. It does not cover memantine (Shelf #1399), other cholinesterase inhibitors, or donepezil's established use in Alzheimer's disease in the general population (separate shelves). Small open-label and crossover studies in this field report rosier results; they are outweighed by the two blinded multicentre trials carded here. Tier C.

shelves.title: Celiprolol for vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome: arterial rupture or dissection in 20% on celiprolol versus 50% untreated in the one randomised trial (n=53, stopped early) — with cohort survival data behind it
shelves.question: In people with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, does celiprolol prevent arterial rupture and dissection and improve survival compared with no preventive treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/therapeutic use · Celiprolol/therapeutic use · Collagen Type III/genetics · Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome/complications · Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome/genetics · Humans · Vascular Diseases/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — scoped exactly to the one Ehlers-Danlos question with comparative treatment data: celiprolol in the vascular type (vEDS, COL3A1). The single randomised trial (BBEST; Ong KT et al., PMID: 20825986) randomised 53 patients with clinical vEDS (33 COL3A1-positive) to celiprolol titrated to 400 mg/day or no treatment, open-label with blinded endpoint assessment: over a mean 47 months, arterial rupture or dissection occurred in 5 of 25 (20%) on celiprolol versus 14 of 28 (50%) controls — hazard ratio 0.36 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.88; P = 0.040), a 64% relative reduction and a 30-percentage-point absolute difference — and the trial was stopped early for benefit, which inflates effect estimates. The large French referral-centre cohort (Frank M et al., PMID: 30999998; 144 molecularly confirmed patients, median follow-up 5.3 years, 90.3% on celiprolol by study end) found celiprolol-treated patients survived better than others (P = 0.0004), with dose-dependent protection (400 mg/day better than <400 mg/day, P = 0.003) — observational, so confounded by everything that goes with being treated at a national centre. A 2025 systematic review (Saputra PBT et al., PMID: 40559232) gathered 323 participants across the 2010–2023 studies and reached the same direction of conclusion. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one small open randomised trial stopped early plus concordant cohort data is a real signal for a disease with no other preventive drug, but it is not LIKELY-grade evidence, and celiprolol does not abolish events — events continue on treatment. BOUNDARY: there are no disease-modifying treatment trials for the other EDS types (classical, hypermobile and the rest); physiotherapy and bracing evidence in hypermobile EDS has no cardable comparative data and is not on this shelf.

cards.headline: Ong 2010 (BBEST, the only RCT): arterial events in 5/25 (20%) on celiprolol versus 14/28 (50%) on no treatment — HR 0.36 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.88), trial stopped early for benefit
cards.summary: Ong 2010 (BBEST, the only RCT): arterial events in 5/25 (20%) on celiprolol versus 14/28 (50%) on no treatment — HR 0.36 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.88), trial stopped early for benefit
cards.type: Prospective randomised, open, blinded-endpoints trial (BBEST; Ong 2010)
cards.people: 53 patients with clinical vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome at eight centres in France and one in Belgium, randomly assigned to celiprolol (25) or no treatment (28) for a planned 5 years; 33 patients were positive for a COL3A1 (collagen 3A1) mutation. Celiprolol was given twice daily, uptitrated in 100 mg steps every 6 months to a maximum of 400 mg/day. Primary endpoint: arterial events (rupture or dissection, fatal or not), assessed blinded.
cards.result: Mean follow-up was 47 (SD 5) months, with the trial stopped early for treatment benefit. The primary endpoint was reached by five patients (20%) in the celiprolol group and 14 (50%) in the control group (hazard ratio 0.36; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.88; P = 0.040) — a 64% relative reduction in hazard, corresponding to a 30-percentage-point absolute difference in event rates (20% versus 50%). Adverse events were severe fatigue in one patient after starting 100 mg celiprolol and mild fatigue in two patients related to dose uptitration. The authors suggest celiprolol might be the treatment of choice for preventing major complications in vEDS, while noting it remains unestablished whether clinically similar patients without a mutation are also protected.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-three patients, open-label treatment (patients and doctors knew who was on the drug — endpoints were blinded, behaviour was not), only 33 of 53 mutation-confirmed, and a trial stopped early for benefit: early stopping is known to exaggerate effect sizes, and the confidence interval (0.15 to 0.88) is wide enough to include a much smaller true effect. This is nonetheless the only randomised evidence that exists for any preventive treatment in vEDS, and no second trial has been run.

cards.headline: Frank 2019 (French national cohort, 144 patients): celiprolol-treated patients survived better (P = 0.0004), with dose-dependent protection — best at 400 mg/day (P = 0.003); overall survival 71.6% at median 5.3 years
cards.summary: Frank 2019 (French national cohort, 144 patients): celiprolol-treated patients survived better (P = 0.0004), with dose-dependent protection — best at 400 mg/day (P = 0.003); overall survival 71.6% at median 5.3 years
cards.people: 144 patients with molecularly confirmed vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (median age at diagnosis 34.5 years; 91 probands) followed at the French National Referral Center for Rare Vascular Diseases between 2000 and 2017, treated or recommended for treatment with celiprolol (≤400 mg/day) in addition to usual care, with yearly follow-up; 51% already had arterial events or arterial lesions at molecular diagnosis, and by the end of the study 90.3% were treated with celiprolol alone or in combination.
cards.result: After a median follow-up of 5.3 years, overall patient survival was 71.6% (95% CI 50% to 90%), and depended on COL3A1 variant type, age at diagnosis and medical treatment. More than two-thirds of patients remained clinically silent. Patients treated with celiprolol had a better survival than others (P = 0.0004), and the observed reduction in mortality was dose-dependent: the best protection was at 400 mg/day versus <400 mg/day (P = 0.003). The authors conclude that patients exhibited a low annual occurrence of arterial complications and a high survival rate, on which the overall medical care seems to have a positive influence.
cards.watchOut: Observational and single-centre: patients who take 400 mg/day for years differ from those who do not (tolerance, adherence, survival long enough to titrate — a built-in immortal-time advantage), and the whole cohort received specialist-centre care, so the survival figure cannot be split cleanly between the drug and the centre. The dose-response pattern (400 mg better than less) is the feature that most argues for a real drug effect, and it agrees with the randomised trial's target dose.
cards.source: Frank M, Adham S, Seigle S, Legrand A, Mirault T, Henneton P, Albuisson J, Denarié N, Mazzella JM, Mousseaux E, Messas E, Boutouyrie P, Jeunemaitre X. cards.headline: Saputra 2025 (systematic review of celiprolol in vEDS): 323 participants across the 2010–2023 studies — major vascular events reduced and survival improved in most studies, with dizziness and hypotension among the side effects
cards.summary: Saputra 2025 (systematic review of celiprolol in vEDS): 323 participants across the 2010–2023 studies — major vascular events reduced and survival improved in most studies, with dizziness and hypotension among the side effects
cards.people: Systematic review of studies comparing celiprolol with placebo or other treatments in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, published 2010–2023 and conducted primarily in European settings; 323 participants in total across the included studies.
cards.result: Celiprolol administration, starting at 100 mg daily and titrated up to 400 mg, significantly reduced the incidence of major vascular events such as arterial dissections and ruptures. Most studies reported improved survival rates and fewer hospitalisations due to acute arterial events. Variations in treatment response and side effects such as dizziness and hypotension were noted across studies, occasionally leading to treatment discontinuation. The reviewers conclude celiprolol appears to be a promising treatment for reducing vascular events in vEDS patients.
cards.watchOut: A review of essentially one small trial plus cohorts drawn from overlapping European referral populations — the 323 participants are not 323 independent confirmations, and several cohorts share patients and centres with the trial programme. Its value here is as a census of the whole literature (nothing contradicts the trial; nothing independent and large confirms it either), not as a second pillar.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one small stopped-early trial and concordant cohorts — a real but fragile signal, in vascular EDS only
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small stopped-early trial and concordant cohorts — a real but fragile signal, in vascular EDS only
cards.people: One randomised trial (Ong 2010, 53 patients, NCT00190411), one national retrospective cohort (Frank 2019, 144 patients) and one systematic review of the whole celiprolol literature (Saputra 2025, 323 participants).
cards.result: Randomised: arterial rupture/dissection 20% on celiprolol versus 50% on no treatment over ~47 months (HR 0.36, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.88 — a 64% relative reduction; 30-percentage-point absolute difference). Observational: better survival on celiprolol (P = 0.0004), dose-dependent (400 mg/day best, P = 0.003), overall cohort survival 71.6% at median 5.3 years. Review-level: consistent direction across all studies found. Events nonetheless continue on treatment, and tolerability issues (fatigue, dizziness, hypotension) occur. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single small open trial stopped early caps the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Vascular EDS only. Nothing here applies to classical, hypermobile or other Ehlers-Danlos types, for which no comparative treatment trials were found — supportive care, physiotherapy and surveillance questions in those types have no cardable comparative data and are not answered by this shelf. Celiprolol is not FDA-approved for vEDS in the United States (the EDSIVO application rests on this same trial); availability differs by country. Tier C.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ong KT et al. The Lancet. 2010 (PMID: 20825986); Frank M et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2019 (PMID: 30999998); Saputra PBT et al. Medical Sciences (Basel). 2025 (PMID: 40559232).
