shelves.title: Eye injuries — patching for corneal abrasion: 12 randomised trials found no faster healing with a patch (healed at 48 hours, relative risk 0.97); a bandage contact lens, not a patch, sped return to normal activities
shelves.question: I scratched my eye (a corneal abrasion) — should it be patched? Does an eye patch speed healing or reduce pain compared with no patch, and how does a bandage contact lens compare?
shelves.mesh: Corneal Injuries/therapy · Occlusive Dressings/adverse effects · Pain Measurement · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Wound Healing · Contact Lenses · Bandages
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — scoped to traumatic/mechanical corneal abrasion, the injury for which comparative trials exist; no cardable comparative evidence was fetched for chemical, penetrating or other eye injuries, and none is claimed. The Cochrane review (Lim 2016, PMID: 27457359) pooled 12 trials with 1,080 participants: the proportion healed did not differ between patch and no patch at 24 hours (relative risk 0.89, 95% CI 0.79–1.00; 7 trials, 531 participants, low certainty), 48 hours (RR 0.97, 0.91–1.02; 6 trials, 497, moderate certainty) or 72 hours (RR 1.01, 0.97–1.05; 4 trials, 430, moderate certainty), and time to heal differed by a mean of +0.14 days (95% CI 0 to 0.27; 6 trials, 642). Pain at 24 hours leaned against the patch (RR 1.51, 0.86–2.65; 2 trials, 193, low certainty), analgesic use did not differ (RR 0.95, 0.69–1.32; 256), and complications leaned against patching without reaching significance (RR 3.24, 0.87–12.05; 8 trials, 660); 22% of patched patients in three trials did not keep the patch on, and in one children's study walking was harder with a patch (activity score 1.7 vs 0.3 cm on a visual analogue scale). Head-to-head randomised comparisons found patching, a bandage contact lens and antibiotic ointment alone all reduced abrasion area equally (Menghini 2013, PMID: 23652196; 66 patients, all healed by day 7), while a bandage contact lens let patients return to normal activities sooner than a patch and adding a topical NSAID reduced pain (Donnenfeld 1995, PMID: 7777307; 47 patients). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): patching a simple corneal abrasion does not speed healing and may add pain and inconvenience; comfort measures and, where used, a bandage lens address symptoms instead.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2016: 12 trials, 1,080 participants — no difference in healing at 24, 48 or 72 hours with a patch; pain and complications leaned against patching
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016: 12 trials, 1,080 participants — no difference in healing at 24, 48 or 72 hours with a patch; pain and complications leaned against patching
cards.people: 12 randomised trials with 1,080 participants with corneal abrasion, comparing eye patching with no patching; healing assessed at 24, 48 and 72 hours, with pain, analgesic use, complications and activities of daily living as secondary outcomes.
cards.result: Healed proportions did not differ: at 24 hours relative risk 0.89 (95% CI 0.79–1.00; 7 trials, 531 participants, low-certainty evidence), at 48 hours RR 0.97 (0.91–1.02; 6 trials, 497, moderate certainty), at 72 hours RR 1.01 (0.97–1.05; 4 trials, 430, moderate certainty). Time to heal differed by a mean of +0.14 days with patching (95% CI 0 to 0.27; 6 trials, 642). Pain at 24 hours was more frequent with a patch (RR 1.51, 0.86–2.65; 2 trials, 193, low certainty) without reaching significance; analgesic use did not differ (RR 0.95, 0.69–1.32; 256 participants); complications were more frequent with patching, again not significantly (RR 3.24, 0.87–12.05; 8 trials, 660). In three trials 22% of participants did not comply with patching, no-patch groups more often received adjuvant antibiotics or cycloplegics, and one study in children found walking harder with a patch (visual analogue score 1.7 vs 0.3 cm).
cards.watchOut: Most pooled estimates are low-to-moderate certainty and the pain and complication signals rest on few trials with confidence intervals crossing 1 — they argue against expecting benefit from a patch, not for proven harm. Trials largely enrolled simple traumatic abrasions; abrasions in contact-lens wearers (where patching over a lens-related abrasion carries infection concern in practice) and very large abrasions are thin in this record.
cards.source: Lim CHL, Turner A, Lim BX. Patching for corneal abrasion. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27457359. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review; Cochrane CD004764). cards.headline: Menghini 2013: patch, bandage contact lens and ointment alone shrank the abrasion equally (day-1 reduction 3.4 vs 4.1 vs 3.5 mm², p=0.789); every patient healed by day 7
cards.summary: Menghini 2013: patch, bandage contact lens and ointment alone shrank the abrasion equally (day-1 reduction 3.4 vs 4.1 vs 3.5 mm², p=0.789); every patient healed by day 7
cards.people: 66 patients presenting with superficial corneal foreign bodies, randomised masked to pressure patching with ofloxacin ointment (n=18), a therapeutic contact lens with ofloxacin drops (n=20), or ofloxacin ointment alone (n=28); abrasion area measured at baseline, day 1 and day 7.
cards.result: Mean initial abrasion area was 3.6 ± 3.4 mm² (patch), 4.2 ± 4.0 mm² (contact lens) and 3.7 ± 3.1 mm² (ointment) (p=0.875). The decrease in area from presentation to day 1 was 3.4 ± 3.3 mm², 4.1 ± 4.0 mm² and 3.5 ± 3.1 mm² respectively (p=0.789) — no statistically significant difference at any time point. The epithelium had healed in all patients by day 7, and the authors concluded the three approaches were equal in reducing abrasion area and pain, so treatment can follow patient needs and preferences.
cards.watchOut: Small (66 patients) and single-centre, with abrasions caused by superficial foreign bodies rather than all trauma mechanisms; it can rule in equivalence only loosely. Its value is as a direct three-way comparison agreeing with the Cochrane patch-versus-no-patch result: no arm, including the patch, healed faster.

cards.headline: Donnenfeld 1995: healing time identical across patch, bandage lens and lens-plus-NSAID — but the lens groups returned to normal activities sooner, and ketorolac cut pain
cards.summary: Donnenfeld 1995: healing time identical across patch, bandage lens and lens-plus-NSAID — but the lens groups returned to normal activities sooner, and ketorolac cut pain
cards.people: 47 consecutive patients with traumatic corneal abrasions, randomised prospectively in a single-masked trial to (1) pressure patching, (2) a bandage contact lens, or (3) a bandage contact lens with topical 0.5% ketorolac tromethamine (an NSAID).
cards.result: There was no significant difference in healing time among the three groups. Psychometric analysis showed a significant decrease in pain in the group receiving the bandage contact lens plus the topical NSAID, and both contact-lens groups differed significantly from the pressure-patch group in ability to return to normal activities (sooner with a lens). There was no significant difference among groups in photophobia, redness, ocular irritation, headache or tearing. The authors concluded a bandage contact lens shortens time to return to normal activities and that adding an NSAID significantly decreases abrasion pain.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports significance without effect sizes, so the size of the pain and activity advantages cannot be quantified from this record — the card claims direction only. Forty-seven patients, one centre, 1995 practice; and a bandage lens is a clinical fitting with its own follow-up needs, not a home remedy — the comparison is between supervised treatments.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the patch adds nothing measurable to healing; symptom relief comes from analgesia and, where fitted, a bandage lens
cards.summary: Synthesis: the patch adds nothing measurable to healing; symptom relief comes from analgesia and, where fitted, a bandage lens
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 12 trials (1,080 participants; Lim 2016), a three-arm randomised trial (66 patients; Menghini 2013), and a randomised trial of patch versus bandage lens with or without topical NSAID (47 patients; Donnenfeld 1995) — all in traumatic/mechanical corneal abrasion.
cards.result: Healing: relative risks for being healed with a patch were 0.89 at 24 hours, 0.97 at 48 hours and 1.01 at 72 hours, all compatible with no difference, and mean time to heal differed by +0.14 days (Cochrane). Abrasion-area reduction was statistically indistinguishable between patch, bandage lens and ointment alone (Menghini), and healing time was identical across patch and lens arms (Donnenfeld). Symptoms and function: pain at 24 hours leaned against patching (RR 1.51, CI crossing 1), bandage-lens patients returned to normal activities sooner, and topical ketorolac added to a lens significantly reduced pain. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) for patching as a healing treatment.
cards.watchOut: Scope is simple traumatic corneal abrasion only. This shelf makes no claim about chemical burns, penetrating injuries, abrasions with retained foreign body or infection, or recurrent corneal erosion syndrome, none of which had comparative evidence fetched for this build. Tier C: developer's personal verdict.

shelves.title: Food intolerance — lactase for lactose intolerance: tablets blunted a lactose challenge (breath hydrogen down 55%, relative), but at a normal glass of milk blinded symptoms were negligible with or without aids
shelves.question: Milk gives me bloating and diarrhoea (lactose intolerance) — do lactase tablets or lactose-free milk actually reduce symptoms, or would I feel the same anyway?
shelves.mesh: Breath Tests · Cross-Over Studies · Dietary Supplements · Lactase/administration & dosage · Lactose Intolerance/physiopathology · Lactose Intolerance/therapy · Milk/adverse effects · Probiotics/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on the dose of lactose being faced. This shelf is scoped strictly to lactase enzyme and lactose-hydrolysed (lactose-reduced) milk for lactose intolerance, the interventions with fetched trial numbers; IgG-test-based elimination diets and other 'food intolerance' treatments had no credible trials to card and are excluded, not endorsed. In breath-test-confirmed intolerance, a randomised double-blind crossover trial of 47 adults found lactase chewable tablets (the tested product was Yamoo lactase 4500 FCC, named in the full text) reduced cumulative breath hydrogen over 180 minutes by 55% relative to placebo and improved symptom scores (P<0.05) after a lactose load (Baijal & Tandon 2021, PMID: 33490624). At ordinary intakes the picture reverses: in a randomised double-blind crossover trial in 30 self-described severely intolerant people drinking 240 ml of milk daily for a week on each milk, symptom severity scores on lactose-hydrolysed versus regular milk were 0.1–1.2 on a scale where 1 is trivial and 2 is mild, with no significant differences, and the authors concluded digestive aids are unnecessary at intakes of 240 ml/day or less (Suarez 1995, PMID: 7776987). The AHRQ systematic review (Shaukat 2010, PMID: 20404262; 36 RCTs) found moderate-quality evidence that most adults tolerate 12–15 g of lactose (about one cup of milk), and rated the evidence insufficient that lactose-reduced products reduce symptoms compared with larger lactose doses. PROPOSED SPLIT: lactase measurably blunts the response to a lactose challenge in the laboratory; at a normal glass of milk, symptoms are minimal either way and the review-level symptom evidence for aids is insufficient.

cards.headline: Baijal & Tandon 2021: in breath-test-confirmed intolerance, lactase tablets cut breath hydrogen by 55% (relative) versus placebo and improved symptom scores (P<0.05)
cards.summary: Baijal & Tandon 2021: in breath-test-confirmed intolerance, lactase tablets cut breath hydrogen by 55% (relative) versus placebo and improved symptom scores (P<0.05)
cards.people: 47 adults (mean age 33.6 years, 30 men) with lactose intolerance confirmed by hydrogen breath test, in a randomised double-blind crossover trial of lactase chewable tablets versus placebo given with a lactose load; the tested product, named in the full text, was Yamoo lactase 4500 FCC chewable tablets.
cards.result: Symptoms and the mean clinical symptom score improved significantly on lactase compared with placebo (P<0.05), and cumulative breath hydrogen excretion over 180 minutes after the lactose load was reduced by 55% relative to placebo. The trial supports a real physiological effect of the enzyme on lactose digestion under challenge conditions.
cards.watchOut: A challenge study, not daily life: a standardised lactose load in confirmed malabsorbers, with breath hydrogen — a digestion marker — as the hardest outcome and symptom scores collected over hours. Forty-seven participants, single product and dose; the 55% figure is a relative reduction in hydrogen excretion, not a 55% reduction in symptoms, and the abstract-level record does not print the absolute symptom scores.
cards.source: Baijal R, Tandon RK. Lactase chewable tablets versus placebo in lactose intolerance: a randomised double-blind crossover trial. JGH Open. 2021. PMID: 33490624. Registry ID: CTRI/2018/03/012295. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Suarez 1995 (NEJM): at 240 ml of milk a day, symptom scores were 0.1–1.2 (trivial to mild) on regular and lactose-hydrolysed milk alike — 'digestive aids are unnecessary' at this dose
cards.summary: Suarez 1995 (NEJM): at 240 ml of milk a day, symptom scores were 0.1–1.2 (trivial to mild) on regular and lactose-hydrolysed milk alike — 'digestive aids are unnecessary' at this dose
cards.people: 30 people who described themselves as severely lactose intolerant (21 confirmed lactose malabsorbers and 9 absorbers on breath testing), in a randomised double-blind crossover trial drinking 240 ml of lactose-hydrolysed milk or regular milk daily for one week each.
cards.result: Symptom severity scores during the two periods ranged from 0.1 to 1.2 (on a scale where 1 = trivial and 2 = mild), with no significant differences between hydrolysed and regular milk for any symptom. The only significant difference was in malabsorbers, who passed flatus 2.5 ± 1.1 more times per day on regular milk than on hydrolysed milk (95% CI 0.2 to 4.8). The authors concluded that at lactose intakes equivalent to 240 ml of milk per day or less, symptoms are negligible and digestive aids unnecessary.
cards.watchOut: Self-reported 'severe' intolerance is the point of the study: nearly a third of participants (9 of 30) absorbed lactose normally on testing, and even the malabsorbers reported trivial-to-mild symptoms at this dose. The trial does not test larger loads — a litre of milk or a lactose challenge drink is a different exposure, which is where the lactase card above applies.
cards.source: Suarez FL, Savaiano DA, Levitt MD. A comparison of symptoms after the consumption of milk or lactose-hydrolyzed milk by people with self-reported severe lactose intolerance. cards.headline: Shaukat 2010 (AHRQ review): most adults tolerate 12–15 g lactose (about a cup of milk); evidence that lactose-reduced products reduce symptoms was rated insufficient
cards.summary: Shaukat 2010 (AHRQ review): most adults tolerate 12–15 g lactose (about a cup of milk); evidence that lactose-reduced products reduce symptoms was rated insufficient
cards.people: Systematic review of 36 randomised trials of management strategies for lactose intolerance: 26 trials of lactase supplements, lactose-hydrolysed or lactose-reduced milk, lactose dose reduction or avoidance; 7 of probiotics; 2 of colonic adaptation; 1 of another intervention.
cards.result: The review found moderate-quality evidence that 12–15 g of lactose — roughly the amount in one cup of milk — is tolerated by most adults with lactose intolerance. It rated the evidence insufficient to determine whether lactose-reduced products (0–2 g lactose) reduce symptoms compared with standard doses above 12 g, and likewise insufficient for probiotics and for colonic adaptation strategies. In other words, at review level the symptom benefit of the aids themselves has not been demonstrated, even though small challenge trials show effects on breath hydrogen.
cards.watchOut: 'Insufficient evidence' is not 'evidence of no effect': the underlying trials were small, used differing lactose doses and symptom measures, and many enrolled people whose intolerance was self-reported rather than breath-test confirmed. The review's firmest finding is the dose threshold — tolerance of about a cup of milk's worth of lactose — which frames when any aid could plausibly matter.
cards.source: Shaukat A, Levitt MD, Taylor BC, MacDonald R, Shamliyan TA, Kane RL, Wilt TJ. Systematic review: effective management strategies for lactose intolerance. cards.headline: Synthesis: lactase works on a challenge load; at a glass of milk there is little symptom for it to remove
cards.summary: Synthesis: lactase works on a challenge load; at a glass of milk there is little symptom for it to remove
cards.people: A 47-person randomised crossover challenge trial of lactase tablets (Baijal & Tandon 2021), a 30-person randomised crossover trial of hydrolysed versus regular milk at 240 ml/day (Suarez 1995), and a 36-trial systematic review (Shaukat 2010).
cards.result: Under challenge conditions in confirmed malabsorbers, lactase reduced breath hydrogen by 55% relative to placebo and improved symptom scores (P<0.05). At 240 ml of milk daily, symptom scores were trivial-to-mild (0.1–1.2) and indistinguishable between hydrolysed and regular milk, and the systematic review rated symptom evidence for lactose-reduced products insufficient while finding most adults tolerate 12–15 g lactose. PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit is plausible and measurable against large lactose loads; at ordinary single-glass intakes, aids address symptoms that blinded testing shows are minimal.
cards.watchOut: Scope is lactase enzyme and lactose-hydrolysed milk for lactose intolerance only. This shelf does not cover IgG-food-intolerance testing or elimination diets (no cardable trials), milk allergy (a different, immune-mediated condition), secondary lactase deficiency, or probiotics and colonic adaptation, whose evidence the AHRQ review also rated insufficient. Tier C: developer's personal verdict.

shelves.title: Food poisoning: antibiotics depend on the organism — Campylobacter illness shortened by 1.32 days, Shigella dysentery reduced, but Salmonella gastroenteritis gained nothing and carriage nearly doubled
shelves.question: I have food poisoning — should I take an antibiotic? When the stool grows Campylobacter, Salmonella or Shigella, do antibiotics shorten the illness?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Campylobacter Infections/drug therapy · Diarrhea/drug therapy · Dysentery, Bacillary/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Salmonella Infections/drug therapy · Shigella
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by organism, because the three classic bacterial causes of food poisoning answer the antibiotic question differently. For Campylobacter, a meta-analysis of 11 randomised placebo-controlled trials found antibiotics shortened intestinal symptoms by 1.32 days (95% CI 0.64–1.99; P<.0001), with the benefit concentrated in treatment started early, while the authors advised a restrictive attitude in uncomplicated cases because of resistance (Ternhag 2007, PMID: 17278062). For Shigella dysentery, the Cochrane review of 16 trials (1,748 participants) concluded antibiotics reduce the duration of dysentery; in the one three-armed trial in moderately severe illness, diarrhoea at follow-up occurred with relative risk 0.21 (95% CI 0.09–0.48; furazolidone vs no drug, 73 participants) and 0.30 (0.15–0.59; cotrimoxazole vs no drug, 76 participants) (Christopher 2010, PMID: 20687081). For non-typhoidal Salmonella, the Cochrane review of 12 trials (767 participants) found no benefit: mean difference in diarrhoea duration 0 days (95% CI −0.54 to 0.54), clinical failure relative risk 0.88 (0.62–1.25), and antibiotics made passage of the same serovar one month later almost twice as likely (RR 1.96, 1.29–2.98), with more non-severe adverse reactions (Onwuezobe 2012, PMID: 23152205). BOUNDARY: empiric antibiotics and loperamide for traveller's diarrhoea are homed on Shelves #1213, #1214 and #5269 and are not re-carded here; typhoid fever is a different, systemic disease (its vaccine is Shelf #726). Fluids and supportive care remain the base treatment for all of these infections. PROPOSED SPLIT: antibiotics shorten Campylobacter symptoms by about a day and treat Shigella dysentery, but for Salmonella gastroenteritis in otherwise healthy people they do nothing measurable and prolong carriage.

cards.headline: Ternhag 2007 (Campylobacter): antibiotics shortened intestinal symptoms by 1.32 days (95% CI 0.64–1.99) across 11 randomised trials — benefit mainly when started early
cards.summary: Ternhag 2007 (Campylobacter): antibiotics shortened intestinal symptoms by 1.32 days (95% CI 0.64–1.99) across 11 randomised trials — benefit mainly when started early
cards.people: Patients with stool-culture-confirmed Campylobacter species infection in 11 randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled trials pooled in a meta-analysis (total participant number not documented in the record); antibiotics tested were mainly macrolides (erythromycin in 6 studies) and fluoroquinolones.
cards.result: Antibiotic treatment shortened the duration of intestinal symptoms by 1.32 days compared with placebo (95% CI 0.64–1.99; P<.0001, random-effects model; the fixed-effect estimate was 1.95 days). All but one study's point estimate favoured antibiotics. The authors note the clinical benefit is most apparent when treatment starts within the first three days of illness, and — because of drug resistance — advise a restrictive attitude towards antibiotics in uncomplicated cases.
cards.watchOut: The trials are old and small (conducted in the 1980s–1990s, largely in adults) and fluoroquinolone resistance in Campylobacter has risen since, so the pooled 1.32 days is best read as the effect of an effective antibiotic started early — not a promise for empiric treatment begun on day four. Most Campylobacter illness resolves within a week untreated; the gain is about a day.
cards.source: Ternhag A, Asikainen T, Giesecke J, Ekdahl K. A meta-analysis on the effects of antibiotic treatment on duration of symptoms caused by infection with Campylobacter species. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2007. PMID: 17278062. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis of pre-registration-era trials). cards.headline: Christopher 2010 (Shigella, Cochrane): antibiotics reduce the duration of dysentery — diarrhoea at follow-up relative risk 0.21–0.30 versus no drug in the one direct three-armed trial
cards.summary: Christopher 2010 (Shigella, Cochrane): antibiotics reduce the duration of dysentery — diarrhoea at follow-up relative risk 0.21–0.30 versus no drug in the one direct three-armed trial
cards.people: 16 randomised trials with 1,748 participants with Shigella dysentery, spanning four decades and differing local antibiotic-sensitivity patterns; the direct antibiotic-versus-no-drug comparison comes from one three-armed trial in people with moderately severe illness.
cards.result: The reviewers concluded that antibiotics reduce the duration of Shigella dysentery. In the three-armed trial, episodes of diarrhoea at follow-up were reduced with furazolidone versus no drug (relative risk 0.21, 95% CI 0.09–0.48; 73 participants) and with cotrimoxazole versus no drug (RR 0.30, 0.15–0.59; 76 participants). There was insufficient evidence to rank any antibiotic class above another, all antibiotics studied were safe, and evidence on preventing relapses was inadequate. Seven of the 16 trials were at risk of bias from inadequate allocation concealment or blinding, and 12 from incomplete outcome reporting.
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison against no treatment rests on a single small three-armed trial using older drugs (furazolidone, cotrimoxazole); much of the review compares one antibiotic with another, which shows drugs work similarly, not that they beat the natural course. Shigella resistance patterns are intensely local and have shifted since these trials — the review itself insists empiric choice must follow current local sensitivity data.
cards.source: Christopher PRH, David KV, John SM, Sankarapandian V. Antibiotic therapy for Shigella dysentery. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2010. PMID: 20687081. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review; Cochrane CD006784). cards.headline: Onwuezobe 2012 (Salmonella, Cochrane): no benefit on diarrhoea, fever or illness duration (mean differences ~0 days) — and shedding of the same serovar at one month was almost twice as likely after antibiotics (RR 1.96)
cards.summary: Onwuezobe 2012 (Salmonella, Cochrane): no benefit on diarrhoea, fever or illness duration (mean differences ~0 days) — and shedding of the same serovar at one month was almost twice as likely after antibiotics (RR 1.96)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials with 767 participants with symptomatic non-typhoidal Salmonella infection, comparing antibiotic treatment with placebo or no treatment; typhoid and paratyphoid infections excluded.
cards.result: No differences were detected: diarrhoea at two to four days (relative risk 1.75, 95% CI 0.42–7.21; one trial, 46 participants, very low quality), diarrhoea at five to seven days (RR 0.83, 0.62–1.12; two trials, 192, very low quality), clinical failure (RR 0.88, 0.62–1.25; seven trials, 440, very low quality); mean difference in diarrhoea duration 0 days (95% CI −0.54 to 0.54; 202 participants, low quality), fever 0.27 days (−0.11 to 0.65), illness duration 0 days (−0.68 to 0.68). Quinolones produced more negative stool cultures in week one (microbiological failure RR 0.33, 0.20–0.56; 166 participants), yet passage of the same Salmonella serovar one month after treatment was almost twice as likely in the antibiotic groups (RR 1.96, 1.29–2.98; 112 participants, three trials), and non-severe adverse drug reactions were more common. The authors concluded there is no evidence of benefit in otherwise healthy people, with effects uncertain in the very young, very old, and severe or extraintestinal disease.
cards.watchOut: The evidence is graded very low quality throughout — small old trials — so this is 'no benefit shown', with wide intervals on several outcomes, rather than proof of exact equivalence. The conclusion is explicitly limited to otherwise healthy people with gut infection: bacteraemia, extraintestinal infection, infancy, old age and immunocompromise are outside it, and antibiotics remain standard there on other grounds.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the organism decides — about a day gained in Campylobacter, a treated disease in Shigella, nothing gained and carriage prolonged in Salmonella
cards.summary: Synthesis: the organism decides — about a day gained in Campylobacter, a treated disease in Shigella, nothing gained and carriage prolonged in Salmonella
cards.people: Three syntheses of randomised evidence: Campylobacter (11 trials, Ternhag 2007), Shigella dysentery (16 trials, 1,748 participants, Christopher 2010), non-typhoidal Salmonella (12 trials, 767 participants, Onwuezobe 2012).
cards.result: Campylobacter: symptoms shortened by 1.32 days (95% CI 0.64–1.99), mostly an early-treatment effect, with a resistance caution against routine use. Shigella: antibiotics reduce dysentery duration; diarrhoea at follow-up RR 0.21–0.30 versus no drug in the single direct trial. Salmonella: diarrhoea, fever and illness-duration differences all ~0 days, clinical failure RR 0.88, and one-month carriage of the same serovar RR 1.96 with more adverse reactions. PROPOSED SPLIT — 'food poisoning' is three different antibiotic answers wearing one label; supportive care is common to all three.
cards.watchOut: These are culture-proven infections, usually identified days into the illness — by which time the early-treatment window for Campylobacter may have passed. Empiric treatment of undifferentiated traveller's diarrhoea is a separate question homed on Shelves #1213, #1214 and #5269; viral food poisoning (e.g. norovirus) has no antibiotic answer at all. Tier C: developer's personal verdict.

shelves.title: Ganglion cyst of the wrist: surgery cured 94% versus 61% for aspiration in the small randomised trial — but long-term, recurrence was 39–58% after either procedure and symptoms settled just as often with no treatment
shelves.question: I have a ganglion cyst on my wrist — should I have it drained (aspirated), cut out, or just leave it alone? How often does each choice work, and how often does the cyst come back?
shelves.mesh: Ganglion Cysts/surgery · Patient Satisfaction · Prospective Studies · Recurrence · Suction · Wrist/surgery
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the short-term and long-term records point different ways. In the only randomised trial (Khan & Hayat 2011, PMID: 23204769; 36 patients with dorsal wrist ganglion), surgical excision succeeded in 17 of 18 patients (94.4%) versus 11 of 18 (61.1%) for aspiration with intralesional triamcinolone and immobilisation (p=0.041). A non-randomised comparison of 86 patients found the two nearly equal at up to 12 months — success 86.8% (59/68) after aspiration with steroid versus 83.3% (15/18) after excision (Shah 2019, PMID: 31309054). The long view is humbling for both: in a prospective cohort of 236 patients followed a mean of 70 months, recurrence was 58% (45/78) after aspiration and 39% (40/103) after excision, symptom resolution did not differ between excision, aspiration and no treatment (p>0.3), 23 of 55 untreated ganglia resolved on their own, and the authors concluded neither intervention gave significant long-term benefit over no treatment — though satisfaction was higher after excision (p<0.0001) and 8 of 103 surgical patients had complications (Dias 2007, PMID: 17950209). PROPOSED SPLIT: excision wins the short-term cure comparison in a small trial; over years, recurrence is common after either procedure and symptoms settle at similar rates with observation alone.

cards.headline: Khan & Hayat 2011 (the randomised trial): excision succeeded in 94.4% (17/18) versus 61.1% (11/18) for aspiration plus triamcinolone injection (p=0.041)
cards.summary: Khan & Hayat 2011 (the randomised trial): excision succeeded in 94.4% (17/18) versus 61.1% (11/18) for aspiration plus triamcinolone injection (p=0.041)
cards.people: 36 patients with dorsal wrist ganglion randomised to surgical excision (18) or aspiration with intralesional triamcinolone injection and immobilisation (18).
cards.result: Treatment success was 94.4% (17 of 18) after surgical excision versus 61.1% (11 of 18) after aspiration with steroid injection — an absolute difference of 33.3 percentage points — with p=0.041. On this small head-to-head test, cutting the ganglion out cured roughly three in three while aspiration cured roughly three in five.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-six patients from one centre: a shift of two patients between outcome categories would erase the significance, so the 33-point gap should be read as 'excision ahead in a small trial', not a precise margin. Follow-up in trials of this size is short — the long-term cohort below shows recurrence accumulating for years after both procedures.
cards.source: Khan MA, Hayat S. Surgical excision versus aspiration and intralesional triamcinolone injection in the management of dorsal wrist ganglion. Journal of Hand and Microsurgery. 2011. PMID: 23204769. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Shah 2019: at up to 12 months, success was 86.8% after aspiration with steroid (59/68) and 83.3% after excision (15/18) — no advantage to surgery in this comparison
cards.summary: Shah 2019: at up to 12 months, success was 86.8% after aspiration with steroid (59/68) and 83.3% after excision (15/18) — no advantage to surgery in this comparison
cards.people: 86 patients with wrist ganglion treated by aspiration with steroid injection (68) or surgical excision (18), in a non-randomised comparative study with follow-up to 12 months.
cards.result: Success was 86.8% (59 of 68) after aspiration plus steroid versus 83.3% (15 of 18) after excision; recurrence was correspondingly 13.2% versus 16.7%. Unlike the randomised trial, this comparison found the needle and the knife level at one year.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised and heavily unbalanced (68 versus 18): patients chosen for excision may have had larger, recurrent or more troublesome ganglia, which would bias the comparison against surgery — or the reverse. Its excision arm is the same size as the randomised trial's, so the disagreement between the two studies is a disagreement between two small, differently-assembled groups.

cards.headline: Dias 2007: over a mean 70 months, recurrence was 58% after aspiration and 39% after excision — and symptoms resolved as often with no treatment; 23 of 55 untreated ganglia disappeared
cards.summary: Dias 2007: over a mean 70 months, recurrence was 58% after aspiration and 39% after excision — and symptoms resolved as often with no treatment; 23 of 55 untreated ganglia disappeared
cards.people: 236 of 283 patients with ganglion cysts followed prospectively for a mean of 70 months after surgical excision (103), aspiration (78) or no treatment (55), with symptom resolution, recurrence, complications and satisfaction recorded.
cards.result: Symptom resolution was similar across excision, aspiration and no treatment (p>0.3 for the comparisons). Among untreated patients, 23 of 55 ganglia resolved spontaneously (the abstract prints '58%' beside the count 23/55, which is arithmetically 42% — the counts are quoted here and the printed percentage appears to be an error in the source). Recurrence was 58% (45/78) after aspiration and 39% (40/103) after excision. Eight of 103 surgical patients had complications. Patient satisfaction was higher after excision (p<0.0001). The authors concluded that neither intervention gave significant long-term benefit over no treatment.
cards.watchOut: Observational — treatment was chosen, not assigned, so the groups differ at baseline (surgery is usually offered for bigger or more symptomatic ganglia). The symptom-resolution equivalence is nonetheless the shelf's most decision-relevant long-term finding, and the spontaneous-resolution count (23 of 55) is the number to set against any procedure's cure claim. Note the source's own percentage error flagged in the result: trust the counts.
cards.source: Dias JJ, Dhukaram V, Kumar P. The natural history, prognosis and treatment outcome of unused and excised ganglia: a prospective cohort. Journal of Hand Surgery (European Volume). 2007. cards.headline: Synthesis: excision leads early, everything converges late — and doing nothing is a real option with a ~4-in-10 spontaneous resolution rate in the cohort
cards.summary: Synthesis: excision leads early, everything converges late — and doing nothing is a real option with a ~4-in-10 spontaneous resolution rate in the cohort
cards.people: One randomised trial (36 patients; Khan & Hayat 2011), one non-randomised comparison (86 patients; Shah 2019), and one prospective cohort (236 patients, mean 70 months; Dias 2007), all for wrist ganglion.
cards.result: Short term: excision success 94.4% vs 61.1% for aspiration plus steroid in the randomised trial; 83.3% vs 86.8% (excision vs aspiration) in the non-randomised study. Long term: recurrence 39% after excision and 58% after aspiration; symptom resolution indistinguishable between excision, aspiration and observation; 23 of 55 untreated ganglia resolved. Satisfaction favoured excision despite this. PROPOSED SPLIT — the procedures differ in early clearance, converge in long-term symptoms, and observation carries a substantial spontaneous-resolution rate.
cards.watchOut: The evidence base is thin — one 36-patient trial and observational data — so this shelf should not be quoted as settling aspiration versus excision; it settles only that long-term expectations must be modest for both. Findings are for wrist (predominantly dorsal) ganglia; ganglia at other sites, mucous cysts of the finger, and ganglia with nerve compression or diagnostic uncertainty are outside it. Tier C: developer's personal verdict.

shelves.title: Severe hand, foot and mouth disease: IVIG shortens fever and rash times in pooled small Chinese RCTs — but the big hospital datasets show no advantage, and steroids and milrinone show none anywhere
shelves.question: In a child with severe hand, foot and mouth disease (mostly enterovirus 71), does anything beyond supportive care — IVIG, corticosteroids, milrinone — improve outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Child · Child, Preschool · Combined Modality Therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Exanthema/therapy · Female · Fever/therapy · Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease/therapy · Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous/administration & dosage · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous/adverse effects · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous/therapeutic use · Infant · Male · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Remission Induction · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the randomised evidence for severe HFMD is thin and surrogate-only. Jiao 2019 (PMID: 30646003) pooled 8 RCTs and 1,450 children and found IVIG plus conventional therapy shortened fever clearance time, rash regression time and clinical cure time versus conventional therapy alone, with the 1 g/kg/day dose subgroup performing best on most measures — but the abstract prints no pooled effect sizes and no mortality or sequelae outcome. The observational record is much larger and colder. Zhang 2018 (PMID: 29925360; 3,778 hospitalised children in Shantou) found no advantage for steroids or IVIG: recovery was lower with IVIG in mild cases and hospital stays were longer with steroid/IVIG in severe cases — patterns the authors themselves attribute in part to sicker children receiving the drugs. Liu & Qi 2020 (PMID: 32754560; 637 severe cases among 50,651 reported in Xiangyang) found an association between IVIG given in early stage IV disease and improved progression (odds ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.57), but no mortality benefit for methylprednisolone or milrinone at any stage. Nothing carded tests any antiviral; the magnesium-sulfate RCT for EV71 autonomic dysregulation found this session is a protocol without results (NCT01940250), and acyclovir rests on a single uncontrolled 13-person series from 1996 — neither is carded as evidence. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for IVIG in severe HFMD; no difference shown for corticosteroids and milrinone on the records fetched.

cards.headline: Jiao 2019 (meta-analysis of 8 RCTs): IVIG plus conventional therapy shortened fever, rash and cure times versus conventional therapy alone — no effect sizes or mortality data in the abstract
cards.summary: Jiao 2019 (meta-analysis of 8 RCTs): IVIG plus conventional therapy shortened fever, rash and cure times versus conventional therapy alone — no effect sizes or mortality data in the abstract
cards.people: 8 RCTs, 1,450 children with severe HFMD, identified from PubMed-Medline, CNKI, Wanfang and VIP databases to June 2017, comparing IVIG (low dose 0.2 g/kg/day, medium 0.4–0.5 g/kg/day, high 1.0 g/kg/day, given 2–3 days) plus conventional therapy against conventional therapy alone.
cards.result: The pooled analysis found shorter fever clearance time, shorter rash regression time and shorter clinical cure time with IVIG added to conventional therapy (directions and significance as reported; the abstract prints no pooled mean differences). In dose subgroups, the high-dose group (1 g/kg/day) had shorter fever clearance time (P < 0.05), shorter rash regression (P < 0.05) and shorter remission time of neurological symptoms (P < 0.05), but a longer clinical cure time that was not significant (P > 0.05). The authors concluded the high-dose group has a better prognosis, while advising that advantages and disadvantages be carefully considered when choosing the dose.
cards.watchOut: Every included trial is small, single-country and at unclear-to-high risk of bias, and the outcomes are times to symptom resolution, not death or neurological sequelae — the outcomes severe HFMD care actually turns on. The abstract does not report the pooled effect sizes, so the size of any time saving cannot be stated from this record; anyone quoting day-counts for IVIG in HFMD is reading the individual small trials, not this meta-analysis.
cards.source: Jiao W, Tan SR, Huang YF, Mu LH, Yang Y, Wang Y, Wu XE. The Effectiveness of Different Doses of Intravenous Immunoglobulin on Severe Hand, Foot and Mouth Disease: A Meta-Analysis. Medical Principles and Practice. 2019. PMID: 30646003. Registry ID: none in the record (meta-analysis). cards.headline: Liu & Qi 2020 (Xiangyang, 637 severe cases): IVIG in early stage IV disease was associated with better progression (OR 0.24); methylprednisolone and milrinone showed no mortality benefit at any stage
cards.summary: Liu & Qi 2020 (Xiangyang, 637 severe cases): IVIG in early stage IV disease was associated with better progression (OR 0.24); methylprednisolone and milrinone showed no mortality benefit at any stage
cards.type: Retrospective surveillance cohort with stage-stratified treatment comparisons (Liu & Qi 2020)
cards.people: 50,651 HFMD cases reported in Xiangyang, China, 2008–2013, of whom 637 (1.26%) were severe (CNS involvement) and 38 (0.075%) fatal; severe cases staged I–V on admission, with treatment comparisons by binary logistic regression. IVIG was given as 2 g/kg once or 1 g/kg daily for 2 days; methylprednisolone and milrinone were the other drugs compared.
cards.result: Risk factors for fatality included age under 3 years, enterovirus 71 positivity, autonomic nervous system dysregulation, pulmonary edema/haemorrhage, C-reactive protein >40 mg/L and cardiac troponin I >0.04 ng/mL (all P < 0.05). IVIG and mechanical ventilation applied in early stage IV significantly improved progression (both P < 0.05), with odds ratios of 0.24 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.57) for IVIG and 0.01 (95% CI 0.00 to 0.10) for ventilation — relative (odds) measures from a retrospective comparison. Neither methylprednisolone nor milrinone administered at any stage made a significant difference to mortality (all P > 0.05).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and confounded by indication and by stage: children given IVIG early in stage IV differ from those who were not, in ways a logistic model on surveillance data cannot fully remove, and the ventilation odds ratio of 0.01 is implausibly large for a treatment effect — it mostly marks which children reached a ventilator in time. Read this card as 'no signal for steroids or milrinone; a hypothesis for early IVIG', not as proof.
cards.source: Liu J, Qi J. Prevalence and Management of Severe Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease in Xiangyang, China, From 2008 to 2013. Frontiers in Pediatrics. 2020. PMID: 32754560. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective observational study). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Zhang 2018 (Shantou, 3,778 hospitalised children): no advantage for steroids or IVIG — recovery was lower with IVIG in mild cases and stays were longer with steroid/IVIG in severe cases
cards.summary: Zhang 2018 (Shantou, 3,778 hospitalised children): no advantage for steroids or IVIG — recovery was lower with IVIG in mild cases and stays were longer with steroid/IVIG in severe cases
cards.people: 3,778 children hospitalised with HFMD at a tertiary hospital in Shantou, China, 2008–2016: 58.4% mild, 41.5% severe, 0.1% very severe. Steroids were prescribed in 60.5%, IVIG in 37.1% and the traditional Chinese herb preparation Lan-Qin in 71.0%; all cases received conventional supportive therapy.
cards.result: Most cases (99.8%) recovered and 6 children died. In mild cases, the recovery rate was lower with the use of IVIG and higher with Lan-Qin, alone or in combination with steroid (P < 0.05 for both comparisons). In severe cases, longer hospital stay was observed with steroid/IVIG, with or without Lan-Qin (P < 0.05). The authors concluded there was no significant advantage to using steroids and IVIG in mild HFMD and that caution should be exercised in their extensive use.
cards.watchOut: Confounding by indication runs through every comparison here: sicker children receive IVIG and steroids, so 'lower recovery with IVIG in mild cases' and 'longer stay in severe cases' cannot be read as harm caused by the drugs. The card's weight is negative in a narrower sense — across nearly 3,800 treated children, no outcome advantage for these widely used therapies was visible. Lan-Qin's higher recovery rate in mild cases is an uncontrolled association for an unstandardised herbal preparation, not trial evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: symptom-time gains in small RCTs, no advantage in thousands of real-world cases — severe HFMD care remains supportive
cards.summary: Synthesis: symptom-time gains in small RCTs, no advantage in thousands of real-world cases — severe HFMD care remains supportive
cards.people: Three sources: a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (1,450 children; Jiao 2019), a stage-stratified retrospective series of 637 severe cases within 50,651 reported cases (Liu & Qi 2020), and a 3,778-child hospital review (Zhang 2018).
cards.result: Randomised evidence exists only for IVIG in severe HFMD and only for symptom-time outcomes: pooled, IVIG shortened fever clearance, rash regression and clinical cure times, with the 1 g/kg/day dose performing best on most measures (Jiao 2019) — no mortality or sequelae outcome, and no effect sizes in the abstract. Observational evidence is larger and colder: no advantage for steroids or IVIG in 3,778 hospitalised children (Zhang 2018); no mortality benefit for methylprednisolone or milrinone at any stage, and an IVIG association confined to early stage IV disease, in 637 severe cases (Liu & Qi 2020). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for IVIG in severe HFMD; no difference shown for corticosteroids and milrinone on the records fetched.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: this shelf covers severe (mostly EV71) HFMD in hospital, the setting of all three sources. Ordinary HFMD is a self-limiting illness managed supportively, and nothing here supports IVIG, steroids or herbals for mild disease — the Shantou data, if anything, point the other way. Acyclovir for HFMD rests on a single uncontrolled series of 12 children and 1 adult from 1996 (PMID: 8727772) and is not carded as evidence; the one randomised test of magnesium sulfate for EV71 autonomic dysregulation found this session is a protocol with no results (NCT01940250).
cards.source: Synthesis of Jiao W et al. Medical Principles and Practice. 2019 (PMID: 30646003); Liu J, Qi J. Frontiers in Pediatrics. 2020 (PMID: 32754560); Zhang D et al. BMC Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29925360).

shelves.title: IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura): prednisone eases abdominal and joint pain and steroids speed abdominal-pain resolution — but no treatment is proven for established kidney disease, and kidney prevention is homed on Shelf #3914
shelves.question: In a child with IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura), do corticosteroids help the abdominal and joint symptoms — and can they treat kidney involvement once it appears? (Whether steroids prevent kidney involvement is a separate question, answered on Shelf #3914.)
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: SPLIT, with an explicit boundary. BOUNDARY: whether early steroids PREVENT kidney involvement in IgA vasculitis is homed on Shelf #3914 (Dudley 2013: proteinuria at 12 months 15% on prednisolone versus 10% on placebo, OR 1.46 — no protection), and that question is not re-carded here; Dudley is not a card on this shelf. This shelf covers the two remaining questions: treating symptoms, and treating kidney disease once present. Symptoms: in the largest placebo-controlled trial, Ronkainen 2006 (PMID: 16887443; 171 children), prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks with a 2-week wean cut abdominal pain intensity scores (2.5 vs 4.8, P = .029) and joint pain scores (4.6 vs 7.3, P = .030), and renal symptoms, once present, resolved in 61% versus 34% (difference 27 percentage points, 95% CI 3 to 47; P = .024); the 8-year follow-up of the same cohort found no long-term differences (Jauhola 2012, PMID: 22311342). Weiss 2007 (PMID: 17974746; 15 studies) found steroids did not shorten the median time to abdominal-pain resolution but did shorten the mean and raised the odds of resolution within 24 hours. The small Huber 2004 trial (PMID: 15059282; ISRCTN85109383; 40 children) found no significant differences in renal involvement at one year (3/21 vs 2/19) or acute GI complications (2/21 vs 3/19). Established kidney disease: the Cochrane review (Hahn 2015, PMID: 26258874; 13 studies, 1,403 patients) found no significant benefit of prednisone for persistent kidney disease (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.32) and no benefit for cyclophosphamide; a single heparin trial (228 children, RR 0.27 at 3 months) stands unreplicated. PROPOSED SPLIT: POSSIBLE benefit for symptom relief; no proven treatment effect for established kidney disease on the fetched record.

cards.headline: Ronkainen 2006 (largest RCT): prednisone cut abdominal pain scores (2.5 vs 4.8) and joint pain scores (4.6 vs 7.3), and renal symptoms, once present, resolved in 61% versus 34%
cards.summary: Ronkainen 2006 (largest RCT): prednisone cut abdominal pain scores (2.5 vs 4.8) and joint pain scores (4.6 vs 7.3), and renal symptoms, once present, resolved in 61% versus 34%
cards.people: 171 children with newly diagnosed Henoch-Schönlein purpura at 14 Finnish hospitals; 84 received prednisone 1 mg/kg/day for 2 weeks followed by a 2-week wean, 87 received placebo; follow-up 6 months.
cards.result: Abdominal pain intensity score was 2.5 on prednisone versus 4.8 on placebo (P = .029); joint pain score 4.6 versus 7.3 (P = .030). Prednisone did not prevent renal symptoms, but among children who had or developed renal symptoms, they resolved in 61% on prednisone versus 34% on placebo (difference 27 percentage points, 95% CI 3 to 47; P = .024). The authors concluded that general use of prednisone is not supported, but that patients with disturbing symptoms may benefit.
cards.watchOut: The 8-year follow-up of this same cohort (Jauhola 2012, PMID: 22311342; questionnaires from 160 of 171, urine and blood-pressure screening in 138) found no differences between the prednisone and placebo groups in any long-term outcome — early prednisone neither protected nor harmed the kidney in the long run. The pain figures are average symptom scores, not proportions of children made pain-free, and the trial does not report how many children were spared severe pain.

cards.headline: Huber 2004 (small RCT): no significant difference in renal involvement at one year (3/21 vs 2/19) or acute GI complications (2/21 vs 3/19)
cards.summary: Huber 2004 (small RCT): no significant difference in renal involvement at one year (3/21 vs 2/19) or acute GI complications (2/21 vs 3/19)
cards.people: 40 children with HSP seen in the emergency department of a tertiary paediatric centre; 21 received oral prednisone 2 mg/kg/day for one week with weaning over a second week, 19 received an identical-appearing placebo.
cards.result: At one year there was no difference in the rate of renal involvement (3 of 21 prednisone versus 2 of 19 placebo; P = 1.0) and no statistically significant difference in acute gastrointestinal complications (2 of 21 versus 3 of 19; P = 0.7). Two children in the placebo group had intussusceptions compared with none in the prednisone group (P = 0.2). The authors concluded that early prednisone does not appear to reduce renal involvement or GI complications and that its routine early use in uncomplicated HSP cannot be recommended.
cards.watchOut: Forty children cannot settle anything — every interval here is wide enough to contain both worthwhile benefit and harm, and the trial was not powered for the symptom-score outcomes on which Ronkainen was positive. Its role on this shelf is directional agreement with the larger trials on prevention and complications, not independent proof.

cards.headline: Weiss 2007 (systematic review): steroids did not shorten median time to abdominal-pain resolution, but did shorten the mean and raised the odds of resolution within 24 hours
cards.summary: Weiss 2007 (systematic review): steroids did not shorten median time to abdominal-pain resolution, but did shorten the mean and raised the odds of resolution within 24 hours
cards.people: 15 eligible studies (randomised trials and observational studies) of corticosteroid treatment in Henoch-Schönlein purpura, from Medline (1956 to January 2007) and the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register.
cards.result: Corticosteroid treatment did not reduce the median time to resolution of abdominal pain, but did significantly reduce the mean resolution time and increased the odds of abdominal pain resolving within 24 hours. Although not statistically significant, the prospective data also suggested reduced odds of surgical intervention and of recurrence. The authors concluded that corticosteroids given early seem to produce consistent benefits for several clinically relevant HSP outcomes.
cards.watchOut: This 2007 review also reported that early steroids reduced the odds of developing persistent renal disease — a signal the later, larger randomised record did not confirm. Renal prevention is homed on Shelf #3914 and is deliberately not re-litigated here; this card is carded for the abdominal-pain findings only, and even those rest partly on observational studies at risk of confounding by severity.

cards.headline: Hahn 2015 (Cochrane): no significant benefit of prednisone for persistent kidney disease (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.32); heparin's one positive trial and cyclophosphamide's null trials do not add up to a treatment
cards.summary: Hahn 2015 (Cochrane): no significant benefit of prednisone for persistent kidney disease (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.32); heparin's one positive trial and cyclophosphamide's null trials do not add up to a treatment
cards.people: 13 studies, 1,403 patients (children and adults) with IgA vasculitis / Henoch-Schönlein purpura, testing interventions to prevent or treat kidney disease — including prednisone for 14–28 days versus placebo or supportive care (5 studies, 746 children), heparin (1 study, 228 children) and cyclophosphamide (2 studies; 56 children and 54 adults).
cards.result: There was no significant difference in persistent kidney disease at any time point for prednisone versus placebo or supportive care (relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.32), nor at 1, 3, 6 or 12 months separately. Heparin reduced persistent kidney disease at 3 months in its single study (RR 0.27, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.55), with no significant bleeding reported. Cyclophosphamide showed no significant benefit in either of its two studies.
cards.watchOut: The heparin result is one trial, never replicated, with an implausibly large effect for an anticoagulant in a small-vessel vasculitis — the review does not recommend it and neither does this shelf. The prednisone interval (0.42 to 1.32) still contains a worthwhile benefit for established kidney disease: 'no significant difference' here means unproven, not disproven, and severe nephritis is managed by specialists on biopsy and clinical grounds, not by this shelf. A 2023 Cochrane update (20 RCTs, 1,963 participants) reached the same conclusion; its PMID was not captured this session.
cards.source: Hahn et al. Interventions for preventing and treating kidney disease in Henoch-Schönlein Purpura (HSP). Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015. PMID: 26258874. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: steroids earn their place for the painful abdomen and joints, not for the kidney — and kidney prevention belongs to another shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: steroids earn their place for the painful abdomen and joints, not for the kidney — and kidney prevention belongs to another shelf
cards.people: Four sources: two placebo-controlled prednisone trials (Ronkainen 2006, 171 children; Huber 2004, 40 children, ISRCTN85109383), a 15-study systematic review (Weiss 2007), and the Cochrane kidney-interventions review (Hahn 2015, 13 studies, 1,403 patients); plus the 8-year follow-up of the Ronkainen cohort (Jauhola 2012), cited in that card's watch-out.
cards.result: Symptoms: prednisone reduced abdominal pain scores (2.5 vs 4.8, P = .029) and joint pain scores (4.6 vs 7.3, P = .030) in the largest trial, and pooled data show steroids shorten mean abdominal-pain resolution time and raise the odds of resolution within 24 hours (Weiss 2007). Kidney: renal symptoms, once present, resolved more often on prednisone in Ronkainen (61% vs 34%), yet the Cochrane pool finds no significant effect on persistent kidney disease (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.32), cyclophosphamide shows no benefit, and 8-year outcomes did not differ. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE benefit for treating abdominal and joint symptoms; no proven benefit for treating established kidney disease on the fetched record; prevention of kidney disease is Shelf #3914's question and is not answered here.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. BOUNDARY, restated: this shelf must not be cited on whether steroids prevent kidney involvement in IgA vasculitis — that question, and the Dudley 2013 trial that answers it, live on Shelf #3914. Severe abdominal complications (intussusception, perforation, major bleeding) and biopsy-proven severe nephritis are surgical and specialist decisions that no card here displaces.

(whether steroids prevent kidney involvement is a separate question, answered on shelf #3914.) synthesis four sources: two placebo-controlled prednisone trials (ronkainen 2006, 171 children; huber 2004, 40 children, isrctn85109383), a 15-study systematic review (weiss 2007), and the cochrane kidney-interventions review (hahn 2015, 13 studies, 1,403 patients); plus the 8-year follow-up of the ronkainen cohort (jauhola 2012), cited in that card's watch-out. symptoms: prednisone reduced abdominal pain scores (2.5 vs 4.8, p = .029) and joint pain scores (4.6 vs 7.3, p = .030) in the largest trial, and pooled data show steroids shorten mean abdominal-pain resolution time and raise the odds of resolution within 24 hours (weiss 2007). kidney: renal symptoms, once present, resolved more often on prednisone in ronkainen (61% vs 34%), yet the cochrane pool finds no significant effect on persistent kidney disease (rr 0.74, 95% ci 0.42 to 1.32), cyclophosphamide shows no benefit, and 8-year outcomes did not differ. proposed split — possible benefit for treating abdominal and joint symptoms; no proven benefit for treating established kidney disease on the fetched record; prevention of kidney disease is shelf #3914's question and is not answered here. tier c — the developer's personal verdict. boundary, restated: this shelf must not be cited on whether steroids prevent kidney involvement in iga vasculitis — that question, and the dudley 2013 trial that answers it, live on shelf #3914. severe abdominal complications (intussusception, perforation, major bleeding) and biopsy-proven severe nephritis are surgical and specialist decisions that no card here displaces. synthesis of ronkainen j et al. the journal of pediatrics. 2006 (pmid: 16887443); huber am et al. bmc medicine. 2004 (pmid: 15059282); weiss pf et al. pediatrics. 2007 (pmid: 17974746); hahn et al. cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015 (pmid: 26258874).

shelves.title: Amifampridine (Firdapse) helps Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome: two phase 3 withdrawal trials met their endpoints on muscle strength and global impression
shelves.question: Does amifampridine (3,4-diaminopyridine) help people with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome?
shelves.mesh: 4-Aminopyridine / analogs & derivatives · Amifampridine · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome / drug therapy · Muscle Strength · Phosphates / therapeutic use · Potassium Channel Blockers / therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Three randomised trials, all positive, in a rare disease. Oh 2009 (PMID 19722254) was a randomised, double-blind, cross-over trial of 3,4-diaminopyridine (up to 75-80 mg/day) versus placebo in only 7 patients with LEMS (QMG score >9) - the n is printed on the card face because it is under 10; one patient withdrew with major side effects. 3,4-DAP was significantly better than placebo on the subjective symptoms score (P=0.01), LEMS classification (P<0.001), muscle strength score (P<0.006), QMG score (P=0.02) and CMAP (P=0.03). Oh 2016 (PMID 26852139; registry NCT01377922, stated in the paper's full text and not printed in the PubMed record) was the phase 3 randomised, double-blind withdrawal trial of amifampridine phosphate (Firdapse): after an open-label run-in of 7-91 days, patients were randomised to continue amifampridine phosphate for 14 days or placebo (7-day taper, 7-day placebo). The co-primary endpoints - change at day 14 in QMG and Subject Global Impression - were met, and all 5 primary, secondary and tertiary endpoints were significant at day 8; the most common adverse events were oral and digital paresthesias, nausea and headache. The PubMed abstract gives no total N, so the card prints 'N not documented'. Shieh 2019 (PMID 30801481) was the confirmatory phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal trial in 26 adults with LEMS (13 amifampridine phosphate vs 13 placebo over 4 days), all previously titrated to 30-80 mg/day: amifampridine phosphate showed significant benefit in QMG and Subject Global Impression at 4 days, with Clinical Global Impression-Improvement, timed up-and-go and QMG limb domain also improved; placebo-group events were mainly withdrawal effects (muscle weakness n=5, fatigue n=4). The tested product is amifampridine phosphate, sold as Firdapse. Two phase 3 trials plus a positive cross-over trial, consistently in the same direction, support: PROPOSED LIKELY.

cards.summary: Oh 2009: in 7 patients, 3,4-diaminopyridine beat placebo on muscle strength, QMG score and CMAP

cards.summary: Shieh 2019: in 26 adults, amifampridine phosphate beat placebo on QMG and global impression at 4 days
cards.type: Phase 3 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal trial (Shieh 2019)
cards.people: 26 adults with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (13 amifampridine phosphate vs 13 placebo) over 4 days; all had been on amifampridine phosphate 30-80 mg/day and titrated to the optimal dose for at least 1 week before randomisation

shelves.title: Long QT syndrome beyond beta-blockers: left cardiac sympathetic denervation cut the yearly cardiac event rate by 86%, and mexiletine cut arrhythmic events in LQT3 from 22% to 3%
shelves.question: Beyond beta-blockers, what treatments help people with long QT syndrome - sympathetic denervation or mexiletine?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists / therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Long QT Syndrome / surgery · Male · Retrospective Studies · Sympathectomy / methods · Syncope / etiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: BOUNDARY: which beta-blocker to use for long QT syndrome is homed on shelf #3074 and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers treatments beyond beta-blockers. All the evidence is observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE - but the effects are large. Dusi 2022 (PMID 35331422) reported a single centre's 50-year experience of left cardiac sympathetic denervation (LCSD) in 125 patients with long QT syndrome (58% women, mean QTc 527 +/- 60 ms, 90% on beta blockers), followed for 12.9 +/- 10.3 years: after LCSD, 17% of the very-high-risk group remained asymptomatic, compared with 52%, 47% and 97% in the aborted-cardiac-arrest, syncope/ICD-shock and primary-prevention groups (P<0.0001), with an overall 86% decrease in the mean yearly cardiac event rate (P<0.0001); among the 45 patients with only syncope or ICD shocks before LCSD, none had aborted cardiac arrest or sudden death as a first symptom afterwards, and a 6-month post-LCSD QTc under 500 ms predicted an excellent outcome. Mazzanti 2016 (PMID 26940925) studied 34 patients with long QT syndrome type 3 (LQT3) (56% male, median age at treatment start 22 years, median baseline QTc 509 ms) on oral mexiletine for a median 36 months at a mean dose of 8 +/- 0.5 mg/kg/day: QTc shortened by 63 +/- 6 ms (p<0.0001), the proportion with arrhythmic events fell from 22% to 3% (p=0.031), mean events per patient from 0.43 +/- 0.17 to 0.03 +/- 0.03 (p=0.027), and the annual event rate from 10.3% to 0.7% (p=0.0097) - a before-after comparison over equal-duration periods. Funasako 2016 (PMID 26632536) gave an intravenous mexiletine infusion test (2 mg/kg) to 31 genotype-positive patients (LQT3 n=15; LQT1 n=4, LQT2 n=12): QTc shortened in both groups (P<0.0001 vs baseline), but the shortening was larger in LQT3 (99 +/- 39 ms) than in LQT1/LQT2 (48 +/- 32 ms), P=0.0004, and the test identified LQT3 with 86.7% sensitivity, 81.3% specificity and 81.3% accuracy at an optimal delta-QTc cut-off of 69 ms, with no pro-arrhythmic event. LCSD and mexiletine are additions to, not replacements for, beta-blockers in these series - 90% of the LCSD patients were on beta blockers. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Dusi 2022: after left cardiac sympathetic denervation, the yearly cardiac event rate fell by 86% in 125 patients followed for 13 years
cards.summary: Dusi 2022: after left cardiac sympathetic denervation, the yearly cardiac event rate fell by 86% in 125 patients followed for 13 years
cards.people: 125 patients with long QT syndrome who had LCSD between 1973 and 2020 at one centre (58% women, mean QTc 527 +/- 60 ms, 90% on beta blockers), followed for 12.9 +/- 10.3 years
cards.result: Groups were very high risk (n=18), aborted cardiac arrest (n=31), syncope and/or ICD shocks on beta blockers (n=45) and primary prevention (n=31). After LCSD, 17% in the very-high-risk group remained asymptomatic, compared with 52%, 47% and 97% in the other three groups (P<0.0001), with an overall 86% decrease in the mean yearly cardiac event rate (P<0.0001). Among the 45 patients with only syncope/ICD shocks before LCSD, none had aborted cardiac arrest or sudden death as a first symptom after LCSD. A 6-month post-LCSD QTc <500 ms predicted an excellent outcome; patients with QTc of 500 ms or more had a 50% chance of shortening it by an average of 60 ms.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single centre, no control group - the 86% fall is a before-after comparison, and the very-high-risk group still did badly (only 17% asymptomatic).
cards.source: Dusi V, Pugliese L, De Ferrari GM, et al. Left Cardiac Sympathetic Denervation for Long QT Syndrome: 50 Years' Experience Provides Guidance for Management. JACC Clin Electrophysiol. 2022. PMID: 35331422. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Funasako 2016: a mexiletine infusion test shortened QTc by 99 ms in LQT3 vs 48 ms in LQT1/LQT2, identifying LQT3 with 86.7% sensitivity
cards.summary: Funasako 2016: a mexiletine infusion test shortened QTc by 99 ms in LQT3 vs 48 ms in LQT1/LQT2, identifying LQT3 with 86.7% sensitivity
cards.people: 31 genotype-positive patients with long QT syndrome (LQT3 n=15; LQT1 n=4 and LQT2 n=12) given intravenous mexiletine 2 mg/kg during sinus rhythm
cards.result: QTc shortened with mexiletine in both groups (P<0.0001 vs baseline). The degree of QTc shortening was significantly larger in LQT3 than in LQT1/LQT2 patients (99 +/- 39 ms vs 48 +/- 32 ms; P=0.0004). Sensitivity, specificity and predictive accuracy of the mexiletine infusion test for differentiating LQT3 from LQT1/LQT2 were 86.7%, 81.3% and 81.3%, respectively, with an optimal delta-QTc cut-off of 69 ms. No pro-arrhythmic event was observed.
cards.watchOut: A diagnostic test, not a treatment trial - it shows mexiletine shortens QTc most in LQT3, which supports using it there, but it does not itself prove fewer events.

cards.headline: Synthesis: LCSD and mexiletine both look strongly protective in long QT syndrome - but only in retrospective, before-after data
cards.summary: Synthesis: LCSD and mexiletine both look strongly protective in long QT syndrome - but only in retrospective, before-after data

cards.result: LCSD cut the mean yearly cardiac event rate by 86% over about 13 years (Dusi 2022). shelves.title: Long-sightedness (hyperopia): no randomised trials compare PRK with LASIK, and the best available data show LASIK is no better than PRK
shelves.question: For long-sightedness (hyperopia), is laser surgery with LASIK or with PRK better?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Hyperopia / surgery · Keratomileusis, Laser In Situ / methods · Lasers, Excimer / therapeutic use · Photorefractive Keratectomy / methods · Refraction, Ocular / physiology · Treatment Outcome · Visual Acuity / physiology
shelves.balance: There is no randomised evidence at all. Settas 2012 (PMID 22696365), a Cochrane review that planned to include only randomised controlled trials comparing PRK with LASIK for hyperopia, identified no studies meeting its inclusion criteria and concluded that no robust, reliable conclusions could be reached - although the non-randomised trials it discussed narratively appeared to show comparable efficacy, and high-quality open RCTs are needed. The best comparative data come from two meta-analyses of non-randomised studies. Almutairi 2025 (PMID 40102791; PROSPERO CRD42023469543) pooled 6 articles (419 participants, 585 eyes; 5 retrospective, 1 case-series): the final mean refractive spherical equivalent differed by a weighted mean difference of -0.05 (P=0.06; the 95% CI is printed in the record as 0.42 to 0.31, apparently missing a minus sign), the odds ratio for uncorrected distance visual acuity of 20/20 or better was 0.58 (95% CI 0.39-0.78, P=0.33) and for 20/40 or better 1.40 (95% CI 0.65-3.02, P=0.81) - LASIK had no significant benefits over PRK on clinical outcomes, with less corneal haze in LASIK-treated eyes at 1-3 months. Hassanzadeh 2025 (PMID 40287029) pooled PRK alone - 750 eyes from 481 patients (49.5% female): postoperative improvement in uncorrected visual acuity, spherical equivalent and cylindrical power was statistically significant (P=0.001), but overall corneal haze incidence was 32.5% (95% CI 26.5-38.4%), significantly higher than in myopic PRK. So the honest answer is that neither operation has been shown better than the other in a randomised trial, and PRK carries a roughly one-in-three chance of corneal haze: PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

shelves.title: Molar pregnancy: prophylactic chemotherapy after evacuation roughly halves later cancerous growth in high-risk complete moles in the pooled trials (relative risk 0.37; 19% versus 39.7% with a single actinomycin D dose in a 426-woman cohort) — but one single methotrexate dose did not significantly help, and routine prophylaxis is not recommended
shelves.question: In women whose molar pregnancy (hydatidiform mole) has been evacuated, does prophylactic chemotherapy reduce the later development of gestational trophoblastic neoplasia (GTN), and does the regimen matter?
shelves.mesh: Antineoplastic Agents / therapeutic use · Dactinomycin / therapeutic use · Female · Gestational Trophoblastic Disease / epidemiology · Gestational Trophoblastic Disease / prevention & control · Humans · Hydatidiform Mole / drug therapy · Incidence · Methotrexate / therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: Evacuation cures most molar pregnancies; the contested question is prophylactic chemotherapy (P-Chem) against later GTN. Wang 2017 (PMID: 28892119; Registry ID: none in the record), the Cochrane review of 3 randomised trials (613 women), found P-Chem reduced GTN after complete mole with a relative risk of 0.37 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.57), but two of the three trials were poor quality; the one good small trial in high-risk women gave a relative risk of 0.28 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.73), and P-Chem delayed GTN diagnosis and increased the courses needed to cure it. Uberti 2025 (PMID: 39799786; Registry ID: none in the record), a 27-year retrospective cohort of 426 high-risk complete moles, found GTN in 19% (55/290) after a single actinomycin D bolus at evacuation versus 39.7% (54/136) without (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.66; NNT 5). Akhavan 2024 (PMID: 39538177; Registry ID: none in the record) found a single methotrexate dose did not significantly reduce progression (18.2% versus 36.3%; p=0.12; n=80). Proposed stamp: SPLIT (multi-course or single-dose actinomycin D prophylaxis in high-risk complete mole: POSSIBLE benefit · single-dose methotrexate: no significant effect · routine use not recommended by the Cochrane authors).

cards.headline: Wang 2017 (Cochrane): prophylactic chemotherapy cut GTN after complete mole (relative risk 0.37) — on mostly poor-quality trials
cards.summary: Wang 2017 (Cochrane): prophylactic chemotherapy cut GTN after complete mole (relative risk 0.37) — on mostly poor-quality trials
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Wang 2017)
cards.people: Women with complete hydatidiform mole in 3 randomised trials; n=613 (550 in the main GTN analysis)
cards.result: GTN after complete mole: relative risk 0.37 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.57; 3 studies, 550 participants; low-quality evidence) with prophylactic methotrexate or dactinomycin versus none. In the single good-quality trial in high-risk women the relative risk was 0.28 (95% CI 0.10 to 0.73; 59 participants). Time to GTN diagnosis was longer with P-Chem (mean difference 28.72 days, 95% CI 13.19 to 44.24), and women who still developed GTN needed more courses to cure it (mean difference 1.10 courses, 95% CI 0.52 to 1.68).
cards.watchOut: Two of the three trials were judged poor quality and high risk of bias; toxicity, drug resistance and survival could not be meta-analysed, and the Cochrane authors conclude P-Chem cannot currently be recommended routinely.
cards.source: Wang Q, Fu J, Hu L, Fang F, Xie L, Chen H, He F, Wu T, Lawrie TA. Prophylactic chemotherapy for hydatidiform mole to prevent gestational trophoblastic neoplasia. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017. PMID: 28892119. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Uberti 2025: a single actinomycin D bolus at evacuation halved later GTN in high-risk complete mole (19% versus 39.7%; relative risk 0.48)
cards.summary: Uberti 2025: a single actinomycin D bolus at evacuation halved later GTN in high-risk complete mole (19% versus 39.7%; relative risk 0.48)
cards.people: Women with high-risk complete hydatidiform mole at one Brazilian trophoblastic disease centre, 1996-2023; n=426 (290 given prophylaxis, 136 not)
cards.result: Post-molar GTN occurred in 19% (55/290) with a single bolus of actinomycin D (1.25 mg/m2) at uterine evacuation versus 39.7% (54/136) without (p<0.001); relative risk 0.48 (95% CI 0.35 to 0.66), number needed to treat 5. The prophylaxis group also had lower hCG at GTN diagnosis (p=0.007), lower recurrence risk (p=0.001) and lower hysterectomy risk (p=0.04), with no difference in time to remission (p=0.72).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective over 27 years: who received prophylaxis was a clinical-era decision, not randomisation, so confounding by era and selection is likely; single centre.
cards.source: Uberti EMH, Medeiros LRF, Cardoso RB, Muller KP, Patias CB, Nunes TF, Reis RJ, Marçal JMB. cards.headline: Akhavan 2024: a single methotrexate dose did not significantly prevent GTN (18.2% versus 36.3%; p=0.12)
cards.summary: Akhavan 2024: a single methotrexate dose did not significantly prevent GTN (18.2% versus 36.3%; p=0.12)
cards.people: Women with high-risk complete molar pregnancy after suction curettage at one Tehran hospital; n=80 (22 given prophylaxis, 58 not)
cards.result: Progression to post-molar GTN was 18.2% (4/22) with a single intramuscular methotrexate dose (50 mg/m2) versus 36.3% (21/58) without (p=0.12). Spontaneous remission was 81.8% versus 63.7% (p=0.12) and time to remission 57 versus 61.24 days (p=0.46); among women who developed GTN, prophylaxis did not reduce metastasis, first-line chemotherapy resistance, or time to hCG normalisation (all p>0.05).
cards.watchOut: Small and unevenly split (22 versus 58) despite the paper describing random allocation, and underpowered: the point estimate favours prophylaxis but the confidence interval is wide and the difference is not significant.
cards.source: Akhavan S, Hoorshad N, Mousavi AS, Sheikhhasani S, Rezayof E, Zamani N. The role of single-dose prophylactic methotrexate in the prevention of post-molar gestational trophoblastic neoplasia in patients with high-risk molar pregnancy. BMC Cancer. 2024. PMID: 39538177. cards.headline: Synthesis: prophylaxis works best as actinomycin D or multi-course regimens in high-risk complete mole; a single methotrexate dose is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: prophylaxis works best as actinomycin D or multi-course regimens in high-risk complete mole; a single methotrexate dose is unproven
cards.people: All carded evidence: 3 randomised trials pooled by Cochrane (n=613), one 426-woman retrospective cohort, and one 80-woman comparative study
cards.result: Pooled randomised relative risk for GTN was 0.37 (Wang 2017); the single-dose actinomycin D cohort showed 19% versus 39.7% (Uberti 2025); single-dose methotrexate showed no significant effect (Akhavan 2024). Prophylaxis also delays GTN diagnosis and can increase the chemotherapy courses needed to cure GTN that still occurs.
cards.watchOut: The strongest single study (Uberti) is retrospective and the randomised base is old and mostly poor quality; standard care where follow-up is reliable remains evacuation plus hCG surveillance, treating GTN only if it develops.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wang 2017 (PMID: 28892119), Uberti 2025 (PMID: 39799786) and Akhavan 2024 (PMID: 39538177).

shelves.question: In oral candidiasis (oral thrush), how do fluconazole and miconazole gel compare with nystatin, and how effective is nystatin itself?
