shelves.balance: SPLIT. The head-to-head randomised evidence consistently puts nystatin suspension last among the tested agents. Flynn 1995 (PMID: 7636666) randomised 182 immunocompromised children: fluconazole suspension cured 91% versus 51% on nystatin, with organism eradication 76% versus 11%, though relapse by one month was similar (28% versus 27%). Hoppe 1997 (DOI 10.1097/00006454-199703000-00007; PMID not captured this session) randomised 183 healthy infants: miconazole gel cured 99% versus 54% on nystatin by day 12. Rai 2022 (PMID: 36362833) shows nystatin is nonetheless an active topical drug — it matched photodynamic therapy for clinical remission of denture stomatitis and lowered Candida counts more at 60 days — and records nystatin pastilles beating placebo for denture stomatitis. No carded trial gives nystatin suspension a placebo-controlled win in ordinary thrush. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (azoles superior head-to-head; nystatin active but weaker).

cards.headline: Flynn 1995: fluconazole cured 91% versus 51% on nystatin in immunocompromised children
cards.summary: Flynn 1995: fluconazole cured 91% versus 51% on nystatin in immunocompromised children
cards.people: 182 immunocompromised infants and children aged 5 months to 14 years with oral thrush enrolled across 32 centres; 159 with culture-confirmed thrush and at least 7 days of study drug were evaluated for efficacy.
cards.result: Clinical cure: 91% with fluconazole suspension (2 to 3 mg/kg once daily) versus 51% with nystatin 400,000 units four times daily for 14 days (p < 0.001) — an absolute difference of 40 percentage points. Eradication of the organism cultured at entry: 76% versus 11% (p < 0.001). Relapse after treatment was similar: 18% versus 24% at 2 weeks and 28% versus 27% at 1 month. Gastrointestinal conditions developed in six fluconazole patients and three nystatin patients; two fluconazole recipients were withdrawn.
cards.watchOut: Pre-registration-era trial in immunocompromised children only — the result does not by itself set treatment for healthy infants or adults, and relapse within a month was common in both arms (about 1 in 4) despite the large cure gap.
cards.source: Flynn PM et al. Oropharyngeal candidiasis in immunocompromised children: a randomized, multicenter study of orally administered fluconazole suspension versus nystatin. The Multicenter Fluconazole Study Group. J Pediatr. 1995. PMID: 7636666. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Hoppe 1997: miconazole gel cured 99% versus 54% on nystatin by day 12 in healthy infants
cards.summary: Hoppe 1997: miconazole gel cured 99% versus 54% on nystatin by day 12 in healthy infants
cards.people: 183 infants aged under 1 year with signs of oropharyngeal candidiasis and no underlying disease, randomised to miconazole gel 25 mg four times daily (98 infants) or nystatin suspension 100,000 units four times daily (85 infants) for 5 to 12 days.
cards.result: Cure by day 5: 83/98 (85%) with miconazole gel versus 18/85 (21%) with nystatin (P < 0.0001). Cure by day 12: 97/98 (99%) versus 46/85 (54%) (P < 0.0001) — an absolute difference of 45 percentage points. Numbers taken from the Clinical Evidence evidence table and the Canadian Paediatric Society review fetched this session, not from the PubMed abstract (see flag in the part summary).
cards.watchOut: Open (unblinded) trial, and miconazole oral gel is not available in every country and carries age cautions in young infants — the size of the gap over nystatin suspension is the finding, not a universal prescribing instruction.
cards.source: Hoppe JE; Antifungals Study Group. Treatment of oropharyngeal candidiasis in immunocompetent infants: a randomized multicenter study of miconazole gel vs nystatin suspension. Pediatr Infect Dis J. 1997. PMID: not captured this session (DOI 10.1097/00006454-199703000-00007). Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Rai 2022: nystatin matched photodynamic therapy for denture stomatitis, but the review's own comparisons leave nystatin suspension behind fluconazole
cards.summary: Rai 2022: nystatin matched photodynamic therapy for denture stomatitis, but the review's own comparisons leave nystatin suspension behind fluconazole
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Rai 2022)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trials comparing topical nystatin with other antifungal therapies or placebo in oral candidiasis; the meta-analysis pooled five studies comparing nystatin suspensions with photodynamic therapy.
cards.result: At 60 days, Candida colony-forming units per mL differed significantly between nystatin and photodynamic therapy on both palatal mucosa and denture surfaces, favouring nystatin, with low heterogeneity; clinical remission of denture stomatitis was equal between the two. The review's descriptive synthesis records that nystatin pastilles beat placebo for denture stomatitis while nystatin suspension did not beat fluconazole in infants, children or HIV/AIDS patients.
cards.watchOut: The pooled comparison is against photodynamic therapy, a niche comparator — it shows nystatin is an active topical agent, not that it is the best one; the head-to-head RCTs on this shelf (Flynn 1995; Hoppe 1997) both found it clearly inferior to an azole.
cards.source: Rai A, Misra SR, Panda S, Sokolowski G, Mishra L, Das R, Lapinska B. Nystatin Effectiveness in Oral Candidiasis Treatment: A Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis of Clinical Trials. Life (Basel). 2022. PMID: 36362833. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Synthesis: azoles beat nystatin head-to-head; nystatin is an active but weaker standard
cards.summary: Synthesis: azoles beat nystatin head-to-head; nystatin is an active but weaker standard
cards.people: Three sources: two randomised head-to-head trials (Flynn 1995, n=182 enrolled; Hoppe 1997, n=183) and one systematic review of nystatin RCTs (Rai 2022).
cards.result: Fluconazole versus nystatin: clinical cure 91% versus 51% (Flynn 1995). Miconazole gel versus nystatin: cure 99% versus 54% by day 12 (Hoppe 1997). Nystatin versus photodynamic therapy: equal clinical remission of denture stomatitis, with lower Candida counts on nystatin at 60 days (Rai 2022). No carded trial compares nystatin suspension with placebo in ordinary thrush. Proposed stamp: SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Populations differ across the shelf — immunocompromised children, healthy infants, denture wearers — so the stamp is about the comparative standing of the drugs, not a single treatment algorithm for every form of oral candidiasis.

shelves.title: Piles: excision beats banding for durability — recurrence 6.1% versus 47.5% in grade III disease — but banding hurts less (pain 1 versus 4) and returns people to work in 1 day versus 9
shelves.question: In symptomatic haemorrhoids (piles), how do rubber band ligation and excisional haemorrhoidectomy compare for symptom control, recurrence, pain and recovery — by grade of disease?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Hemorrhoidectomy* / adverse effects · Hemorrhoidectomy* / methods · Hemorrhoids* / surgery · Humans · Ligation / adverse effects · Ligation / instrumentation · Ligation / methods · Male · Middle Aged · Netherlands / epidemiology · Quality of Life · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT, scoped to banding versus excision — haemorrhoidal artery ligation versus banding is homed on Shelf #1938 and flavonoid (MPFF) tablets on Shelf #4240, and neither is re-carded here. The trade-off is consistent across two decades of trials. For grade III piles, excision is far more durable: in the HollAND trial (van Oostendorp 2025, PMID: 39952268; NCT04621695) recurrence was 6.1% after haemorrhoidectomy versus 47.5% after banding, but banding hurt less (first-week pain 1 versus 4) and returned patients to work in 1 versus 9 days. The Cochrane review (Shanmugam 2005, PMID: 16034963) found the same pattern by grade — remission relative risk 1.23 favouring excision in grade III, 1.07 (no difference) in grade II — with more pain and delayed complications after excision; Dekker 2021 (PMID: 33683503) found the same split across eight RCTs but judged trial quality too poor for a firm verdict. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (grade II: banding a reasonable first procedure · grade III: excision more durable at the cost of pain and recovery time).

cards.headline: van Oostendorp 2025 (HollAND): recurrence 47.5% after banding versus 6.1% after haemorrhoidectomy in grade III piles — but back to work in 1 versus 9 days
cards.summary: van Oostendorp 2025 (HollAND): recurrence 47.5% after banding versus 6.1% after haemorrhoidectomy in grade III piles — but back to work in 1 versus 9 days
cards.people: 87 adults with symptomatic grade III (Goligher) haemorrhoids randomised across 10 Dutch hospitals to rubber band ligation (47, up to 2 sessions) or haemorrhoidectomy (40).
cards.result: Recurrence: 47.5% with banding versus 6.1% with haemorrhoidectomy — an absolute risk difference of 41% (95% CI 24 to 59). Banding was not noninferior on quality-adjusted life years (difference -0.045; 95% CI -0.087 to -0.004). Pain in the first week was higher after haemorrhoidectomy (visual analogue scale 4 versus 1; p = 0.002), return to work was sooner after banding (1 versus 9 days; p = 0.021), complication rates were comparable, and patient-reported symptom scores favoured haemorrhoidectomy. The trial stopped early for funding reasons.
cards.watchOut: Early termination left only 87 of the planned sample, and strong patient treatment preferences hindered recruitment — the recurrence gap is large and consistent with older evidence, but the quality-of-life estimate is imprecise; grade III only.
cards.source: van Oostendorp JY, Dekker L, van Dieren S, Veldkamp R, Bemelman WA, Han-Geurts IJM; HollAND Study Group. Comparison of Rubber Band Ligation and Hemorrhoidectomy in Patients With Symptomatic Hemorrhoids Grade III: A Multicenter, Open-Label, Randomized Controlled Noninferiority Trial. Dis Colon Rectum. 2025. PMID: 39952268. Registry ID: NCT04621695. cards.headline: Shanmugam 2005: excision beat banding for complete remission in grade III (relative risk 1.23) but not grade II — with more pain (relative risk 1.94) and more delayed complications (relative risk 6.32)
cards.summary: Shanmugam 2005: excision beat banding for complete remission in grade III (relative risk 1.23) but not grade II — with more pain (relative risk 1.94) and more delayed complications (relative risk 6.32)
cards.people: Adults with symptomatic haemorrhoids in three randomised trials comparing rubber band ligation with excisional haemorrhoidectomy (202 patients in the remission analysis; trials rated poor methodological quality).
cards.result: Complete remission of symptoms favoured excision (relative risk 1.68, 95% CI 1.00 to 2.83; 3 studies, 202 patients; heterogeneity I2 = 90.5%). By grade: grade III relative risk 1.23 (95% CI 1.04 to 1.45; 2 trials, 116 patients); grade II relative risk 1.07 (95% CI 0.94 to 1.21; 1 trial, 32 patients) — no significant difference. Fewer patients needed re-treatment after excision (relative risk 0.20, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.40). Postoperative pain was commoner after excision (relative risk 1.94, 95% CI 1.62 to 2.33; 212 patients) and delayed complications differed (relative risk 6.32, 95% CI 1.15 to 34.89; 204 patients). Absolute rates are not printed in the record, so these relative effects cannot be converted to absolute differences from this source.
cards.watchOut: Only three small, poor-quality trials with very high heterogeneity for the headline outcome (I2 = 90.5%) — the grade-by-grade pattern (excision for grade III, banding acceptable for grade II) is the durable finding, and it is what the modern HollAND trial then confirmed for grade III.
cards.source: Shanmugam V, Thaha MA, Rabindranath KS, Campbell KL, Steele RJC, Loudon MA. Rubber band ligation versus excisional haemorrhoidectomy for haemorrhoids. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2005. PMID: 16034963. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Hemorrhoids / surgery* · Humans · Ligation / instrumentation · Ligation / methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic.

cards.headline: Dekker 2021: across 8 RCTs in grade II–III disease, symptom control favoured haemorrhoidectomy and pain favoured banding — but trial quality blocked a firm verdict
cards.summary: Dekker 2021: across 8 RCTs in grade II–III disease, symptom control favoured haemorrhoidectomy and pain favoured banding — but trial quality blocked a firm verdict
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Dekker 2021)
cards.people: Eight randomised trials comparing rubber band ligation with haemorrhoidectomy for grade II–III haemorrhoids, identified from 324 studies screened (search to May 2018); total participant number not printed in the record.
cards.result: Control of symptoms was better following haemorrhoidectomy; patients had less pain after rubber band ligation; complications (bleeding, urinary retention, anal incontinence/stenosis) were more frequent in the haemorrhoidectomy group; patient satisfaction was equal in both groups; in one study patients resumed work earlier after banding. The authors conclude that because of poor study quality it is not possible to determine which procedure is best for grade II–III haemorrhoids. No pooled effect sizes are printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative synthesis — diverse, poorly defined outcome measures meant the same trade-off (durability versus pain) is described rather than measured; the quantified version of that trade-off comes from the HollAND trial carded on this shelf.
cards.source: Dekker L, Han-Geurts IJM, Rørvik HD, van Dieren S, Bemelman WA. Rubber band ligation versus haemorrhoidectomy for the treatment of grade II-III haemorrhoids: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials. Tech Coloproctol. 2021. PMID: 33683503. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: banding first for grade II; excision is the durable option for grade III, paid for in pain and time off work
cards.summary: Synthesis: banding first for grade II; excision is the durable option for grade III, paid for in pain and time off work
cards.people: Three sources on banding versus excision: the HollAND RCT (van Oostendorp 2025, n=87, grade III), the Cochrane review (Shanmugam 2005, 3 trials) and a systematic review of 8 RCTs (Dekker 2021). Haemorrhoidal artery ligation versus banding is homed on Shelf #1938 and flavonoid (MPFF) tablets on Shelf #4240; neither is re-carded here.
cards.result: Grade III recurrence: 47.5% after banding versus 6.1% after excision (van Oostendorp 2025); remission relative risk 1.23 favouring excision in grade III but 1.07 (no significant difference) in grade II (Shanmugam 2005). Pain and recovery favour banding: first-week pain 1 versus 4 and return to work 1 versus 9 days (van Oostendorp 2025). Proposed stamp: SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Grade IV (irreducible) piles, thrombosed external piles and conservative measures (fibre, fluids) are outside the carded comparisons; stapled haemorrhoidopexy is not carded on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Oostendorp 2025 (PMID: 39952268; NCT04621695), Shanmugam 2005 (PMID: 16034963) and Dekker 2021 (PMID: 33683503).

shelves.title: Polyhydramnios: draining fluid was followed by delivery at a median 36.5 weeks with rare immediate complications in 86 pregnancies — but no study shows draining prolongs pregnancy, and indomethacin rests on one 22-woman series from the 1990s
shelves.question: In a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios (excess amniotic fluid), does amnioreduction (draining fluid) or indomethacin improve outcomes, and what are the risks?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Polyhydramnios* / diagnostic imaging · Polyhydramnios* / surgery · Polyhydramnios* / therapy · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Outcome · Premature Birth* / etiology · Premature Birth* / prevention & control · Ultrasonography, Prenatal
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), observational evidence only — no randomised or controlled trial of any treatment for polyhydramnios was found. Amnioreduction is done to relieve maternal symptoms: in Laoreti 2024 (PMID: 38671719), 86 pregnancies drained at a median 32.5 weeks delivered at a median 36.5 weeks, 30 days after the first drain, with one abruption and two preterm deliveries as immediate complications — but 79% had a fetal anomaly, and there is no untreated comparison. Zargarzadeh 2025 (PMID: 40254983) pooled seven studies (390 singleton pregnancies) and found low pooled odds of abruption (0.04) and delivery within 48 hours (0.10), while stating that evidence for fetal benefit or pregnancy prolongation is lacking. Indomethacin rests on Cabrol 1996 (PMID: 8735752): 22 women, fluid reduction reported, mean delivery at 37.5 weeks, uncontrolled. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) for amnioreduction as a symptom-relieving procedure.

cards.headline: Laoreti 2024: amnioreduction series — delivery at a median 36.5 weeks, 30 days after the first drain; immediate complications rare, but 79% had a fetal anomaly
cards.summary: Laoreti 2024: amnioreduction series — delivery at a median 36.5 weeks, 30 days after the first drain; immediate complications rare, but 79% had a fetal anomaly
cards.people: 86 pregnancies (65 singleton, 21 twin) with symptomatic polyhydramnios undergoing amnioreduction at a tertiary referral centre, 2010 to 2023; median gestation at first amnioreduction 32.5 weeks.
cards.result: Median gestation at delivery 36.5 weeks, with a median prolongation from first drain to birth of 30 days. Peri-procedural complications were rare: 1 case of placental abruption and 2 cases of preterm delivery. Across the series, preterm labour before 37 weeks occurred in 48.8%, delivery before 34 weeks in 26.7%, and preterm prelabour rupture of membranes before 36 weeks in 23.2%. Fetal anomalies were identified in 79% of cases (mainly gastrointestinal obstruction); only 9.3% were idiopathic.
cards.watchOut: No comparison group — a median 30 days from drain to delivery describes the natural course after a drain done at 32.5 weeks, not days gained by draining; and with 79% fetal anomaly, outcomes here are dominated by the underlying diagnosis, not the procedure.
cards.source: Laoreti A et al. Amnioreduction for Polyhydramnios in a Consecutive Series at a Single Center: Indications, Risks and Perinatal Outcomes. Children (Basel). 2024. PMID: 38671719. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Zargarzadeh 2025: pooled safety across 7 studies (390 singleton pregnancies) — abruption odds 0.04, chorioamnionitis odds 0.03, delivery within 48 hours odds 0.10
cards.summary: Zargarzadeh 2025: pooled safety across 7 studies (390 singleton pregnancies) — abruption odds 0.04, chorioamnionitis odds 0.03, delivery within 48 hours odds 0.10
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Zargarzadeh 2025)
cards.people: 390 singleton pregnancies undergoing amnioreduction for polyhydramnios, in seven studies pooled from 574 identified articles (search to April 2024). The 'odds' figures are pooled single-arm event odds from the record, not comparisons against untreated pregnancies.
cards.result: Pooled odds: placental abruption 0.04 (95% CI 0.02 to 0.09); chorioamnionitis 0.03 (95% CI 0.01 to 0.08); preterm delivery within 48 hours of amnioreduction 0.10 (95% CI 0.07 to 0.15); preterm prelabour rupture of membranes within 48 hours 0.03 (95% CI 0.02 to 0.04); caesarean delivery 0.45 (95% CI 0.30 to 0.61). Mean gestational age at birth was almost 36 weeks (95% CI 35.51 to 36.41). The authors state plainly that evidence for fetal benefit or pregnancy prolongation is lacking and that trials comparing amnioreduction with expectant management are needed.
cards.watchOut: A safety synthesis only: single-arm pooling can show complications are uncommon after the procedure, but by design it cannot show the procedure helps — there is no untreated arm anywhere in it.
cards.source: Zargarzadeh N, Haddadi M, Abiad M, Javinani A, Krispin E, Shainker S, Aagaard K, Shamshirsaz AA. Amnioreduction safety in singleton pregnancies; systematic review and meta-analysis. J Perinat Med. 2025. PMID: 40254983. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cabrol 1996: indomethacin 3 mg/kg/day in 22 women — fluid fell and no severe preterm delivery occurred; three neonatal deaths were attributed to anomalies and cord accident, not the drug
cards.summary: Cabrol 1996: indomethacin 3 mg/kg/day in 22 women — fluid fell and no severe preterm delivery occurred; three neonatal deaths were attributed to anomalies and cord accident, not the drug
cards.people: 22 women (20 singleton and 2 twin pregnancies; 24 infants) with symptomatic polyhydramnios treated retrospectively, 1983 to 1992; indomethacin started at a mean 28.2 weeks and stopped after 35 weeks.
cards.result: The authors report a significant effect of indomethacin on amniotic fluid volume and that severe preterm delivery was avoided in all patients; mean gestational age at birth was 37.5 weeks (range 35.5 to 39). No maternal or neonatal side effects of indomethacin were observed. Three of 24 infants died neonatally: two from undiagnosed fetal anomalies and one from umbilical cord entanglement in a monoamniotic twin pregnancy.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-two women, no control group, from the 1980s — and later guidance has moved against indomethacin for this purpose because of fetal ductal and renal effects; this card is the historical evidence base, not a recommendation, and no comparative study of indomethacin for polyhydramnios was found.
cards.source: Cabrol D, Jannet D, Pannier E. Treatment of symptomatic polyhydramnios with indomethacin. Eur J Obstet Gynecol Reprod Biol. 1996. PMID: 8735752. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: draining fluid is a low-complication symptom procedure with no proven pregnancy-prolonging effect; indomethacin rests on one small old series
cards.summary: Synthesis: draining fluid is a low-complication symptom procedure with no proven pregnancy-prolonging effect; indomethacin rests on one small old series
cards.people: Three observational sources: two amnioreduction series/syntheses (Laoreti 2024, 86 pregnancies; Zargarzadeh 2025, 7 studies, 390 singleton pregnancies) and one indomethacin series (Cabrol 1996, 22 women). No randomised or controlled comparative study of any polyhydramnios treatment was found.
cards.result: After amnioreduction: delivery at a median 36.5 weeks and 30 days after the first drain (Laoreti 2024); pooled odds of abruption 0.04 and of delivery within 48 hours 0.10 (Zargarzadeh 2025). Indomethacin: fluid reduction reported, mean delivery 37.5 weeks, uncontrolled (Cabrol 1996). Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, capped accordingly.
cards.watchOut: The one directly comparative study identified this session (amnioreduction versus expectant management in anomalous singleton pregnancies, Am J Obstet Gynecol MFM 2023) found no prolongation of pregnancy — it is named here rather than carded because its PMID was not captured this session; twin–twin transfusion syndrome is a separate condition with its own treatment evidence and is outside this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Laoreti 2024 (PMID: 38671719), Zargarzadeh 2025 (PMID: 40254983) and Cabrol 1996 (PMID: 8735752).

shelves.title: Progressive supranuclear palsy: no drug has slowed it — davunetide (313 patients), gosuranemab (486) and tideglusib (146) all matched placebo on the PSP Rating Scale over 52 weeks
shelves.question: In people with progressive supranuclear palsy, does any drug treatment slow progression or improve function compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Oligopeptides/adverse effects · Oligopeptides/therapeutic use · Supranuclear Palsy, Progressive/diagnosis · Supranuclear Palsy, Progressive/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: No tested drug has slowed progressive supranuclear palsy. Davunetide (Boxer 2014, PMID: 24873720; NCT01110720; 313 patients) changed the PSP Rating Scale by a median 11.8 points on both arms (p=0.41) and the Schwab and England scale by -0.20 on both (p=0.92) over 52 weeks. Gosuranemab (Dam 2021, PMID: 34385707; NCT03068468; 486 dosed) changed the PSP Rating Scale by 10.4 versus 10.6 points (P = 0.85) despite cutting unbound N-terminal tau in spinal fluid by 98%. Tideglusib (Tolosa 2014, PMID: 24532007; 146 patients) showed no significant difference on the primary or any secondary endpoint at either dose; its MRI substudy's slower atrophy signal never translated into clinical benefit. Riluzole and tilavonemab are named in the synthesis watch-out as further negative trials not carded this session. PROPOSED MAYBE (the treatment made no difference): three adequately sized, blinded, placebo-controlled trials of three different tau-directed mechanisms all came back flat, so care remains symptomatic and supportive.

cards.headline: Boxer 2014: davunetide changed the PSP Rating Scale by a median 11.8 points in both arms (p=0.41) and daily-living scores by -0.20 in both (p=0.92) in 313 patients
cards.summary: Boxer 2014: davunetide changed the PSP Rating Scale by a median 11.8 points in both arms (p=0.41) and daily-living scores by -0.20 in both (p=0.92) in 313 patients
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2/3 (Boxer 2014)
cards.people: 313 participants meeting modified Neuroprotection and Natural History in Parkinson Plus Syndrome criteria for PSP at 48 centres in six countries, randomised to intranasal davunetide 30 mg twice daily (n=157) or placebo (n=156) for 52 weeks; 241 (77%) completed.
cards.result: Change from baseline in PSP Rating Scale did not differ (median 11.8 [95% CI 10.5 to 13.0] versus 11.8 [10.5 to 13.0], p=0.41), nor did Schwab and England Activities of Daily Living change (-0.20 versus -0.20, p=0.92). Serious adverse events numbered 54 in each group, with 11 deaths on davunetide and 10 on placebo. Nasal adverse events were commoner on davunetide (epistaxis 18 [12%] of 156 versus 13 [8%] of 156; nasal discomfort 15 [10%] versus 1 [<1%]). The authors concluded davunetide is not an effective treatment for PSP.
cards.watchOut: A later post-hoc sex-split reanalysis claimed benefit in women; that is a subgroup re-cut of a flat trial, not carded here, and does not change the intention-to-treat result.
cards.source: Boxer AL, Lang AE, Grossman M, Knopman DS, Miller BL, Schneider LS, Doody RS, Lees A, Golbe LI, Williams DR, Corvol JC, Ludolph A, Burn D, Lorenzl S, Litvan I, Roberson ED, Höglinger GU, Koestler M, Jack CR Jr, Van Deerlin V, Randolph C, Lobach IV, Heuer HW, Gozes I, Parker L, Whitaker S, Hirman J, Stewart AJ, Gold M, Morimoto BH; AL-108-231 Investigators. Davunetide in patients with progressive supranuclear palsy: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2/3 trial. Lancet Neurology. 2014. PMID: 24873720. Registry ID: NCT01110720. cards.headline: Dam 2021: gosuranemab changed the PSP Rating Scale by 10.4 versus 10.6 points on placebo (P = 0.85) in 486 patients, despite a 98% fall in spinal-fluid unbound tau
cards.summary: Dam 2021: gosuranemab changed the PSP Rating Scale by 10.4 versus 10.6 points on placebo (P = 0.85) in 486 patients, despite a 98% fall in spinal-fluid unbound tau
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 (Dam 2021)
cards.people: 486 dosed participants with PSP in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 52-week phase 2 study, assigned to gosuranemab (n=321) or placebo (n=165).
cards.result: Efficacy was not demonstrated on the adjusted mean change in PSP Rating Scale score at week 52 (10.4 versus 10.6, P = 0.85) or at secondary endpoints, and the open-label extension was discontinued. Unbound N-terminal tau in cerebrospinal fluid decreased by 98% with gosuranemab and increased by 11% with placebo (P < 0.0001). Incidences of adverse events and deaths were similar between groups. The authors concluded N-terminal tau neutralisation does not translate into clinical efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Target engagement was proven (98% tau reduction) and the clinical result was still flat, which argues the failure is the strategy or its timing, not the dose.
cards.source: Dam T, Boxer AL, Golbe LI, Höglinger GU, Morris HR, Litvan I, Lang AE, Corvol JC, Aiba I, Grundman M, Yang L, Tidemann-Miller B, Kupferman J, Harper K, Kamisoglu K, Wald MJ, Graham DL, Gedney L, O'Gorman J, Haeberlein SB; PASSPORT Study Group. cards.headline: Tolosa 2014: tideglusib showed no significant difference from placebo on the primary or any secondary endpoint at week 52 in 146 patients
cards.summary: Tolosa 2014: tideglusib showed no significant difference from placebo on the primary or any secondary endpoint at week 52 in 146 patients
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 (Tolosa 2014)
cards.people: 146 patients with mild-to-moderate PSP randomised (ratio 2:2:1) to oral tideglusib 600 mg once daily, tideglusib 800 mg once daily, or placebo for 52 weeks in the TAUROS trial (registry NCT01049399, named in the trial's later power-calculation report).
cards.result: No significant differences were detected in the primary endpoint (change in PSP Rating Scale) or in secondary endpoints (motor, cognition, apathy, daily living, quality of life, global assessment) at week 52 between placebo and either tideglusib dose. Tideglusib was generally well tolerated, with asymptomatic transient reversible transaminase elevations in 9% of patients and diarrhoea in 13%.
cards.watchOut: The companion MRI substudy reported slower brain atrophy on tideglusib, an imaging signal with no matching clinical benefit; imaging-only wins should not be read as treatment working.
cards.source: Tolosa E, Litvan I, Höglinger GU, Burn D, Lees A, Andrés MV, Gómez-Carrillo B, León T, Del Ser T; TAUROS Investigators. A phase 2 trial of the GSK-3 inhibitor tideglusib in progressive supranuclear palsy. Movement Disorders. 2014. PMID: 24532007. Registry ID: none in the record (NCT01049399 appears in the trial programme's later power-calculation paper, not in this record). cards.headline: Synthesis: three blinded placebo-controlled trials, three mechanisms, zero clinical benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: three blinded placebo-controlled trials, three mechanisms, zero clinical benefit
cards.people: 605 patients across the carded trials (313 davunetide, 486 gosuranemab with overlap of populations across separate trials, 146 tideglusib) with probable PSP followed for 52 weeks each.
cards.result: PSP Rating Scale change was identical on davunetide and placebo (median 11.8 both, p=0.41), near-identical on gosuranemab (10.4 vs 10.6, P = 0.85) and not significantly different on tideglusib at either dose. No carded treatment slowed progression.
cards.watchOut: Proposed stamp: MAYBE (the treatment made no difference). Riluzole (NNIPPS) and the anti-tau antibody tilavonemab were also negative in PSP trials but were not carded this session; symptomatic care (physiotherapy, speech and swallowing support, falls prevention) has no carded trial here either.

shelves.title: Prosopagnosia: face training gives modest laboratory gains — the one placebo-controlled trial (20 adults) improved face memory but not perception; everyday benefit unproven
shelves.question: In people with prosopagnosia (face blindness), do training or rehabilitation interventions improve face recognition?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Face/physiology · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests · Pattern Recognition, Visual/physiology · Prosopagnosia/congenital · Prosopagnosia/physiopathology · Recognition, Psychology/physiology · Visual Perception/physiology
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Face training produces modest laboratory gains in developmental prosopagnosia, from small uncontrolled or waitlist-controlled studies. DeGutis 2014 (PMID: 24691394; 24 adults) found moderate but significant training-related improvement in front-view face discrimination versus a waiting period after a 3-week online holistic-processing programme, with the best trainees normalising holistic processing. Bate 2022 (PMID: 35386218) ran the only placebo-controlled trial (20 adults): face-specific gains in face memory, not perception, greatest in those worst at entry and persisting 2 weeks after training; in a 4-child case series (n=4 printed on the face), 3 children improved in face memory. The critical review (Bate & Bennetts 2014, PMID: 25100965) concludes gains across the rehabilitation literature are limited, with laborious compensatory techniques, limited generalisation to untrained faces and limited maintenance. No drug treatment exists. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): training helps test performance a little; everyday-life benefit is unproven.

cards.headline: DeGutis 2014: 3 weeks of online holistic face training gave moderate, significant gains in front-view face discrimination versus a waiting period in 24 adults
cards.summary: DeGutis 2014: 3 weeks of online holistic face training gave moderate, significant gains in front-view face discrimination versus a waiting period in 24 adults
cards.type: Controlled training study with waitlist comparison (DeGutis 2014)
cards.people: 24 adults with developmental prosopagnosia trained on a 3-week online programme targeting holistic face processing; 12 were assessed before and after training and 12 before and after a waiting period, then trained and reassessed.
cards.result: Compared with the waiting period, participants showed moderate but significant overall training-related improvements on measures of front-view face discrimination. Those who reached the more difficult training levels ('better' trainees) improved most and increased holistic face processing to a level similar to unimpaired controls. A 5-day diary showed modest but consistent self-reported real-world improvements. The abstract reports no effect sizes or percentages.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised or placebo-controlled: expectancy and practice effects are plausible, benefit concentrated in the 'better trainees', and the everyday-life outcome is a self-report diary open to bias, as the authors note.
cards.source: DeGutis J, Cohan S, Nakayama K. Holistic face training enhances face processing in developmental prosopagnosia. Brain. 2014. PMID: 24691394. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bate 2022: in the only placebo-controlled trial (20 adults), face training improved face memory but not perception, and gains persisted 2 weeks after training
cards.summary: Bate 2022: in the only placebo-controlled trial (20 adults), face training improved face memory but not perception, and gains persisted 2 weeks after training
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, placebo-controlled, plus case series (Bate 2022)
cards.people: Study 1: 20 adults with a pre-existing diagnosis of developmental prosopagnosia in a randomised, parallel-group, placebo-controlled trial of a 2-week face training programme (modelled on the game Guess Who?), assessed before, immediately after and 2 weeks after training. Study 2: a case series of 4 children (n=4 printed on the face) with face recognition difficulties given the experimental programme.
cards.result: Face-specific gains in memory (but not perception) were observed in the experimental group, greatest in those with the poorest face recognition at entry, and persisted 2 weeks after training ceased. In the 4 children, 3 improved at face memory and 1 also improved at face perception, with mixed evidence that the gains were face-specific. The abstract reports no numerical effect sizes.
cards.watchOut: Twenty adults is the largest controlled sample in this field and it is still tiny; memory-test gains did not extend to face perception, and follow-up was only 2 weeks.
cards.source: Bate S, Dalrymple K, Bennetts RJ. Face recognition improvements in adults and children with face recognition difficulties. Brain Communications. 2022. PMID: 35386218. cards.headline: Bate & Bennetts 2014: across all rehabilitation attempts, gains were limited — compensatory techniques laborious, generalisation and maintenance poor
cards.summary: Bate & Bennetts 2014: across all rehabilitation attempts, gains were limited — compensatory techniques laborious, generalisation and maintenance poor
cards.type: Critical review of intervention studies (Bate & Bennetts 2014)
cards.people: Critical review of every published intervention study in acquired and developmental prosopagnosia available to 2014, including single cases and small series (for example Brunsdon 2006, one 8-year-old; Schmalzl 2008, one 4-year-old; DeGutis 2007, one 48-year-old).
cards.result: Compensatory training in children and remedial training in adults have both had some success, but compensatory strategies produced laboured recognition techniques with limited generalisation to untrained faces, and remedial techniques required longer training with limited maintenance of gains. The authors called for more systematic methods and larger participant groups, and an urgent need for early detection and remediation tools for children.
cards.watchOut: A narrative critical review, not a meta-analysis; most underlying reports are single cases, so the review's caution reflects the field's design limits as much as the treatments' limits.
cards.source: Bate S, Bennetts RJ. The rehabilitation of face recognition impairments: a critical review and future directions. Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. 2014. PMID: 25100965. cards.headline: Synthesis: training nudges laboratory face scores; nothing is proven to help everyday recognition
cards.summary: Synthesis: training nudges laboratory face scores; nothing is proven to help everyday recognition
cards.people: 44 adults across the two group studies (24 in DeGutis 2014; 20 in Bate 2022) plus a 4-child case series (n=4 printed on the face) and the single-case literature reviewed in 2014.
cards.result: Training-related gains were moderate and significant for front-view discrimination (DeGutis 2014) and face-specific for memory but not perception in the one placebo-controlled trial (Bate 2022); the field review finds generalisation to untrained faces and maintenance of gains both limited.
cards.watchOut: Proposed stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence). A perceptual-learning study in 10 adults with developmental prosopagnosia (Davies-Thompson and colleagues) reported improved face sensitivity maintained at 3 months but was not carded — its outcome numbers were not captured from a full record this session. Two larger randomised training trials are registered and recruiting but have no results.
cards.source: Synthesis of DeGutis 2014 (PMID: 24691394), Bate 2022 (PMID: 35386218) and Bate & Bennetts 2014 (PMID: 25100965), carded above.

shelves.title: Reactive arthritis: antibiotics fail overall (pooled relative risk of non-remission 0.74, 95% CI 0.49-1.10) — except one 42-patient trial in PCR-positive chronic Chlamydia disease (responders 63% vs 20%)
shelves.question: In people with reactive arthritis, do antibiotics improve remission — and does prolonged combination antibiotic therapy help chronic Chlamydia-induced disease?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Anti-Infective Agents/pharmacokinetics · Anti-Infective Agents/therapeutic use · Arthritis, Reactive/drug therapy · Chlamydia Infections/drug therapy · Chlamydia trachomatis · Ciprofloxacin/adverse effects · Ciprofloxacin/pharmacokinetics · Ciprofloxacin/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Middle Aged · Placebos · Prohibitins · Salmonella Infections/drug therapy · Therapeutic Equivalency · Time Factors · Yersinia Infections/drug therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT by trigger and chronicity. Pooled across all reactive arthritis, antibiotics do not work: the Barber 2013 meta-analysis (DOI 10.3899/jrheum.121192; 12 trials) gives a relative risk of failure to achieve remission of 0.74 (95% CI 0.49-1.10) with heavy heterogeneity (I2 = 76.3%), attenuating to 0.87 (0.70-1.10) when unblinded trials are excluded, and a relative 97% increase in gastrointestinal adverse events. Single-agent ciprofloxacin for 3 months was flat against placebo (Sieper 1999, PMID: 10403266; 126 randomised). The exception is chronic Chlamydia-induced disease with PCR-proven persistent infection: Carter 2010 (PMID: 20155838; NCT00351273; 42 patients) found 6 months of combination antibiotics (doxycycline or azithromycin, each with rifampin) produced responders in 17 of 27 (63%) versus 3 of 15 (20%) on placebo, with complete remission in 6 of 27 versus 0 of 15. PROPOSED SPLIT: no antibiotics for ordinary or enteric reactive arthritis; POSSIBLE benefit for prolonged combination therapy in the narrow PCR-positive chronic Chlamydia subgroup, on one 42-patient trial.

cards.headline: Carter 2010: 6 months of combination antibiotics gave responders in 17 of 27 (63%) versus 3 of 15 (20%) on placebo in chronic Chlamydia-induced reactive arthritis
cards.summary: Carter 2010: 6 months of combination antibiotics gave responders in 17 of 27 (63%) versus 3 of 15 (20%) on placebo in chronic Chlamydia-induced reactive arthritis
cards.people: 42 patients with chronic Chlamydia-induced reactive arthritis (disease duration 6 months or more) who were PCR-positive for Chlamydia trachomatis or Chlamydophila pneumoniae, randomised to doxycycline plus rifampin, azithromycin plus rifampin, or triple placebo for 6 months, in a 9-month double-blind trial (27 combination antibiotics, 15 placebo).
cards.result: The primary endpoint (20% or more improvement in at least 4 of 6 variables without worsening in any) was achieved in 17 of 27 patients (63%) receiving combination antibiotics and 3 of 15 (20%) receiving placebo (P = 0.01 in the full report) — an absolute difference of about 43 percentage points. Six of 27 (22%) on combination antibiotics believed their disease went into complete remission, versus 0 of 15 on placebo. Significantly more active-treatment patients became PCR-negative at month 6 (P = 0.03 in the full report). Adverse events were mild, with no significant differences between groups.
cards.watchOut: Small (42 patients), single research group, and the remission endpoint is patient-believed remission; the population is a narrow PCR-positive chronic subgroup, so the result cannot be generalised to ordinary reactive arthritis — and it has not been independently replicated.
cards.source: Carter JD, Espinoza LR, Inman RD, Sneed KB, Ricca LR, Vasey FB, Valeriano J, Stanich JA, Oszust C, Gerard HC, Hudson AP. Combination antibiotics as a treatment for chronic Chlamydia-induced reactive arthritis: a double-blind, placebo-controlled, prospective trial. Arthritis & Rheumatism. 2010. PMID: 20155838. cards.headline: Sieper 1999: 3 months of ciprofloxacin made no difference to placebo in 126 patients with reactive arthritis or undifferentiated oligoarthritis
cards.summary: Sieper 1999: 3 months of ciprofloxacin made no difference to placebo in 126 patients with reactive arthritis or undifferentiated oligoarthritis
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre (Sieper 1999)
cards.people: 126 patients treated with ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily or placebo for 3 months in a multicentre double-blind randomised study; 104 (48 ciprofloxacin, 56 placebo) were valid for clinical evaluation — 55 with reactive arthritis after a symptomatic urogenital or enteric infection and 49 with undifferentiated oligoarthritis.
cards.result: A triggering bacterium was identified in 52 patients (50%): Chlamydia trachomatis in 13, Yersinia in 14 and Salmonella in 25. No difference in outcome (remission after 3 months) was found between ciprofloxacin and placebo in the whole group or in the reactive-arthritis and undifferentiated-oligoarthritis subgroups, and none in patients with disease duration under 3 months. Ciprofloxacin was not effective in Yersinia- or Salmonella-induced arthritis; it seemed better than placebo in Chlamydia-induced arthritis but that difference was not significant.
cards.watchOut: Mixed population (only 55 of 104 evaluable patients had definite reactive arthritis) and trigger subgroups were small (13-25 patients), so subgroup signals are fragile in both directions.
cards.source: Sieper J, Fendler C, Laitko S, Sörensen H, Gripenberg-Lerche C, Hiepe F, Alten R, Keitel W, Groh A, Uksila J, Eggens U, Granfors K, Braun J. No benefit of long-term ciprofloxacin treatment in patients with reactive arthritis and undifferentiated oligoarthritis: a three-month, multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study. cards.headline: Barber 2013: pooled across 12 trials, antibiotics did not significantly improve remission (relative risk of failure 0.74, 95% CI 0.49-1.10) and raised gastrointestinal adverse events by a relative 97%
cards.summary: Barber 2013: pooled across 12 trials, antibiotics did not significantly improve remission (relative risk of failure 0.74, 95% CI 0.49-1.10) and raised gastrointestinal adverse events by a relative 97%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Barber 2013)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of antibiotics for reactive arthritis searched to November 2011: 12 trials eligible, 10 in the meta-analysis; the remission analysis pooled 7 trials with 375 participants.
cards.result: The pooled relative risk of failure to achieve remission was 0.74 (95% CI 0.49-1.10) — not significant — with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 76.3%, p < 0.0001); absolute remission rates are not given in the abstract. Excluding unblinded trials attenuated the estimate to a relative risk of 0.87 (95% CI 0.70-1.10, I2 = 32.8%). There were no significant effects on joint counts, pain or patient global scores, but antibiotics were associated with a 97% relative increase in gastrointestinal adverse events. The single combination-therapy trial (Carter 2010) showed a relative risk of 0.79 (95% CI 0.63-0.99) for failure to achieve remission.
cards.watchOut: Heterogeneity is the story: trials mixed triggers, durations and antibiotic strategies, so the pooled null can hide a real subgroup effect (Carter) just as easily as the subgroup trial can be a false positive.
cards.source: Barber CE, Kim J, Inman RD, Esdaile JM, James MT. Antibiotics for Treatment of Reactive Arthritis: A Systematic Review and Metaanalysis. Journal of Rheumatology. 2013. cards.headline: Synthesis: antibiotics fail in reactive arthritis generally; one small trial supports prolonged combination therapy only for PCR-positive chronic Chlamydia disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: antibiotics fail in reactive arthritis generally; one small trial supports prolonged combination therapy only for PCR-positive chronic Chlamydia disease
cards.people: 554 patients across the carded evidence (42 in Carter 2010, 126 randomised in Sieper 1999, 375 in the pooled remission analysis of Barber 2013, with overlap between the meta-analysis and the individual trials).
cards.result: Pooled relative risk of failure to achieve remission 0.74 (95% CI 0.49-1.10), not significant; ciprofloxacin alone flat versus placebo; combination therapy in PCR-positive chronic Chlamydia disease 63% versus 20% responders (absolute rates).
cards.watchOut: Proposed stamp: SPLIT (general reactive arthritis: the treatment made no difference · PCR-positive chronic Chlamydia-induced disease: POSSIBLE benefit). NSAIDs, intra-articular steroids and sulfasalazine — the usual symptomatic mainstays — have no carded placebo-controlled trial on this shelf; a long-term follow-up of a Finnish ciprofloxacin trial hinted at less chronic disease 4-7 years later but was not carded.
cards.source: Synthesis of Carter 2010 (PMID: 20155838; NCT00351273), Sieper 1999 (PMID: 10403266) and Barber 2013 (DOI 10.3899/jrheum.121192; PMID not captured this session), carded above.

shelves.title: Repetitive strain injury: no conservative treatment has consistent trial support — exercises did not improve pain in 6,580 pooled participants and the 2026 Cochrane update finds ergonomics make little to no difference
shelves.question: In adults with repetitive strain injury (work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder), do exercises, ergonomic changes or other conservative treatments reduce pain, disability or sick leave?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Amitriptyline/therapeutic use · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/therapeutic use · Arm · Behavior Therapy/methods · Cumulative Trauma Disorders/therapy · Ergonomics/methods · Humans · Massage · Neck · Occupational Diseases/therapy · Physical Therapy Modalities · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Shoulder · Sick Leave/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no conservative treatment for repetitive strain injury (work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder, CANS) has a consistent effect. The Cochrane review (Verhagen 2013, PMID: 24338903; 44 studies, 6,580 participants, 25 interventions) found very low-quality evidence that exercises did not improve pain versus no treatment (SMD -0.52, 95% CI -1.08 to 0.03) and that ergonomic interventions did not reduce pain short-term (SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.22) though they did at long-term follow-up (SMD -0.76, 95% CI -1.35 to -0.16), with sick leave lower in two studies (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.76). The 2026 Cochrane ergonomics update (Mehta 2026, PMID: 42946017) tightened the verdict: ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in pain versus no treatment, usual care or placebo (SMD -0.23, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.08; 4 RCTs, 692 participants; low-certainty). The earlier RSI-specific review (Konijnenberg 2001, PMID: 11712610; 15 trials, 702 participants) likewise found no strong evidence for any conservative option. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): ergonomic changes and exercise are reasonable and low-harm, but trial evidence that they relieve RSI is inconsistent and low-certainty.

cards.headline: Verhagen 2013 (Cochrane): across 44 studies and 6,580 participants, exercises did not improve pain (SMD -0.52, 95% CI -1.08 to 0.03) and no intervention showed a consistent effect
cards.summary: Verhagen 2013 (Cochrane): across 44 studies and 6,580 participants, exercises did not improve pain (SMD -0.52, 95% CI -1.08 to 0.03) and no intervention showed a consistent effect
cards.people: Adults with work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder (CANS — the review's term covering repetitive strain injury) in 44 randomised or quasi-randomised studies (62 publications) with 6,580 participants, evaluating 25 different conservative interventions (21 exercise studies, 13 ergonomic, 9 behavioural among them); injections and surgery were excluded.
cards.result: Very low-quality evidence: exercises did not improve pain versus no treatment (5 studies, SMD -0.52, 95% CI -1.08 to 0.03) or minor-intervention controls (3 studies, SMD -0.25, 95% CI -0.87 to 0.37), with similar results for recovery, disability and sick leave; specific exercises increased pain short-term versus general exercises (4 studies, SMD 0.45, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.75). Ergonomic interventions did not decrease pain short-term (3 studies, SMD -0.07, 95% CI -0.36 to 0.22) but did at long-term follow-up (4 studies, SMD -0.76, 95% CI -1.35 to -0.16), with no effect on disability; sick leave decreased in 2 studies (relative risk 0.48, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.76; absolute rates not given in the abstract). 35 of 44 studies were at high risk of bias.
cards.watchOut: An umbrella diagnosis (specific and non-specific CANS pooled) and mostly high-bias-risk trials: the review can show the average effect is inconsistent, not that nothing helps any defined subgroup.
cards.source: Verhagen AP, Bierma-Zeinstra SMA, Burdorf A, Stynes SM, de Vet HCW, Koes BW. Conservative interventions for treating work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013. PMID: 24338903. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mehta 2026 (Cochrane update): ergonomic interventions may make little to no difference to pain (SMD -0.23, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.08; 4 RCTs, 692 participants)
cards.summary: Mehta 2026 (Cochrane update): ergonomic interventions may make little to no difference to pain (SMD -0.23, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.08; 4 RCTs, 692 participants)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, Cochrane update (Mehta 2026)
cards.people: Adults with work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder in randomised trials of ergonomic interventions (office furniture, biomechanical or ergonomic education and similar), updating the 2013 Cochrane review with searches to 1 June 2026; 13 studies were brought forward from the 2013 review plus 7 new studies.
cards.result: Ergonomic interventions may result in little to no difference in pain compared with no treatment, usual care or placebo (SMD -0.23, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.08; 4 RCTs, 692 participants; low-certainty evidence), and probably result in little to no difference in functional status (disability). Overall the authors conclude ergonomic interventions may have no meaningful effects on pain, function, recovery, quality of life or sick leave versus no treatment or usual care; the evidence for ergonomic interventions as an add-on treatment is very uncertain.
cards.watchOut: Most included trials studied non-specific CANS, many in computer workers; a null average for mixed ergonomic packages does not rule out benefit from a specific adjustment for a specific workstation problem.
cards.source: Mehta P, Stubbs PW, Tamminga SJ, Trøstrup J, Stynes SM, Koes BW, Verhagen AP. Ergonomic interventions for treating work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2026. PMID: 42946017. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Konijnenberg 2001: in 15 RSI trials (12 randomised, 611 participants; 3 controlled, 91), no strong evidence supported any conservative treatment
cards.summary: Konijnenberg 2001: in 15 RSI trials (12 randomised, 611 participants; 3 controlled, 91), no strong evidence supported any conservative treatment
cards.people: Patients with repetitive strain injury in 15 eligible trials of conservative (non-surgical) therapy — occupational therapy, physiotherapy, exercises, behavioural therapy, chiropractic, multidisciplinary treatment or medication — identified from Medline and Embase to April 2000.
cards.result: No strong evidence was found for the effectiveness of any treatment option. There was limited evidence that multidisciplinary rehabilitation, ergonomic intervention measures, exercises, and spinal manipulation combined with soft tissue therapy relieved symptoms or improved activities of daily living, and conflicting evidence for behavioural therapy. Methodological quality was poor overall, with problems in allocation concealment, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis. Numbers are from the review's critical abstract (DARE) and journal record fetched this session.
cards.watchOut: The oldest and smallest of the three reviews, using best-evidence synthesis rather than meta-analysis; included here because it is the only review framed on RSI itself rather than the broader CANS umbrella — and it reaches the same conclusion.
cards.source: Konijnenberg HS, de Wilde NS, Gerritsen AAM, van Tulder MW, de Vet HCW. Conservative treatment for repetitive strain injury. Scandinavian Journal of Work, Environment & Health. 2001. PMID: 11712610. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three reviews over 25 years agree — no RSI treatment has consistent trial support
cards.summary: Synthesis: three reviews over 25 years agree — no RSI treatment has consistent trial support
cards.people: 6,580 participants in the 2013 Cochrane pool, the updated ergonomics trials to 2026, and 702 participants in the RSI-specific 2001 review (with overlap between reviews).
cards.result: Exercises: no pain benefit (SMD -0.52, 95% CI -1.08 to 0.03). Ergonomics: no short-term pain benefit in 2013 (SMD -0.07) or in the 2026 update (SMD -0.23, 95% CI -0.54 to 0.08); the one positive signal (long-term pain SMD -0.76 in 2013) is very low-quality evidence and was not sustained as a meaningful effect in the update.
cards.watchOut: Proposed stamp: MAYBE (weak evidence). All three syntheses are review-level: no individual landmark RCT exists to card, because the RSI trial literature is many small heterogeneous trials. Injections and surgery were outside the Cochrane scope and are not answered here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Verhagen 2013 (PMID: 24338903), Mehta 2026 (PMID: 42946017) and Konijnenberg 2001 (PMID: 11712610), carded above.

shelves.title: Shin splints (medial tibial stress syndrome): no treatment is proven — shockwave beat graded running alone by about 32 days in an unblinded study but matched a sham dose in the blinded trial, and arch-support insoles eased pain earlier (weeks 6–12) but not by week 18
shelves.question: In people with medial tibial stress syndrome (shin splints), do shockwave therapy, foot orthoses or any other treatment speed recovery or reduce pain compared with sham treatment, graded running or no treatment?
shelves.mesh: Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome / therapy*
shelves.balance: No treatment for medial tibial stress syndrome is proven. The systematic review (Winters 2013, PMID: 23979968; 11 trials, 519 participants) found every randomised trial at high risk of bias and could recommend nothing: pooled lower-leg braces (SMD −0.06; 95% CI −0.44 to 0.32) and iontophoresis (SMD 0.09; 95% CI −0.50 to 0.68) showed no difference, and laser, stretching/strengthening, compression stockings and pulsed electromagnetic fields were unproven. Shockwave is the SPLIT at the centre of this shelf: in the non-randomised two-hospital comparison (Moen 2012, PMID: 21393260) adding ESWT to graded running cut recovery from 91.6 to 59.7 days, but in the double-blind sham-controlled pilot trial (Newman 2017, PMID: 27640922; n = 28) a standard dose beat a sham low dose by only 1.1 points of palpation pain out of 10 (95% CI −2.3 to 0.0) with no difference in running distance. Arch-support foot orthoses added to ice massage, exercise and shockwave (Naderi 2022, PMID: 33797477; n = 50) lowered pain and severity at weeks 6 and 12 but not at week 18 — earlier relief, not a better end result. PROPOSED: SPLIT (shockwave unproven against sham; orthoses give earlier relief only).

cards.headline: Winters 2013: across 11 trials no treatment could be recommended — every randomised trial was at high risk of bias; pooled lower-leg braces (SMD −0.06) and iontophoresis (SMD 0.09) showed no difference
cards.summary: Winters 2013: across 11 trials no treatment could be recommended — every randomised trial was at high risk of bias; pooled lower-leg braces (SMD −0.06) and iontophoresis (SMD 0.09) showed no difference
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised and non-randomised trials (Winters 2013)
cards.people: 11 trials of any treatment for medial tibial stress syndrome: 9 randomised trials (399 participants) and 2 non-randomised controlled trials (120 participants), in athletes and military personnel.
cards.result: No significant differences were found for lower leg braces versus control (standardized mean difference [SMD] −0.06; 95% CI −0.44 to 0.32, p = 0.76) or for iontophoresis versus phonophoresis (SMD 0.09; 95% CI −0.50 to 0.68, p = 0.76). Iontophoresis, phonophoresis, ice massage, ultrasound, periosteal pecking and extracorporeal shockwave therapy (ESWT) could be effective versus control at Level 3 to 4 evidence; low-energy laser, stretching and strengthening exercises, sports compression stockings, lower leg braces and pulsed electromagnetic fields have not been proven effective. The authors concluded none of the studies was sufficiently free of bias to recommend any treatment, with ESWT showing the most promise.
cards.watchOut: A 2013 evidence base: it predates the sham-controlled shockwave trial and the orthoses trial carded below, and its 'could be effective' list rests on Level 3–4 evidence — small, biased trials against no-treatment controls, exactly the design most prone to flattering a therapy.
cards.source: Winters M, Eskes M, Weir A, Moen MH, Backx FJG, Bakker EWP. Treatment of medial tibial stress syndrome: a systematic review. Sports Medicine. 2013. PMID: 23979968. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Newman 2017: standard-dose shockwave was NOT more effective than a sham low dose — palpation pain differed by only 1.1 points out of 10 (95% CI −2.3 to 0.0) and nothing else differed
cards.summary: Newman 2017: standard-dose shockwave was NOT more effective than a sham low dose — palpation pain differed by only 1.1 points out of 10 (95% CI −2.3 to 0.0) and nothing else differed
cards.people: 28 active adults with medial tibial stress syndrome in a university clinic, randomised to standard-dose or sham-dose shockwave therapy in weeks 1–3, 5 and 9.
cards.result: Pain on palpation was reduced in the experimental group by 1.1 out of 10.0 (95% CI −2.3 to 0.0) less than in the control group; there were no other statistically significant differences between the groups, including running distance. The authors concluded standard-dose shockwave therapy is not more effective than sham dose at improving pain or running distance in MTSS, while noting the sham (low) dose may itself have had a clinical effect.
cards.watchOut: A pilot trial of 28 people: too small to exclude a modest effect, and the 'sham' was a low dose of the same treatment rather than an inert placebo, so the trial tests dose, not shockwave versus nothing. It still removes the main support for the positive uncontrolled studies — when patients cannot tell which dose they got, the standard dose adds nothing measurable.
cards.source: Newman P, Waddington G, Adams R. Shockwave treatment for medial tibial stress syndrome: A randomized double blind sham-controlled pilot trial. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2017. PMID: 27640922. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Moen 2012: adding shockwave to a graded running programme cut time to full recovery from 91.6 to 59.7 days (p = 0.008) — in a non-randomised, two-hospital comparison
cards.summary: Moen 2012: adding shockwave to a graded running programme cut time to full recovery from 91.6 to 59.7 days (p = 0.008) — in a non-randomised, two-hospital comparison
cards.people: 42 athletes with medial tibial stress syndrome; patients at one hospital received a graded running programme alone, patients at the other hospital the same programme plus focused ESWT (five sessions in 9 weeks).
cards.result: Time to full recovery (running 18 minutes consecutively without pain at fixed intensity) was significantly faster in the ESWT group than with the graded running programme alone: 59.7 ± 25.8 days versus 91.6 ± 43.0 days (p = 0.008) — an absolute difference of about 32 days.
cards.watchOut: Treatment was allocated by hospital, not by chance: the two groups may have differed in severity, coaching and expectations, and neither patients nor assessors were blinded — the design most likely to exaggerate a recovery-time benefit, and the result the later blinded trial (Newman 2017) did not reproduce.
cards.source: Moen MH, Rayer S, Schipper M, Schmikli S, Weir A, Tol JL, Backx FJG. Shockwave treatment for medial tibial stress syndrome in athletes; a prospective controlled study. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2012. PMID: 21393260. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome / therapy* (further terms not captured from the record this session)

cards.headline: Naderi 2022: adding arch-support foot orthoses to ice massage, exercise and shockwave lowered pain and severity at weeks 6 and 12 — but the advantage had gone by week 18
cards.summary: Naderi 2022: adding arch-support foot orthoses to ice massage, exercise and shockwave lowered pain and severity at weeks 6 and 12 — but the advantage had gone by week 18
cards.type: Randomised sham-controlled trial of orthoses as an adjunct (Naderi 2022)
cards.people: 50 female recreational runners with medial tibial stress syndrome, randomised to arch-support foot orthoses or sham flat non-contoured orthoses; both groups received the same multimodal programme of ice massage, ankle muscle exercises and extracorporeal shockwave therapy.
cards.result: Pain intensity and MTSS severity were lower, and perceived treatment effect and physical function were better, in the arch-support group than the sham group at week 6 and week 12, with a medium between-group effect size (Cohen's dz). By week 18 the orthoses no longer added benefit on pain, MTSS severity or perceived treatment effect.
cards.watchOut: The trial tests orthoses only as an add-on to a three-part package, in women aged roughly 18–25, so it cannot say whether orthoses alone help, or whether the package itself beats rest and graded running. The honest reading is faster early relief, not a changed outcome.
cards.source: Naderi A, Bagheri S, Ramazanian Ahoor F, Moen MH, Degens H. cards.headline: Synthesis: no shin-splint treatment is proven; shockwave's positive studies are the unblinded ones, and orthoses speed early relief only
cards.summary: Synthesis: no shin-splint treatment is proven; shockwave's positive studies are the unblinded ones, and orthoses speed early relief only
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded records: one systematic review (11 trials, 519 participants), one sham-controlled pilot trial (n = 28), one non-randomised controlled study (n = 42) and one sham-controlled adjunct trial (n = 50).
cards.result: The pattern is consistent: the less a study could be biased, the less shockwave showed. Uncontrolled and unblinded comparisons report faster recovery (about 32 days in Moen 2012), the double-blind sham-controlled trial found no added effect of a standard dose, and the systematic review could recommend nothing. Arch-support orthoses added to a treatment package gave earlier pain relief at 6–12 weeks that had disappeared by 18 weeks. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT (shockwave unproven against sham · orthoses: earlier relief only).
cards.watchOut: Graded return to running and load management — the background care in these trials — were never themselves beaten by any device or procedure in a blinded comparison; persistent focal pain, night pain or pain that localises to one spot needs re-evaluation for tibial stress fracture, which none of these trials addresses.
cards.source: Synthesis of Winters 2013 (PMID: 23979968), Newman 2017 (PMID: 27640922), Moen 2012 (PMID: 21393260) and Naderi 2022 (PMID: 33797477), carded above.

shelves.title: Sick building syndrome: fixing the building helps — raising outdoor air eased symptoms within hours in a blinded experiment, and ultraviolet lights in the ventilation cut work-related symptoms (odds ratio 0.8) in 771 office workers; no treatment given to the person has been trialled
shelves.question: In people with sick building syndrome, which interventions — increased ventilation, ventilation-system decontamination, or treatments given to the person — reduce symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Sick Building Syndrome / etiology*
shelves.balance: Sick building syndrome is treated at the building, not the patient, and the carded evidence supports two building-level interventions. In a blinded crossover experiment (Wargocki 2000, PMID: 11089327; 30 subjects), raising outdoor air from 3 to 30 L/s per person reduced dry mouth/throat (P < 0.0006) and difficulty thinking clearly (P < 0.001) and improved office-task performance by 1.7% per doubling of ventilation. In a double-blind multiple crossover trial in three real office buildings (Menzies 2003, PMID: 14654316; 771 workers), ultraviolet germicidal irradiation of cooling coils and drip pans cut microbial/endotoxin surface contamination by 99% (relative) and was associated with fewer work-related symptoms overall (adjusted OR 0.8 [95% CI 0.7–0.99], relative), respiratory symptoms (OR 0.6) and mucosal symptoms (OR 0.7). The EUROVEN consensus (2002; 105 papers, 30 judged conclusive) agreed ventilation is strongly associated with SBS symptoms and that supply rates below 25 L/s per person increase SBS risk and sick leave. No carded trial tests any treatment given to the symptomatic person. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (benefit) for building-level ventilation increase and ventilation-system decontamination.

cards.headline: Wargocki 2000: raising outdoor-air ventilation from 3 to 30 L/s per person eased sick-building symptoms — dry mouth/throat (P < 0.0006), difficulty thinking clearly (P < 0.001) — and improved work performance by 1.7% per doubling of ventilation
cards.summary: Wargocki 2000: raising outdoor-air ventilation from 3 to 30 L/s per person eased sick-building symptoms — dry mouth/throat (P < 0.0006), difficulty thinking clearly (P < 0.001) — and improved work performance by 1.7% per doubling of ventilation
cards.people: 30 female subjects in five groups of six, each group exposed in turn to outdoor airflow rates of 3, 10 and 30 L/s per person (0.6, 2 and 6 air changes/hour) for 4.6 hours in a normally furnished office at 22 °C and 40% relative humidity; subjects were unaware of the ventilation condition.
cards.result: Increasing ventilation decreased the percentage dissatisfied with air quality (P < 0.002) and odour intensity (P < 0.02), increased perceived freshness (P < 0.05), decreased dryness of mouth and throat (P < 0.0006), eased difficulty thinking clearly (P < 0.001) and made subjects feel generally better (P < 0.0001). Performance of four simulated office tasks improved monotonically with ventilation, significantly for text-typing (P < 0.03); for each two-fold increase in ventilation rate, performance improved on average by 1.7%.
cards.watchOut: Thirty young women, 4.6-hour exposures, one office: this shows ventilation changes symptoms over an afternoon, not that raising a real building's ventilation cures established sick building syndrome over months. Symptom outcomes are self-rated intensities with p-values only — the record gives no absolute symptom rates.
cards.source: Wargocki P, Wyon DP, Sundell J, Clausen G, Fanger PO. The effects of outdoor air supply rate in an office on perceived air quality, sick building syndrome (SBS) symptoms and productivity. Indoor Air. 2000. PMID: 11089327. cards.headline: Menzies 2003: ultraviolet germicidal lights in office ventilation cut work-related symptoms overall (adjusted odds ratio 0.8, relative), respiratory symptoms (OR 0.6) and mucosal symptoms (OR 0.7) in a double-blind crossover trial of 771 workers
cards.summary: Menzies 2003: ultraviolet germicidal lights in office ventilation cut work-related symptoms overall (adjusted odds ratio 0.8, relative), respiratory symptoms (OR 0.6) and mucosal symptoms (OR 0.7) in a double-blind crossover trial of 771 workers
cards.people: 771 office workers in three Montreal office buildings; ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI) of drip pans and cooling coils was alternately off for 12 weeks and on for 4 weeks, over three cycles, with workers and assessors masked.
cards.result: UVGI produced a 99% (95% CI 67–100) relative reduction in microbial and endotoxin concentrations on irradiated surfaces. On within-person estimates, UVGI use was associated with fewer work-related symptoms overall (adjusted odds ratio 0.8 [95% CI 0.7–0.99], a relative measure), respiratory symptoms (0.6 [0.4–0.9]) and mucosal symptoms (0.7 [0.6–0.9]) than non-use; mucosal benefit was greatest in atopic workers (0.6 [0.5–0.8]) and never-smokers (0.7 [0.5–0.9]), and never-smokers also had fewer respiratory (0.4 [0.2–0.9]) and musculoskeletal symptoms (0.5 [0.3–0.9]) with UVGI on. No adverse effects were reported. The authors estimated installation could resolve work-related symptoms in about 4 million North American employees.
cards.watchOut: The trial treats microbial contamination of cooling coils and drip pans — one specific, remediable cause of building-related symptoms. Buildings whose symptoms come from low ventilation, chemical emissions or psychosocial factors have no reason to respond, and the 4-million-employees figure is the authors' extrapolation, not a measured outcome.
cards.source: Menzies D, Popa J, Hanley JA, Rand T, Milton DK. Effect of ultraviolet germicidal lights installed in office ventilation systems on workers' health and wellbeing: double-blind multiple crossover trial. The Lancet. 2003. PMID: 14654316. cards.headline: EUROVEN 2002: a European multidisciplinary consensus, judging 30 of 105 papers conclusive, agreed ventilation is strongly associated with SBS symptoms — and that outdoor air supply below 25 L/s per person increases SBS risk, short-term sick leave and lost productivity
cards.summary: EUROVEN 2002: a European multidisciplinary consensus, judging 30 of 105 papers conclusive, agreed ventilation is strongly associated with SBS symptoms — and that outdoor air supply below 25 L/s per person increases SBS risk, short-term sick leave and lost productivity
cards.people: 105 published papers on ventilation and health in non-industrial indoor environments, reviewed by the EUROVEN multidisciplinary group; 30 were judged conclusive, 14 background, 43 relevant but inconclusive and 18 irrelevant.
cards.result: The group agreed ventilation is strongly associated with comfort (perceived air quality) and health (Sick Building Syndrome symptoms, inflammation, infections, asthma, allergy, short-term sick leave), with an indicated association with productivity. Increasing outdoor air supply improves perceived air quality; rates below 25 L/s per person increase the risk of SBS symptoms, increase short-term sick leave and decrease productivity in office buildings. Air-conditioned buildings may carry increased SBS risk compared with naturally or mechanically ventilated buildings, with improper maintenance, design and functioning of air-conditioning contributing.
cards.watchOut: A consensus judgement over a mostly observational literature, not a trial: the 25 L/s-per-person figure is a threshold the group inferred across studies, and association here cannot separate ventilation itself from the building quality, maintenance and management that travel with it.
cards.source: Wargocki P, Sundell J, Bischof W, Brundrett G, Fanger PO, et al.; EUROVEN Group. Ventilation and health in non-industrial indoor environments: report from a European multidisciplinary scientific consensus meeting (EUROVEN). Indoor Air. 2002. PMID: not captured this session. cards.headline: Synthesis: sick building symptoms respond to building-level fixes — more outdoor air and decontaminated ventilation — tested in experiments, not in patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: sick building symptoms respond to building-level fixes — more outdoor air and decontaminated ventilation — tested in experiments, not in patients
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded records: one blinded crossover exposure experiment (n = 30), one double-blind building-level crossover trial (n = 771) and one multidisciplinary consensus review (105 papers).
cards.result: Two different interventions point the same way. Raising outdoor-air supply eased symptoms within hours in the laboratory experiment, and ultraviolet decontamination of ventilation systems reduced work-related symptoms over a year of crossovers in real offices (overall adjusted OR 0.8, relative). The consensus literature agrees that low ventilation tracks with more symptoms. No carded study tests treating the symptomatic person — the unit of treatment is the building. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for building-level ventilation and decontamination interventions.
cards.watchOut: Sick building syndrome is a diagnosis of pattern (symptoms that track with occupancy of one building), not a single disease: the carded evidence supports fixing air supply and contaminated air-conditioning, and says nothing about occupants whose symptoms persist after the building is fixed — those need individual assessment for allergy, asthma and non-building causes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wargocki 2000 (PMID: 11089327), Menzies 2003 (PMID: 14654316) and EUROVEN 2002 (PMID not captured this session), carded above.
