shelves.title: Thoracic outlet syndrome: almost no controlled evidence — one small trial favoured removing the first rib for pain, botulinum toxin matched placebo, and surgery's 76–85% 'success' comes entirely from uncontrolled case series with 13–26% complication rates
shelves.question: In people with thoracic outlet syndrome, do surgery (first rib resection, scalenectomy), botulinum toxin injections or conservative treatment improve pain, disability and paresthesias compared with each other, placebo or no treatment?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Thoracic outlet syndrome has the thinnest controlled evidence on this shelf. Cochrane (Povlsen 2014, PMID: 25427003) found only two randomised trials with adequate follow-up: first rib resection decreased pain more than brachial plexus neuroplasty in 55 patients with 'disputed' TOS (high risk of bias), and botulinum toxin injection into the scalene muscles did not significantly improve pain or disability versus saline placebo in 37 patients (low risk of bias), though paresthesias improved. All surgical enthusiasm comes from uncontrolled series: pooled success rates of 76–85% and complete relief of 53–61%, with complication rates of 12.6–25.9% (2019 review, PMID: 30122304), and a 2023 meta-analysis (PMID: 37055338; 22 series, 2,010 patients) ranking rib-sparing scalenectomy best on DASH improvement (43.0 points) and complications (3.6%). No trial compares surgery with physiotherapy or no treatment, and the diagnosis lacks generally accepted criteria. PROPOSED: MAYBE (weak evidence) for surgery in selected patients failing conservative care.

cards.headline: Povlsen 2014 (Cochrane): the entire randomised evidence for thoracic outlet syndrome is two trials — first rib resection beat neuroplasty for pain in 55 patients (high risk of bias), and botulinum toxin matched placebo for pain and disability in 37
cards.summary: Povlsen 2014 (Cochrane): the entire randomised evidence for thoracic outlet syndrome is two trials — first rib resection beat neuroplasty for pain in 55 patients (high risk of bias), and botulinum toxin matched placebo for pain and disability in 37
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Povlsen 2014)
cards.people: All randomised or quasi-randomised trials of any operative or non-operative treatment for thoracic outlet syndrome of any type (neurogenic, vascular or 'disputed') with at least 6 months' follow-up; two trials met the follow-up requirement.
cards.result: One trial (55 participants with 'disputed' TOS, high risk of bias) compared transaxillary first rib resection with supraclavicular neuroplasty of the brachial plexus: first rib resection decreased pain more than neuroplasty, with no adverse effects in either group. The second trial (37 participants, low risk of bias) compared botulinum toxin injection into the scalene muscles with saline placebo: no significant effect on pain relief or disability, but paresthesias improved significantly at 6 months, with no adverse events above placebo. A third randomised trial existed but lacked 6-month follow-up. The reviewers stressed the lack of generally accepted diagnostic criteria for TOS.
cards.watchOut: The review was last searched in June 2014 — old, and nothing in this shelf's other cards is a newer randomised trial either. The surgical result rests on one small high-bias trial in the 'disputed' subtype, the category with the least certain diagnosis; it cannot be generalised to neurogenic TOS with objective neurological loss.
cards.source: Povlsen B, Hansson T, Falk DE. Treatment for thoracic outlet syndrome. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2014. PMID: 25427003. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: 2023 meta-analysis: across 22 surgical case series (2,010 patients), rib-sparing scalenectomy showed the largest pre–post DASH improvement (43.0 points) and lowest complication rate (3.6%) versus transaxillary (26.8; 14.5%) and supraclavicular (21.8; 8.7%) first rib resection
cards.summary: 2023 meta-analysis: across 22 surgical case series (2,010 patients), rib-sparing scalenectomy showed the largest pre–post DASH improvement (43.0 points) and lowest complication rate (3.6%) versus transaxillary (26.8; 14.5%) and supraclavicular (21.8; 8.7%) first rib resection
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of uncontrolled surgical series (2023)
cards.people: 22 articles on surgery for neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome: 11 supraclavicular first rib resection (812 patients), 6 transaxillary first rib resection (478 patients) and 5 rib-sparing scalenectomy (720 patients); all uncontrolled case series pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis.
cards.result: The mean pre-to-postoperative improvement in Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) score was 43.0 points for rib-sparing scalenectomy, 26.8 for transaxillary first rib resection and 21.8 for supraclavicular first rib resection. Derkash success rates were 97.4% (rib-sparing), 93.2% (supraclavicular) and 87.9% (transaxillary). Complication rates were 3.6% (rib-sparing), 8.7% (supraclavicular) and 14.5% (transaxillary). The authors (level of evidence: Therapeutic IV) suggested rib-sparing scalenectomy is an effective option for neurogenic TOS.
cards.watchOut: Pre–post improvements in uncontrolled series are the weakest currency in surgery: regression to the mean, natural history, placebo effects of an operation and selective reporting all push the same way, and the approach with the best numbers (rib-sparing) is also the one offered by the fewest, most selected centres. These data rank surgeons' series, not treatments.

cards.summary: 2019 systematic review: pooled surgical success rates were 76–85% and complete relief 53–61% across the three operations, with complication rates of 12.6–25.9% — all from uncontrolled series
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of uncontrolled surgical series (2019)
cards.people: 40 study groups extracted from the literature on neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome surgery: 17 studies of transaxillary first rib excision, 9 of supraclavicular first rib excision with scalenectomy and 14 of supraclavicular release leaving the first rib intact; random-effects meta-analysis with Bayesian interpretation.
cards.result: Pooled success rates were 0.76 (95% CI 0.65–0.85) for transaxillary excision, 0.77 (0.68–0.85) for supraclavicular excision with scalenectomy and 0.85 (0.76–0.92) for supraclavicular release; complete relief rates were 0.53 (0.38–0.68), 0.57 (0.41–0.72) and 0.61 (0.35–0.84) respectively. The probabilities of a success rate above 70% were 90%, 87% and 99%. Complication rates were 22.5%, 25.9% and 12.6% respectively. The authors concluded supraclavicular release has a high probability of a success rate above 80%, and that both rib-excision approaches carry more complications.
cards.watchOut: 'Success' is each series' own definition, follow-up varies, and there is still no comparison against physiotherapy or no treatment anywhere in the pooled data — a 76–85% success rate after surgery is compatible with almost any true surgical effect, including a small one, in a condition whose symptoms fluctuate.
cards.source: Outcomes of Surgical Management of Neurogenic Thoracic Outlet Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Bayesian Perspective. Journal of Hand Surgery (American Volume). 2019. PMID: 30122304. cards.headline: Synthesis: thoracic outlet syndrome has operations with large case-series success rates and almost no controlled evidence — the honest stamp is weak-evidence MAYBE for surgery in selected patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: thoracic outlet syndrome has operations with large case-series success rates and almost no controlled evidence — the honest stamp is weak-evidence MAYBE for surgery in selected patients
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded records: one Cochrane review (2 eligible randomised trials, 92 participants) and two meta-analyses of uncontrolled surgical series (22 and 40 study groups).
cards.result: Controlled evidence: one small high-bias trial favouring first rib resection over neuroplasty for pain, and one good small trial in which botulinum toxin matched placebo for pain and disability. Everything else is before-and-after surgery data: success 76–85%, complete relief 53–61%, complications 12.6–25.9%, with rib-sparing/supraclavicular release approaches looking best on both benefit and harm. No trial compares surgery with physiotherapy or with no treatment, and the diagnosis itself lacks accepted criteria. PROPOSED STAMP: MAYBE (weak evidence) — surgery may help selected patients who fail conservative care; the size of any true effect is unknown.
cards.watchOut: Vascular thoracic outlet syndrome (arterial or venous compression with clot or ischaemia) is a different, urgent problem managed with anticoagulation, thrombolysis and decompression on vascular-surgery evidence that is also uncontrolled but mechanistically direct; this shelf's weak-evidence verdict concerns the common neurogenic/disputed presentations, where diagnostic uncertainty is the first problem to solve.
cards.source: Synthesis of Povlsen 2014 (PMID: 25427003), the 2023 surgical meta-analysis (PMID: 37055338) and the 2019 surgical systematic review (PMID: 30122304), carded above.

shelves.title: Toe pain from a bunion (hallux valgus): surgery cut pain more than waiting or an insole at 1 year (about 19 points on a 0-100 scale in the one head-to-head trial) — but waiting a year first did not worsen the final result
shelves.question: In adults with toe pain from hallux valgus (a bunion), does surgery relieve pain better than an orthosis or watchful waiting, and does delaying surgery harm the final result?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bias · Bunion/surgery · Female · Hallux Valgus/surgery · Humans · Male · Osteotomy/adverse effects · Osteotomy/methods · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Reoperation/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: For painful hallux valgus (bunion) — the commonest specific, trial-tested cause of great-toe pain — surgery beats waiting and beats an orthosis on pain at one year, but the margin rests on one unblinded Finnish trial. Torkki 2001 (PMID: 11368700; 209 patients randomised to chevron osteotomy, foot orthosis or a 1-year waiting list) found pain fell more with surgery than with no treatment at 6 months (adjusted mean difference -20 points, 95% CI -28 to -12) and at 1 year (-19, 95% CI -28 to -10); the orthosis helped at 6 months (-14, 95% CI -22 to -6) but not by 1 year, and 83% of the surgery group versus 46% orthosis and 24% control felt improved at 1 year. The 2-year follow-up (PMID: 12807332) found waiting a year, with or without orthoses, did not jeopardise the final result. The Cochrane review (Dias 2024, PMID: 39051477; 25 RCTs, 1,597 participants) found surgery may give a clinically important pain reduction versus no treatment (mean pain 21 vs 39 points at 12 months, MD -18.00, 95% CI -26.14 to -9.86; low-certainty, from that same single trial), a slight function gain (AOFAS 75 vs 66), and little to no difference in quality of life (93 vs 93 points); complex osteotomies probably match simple ones for pain and may increase reoperation. Other toe-pain causes (acute gout flare, Morton's neuroma, plantar heel pain) are homed on their own shelves. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit) for surgery over conservative care for painful bunion, on low-certainty evidence dominated by one unblinded trial.

cards.headline: Torkki 2001: surgery beat waiting on pain at 1 year (adjusted difference -19 points); an orthosis helped at 6 months only
cards.summary: Torkki 2001: surgery beat waiting on pain at 1 year (adjusted difference -19 points); an orthosis helped at 6 months only
cards.people: 209 adults (mean age 48 years, 93% women in the companion report) with painful hallux valgus referred in Finland, randomised to distal chevron osteotomy (n=71), functional foot orthosis (n=69) or a 1-year waiting list (n=69); follow-up 98-99%.
cards.result: At 6 months pain intensity fell more with surgery than control (adjusted mean difference -20, 95% CI -28 to -12) and more with orthosis than control (-14, 95% CI -22 to -6). At 1 year pain fell more with surgery than control (-19, 95% CI -28 to -10) and more with surgery than orthosis (-14, 95% CI -22 to -5). At 1 year 83% of the surgery group, 46% of the orthosis group and 24% of controls thought they had improved (number needed to treat 1.7 for surgery versus control, as printed in the record). Four surgical complications occurred, including one recurrence of hallux valgus.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, with subjective self-reported pain outcomes: patients knew whether they had had an operation, which can inflate the surgical advantage. It is also the only trial of surgery versus no treatment in the Cochrane review, so the whole surgery-versus-waiting estimate rests on it.
cards.source: Torkki M, Malmivaara A, Seitsalo S, Hoikka V, Laippala P, Paavolainen P. Surgery vs orthosis vs watchful waiting for hallux valgus: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2001. PMID: 11368700. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session. cards.headline: Torkki 2003 (2-year follow-up): waiting a year for surgery, with or without orthoses, did not jeopardise the final outcome
cards.summary: Torkki 2003 (2-year follow-up): waiting a year for surgery, with or without orthoses, did not jeopardise the final outcome
cards.people: The same 209 consecutive patients (mean age 48 years, 93% female) with painful hallux valgus, randomised to immediate operation or 1 year of waiting with or without foot orthoses, followed for 2 years.
cards.result: At the 1-year follow-up pain was least intense in the surgery group. The authors concluded that immediate operation is superior to delayed operation or foot orthoses, but that if surgery is not possible, waiting for 1 year, with or without an orthosis, does not jeopardise the final outcome.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up report of the same trial as the Torkki 2001 card, not independent evidence; its abstract reports the conclusion qualitatively, without new effect sizes captured this session.

cards.headline: Dias 2024 (Cochrane): surgery may cut pain importantly versus no treatment (21 vs 39 points at 12 months) but quality of life was identical, and complex osteotomies matched simple ones
cards.summary: Dias 2024 (Cochrane): surgery may cut pain importantly versus no treatment (21 vs 39 points at 12 months) but quality of life was identical, and complex osteotomies matched simple ones
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, Cochrane (Dias 2024)
cards.people: 25 randomised trials, 1,597 adults with hallux valgus (most women), comparing surgery with placebo/sham, no treatment, non-surgical treatment, or other surgical techniques; searches to 20 April 2023.
cards.result: Surgery versus no treatment (1 study, 140 participants): mean pain at 12 months 21 points after surgery versus 39 points with no treatment (0-100 scale; MD -18.00, 95% CI -26.14 to -9.86; low-certainty); function 75 versus 66 AOFAS points (MD 9.00, 95% CI 5.16 to 12.84); quality of life 93 points in both groups (MD 0, 95% CI -2.12 to 2.12); global treatment success 80 versus 61 points (MD 19.00, 95% CI 8.11 to 29.89); adverse events RR 8.75 (95% CI 0.48 to 159.53; very low-certainty). Surgery versus non-surgical treatment showed the same pattern. Complex versus simple osteotomies (7 studies, 414 participants) probably differ little on pain (moderate-certainty) and complex osteotomies may increase reoperation. No trial compared surgery with placebo or sham surgery. Most trials were at high risk of bias (detection bias 96%, performance bias 88%).
cards.watchOut: The headline surgery-versus-no-treatment numbers come from a single unblinded trial, and certainty is low or very low throughout; the review cannot separate a true surgical effect from expectation effects, because no sham-controlled trial exists.
cards.source: Dias CGP, Godoy-Santos AL, Ferrari J, Ferretti M, Lenza M. Surgical interventions for treating hallux valgus and bunions. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2024. PMID: 39051477. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for a painful bunion, surgery relieves pain more than waiting or an insole at one year, but waiting a year costs nothing in the final result
cards.summary: Synthesis: for a painful bunion, surgery relieves pain more than waiting or an insole at one year, but waiting a year costs nothing in the final result
cards.people: Synthesis of the 3 carded records: one randomised trial and its 2-year follow-up (209 patients) and the 2024 Cochrane review of 25 trials (1,597 participants).
cards.result: Surgery reduced pain by about 18-20 points (0-100) more than no treatment at 12 months and improved function slightly, with no difference in quality of life; an orthosis relieved pain at 6 months but not at 12. Because the comparative evidence is one unblinded trial graded low-certainty, and delay did not worsen final outcomes, the balance supports offering surgery for persistent painful bunion while reassuring patients that a year of conservative care first is safe. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Scoped to hallux valgus/bunion, the cardable toe-pain question: acute gout flare is homed on Shelf #390, Morton's neuroma on #4210 and plantar heel pain on #1024/#2728; this shelf makes no claim about those causes.
cards.source: Synthesis of Torkki 2001 (PMID: 11368700), Torkki 2003 (PMID: 12807332) and Dias 2024 Cochrane review (PMID: 39051477), carded above.

shelves.title: IL-6 inhibition in rheumatoid arthritis: tocilizumab and sarilumab beat placebo on ACR20 by about 22-33 percentage points across three phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In rheumatoid arthritis with an inadequate response to methotrexate or to TNF inhibitors, does IL-6 receptor inhibition with tocilizumab or sarilumab improve disease activity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/classification · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/drug therapy · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/physiopathology · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Quality of Life · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Tocilizumab versus adalimumab monotherapy (ADACTA) is homed on Shelf #3718 and is not re-carded here. This shelf covers placebo-controlled IL-6 receptor inhibition. OPTION (Smolen 2008, PMID: 18358926, NCT00106548): tocilizumab 8 mg/kg plus methotrexate gave ACR20 at week 24 in 59% versus 26% on placebo (relative OR 4.0). MOBILITY (Genovese 2015, PMID: 25733246, NCT01061736): sarilumab 200 mg plus methotrexate gave ACR20 66.4% versus 33.4%, and slowed radiographic progression (Sharp score change 0.25 vs 2.78 at week 52). TARGET (Fleischmann 2017, PMID: 27860410, NCT01709578), in patients who had failed TNF inhibitors: sarilumab ACR20 60.9% (200 mg) versus 33.7% on placebo. Serious infections ran slightly above placebo in OPTION and MOBILITY (up to 4.0% vs 2.3%) but not in TARGET (1.1% vs 1.1%); liver-enzyme and neutrophil effects are class effects. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: Smolen 2008 (OPTION): tocilizumab 8 mg/kg ACR20 at week 24 was 59% versus 26% on placebo (relative OR 4.0)
cards.summary: Smolen 2008 (OPTION): tocilizumab 8 mg/kg ACR20 at week 24 was 59% versus 26% on placebo (relative OR 4.0)
cards.people: 623 patients with moderate-to-severe active rheumatoid arthritis on stable methotrexate randomised to tocilizumab 8 mg/kg (n=205), 4 mg/kg (214) or placebo (204) intravenously every 4 weeks; intention-to-treat population 622.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 59% (8 mg/kg) and 48% (4 mg/kg) versus 26% on placebo - relative odds ratio 4.0 (95% CI 2.6-6.1) and 2.6 (1.7-3.9), both P<0.0001, with the absolute rates as printed. Serious infections or infestations occurred in 6 patients on 8 mg/kg, 3 on 4 mg/kg and 2 on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Rescue tocilizumab was offered from week 16 to inadequate responders, and the trial predates routine IL-6 inhibitor safety monitoring (lipids, neutrophils, liver enzymes).
cards.source: Smolen JS et al. Effect of interleukin-6 receptor inhibition with tocilizumab in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (OPTION study): a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial. Lancet. 2008. PMID: 18358926. Registry ID: NCT00106548. cards.headline: Genovese 2015 (MOBILITY): sarilumab 200 mg ACR20 was 66.4% versus 33.4% on placebo, with less joint damage at 1 year
cards.summary: Genovese 2015 (MOBILITY): sarilumab 200 mg ACR20 was 66.4% versus 33.4% on placebo, with less joint damage at 1 year
cards.people: 1,197 adults with moderate-to-severe rheumatoid arthritis and inadequate response to methotrexate, randomised to sarilumab 150 mg or 200 mg or placebo every 2 weeks, all with weekly methotrexate, for 52 weeks.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 58.0% (150 mg), 66.4% (200 mg) and 33.4% (placebo), P<0.0001. HAQ disability change at week 16: -0.53, -0.55 and -0.29. Radiographic Sharp/van der Heijde change at week 52: 0.90, 0.25 and 2.78 (less progression on sarilumab). Serious infections: 2.6%, 4.0% and 2.3%. ALT above 3 times the upper limit of normal: 9.5%, 8.0% and 2.1%.
cards.watchOut: Industry-sponsored registration trial in methotrexate inadequate responders; neutropenia and transaminase elevations were commoner on sarilumab and occasionally stopped treatment.
cards.source: Genovese MC et al. Sarilumab Plus Methotrexate in Patients With Active Rheumatoid Arthritis and Inadequate Response to Methotrexate: Results of a Phase III Study. shelves.title: Rituximab in rheumatoid arthritis: one course (2 infusions) roughly tripled ACR20 responses versus placebo - 51-55% versus 18-28% across three trials
shelves.question: In rheumatoid arthritis with an inadequate response to methotrexate or to TNF inhibitors, does rituximab plus methotrexate improve disease activity versus placebo plus methotrexate?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Murine-Derived · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Selection · Placebos · Rituximab · Safety · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: Three placebo-controlled trials of rituximab plus methotrexate. REFLEX (Cohen 2006, PMID: 16947627), in patients who had failed TNF inhibitors: ACR20 at week 24 was 51% versus 18% on placebo, ACR50 27% versus 5%, with serious infections 5.2 versus 3.7 per 100 patient-years. DANCER (Emery 2006, PMID: 16649186), a dose-ranging trial: ACR20 55% (2 x 500 mg) and 54% (2 x 1,000 mg) versus 28%, and glucocorticoid premedication did not add efficacy. SERENE (Emery 2010, PMID: 20488885), in biologic-naive methotrexate inadequate responders: ACR20 54% and 51% versus 23%, with no difference between the 500 mg and 1,000 mg courses. No registry ID appears in any of the three records (all predate routine registration reporting). Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: Cohen 2006 (REFLEX): after TNF-inhibitor failure, rituximab ACR20 was 51% versus 18% on placebo at week 24
cards.summary: Cohen 2006 (REFLEX): after TNF-inhibitor failure, rituximab ACR20 was 51% versus 18% on placebo at week 24
cards.people: 520 patients with active, longstanding rheumatoid arthritis and inadequate response to one or more TNF inhibitors, randomised to one course of rituximab (2 infusions of 1,000 mg; n=311) or placebo (n=209), both with background methotrexate.
cards.result: At week 24: ACR20 51% versus 18%, ACR50 27% versus 5%, ACR70 12% versus 1%, and moderate-to-good EULAR responses 65% versus 22% (all P<0.0001). Serious infections: 5.2 per 100 patient-years on rituximab versus 3.7 on placebo. Most adverse events occurred with the first infusion and were mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: A single course was studied to 24 weeks; retreatment timing and long-term infection and immunoglobulin effects are not answered by this trial.
cards.source: Cohen SB et al. Rituximab for rheumatoid arthritis refractory to anti-tumor necrosis factor therapy: Results of a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase III trial evaluating primary efficacy and safety at twenty-four weeks. Arthritis Rheum. 2006. PMID: 16947627. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2b dose-ranging trial (Emery 2006)
cards.people: 465 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate, randomised across 9 groups: rituximab placebo (n=149), 2 x 500 mg (124) or 2 x 1,000 mg (192), each with placebo glucocorticoids, intravenous methylprednisolone premedication, or premedication plus 2 weeks of oral prednisone; all on methotrexate.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 55% (2 x 500 mg) and 54% (2 x 1,000 mg) versus 28% on placebo (P<0.0001). ACR50: 33%, 34% and 13%. ACR70: 13%, 20% and 5%. DAS28 change: -1.79, -2.05 and -0.67. Glucocorticoids did not significantly change ACR20, but intravenous premedication reduced first-infusion reactions.
cards.watchOut: A phase 2b dose-ranging design with nine small treatment cells; infection rates looked similar to placebo over 24 weeks, which is too short to judge B-cell depletion risks.

cards.summary: Emery 2010 (SERENE): in biologic-naive patients, rituximab ACR20 was 54% (2 x 500 mg) and 51% (2 x 1,000 mg) versus 23% on placebo
cards.people: 512 biologic-naive patients with active rheumatoid arthritis and inadequate response to methotrexate, randomised to rituximab 2 x 500 mg (n=168), 2 x 1,000 mg (172) or placebo (172), all with methotrexate 10-25 mg/week, followed to week 48.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 54% (2 x 500 mg), 51% (2 x 1,000 mg) and 23% (placebo), P<0.0001 for both doses, with further improvement by week 48 after a second course in non-remitters. cards.watchOut: From week 24, non-remitters received a second course and placebo patients switched to rituximab, so week-48 results are no longer a clean placebo comparison.

cards.headline: Fleischmann 2012 (ORAL Solo): tofacitinib monotherapy ACR20 at month 3 was 59.8% and 65.7% versus 26.7% on placebo
cards.summary: Fleischmann 2012 (ORAL Solo): tofacitinib monotherapy ACR20 at month 3 was 59.8% and 65.7% versus 26.7% on placebo
cards.people: 611 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis randomised to tofacitinib 5 mg or 10 mg twice daily, or placebo for 3 months followed by tofacitinib, in a 6-month phase 3 monotherapy trial (no background methotrexate).
cards.result: ACR20 at month 3: 59.8% (5 mg) and 65.7% (10 mg) versus 26.7% on placebo (P<0.001 for both). HAQ disability change: -0.50 and -0.57 versus -0.19. DAS28-4(ESR) below 2.6: 5.6% and 8.7% versus 4.4% (not significant). Serious infections developed in six patients receiving tofacitinib; LDL cholesterol rose and neutrophil counts fell.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled period was only 3 months, and remission (DAS28 below 2.6) was not significantly improved despite the large ACR20 gap.

cards.people: 717 patients with rheumatoid arthritis on stable methotrexate randomised to tofacitinib 5 mg or 10 mg twice daily, adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks, or placebo (with blinded switch to tofacitinib from months 3-6), over 12 months.
cards.result: ACR20 at month 6: 51.5% (tofacitinib 5 mg), 52.6% (10 mg), 47.2% (adalimumab) and 28.3% (placebo), P<0.001 for each active treatment versus placebo. HAQ disability and DAS28 remission also favoured the active groups. Pulmonary tuberculosis developed in two patients on tofacitinib 10 mg; LDL and HDL cholesterol rose and neutrophil counts fell on tofacitinib.
cards.watchOut: Tofacitinib was numerically, not statistically, compared with adalimumab - the trial was not powered as a head-to-head non-inferiority test.
cards.source: van Vollenhoven RF et al. Tofacitinib or adalimumab versus placebo in rheumatoid arthritis. N Engl J Med. 2012. PMID: 22873531. Registry ID: NCT00853385. cards.headline: Burmester 2018 (SELECT-NEXT): upadacitinib ACR20 at week 12 was 64% and 66% versus 36% on placebo
cards.summary: Burmester 2018 (SELECT-NEXT): upadacitinib ACR20 at week 12 was 64% and 66% versus 36% on placebo
cards.people: 661 patients with moderate-to-severe rheumatoid arthritis and inadequate response to conventional DMARDs, randomised to upadacitinib 15 mg (n=221) or 30 mg (219) once daily or placebo (221), on stable background conventional DMARDs, for a 12-week placebo-controlled period.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 12: 141/221 (64%) on 15 mg and 145/219 (66%) on 30 mg versus 79/221 (36%) on placebo (P<0.0001). DAS28(CRP) of 3.2 or less: 48% and 48% versus 17%. Infections were reported in 29% and 32% versus 21%; there were five serious infections across the groups and no deaths.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled window was 12 weeks; this card addresses efficacy only - long-term cardiovascular and malignancy safety for the class is on Shelf #384.

shelves.title: Risankizumab in psoriatic arthritis: ACR20 at week 24 was 57.3% versus 33.5% (KEEPsAKE 1) and 51.3% versus 26.5% (KEEPsAKE 2) on placebo, sustained to week 100
shelves.question: In psoriatic arthritis, does the IL-23 inhibitor risankizumab improve joint disease versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use · Arthritis, Psoriatic/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Guselkumab in psoriatic arthritis (DISCOVER-1 and DISCOVER-2) is homed on Shelf #3719 and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers the other IL-23 inhibitor, risankizumab. KEEPsAKE 1 (Kristensen 2022, PMID: 34911706, NCT03675308), in conventional-DMARD inadequate responders: ACR20 at week 24 was 57.3% versus 33.5% on placebo. KEEPsAKE 2, reported at 52 weeks (Ostör 2023, PMID: 36282537, NCT03671148), which also enrolled biologic inadequate responders: ACR20 at week 24 was 51.3% versus 26.5%, rising to 58.5% at week 52 on continuous risankizumab. The 100-week KEEPsAKE 1 report (Kristensen 2024, PMID: 38498141, NCT03675308) shows durability: ACR20 64.3% at week 100 on continuous risankizumab, with 81.2% of week-52 responders maintaining their response. Serious infections in KEEPsAKE 1 were 1.0% on risankizumab versus 1.2% on placebo. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: Kristensen 2022 (KEEPsAKE 1): risankizumab ACR20 at week 24 was 57.3% versus 33.5% on placebo
cards.summary: Kristensen 2022 (KEEPsAKE 1): risankizumab ACR20 at week 24 was 57.3% versus 33.5% on placebo
cards.people: 964 patients with active psoriatic arthritis and inadequate response or intolerance to at least one conventional DMARD, randomised 1:1 to risankizumab 150 mg (n=483) or placebo (481) at weeks 0, 4 and 16.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 57.3% on risankizumab versus 33.5% on placebo (P<0.001). The first eight ranked secondary endpoints - including skin and nail psoriasis, minimal disease activity, and resolution of enthesitis and dactylitis - also significantly favoured risankizumab (P<0.001). Serious infections: 1.0% versus 1.2%. One death (urosepsis, judged unrelated to the study drug) occurred in the risankizumab group.
cards.watchOut: Conventional-DMARD inadequate responders who were largely biologic-naive; the results do not directly cover patients who have failed a biologic (see the KEEPsAKE 2 card).
cards.source: Kristensen LE et al. Efficacy and safety of risankizumab for active psoriatic arthritis: 24-week results from the randomised, double-blind, phase 3 KEEPsAKE 1 trial. Ann Rheum Dis. 2022. PMID: 34911706. Registry ID: NCT03675308. cards.headline: Östör 2023 (KEEPsAKE 2): risankizumab ACR20 was 51.3% versus 26.5% at week 24 and 58.5% at week 52
cards.summary: Östör 2023 (KEEPsAKE 2): risankizumab ACR20 was 51.3% versus 26.5% at week 24 and 58.5% at week 52
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, 52-week report (Östör 2023)
cards.people: 444 patients with active psoriatic arthritis and prior inadequate response or intolerance to one or two biologic therapies or to conventional DMARDs, randomised 1:1 to risankizumab 150 mg (n=224) or placebo (220) at weeks 0, 4 and 16, with placebo patients switching to risankizumab at week 24.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 51.3% on risankizumab versus 26.5% on placebo (P<0.001). At week 52, ACR20 was 58.5% in patients on continuous risankizumab and 55.7% in patients who switched from placebo at week 24. Serious treatment-emergent adverse event rates remained stable through week 52 and no deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: This is the 52-week report of KEEPsAKE 2; after week 24 there was no placebo group, so the week-52 figures show maintenance, not a controlled comparison.
cards.source: Östör A et al. Efficacy and safety of risankizumab for active psoriatic arthritis: 52-week results from the KEEPsAKE 2 study. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2023. PMID: 36282537. cards.headline: Kristensen 2024 (KEEPsAKE 1 at 100 weeks): ACR20 held at 64.3% on continuous risankizumab, and 81.2% of week-52 responders kept their response
cards.summary: Kristensen 2024 (KEEPsAKE 1 at 100 weeks): ACR20 held at 64.3% on continuous risankizumab, and 81.2% of week-52 responders kept their response
cards.type: Open-label extension report of a randomised phase 3 trial (Kristensen 2024)
cards.people: The 964 patients of KEEPsAKE 1 followed through the open-label extension to week 100; 828 (85.9%) completed week 100, with all patients on open-label risankizumab every 12 weeks after week 24.
cards.result: ACR20 on continuous risankizumab: 57.3% at week 24, 70.6% at week 52 and 64.3% at week 100. In the placebo-to-risankizumab group: 33.5%, 63.7% and 62.1%. Of week-52 ACR20 responders, 81.2% in both cohorts maintained the response at week 100. Minimal disease activity on continuous risankizumab: 25.0%, 38.3% and 38.2% at weeks 24, 52 and 100. Risankizumab was generally well tolerated through week 100.
cards.watchOut: Open-label extension data without a comparator, in the 85.9% who completed 100 weeks - responder maintenance is subject to completer bias. The record carries no MeSH section.
cards.source: Kristensen LE et al. Efficacy and Safety of Risankizumab for Active Psoriatic Arthritis: 100-Week Results from the Phase 3 KEEPsAKE 1 Randomized Clinical Trial. Rheumatol Ther. 2024. PMID: 38498141. Registry ID: NCT03675308. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Ustekinumab in psoriatic arthritis: ACR20 at week 24 was 42.4-49.5% versus 22.8% on placebo (PSUMMIT-1), and joint damage progressed less (vdH-S change 0.4 vs 1.0)
shelves.question: In psoriatic arthritis, does ustekinumab (IL-12/23 p40 blockade) improve joint disease and slow radiographic progression versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Arthritis, Psoriatic/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Ustekinumab · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PSUMMIT-1 (McInnes 2013, PMID: 23769296, NCT01009086): ACR20 at week 24 was 42.4% on ustekinumab 45 mg and 49.5% on 90 mg versus 22.8% on placebo, maintained to week 52. PSUMMIT-2 (Ritchlin 2014, PMID: 24482301, NCT01077362), in which 180 of 312 patients had already failed TNF inhibitors: ACR20 43.8% on combined ustekinumab versus 20.2% on placebo, and 35.6% versus 14.5% within the TNF-experienced subgroup. The preplanned integrated radiographic analysis of both trials (Kavanaugh 2014, PMID: 24553909; 927 patients) found less joint damage progression on ustekinumab at week 24 (mean van der Heijde-Sharp change 0.4 versus 1.0 on placebo, all P<0.02). Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).

cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 87/205 (42.4%) on 45 mg and 101/204 (49.5%) on 90 mg versus 47/206 (22.8%) on placebo (P<0.0001 for both), with responses maintained at week 52. Adverse events by week 16 were similar: 171/409 (41.8%) on ustekinumab versus 86/205 (42.0%) on placebo.

cards.summary: Ritchlin 2014 (PSUMMIT-2): ustekinumab ACR20 was 43.8% versus 20.2% on placebo - and 35.6% versus 14.5% after TNF-inhibitor failure
cards.people: 312 adults with active psoriatic arthritis despite conventional and/or TNF-inhibitor therapy (180 anti-TNF-experienced, 132 anti-TNF-naive), randomised to ustekinumab 45 mg or 90 mg or placebo at weeks 0 and 4 then every 12 weeks, with crossover at week 24.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 43.8% on combined ustekinumab versus 20.2% on placebo (P<0.001); in anti-TNF-experienced patients 35.6% versus 14.5%, with PASI75 47.1% versus 2.0% and median HAQ disability change -0.13 versus 0.0. Benefits were sustained through week 52 (ACR20 38.9% in TNF-experienced patients on ustekinumab). No unexpected adverse events through week 60.
cards.watchOut: The headline ACR20 combines both ustekinumab doses; MeSH terms were not captured from this record this session.
cards.source: Ritchlin C et al. Efficacy and safety of the anti-IL-12/23 p40 monoclonal antibody, ustekinumab, in patients with active psoriatic arthritis despite conventional non-biological and biological anti-tumour necrosis factor therapy: 6-month and 1-year results of the phase 3, multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised PSUMMIT 2 trial. Ann Rheum Dis. 2014. PMID: 24482301. Registry ID: NCT01077362. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Kavanaugh 2014: ustekinumab slowed joint damage - mean vdH-S change 0.4 versus 1.0 on placebo over 24 weeks
cards.summary: Kavanaugh 2014: ustekinumab slowed joint damage - mean vdH-S change 0.4 versus 1.0 on placebo over 24 weeks
cards.type: Integrated radiographic analysis of two randomised phase 3 trials (Kavanaugh 2014)
cards.people: Preplanned integrated radiographic analysis of PSUMMIT-1 (n=615) and PSUMMIT-2 (n=312) - 927 patients with active psoriatic arthritis, with hand and foot radiographs at weeks 0, 24 and 52 scored by the PsA-modified van der Heijde-Sharp method.
cards.result: Mean change in total vdH-S score from week 0 to 24: 0.4 in the combined and individual ustekinumab dose groups versus 1.0 on placebo (all P<0.02). From weeks 24 to 52, inhibition of progression was maintained on ustekinumab, and progression slowed in former placebo patients after they started ustekinumab (mean change 0.08).
cards.watchOut: The absolute difference in progression over 24 weeks is small (0.6 vdH-S units) and its long-term clinical meaning is uncertain; the record lists no registry ID.
cards.source: Kavanaugh A et al. Ustekinumab, an anti-IL-12/23 p40 monoclonal antibody, inhibits radiographic progression in patients with active psoriatic arthritis: results of an integrated analysis of radiographic data from the phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled PSUMMIT-1 and PSUMMIT-2 trials. Ann Rheum Dis. 2014. PMID: 24553909. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Apremilast in psoriatic arthritis: ACR20 at week 16 was 28-41% versus 18-19% on placebo across the three PALACE trials - real but modest gains
shelves.question: In psoriatic arthritis, does oral apremilast improve joint disease versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Antirheumatic Agents/administration & dosage · Arthritis, Psoriatic/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Methotrexate/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Phosphodiesterase 4 Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Psoriasis/drug therapy · Thalidomide/administration & dosage · Thalidomide/analogs & derivatives · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Three phase 3 placebo-controlled trials of the oral PDE4 inhibitor apremilast, all with an early-escape design. PALACE-1 (Kavanaugh 2014, PMID: 24595547, NCT01172938): ACR20 at week 16 was 31% (20 mg twice daily) and 40% (30 mg) versus 19% on placebo. PALACE-2 (Cutolo 2016, PMID: 27422893, NCT01212757): 37.4% and 32.1% versus 18.9% - note the 20 mg dose scored numerically above the 30 mg dose. PALACE-3 (Edwards 2016, PMID: 26792812, NCT01212770), in patients all with skin involvement: 28% and 41% versus 18%, with PASI50 in 41% versus 24% at the 30 mg dose. Absolute gains are modest (about 9-22 percentage points) and smaller than those on the biologic shelves; gastrointestinal effects (diarrhoea, nausea) were the commonest adverse events and usually settled. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit), with modest effect size.

cards.headline: Kavanaugh 2014 (PALACE-1): apremilast ACR20 at week 16 was 31% (20 mg) and 40% (30 mg) versus 19% on placebo
cards.summary: Kavanaugh 2014 (PALACE-1): apremilast ACR20 at week 16 was 31% (20 mg) and 40% (30 mg) versus 19% on placebo
cards.people: 504 patients with active psoriatic arthritis despite prior conventional DMARD and/or biologic therapy, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, apremilast 20 mg twice daily or apremilast 30 mg twice daily, with stable background DMARDs allowed.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 16: 31% (20 mg) and 40% (30 mg) versus 19% on placebo (P<0.001). Physical function and psoriasis measures also improved significantly. The commonest adverse events were gastrointestinal, generally early and self-limiting; there was no imbalance in major cardiac events, serious or opportunistic infections, malignancies or laboratory abnormalities.
cards.watchOut: Patients without at least 20% joint-count improvement at week 16 were re-randomised or escaped early, so later time points are not clean placebo comparisons.
cards.source: Kavanaugh A et al. Treatment of psoriatic arthritis in a phase 3 randomised, placebo-controlled trial with apremilast, an oral phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitor. Ann Rheum Dis. 2014. PMID: 24595547. Registry ID: NCT01172938. cards.headline: Cutolo 2016 (PALACE-2): apremilast ACR20 at week 16 was 37.4% (20 mg) and 32.1% (30 mg) versus 18.9% on placebo
cards.summary: Cutolo 2016 (PALACE-2): apremilast ACR20 at week 16 was 37.4% (20 mg) and 32.1% (30 mg) versus 18.9% on placebo
cards.people: 484 patients with active psoriatic arthritis despite prior conventional DMARDs and/or biologic therapy, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, apremilast 20 mg twice daily or apremilast 30 mg twice daily (intention-to-treat population).
cards.result: ACR20 at week 16: 37.4% on 20 mg (P=0.0002) and 32.1% on 30 mg (P=0.0060) versus 18.9% on placebo. Improvements in signs and symptoms, physical function and psoriasis were maintained through week 52. The commonest adverse events were diarrhoea, nausea, headache and upper respiratory tract infection; laboratory abnormalities were infrequent and transient.
cards.watchOut: The dose order inverted here (20 mg numerically above 30 mg), so there is no consistent dose-response across the PALACE programme.
cards.source: Cutolo M et al. A Phase III, Randomized, Controlled Trial of Apremilast in Patients with Psoriatic Arthritis: Results of the PALACE 2 Trial. J Rheumatol. 2016. PMID: 27422893. cards.headline: Edwards 2016 (PALACE-3): apremilast ACR20 was 28% (20 mg) and 41% (30 mg) versus 18% on placebo, with PASI50 41% versus 24%
cards.summary: Edwards 2016 (PALACE-3): apremilast ACR20 was 28% (20 mg) and 41% (30 mg) versus 18% on placebo, with PASI50 41% versus 24%
cards.people: 505 patients with active psoriatic arthritis and current skin involvement despite prior conventional DMARDs and/or biologics, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, apremilast 20 mg twice daily or apremilast 30 mg twice daily.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 16: 28% (20 mg, P=0.0295) and 41% (30 mg, P<0.0001) versus 18% on placebo. HAQ disability change at 30 mg: -0.20 versus -0.07 on placebo (P=0.0073). In patients with at least 3% body surface area psoriasis, PASI50 at week 16 was 41% (30 mg) versus 24% (P=0.0098). Improvements were sustained to week 52; most adverse events were mild to moderate, with diarrhoea, nausea, headache and upper respiratory tract infection commonest.
cards.watchOut: The 20 mg dose's ACR20 advantage was marginal (P=0.0295) and the absolute gains are smaller than those seen with biologic therapies; there is no radiographic-progression endpoint in the abstract.
cards.source: Edwards CJ et al. Apremilast, an oral phosphodiesterase 4 inhibitor, in patients with psoriatic arthritis and current skin involvement: a phase III, randomised, controlled trial (PALACE 3). Ann Rheum Dis. 2016. PMID: 26792812. Registry ID: NCT01212770. cards.headline: Synthesis: apremilast beats placebo in all three PALACE trials, but absolute ACR20 gains are modest - LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: apremilast beats placebo in all three PALACE trials, but absolute ACR20 gains are modest - LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PALACE-1 (504 patients), PALACE-2 (484) and PALACE-3 (505).
cards.result: ACR20 at week 16 versus placebo: 31% and 40% vs 19% (PALACE-1); 37.4% and 32.1% vs 18.9% (PALACE-2); 28% and 41% vs 18% (PALACE-3, all with skin disease, where PASI50 was 41% vs 24% at 30 mg). Effects are consistent but modest, with no consistent dose-response and mainly gastrointestinal tolerability issues. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit), modest effect size.
cards.watchOut: No PALACE trial measured radiographic progression, and none compared apremilast with a biologic; positioning against biologics rests on cross-trial comparison only.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kavanaugh et al. 2014 (PMID: 24595547), Cutolo et al. 2016 (PMID: 27422893) and Edwards et al. 2016 (PMID: 26792812). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.balance: Upadacitinib in psoriatic arthritis (SELECT-PsA 1 and 2) is homed on pack Shelf #5092 and is not re-carded here; this shelf covers tofacitinib. OPAL Broaden (Mease 2017, PMID: 29045212, NCT01877668), in conventional-DMARD inadequate responders: ACR20 at month 3 was 50% on tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily and 61% on 10 mg versus 33% on placebo, with adalimumab at 52% in the same trial. OPAL Beyond (Gladman 2017, PMID: 29045207, NCT01882439), in TNF-inhibitor inadequate responders: ACR20 50% and 47% versus 24% on placebo, with serious adverse events in 4% and 6% on the continuous tofacitinib doses. A post hoc analysis of the OPAL Balance extension (Gladman 2024, PMID: 39702318) found efficacy was maintained when patients switched directly from adalimumab to tofacitinib (n=91) or continued tofacitinib (n=89). Class safety for JAK inhibitors is covered on Shelf #384. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: Mease 2017 (OPAL Broaden): tofacitinib ACR20 at month 3 was 50% (5 mg) and 61% (10 mg) versus 33% on placebo; adalimumab 52%
cards.summary: Mease 2017 (OPAL Broaden): tofacitinib ACR20 at month 3 was 50% (5 mg) and 61% (10 mg) versus 33% on placebo; adalimumab 52%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active- and placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Mease 2017)
cards.people: 422 patients with active psoriatic arthritis and inadequate response to conventional DMARDs (TNF-inhibitor-naive), randomised to tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily (n=107), 10 mg twice daily (104), adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks (106), or placebo with blinded switch to tofacitinib at month 3 (52 and 53).
cards.result: ACR20 at month 3: 50% (5 mg, P=0.01) and 61% (10 mg, P<0.001) versus 33% on placebo; adalimumab 52%. HAQ disability change: -0.35 and -0.40 versus -0.18 on placebo (adalimumab -0.38). Adverse events through month 12: 66% and 71% on tofacitinib, 72% on adalimumab. Four cancers, three serious infections and four herpes zoster cases occurred in patients receiving tofacitinib.
cards.watchOut: The placebo comparison ends at month 3 (placebo patients switched to tofacitinib); adalimumab was an active reference arm, not a powered head-to-head comparison.
cards.source: Mease P et al. Tofacitinib or Adalimumab versus Placebo for Psoriatic Arthritis. N Engl J Med. 2017. PMID: 29045212. Registry ID: NCT01877668. cards.headline: Gladman 2017 (OPAL Beyond): after TNF-inhibitor failure, tofacitinib ACR20 was 50% and 47% versus 24% on placebo
cards.summary: Gladman 2017 (OPAL Beyond): after TNF-inhibitor failure, tofacitinib ACR20 was 50% and 47% versus 24% on placebo
cards.people: 395 patients with active psoriatic arthritis and inadequate response to TNF inhibitors, randomised to tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily (n=132), 10 mg twice daily (132), or placebo with switch to tofacitinib at month 3 (66 and 65).
cards.result: ACR20 at month 3: 50% (5 mg) and 47% (10 mg) versus 24% on placebo (P<0.001 for both). HAQ disability change: -0.39 and -0.35 versus -0.14. Serious adverse events occurred in 4% (5 mg) and 6% (10 mg) of continuously treated patients; over 6 months there were four serious infections, three herpes zoster infections, one myocardial infarction and one ischaemic stroke among tofacitinib-treated patients.
cards.watchOut: A TNF-inhibitor-experienced population with only a 3-month placebo window; liver-enzyme elevations of at least 3 times the upper limit of normal were commoner on tofacitinib.
cards.source: Gladman D et al. Tofacitinib for Psoriatic Arthritis in Patients with an Inadequate Response to TNF Inhibitors. N Engl J Med. 2017. PMID: 29045207. Registry ID: NCT01882439. cards.headline: Gladman 2024: switching directly from adalimumab to tofacitinib maintained efficacy in the OPAL Balance extension
cards.summary: Gladman 2024: switching directly from adalimumab to tofacitinib maintained efficacy in the OPAL Balance extension
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of an open-label long-term extension study (Gladman 2024)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of 180 patients with psoriatic arthritis who entered the open-label OPAL Balance extension after OPAL Broaden: 91 switched directly from adalimumab to tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily and 89 continued tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily.
cards.result: Efficacy in the phase 3 study was similar between the groups and was maintained to month 3 or 6 of the extension across ACR responses, PASI75, HAQ disability response, disease activity and minimal disease activity measures. Treatment-emergent adverse events, serious adverse events and serious infections were generally similar between groups and across the two studies, supporting direct switching from adalimumab to tofacitinib without a washout period. The abstract reports this comparison qualitatively, without printing the group response rates.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc, open-label and without a control group; the switch group was younger with less active disease at baseline, and no numeric response rates are printed in the abstract.
cards.source: Gladman D et al. Efficacy and safety of tofacitinib in an open-label, long-term extension study in patients with psoriatic arthritis who received adalimumab or tofacitinib in a Phase 3 randomized controlled study: a post hoc analysis. Arthritis Res Ther. 2024. PMID: 39702318. Registry ID: NCT01877668; NCT01976364. cards.summary: Synthesis: tofacitinib beats placebo in both DMARD- and TNF-inhibitor-inadequate responders - LIKELY

shelves.title: Non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis: certolizumab, secukinumab, ixekizumab and upadacitinib all beat placebo — ASAS40 gains of about 12–23 percentage points across the phase 3 trials
shelves.question: In adults with active non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis who have not responded to NSAIDs, do TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors or a JAK inhibitor improve disease activity versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antirheumatic Agents · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Spondylarthropathies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (nr-axSpA) treatment beyond the adalimumab trial homed on Shelf #4780 (ABILITY-1, PMID: 22772328) and the radiographic-disease shelf #680. Four placebo-controlled programmes are carded here. Certolizumab (RAPID-axSpA, PMID: 24013647, NCT01087762): ASAS20 at week 12 of 57.7% and 63.6% versus 38.3% on placebo in the whole axSpA population, with similar effects in the nr-axSpA subpopulation. Secukinumab (PREVENT, PMID: 32770640, NCT02696031): ASAS40 in TNFi-naive patients 41.5% versus 29.2% at week 16 and 39.8% versus 19.9% at week 52. Ixekizumab (COAST-X, PMID: 31813637, NCT02757352): ASAS40 35–40% versus 19% at week 16, sustained at week 52 (30–31% vs 13%). Upadacitinib (SELECT-AXIS 2, PMID: 38747163, NCT04169373): ASAS40 63% versus 43% at week 52. Every class clears its placebo bar; no head-to-head or structural-progression data are carded. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: Landewé 2014 (RAPID-axSpA): certolizumab ASAS20 at week 12 was 57.7% (200 mg Q2W) and 63.6% (400 mg Q4W) versus 38.3% on placebo
cards.summary: Landewé 2014 (RAPID-axSpA): certolizumab ASAS20 at week 12 was 57.7% (200 mg Q2W) and 63.6% (400 mg Q4W) versus 38.3% on placebo
cards.people: 325 patients with active axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis and non-radiographic axSpA subpopulations) randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, certolizumab pegol 200 mg every 2 weeks or 400 mg every 4 weeks; primary endpoint ASAS20 at week 12.
cards.result: At week 12, ASAS20 response was 57.7% on certolizumab 200 mg Q2W and 63.6% on 400 mg Q4W versus 38.3% on placebo (p≤0.004). At week 24, combined certolizumab arms beat placebo on change in BASFI (−2.28 vs −0.40), BASDAI (−3.05 vs −1.05) and BASMI (−0.52 vs −0.07), all p<0.001. Similar improvements were reported in both the AS and nr-axSpA subpopulations. Adverse events 70.4% vs 62.6%; serious adverse events 4.7% vs 4.7%.
cards.watchOut: The headline endpoint is for the whole axSpA population; the abstract reports similar effects in the nr-axSpA subpopulation without printing separate nr-axSpA response rates.
cards.source: Landewé R et al. Efficacy of certolizumab pegol on signs and symptoms of axial spondyloarthritis including ankylosing spondylitis: 24-week results of a double-blind randomised placebo-controlled Phase 3 study. Ann Rheum Dis. 2014. PMID: 24013647. Registry ID: NCT01087762. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Deodhar 2021 (PREVENT): secukinumab ASAS40 in TNFi-naive nr-axSpA was 41.5% versus 29.2% on placebo at week 16, and 39.8% versus 19.9% at week 52
cards.summary: Deodhar 2021 (PREVENT): secukinumab ASAS40 in TNFi-naive nr-axSpA was 41.5% versus 29.2% on placebo at week 16, and 39.8% versus 19.9% at week 52
cards.people: 555 patients with active non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis randomised 1:1:1 to subcutaneous secukinumab 150 mg with loading dose, 150 mg without loading dose, or placebo; 481 completed 52 weeks.
cards.result: In TNFi-naive patients, ASAS40 was significantly higher on secukinumab: loading-dose group 41.5% versus placebo 29.2% at week 16, and non-loading-dose group 39.8% versus placebo 19.9% at week 52 (both P<0.05). All secondary endpoints were met at week 16. Switching to open-label treatment between weeks 20 and 48 occurred in 50.8% (loading), 47.3% (non-loading) and 64.0% (placebo). No new safety findings.
cards.watchOut: The week-52 placebo comparison is weakened by permitted switching to open-label secukinumab or standard care after week 20, which was commonest in the placebo group.
cards.source: Deodhar A et al. Improvement of Signs and Symptoms of Nonradiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis in Patients Treated With Secukinumab: Primary Results of a Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Phase III Study. Arthritis Rheumatol. 2021. PMID: 32770640. Registry ID: NCT02696031. cards.summary: Deodhar 2020 (COAST-X): ixekizumab ASAS40 at week 16 was 35% (Q4W) and 40% (Q2W) versus 19% on placebo in nr-axSpA

cards.result: ASAS40 at week 16: ixekizumab Q4W 34/96 (35%, p=0.0094 vs placebo), Q2W 41/102 (40%, p=0.0016), placebo 20/105 (19%). ASAS40 at week 52: Q4W 29/96 (30%, p=0.0045), Q2W 32/102 (31%, p=0.0037), placebo 14/105 (13%). Both primary endpoints were met.

cards.headline: Van den Bosch 2024 (SELECT-AXIS 2, 1-year): upadacitinib ASAS40 at week 52 was 63% versus 43% on placebo in nr-axSpA
cards.summary: Van den Bosch 2024 (SELECT-AXIS 2, 1-year): upadacitinib ASAS40 at week 52 was 63% versus 43% on placebo in nr-axSpA
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial, 1-year report (Van den Bosch 2024)
cards.people: 314 patients aged ≥18 years with nr-axSpA fulfilling ASAS classification criteria on stable background therapy, randomised to upadacitinib 15 mg once daily or placebo for a 52-week double-blind period; 259 (129 upadacitinib, 130 placebo) completed 52 weeks.
cards.result: At week 52, ASAS40 was achieved by 63% on upadacitinib versus 43% on placebo (NRI-MI; nominal P<0.001), and ASDAS inactive disease by 33% versus 11% (nominal P<0.001). Greater improvements were also seen in disease activity, inflammation, pain, function, enthesitis and quality of life. No opportunistic infections, malignancies, major adverse cardiovascular events, venous thromboembolism, inflammatory bowel disease or deaths were reported on upadacitinib through 1 year.
cards.watchOut: The week-52 p-values are nominal, and about a third of participants had previously had an inadequate response to a biologic, so this is a mixed biologic-naive and biologic-experienced population.
cards.source: Van den Bosch F et al. Upadacitinib in Active Non-radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis: 1-Year Data From a Double-Blind, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Phase 3 Trial. ACR Open Rheumatol. 2024. PMID: 38747163. Registry ID: NCT04169373. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: four drug classes beat placebo in nr-axSpA, with ASAS40 gains of roughly 12–23 percentage points — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: four drug classes beat placebo in nr-axSpA, with ASAS40 gains of roughly 12–23 percentage points — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: RAPID-axSpA (325 patients, certolizumab), PREVENT (555, secukinumab), COAST-X (303, ixekizumab) and SELECT-AXIS 2 (314, upadacitinib).
cards.result: Across mechanisms, active treatment separated from placebo on response composites: ASAS20 57.7–63.6% vs 38.3% (certolizumab, week 12); ASAS40 41.5% vs 29.2% at week 16 and 39.8% vs 19.9% at week 52 (secukinumab); ASAS40 35–40% vs 19% at week 16 (ixekizumab); ASAS40 63% vs 43% at week 52 (upadacitinib). Adalimumab in nr-axSpA (ABILITY-1) is homed on Shelf #4780 and radiographic-disease IL-17/JAK evidence on Shelf #680; neither is re-carded here. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).

shelves.title: Axial spondyloarthritis after TNF failure: switching to an IL-17 inhibitor was NOT better than a second TNF inhibitor in the one randomised trial (ASAS40 15.2% vs 14.5%) — except possibly after primary non-response
shelves.question: In axial spondyloarthritis with an inadequate response to a first TNF inhibitor, does switching to an IL-17 inhibitor outperform cycling to a second TNF inhibitor — and which class should come first?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: The sequencing question has one randomised trial. ROC-SpA (NCT03445845; results reported as a 2025 congress abstract): 300 TNF-inadequate responders randomised to an IL-17 inhibitor or a second TNF inhibitor; ASAS40 at week 24 was 15.2% versus 14.5% (adjusted OR for non-response 0.96, 95% CI 0.68–1.34) — no superiority. Observational data point the same way overall: a Korean nationwide cohort of 1,660 switchers (PMID: 41743540) found similar persistence, except after primary TNF failure, where a second TNF inhibitor was discontinued more (adjusted HR 1.54–2.11); the CorEvitas registry axSpA cohort found similar or numerically better outcomes for switchers. For first-biologic choice, a network meta-analysis in nr-axSpA (Li 2025, DOI: 10.1159/000542744) ranked TNF inhibitors above IL-17 and JAK inhibitors on ASAS40. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (the two sequencing strategies made no difference overall, with a possible switch advantage after primary failure).

cards.headline: ROC-SpA 2025: after a first TNF inhibitor fails, ASAS40 at week 24 was 15.2% on an IL-17 inhibitor versus 14.5% on a second TNF inhibitor — no superiority
cards.summary: ROC-SpA 2025: after a first TNF inhibitor fails, ASAS40 at week 24 was 15.2% on an IL-17 inhibitor versus 14.5% on a second TNF inhibitor — no superiority
cards.type: Prospective randomised open-label phase 4 trial, congress-abstract report (ROC-SpA 2025)
cards.people: 300 adults with active axial spondyloarthritis (BASDAI >4 or ASDAS >3.5) and an inadequate 3-month response to a first TNF inhibitor, at 31 centres in France and Monaco, randomised open-label to an IL-17 inhibitor (n=158; secukinumab 77.6%, ixekizumab 22.4%) or a second TNF inhibitor (n=142).
cards.result: ASAS40 response at week 24 was 15.2% with the IL-17 inhibitor and 14.5% with the second TNF inhibitor; the adjusted odds ratio for ASAS40 non-response was 0.96 (95% CI 0.68–1.34). Mean ASDAS fell from 3.2 to 2.5 in both groups. No significant differences in ASAS20/40, partial remission or ASDAS-CRP at weeks 12–52. On-treatment maintenance at week 54 was 62.8% (IL-17 inhibitor) versus 54.9% (second TNF inhibitor). Non-significant trends favoured the IL-17 inhibitor after primary non-response, with cutaneous psoriasis, HLA-B27 negativity or CRP <5 mg/L, and favoured a second TNF inhibitor when the first was stopped for an adverse event.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the results are available only as a congress abstract this session; absolute ASAS40 rates (~15%) are far lower than in the placebo-controlled licensing trials, reflecting a TNF-inadequate-responder population.
cards.source: Dalix E, Marotte H et al. [Rotation or Change of Biologic After TNF blocker treatment failure for axial Spondyloarthritis — ROC-SpA results, conference abstract; bracketed descriptive title, as the results are published as a congress abstract (Arthritis Rheumatol. 2025; 77 (suppl 9)), not a full journal article]. 2025. cards.headline: Korean nationwide cohort 2026: overall persistence on a second-line IL-17 inhibitor versus TNF inhibitor was similar, but after primary TNF failure the TNF-inhibitor group stopped treatment more (adjusted HR 1.54–2.11)
cards.summary: Korean nationwide cohort 2026: overall persistence on a second-line IL-17 inhibitor versus TNF inhibitor was similar, but after primary TNF failure the TNF-inhibitor group stopped treatment more (adjusted HR 1.54–2.11)
cards.people: 1,660 patients with axial spondyloarthritis in the Korean National Health Insurance Service database (2010–2023) who started a TNF inhibitor first-line and then received an IL-17 inhibitor (n=375) or a second TNF inhibitor (n=1,285) as second-line therapy; primary outcome was discontinuation of the second-line drug within 1 year.
cards.result: Overall treatment persistence and discontinuation risk were similar between the IL-17 inhibitor and TNF inhibitor groups. In patients whose first TNF inhibitor had failed primarily (insufficient effect), discontinuation risk was significantly higher with a second TNF inhibitor than with an IL-17 inhibitor, with adjusted hazard ratios ranging from 1.54 (95% CI 1.14–2.07) to 2.11 (95% CI 1.13–3.94) across analytic approaches.
cards.watchOut: Persistence is a proxy outcome, not symptom response; residual confounding by indication is likely despite adjustment, and the primary-failure subgroup finding is hypothesis-generating.

cards.headline: CorEvitas registry: in axSpA, switching to an IL-17A inhibitor gave similar or numerically better 6-month outcomes than cycling to a second TNF inhibitor
cards.summary: CorEvitas registry: in axSpA, switching to an IL-17A inhibitor gave similar or numerically better 6-month outcomes than cycling to a second TNF inhibitor
cards.type: Registry cohort study with inverse-probability weighting (2026)
cards.people: Registry patients with axial spondyloarthritis who discontinued a first TNF inhibitor: 119 cycled to a second TNF inhibitor and 53 switched to an IL-17A inhibitor (a parallel psoriatic arthritis cohort is not carded here); outcomes at 6 months, analysed before and after inverse-probability weighting.
cards.result: Before weighting, switchers improved more on BASDAI (change-from-baseline difference −0.7, 95% CI −1.2 to −0.2). After weighting, switchers showed a significantly greater improvement in patient fatigue (−9.4, 95% CI −15.8 to −3.1, p=0.004) and numerically greater improvements across the remaining secondary outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Small axSpA switcher group (n=53) and an observational design: the comparison is vulnerable to channelling of harder-to-treat patients to a new mechanism.

cards.headline: Li 2025 network meta-analysis (nr-axSpA): TNF inhibitors ranked above IL-17 and JAK inhibitors for ASAS40, with certolizumab regimens at the top and secukinumab regimens just above placebo
cards.summary: Li 2025 network meta-analysis (nr-axSpA): TNF inhibitors ranked above IL-17 and JAK inhibitors for ASAS40, with certolizumab regimens at the top and secukinumab regimens just above placebo
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of RCTs (Li 2025)
cards.people: Systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised trials in non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis published to June 2023, comparing 12 interventions (TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, JAK inhibitors) on ASAS40, ASAS20 and adverse events.
cards.result: For ASAS40, interventions ranked: certolizumab 200 mg Q2W > certolizumab 400 mg Q4W > golimumab > bimekizumab > adalimumab > upadacitinib > etanercept > brodalumab > ixekizumab > secukinumab 150 mg (no loading) > secukinumab 150 mg (loading) > placebo. The authors concluded that most TNF inhibitors may be more effective than JAK and IL-17 inhibitors, that all were well tolerated, and that larger, longer studies are still needed.
cards.watchOut: Rankings come from indirect comparisons across trials with different populations and placebo response rates; a higher rank is not evidence of superiority in a head-to-head test.
cards.source: Li D et al. Efficacy and Safety of Tumor Necrosis Factor Inhibitors, Interleukin-17 Inhibitors, and Janus Kinase Inhibitors in Patients with Non-Radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis. Int Arch Allergy Immunol. 2025. PMID: not captured this session. DOI: 10.1159/000542744. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: after a first TNF inhibitor, switching class and cycling within class perform about the same — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: after a first TNF inhibitor, switching class and cycling within class perform about the same — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ROC-SpA (300 randomised patients), the Korean nationwide cohort (1,660 patients), the CorEvitas registry axSpA cohort (172 patients) and the Li 2025 nr-axSpA network meta-analysis.
cards.result: The only randomised sequencing trial found no superiority for switching to an IL-17 inhibitor over a second TNF inhibitor (ASAS40 15.2% vs 14.5% at week 24). Registry data agree on overall equivalence, with a consistent signal that patients whose first TNF inhibitor never worked (primary failure) may do better changing mechanism — higher discontinuation on a second TNF inhibitor (adjusted HR 1.54–2.11) — while indirect rankings in biologic-naive nr-axSpA favour TNF inhibitors as a first biologic class. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (no difference between switch and cycle overall · possible advantage to switching class after primary TNF failure).
cards.watchOut: Sequencing evidence is one open-label trial reported as an abstract plus observational data; comorbidity-driven choices (psoriasis, uveitis, inflammatory bowel disease) are not tested by any card here.
cards.source: Synthesis of ROC-SpA 2025 (Registry ID: NCT03445845), the Korean nationwide cohort 2026 (PMID: 41743540), the CorEvitas registry analysis 2026 (DOI: 10.1007/s12325-026-03531-5) and Li et al. 2025 (DOI: 10.1159/000542744).

shelves.title: Hip osteoarthritis: one triamcinolone injection eased pain versus advice alone (−1.43 points over 6 months) but not versus a plain lidocaine injection, pooled placebo data are null, and PRP matched saline
shelves.question: In adults with hip osteoarthritis, do intra-articular corticosteroid or platelet-rich plasma injections reduce pain compared with advice, local anaesthetic or placebo?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Hip-specific treatment evidence (exercise for knee and hip OA is homed on Shelf #683). The HIT trial (Paskins 2022, ISRCTN50550256) found one ultrasound-guided triamcinolone injection added to advice and education improved pain over 6 months by −1.43 points versus advice alone, but by only −0.52 (not significant) versus a lidocaine-only injection, and the 2025 meta-analysis (PMID: 40375257) found no statistically significant corticosteroid benefit over placebo. Kullenberg 2004 (PMID: 15517641) found fluoroscopic triamcinolone beat local anaesthetic at 3 weeks. Platelet-rich plasma was no better than saline in a 60-patient double-blind trial (PMID: 38948640). Proposed stamp: SPLIT.

cards.headline: Paskins 2022 (HIT trial): adding one ultrasound-guided triamcinolone hip injection to advice and education cut average pain by 1.43 points more over 6 months — but beat lidocaine-only injection by only 0.52, not significantly
cards.summary: Paskins 2022 (HIT trial): adding one ultrasound-guided triamcinolone hip injection to advice and education cut average pain by 1.43 points more over 6 months — but beat lidocaine-only injection by only 0.52, not significantly
cards.type: Pragmatic three-arm single-blind randomised controlled trial (Paskins 2022)
cards.people: 199 adults aged ≥40 years with hip osteoarthritis and at least moderate pain in two English community musculoskeletal services: 67 advice and education (best current treatment, BCT), 66 BCT plus ultrasound-guided triamcinolone 40 mg with lidocaine, 66 BCT plus lidocaine only; mean age 62.8 years, 57% women; primary outcome hip pain intensity (0–10) over 6 months.
cards.result: Mean improvement in pain over 6 months was greater with BCT plus triamcinolone-lidocaine than with BCT alone: mean difference −1.43 (95% CI −2.15 to −0.72, P<0.001; standardised mean difference −0.55). Against BCT plus lidocaine alone the difference was −0.52 (95% CI −1.21 to 0.18), not significant. Ultrasound-confirmed synovitis or effusion strengthened the triamcinolone effect (interaction −1.70, 95% CI −3.10 to −0.30). One participant with a bioprosthetic aortic valve died from subacute bacterial endocarditis 4 months after injection, deemed possibly related.
cards.watchOut: The comparison against BCT alone was unblinded (no sham injection), so part of the −1.43 difference may be contextual; the blinded-relevant contrast, against lidocaine injection, was not significant.
cards.source: Paskins Z et al. Clinical effectiveness of one ultrasound guided intra-articular corticosteroid and local anaesthetic injection in addition to advice and education for hip osteoarthritis (HIT trial): single blind, parallel group, three arm, randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2022. PMID: not captured this session. DOI: 10.1136/bmj-2021-068446. Registry ID: ISRCTN50550256. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Kullenberg 2004: fluoroscopic triamcinolone 80 mg significantly reduced hip OA pain at 3 weeks where local anaesthetic alone did not
cards.summary: Kullenberg 2004: fluoroscopic triamcinolone 80 mg significantly reduced hip OA pain at 3 weeks where local anaesthetic alone did not
cards.people: 80 patients with hip osteoarthritis and pain at rest and on weight-bearing for more than 4 weeks, randomised to intra-articular corticosteroid (80 mg triamcinolone acetonide, n=40) or local anaesthetic (1% mepivacaine, n=40) under fluoroscopy; outcomes at 3 weeks (and 12 weeks).
cards.result: Pain in all modalities decreased after corticosteroid injection, most at rest, with significant pain reduction at the 3-week (and 12-week) follow-up; joint range of motion increased significantly in all directions and functional ability improved significantly. No significant pain relief or functional improvement occurred with local anaesthetic alone. The abstract reports significance without printing the group mean pain scores.
cards.watchOut: Small, old and short: 80 patients, 3-week primary follow-up, and no printed effect sizes in the abstract — it supports direction, not magnitude.

cards.headline: Platelet-rich plasma vs saline 2024: PRP showed no advantage over a saline placebo injection in hip osteoarthritis over 6 months (n=60)
cards.summary: Platelet-rich plasma vs saline 2024: PRP showed no advantage over a saline placebo injection in hip osteoarthritis over 6 months (n=60)
cards.people: 60 patients (29 men, 31 women; mean age 57.9 years) with Kellgren–Lawrence grade 2/3 hip osteoarthritis randomised double-blind to intra-articular platelet-rich plasma (n=30) or saline placebo (n=30).
cards.result: PRP showed no advantage over saline on VAS pain during activity; both groups improved significantly on activity VAS at 1 and 6 months. The placebo group improved on resting VAS while the PRP group did not, neither group improved on WOMAC-total, and most SF-36 domains did not improve in either group. The authors concluded PRP shows no significant difference from saline placebo on pain, function or quality of life over 6 months.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre 60-patient trial; it rules out a large PRP effect but cannot exclude a small one, and PRP preparations vary between studies.

cards.headline: Hip injection meta-analysis 2025: pooled corticosteroid injections did NOT significantly beat placebo or hyaluronic acid on WOMAC pain
cards.summary: Hip injection meta-analysis 2025: pooled corticosteroid injections did NOT significantly beat placebo or hyaluronic acid on WOMAC pain
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (2025)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of intra-articular injections for symptomatic hip osteoarthritis (PROSPERO CRD42024526221), comparing corticosteroids with placebo and with hyaluronic acid on WOMAC and VAS outcomes.
cards.result: Corticosteroid versus placebo on WOMAC pain at 2 months reached only p=0.05, and WOMAC stiffness and function p=0.05 and p=0.08 — all statistically non-significant; corticosteroid versus hyaluronic acid on overall WOMAC at 6 months gave p=0.46. The authors concluded intra-articular corticosteroids do not provide statistically significant symptomatic improvement over placebo in hip OA, despite individual trials reporting improvements.
cards.watchOut: The pooled null sits in tension with the positive HIT trial; the meta-analysis pools older, smaller, variably guided injections, and borderline p-values (0.05) mean the honest reading is 'unproven against placebo', not 'proven useless'.
cards.source: [Authors not captured from the record this session]. Pain management of hip osteoarthritis with corticosteroids vs injection therapies: a systematic review and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: hip steroid injection helps against advice alone but is unproven against a placebo injection; PRP made no difference — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: hip steroid injection helps against advice alone but is unproven against a placebo injection; PRP made no difference — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: HIT (199 patients), Kullenberg 2004 (80 patients), the PRP-versus-saline trial (60 patients) and the 2025 hip-injection meta-analysis.
cards.result: A single triamcinolone injection added to advice and education improved pain over 6 months (−1.43 points vs advice alone), but the advantage over a lidocaine-only injection was small and non-significant (−0.52), and pooled placebo-controlled data show no significant corticosteroid benefit. PRP was indistinguishable from saline. Exercise therapy for hip OA is homed on Shelf #683 and is not re-carded here. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (POSSIBLE short-term benefit of steroid injection · no proven benefit over placebo injection · PRP: the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: No card here addresses total hip replacement timing or outcomes; this shelf covers non-operative injection treatment only.
cards.source: Synthesis of Paskins et al. 2022 (DOI: 10.1136/bmj-2021-068446), Kullenberg et al. 2004 (PMID: 15517641), the PRP-versus-placebo trial 2024 (PMID: 38948640) and the hip-injection meta-analysis 2025 (PMID: 40375257). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.
