shelves.title: Hand osteoarthritis: exercises improved function and grip, a splint added nothing to good self-management at 8 weeks (OTTER II, 349 patients) — but a custom night splint worn for a year cut pain by 14.3 mm
shelves.question: In adults with hand osteoarthritis, do thumb splints/orthoses and hand exercise programmes reduce pain and improve function?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Non-drug treatment of hand osteoarthritis; the drug shelves are already homed (methotrexate/hydroxychloroquine #2014, topical diclofenac #2567, prednisolone #3720, denosumab #3760) and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. OTTER II (Adams 2021, ISRCTN54744256; 349 patients) found adding a verum or placebo thumb splint to a supported self-management programme made no difference at 8 weeks (−0.5, 95% CI −1.4 to 0.4). Rannou 2009 (112 patients) found a custom night splint useless at 1 month but better by 14.3 mm at 12 months. Exercise trials were positive: Hennig 2015 (PMID: 24667900) improved activity performance (responders 16 vs 2) and Stamm 2018 (PMID: 30413191) improved grip strength. Proposed stamp: SPLIT.

cards.headline: Adams 2021 (OTTER II): adding a thumb splint to a self-management programme made no difference — AUSCAN pain difference −0.5 (95% CI −1.4 to 0.4) at 8 weeks
cards.summary: Adams 2021 (OTTER II): adding a thumb splint to a self-management programme made no difference — AUSCAN pain difference −0.5 (95% CI −1.4 to 0.4) at 8 weeks
cards.type: Pragmatic multicentre three-arm randomised controlled trial with placebo splint (Adams 2021)
cards.people: 349 adults with symptomatic basal thumb joint osteoarthritis and at least moderate pain and dysfunction at 17 NHS hospital departments, randomised 1:1:1 to therapist-supported self-management (SSM, n=116), SSM plus a verum thumb splint (n=116) or SSM plus a placebo thumb splint (n=117); 292 (84%) provided the 8-week primary outcome.
cards.result: All groups improved, with no mean treatment difference: SSM plus splint versus SSM −0.5 (95% CI −1.4 to 0.4, P=0.255); SSM plus placebo splint versus SSM −0.1 (95% CI −1.0 to 0.8, P=0.829); verum versus placebo splint −0.4 (95% CI −1.4 to 0.5, P=0.378). Twelve-week costs were £586 (SSM), £738 (SSM plus splint) and £685 (SSM plus placebo splint). The authors concluded there was no additional benefit from adding a thumb splint to a high-quality self-management programme.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up was only 12 weeks and most splints were prefabricated neoprene; the trial does not test long-term night splinting of the kind that was positive in Rannou 2009.
cards.source: Adams J et al. The clinical and cost effectiveness of splints for thumb base osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled clinical trial. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2021. PMID: not captured this session. Registry ID: ISRCTN54744256. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Rannou 2009: a custom night splint for thumb-base OA did nothing at 1 month but cut pain by 14.3 mm more than usual care at 12 months
cards.summary: Rannou 2009: a custom night splint for thumb-base OA did nothing at 1 month but cut pain by 14.3 mm more than usual care at 12 months
cards.people: 112 patients (101 women) with base-of-thumb osteoarthritis at two French tertiary hospitals, randomised to a custom-made neoprene night splint (n=57) or usual care (n=55); 98 (87%) completed the study; 86% of the splint group wore it more than 5 nights a week at 12 months.
cards.result: At 1 month, pain change did not differ (adjusted mean change −10.1 vs −10.7 mm; between-group difference 0.6, 95% CI −7.9 to 9.1; P=0.89). At 12 months, pain fell more with the splint (adjusted mean change −22.2 vs −7.9 mm; difference −14.3, 95% CI −23.4 to −5.2; P=0.002), and disability scores also improved more (Cochin difference 6 points in the summarised report). No adverse effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded with self-reported outcomes and a usual-care comparator, so expectation effects could inflate the late benefit; the 12-month horizon is exactly what OTTER II lacked.
cards.source: Rannou F et al. Splint for base-of-thumb osteoarthritis: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2009. PMID: not captured this session. DOI: 10.7326/0003-4819-150-10-200905190-00003. Registry ID: NCT00350896. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Hennig 2015: home hand exercises improved activity performance in women with hand OA — 16 of 40 responders versus 2 of 40 on information alone
cards.summary: Hennig 2015: home hand exercises improved activity performance in women with hand OA — 16 of 40 responders versus 2 of 40 on information alone
cards.people: 80 women with hand osteoarthritis (mean age 60.8 years) randomised to information plus a home-based hand exercise programme (n=40) or information only (n=40); follow-up 89% (n=71); primary outcome Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS).
cards.result: The adjusted mean difference favoured exercise by 1.4 points on the PSFS (95% CI 0.6 to 2.2; effect size 1.0). Thirteen exercise-group patients versus three controls reached the minimal clinically important difference of 2.2 points, and 16 versus 2 fulfilled OMERACT-OARSI response criteria (p<0.001). Grip strength, thumb web space, fatigue, joint pain and activity-performance scores also improved significantly. Exercises were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Women only, unblinded, and a patient-specific primary outcome chosen by participants; effects on standardised pain scales were secondary.
cards.source: Hennig T et al. Effect of home-based hand exercises in women with hand osteoarthritis: a randomised controlled trial. Ann Rheum Dis. 2015. PMID: 24667900. Registry ID: ISRTCN79019063 (as printed in the record). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Stamm 2018: one combined functional-consultation and exercise session improved grip strength at 8 weeks in hand OA (+0.03 vs −0.03 bar, p=0.001)
cards.summary: Stamm 2018: one combined functional-consultation and exercise session improved grip strength at 8 weeks in hand OA (+0.03 vs −0.03 bar, p=0.001)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with blinded assessor (Stamm 2018)
cards.people: 151 patients with hand osteoarthritis randomised to a one-session interdisciplinary intervention (functioning, activities of daily living, physical activity, nutrition, assistive devices, pain management and exercise instruction; n=74) or routine care plus placebo (n=77); 2-month follow-up attendance 84% (n=128); primary outcome grip strength.
cards.result: Grip strength increased in the intervention group and decreased in controls (dominant hand mean +0.03 bar [SD 0.11] versus −0.03 [SD 0.13], p=0.001, baseline-corrected). Self-reported satisfaction with treatment also improved significantly; pain and AUSCAN outcomes are reported as secondary in the abstract without a significant headline difference.
cards.watchOut: A single-session, multi-component intervention: the grip gain cannot be attributed to exercise alone, and 8 weeks is short.
cards.source: Stamm TA et al. Functional consultation and exercises improve grip strength in osteoarthritis of the hand – a randomised controlled trial. Arthritis Res Ther. 2018. PMID: 30413191. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Silva 2008: a functional splint worn during daily activities reduced trapeziometacarpal OA pain from 45 days, without changing strength or dexterity
cards.summary: Silva 2008: a functional splint worn during daily activities reduced trapeziometacarpal OA pain from 45 days, without changing strength or dexterity
cards.people: 40 patients with painful trapeziometacarpal (thumb-base) osteoarthritis of the dominant hand randomised to use a functional splint during activities of daily living for 180 days, or to use it only during evaluations for the first 90 days and during activities for the following 90 days.
cards.result: Pain without the splint differed significantly between groups over time: the immediate-use group improved from the first (45-day) evaluation, while the delayed group improved only at the end of the study, after 90 days of splint use. The authors concluded splint use during daily activities reduces pain but does not alter function, grip strength, pinch strength or dexterity. The abstract reports the pattern without printing group pain scores.
cards.watchOut: Only 40 patients, a delayed-start rather than no-treatment control, and no printed effect sizes — supportive, not decisive.
cards.source: Silva P et al. Assessment of the effectiveness of a functional splint for osteoarthritis of the trapeziometacarpal joint on the dominant hand: a randomized controlled study. cards.headline: Synthesis: exercises help function and grip; splints help only with long, adherent use and add nothing to good self-management at 8 weeks — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: exercises help function and grip; splints help only with long, adherent use and add nothing to good self-management at 8 weeks — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: OTTER II (349 patients), Rannou 2009 (112), Hennig 2015 (80), Stamm 2018 (151) and Silva 2008 (40). Drug treatment of hand OA is homed elsewhere (methotrexate/hydroxychloroquine Shelf #2014, topical diclofenac #2567, prednisolone #3720, denosumab #3760) and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Exercise-based care improved activity performance (PSFS +1.4 points; responders 16 vs 2) and grip strength (+0.03 vs −0.03 bar). Splinting split by context: no added benefit over 8–12 weeks when layered on a strong self-management programme (OTTER II, −0.5 points, NS) or at 1 month (Rannou), but a 14.3 mm pain advantage at 12 months with a custom night splint worn >5 nights a week, and earlier pain relief with daytime functional splinting in a small delayed-start trial. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (exercise: POSSIBLE benefit · splint added to self-management: the treatment made no difference at 8 weeks · long-term night splint: POSSIBLE benefit).
cards.watchOut: Almost all splint evidence is for thumb-base (trapeziometacarpal) disease; finger-joint hand OA splinting is essentially untested in these cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Adams et al. 2021 (ISRCTN54744256), Rannou et al. 2009 (DOI: 10.7326/0003-4819-150-10-200905190-00003), Hennig et al. 2015 (PMID: 24667900), Stamm et al. 2018 (PMID: 30413191) and Silva et al. 2008 (PMID: 20544159).

shelves.title: CPPD (pseudogout): colchicine and prednisone were equivalent in the first head-to-head trial (pain −36 vs −38 mm at 24 h, 111 patients); anakinra helped 76% in uncontrolled series
shelves.question: In older adults with an acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis flare, how do colchicine, prednisone and anakinra compare for pain relief and safety?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Treatment of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, scoped to the acute flare and IL-1 blockade; colchicine prophylaxis is homed on Shelf #2713 and methotrexate on Shelf #2723 and is not re-carded. COLCHICORT (Pascart 2023, NCT03128905; 111 patients, median age 88) showed low-dose colchicine and prednisone 30 mg are equivalent at 24 hours (pain −36 vs −38 mm; difference −1 mm, 95% CI −12 to 10; ~65% responders each). Anakinra rests on a 15-patient double-blind pilot versus prednisone (Dumusc 2021), a meta-analysis of mostly uncontrolled series (PMID: 41206733; 84 patients, 76% response) and a 292-patient mixed-crystal cohort (PMID: 41926750; 92.8% judged effective, 4.5% infection). Proposed stamp: SPLIT.

cards.headline: Pascart 2023 (COLCHICORT): low-dose colchicine and prednisone were equivalent for acute CPP crystal arthritis — pain fell 36 mm versus 38 mm at 24 hours
cards.summary: Pascart 2023 (COLCHICORT): low-dose colchicine and prednisone were equivalent for acute CPP crystal arthritis — pain fell 36 mm versus 38 mm at 24 hours
cards.people: 111 hospitalised patients aged ≥65 years (per-protocol 95; median age 88 years, 73% women) with acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis of <36 hours' duration at six French hospitals, randomised to colchicine 1.5 mg on day 1 and 1 mg on day 2 (n=57) or prednisone 30 mg on days 1 and 2 (n=54); baseline pain VAS 68 mm (SD 17); knee affected in 48%.
cards.result: Change in pain VAS at 24 hours was −36 mm (SD 32) on colchicine and −38 mm (SD 23) on prednisone; the between-group difference was −1 mm (95% CI −12 to 10), within the ±13 mm equivalence margin. About 65% of each group were responders. Adverse events occurred in about a third of each group: diarrhoea predominated with colchicine, and raised blood pressure, insomnia, delirium and hyperglycaemia with prednisone; two deaths in the prednisone group were deemed unrelated.
cards.watchOut: No placebo group and open-label: equivalence of two active drugs in a self-limiting flare cannot show how much either beats natural history; only 39% of cases were crystal-proven in the companion report.
cards.source: Pascart T et al. Evaluating the safety and short-term equivalence of colchicine versus prednisone in older patients with acute calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis (COLCHICORT): an open-label, multicentre, randomised trial. cards.headline: Dumusc 2021: in a 15-patient double-blind pilot, anakinra and prednisone both gave rapid pain relief in acute CPPD crystal arthritis (n=15 on the face)
cards.summary: Dumusc 2021: in a 15-patient double-blind pilot, anakinra and prednisone both gave rapid pain relief in acute CPPD crystal arthritis (n=15 on the face)
cards.people: 15 patients with acute calcium pyrophosphate deposition crystal arthritis randomised double-blind to anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) or prednisone in a single-centre pilot study.
cards.result: The pilot recruited only 15 patients and indicated that both drugs provided rapid pain relief; the fetched record reports no comparative effect size, and the trial was not powered to distinguish the treatments.
cards.watchOut: With 15 patients this is a feasibility signal only; it cannot support an efficacy claim for anakinra on its own.

cards.headline: Anakinra meta-analysis 2026: across 84 patients, 76% responded to anakinra for an acute CPPD flare and pain scores fell by 48 mm
cards.summary: Anakinra meta-analysis 2026: across 84 patients, 76% responded to anakinra for an acute CPPD flare and pain scores fell by 48 mm
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, mostly observational studies (2026)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of six studies (five observational, one randomised trial) of anakinra for acute calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease flare, totalling 84 patients; primary outcome a positive treatment response at day 3–5.
cards.result: The pooled positive treatment response rate was 76% (95% CI 61–86, I²=0%). Pain VAS fell by 48.12 mm (95% CI 43.03–53.21) and CRP by 62.09 mg/L (95% CI 26.44–97.74) from baseline; tender and swollen joint counts also fell. Reported adverse reactions included injection-site reaction, rash, bacterial pneumonitis and neutropenia.
cards.watchOut: Five of six studies had no control group, so the 76% response mixes drug effect with the natural resolution of a self-limiting flare; responses were subjective physician assessments.
cards.source: Nakaphan P et al. Efficacy and safety of anakinra for acute calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease flare: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Mod Rheumatol. 2026. PMID: 41206733. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Moriot 2026: anakinra was judged effective in 92.8% of 292 crystal-related flares, with infection in 4.5% within a month
cards.summary: Moriot 2026: anakinra was judged effective in 92.8% of 292 crystal-related flares, with infection in 4.5% within a month
cards.people: 292 adults treated with anakinra for a crystal-related disease flare (gout, calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease and hydroxyapatite disease combined) at a single centre, 2011–2024; treatment failure meant insufficient response requiring escalation or persistent symptoms.
cards.result: Anakinra was effective in 92.8% of patients after a median treatment duration of 3 days. Longer crystal-disease duration (OR 1.11, 95% CI 1.03–1.19) and diabetes (OR 4.00, 95% CI 1.25–14.29) were independently associated with treatment failure. Thirteen patients (4.5%) developed an infection within one month (median delay 11 days); no variable independently predicted infection.
cards.watchOut: Mixed crystal diseases — the 92.8% figure is not CPPD-specific — and there is no comparator group, so effectiveness is judged against the treating team's expectations.
cards.source: Moriot C et al. Factors associated with anakinra effectiveness and risk of infection in crystal-related flares. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2026. PMID: 41926750. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: acute CPPD — colchicine and prednisone are equivalent; anakinra is a plausible rescue on uncontrolled data — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: acute CPPD — colchicine and prednisone are equivalent; anakinra is a plausible rescue on uncontrolled data — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: COLCHICORT (111 randomised patients), the Dumusc pilot (15 patients, n on the face), the anakinra meta-analysis (84 patients) and the Moriot cohort (292 mixed crystal flares). Colchicine prophylaxis is homed on Shelf #2713 and methotrexate on Shelf #2723; neither is re-carded here.
cards.result: For an acute flare, the one adequately sized trial shows low-dose colchicine and 30 mg prednisone are equivalent at 24 hours (−36 vs −38 mm; difference −1 mm, 95% CI −12 to 10), with about 65% responders on each and different harm profiles (diarrhoea vs metabolic/pressor effects). Anakinra's case rests on uncontrolled series (76% pooled response) and one 15-patient pilot. No treatment dissolves the crystals or is proven to prevent flares in this shelf. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (colchicine vs prednisone: the two treatments made no difference to each other · anakinra: POSSIBLE benefit on weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: All acute-flare trials are short (24 hours to a few days) and none is placebo-controlled; chronic CPP inflammatory arthritis treatment remains essentially untested by randomised trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pascart et al. 2023 (DOI: 10.1016/S2665-9913(23)00165-0; NCT03128905), Dumusc et al. 2021 (DOI: 10.1016/j.jbspin.2020.105088), Nakaphan et al. 2026 (PMID: 41206733) and Moriot et al. 2026 (PMID: 41926750).

shelves.title: Spaceflight bone loss: alendronate plus ARED exercise protected spine, hip and pelvis bone density in 7 ISS astronauts — exercise alone left hip trabecular bone unprotected
shelves.question: In astronauts on long-duration spaceflight, does adding a bisphosphonate (alendronate) to resistive exercise prevent the bone mineral density loss, raised bone resorption and urinary calcium of microgravity?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Spaceflight bone loss: the flight evidence is two small NASA/JAXA ISS cohorts. LeBlanc 2013 (PMID: 23334732): 7 astronauts on alendronate 70 mg weekly plus ARED exercise for ~5.5 months showed attenuation of essentially all bone-loss indices. Sibonga 2019 (PMID: 31400472): 10 ARED-only astronauts were only partially protected — hip trabecular bone and resorption markers were not protected — isolating the drug's contribution. A 17-week bed-rest analogue (NASA report; alendronate n=6) concurs mechanistically and is labelled an analogue on its card. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit), capped by n=7 treated flight subjects and no randomisation.

cards.headline: LeBlanc 2013: in 7 ISS astronauts (n=7 on the face), weekly alendronate plus ARED exercise attenuated essentially all indices of spaceflight bone loss over ~5.5 months
cards.summary: LeBlanc 2013: in 7 ISS astronauts (n=7 on the face), weekly alendronate plus ARED exercise attenuated essentially all indices of spaceflight bone loss over ~5.5 months
cards.type: Controlled clinical trial in ISS astronauts (LeBlanc 2013)
cards.people: Seven International Space Station astronauts (n=7) who spent a mean of 5.5 months on the ISS and took oral alendronate 70 mg weekly, starting 3 weeks before flight and continuing throughout the mission, exercising with the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED); compared with earlier crew experience reported in the same paper.
cards.result: The combination of ARED and bisphosphonate attenuated the expected decline in essentially all indices of altered bone physiology during spaceflight, including DXA losses in bone mineral density of spine, hip and pelvis, QCT trabecular and cortical losses in the hip, calculated hip bone strength, elevated bone resorption markers and urinary calcium excretion. ARED alone (in the comparison experience) attenuated bone loss significantly versus the older exercise device, although post-flight decreases in femoral neck and hip remained.
cards.watchOut: Only 7 treated astronauts (n on the face), not randomised, with historical comparison groups; the abstract reports the protection qualitatively rather than as group mean percentage changes.
cards.source: LeBlanc A et al. Bisphosphonates as a supplement to exercise to protect bone during long-duration spaceflight. Osteoporos Int. 2013. PMID: 23334732. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Sibonga 2019: ARED exercise alone only partially protected bone — it did not prevent hip trabecular bone loss or suppress resorption markers, unlike ARED plus alendronate
cards.summary: Sibonga 2019: ARED exercise alone only partially protected bone — it did not prevent hip trabecular bone loss or suppress resorption markers, unlike ARED plus alendronate
cards.type: Clinical trial comparison across ISS astronaut cohorts (Sibonga 2019)
cards.people: 10 additional ISS astronauts who used the ARED without any drug (ARED group), compared with the earlier bisphosphonate-plus-ARED group and a pre-ARED group, using densitometry, biochemical assays and finite-element hip strength models; flight durations did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.result: Combined bisphosphonate plus ARED prevented declines in all DXA and QCT hip measures and finite-element hip strength, increased lumbar spine areal BMD and prevented rises in urinary resorption markers. ARED without alendronate partially attenuated declines in bone mass but did not suppress bone resorption biomarkers or prevent trabecular bone loss: it did not prevent declines in hip trabecular volumetric BMD, though it prevented reductions in femoral neck cortical volumetric BMD, finite-element hip strength for non-linear stance and femoral neck areal BMD. Post-flight bone density was significantly reduced from pre-flight in the pre-ARED group.
cards.watchOut: Small sequential cohorts rather than a randomised comparison; era, diet and exercise adherence differ between groups. The ARED-alone side of this comparison is developed on Shelf #5460.
cards.source: Sibonga J et al. Resistive exercise in astronauts on prolonged spaceflights provides partial protection against spaceflight-induced bone loss. Bone. 2019. PMID: 31400472. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Bed-rest analogue (labelled analogue, not flight data): alendronate blunted the resorption rise of 17 weeks' bed rest — urinary N-telopeptide fell 20% on alendronate versus rising 40–50% in controls
cards.summary: Bed-rest analogue (labelled analogue, not flight data): alendronate blunted the resorption rise of 17 weeks' bed rest — urinary N-telopeptide fell 20% on alendronate versus rising 40–50% in controls
cards.type: Bed-rest analogue study — analogue, not flight data (Smith, NASA report)
cards.people: BED-REST ANALOGUE: healthy volunteers in a 17-week horizontal bed-rest study assigned to alendronate 10 mg/day (n=6), resistive exercise (n=8) or no countermeasure (control, n=8), with a 3-week ambulatory adaptation period; biochemical markers of bone and calcium metabolism.
cards.result: Urinary calcium increased 50% in controls but was unchanged or decreased in both the alendronate and exercise groups. Urinary N-telopeptide (resorption marker) increased 40–50% in control and exercise subjects but decreased 20% in alendronate subjects. Serum calcium changed little, tending to decrease 4–8% in alendronate subjects, while bone formation markers (bone alkaline phosphatase, osteocalcin) rose >65% and >30% with exercise but not with alendronate.
cards.watchOut: An analogue study with 6 alendronate subjects and biochemical endpoints only; it supports the mechanism (resorption suppression) but is not evidence about fractures or flight outcomes.
cards.source: Smith SM et al. [Alendronate and Resistive Exercise Countermeasures Against Bed Rest-Induced Bone Loss: Biochemical Markers of Bone and Calcium Metabolism — bracketed descriptive title; NASA technical report, not a journal article]. cards.headline: Synthesis: alendronate plus ARED exercise protected bone in the small flight cohorts; exercise alone left trabecular bone unprotected — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: alendronate plus ARED exercise protected bone in the small flight cohorts; exercise alone left trabecular bone unprotected — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: LeBlanc 2013 (7 treated ISS astronauts), Sibonga 2019 (10 ARED-only astronauts plus comparison cohorts) and a 17-week bed-rest analogue (22 subjects).
cards.result: In flight, alendronate 70 mg weekly combined with ARED exercise attenuated essentially all measured bone losses, and the head-to-head cohort contrast shows the drug's added value is specifically in trabecular bone and resorption suppression, which exercise alone did not achieve. The bed-rest analogue concurs mechanistically (resorption marker −20% on alendronate vs +40–50% in controls). Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent direction across flight and analogue data, capped by tiny, non-randomised flight cohorts.
cards.watchOut: No astronaut trial is randomised and total treated flight experience is in single figures; long-term bisphosphonate safety in healthy young crew (atypical fracture, jaw osteonecrosis) is untested in this setting.
cards.source: Synthesis of LeBlanc et al. 2013 (PMID: 23334732), Sibonga et al. 2019 (PMID: 31400472) and Smith et al. (NASA technical report, bed-rest analogue).

shelves.title: ARED resistance exercise in space: crews with the heavier device kept hip and pelvis bone density — but still lost 1.7% femoral neck BMD, 5.8% leg strength and 6.1% VO2peak per mission
shelves.question: In astronauts on long-duration spaceflight, how well do ARED resistance-exercise countermeasures protect bone mineral density, muscle strength and aerobic fitness?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Resistance-exercise countermeasures in flight. Smith 2012 (DOI: 10.1002/jbmr.1647): among 13 ISS crewmembers, pelvis and hip BMD were unchanged from pre-flight only in the 5 with ARED access (up to 600 lbf) versus 8 iRED crew (297 lbf). English 2020 Sprint (PMID: 32864428; 26 crew): high-intensity lower-volume training matched the standard programme, but both groups lost femoral neck BMD (−1.7%), knee extensor torque (−5.8%) and VO2peak (−6.1%). Loehr 2011 (PMID: 20473227) is an Earth training analogue showing ARED loads muscle like free weights. The drug-plus-exercise contrast is homed on Shelf #5459. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — partial protection only.

cards.headline: Smith 2012: only ARED crews kept pelvis and hip bone density unchanged over 4–6 month ISS missions — 5 ARED versus 8 iRED crewmembers
cards.summary: Smith 2012: only ARED crews kept pelvis and hip bone density unchanged over 4–6 month ISS missions — 5 ARED versus 8 iRED crewmembers
cards.type: Observational cohort comparison within ISS crews (Smith 2012)
cards.people: 13 ISS crewmembers on missions from 2006 to 2009 (8 with access to the interim Resistive Exercise Device, iRED, maximum load 297 lbf; 5 with access to the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device, ARED, up to 600 lbf), with dietary intake, densitometry and biochemical markers; body mass unchanged in both groups and vitamin D status nominal (75 ± 17 nmol/L) before and during flight.
cards.result: Bone densitometry showed significant time-by-device interactions for pelvis BMD and bone mineral content (p<0.01), femoral neck BMD (p<0.05), trochanter BMD (p<0.05) and total hip BMD (p<0.05). These variables were unchanged from pre-flight only in ARED crewmembers, who also returned with higher percent lean mass and lower percent fat mass. Bone resorption markers rose in both groups during flight and 30 days after landing (p<0.05), while bone-specific alkaline phosphatase rose after landing (p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Five ARED crewmembers, non-randomised and flown later than the iRED group: device, era, nutrition and crew differences are entangled, and resorption rose despite the densitometry protection.

cards.headline: English 2020 (NASA Sprint Study): high-intensity, lower-volume training matched the standard programme — both groups still lost 1.7% femoral neck BMD and 5.8% knee extensor torque
cards.summary: English 2020 (NASA Sprint Study): high-intensity, lower-volume training matched the standard programme — both groups still lost 1.7% femoral neck BMD and 5.8% knee extensor torque
cards.type: Non-randomised programme comparison in ISS crews (English 2020)
cards.people: 26 ISS crewmembers on long-duration spaceflight: 9 performed the high-intensity/lower-volume Sprint programme (resistance 3 days/week plus alternating interval and continuous aerobic work) and 17 the standard daily ISS resistance and aerobic programme; mean ages 48 and 46 years.
cards.result: After spaceflight, femoral neck bone mineral density (−1.7%), knee extensor peak torque (−5.8%), cone agility test time (+7.4%) and VO2peak (−6.1%) all worsened in both groups (main effects of time, all P<0.05), with a few interactions where Sprint showed attenuated or no loss. The authors concluded outcomes were not appreciably different between programmes, and that high-intensity/lower-volume training should be part of prescriptions because it conserves crew time.
cards.watchOut: Crewmembers self-selected their programme and the standard programme itself changed over the study years; 26 subjects cannot exclude meaningful differences.
cards.source: English KL et al. High intensity training during spaceflight: results from the NASA Sprint Study. NPJ Microgravity. 2020. PMID: 32864428. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Loehr 2011 (ground training study, labelled analogue): 16 weeks of ARED training built strength, muscle volume and spine BMD indistinguishably from free weights
cards.summary: Loehr 2011 (ground training study, labelled analogue): 16 weeks of ARED training built strength, muscle volume and spine BMD indistinguishably from free weights
cards.type: Randomised Earth-based training comparison — analogue, not flight data (Loehr 2011)
cards.people: GROUND ANALOGUE (Earth-based training study, not flight data): 20 previously untrained ambulatory adults — free-weight group 9 (6 men, 3 women), ARED group 11 (8 men, 3 women) — performing squat, heel raise and dead lift 3 days/week for 16 weeks.
cards.result: Muscle strength, muscle volume, vertical jump height and lumbar spine bone mineral density (by DXA and QCT) increased significantly (P≤0.05) in both groups, with no significant differences between ARED and free-weight training in any variable at any time. The authors concluded ARED exercise produces musculoskeletal effects not significantly different from free weights and should be validated in flight.
cards.watchOut: Untrained Earth volunteers over 16 weeks say the device loads muscle like free weights; they say nothing directly about microgravity, where the flight cohorts above are the evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ARED-era crews kept hip and pelvis bone density, but still lost strength and fitness; no exercise prescription fully protects — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: ARED-era crews kept hip and pelvis bone density, but still lost strength and fitness; no exercise prescription fully protects — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Smith 2012 (13 ISS crewmembers), English 2020 Sprint (26 ISS crewmembers) and Loehr 2011 (20 Earth trainees, analogue). The bisphosphonate-plus-ARED comparison that isolates what exercise alone cannot do is on Shelf #5459 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: ARED access was associated with unchanged pelvis and hip BMD where iRED crews lost bone, and ARED training loads muscle like free weights on Earth. But even in the ARED era, crews lost femoral neck BMD (−1.7%), knee extensor torque (−5.8%) and VO2peak (−6.1%) over a mission, and bone resorption markers rose throughout. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but partial protection, from small non-randomised flight cohorts.
cards.watchOut: Every flight comparison is confounded by era and self-selection; there is no randomised in-flight exercise trial, and muscle outcomes are thinner than bone outcomes in these cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Smith et al. 2012 (DOI: 10.1002/jbmr.1647), English et al. 2020 (PMID: 32864428) and Loehr et al. 2011 (PMID: 20473227).

shelves.title: Potassium citrate in spaceflight: 20 mEq/day held calcium oxalate supersaturation at pre-flight levels and lowered urinary calcium in a double-blind ISS study of 30 crew
shelves.question: In astronauts on long-duration spaceflight, does potassium citrate supplementation reduce the urinary stone-forming risk created by microgravity?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Spaceflight stone prevention. Whitson 2009 (J Urol, DOI: 10.1016/j.juro.2009.07.010): in 30 long-duration crew, potassium citrate 20 mEq/day (double-blind, placebo-controlled on the ISS) decreased urinary calcium and maintained calcium oxalate supersaturation at pre-flight levels, with higher urinary pH lowering uric acid stone risk. Zerwekh 2007 (PMID: 17509313) is the controlled bed-rest analogue (n=20) showing the same chemistry effect, labelled an analogue on its card. Whitson 1997 documents the underlying risk shift (323 post-flight crew). Earth stone prevention with potassium citrate is homed on Shelf #2645. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) on surrogate endpoints.

cards.headline: Whitson 2009: potassium citrate 20 mEq/day kept calcium oxalate supersaturation at pre-flight levels in long-duration crew, in a double-blind placebo-controlled ISS study
cards.summary: Whitson 2009: potassium citrate 20 mEq/day kept calcium oxalate supersaturation at pre-flight levels in long-duration crew, in a double-blind placebo-controlled ISS study
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled study in ISS crew with Mir comparison crew (Whitson 2009)
cards.people: 30 long-duration spaceflight crew members to Mir and the ISS with 24-hour urine collections before, during and after flight; ISS crew ingested potassium citrate 20 mEq daily in a double-blind, placebo-controlled study, while Mir crew followed the identical protocol without medication.
cards.result: Potassium-citrate-treated crew members had decreased urinary calcium excretion and maintained the calcium oxalate supersaturation risk at pre-flight levels compared with controls. Increased urinary pH in the treatment group decreased the risk of uric acid stones. The authors concluded supplementation with potassium citrate may decrease the risk of renal stone formation during and immediately after spaceflight. The abstract reports directions of effect without printing the group urinary values.
cards.watchOut: Surrogate urinary-chemistry endpoints only — no stone events were or could be counted in 30 crew — and the abstract gives no numerical supersaturation values.
cards.source: Whitson PA et al. Effect of potassium citrate therapy on the risk of renal stone formation during spaceflight. J Urol. 2009. PMID: not captured this session. DOI: 10.1016/j.juro.2009.07.010. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Zerwekh 2007 (bed-rest analogue, labelled analogue): potassium-magnesium citrate lowered calcium oxalate saturation despite bed rest raising urinary calcium by ~50 mg/day
cards.summary: Zerwekh 2007 (bed-rest analogue, labelled analogue): potassium-magnesium citrate lowered calcium oxalate saturation despite bed rest raising urinary calcium by ~50 mg/day
cards.people: BED-REST ANALOGUE (not flight data): 20 normocalciuric subjects randomised double-blind to potassium-magnesium citrate (42 mEq potassium, 21 mEq magnesium, 63 mEq citrate per day) or placebo, before and during 5 weeks of strict bed rest.
cards.result: Bed rest rapidly increased urinary calcium excretion by approximately 50 mg/day in both groups. Despite this, the citrate group showed significant decreases in the relative saturation of calcium oxalate and in the concentration of undissociated uric acid compared with placebo — citrate chelation lowered calcium oxalate saturation even as urine calcium rose, and higher urine pH lowered uric acid risk.
cards.watchOut: An analogue: strict bed rest mimics the urinary chemistry of flight but the subjects were not astronauts, and the formulation adds magnesium to the potassium citrate used in flight.
cards.source: Zerwekh JE et al. Reduction of renal stone risk by potassium-magnesium citrate during 5 weeks of bed rest. J Urol. 2007. PMID: 17509313. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Whitson 1997: spaceflight urine chemistry shifts towards stone formation — the risk the countermeasure targets
cards.summary: Whitson 1997: spaceflight urine chemistry shifts towards stone formation — the risk the countermeasure targets
cards.type: Observational risk-assessment study across Shuttle and Mir crews (Whitson 1997)
cards.people: Renal stone risk assessment across Space Shuttle and Mir programmes: urinary data from 323 crew members immediately after spaceflight, 6 Shuttle crew during short flights and 9 crew on long-duration Shuttle/Mir missions, with dietary monitoring.
cards.result: After flight, urinary changes favoured increased calcium oxalate and uric acid stone-forming potential. During flight, urinary output and citrate (a potent inhibitor of calcium-containing stones) were slightly reduced while urinary calcium rose, producing a urine saturated with calcium stone-forming salts; dietary intakes of fluid, energy, protein, potassium, phosphorus and magnesium also fell significantly during flight.
cards.watchOut: Risk chemistry, not events: it establishes why a countermeasure is needed, not that any countermeasure prevents actual stones.
cards.source: Whitson PA et al. Renal stone risk assessment during Space Shuttle flights. J Urol. 1997. PMID: not captured this session. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: citrate alkali holds stone-risk chemistry at pre-flight levels in flight and in bed rest — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: citrate alkali holds stone-risk chemistry at pre-flight levels in flight and in bed rest — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Whitson 2009 (30 long-duration crew), Zerwekh 2007 (20 bed-rest subjects, analogue) and Whitson 1997 (risk assessment in 323 post-flight and 15 in-flight crew). Terrestrial potassium citrate for recurrent calcium stones is homed on Shelf #2645 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Flight raises urinary calcium and lowers volume, pH and citrate, pushing urine towards calcium oxalate and uric acid saturation. Potassium citrate 20 mEq/day in a double-blind ISS study decreased urinary calcium and held calcium oxalate supersaturation at pre-flight levels while raising pH; the bed-rest analogue with potassium-magnesium citrate showed the same chemistry win under controlled conditions. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent surrogate-endpoint evidence, no stone-event data.
cards.watchOut: No study is powered for actual kidney stone events, which are uncommon per mission; the entire case rests on urinary supersaturation, a validated but surrogate endpoint.
cards.source: Synthesis of Whitson et al. 2009 (DOI: 10.1016/j.juro.2009.07.010), Zerwekh et al. 2007 (PMID: 17509313) and Whitson et al. 1997.

shelves.title: Post-flight orthostatic intolerance: compression garments held standing heart rate and pressure at pre-flight levels — fluid loading helps for 1–3 hours, and midodrine failed in 2 of 5 astronauts tested
shelves.question: In astronauts returning from spaceflight, do fluid loading, midodrine or gradient compression garments prevent post-flight orthostatic intolerance?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Male · Hemodynamics · Middle Aged · Sodium Chloride · Body Fluids · Head-Down Tilt · Young Adult · Aerospace Medicine · Humans · Female · Monitoring, Physiologic
shelves.balance: Post-flight orthostatic intolerance countermeasures. Gradient compression garments have the strongest flight data: Stenger 2013 (PMID: 23713210; 14 Shuttle astronauts) — heart-rate rise 11 vs 21 beats/min and systolic change +2 vs −9 mmHg on landing day; Lee 2020 (PMID: 32765292; 11 long-duration astronauts) — standing responses held at pre-flight levels while wearing the garment. Fluid loading rests on a head-down-tilt analogue (Cowings 2015; n=16) showing a 10 mmHg pressure advantage confined to hours 1–3. Midodrine's only flight test (Platts, NASA report; n=5) failed to prevent hypotension in 2 of 5 and routine use was judged unlikely. Terrestrial midodrine shelves #2498/#1557 are cross-pointed, not re-carded. Proposed stamp: SPLIT.

cards.headline: Cowings 2015 (head-down-tilt analogue, labelled analogue): salt-and-water fluid loading raised mean arterial pressure by 10 mmHg in hours 1–3 — the window 1–3 hours before re-entry
cards.summary: Cowings 2015 (head-down-tilt analogue, labelled analogue): salt-and-water fluid loading raised mean arterial pressure by 10 mmHg in hours 1–3 — the window 1–3 hours before re-entry
cards.people: ANALOGUE (head-down tilt simulation, not flight data): 16 subjects given two 6-hour exposures to head-down tilt, with and without fluid loading (salt tablets and water), to simulate microgravity's plasma-volume effects.
cards.result: Significant increases in mean arterial pressure occurred between hours 1 and 3 of head-down tilt after fluid loading (10 mmHg higher than without fluid loading). Other cardiovascular responses showed non-significant trends with similar time profiles. The authors concluded the optimal time to begin fluid loading is within 1 to 3 hours before re-entry, while noting large individual variability suggesting fluid loading alone may be inadequate for all crewmembers.
cards.watchOut: A 6-hour tilt analogue in 16 ground subjects: it times the fluid load, it does not show that fluid loading prevents post-flight presyncope in astronauts.
cards.source: Cowings PS et al. Fluid Loading Effects on Temporal Profiles of Cardiovascular Responses to Head-Down Tilt. Aerosp Med Hum Perform. 2015. PMID: not captured this session. cards.headline: Platts (midodrine, flight): taken before re-entry, midodrine did not prevent post-flight hypotension in 2 of 5 astronauts (n=5 on the face), and routine use was judged unlikely
cards.summary: Platts (midodrine, flight): taken before re-entry, midodrine did not prevent post-flight hypotension in 2 of 5 astronauts (n=5 on the face), and routine use was judged unlikely
cards.people: Five male astronauts (n=5) whose cardiovascular responses to 10 minutes of 80° head-up tilt were compared before flight and within 60 minutes of Space Shuttle landing (in the Crew Transport Vehicle on the runway); midodrine was self-administered before re-entry. A preceding phase had given 10 mg midodrine 2 hours after landing, 1 hour before a laboratory tilt test.
cards.result: Midodrine did not prevent post-flight orthostatic hypotension in two of the five astronauts, but the rate of presyncope across the group did not increase from pre- to post-flight (p=0.17). Systolic blood pressure decreased more after spaceflight (p=0.05) and diastolic tended to decrease (p=0.08); the heart-rate change from supine to standing was unaffected. The authors concluded that, with no control subjects tested in the vehicle, and with drug-interaction concerns (antiemetics) and QTc prolongation seen in long-duration astronauts, routine midodrine use for immediate post-flight hypotension is unlikely.
cards.watchOut: No untreated comparison in the same setting and only 5 subjects: this can raise doubts about midodrine, it cannot quantify any benefit. Terrestrial midodrine evidence is homed on Shelves #2498 and #1557 and is not re-carded here.
cards.source: Platts SH et al. [Midodrine as a Countermeasure to Orthostatic Hypotension Immediately After Space Shuttle Landing — bracketed descriptive title; NASA technical report]. cards.headline: Stenger 2013: an abdomen-high gradient compression garment blunted the landing-day stand-test response — heart rate rise 11 versus 21 beats/min, systolic pressure +2 versus −9 mmHg
cards.summary: Stenger 2013: an abdomen-high gradient compression garment blunted the landing-day stand-test response — heart rate rise 11 versus 21 beats/min, systolic pressure +2 versus −9 mmHg
cards.type: Controlled stand-test study in Shuttle astronauts (Stenger 2013)
cards.people: 14 astronauts around Space Shuttle missions (12–16 days) performing a 3.5-minute stand test ~30 days before flight (no garment) and ~2 hours after flight: 7 wore a custom three-piece foot-to-breast gradient compression garment (55 mmHg at the ankle grading to 15 mmHg over the abdomen) and 7 were controls.
cards.result: On landing day the garment group had a smaller rise in heart rate on standing (11±1 vs 21±4 beats/min, p≤0.05) and no fall in systolic blood pressure (+2±4 vs −9±2 mmHg, p≤0.05). No subject in either group became presyncopal during the short stand test, before or after flight. The authors concluded the garment prevented the tachycardia and hypotension typically seen post-spaceflight in this small group.
cards.watchOut: The 3.5-minute stand test was deliberately too short to provoke presyncope, so the garment is proven on physiology, not on preventing fainting; Shuttle flights were short-duration.

cards.headline: Lee 2020: after ~6-month missions, a gradient compression garment kept landing-day standing heart rate and pressure responses at pre-flight levels in 11 astronauts
cards.summary: Lee 2020: after ~6-month missions, a gradient compression garment kept landing-day standing heart rate and pressure responses at pre-flight levels in 11 astronauts
cards.type: Within-subject flight study in long-duration astronauts (Lee 2020)
cards.people: 11 astronauts (9 men, 2 women) after long-duration spaceflight, tested prone-then-standing (3.5 minutes) before flight in standard clothing and on landing day wearing a lower-body gradient compression garment at 1–4 hours, ~12 hours and ~28 hours after landing; historically, >60% of returning long-duration astronauts could not complete a 10-minute 80° tilt test on landing day.
cards.result: Three astronauts were unable to attempt the stand test at the first landing-day session and one could not complete standing at the second. In those tested, heart rate and mean arterial pressure responses to standing while wearing the garment were not different from pre-flight at any landing-day session. The authors concluded the garment prevented the tachycardia that normally occurs on standing after spaceflight without compression and protected against a fall in blood pressure during the short stand test.
cards.watchOut: No randomised no-garment landing-day arm (the comparison is to pre-flight responses and historical experience), and the frailest crew — those unable to attempt the test — are missing from the physiology.

cards.headline: Synthesis: compression garments work on landing-day physiology; fluid loading is a timing-limited partial measure; midodrine is unproven in flight — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: compression garments work on landing-day physiology; fluid loading is a timing-limited partial measure; midodrine is unproven in flight — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Cowings 2015 (16 analogue subjects), Platts 2010 (5 astronauts), Stenger 2013 (14 astronauts) and Lee 2020 (11 astronauts).
cards.result: Gradient compression garments are the best-supported countermeasure: they abolished the excess tachycardia and systolic fall on standing after both short (Stenger) and long (Lee) missions. Fluid loading raises arterial pressure for a 1–3 hour window in analogue studies but is acknowledged to be inadequate alone. Midodrine, effective in terrestrial orthostatic hypotension (Shelves #2498, #1557), failed to prevent hypotension in 2 of 5 astronauts in its only flight test and carries QTc/antiemetic interaction concerns. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (compression: POSSIBLE benefit · fluid loading: POSSIBLE partial benefit · midodrine in flight: unproven).
cards.watchOut: No countermeasure has been tested against the outcome that matters most — presyncope or syncope on landing day — in a randomised flight trial; all stamps here rest on stand-test physiology.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cowings et al. 2015, Platts et al. 2010 (NASA technical report), Stenger et al. 2013 (PMID: 23713210) and Lee et al. 2020 (PMID: 32765292).

shelves.title: Sleep in spaceflight: crews get only ~6 hours despite 3 in 4 using sleeping pills — and melatonin 0.3 mg, the one drug trialled in flight, did not improve sleep at all
shelves.question: In spaceflight crewmembers, do melatonin, sleep-promoting medications or light-based circadian countermeasures improve sleep duration and circadian alignment?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Sleep and circadian countermeasures in flight. Dijk 2001 (PMID: 11641138): 5 Shuttle astronauts slept ~6.5 hours/day and melatonin 0.3 mg on alternate nights did not improve sleep. Barger 2014 (PMID: 25127232): 85 astronauts obtained 5.96 hours (Shuttle) and 6.09 hours (ISS) per night, while 78% of Shuttle crew used sleep-promoting drugs on 52% of nights and 75% of ISS crew used them — use is pervasive but untested against placebo in flight. The 2023 review (PMID: 37533816) puts medication use at 71–78% of crewmembers. No cardable in-flight randomised trial of timed light was captured this session — flagged as a gap. Proposed stamp: SPLIT.

cards.headline: Dijk 2001: astronauts slept only ~6.5 hours a day in flight, and melatonin 0.3 mg on alternate nights did not improve sleep (n=5 on the face)
cards.summary: Dijk 2001: astronauts slept only ~6.5 hours a day in flight, and melatonin 0.3 mg on alternate nights did not improve sleep (n=5 on the face)
cards.type: Flight study with melatonin administration in 5 astronauts (Dijk 2001)
cards.people: Five astronauts (n=5) studied before, during and after a 16-day and a 10-day Space Shuttle mission, with questionnaires, actigraphy, circadian and neurobehavioral performance measures; melatonin 0.3 mg was administered on alternate nights in flight.
cards.result: Sleep duration in flight was only approximately 6.5 hours per day and subjective sleep quality diminished. Administration of melatonin (0.3 mg) on alternate nights did not improve sleep. After return to Earth, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep was markedly increased.
cards.watchOut: Five astronauts and a low, physiologic melatonin dose: the null applies to 0.3 mg on alternate nights, not to every melatonin regimen, and predates modern ISS lighting.
cards.source: Dijk DJ et al. Sleep, performance, circadian rhythms, and light-dark cycles during two space shuttle flights. Am J Physiol Regul Integr Comp Physiol. 2001. PMID: 11641138. cards.headline: Barger 2014: crews obtained only 5.96 hours (Shuttle) and 6.09 hours (ISS) of sleep in flight — yet 78% of Shuttle crew used sleep-promoting drugs, on 52% of nights
cards.summary: Barger 2014: crews obtained only 5.96 hours (Shuttle) and 6.09 hours (ISS) of sleep in flight — yet 78% of Shuttle crew used sleep-promoting drugs, on 52% of nights
cards.type: Large observational actigraphy study of Shuttle and ISS crews (Barger 2014)
cards.people: 64 astronauts on 80 Space Shuttle missions (1,063 in-flight days) and 21 astronauts on 13 ISS missions (3,248 in-flight days), with wrist actigraphy and daily logs before, during and after flight (4,014 ground-based days).
cards.result: Actigraphic sleep obtained per night was 5.96 hours (SD 0.56) on Shuttle missions and 6.09 hours (0.67) on ISS missions, versus 6.74 and 6.95 hours in the first week post-mission (p<0.0001); sleep was already curtailed 3 months before launch (6.29 and 6.41 hours). Of 78 Shuttle crew members, 61 (78%) reported taking a sleep-promoting drug on 500 (52%) of 963 nights; 12 (75%) of 16 ISS crew reported using sleep-promoting drugs.
cards.watchOut: Observational: hypnotic use is recorded, not randomised, so these data cannot show whether the drugs improved sleep, performance or safety — only that use was pervasive despite short sleep.
cards.source: Barger LK et al. Prevalence of sleep deficiency and use of hypnotic drugs in astronauts before, during, and after spaceflight: an observational study. Lancet Neurol. 2014. PMID: 25127232. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Sleep-in-spaceflight review 2023: sleep-promoting medication use ranges from 71% to 78% of crewmembers, highest on circadian-misaligned sleep episodes
cards.summary: Sleep-in-spaceflight review 2023: sleep-promoting medication use ranges from 71% to 78% of crewmembers, highest on circadian-misaligned sleep episodes
cards.type: Systematic review of spaceflight sleep literature (2023)
cards.people: Systematic review of the low-Earth-orbit literature (182 articles retrieved from PubMed and Scopus) on sleep disruption, sleep-promoting medication use and circadian desynchronisation in spaceflight crewmembers, with implications for deep-space missions.
cards.result: Evidence consistently indicates loss of sleep and circadian disruption during low-Earth-orbit missions; sleep is shortest the night before a critical operation and during circadian-misaligned sleep episodes. The prevalence of sleep-promoting medication use ranges between 71% and 78% of crewmembers, and medication is taken more frequently on circadian-misaligned sleep episodes.
cards.watchOut: A narrative-systematic review without pooled effect sizes; it documents practice and problems rather than testing any countermeasure.

cards.headline: Synthesis: sleep in flight runs at ~6 hours despite pervasive hypnotic use, and the one tested drug countermeasure — low-dose melatonin — made no difference — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: sleep in flight runs at ~6 hours despite pervasive hypnotic use, and the one tested drug countermeasure — low-dose melatonin — made no difference — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Dijk 2001 (5 astronauts), Barger 2014 (85 astronauts across Shuttle and ISS programmes) and the 2023 systematic review.
cards.result: Crews sleep about 6–6.5 hours in flight, less than post-flight, and the deficit starts before launch. Hypnotics (zolpidem-class agents in the Shuttle era) are used by roughly three quarters of crew on about half of nights, but no card here tests them against placebo in flight, so their benefit is unproven rather than established. The single drug actually trialled in flight, melatonin 0.3 mg on alternate nights, did not improve sleep. Timed light — the main circadian countermeasure used operationally — has no cardable in-flight randomised trial in this session's records and is flagged as a gap. Proposed stamp: SPLIT (melatonin 0.3 mg: the treatment made no difference · hypnotics: widely used, benefit unproven in flight · light: untested in cardable flight trials).
cards.watchOut: Terrestrial insomnia evidence (CBT-I, melatonin for sleep onset — Shelves #437, #499, #116) does not transfer automatically to the spaceflight environment and is not re-carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dijk et al. 2001 (PMID: 11641138), Barger et al. 2014 (PMID: 25127232) and the 2023 spaceflight sleep review (PMID: 37533816).

shelves.title: SANS eye swelling in space: only standing upright (in the Earth bed-rest model) kept retinal thickening under NASA's danger line (18.6 vs >20 µm) — suction trousers and thigh cuffs did nothing extra, and the B-vitamin idea rests on risk genes, not a treatment trial
shelves.question: In astronauts and in head-down bed-rest analogues of spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS), do countermeasures — fluid-shift reversal (upright posture, lower body negative pressure, thigh cuffs) or B-vitamin supplementation aimed at one-carbon metabolism — prevent optic disc edema, and who is at highest risk?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bed Rest/adverse effects · Female · Fluid Shifts/physiology · Fluorescein Angiography · Head-Down Tilt · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Optic Nerve/blood supply · Papilledema/etiology · Papilledema/physiopathology · Prospective Studies · Retinal Vessels · Space Flight · Syndrome · Tomography, Optical Coherence · Vision Disorders
shelves.balance: SPLIT — fluid-shift reversal works in the analogue, no deployable countermeasure is proven, and the B-vitamin lead is risk genetics, not a treatment trial. In the randomised 30-day head-down bed-rest trial of He 2025 (PMID: 40545016; 47 volunteers), only intermittent upright posture kept retinal thickening below NASA's 20 µm disc-edema threshold (18.6 ± 5.5 µm); lower body negative pressure and exercise with thigh cuffs did not differ from no countermeasure. Susceptibility is real and measurable before flight: Zwart 2012 (PMID: 22298570) found one-carbon metabolites 25–45% higher (P < 0.001) in the 5 astronauts with eye changes than in 15 without, before, during and after flight, and Zwart 2019 (JAMA Ophthalmology, DOI: 10.1001/jamaophthalmol.2019.3124) found edema in 5 of 11 bed-rest subjects tracking MTRR/SHMT1 risk alleles and B-vitamin status. That makes B-vitamin supplementation a plausible, currently untested countermeasure — not a proven one. PROPOSED SPLIT (analogue posture effect: positive · mechanical countermeasures as tested: the treatment made no difference · B vitamins: association only, no trial).

cards.headline: He 2025: only intermittent upright posture kept retinal thickening below NASA's 20 µm disc-edema threshold (18.6 µm); lower body negative pressure and exercise plus thigh cuffs did not differ from no countermeasure
cards.summary: He 2025: only intermittent upright posture kept retinal thickening below NASA's 20 µm disc-edema threshold (18.6 µm); lower body negative pressure and exercise plus thigh cuffs did not differ from no countermeasure
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in a head-down bed-rest analogue (He 2025)
cards.people: 47 healthy volunteers in 30 days of strict head-down tilt bed rest (a SANS analogue), randomised to no countermeasure, lower body negative pressure, exercise with veno-constrictive thigh cuffs, or intermittent upright posture (n = 11–12 per group).
cards.result: Change in total retinal thickness 250 µm from Bruch's membrane opening (ΔTRT250): only the upright-posture group stayed below the NASA >20 µm disc-edema convention, at 18.6 ± 5.5 µm (mean ± 95% CI). The other three groups, including both mechanical countermeasures, all exceeded 20 µm with no differences between groups. Smaller pre-bed-rest optic cup width, depth and volume predicted greater ΔTRT250 (P = .001–.002).
cards.watchOut: This is an Earth-bound analogue, not spaceflight: upright posture works by intermittently reversing the headward fluid shift, which no current spacecraft countermeasure replicates, and 30 days is far shorter than a 6-month mission.
cards.source: He Y et al. Optic Nerve Vasculature and Countermeasure Assessment in a Bedrest Analogue of Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome. American Journal of Ophthalmology. 2025. PMID: 40545016. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zwart 2012: astronauts who developed eye changes had one-carbon metabolites 25–45% higher before, during and after flight (n = 5 affected vs 15 unaffected)
cards.summary: Zwart 2012: astronauts who developed eye changes had one-carbon metabolites 25–45% higher before, during and after flight (n = 5 affected vs 15 unaffected)
cards.people: 20 astronauts on ISS missions of 48–215 days with nutritional biochemistry modelled (5 with ophthalmic changes, 15 without); about 20% (7 of 38) of ISS astronauts in the programme had developed measurable ophthalmic changes after flight.
cards.result: Serum homocysteine, cystathionine, 2-methylcitric acid and methylmalonic acid concentrations were 25–45% higher (P < 0.001) in astronauts with ophthalmic changes than in those without, and the differences existed before, during and after flight. Preflight homocysteine and cystathionine, and mean in-flight serum folate, correlated with the postflight change in refraction (P < 0.05).
cards.watchOut: Association only, in 5 affected astronauts: it identifies a susceptibility pathway (and the rationale for B-vitamin supplementation) but does not show that giving B vitamins prevents or treats SANS; no supplementation trial with ocular outcomes is carded anywhere in this pack because none was found.

cards.headline: Zwart 2019: optic disc edema developed in 5 of 11 volunteers during 30-day strict head-down bed rest with 0.5% CO2, and its size tracked one-carbon risk alleles and B-vitamin status (n = 11, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Zwart 2019: optic disc edema developed in 5 of 11 volunteers during 30-day strict head-down bed rest with 0.5% CO2, and its size tracked one-carbon risk alleles and B-vitamin status (n = 11, printed on the face)
cards.people: 11 healthy volunteers (6 men, 5 women; 33 ± 8 years) in 30 days of strict 6° head-down tilt bed rest with 0.5% CO2 exposure (the VaPER analogue study).
cards.result: Optic disc edema occurred in 5 of 11 subjects. The change in total retinal thickness was strongly associated with the number of MTRR 66 G alleles and SHMT1 1420 C alleles (one-carbon pathway variants), together with B-vitamin status — the same risk pattern seen in astronauts.
cards.watchOut: Only 11 subjects (n printed on the face), an analogue with added CO2, and again a risk-factor association — not a test of B-vitamin treatment. A single severe in-flight case improved while B vitamins were given and cabin CO2 fell at the same time, so the two cannot be separated.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one analogue RCT supports fluid-shift reversal in principle, but no flight-ready countermeasure is proven, and B vitamins remain an untested hypothesis built on risk genetics
cards.summary: Synthesis: one analogue RCT supports fluid-shift reversal in principle, but no flight-ready countermeasure is proven, and B vitamins remain an untested hypothesis built on risk genetics
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised analogue trial (47 volunteers), one astronaut cohort (20 analysed of 38 in the programme) and one 11-person analogue cohort.
cards.result: In the only randomised test, intermittent upright posture held ΔTRT250 to 18.6 µm, below NASA's 20 µm edema threshold, while lower body negative pressure and exercise plus thigh cuffs were indistinguishable from no countermeasure (all >20 µm). Risk concentrates in people with one-carbon pathway variants (MTRR 66 G, SHMT1 1420 C) and poorer B-vitamin status: metabolites 25–45% higher in affected astronauts (P < 0.001), and edema in 5 of 11 analogue subjects tracking the same alleles. No randomised trial of B-vitamin supplementation for SANS exists. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Everything here is analogue or observational except the posture finding, and upright posture is not itself deployable in weightlessness; artificial gravity, the closest deployable analogue of posture reversal, is carded separately on the artificial-gravity shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of He et al. American Journal of Ophthalmology. 2025 (PMID: 40545016); Zwart SR et al. The Journal of Nutrition. 2012 (PMID: 22298570); Zwart SR et al. JAMA Ophthalmology. 2019 (DOI: 10.1001/jamaophthalmol.2019.3124).

shelves.title: Medicines in space: the one drug measured in flight reached blood levels 4–5 times higher than on Earth (4 crew), and after 28 months on the space station only 9 of 35 medicines still met potency standards versus 17 of 35 stored on Earth
shelves.question: During spaceflight, are drug pharmacokinetics altered in microgravity, and do medications lose stability or potency faster in the space environment than on Earth?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: SPLIT — exposure changes in flight, and long storage degrades medicines faster, but the evidence is one drug in 4 people plus formulation chemistry. Mampre 2026 (PMID: 42530224) made the first blood-sampled in-flight pharmacokinetic measurements: in 4 Polaris Dawn crew, acetaminophen Cmax rose from 9,110 to 43,300 ng/mL and AUC roughly quadrupled versus pre-flight, with changes still present 3 days after landing. For stability, Du 2011 (PMID: 21479701) found only 9 of 35 ISS formulations still met USP potency criteria after 28 months versus 17 of 35 ground controls, with faster degradation in space; Wotring 2015 (DOI: 10.1208/s12248-015-9834-5) found most of 9 medicines still potent after 550 days on the ISS, 4 of them up to 8 months past expiry. PROPOSED SPLIT (in-flight pharmacokinetics: changed, direction drug-specific · long-duration storage: faster degradation · ~18-month storage: potency mostly held).

cards.headline: Mampre 2026: in the first blood-sampled flight study, acetaminophen peak levels were nearly 5 times higher in flight than before flight in 4 crew (n = 4, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Mampre 2026: in the first blood-sampled flight study, acetaminophen peak levels were nearly 5 times higher in flight than before flight in 4 crew (n = 4, printed on the face)
cards.people: 4 SpaceX Polaris Dawn crewmembers (n = 4, printed on the face) who took a single 500 mg oral acetaminophen dose before, during and after a short commercial spaceflight, with capillary microsampling (VAMS).
cards.result: Compared with pre-flight: in-flight Cmax rose from 9,110 (SD 3,290) to 43,300 (SD 5,700) ng/mL (P < .001) and AUC0-last from 26,100 (SD 4,520) to 109,000 (SD 29,400) h·ng/mL; half-life fell from 3.27 (SD 0.95) to 2.07 (SD 0.13) h, apparent clearance from 16,200 (SD 2,990) to 3,890 (SD 559) mL/h, and tmax from 1.06 to 0.688 h. Cmax, AUC, Vz/F and CL/F still differed 3 days after landing. The authors flag supratherapeutic levels at standard terrestrial doses as a toxicity concern.
cards.watchOut: Only 4 people (n printed on the face), one drug, one short mission, and whole-blood microsamples rather than plasma: the direction (higher, faster exposure in flight) is striking but the size cannot be generalised to other drugs or to 6-month missions.
cards.source: Mampre D et al. Volumetric Absorptive Microsampling During Spaceflight for Analysis of Acetaminophen Pharmacokinetics in Whole Blood. The Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2026. PMID: 42530224. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Du 2011: after 28 months on the ISS, only 9 of 35 medication formulations still met US Pharmacopeia potency standards, versus 17 of 35 ground controls — degradation ran faster in space
cards.summary: Du 2011: after 28 months on the ISS, only 9 of 35 medication formulations still met US Pharmacopeia potency standards, versus 17 of 35 ground controls — degradation ran faster in space
cards.type: Controlled stability comparison, flight versus ground kits (Du 2011)
cards.people: 35 medication formulations carried in identical pharmaceutical kits stored on the International Space Station and in matched ground controls, assayed after return at intervals up to 28 months.
cards.result: After 28 months of stowage, 9 medications from the ISS kits and 17 from ground controls met USP acceptance criteria for active ingredient content; 6 ISS and 2 ground formulations showed physical changes. A higher percentage of flight medications had lower active content than their ground controls, the number failing rose with time in space independent of the labelled expiration date, and degradation was faster in space for many medications, although most solid dosage forms still met dissolution standards. Cumulative radiation dose was higher in space; temperature and humidity were similar.
cards.watchOut: Formulations, not patients: potency loss is a chemistry endpoint, and the study cannot separate radiation from the repackaging of solid medicines into flight dispensers, which the authors themselves name as a suspect.
cards.source: Du B et al. Evaluation of physical and chemical changes in pharmaceuticals flown on space missions. The AAPS Journal. 2011. PMID: 21479701. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Wotring 2015: medicines stored 550 days on the ISS mostly kept their potency — 4 of 9 were still within US Pharmacopeia limits up to 8 months past their expiry dates, with no unusual breakdown products
cards.summary: Wotring 2015: medicines stored 550 days on the ISS mostly kept their potency — 4 of 9 were still within US Pharmacopeia limits up to 8 months past their expiry dates, with no unusual breakdown products
cards.type: Opportunistic stability study of returned flight medicines (Wotring 2015)
cards.people: 9 medications (sleeping aids, pain relievers, antihistamine/decongestants, an antidiarrhoeal and an alertness drug) stored unused on the ISS for 550 days and assayed after return to Earth.
cards.result: One medication met USP requirements 5 months after its expiration date and 4 of the 9 were still viable up to 8 months after expiring; 3 met guidelines when tested 3 months before expiry; a dietary supplement/sleeping aid failed 11 months after expiry. No unusual degradation products were identified in any medication.
cards.watchOut: A single time point, 9 medicines and no parallel ground control in this pilot: it reassures for ~18-month storage but cannot be extrapolated to other drugs, longer storage, or a Mars-length mission without resupply.

cards.headline: Synthesis: drug handling genuinely changes in flight, and long storage genuinely degrades medicines faster — but each claim rests on very small, single-drug or formulation-level evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: drug handling genuinely changes in flight, and long storage genuinely degrades medicines faster — but each claim rests on very small, single-drug or formulation-level evidence
cards.people: The carded evidence: one 4-person in-flight pharmacokinetic study, one 35-formulation controlled stability comparison, and one 9-medicine opportunistic potency study.
cards.result: Acetaminophen exposure in flight was far higher and faster than pre-flight in 4 crew (Cmax 43,300 vs 9,110 ng/mL; AUC roughly fourfold). Over 28 months, ISS-stored kits failed potency standards far more often than ground kits (9 vs 17 of 35 passing), yet over 550 days most of 9 returned medicines still met potency limits, several past expiry. Together: terrestrial doses and terrestrial shelf lives cannot simply be assumed in space, in either direction of risk. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: No carded study measures a clinical outcome of a changed dose; the pharmacokinetic signal is one drug in 4 people on a days-long flight, and the two stability studies differ in design and duration, which is why their emphases differ.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mampre D et al. The Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2026 (PMID: 42530224); Du B et al. The AAPS Journal. 2011 (PMID: 21479701); Wotring VE. The AAPS Journal. 2015 (DOI: 10.1208/s12248-015-9834-5).

shelves.title: Dormant viruses wake up in space: 22 of 23 long-mission astronauts shed a herpesvirus — but the fittest crew had a 29–39% lower relative risk, and shedding fell after 2012 as exercise, food and scheduling countermeasures improved
shelves.question: In long-duration spaceflight, how common is immune dysregulation with latent herpesvirus reactivation, and do countermeasures — preflight fitness, exercise, nutritional supplementation, scheduling and other operational measures — reduce it?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only. Reactivation is near-universal on long missions: Mehta 2017 (PMID: 28649633) found 22 of 23 ISS astronauts shed a latent herpesvirus (15 VZV, 22 EBV, 14 CMV at some phase), with shedding heavier than on short shuttle flights. Two countermeasure signals, neither randomised: Agha 2020 (PMID: 31908052) found higher preflight cardiorespiratory fitness carried a 29% lower relative risk of reactivation and higher upper-body endurance a 39% lower relative risk in 22 crew; Crucian 2020 (PMID: 32464118) found stress, immune dysregulation and reactivation all improved across 12 years of ISS operations as the exercise, nutrition, supplementation and scheduling bundle improved from about 2012. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for fitness and the combined operational countermeasure bundle; no drug or vaccine countermeasure has been tested in flight.

cards.headline: Mehta 2017: 22 of 23 long-duration astronauts shed a reactivated latent herpesvirus; shedding grew in frequency, duration and copy number compared with short shuttle flights
cards.summary: Mehta 2017: 22 of 23 long-duration astronauts shed a reactivated latent herpesvirus; shedding grew in frequency, duration and copy number compared with short shuttle flights
cards.people: 23 astronauts (18 men, 5 women) on long-duration ISS missions up to 180 days, with 20 age- and sex-matched ground controls; saliva, urine and blood sampled before, during and after flight.
cards.result: Twenty-two of 23 astronauts shed one or more target viruses at some point: 15 shed varicella-zoster virus, 22 Epstein–Barr virus and 14 cytomegalovirus (full-text counts). The PubMed abstract reports shedding of EBV, VZV and CMV detected in 8 of the 23 astronauts during flight. Reactivation increased in frequency, duration and amplitude (viral copy numbers) compared with short-duration (10–16 day) shuttle missions; no HSV-1, HSV-2 or HHV-6 reactivation was found. The mean diurnal trajectory of salivary cortisol changed significantly in flight (P = 0.010).
cards.watchOut: Shedding is a biomarker of immune dysregulation, not illness: almost all reactivation was asymptomatic, and the abstract and full-text shedding counts differ in framing (in-flight detection vs any-phase shedding), so both are printed here rather than merged.
cards.source: Mehta SK et al. Latent virus reactivation in astronauts on the international space station. NPJ Microgravity. 2017. PMID: 28649633. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Agha 2020: fitter crew reactivated less — higher preflight cardiorespiratory fitness carried a 29% lower relative risk of viral reactivation, and higher upper-body endurance a 39% lower relative risk
cards.summary: Agha 2020: fitter crew reactivated less — higher preflight cardiorespiratory fitness carried a 29% lower relative risk of viral reactivation, and higher upper-body endurance a 39% lower relative risk
cards.people: 22 ISS crewmembers on ~6-month missions, with standardised preflight tests of maximal strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF), and CMV, EBV and VZV reactivation measured before, during and after flight against ground controls.
cards.result: Crewmembers with higher preflight CRF had a 29% reduced relative risk of latent viral reactivation compared with crew with lower CRF. Higher preflight upper-body muscular endurance was associated with a 39% reduced relative risk of reactivation, a longer time to reactivation, and lower peak viral DNA concentrations, particularly for EBV and VZV. Reactivation rates were highest in crew with lower preflight CRF and more CRF deconditioning on return to Earth. Absolute reactivation rates by fitness group were not printed in the record fetched this session, so the relative figures stand alone and are labelled relative.
cards.watchOut: Observational: fitness was measured, not assigned, so fitter crew may differ in other protective ways, and no trial has tested whether raising fitness before flight prevents reactivation. Relative risks are printed without absolute rates because the record did not give them.
cards.source: Agha NH et al. Exercise as a countermeasure for latent viral reactivation during long duration space flight. The FASEB Journal. 2020. PMID: 31908052. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Crucian 2020: across 12 years of ISS operations, astronaut stress, immune dysregulation and herpesvirus reactivation all improved as onboard countermeasures improved from about 2012
cards.summary: Crucian 2020: across 12 years of ISS operations, astronaut stress, immune dysregulation and herpesvirus reactivation all improved as onboard countermeasures improved from about 2012
cards.type: Review with cross-era comparison of monitored crews (Crucian 2020)
cards.people: ISS astronaut monitoring data compared across 12 years of station construction and operations (cohort sizes by era: N not documented in the record fetched this session).
cards.result: Immunity, stress and latent herpesvirus reactivation all improved in ISS astronauts over the period. The major improvements began around 2012, coinciding with a bundle of operational and biomedical countermeasures: more frequent cargo resupply, personal communication, better exercise equipment and protocols, better food quality and variety, nutritional supplementation, and schedule management. The authors conclude spaceflight immune dysregulation has been positively influenced by these countermeasures and that they should be designed into deep-space missions.
cards.watchOut: An era comparison of a bundle: no single countermeasure (exercise, food, supplements, scheduling, communication) can be credited individually, era crews differ, and the paper is classified as a review — this is the weakest design on the shelf.
