cards.headline: Synthesis: reactivation is near-universal on long missions; fitness and the modern countermeasure bundle are associated with less of it, but nothing has been randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: reactivation is near-universal on long missions; fitness and the modern countermeasure bundle are associated with less of it, but nothing has been randomised
cards.people: The carded evidence: two prospective astronaut cohorts (23 and 22 crew) and one 12-year cross-era comparison.
cards.result: Reactivation is the norm, not the exception: 22 of 23 long-duration astronauts shed a latent herpesvirus, more heavily than on short flights (Mehta 2017). The two countermeasure signals are both observational: higher preflight fitness, 29–39% lower relative risk of reactivation (Agha 2020), and a post-2012 era improvement coinciding with the upgraded exercise, nutrition, supplementation and scheduling bundle (Crucian 2020). No randomised immune countermeasure trial in spaceflight was found. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence only, capped at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: A laboratory-confirmed case of shingles did occur on a 6-month ISS mission despite the modern bundle (treated successfully with oral valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days), so improvement is not elimination; vaccination and antiviral strategies remain proposals, not tested countermeasures, in the carded record.

shelves.title: Spinning as medicine: 30 minutes a day in a small centrifuge blunted fainting-proneness after 60 days of bed rest (standing tolerance fell ~300 vs 801 seconds) — but it did not protect blood volume or fitness, and spinning while exercising added nothing
shelves.question: Does artificial gravity from short-radius (short-arm) centrifugation, daily or combined with exercise, protect against cardiovascular and other deconditioning during spaceflight or its head-down bed-rest analogue?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bed Rest/adverse effects · Blood Volume/physiology · Cross-Over Studies · Gravity, Altered · Humans · Male · Orthostatic Intolerance/etiology · Orthostatic Intolerance/physiopathology · Orthostatic Intolerance/therapy · Supine Position · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a real orthostatic benefit at rest in analogues; no protection for plasma volume or fitness, and no added benefit when combined with exercise. Linnarsson 2015 (PMID: 25342708; 11 men, crossover) found tilt tolerance after 5 days of bed rest was 78% of baseline with 6 × 5 min daily centrifugation versus 36% with no countermeasure, while plasma volume (85% of baseline) and aerobic power (95%) were unprotected. Hoenemann 2023 (PMID: 37347452; DRKS00015677; AGBRESA, 24 people, 60 days) found time to presyncope fell ~300 s in both centrifugation groups versus 801 s in controls (P = 0.0249). Hedge 2025 (PMID: 40953072; BRACE, 24 men, 60 days) found exercise during centrifugation protected aerobic fitness exactly as exercise alone did (Δ +4% vs 0%, controls −24%) and standing tolerance fell in all groups. PROPOSED SPLIT (orthostatic tolerance at rest: POSSIBLE benefit in analogues · plasma volume, fitness, and exercise-combined use: the treatment made no difference beyond exercise).

cards.headline: Linnarsson 2015 (BR-AG1): split-dose centrifugation preserved standing tolerance best — tilt tolerance was 78% of baseline with 6 × 5 min daily spins vs 36% with no countermeasure after 5 days of bed rest
cards.summary: Linnarsson 2015 (BR-AG1): split-dose centrifugation preserved standing tolerance best — tilt tolerance was 78% of baseline with 6 × 5 min daily spins vs 36% with no countermeasure after 5 days of bed rest
cards.type: Randomised crossover trial in a bed-rest analogue (Linnarsson 2015)
cards.people: 11 healthy men in a randomised crossover of three 5-day head-down bed-rest campaigns: no countermeasure, 30 min of artificial gravity once daily (AG1), or 6 × 5 min daily (AG2), at 1 G at the centre of mass; complete datasets in 8 subjects.
cards.result: After bed rest, head-up tilt tolerance times were 36% (control), 64% (AG1) and 78% (AG2) of pre-bed-rest baseline, with a significant difference between AG2 and control. Plasma volume fell to 85% and peak oxygen uptake to 95% of baseline with no differences between treatments. AG2 was better tolerated than AG1.
cards.watchOut: Five days of bed rest in 11 men (8 complete datasets) is a very short, small analogue: it shows an orthostatic signal for split-dose spinning, not protection over a 6-month mission, and neither plasma volume nor aerobic power was protected at all.
cards.source: Linnarsson D et al. Effects of an artificial gravity countermeasure on orthostatic tolerance, blood volumes and aerobic power after short-term bed rest (BR-AG1). cards.headline: Hoenemann 2023 (AGBRESA): daily centrifugation blunted the fall in time to presyncope after 60 days of bed rest — a fall of ~300 s in both spin groups vs 801 s in controls (P = 0.0249)
cards.summary: Hoenemann 2023 (AGBRESA): daily centrifugation blunted the fall in time to presyncope after 60 days of bed rest — a fall of ~300 s in both spin groups vs 801 s in controls (P = 0.0249)
cards.type: Controlled trial in a 60-day bed-rest analogue (Hoenemann 2023)
cards.people: 24 healthy people (8 women; age 33.3 ± 9.0 years) in the 60-day strict head-down tilt AGBRESA bed-rest study, assigned to 30 min/day continuous centrifugation, 6 × 5 min intermittent centrifugation (both 1 Gz at the centre of mass), or control.
cards.result: Time to presyncope on tilt testing fell by 323 ± 235 s (continuous) and 296 ± 508 s (intermittent) versus 801 ± 354 s in controls (P = 0.0249 between interventions). Supine and upright heart rate still rose in all groups, and the orthostatic benefit was not correlated with changes in plasma volume — centrifugation attenuated, but did not prevent, cardiovascular deconditioning.
cards.watchOut: Still an analogue with 8 people per group and wide variability (the intermittent group's SD of 508 s exceeds its mean effect); baseline orthostatic tolerance differed between groups, and no in-flight centrifuge trial exists.
cards.source: Hoenemann JN et al. Effects of daily artificial gravity training on orthostatic tolerance following 60-day strict head-down tilt bedrest. Clinical Autonomic Research. 2023. PMID: 37347452. Registry ID: DRKS00015677. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Hedge 2025 (BRACE): exercising while spinning protected aerobic fitness exactly as well as exercise alone — and neither protected standing tolerance, which fell in every group
cards.summary: Hedge 2025 (BRACE): exercising while spinning protected aerobic fitness exactly as well as exercise alone — and neither protected standing tolerance, which fell in every group
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in a 60-day bed-rest analogue (Hedge 2025)
cards.people: 24 healthy men (age 29 ± 6 years) randomised for 60 days of head-down bed rest to sedentary control (n = 8), high-intensity interval cycling exercise (n = 8), or the same exercise performed while spinning in a short-arm centrifuge (exercise + AG, n = 8); exercise on 49 of 60 days.
cards.result: Peak oxygen uptake fell 24 ± 5% in controls but was protected by exercise (Δ 0 ± 6%) and by exercise + AG (Δ +4 ± 6%; HDBR × group P < 0.001) — no added benefit from spinning during exercise. Time to presyncope fell in all groups: control −9.0 ± 3.4 min, exercise −12.4 ± 5.2 min, exercise + AG −4.5 ± 8.8 min (main effect P < 0.001). The authors conclude AG should be applied at rest or after exercise, not during it, to protect orthostatic tolerance.
cards.watchOut: The exercise + AG orthostatic figure (−4.5 min) looks gentler but carries an 8.8-minute SD in 8 men, and the trial's own interpretation is that muscle-pump activity during exercise cancels the centrifuge's orthostatic stimulus — timing, not spinning itself, is the open question.
cards.source: Hedge ET et al. Exercise during artificial gravity preserves cardiorespiratory fitness but not orthostatic tolerance following 60 days of head-down bed rest (BRACE). cards.headline: Synthesis: centrifugation at rest genuinely blunts orthostatic intolerance in bed-rest analogues; it does not protect plasma volume or fitness, and spinning during exercise adds nothing
cards.summary: Synthesis: centrifugation at rest genuinely blunts orthostatic intolerance in bed-rest analogues; it does not protect plasma volume or fitness, and spinning during exercise adds nothing
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised analogue trials — 5-day crossover (11 men), 60-day AGBRESA (24 people) and 60-day BRACE (24 men).
cards.result: Orthostatic tolerance after bed rest: 78% of baseline preserved with split-dose spins vs 36% without (Linnarsson 2015); time-to-presyncope losses of ~300 s with daily spins vs 801 s in controls at 60 days (Hoenemann 2023). But plasma volume and aerobic power were unprotected by spinning alone (Linnarsson 2015), and exercising on the centrifuge matched exercise alone for fitness while standing tolerance still fell in every group (Hedge 2025). No trial has flown a centrifuge with crew. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are head-down bed-rest analogues; the same AGBRESA campaign also found 30 min of daily centrifugation did not prevent optic disc edema, so artificial gravity at this dose is a cardiovascular countermeasure signal, not a whole-body solution.
cards.source: Synthesis of Linnarsson D et al. Journal of Applied Physiology. 2015 (PMID: 25342708); Hoenemann JN et al. Clinical Autonomic Research. 2023 (PMID: 37347452; DRKS00015677); Hedge ET et al. Journal of Applied Physiology. 2025 (PMID: 40953072).

shelves.title: Vitamin D in space: levels fell after long missions despite the old supplement dose — in the Antarctic no-sunlight test, 1,000–2,000 IU a day raised levels about 60%, and bones were protected only when good nutrition came with heavy resistance exercise
shelves.question: In spaceflight, does vitamin D supplementation (and adequate energy/nutrition generally) maintain vitamin D status and protect bone, and what dose is needed when there is no ultraviolet light?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for vitamin D status and for bone as part of an inseparable exercise-plus-nutrition package; no isolated nutritional countermeasure has a flight trial. Smith 2005 (PMID: 15735075; 11 astronauts) found serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol fell after 128–195-day missions despite supplement use (P < 0.01), with bone resorption increased. The blinded Antarctic winter-over dose study (Smith 2009, FASEB conference abstract; 66 volunteers) found 1,000 and 2,000 IU/day raised levels ~61–63% while no supplement meant a 13% fall. Smith 2012 (PMID: 22549960; 13 crew) found bone density maintained in most regions when ARED resistance exercise came with adequate energy intake and vitamin D status. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Smith 2005: despite taking vitamin D supplements in flight, astronauts' vitamin D blood levels fell by landing day (P < 0.01), while bone resorption rose
cards.summary: Smith 2005: despite taking vitamin D supplements in flight, astronauts' vitamin D blood levels fell by landing day (P < 0.01), while bone resorption rose
cards.people: 11 astronauts studied before and after long-duration (128–195 day) ISS missions, with dietary intake and limited biochemistry during flight.
cards.result: Crew ate a mean of 80% of their recommended energy intake and weighed less on landing day (P = 0.051). Despite vitamin D supplement use during flight, serum 25-hydroxycholecalciferol was decreased after flight (P < 0.01) — by 32–36% in the full text. Bone resorption markers were increased after flight, while bone formation markers did not consistently rise 1 day after landing; urinary 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine rose and red-cell superoxide dismutase fell (P < 0.05), indicating oxidative damage.
cards.watchOut: No unsupplemented comparison group — everyone supplemented — so this shows the era's supplement dose did not hold vitamin D status, not that supplementation is useless; the 32–36% figure comes from the full text rather than the abstract.
cards.source: Smith SM et al. The nutritional status of astronauts is altered after long-term space flight aboard the International Space Station. The Journal of Nutrition. 2005. PMID: 15735075. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Smith 2012: crew with the heavier resistance device, adequate energy intake and maintained vitamin D status came home with bone density virtually unchanged in most regions — the first such protection shown
cards.summary: Smith 2012: crew with the heavier resistance device, adequate energy intake and maintained vitamin D status came home with bone density virtually unchanged in most regions — the first such protection shown
cards.type: Prospective cohort comparison across exercise-device eras (Smith 2012)
cards.people: 13 crewmembers on ISS missions from 2006 to 2009 (8 with the older interim resistive exercise device, iRED; 5 with the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device, ARED, from 2008), with dietary intake, densitometry and bone biochemistry.
cards.result: Bone densitometry showed significant time-by-device interactions for pelvis BMD and bone mineral content (P < 0.01) and for femoral neck, trochanter and total hip BMD (P < 0.05), favouring ARED. Bone resorption markers rose in both groups during flight and 30 days after landing (P < 0.05), while bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (a formation marker) tended to rise in flight (P = 0.06) and rose after landing (P < 0.001). The authors conclude resistance exercise coupled with adequate energy intake and vitamin D status can maintain bone in most regions during 4- to 6-month missions.
cards.watchOut: Nutrition and the new exercise device arrived together and were never separated: this card cannot say how much of the protection was vitamin D or calories and how much was the ARED, and resorption stayed elevated throughout — formation rose to match it rather than loss being switched off.
cards.source: Smith SM et al. Benefits for bone from resistance exercise and nutrition in long-duration spaceflight: Evidence from biochemistry and densitometry. Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. 2012. PMID: 22549960. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Smith 2009 (Antarctic analogue): in a blinded winter-over dose trial, 2,000 and 1,000 IU/day of vitamin D raised blood levels by ~63% and ~61%, while levels fell 13% with no supplement
cards.summary: Smith 2009 (Antarctic analogue): in a blinded winter-over dose trial, 2,000 and 1,000 IU/day of vitamin D raised blood levels by ~63% and ~61%, while levels fell 13% with no supplement
cards.type: Blinded randomised dose-ranging study in an Antarctic analogue (Smith 2009)
cards.people: 66 volunteers wintering at McMurdo Station, Antarctica (essentially zero UV-B — a ground analogue for spaceflight), randomly divided in a blinded study to vitamin D 2,000 IU/day (n = 18), 1,000 IU/day (n = 18), 400 IU/day (n = 19) or no pill.
cards.result: In subjects completing four blood draws (n = 9, 5, 11 and 3 by group), serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D after ~5 months rose 63% on 2,000 IU/day (to 82 ± 28 nmol/L), 61% on 1,000 IU/day (to 85 ± 36 nmol/L) and 51% on 400 IU/day (to 64 ± 13 nmol/L), and fell 13% with no supplement (to 35 ± 16 nmol/L). The authors used these data to set evidence-based vitamin D doses for space crews.
cards.watchOut: A conference abstract, not a full paper, with only 28 of 66 subjects in the four-draw analysis and a non-monotonic result (1,000 IU/day ended marginally higher than 2,000 IU/day) that underlines the small numbers; it answers the blood-level question, not bone or fracture outcomes.

cards.headline: Synthesis: vitamin D status genuinely falls in flight at old supplement doses, ~1,000–2,000 IU/day holds blood levels in the Antarctic analogue, and bone protection is proven only for the combined exercise-plus-nutrition package
cards.summary: Synthesis: vitamin D status genuinely falls in flight at old supplement doses, ~1,000–2,000 IU/day holds blood levels in the Antarctic analogue, and bone protection is proven only for the combined exercise-plus-nutrition package
cards.people: The carded evidence: two astronaut cohorts (11 and 13 crew) and one blinded Antarctic dose trial (66 volunteers).
cards.result: Vitamin D status fell after flight despite supplementation (P < 0.01; Smith 2005). In the no-UV Antarctic analogue, 1,000–2,000 IU/day raised 25-hydroxyvitamin D by ~61–63% versus a 13% fall unsupplemented (Smith 2009). Bone density was maintained in most regions only when heavy resistance exercise came with adequate energy intake and vitamin D status (Smith 2012) — an inseparable package. No trial isolates a nutritional countermeasure against a clinical endpoint in flight. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for maintaining vitamin D status and, as part of the combined package, bone density; observational and analogue evidence only.
cards.watchOut: Doses on this shelf are the studied ones (400–2,000 IU/day); nothing here tests higher doses, other nutrients as isolated countermeasures, or fracture and kidney-stone outcomes, and the Antarctic trial's completer analysis is small.

shelves.title: Drugs for space muscle loss: testosterone is the only one with trial evidence — added to exercise it increased lean mass in 70 days of bed rest, but it never improved strength beyond exercise alone, and no other muscle drug has human space-analogue data
shelves.question: Beyond exercise, do pharmacologic countermeasures (testosterone or other anabolic agents) prevent muscle atrophy and strength loss during spaceflight or its bed-rest analogue?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for lean mass as an adjunct to exercise, from two small bed-rest trials of one drug; no drug preserved strength beyond exercise, and no other drug has cardable human evidence. Dillon 2018 (PMID: 29924745; NCT00891449; 70-day head-down bed rest) found lean body mass decreased in controls, held with exercise plus placebo, and increased with exercise plus cycled testosterone 100 mg/week, while leg strength was protected equally by exercise with or without the drug. The same cohort's metabolic report (Dillon 2020, NCT00891449) found testosterone protected against insulin resistance (HOMA-IR 1.45→1.07 vs 1.74→2.24 in controls) though 2-hour glucose rose. Zachwieja 1999 (10 men, 28 days) found testosterone preserved nitrogen balance and lean mass but knee extensor strength fell as much as on placebo. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), lean-mass adjunct only.

cards.headline: Dillon 2018: adding cycled low-dose testosterone to exercise made lean body mass increase during 70 days of bed rest, while exercise plus placebo merely held it and no countermeasure lost it
cards.summary: Dillon 2018: adding cycled low-dose testosterone to exercise made lean body mass increase during 70 days of bed rest, while exercise plus placebo merely held it and no countermeasure lost it
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in a bed-rest analogue (Dillon 2018)
cards.people: Healthy men (35 ± 8 years) randomised during 70 days of 6° head-down bed rest to inactive control (CON), NASA SPRINT exercise plus placebo (PEX), or exercise plus testosterone (TEX, 100 mg/week, injected 2 weeks on, 2 weeks off); arm sizes 8–9 per group in the trial reports (NCT00891449).
cards.result: Total, leg and trunk lean body mass consistently decreased in CON, increased in TEX, and showed little or no change in PEX. Total, leg and trunk fat mass consistently increased in CON and PEX and decreased in TEX. Leg strength decreased in CON, while both PEX and TEX were protected against strength loss, and changes in leg lean mass correlated positively with changes in leg strength. The abstract reports directions of change rather than kilogram values.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one cohort of young eugonadal men, an analogue — and testosterone added nothing for strength beyond exercise alone; the gain was in lean mass and fat mass. Long-term safety of androgen countermeasures in crew is untested.
cards.source: Dillon EL et al. Efficacy of Testosterone plus NASA Exercise Countermeasures during Head-Down Bed Rest. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2018. PMID: 29924745. Registry ID: NCT00891449. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Dillon 2020 (same cohort): testosterone also protected against bed-rest insulin resistance — HOMA-IR fell in the testosterone group (1.45 to 1.07) while it rose in controls (1.74 to 2.24)
cards.summary: Dillon 2020 (same cohort): testosterone also protected against bed-rest insulin resistance — HOMA-IR fell in the testosterone group (1.45 to 1.07) while it rose in controls (1.74 to 2.24)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, metabolic outcomes, same cohort as Dillon 2018 (Dillon 2020)
cards.people: The same 70-day head-down bed-rest cohort (NCT00891449): control (CON, n = 9), exercise plus placebo (PEX, n = 9) and exercise plus testosterone (TEX, n = 8), with metabolic testing before, during and after bed rest.
cards.result: HOMA-IR from pre-bed-rest to day 66 changed from 1.74 to 2.24 (CON), 1.18 to 1.47 (PEX) and 1.45 to 1.07 (TEX) — testosterone protected against bed-rest-induced insulin resistance. Two-hour oral glucose tolerance values nonetheless rose in TEX, from 5.87 to 7.08 mmol/L (approximately 106 to 128 mg/dL), and basal metabolic rate fell least in the exercise groups. The authors conclude daily exercise was beneficial but not completely protective, and testosterone may add metabolic benefit.
cards.watchOut: This is the same single cohort as the Dillon 2018 card, not independent confirmation, and its glucose-tolerance result points the other way (2-hour glucose rose most in the testosterone group) — the metabolic picture is mixed, and glucose values are printed with mg/dL equivalents per the library's US-units rule.

cards.headline: Zachwieja 1999: testosterone preserved nitrogen balance and lean mass over 28 days of bed rest but did not preserve strength — knee extensor strength fell just as much as on placebo
cards.summary: Zachwieja 1999: testosterone preserved nitrogen balance and lean mass over 28 days of bed rest but did not preserve strength — knee extensor strength fell just as much as on placebo
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial in a bed-rest analogue (Zachwieja 1999)
cards.people: 10 healthy men (age 36 ± 2 years) confined to bed for 28 days at 6° head-down tilt, all receiving daily triiodothyronine, randomised double-blind to testosterone enanthate 200 mg/week by injection (n = 6) or placebo (n = 4) (n printed on the face).
cards.result: Despite improved [13C]leucine kinetics and maintenance of nitrogen balance and lean body mass in testosterone-treated men, muscle strength was little preserved: right knee extensor best work fell from 165 ± 15 to 126 ± 18 foot-pounds on testosterone and from 179 ± 22 to 149 ± 13 foot-pounds on placebo (P = 0.011 for the decline), with no benefit from testosterone, particularly in the knee extensors.
cards.watchOut: Only 10 men (n printed on the face), and everyone also received triiodothyronine to accelerate wasting — a deliberate catabolic co-intervention that limits generalisation to astronauts; the mass–strength dissociation is the key lesson.
cards.source: Zachwieja JJ et al. Testosterone Administration Preserves Protein Balance But Not Muscle Strength during 28 Days of Bed Rest. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 1999. cards.headline: Synthesis: testosterone is the only drug with randomised analogue evidence for muscle — it adds lean mass on top of exercise and preserves protein balance, but in neither trial did it preserve strength beyond exercise or bed rest alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: testosterone is the only drug with randomised analogue evidence for muscle — it adds lean mass on top of exercise and preserves protein balance, but in neither trial did it preserve strength beyond exercise or bed rest alone
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised bed-rest trials of testosterone (the 70-day NASA cohort reported twice, NCT00891449, and a 10-man 28-day trial), all analogues, no in-flight drug trial.
cards.result: Lean mass: increased with exercise plus testosterone, held with exercise plus placebo, lost without countermeasures (Dillon 2018); nitrogen balance and lean mass likewise preserved in Zachwieja 1999. Strength: protected by exercise with or without testosterone (Dillon 2018) and not protected by testosterone without exercise (Zachwieja 1999). No other pharmacologic agent — no myostatin inhibitor or other anabolic drug — has published human spaceflight or bed-rest countermeasure evidence that could be carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for lean mass as an adjunct to exercise only.
cards.watchOut: Two of the three cards report one cohort, so the independent evidence is two small trials in young men; nothing here addresses women crew, older crew, bone (bisphosphonate flight data answer a bone question, not this muscle one), or the safety of routine androgen use on missions.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dillon EL et al. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2018 (PMID: 29924745; NCT00891449); Dillon EL et al. Life Sciences in Space Research. 2020 (PMID: not captured this session; NCT00891449); Zachwieja JJ et al. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism. 1999 (PMID: not captured this session).

shelves.title: Space motion sickness: promethazine is the proven treatment — relief within 2 hours in 14 of 15 sick crew, and in a blinded test flight sickness on only 12.6% of parabolas versus 51.8% on placebo
shelves.question: In spaceflight and its analogues, how effective are promethazine and other drugs for preventing and treating space motion sickness, and what cognitive price do they carry?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for promethazine as treatment. Davis 1993 (PMID: 11541638), comparing Shuttle debriefings, found intramuscular promethazine gave relief within 1–2 hours in 14 of 15 treated crew with no delayed symptom onset, while oral scopolamine-dextroamphetamine prophylaxis was dropped over delayed symptoms and variable early-flight absorption. Abbott 2025 (PMID: 41253367), a blinded parabolic-flight trial in 12 subjects, found motion sickness on 12.6% of parabolas with 25 mg oral promethazine versus 51.8% on placebo. Bos 2004 (PMID: 15451046; 67 volunteers) ranked the cognitive cost of the options: meclizine best, then scopolamine, promethazine, lorazepam worst. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Davis 1993: intramuscular promethazine relieved space motion sickness within 1–2 hours in 14 of 15 treated crew, with no delayed symptom onset — the result that made it NASA's treatment of choice
cards.summary: Davis 1993: intramuscular promethazine relieved space motion sickness within 1–2 hours in 14 of 15 treated crew, with no delayed symptom onset — the result that made it NASA's treatment of choice
cards.type: Comparative study of postflight debriefing data (Davis 1993)
cards.people: Crewmembers from Space Shuttle postflight debriefings: 19 treated with oral scopolamine plus dextroamphetamine (scopdex) and 15 treated with promethazine by intramuscular injection or suppository after symptoms developed.
cards.result: Fourteen of 15 crewmembers treated with intramuscular promethazine and 6 of 8 treated with promethazine suppositories had immediate (within 1–2 h) symptom relief and required no additional medication. There were no cases of delayed symptom presentation in promethazine-treated crew, whereas oral scopdex prophylaxis was associated with delayed symptom development and variable absorption of oral medications in early flight. The authors conclude promethazine is an effective in-flight treatment and NASA policy moved to treating after symptom onset rather than scopdex prophylaxis.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: treatments were compared across different crews and eras of debriefing data, relief was self-reported, and the suppository subgroup is only 8 people — but it remains the largest in-flight treatment comparison available.
cards.source: Davis JR et al. Comparison of treatment strategies for Space Motion Sickness. Acta Astronautica. 1993. PMID: 11541638. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Abbott 2025: oral promethazine 25 mg cut motion-sick parabolas from 51.8% on placebo to 12.6% in a blinded parabolic-flight trial (n = 12, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Abbott 2025: oral promethazine 25 mg cut motion-sick parabolas from 51.8% on placebo to 12.6% in a blinded parabolic-flight trial (n = 12, printed on the face)
cards.type: Controlled clinical trial in a parabolic-flight analogue (Abbott 2025)
cards.people: 12 subjects (6 women) in parabolic flight (n = 12, printed on the face), each flying a 0-g and a partial-g profile of 10 parabolas at 0, 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75 g; half received 25 mg oral promethazine before flight and half placebo, counterbalanced by sex.
cards.result: Placebo-group Pensacola Motion Sickness Questionnaire scores rose from 2.0 (SD 1.55) preflight to 9.17 (SD 5.42) postflight on the 0-g flight. Placebo subjects reported motion sickness on 51.8% of parabolas versus 12.6% with promethazine. All 6 placebo subjects reported some motion sickness; 4 of the 6 promethazine subjects reported none at all. Promethazine was effective in both 0 g and partial gravity.
cards.watchOut: Only 12 subjects (n printed on the face) and minutes-long parabolas rather than days of spaceflight; sedation and performance effects were not the outcome here, and oral dosing in real early flight is complicated by the variable absorption Davis 1993 described.
cards.source: Abbott R et al. Promethazine Effects on Motion Sickness During Altered Gravity Induced by Parabolic Flight. Aerospace Medicine and Human Performance. 2025. PMID: 41253367. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Bos 2004: among candidate space motion sickness drugs tested with rotary-chair provocation, meclizine had the best cognitive profile and lorazepam the worst — promethazine impaired working memory only when combined with spinning
cards.summary: Bos 2004: among candidate space motion sickness drugs tested with rotary-chair provocation, meclizine had the best cognitive profile and lorazepam the worst — promethazine impaired working memory only when combined with spinning
cards.type: Clinical trial of drug cognitive side effects with vestibular provocation (Bos 2004)
cards.people: 67 healthy volunteers (mean age 26.6 ± 4.8 years; 24 women, 43 men), each tested off and on drug (meclizine 25 mg, scopolamine 0.4 mg, promethazine 25 mg or lorazepam 1 mg, oral, ~45 min before testing) with a delayed matching-to-sample working-memory task, with and without vestibular stimulation by rotary chair.
cards.result: Spinning alone significantly decreased task accuracy and choice response speed, especially at longer recall delays. Promethazine alone had no adverse effect, but combined with spinning it decreased accuracy and speed. The authors' rank order for cognitive profile at clinically useful doses was meclizine > scopolamine > promethazine > lorazepam.
cards.watchOut: A ground laboratory study of side effects, not of anti-sickness efficacy in flight: it ranks the cognitive cost of the options, and separate ground data show promethazine injections can impair performance substantially — while in-flight reports paradoxically found sedation in under 5% of treated crew versus 60–73% on the ground.
cards.source: Bos JE et al. [Effects of drug countermeasures for space motion sickness on working memory in humans — bracketed descriptive title; the verbatim article title was not captured this session]. cards.headline: Synthesis: promethazine works — in-flight relief in 14 of 15 treated crew and a fourfold lower rate of sick parabolas than placebo — and its cognitive cost, while real, ranks mid-pack among the alternatives
cards.summary: Synthesis: promethazine works — in-flight relief in 14 of 15 treated crew and a fourfold lower rate of sick parabolas than placebo — and its cognitive cost, while real, ranks mid-pack among the alternatives
cards.people: The carded evidence: one in-flight comparative debriefing study (34 treated crew), one blinded parabolic-flight trial (12 subjects) and one 67-volunteer cognitive side-effect trial.
cards.result: Efficacy: immediate relief in 14/15 with intramuscular promethazine and no delayed-onset cases (Davis 1993); motion sickness on 12.6% of parabolas with oral promethazine versus 51.8% on placebo (Abbott 2025). Cost: working memory spared by promethazine alone but impaired when combined with provocation, ranking behind meclizine and scopolamine and ahead of lorazepam (Bos 2004). Scopdex oral prophylaxis was abandoned because of delayed symptoms and erratic early-flight absorption. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent efficacy across flight and analogue data, none of it from a large randomised in-flight trial.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial compares promethazine head-to-head with meclizine or scopolamine for efficacy in flight, and the sedation paradox (rare in flight, common on the ground) is unexplained — dosing route (injection after symptoms) is part of the operational answer, not a tested variable.

shelves.title: Heart and fitness in space: exercise programmes fully protected aerobic fitness in Earth bed-rest trials, yet on real station missions fitness still fell about 17% in the first two weeks despite daily exercise
shelves.question: In spaceflight and its bed-rest analogue, do exercise and other countermeasures (including post-exercise venoconstrictive thigh cuffs) prevent cardiovascular deconditioning — loss of aerobic capacity, plasma volume and cardiac function?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for exercise-based countermeasures, with documented breakthrough in flight. Moore 2014 (PMID: 24970852; 14 astronauts) found VO2peak fell ~17% by flight day 15 despite routine in-flight exercise, then partly recovered but stayed below preflight until after landing. In randomised bed-rest analogues the programmes work better: Ploutz-Snyder 2018 (PMID: 29924746; NCT00891449; 34 subjects) found integrated SPRINT exercise held peak aerobic capacity while sedentary controls lost ~10%, and the 2025 thigh-cuff randomised trial (PMID: 40605173; 24 subjects) found exercise plus post-exercise thigh cuffs limited the VO2peak fall to −106 versus −607 mL/min in controls (P < 0.001) and blunted plasma volume, stroke volume and cardiac output losses — without protecting muscle. Artificial gravity is homed on its own shelf (#5467) and not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Moore 2014: even with regular in-flight exercise, astronauts' peak oxygen uptake fell ~17% by flight day 15, then partly recovered but never regained preflight levels in flight
cards.summary: Moore 2014: even with regular in-flight exercise, astronauts' peak oxygen uptake fell ~17% by flight day 15, then partly recovered but never regained preflight levels in flight
cards.people: 14 astronauts (9 men, 5 women; 49 ± 5 years; preflight VO2peak 40.6 ± 6.4 mL·kg−1·min−1) on ISS missions of 91–192 days, exercising ~30 min/day on 5–6 days/week at ~73% of peak heart rate, with peak cycle tests ~90 days preflight, on flight day 15, every ~30 days in flight, and on recovery days 1, 10 and 30.
cards.result: VO2peak decreased early in flight (~17%) then gradually increased during flight but never returned to preflight levels; it was lower than preflight on recovery days 1 and 10 and had recovered by day 30. Peak heart rate did not differ from preflight at any point. Seven astronauts did attain their preflight VO2peak at some point in flight or on recovery day 1 — four of them exercised at higher intensities in flight — so a sustained decline was not universal.
cards.watchOut: Uncontrolled: everyone exercised, so this measures how much deconditioning breaks through the standard countermeasure rather than exercise versus none; the ~17% figure and trajectory are from the fetched abstract and full text of the record.

cards.headline: Ploutz-Snyder 2018 (SPRINT): an integrated aerobic-plus-resistance programme held peak aerobic capacity through 70 days of bed rest while sedentary controls lost ~10%, and mitigated cardiac and muscle deconditioning on either equipment suite
cards.summary: Ploutz-Snyder 2018 (SPRINT): an integrated aerobic-plus-resistance programme held peak aerobic capacity through 70 days of bed rest while sedentary controls lost ~10%, and mitigated cardiac and muscle deconditioning on either equipment suite
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in a bed-rest analogue (Ploutz-Snyder 2018)
cards.people: 34 subjects in 70 days of 6° head-down tilt bed rest, randomised to sedentary control (n = 9), exercise on traditional ISS-like equipment (n = 9), exercise plus low-dose testosterone (n = 8), or exercise on a combined flywheel device (n = 8) (NCT00891449 cohort).
cards.result: Peak aerobic capacity was maintained from pre- to post-bed-rest in all exercise groups, whereas the sedentary group declined ~10%. The SPRINT protocol mitigated bed-rest-induced muscle and cardiac deconditioning regardless of which exercise device was used, with significant interactions favouring all exercise groups over control for leg press work, isokinetic strength, vertical jump power and muscle size; bone molecular markers did not change in control or exercise groups.
cards.watchOut: An analogue trial of a programme, not of any single element: aerobic, resistance and (in one arm) testosterone elements are bundled, and 70 days of bed rest is not 6 months of flight — Moore 2014 shows breakthrough losses in flight that this analogue programme did not show.
cards.source: Ploutz-Snyder LL et al. Exercise Training Mitigates Multisystem Deconditioning during Bed Rest. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2018. PMID: 29924746. Registry ID: NCT00891449. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Thigh-cuff randomised trial 2025: aerobic exercise plus 6 hours of venoconstrictive thigh cuffs preserved fitness in 30 days of bed rest — peak oxygen uptake fell 106 mL/min with the countermeasure versus 607 mL/min in controls (P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Thigh-cuff randomised trial 2025: aerobic exercise plus 6 hours of venoconstrictive thigh cuffs preserved fitness in 30 days of bed rest — peak oxygen uptake fell 106 mL/min with the countermeasure versus 607 mL/min in controls (P < 0.001)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in a bed-rest analogue (Thigh-cuff RCT 2025)
cards.people: 24 men and women randomised to a countermeasure group (n = 12; age 34 ± 9 years) or control (n = 12; age 35 ± 8 years) for 30 days of strict 6° head-down tilt bed rest; the countermeasure was 60 min of submaximal cycling 6 days/week followed by 6 h of thigh cuffs at 50 ± 5 mmHg.
cards.result: Peak oxygen uptake was maintained in the countermeasure group (−106 ± 148 mL/min) versus controls (−607 ± 343 mL/min; P < 0.001). Plasma volume loss was blunted (−147 ± 95 vs −286 ± 153 mL; P = 0.014), as were falls in peak stroke volume (−6 ± 5 vs −21 ± 13 mL; P < 0.001) and cardiac output (−0.7 ± 0.9 vs −3.8 ± 2.1 L/min; P < 0.001). Both groups still lost fat-free mass and muscle strength — the countermeasure protected the cardiovascular system, not muscle.
cards.watchOut: Exercise and cuffs were bundled, so the cuffs' separate contribution is unknown, and 30 days is the shortest analogue on this shelf; muscle was explicitly not protected, which is why this shelf's stamp is cardiovascular only.

cards.headline: Synthesis: exercise-based countermeasures preserve aerobic capacity and blunt plasma-volume and cardiac losses in bed-rest analogues, but in real flight a ~17% early fall in aerobic capacity breaks through the standard programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: exercise-based countermeasures preserve aerobic capacity and blunt plasma-volume and cardiac losses in bed-rest analogues, but in real flight a ~17% early fall in aerobic capacity breaks through the standard programme
cards.people: The carded evidence: one in-flight astronaut cohort (14 crew), and two randomised bed-rest trials (34 and 24 subjects).
cards.result: In flight, VO2peak fell ~17% by day 15 despite routine exercise, recovering only partly in flight and fully by 30 days after landing (Moore 2014). In analogues, integrated exercise held aerobic capacity while controls lost ~10% (Ploutz-Snyder 2018), and exercise plus post-exercise thigh cuffs nearly abolished the fitness fall (−106 vs −607 mL/min) and blunted plasma volume, stroke volume and cardiac output losses (thigh-cuff RCT, PMID: 40605173). Artificial gravity, the other major cardiovascular countermeasure candidate, is homed on its own shelf and not re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — strong analogue trials, but the only flight data show partial breakthrough.
cards.watchOut: Orthostatic intolerance after flight is only partly addressed by these fitness outcomes: the BRACE trial on the artificial-gravity shelf found standing tolerance fell even when fitness was fully preserved, so a preserved VO2peak should not be read as a preserved ability to stand.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moore AD Jr et al. Journal of Applied Physiology. 2014 (PMID: 24970852); Ploutz-Snyder LL et al. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2018 (PMID: 29924746; NCT00891449); Aerobic Exercise and Subsequent Venoconstrictive Thigh Cuffs Preserve Cardiorespiratory Fitness but Not Muscle Function after 30 Days of Bed Rest. shelves.title: Social prescribing: implemented ahead of its evidence — 15 foundation evaluations all at high risk of bias, and the best trial reading is a modest activity gain (odds ratio 1.31) tied to participation, not referral
shelves.question: In primary care, does referral to a link worker / community connector (social prescribing) improve well-being and reduce loneliness?
shelves.mesh: Exercise · Humans · Prescriptions · Primary Health Care · Social Support · Social Welfare · Social Work · State Medicine · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the evidence weakness is the finding. Bickerdike 2017 (PMID: 28389486) found all 15 UK evaluations at high risk of bias and the evidence insufficient to judge success or value for money. O'Sullivan 2024 (PMID: 38863236) found 12 controlled trials (3,566 people) with poor quality overall: condition-targeted programmes improved quality of life, but general psychological well-being did not significantly change. Huang 2026 (PMID: 42865730), re-analysing 10 trial reports (4,840 participants), found higher odds of meeting physical-activity targets (OR 1.31) and suggested benefit tracks participation rather than referral. No card isolates loneliness as an outcome with an adequate trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Bickerdike 2017: 15 UK social-prescribing evaluations, every one at high risk of bias — most concluded positively anyway, and the reviewers said the evidence could not judge success or value for money
cards.summary: Bickerdike 2017: 15 UK social-prescribing evaluations, every one at high risk of bias — most concluded positively anyway, and the reviewers said the evidence could not judge success or value for money
cards.people: 15 evaluations of UK social prescribing programmes in which primary care referred patients to a link worker or facilitator, identified from nine databases (2000 to January 2016) plus reports, guidelines and websites; outcomes were health and well-being measures and health-service use.
cards.result: Most evaluations were small and limited by poor design and reporting; all were rated high risk of bias, with common problems including no comparative controls, short follow-up, non-standardised measures, missing data and unconsidered confounding. Despite this, most presented positive conclusions. The reviewers concluded that current evidence fails to provide sufficient detail to judge either success or value for money, and that future evaluations must be comparative by design.
cards.watchOut: UK-only, pre-2017 evidence: this is the baseline caution. Later cards test whether the trial base has since improved — it has, only partly.
cards.source: Bickerdike L, Booth A, Wilson PM, Farley K, Wright K. Social prescribing: less rhetoric and more reality. A systematic review of the evidence. BMJ Open. 2017. PMID: 28389486. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Exercise · Humans · Prescriptions · Primary Health Care · Social Support · Social Welfare · Social Work · State Medicine · United Kingdom

cards.headline: O'Sullivan 2024: 12 controlled trials of social prescribing in long-term conditions (3,566 people) — condition-targeted programmes improved quality of life, but general psychological well-being did not significantly change
cards.summary: O'Sullivan 2024: 12 controlled trials of social prescribing in long-term conditions (3,566 people) — condition-targeted programmes improved quality of life, but general psychological well-being did not significantly change
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of controlled trials (O'Sullivan 2024)
cards.people: 12 randomised and quasi-randomised controlled trials (n = 3,566) of social prescribing interventions in community-based adults with long-term conditions, from 11 databases; outcomes included quality of life, physical activity, psychological well-being and disease-specific measures; bias assessed with Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.
cards.result: Interventions were heterogeneous, with poor blinding and high attrition the commonest biases. Social prescribing designed for specific conditions (cancer, diabetes) showed significant improvements in quality of life (2 studies) and disease-specific psychological outcomes (3 studies); there was some evidence for physical-activity improvement (2 studies, with most changes within-group only), and no significant change in general psychological well-being. Evidence quality remains poor.
cards.watchOut: Within-group improvements are not treatment effects; the credible signal is confined to condition-targeted programmes and specific outcomes, not to social prescribing in general.
cards.source: O'Sullivan DJ, Bearne LM, Harrington JM, Cardoso JR, McVeigh JG. The effectiveness of social prescribing in the management of long-term conditions in community-based adults: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical Rehabilitation. 2024. PMID: 38863236. cards.headline: Huang 2026: Bayesian re-analysis of 10 social-prescribing trial reports (4,840 participants) — higher odds of meeting physical-activity targets (odds ratio 1.31), with benefit tied to participation rather than referral, and no dose-response
cards.summary: Huang 2026: Bayesian re-analysis of 10 social-prescribing trial reports (4,840 participants) — higher odds of meeting physical-activity targets (odds ratio 1.31), with benefit tied to participation rather than referral, and no dose-response
cards.people: 10 reports of randomised trials of social prescribing in chronic diseases, totalling 4,840 participants, re-analysed with Bayesian hierarchical models: intention-to-treat effects on physical activity, dose-response, the added benefit of programme participation, patient-reported outcomes of link-worker prescribing, and published economic evaluations.
cards.result: Social prescribing increased the likelihood of achieving recommended physical activity levels (odds ratio 1.31, 95% credible interval 1.07 to 1.67; posterior probability of benefit 0.991). No consistent dose-response was found (slope −1.29 benefit units, 95% credible interval −6.17 to 3.48). High programme participation was associated with an additional 0.26 clinically meaningful benefit units (95% credible interval −0.07 to 0.63; posterior probability of benefit 0.940). Positive effects were reported across activity, weight, blood pressure, mental health, quality of life, patient activation and function; exercise-oriented prescribing remained cost-effective at conventional thresholds, while link-worker value depended on implementation capacity.
cards.watchOut: A re-analysis, not new trial data: the participation finding is observational within trials (people who participate differ from those who do not), so 'participation, not referral' is a mechanism hypothesis, not a randomised contrast.
cards.source: Huang M, Fu G, Du Z. Bayesian re-analysis suggests participation rather than referral underlies the benefits of social prescribing for chronic diseases. Frontiers in Public Health. 2026. PMID: 42865730. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: social prescribing is widely implemented ahead of its evidence — targeted programmes show some quality-of-life gains, activity probably rises modestly, and referral alone, without participation, has no demonstrated benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: social prescribing is widely implemented ahead of its evidence — targeted programmes show some quality-of-life gains, activity probably rises modestly, and referral alone, without participation, has no demonstrated benefit
cards.people: The carded evidence: one systematic review of 15 UK evaluations, one systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 controlled trials (3,566 participants), and one Bayesian re-analysis of 10 trial reports (4,840 participants).
cards.result: The foundation evaluations were uniformly high risk of bias (Bickerdike 2017). Controlled trials since show significant quality-of-life gains only for condition-targeted programmes and no significant change in general psychological well-being (O'Sullivan 2024). The most favourable reading — activity odds ratio 1.31 with benefit concentrated in actual participants — comes from re-analysis, not from a definitive trial (Huang 2026). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Loneliness is the outcome most often claimed for social prescribing in policy, yet none of the carded syntheses rests on an adequate loneliness-outcome trial; do not read activity or quality-of-life signals as loneliness evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bickerdike L et al. BMJ Open. 2017 (PMID: 28389486); O'Sullivan DJ et al. Clinical Rehabilitation. 2024 (PMID: 38863236); Huang M, Fu G, Du Z. Frontiers in Public Health. 2026 (PMID: 42865730).

shelves.title: IMPaCT community health workers: every $1 invested returned $2.47 to a Medicaid payer within a year on randomised-trial accounting — and a 1,230-person randomised rollout in a second system cut hospital days
shelves.question: In low-income patients, does a standardised community-health-worker programme addressing social needs improve health and return on investment?
shelves.mesh: Community Health Workers · Delivery of Health Care · Humans · Investments · Medicaid · Socioeconomic Factors · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The programme's clinical-outcome trials are homed at live shelf #2004 and are cross-pointed, not re-carded; this shelf homes the value and scale-up questions. Kangovi 2020 (PMID: 32011942) calculated from the randomised trial that each $1 invested returned $2.47 to an average Medicaid payer within the fiscal year. Vasan 2026 (PMID: 40216669) randomised 1,230 patients in a second system and found fewer hospital days and better primary-care engagement, with no emergency-department difference. Knowles 2025 (PMID: 40238902) found faithful implementation at five sites, with three of five sustaining the programme and reducing acute-care use over 3 years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the return-on-investment and utilisation claims.

cards.headline: Kangovi 2020: IMPaCT's return on investment, calculated from its randomised trial, was $2.47 returned to an average Medicaid payer for every $1 invested, within the fiscal year
cards.summary: Kangovi 2020: IMPaCT's return on investment, calculated from its randomised trial, was $2.47 returned to an average Medicaid payer for every $1 invested, within the fiscal year
cards.type: Return-on-investment analysis of a randomised trial (Kangovi 2020)
cards.people: Patients in the randomised controlled trial of IMPaCT (Individualized Management for Patient-Centered Targets), a standardised community-health-worker intervention addressing unmet social needs for disadvantaged people; the return-on-investment analysis was performed for an average Medicaid payer. Trial participant N not documented in this record (the trial's clinical outcomes are homed at live shelf #2004).
cards.result: Every dollar invested in the intervention would return $2.47 to an average Medicaid payer within the fiscal year. The authors emphasise that, unlike many published return-on-investment estimates based on pre-post designs susceptible to regression to the mean, this estimate is based on a randomised controlled trial.
cards.watchOut: A payer-perspective, single-fiscal-year estimate for Medicaid: returns to other payers, over longer horizons, or counting patient and societal benefits, would differ; the figure inherits every limitation of the one trial beneath it.
cards.source: Kangovi S, Mitra N, Grande D, Long JA, Asch DA. Evidence-Based Community Health Worker Program Addresses Unmet Social Needs And Generates Positive Return On Investment. cards.headline: Vasan 2026: IMPaCT transplanted to an integrated delivery system — 1,230 low-income adults randomised — cut total hospital days (−172.3 per 1,000 members per month at 6 months) and raised primary-care engagement (85.7% vs 79.5% with at least one visit)
cards.summary: Vasan 2026: IMPaCT transplanted to an integrated delivery system — 1,230 low-income adults randomised — cut total hospital days (−172.3 per 1,000 members per month at 6 months) and raised primary-care engagement (85.7% vs 79.5% with at least one visit)
cards.type: Randomised evaluation in an integrated delivery system (Vasan 2026)
cards.people: 1,230 adults living in low-income zip codes at two clinics of an integrated health system in Portland, Oregon, randomised 2:1 to IMPaCT (n = 820) or usual care (n = 410); community health workers built tailored action plans from an in-depth interview and coached patients at least weekly for 3 months, delivered predominantly remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic. Analysis was a prospective randomised difference-in-differences evaluation.
cards.result: Compared with usual care, IMPaCT patients had a relative reduction in total hospital days at 6 months (−172.3 days per 1,000 members per month, 95% CI −320.05 to −24.53; p = 0.022), and a greater proportion attended at least one primary-care visit (85.7% vs 79.5%; p = 0.006). There were no differences in emergency department utilisation.
cards.watchOut: Remote pandemic-era delivery in one integrated system: hospital-day reductions without emergency-department change is a specific pattern, and difference-in-differences adjustment is not identical to a simple randomised contrast.
cards.source: Vasan A, Knowles M, Flerchinger S et al. Effects of a Standardized Community Health Worker Intervention on Health Care Utilization Within an Integrated Delivery System. Journal of General Internal Medicine. 2026. PMID: 40216669. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Knowles 2025: scaling IMPaCT to five distinct sites — core components were implemented with fidelity everywhere, and three of five sites both sustained the programme for 3 years and significantly reduced acute-care use
cards.summary: Knowles 2025: scaling IMPaCT to five distinct sites — core components were implemented with fidelity everywhere, and three of five sites both sustained the programme for 3 years and significantly reduced acute-care use
cards.people: Implementation of the IMPaCT community-health-worker model across five geographically and structurally distinct sites serving diverse, low-income patient populations; fidelity assessed across seven best-practice domains by structured virtual observation of community health workers, supervisors and programme directors; acute-care use evaluated by difference-in-differences against propensity-matched controls.
cards.result: Core programme components were implemented consistently across sites. Three of five sites sustained implementation over a three-year period and demonstrated significant reductions in acute-care use, consistent with the programme's previous randomised trials. The authors argue funding should be tied to evidence-based best practices (hiring, training, support, supervision) while allowing context-specific adaptation.
cards.watchOut: Two of five sites did not both sustain and show reductions — scale-up failure is part of this result, and the acute-care comparisons at scale are matched observational analyses, not randomised contrasts.
cards.source: Knowles M, Vasan A, Pan Z, Long JA, Kangovi S. Scaling an Evidence-Based Community Health Worker Program With Fidelity: Results and Lessons Learned. The Milbank Quarterly. 2025. cards.headline: Synthesis: IMPaCT is the rare social-needs programme with randomised roots — a $2.47-to-$1 Medicaid return in its home trial's accounting, fewer hospital days when transplanted and randomised elsewhere, and faithful scale-up at most, not all, sites
cards.summary: Synthesis: IMPaCT is the rare social-needs programme with randomised roots — a $2.47-to-$1 Medicaid return in its home trial's accounting, fewer hospital days when transplanted and randomised elsewhere, and faithful scale-up at most, not all, sites
cards.people: The carded evidence: one return-on-investment analysis of the programme's randomised trial, one 1,230-patient randomised evaluation in an integrated delivery system, and one five-site implementation evaluation. The programme's primary clinical-outcome reports are homed at live shelf #2004 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: The economic claim ($2.47 per $1, Kangovi 2020) rests on randomised data rather than pre-post comparison, which is its strength and its boundary: one payer, one year, one trial. Utilisation benefit replicated under randomisation in a second system (Vasan 2026). Scale-up preserved fidelity at all five sites but sustained benefit at three (Knowles 2025). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: One-home note: shelf #2004 already homes whether IMPaCT improves chronic-disease control, mental health and hospital use. This shelf must not be read as a second verdict on those outcomes; it covers return on investment, replication of utilisation effects, and scale-up fidelity.

shelves.title: Lay-led self-management programmes: small short-term gains in pain, fatigue, disability and self-efficacy across 17 trials and 7,442 participants — but no significant change in healthcare use or quality of life
shelves.question: Do lay-led self-management education programmes improve outcomes in chronic conditions?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: Small, short-term, self-reported gains — consistent across a Cochrane synthesis and the programme's own trials, with no demonstrated change in healthcare use or clinical outcomes. Foster 2007 (PMID: 17943839; 17 trials, 7,442 participants) found small statistically significant improvements in pain, disability, fatigue, depression, self-rated health, aerobic exercise and self-efficacy, and no significant differences in physician attendance, days in hospital or health-related quality of life. The founding randomised trial, Lorig 1999 (PMID: 10413387; 952 patients), found the same pattern at 6 months plus fewer hospitalisations, and a real-world before-after cohort, Lorig 2001 (PMID: 11769298; 489 with complete data), reproduced similar gains at 1 year with fewer emergency department visits. Only one trial in the Cochrane set reported outcomes beyond six months and only two reported clinical outcomes, so durability and disease control are unproven. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Foster 2007 (Cochrane): across 17 randomised trials with 7,442 participants, lay-led self-management programmes produced small improvements in pain, disability, fatigue, depression and self-efficacy — and no significant change in healthcare use or quality of life
cards.summary: Foster 2007 (Cochrane): across 17 randomised trials with 7,442 participants, lay-led self-management programmes produced small improvements in pain, disability, fatigue, depression and self-efficacy — and no significant change in healthcare use or quality of life
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Foster 2007, Cochrane)
cards.people: 17 randomised controlled trials involving 7,442 participants with chronic conditions, comparing structured lay-led self-management education programmes against no intervention or clinician-led programmes; there were no studies of children and adolescents, only one study provided data on outcomes beyond six months, and only two studies reported clinical outcomes.
cards.result: There were small, statistically significant improvements in pain (11 studies, standardised mean difference −0.10, 95% CI −0.17 to −0.04), disability (8 studies, SMD −0.15, 95% CI −0.25 to −0.05), fatigue (7 studies, SMD −0.16, 95% CI −0.23 to −0.09), depression (6 studies, SMD −0.16, 95% CI −0.24 to −0.07), self-rated general health (6 studies, weighted mean difference −0.20, 95% CI −0.31 to −0.10), aerobic exercise and cognitive symptom management, and self-efficacy (10 studies, SMD −0.30, 95% CI −0.41 to −0.19). There were no statistically significant differences in physician or general practitioner attendance, days or nights in hospital, or health-related quality of life. No adverse events were reported in any study.
cards.watchOut: Effects are small, self-reported and almost entirely short-term; the review's own conclusion is that there is no evidence these programmes improve psychological health or health-related quality of life or significantly alter healthcare use, despite the statistically significant symptom scores.
cards.source: Foster G, Taylor SJ, Eldridge SE, Ramsay J, Griffiths CJ. Self-management education programmes by lay leaders for people with chronic conditions. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2007. PMID: 17943839. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lorig 1999: in a 6-month randomised trial of 952 patients with heart disease, lung disease, stroke or arthritis, the lay-led Chronic Disease Self-Management Program improved exercise, symptom management, self-reported health, fatigue and disability, with fewer hospitalisations
cards.summary: Lorig 1999: in a 6-month randomised trial of 952 patients with heart disease, lung disease, stroke or arthritis, the lay-led Chronic Disease Self-Management Program improved exercise, symptom management, self-reported health, fatigue and disability, with fewer hospitalisations
cards.people: 952 patients aged 40 years or older with a physician-confirmed diagnosis of heart disease, lung disease, stroke or arthritis, in a six-month randomised controlled trial at community-based sites comparing the self-management programme with wait-list control; outcomes were measured by mailed, self-administered questionnaires.
cards.result: At 6 months, treatment subjects compared with controls demonstrated improvements in weekly minutes of exercise, frequency of cognitive symptom management, communication with physicians, self-reported health, health distress, fatigue, disability and social/role activities limitations. They also had fewer hospitalizations and days in the hospital. No differences were found in pain/physical discomfort (outcome list as reported in the record).
cards.watchOut: A wait-list control and self-reported outcomes invite expectancy effects, and the comparison lasts only 6 months; this programme's trials are also inside the Foster 2007 synthesis, so the two cards are not fully independent evidence.

cards.headline: Lorig 2001: in a real-world Kaiser Permanente cohort, the same lay-led programme reproduced the trial's gains at 1 year — better health behaviours, self-efficacy and health status, and fewer emergency department visits (0.4 to 0.3 per 6 months, P = 0.05)
cards.summary: Lorig 2001: in a real-world Kaiser Permanente cohort, the same lay-led programme reproduced the trial's gains at 1 year — better health behaviours, self-efficacy and health status, and fewer emergency department visits (0.4 to 0.3 per 6 months, P = 0.05)
cards.type: Before-after cohort study in a real-world setting (Lorig 2001)
cards.people: 613 patients recruited from Kaiser Permanente hospitals and clinics, of whom 489 had complete baseline and follow-up data; the programme is a 7-week, small-group intervention for people with different chronic conditions, taught largely by peer instructors from a highly structured manual.
cards.result: At 1 year, participants experienced statistically significant improvements in health behaviors (exercise, cognitive symptom management and communication with physicians), self-efficacy, and health status (fatigue, shortness of breath, pain, role function, depression and health distress), and had fewer visits to the emergency department (0.4 visits in the 6 months prior to baseline, compared with 0.3 in the 6 months prior to follow-up; P = 0.05). Outpatient physician visits and days in hospital were slightly fewer but not statistically significant. Programme costs were estimated at about $200 per participant.
cards.watchOut: No control group: before-after gains in a self-selected programme cohort can reflect regression to the mean and volunteer effects, which is why this card supports, but cannot substitute for, the randomised evidence.
cards.source: Lorig KR, Sobel DS, Ritter PL, Laurent D, Hobbs M. Effect of a self-management program on patients with chronic disease. Effective Clinical Practice. 2001. PMID: 11769298. cards.headline: Synthesis: lay-led self-management programmes give small, short-term improvements in symptoms, self-efficacy and exercise, with no proven change in healthcare use, quality of life or clinical disease outcomes
cards.summary: Synthesis: lay-led self-management programmes give small, short-term improvements in symptoms, self-efficacy and exercise, with no proven change in healthcare use, quality of life or clinical disease outcomes
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane synthesis (17 trials, 7,442 participants), one randomised trial of the flagship programme (952 patients) and one real-world before-after cohort (489 with complete data).
cards.result: Foster 2007 pooled small significant effects on pain (SMD −0.10), disability (−0.15), fatigue (−0.16), depression (−0.16) and self-efficacy (−0.30), with no significant differences in physician attendance, hospital days or health-related quality of life (PMID: 17943839). Lorig 1999 found the same pattern under randomisation at 6 months, plus fewer hospitalisations (PMID: 10413387), and Lorig 2001 found similar gains and fewer emergency department visits at 1 year in routine practice (PMID: 11769298). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but small and short-term, on self-reported outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Almost nothing is known beyond six months and almost nothing about clinical measures of disease: a programme can honestly be offered as helping people feel and function a little better, not as controlling their condition.

shelves.title: Nurse staffing, skill mix and inpatient mortality (observational only): each additional patient per nurse was associated with about 7% higher odds of 30-day mortality in Pennsylvania and in nine European countries, and shifts staffed below target with higher mortality in a US centre
shelves.question: In hospital inpatients, do higher nurse staffing levels and richer skill mix reduce patient mortality versus leaner staffing?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Comorbidity · Education, Nursing · Educational Status · Europe · Female · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nursing Administration Research · Nursing Staff, Hospital · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Personnel Staffing and Scheduling · Postanesthesia Nursing · Quality Indicators, Health Care · Retrospective Studies · Workforce · Workload
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only, printed on the face: leaner registered-nurse staffing is associated with higher inpatient mortality. Each additional patient per nurse carried 7% higher odds of 30-day mortality in 168 Pennsylvania hospitals (odds ratio 1.07; PMID: 12387650) and in 300 European hospitals in RN4CAST (odds ratio 1.068; PMID: 24581683), where every 10% increase in bachelor's-degree nurses was associated with 7% lower mortality odds (0.929). Within one US academic centre, exposure to shifts staffed 8 or more hours below target carried a hazard ratio of 1.02 per shift (PMID: 21410372). No randomised staffing trial is carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: leaner staffing and leaner skill mix are associated with higher patient mortality.

cards.headline: Aiken 2014 (RN4CAST): in 300 European hospitals, each additional patient per nurse was associated with 7% higher odds of 30-day mortality, and each 10% more bachelor's-degree nurses with 7% lower odds
cards.summary: Aiken 2014 (RN4CAST): in 300 European hospitals, each additional patient per nurse was associated with 7% higher odds of 30-day mortality, and each 10% more bachelor's-degree nurses with 7% lower odds
cards.people: 422,730 patients aged 50 years or older who underwent common surgeries in 300 hospitals in nine European countries, with discharge data for 30-day in-hospital mortality; staffing and education measured by surveys of 26,516 nurses practising in the study hospitals.
cards.result: An increase in a nurse's workload by one patient increased the likelihood of an inpatient dying within 30 days of admission by 7% (odds ratio 1.068, 95% CI 1.031 to 1.106), and every 10% increase in bachelor's degree nurses was associated with a decrease in this likelihood by 7% (odds ratio 0.929, 95% CI 0.886 to 0.973), after adjusting for hospital and patient characteristics including age, sex, admission type, surgery type and comorbidities.
cards.watchOut: Hospital-level staffing measured by nurse survey, linked to patient outcomes at hospital level: hospitals with richer staffing differ in funding, case mix and everything else, and risk adjustment cannot make this a randomised comparison.
cards.source: Aiken LH et al. Nurse staffing and education and hospital mortality in nine European countries: a retrospective observational study. Lancet. 2014. PMID: 24581683. cards.headline: Needleman 2011: within one large academic centre, patient exposure to shifts staffed 8 or more hours below the registered-nurse target was associated with higher mortality (hazard ratio 1.02 per such shift)
cards.summary: Needleman 2011: within one large academic centre, patient exposure to shifts staffed 8 or more hours below the registered-nurse target was associated with higher mortality (hazard ratio 1.02 per such shift)
cards.people: 197,961 admissions and 176,696 nursing shifts of 8 hours in 43 hospital units of a large tertiary academic medical centre in the United States; staffing was within 8 hours of target on 84% of shifts. Overall mortality was 61% of the expected rate for similar patients.
cards.result: There was a significant association between increased mortality and increased exposure to unit shifts during which registered-nurse staffing was 8 hours or more below the target level (hazard ratio per such shift 1.02, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.03, P<0.001), adjusted for patient and unit characteristics. High patient turnover (admissions, transfers and discharges) was also associated with mortality (hazard ratio per high-turnover shift 1.04, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.06, P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The strongest design here — it links individual patients to the shifts they actually experienced — but it is a single centre whose overall mortality was already 61% of expected, and a hazard ratio of 1.02 per understaffed shift is small and observational.
cards.source: Needleman J et al. Nurse staffing and inpatient hospital mortality. New England Journal of Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21410372. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Aiken 2002: in 168 Pennsylvania hospitals, each additional patient per nurse was associated with 7% higher odds of dying within 30 days and 7% higher odds of failure-to-rescue
cards.summary: Aiken 2002: in 168 Pennsylvania hospitals, each additional patient per nurse was associated with 7% higher odds of dying within 30 days and 7% higher odds of failure-to-rescue
cards.people: 232,342 general, orthopaedic and vascular surgery patients discharged from 168 nonfederal adult general hospitals in Pennsylvania between 1 April 1998 and 30 November 1999, linked to surveys of 10,184 staff nurses and hospital administrative data.
cards.result: After adjusting for patient and hospital characteristics (size, teaching status and technology), each additional patient per nurse was associated with a 7% increase in the likelihood of dying within 30 days of admission (odds ratio 1.07, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.12) and a 7% increase in the odds of failure-to-rescue (odds ratio 1.07, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.11). Each additional patient per nurse was also associated with 23% higher odds of nurse burnout (1.23, 95% CI 1.13 to 1.34) and 15% higher odds of job dissatisfaction (1.15, 95% CI 1.07 to 1.25).
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional: staffing and outcomes measured in the same period, so sicker, harder-to-staff hospitals can generate the association in either direction; the consistency with the later European and within-centre studies is what carries weight.
cards.source: Aiken LH et al. Hospital nurse staffing and patient mortality, nurse burnout, and job dissatisfaction. JAMA. 2002. PMID: 12387650. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three observational studies on three designs agree — leaner registered-nurse staffing is associated with higher inpatient mortality, at about 7% higher odds per additional patient per nurse, and richer degree-level skill mix with lower mortality
cards.summary: Synthesis: three observational studies on three designs agree — leaner registered-nurse staffing is associated with higher inpatient mortality, at about 7% higher odds per additional patient per nurse, and richer degree-level skill mix with lower mortality
cards.people: The carded evidence: one nine-country retrospective study (422,730 surgical patients, 300 hospitals), one within-centre shift-level study (197,961 admissions, 176,696 shifts) and one cross-sectional study (232,342 surgical patients, 168 hospitals). All evidence is observational; no randomised staffing trial is carded.
cards.result: Each additional patient per nurse was associated with 7% higher odds of 30-day mortality in both Pennsylvania in 1998–99 (odds ratio 1.07; Aiken 2002) and Europe two decades later (odds ratio 1.068; RN4CAST, Aiken 2014), and RN4CAST also found every 10% more bachelor's-degree nurses associated with 7% lower mortality odds (0.929). At shift level, exposure to shifts staffed 8 or more hours below target carried a hazard ratio of 1.02 per shift (Needleman 2011). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only: leaner nurse staffing is associated with higher inpatient mortality.
cards.watchOut: All three studies are observational and two share a research group and method family; hospitals that can staff richly differ systematically from hospitals that cannot, so the per-patient odds ratios should not be read as the certain effect of adding one nurse.
cards.source: Synthesis of Aiken LH et al. Lancet. 2014 (PMID: 24581683); Needleman J et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21410372); Aiken LH et al. JAMA. 2002 (PMID: 12387650).
