shelves.title: Folic acid dose in pregnancy on anti-seizure medications: SPLIT — guidelines say high-dose 5 mg, but register data show no dose benefit against malformations
shelves.question: Does folic acid dose need to be higher in pregnant women taking anti-seizure medications?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Folic Acid · Pregnancy · Anticonvulsants · Epilepsy · Adult · Preconception Care · Neural Tube Defects · Dietary Supplements · Pregnancy Complications · Young Adult · Retrospective Studies · Prenatal Care
shelves.balance: SPLIT — guideline practice and outcome data point in different directions. International guidelines, as documented in a 10-year maternity-hospital review, recommend high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily, at least three months before conception) for women at increased neural-tube-defect risk, and women taking anti-seizure medications are treated as that group; in that review 65.6% of 250 women with epilepsy on anti-seizure medications took high-dose 5 mg before conception. But the largest dose-specific outcome dataset carded — the Australian pregnancy register, 2,104 folic-acid-treated pregnancies — found no statistically significant effect of folic acid dosage on overall fetal malformation rates (P = 0.640 for use before and during pregnancy) or on spina bifida (P = 0.409), and its authors conclude it would be misguided to hope 5 mg/day protects against valproate- and other drug-associated malformations. Safety is not settled either: a Scandinavian register cohort found prenatal high-dose folic acid exposure (mean 4.3 mg) in children of mothers with epilepsy was associated with childhood cancer at an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.7 (a relative measure; absolute risk 1.4% versus 0.6%), and a 2015 review urged against advocating high doses until safe, optimal dosing is known, citing drug interactions and animal data. So the higher dose is what guidelines direct, but no carded study demonstrates that the higher dose prevents more malformations than standard doses. PROPOSED SPLIT (guidelines: use high-dose 5 mg periconceptionally; register outcome data: no demonstrated dose benefit, with an unresolved safety signal).

cards.headline: Turner 2025: guidelines recommend high-dose 5 mg folic acid before conception for women on anti-seizure medications — and two-thirds complied, but compliance was worst (30.8%) in women on valproate
cards.summary: Turner 2025: guidelines recommend high-dose 5 mg folic acid before conception for women on anti-seizure medications — and two-thirds complied, but compliance was worst (30.8%) in women on valproate
cards.type: Retrospective review of periconceptual supplementation practice (Turner 2025)
cards.people: Ten-year review (2013–2022) at a large maternity hospital: of 75,869 women who delivered a baby over 499 g, 632 (0.83%) had epilepsy and 250 (0.33%) were taking anti-seizure medications at antenatal presentation — most often lamotrigine (n = 98) and levetiracetam (n = 89); 211 (84.4%) were on monotherapy and 39 (15.6%) on polytherapy.
cards.result: The review states the governing recommendation: women at increased risk of a neural-tube-defect pregnancy should start high-dose folic acid (5 mg daily) at least three months before conceiving, and periconceptual folic acid potentially prevents two-thirds of neural tube defect cases. Of the 250 women, 188 (75.2%) took folic acid before conception — 164 (65.6%) at high-dose 5 mg and 24 (9.6%) at low-dose 0.4 mg — while 59 (23.6%) started only after conception and 3 (1.2%) took none. Guideline compliance in the 16 women taking valproate was 30.8% versus 76.0% for the other 234 women (P < 0.03), and 72.5% on monotherapy versus 25.6% on polytherapy (P < 0.03). The study measures compliance, not whether the 5 mg dose prevents more defects than 0.4 mg, and reports no malformation outcomes by dose.
cards.watchOut: A compliance audit cannot answer a dose-effectiveness question: it documents what guidelines say and what women took, and its two-thirds-prevention figure is the guideline rationale, not a result measured in these 250 women.
cards.source: Turner C et al. A 10-year review of periconceptual folic acid supplementation in women with epilepsy taking antiseizure medications. J Matern Fetal Neonatal Med. 2025. PMID: 40588438. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vajda 2021: in 2,104 folic-acid-treated pregnancies, folic acid DOSE showed no significant relationship with malformation rates (P = 0.640) or spina bifida (P = 0.409)
cards.summary: Vajda 2021: in 2,104 folic-acid-treated pregnancies, folic acid DOSE showed no significant relationship with malformation rates (P = 0.640) or spina bifida (P = 0.409)
cards.people: Statistical analysis of the Australian Register of Antiepileptic Drugs in Pregnancy: 2,104 folic-acid-treated pregnancies in women with epilepsy taking antiepileptic drugs, examining whether folic acid dose related to protection against valproate-associated and other drug-associated fetal structural malformations.
cards.result: Multiple-variable logistic regression failed to demonstrate any statistically significant effect of folic acid dosage in reducing overall fetal malformation rates in women taking folic acid before and during pregnancy (P = 0.640) or during early pregnancy only (P = 0.801), and in reducing spina bifida occurrence rates (P = 0.409) — on dose, the treatment made no difference that this register could detect. The authors conclude that, in the present state of knowledge, it would seem misguided to hope that a folic acid dose of 5 mg/day taken before and during pregnancy would protect against valproate-associated and other antiepileptic-drug-associated fetal structural malformations, and that future studies must test other outcomes such as postnatal neurobehavioral development. The record reports P values without dose-stratified malformation rates, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Register data are observational: women prescribed 5 mg differ from women prescribed 0.4 mg (higher-risk drugs, prior affected pregnancies), which biases against finding a dose benefit — but the burden of proof for 'higher is better' sits with the higher dose, and this dataset does not meet it.
cards.source: Vajda FJE et al. Folic acid dose, valproate, and fetal malformations. Epilepsy Behav. 2021. PMID: 33272896. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Vegrim 2022: prenatal high-dose folic acid in mothers with epilepsy was associated with childhood cancer — adjusted hazard ratio 2.7 (relative); absolute risk 1.4% versus 0.6%
cards.summary: Vegrim 2022: prenatal high-dose folic acid in mothers with epilepsy was associated with childhood cancer — adjusted hazard ratio 2.7 (relative); absolute risk 1.4% versus 0.6%
cards.people: Nationwide register cohort from Denmark, Norway and Sweden (1997–2017): 3,379,171 children, of whom 27,784 were born to mothers with epilepsy; 5,934 (21.4%) of those were exposed to high-dose folic acid (prescription fills of at least 1 mg daily from 90 days before pregnancy to birth; mean dose 4.3 mg). Median follow-up age was 7.3 years.
cards.result: Among children of mothers with epilepsy, 18 exposed versus 29 unexposed cancer cases gave an adjusted hazard ratio of 2.7 (95% CI 1.2 to 6.3 — a relative measure), with absolute risk 1.4% (95% CI 0.5% to 3.6%) if exposed versus 0.6% (95% CI 0.3% to 1.1%) if unexposed. In children of mothers without epilepsy, high-dose exposure gave an adjusted hazard ratio of 1.1 (95% CI 0.9 to 1.4; absolute risk 0.4%). There was no increased cancer risk in children of mothers with epilepsy who were exposed to anti-seizure medications but not high-dose folic acid (absolute risk 0.6%).
cards.watchOut: Only 18 exposed cancer cases drive the headline ratio, the confidence interval is wide, and mothers prescribed high-dose folate differ systematically from those who are not — this is a signal demanding study, not proof that 5 mg causes cancer.
cards.source: Vegrim HM et al. Cancer Risk in Children of Mothers With Epilepsy and High-Dose Folic Acid Use During Pregnancy. JAMA Neurol. 2022. PMID: 36156660. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Asadi-Pooya 2015: a safety review concludes high-dose folic acid should NOT be advocated in women with epilepsy until safe, optimal dosing is known
cards.summary: Asadi-Pooya 2015: a safety review concludes high-dose folic acid should NOT be advocated in women with epilepsy until safe, optimal dosing is known
cards.people: Expert review of high-dose folic acid supplementation in women with epilepsy, weighing the established role of folic acid in preventing neural tube defects against potential drug–drug interactions between high folic acid doses and some antiepileptic drugs and emerging animal evidence that high folate levels throughout gestation may adversely affect fetal brain development.
cards.result: The review records the standard recommendation that all women of childbearing potential take at least 0.4 mg folic acid daily before conception and during pregnancy, and that women with epilepsy should be supplemented daily before conception and during pregnancy. It reports no new comparative outcome data and no effect size for any dose — none is printed here. Its conclusion is cautionary: it is not suggested to advocate high-dose folic acid supplementation in women with epilepsy until more information is available about its appropriate, safe and optimal dosing.
cards.watchOut: An opinion-bearing review resting partly on animal data: it marks genuine professional disagreement about the high-dose policy, but it is not outcome evidence and does not show standard doses are equally protective.
cards.source: Asadi-Pooya AA et al. High dose folic acid supplementation in women with epilepsy: are we sure it is safe? Seizure. 2015. PMID: 25891927. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — guidelines direct high-dose 5 mg, but the register data show no dose benefit for malformations and carry an unresolved childhood-cancer signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — guidelines direct high-dose 5 mg, but the register data show no dose benefit for malformations and carry an unresolved childhood-cancer signal
cards.people: The carded evidence: a 10-year practice review documenting the guideline (250 women on anti-seizure medications), a 2,104-pregnancy register dose analysis, a 3.38-million-child register cohort for the safety outcome, and a cautionary expert review. No randomised trial of folic acid dose in this population is carded, because none was found in the records fetched.
cards.result: Guideline dose: 5 mg daily from at least 3 months before conception (Turner 2025). Dose versus malformations: no significant effect (P = 0.640; spina bifida P = 0.409) (Vajda 2021). High-dose exposure and childhood cancer in epilepsy: adjusted hazard ratio 2.7 relative, absolute 1.4% versus 0.6% (Vegrim 2022). PROPOSED SPLIT (guideline recommendation: higher dose; demonstrated outcome benefit of the higher dose: none in the carded data).
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not advise any woman to stop or reduce prescribed folate: it records that the high-dose policy is guideline-based while its incremental benefit over standard doses is unproven — a question only a prospective study can close.

shelves.title: Tapering gabapentin after long-term use (weak evidence): no taper-schedule trial exists — reduce gradually rather than stopping abruptly, slower after long use, high doses, or a substance-use history
shelves.question: How should gabapentin be tapered in patients taking it long term for chronic pain?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Anxiety Agents · Anxiety Disorders · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Lorazepam · Male · Middle Aged · Pregabalin · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Recurrence · Severity of Illness Index · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). No randomised trial of gabapentin taper schedules in chronic pain was found in the records fetched this session — the 'how' of tapering rests on gabapentinoid discontinuation data and the dependence literature, and the shelf grades itself accordingly. The closest controlled evidence is for the sister drug pregabalin: in a randomised trial programme, a 1-week taper after 12 or 24 weeks of treatment produced low discontinuation symptom scores (Physician Withdrawal Checklist increases of 1.7–2.8 points across pregabalin dose groups) and rebound anxiety rates of 0–6% (Kasper 2014, PMID: 24351233). The dependence reviews explain who needs a slower taper: across 106 studies there was no convincing evidence of strong addictive power in ordinary patients — only 4 reported cases of behavioural dependence without a prior abuse history — with risk concentrated in people with current or past substance-use disorders, especially opioid use (Bonnet 2017, PMID: 28988943); a second review put gabapentinoid abuse prevalence at 1.6% in the general population versus 3–68% among opioid abusers (Evoy 2017, PMID: 28144823). At the severe end, a 38-patient inpatient gabapentinoid detoxification cohort records that abrupt cessation is associated with adverse events such as seizures, and most patients completed a supervised detoxification (Priyam 2026, PMID: 42366702). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): taper gradually rather than stopping abruptly — a short taper sufficed after months of pregabalin in trial conditions, but long-term, high-dose gabapentin use, and any substance-use history, argue for a slower, monitored reduction; the specific week-by-week schedule is practice consensus, not trial evidence, and is not dressed up as such here.

cards.headline: Kasper 2014: after 12–24 weeks of pregabalin (the sister gabapentinoid), a 1-week taper produced low discontinuation symptoms and 0–6% rebound anxiety — the only controlled taper data carded
cards.summary: Kasper 2014: after 12–24 weeks of pregabalin (the sister gabapentinoid), a 1-week taper produced low discontinuation symptoms and 0–6% rebound anxiety — the only controlled taper data carded
cards.type: Randomised discontinuation study — pregabalin class evidence (Kasper 2014)
cards.people: Randomised, double-blind, placebo- and lorazepam-controlled multicentre trial programme in generalised anxiety disorder across 16 countries: pregabalin 450–600 mg/day, pregabalin 150–300 mg/day, or lorazepam 3–4 mg/day, in two 12-week treatment periods each followed by a 1-week taper and two post-discontinuation assessments. Total participant N is not documented in the record fetched. Evidence type: randomised discontinuation assessment — for pregabalin, not gabapentin, and labelled as class evidence.
cards.result: Low levels of discontinuation symptoms were seen in all groups. For patients treated through both periods, mean increases on the Physician Withdrawal Checklist from the last on-treatment visit to the second post-discontinuation assessment were 2.8 (95% CI 1.6 to 3.9) for pregabalin 450–600 mg/day, 1.7 (0.7 to 2.8) for pregabalin 150–300 mg/day and 2.2 (1.0 to 3.5) for lorazepam. Rates of rebound anxiety were low at both 12 and 24 weeks (0–6%). The authors conclude the risk of discontinuation symptoms and rebound anxiety is low for pregabalin after 12 and 24 weeks of treatment, using a 1-week taper.
cards.watchOut: Pregabalin is not gabapentin, 24 weeks is not years of chronic-pain use, and trial patients were not selected for dependence — this card shows a short taper can suffice in favourable conditions, not that it will after long-term high-dose gabapentin.
cards.source: Kasper S et al. Pregabalin long-term treatment and assessment of discontinuation in patients with generalized anxiety disorder. The international journal of neuropsychopharmacology. 2014. PMID: 24351233. Registry ID: NCT00624780. cards.headline: Bonnet 2017: across 106 studies, gabapentinoid dependence in patients without a substance-use history was rare (4 behavioural-dependence cases) — risk concentrates in people with substance-use disorders
cards.summary: Bonnet 2017: across 106 studies, gabapentinoid dependence in patients without a substance-use history was rare (4 behavioural-dependence cases) — risk concentrates in people with substance-use disorders
cards.people: Systematic review of 106 studies of gabapentin and pregabalin addiction risk, drawing on clinical studies and pharmacovigilance databases. Evidence type: systematic review of dependence and withdrawal literature.
cards.result: The reviewers found no convincing evidence of a vigorous addictive power of gabapentinoids: rewarding properties were limited, relapses marginal, and there were very few cases of gabapentinoid-related behavioural dependence symptoms in patients without a prior abuse history (N = 4). No publication described people seeking treatment for gabapentinoid use. Pregabalin appeared somewhat more addictive than gabapentin. The principal at-risk population was patients with other current or past substance-use disorders, mostly opioid and multi-drug users; pure gabapentinoid overdoses appeared relatively safe but can be lethal in mixture with opioids and sedatives. The authors recommend avoiding gabapentinoids in patients with a substance-use history, or using them with strict monitoring.
cards.watchOut: A review of addiction liability is not a taper trial: it identifies who is at risk of a hard discontinuation (substance-use history) rather than how fast anyone should reduce — and absence of treatment-seeking reports may reflect under-recognition as much as safety.
cards.source: Bonnet U et al. How addictive are gabapentin and pregabalin? A systematic review. European neuropsychopharmacology : the journal of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology. 2017. PMID: 28988943. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Evoy 2017: gabapentinoid abuse prevalence was 1.6% in the general population but 3–68% among opioid abusers — the taper-risk gradient in one pair of numbers
cards.summary: Evoy 2017: gabapentinoid abuse prevalence was 1.6% in the general population but 3–68% among opioid abusers — the taper-risk gradient in one pair of numbers
cards.people: Systematic review of 59 studies (24 epidemiological, 3 clinical abuse-liability, 16 abuse/misuse/dependence case reports or series, and 17 acute-overdose reports) of pregabalin and gabapentin abuse, misuse and overdose, indexed to July 2016, including US FDA data. Evidence type: systematic review.
cards.result: Increasing numbers of patients self-administer higher-than-recommended doses for euphoric effects. Abuse prevalence was 1.6% in the general population and ranged from 3% to 68% among opioid abusers. An international adverse-event database held 11,940 reports of gabapentinoid abuse from 2004–2015, over 75% of them since 2012. Risk factors were a history of substance abuse (particularly opioids) and psychiatric comorbidity; high-dose effects are generally non-lethal, though gabapentinoids are increasingly found in post-mortem toxicology.
cards.watchOut: Abuse epidemiology is not withdrawal physiology: these numbers justify screening for substance-use history before setting taper speed, but they do not measure how often ordinary long-term pain patients get withdrawal symptoms on a slow taper.
cards.source: Evoy KE et al. Abuse and Misuse of Pregabalin and Gabapentin. Drugs. 2017. PMID: 28144823. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Priyam 2026: in the largest inpatient gabapentinoid detoxification cohort (N = 38 on the face), abrupt cessation is associated with seizures — and most patients completed a supervised detoxification
cards.summary: Priyam 2026: in the largest inpatient gabapentinoid detoxification cohort (N = 38 on the face), abrupt cessation is associated with seizures — and most patients completed a supervised detoxification
cards.people: Retrospective observational cohort of all 38 patients admitted for gabapentinoid detoxification to a large regional specialist unit in Manchester, UK, 2017–2022 (mean age 38.9 years; 35 of 38 required detoxification from multiple substances). Cohort N = 38.
cards.result: The majority completed detoxification successfully. Relapse (p < 0.001), complications (p = 0.001), personality disorders (p = 0.034) and concurrent benzodiazepine (p = 0.011) or opioid detoxification (p = 0.025) were significantly associated with incomplete detoxification; illicit pregabalin use and multiple concurrent detoxifications were not related to outcome. The record states that abrupt cessation is associated with adverse events such as seizures, and that no standardised withdrawal scales or treatment regimens exist.
cards.watchOut: These are dependent, mostly multi-substance inpatients — the severe extreme of gabapentinoid use, not chronic-pain patients on stable prescribed doses. The card's transferable lesson is narrow: do not stop abruptly; supervised gradual reduction usually succeeds.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no gabapentin taper trial exists in the fetched records — taper gradually, faster only when use has been short and uncomplicated, slower after long use, high doses or a substance-use history
cards.summary: Synthesis: no gabapentin taper trial exists in the fetched records — taper gradually, faster only when use has been short and uncomplicated, slower after long use, high doses or a substance-use history
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised pregabalin discontinuation programme using a 1-week taper (total N not documented in the record), two systematic reviews of gabapentinoid dependence (106 and 59 studies), and one 38-patient inpatient detoxification cohort. No study carded randomised long-term gabapentin users with chronic pain to different taper schedules. The reviews and cohort each exceed or describe populations over 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the detoxification cohort's N = 38 is printed on its face.
cards.result: A 1-week pregabalin taper after 12–24 weeks produced small withdrawal-checklist increases (1.7–2.8 points) and 0–6% rebound anxiety (Kasper 2014). Dependence without a prior abuse history was rare across 106 studies (4 cases; Bonnet 2017), with abuse prevalence of 1.6% generally versus 3–68% in opioid abusers (Evoy 2017). Abrupt cessation is associated with seizures, and most supervised detoxifications completed (Priyam 2026). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Any specific taper calendar (per-week percentage cuts, total duration) offered for long-term gabapentin in chronic pain is extrapolation and consensus, not something a carded trial has tested — this shelf deliberately prints the evidence gradient (duration, dose, substance-use history) instead of inventing a schedule.

shelves.title: Blepharitis: warm compresses and lid hygiene relieve symptoms about as well as antibiotic ointment in the available evidence — but no adequate head-to-head trial exists, and no treatment is proven to cure chronic blepharitis
shelves.question: For blepharitis, is warm compress and lid hygiene as effective as antibiotic ointment?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Bacterial Agents · Blepharitis · Chronic Disease · Humans · Hygiene · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Steroids
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no head-to-head trial establishes either treatment as superior, and the Cochrane review (Lindsley 2012, PMID: 22592706; 34 studies, 2,169 participants) found topical antibiotics gave some symptomatic relief and eradicated bacteria from the lid margin in anterior blepharitis, while lid hygiene may provide symptomatic relief for both anterior and posterior blepharitis — and concluded there is no strong evidence for any treatment in terms of curing chronic blepharitis. Direct warm-compress studies are small and device-focused: in 42 patients, heated eye masks improved meibomian gland function while a warm face cloth did not (Murphy 2020, PMID: 31657234), and in a 75-patient randomised trial a steam device beat a warm towel on symptoms while the towel itself still helped about half of users (Sim 2014, PMID: 25156975). A meta-analysis of thermal pulsation versus warm compresses (Pang 2019, PMID: 30844843) shows device treatment can beat compresses on gland measures, which underlines that 'warm compress' is not one uniform treatment. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): warm compresses and lid hygiene appear to give symptomatic relief of the same order as antibiotic ointment and remain the reasonable first step, but equivalence has never been tested in an adequate head-to-head trial, and antibiotics additionally clear lid-margin bacteria in anterior disease.

cards.headline: Lindsley 2012 (Cochrane): across 34 studies and 2,169 participants, topical antibiotics relieved symptoms and eradicated lid-margin bacteria, lid hygiene may relieve symptoms — and no treatment had strong evidence of curing chronic blepharitis
cards.summary: Lindsley 2012 (Cochrane): across 34 studies and 2,169 participants, topical antibiotics relieved symptoms and eradicated lid-margin bacteria, lid hygiene may relieve symptoms — and no treatment had strong evidence of curing chronic blepharitis
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised and quasi-randomised trials in adults aged 16 or older with chronic blepharitis: 34 studies with 2,169 participants — 20 studies (1,661 participants) in anterior or mixed blepharitis and 14 studies (508 participants) in posterior blepharitis (meibomian gland dysfunction). Interventions included medical treatment and lid hygiene measures; heterogeneity limited meta-analysis.
cards.result: Topical antibiotics were shown to provide some symptomatic relief and were effective in eradicating bacteria from the eyelid margin for anterior blepharitis. Lid hygiene may provide symptomatic relief for anterior and posterior blepharitis. The effectiveness of other treatments, such as topical steroids and oral antibiotics, was inconclusive. The authors conclude that despite 34 trials there is no strong evidence for any of the treatments in terms of curing chronic blepharitis, and that medical interventions should be compared with conventional lid hygiene measures such as warm compresses and eyelid margin washing, as well as head-to-head.
cards.watchOut: The review predates newer Demodex-directed and device therapies and pools many small, heterogeneous trials; its central message for this shelf is the absence of a demonstrated winner, not proof that all treatments are equal.
cards.source: Lindsley K et al. Interventions for chronic blepharitis. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2012. PMID: 22592706. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Murphy 2020: in 42 patients, heated eye masks improved meibomian gland dysfunction over 8 weeks while a warm face cloth did not — how the compress is delivered changes what it does (small study, N on the face)
cards.summary: Murphy 2020: in 42 patients, heated eye masks improved meibomian gland dysfunction over 8 weeks while a warm face cloth did not — how the compress is delivered changes what it does (small study, N on the face)
cards.type: Prospective comparative study of warm compress therapies (Murphy 2020)
cards.people: 42 subjects (13 male, 29 female; mean age 56.45 years) with meibomian gland dysfunction and Demodex folliculorum blepharitis completed a 2-month warm compress study comparing three therapies — warm face cloth, a heated eye bag device (MGDRx EyeBag) and a moist heat mask (OPTASE Moist Heat Mask) — with assessments at baseline and at 2, 4 and 8 weeks. Study N = 42.
cards.result: Meibomian gland dysfunction, scored by meibum quality and expressibility, reduced significantly with the heated eye bag and the moist heat mask (P < .05), with no significant difference between the two devices (P = .29); no improvement in meibomian gland dysfunction was detected with the warm face cloth. Only the moist heat mask significantly reduced the quantity of Demodex folliculorum over 8 weeks. Symptoms and ocular surface staining improved significantly in all three groups (P < .05), while osmolarity, tear break-up time and Schirmer I test did not change significantly in any group.
cards.watchOut: A 42-person, three-arm device comparison with no antibiotic arm and no untreated control: it shows a plain warm cloth may under-deliver heat, not how compresses compare with antibiotic ointment. (The record's MeSH includes 'Animals' and 'Mites' for the Demodex organism; all 42 participants were human patients.)
cards.source: Murphy O et al. The Efficacy of Warm Compresses in the Treatment of Meibomian Gland Dysfunction and Demodex Folliculorum Blepharitis. Current eye research. 2020. PMID: 31657234. cards.headline: Sim 2014: randomised trial of eyelid warming in 75 patients — a steam device improved symptom severity in 78.3% versus 45.5% with a warm towel, and the towel still helped nearly half
cards.summary: Sim 2014: randomised trial of eyelid warming in 75 patients — a steam device improved symptom severity in 78.3% versus 45.5% with a warm towel, and the towel still helped nearly half
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of eyelid-warming therapies (Sim 2014)
cards.people: 3-month assessor-blinded randomised controlled trial at the Singapore National Eye Centre in patients with meibomian gland dysfunction and frequent dry-eye symptoms: warm towel (n = 25), EyeGiene warming device (n = 25) and Blephasteam steam device (n = 25); patients who wore contact lenses or had active infection, thyroid dysfunction or rheumatoid arthritis were excluded.
cards.result: After 3 months, 78.3% of steam-device participants reported improvement in symptom severity compared with 45.5% of warm-towel participants (P = 0.023); for symptom frequency the proportions were 82.6% and 50.0% (P = 0.020). EyeGiene results were not significantly different from warm towel. Lid-warming treatments did not significantly change tear break-up time, Schirmer test results or the number of visibly occluded meibomian gland orifices, and no treatment worsened best-corrected visual acuity.
cards.watchOut: No antibiotic comparator and no placebo arm: symptom improvement with a warm towel (45.5%) cannot be separated from natural fluctuation and expectation effects, and the population is meibomian gland dysfunction rather than all blepharitis.
cards.source: Sim HS et al. A Randomized, Controlled Treatment Trial of Eyelid-Warming Therapies in Meibomian Gland Dysfunction. Ophthalmology and therapy. 2014. PMID: 25156975. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Pang 2019: meta-analysis of 4 trials (385 patients) — a single thermal pulsation treatment beat warm compresses on gland function and symptom scores, showing compresses are a beatable standard, not a proven equal of drug therapy
cards.summary: Pang 2019: meta-analysis of 4 trials (385 patients) — a single thermal pulsation treatment beat warm compresses on gland function and symptom scores, showing compresses are a beatable standard, not a proven equal of drug therapy
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Pang 2019)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing vectored thermal pulsation treatment with warm compress treatment in dry eye disease due to meibomian gland dysfunction: 4 trials with 385 patients, searched to July 2018.
cards.result: Thermal pulsation gave significantly greater improvement than warm compresses in meibomian gland function (mean difference 2.19, 95% CI 0.95 to 3.43), tear break-up time (MD 1.08, 95% CI 0.06 to 2.10) and Standard Patient Evaluation of Eye Dryness (MD −2.76, 95% CI −4.22 to −1.30) at 2 to 4 weeks, and a greater decrease in Ocular Surface Disease Index at 2 to 4 weeks (MD −8.61, 95% CI −13.62 to −3.61) and 3 months (MD −6.92, 95% CI −11.95 to −1.89). The authors recommend choosing treatment after shared decision-making.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is an in-office device, not antibiotic ointment, and the population is meibomian-gland dry eye; the card is here to calibrate how much room exists above warm compresses, not to answer the antibiotic comparison.
cards.source: Pang SP et al. Efficacy of Vectored Thermal Pulsation and Warm Compress Treatments in Meibomian Gland Dysfunction: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Cornea. 2019. PMID: 30844843. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: lid hygiene relieves symptoms and antibiotics additionally clear lid bacteria, but no adequate head-to-head trial has ever shown one superior — 'as effective as' is unproven in both directions
cards.summary: Synthesis: lid hygiene relieves symptoms and antibiotics additionally clear lid bacteria, but no adequate head-to-head trial has ever shown one superior — 'as effective as' is unproven in both directions
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review (34 studies, 2,169 participants), one 42-patient warm-compress comparison, one 75-patient randomised warming trial, and one meta-analysis of 4 trials (385 patients) using warm compresses as the control treatment. Total carded participants exceed 2,600, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the individual compress studies are small and their Ns are printed on their faces.
cards.result: The Cochrane review found some symptomatic relief from topical antibiotics plus bacterial eradication in anterior blepharitis, possible symptomatic relief from lid hygiene in anterior and posterior disease, and no strong evidence that any treatment cures chronic blepharitis (Lindsley 2012). Heated masks improved gland scores where a warm face cloth did not (Murphy 2020); a warm towel improved symptoms in about half of users (Sim 2014); and device therapy can outperform compresses on gland and symptom measures (Pang 2019). No carded study compares warm compress plus lid hygiene directly with antibiotic ointment. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for the equivalence claim.
cards.watchOut: Blepharitis is several diseases — staphylococcal anterior, seborrhoeic, Demodex and meibomian gland dysfunction — pooled loosely in this evidence; a patient with clear bacterial anterior disease or Demodex infestation may need the targeted treatment the pooled data cannot judge.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lindsley K et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2012 (PMID: 22592706); Murphy O et al. Current eye research. 2020 (PMID: 31657234); Sim HS et al. Ophthalmology and therapy. 2014 (PMID: 25156975); Pang SP et al. Cornea. 2019 (PMID: 30844843).

shelves.title: Vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy: topical clotrimazole is effective in pregnancy trials and safer than oral fluconazole on consistent cohort evidence — but the two have never been randomised head-to-head in pregnancy
shelves.question: For vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy, is topical clotrimazole safer and as effective as oral fluconazole?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Antifungal Agents · Candidiasis, Vulvovaginal · Female · Humans · Pregnancy · Pregnancy Complications, Infectious · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (topical safer; comparative effectiveness untested head-to-head in pregnancy) — observational only for the safety comparison. On effectiveness, the pregnancy trial literature supports topical treatment on its own terms: imidazoles beat nystatin (odds ratio 0.21, relative), clotrimazole beat placebo (odds ratio 0.14, relative), and 7-day courses beat 4-day courses in pregnancy (Young 2001) — but no included trial randomised topical clotrimazole against oral fluconazole in pregnancy, so 'as effective' cannot be printed as a measured result. On safety, three large cohorts point the same way with small absolute numbers: against topical azoles as comparator, oral fluconazole carried an adjusted relative risk of 1.30 (relative) for musculoskeletal malformations, about 12 extra cases per 10,000 pregnancies (Zhu 2020); against no exposure, dose-graded miscarriage odds of 2.23 at 150 mg and 3.20 above it, plus a cardiac-septal signal at high dose (Bérard 2019); and a tetralogy-of-Fallot signal (odds ratio 3.16, relative) despite an overall birth-defect null (Mølgaard-Nielsen 2013). PROPOSED POSSIBLE, as stated above: topical clotrimazole is the safer choice in pregnancy on consistent observational evidence, and it is effective in pregnancy trials — while the direct comparative-effectiveness trial does not exist in the records fetched.

cards.headline: Young 2001 (Cochrane): in pregnancy, topical imidazoles beat nystatin (odds ratio 0.21, relative) and clotrimazole beat placebo (odds ratio 0.14, relative) — and 7-day courses beat 4-day courses; no included trial compared topical treatment with oral fluconazole
cards.summary: Young 2001 (Cochrane): in pregnancy, topical imidazoles beat nystatin (odds ratio 0.21, relative) and clotrimazole beat placebo (odds ratio 0.14, relative) — and 7-day courses beat 4-day courses; no included trial compared topical treatment with oral fluconazole
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Young 2001)
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials of any treatment for vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy (searches to March 2001): 10 trials included. Comparisons were among topical agents, durations and placebo.
cards.result: Based on five trials, imidazole drugs were more effective than nystatin for treating vaginal candidiasis in pregnancy (odds ratio 0.21 [95% CI 0.16 to 0.29], a relative measure). A trial of clotrimazole was more effective than placebo (odds ratio 0.14 [95% CI 0.06 to 0.31], relative). Single-dose treatment was no more or less effective than 3- or 4-day treatment, but two trials involving 81 women showed 4-day treatment was less effective than 7-day treatment (odds ratio 11.7 [95% CI 4.21 to 29.15], relative), and 7 days was no more or less effective than 14 days (odds ratio 0.41 [95% CI 0.16 to 1.05]). Terconazole was as effective as clotrimazole (odds ratio 1.41 [95% CI 0.28 to 7.10]). The review contains no trial of topical therapy versus oral fluconazole in pregnancy — printed plainly, because that absence is central to this shelf's question.
cards.watchOut: A 2001 review of small older trials: it establishes that topical imidazoles work in pregnancy and that courses may need to run 7 days, but it cannot rank topical clotrimazole against oral fluconazole for effectiveness, in either direction.
cards.source: Young GL et al. Topical treatment for vaginal candidiasis (thrush) in pregnancy. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2001. PMID: 11687074. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zhu 2020: against topical azoles as the comparator, first-trimester oral fluconazole carried more musculoskeletal malformations (52.1 versus 37.3 per 10,000 pregnancies; adjusted relative risk 1.30, relative) and no increase in conotruncal malformations or oral clefts
cards.summary: Zhu 2020: against topical azoles as the comparator, first-trimester oral fluconazole carried more musculoskeletal malformations (52.1 versus 37.3 per 10,000 pregnancies; adjusted relative risk 1.30, relative) and no increase in conotruncal malformations or oral clefts
cards.people: Population-based cohort study of US Medicaid data (2000–2014): 1,969,954 pregnancies, including 37,650 (1.9%) exposed to oral fluconazole and 82,090 (4.2%) exposed to topical azoles in the first trimester — the topical group serving as the active comparator, which is what makes this study speak directly to this shelf's comparison.
cards.result: The risk of musculoskeletal malformations was 52.1 (95% CI 44.8 to 59.3) per 10,000 pregnancies exposed to fluconazole versus 37.3 (95% CI 33.1 to 41.4) per 10,000 exposed to topical azoles; the adjusted relative risk was 1.30 (95% CI 1.09 to 1.56), corresponding to an adjusted risk difference of about 12 incidents per 10,000 exposed pregnancies. Conotruncal malformations were 9.6 versus 8.3 per 10,000 (adjusted relative risk 1.04 [95% CI 0.70 to 1.55]) and oral clefts 9.3 versus 10.6 per 10,000 (adjusted relative risk 0.91 [95% CI 0.61 to 1.35]) — no association for either. For cumulative fluconazole doses over 450 mg, the musculoskeletal adjusted relative risk was 1.98 (95% CI 1.23 to 3.17).
cards.watchOut: Observational: women prescribed oral fluconazole may have more severe or recurrent infection and other differences from topical users that propensity adjustment cannot fully remove; the absolute excess is small (about 12 per 10,000) even where the relative increase is real.
cards.source: Zhu Y et al. Oral fluconazole use in the first trimester and risk of congenital malformations: population based cohort study. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2020. PMID: 32434758. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bérard 2019: oral fluconazole in early pregnancy was associated with more spontaneous abortions at both low dose (adjusted odds ratio 2.23, relative) and high dose (3.20), and high-dose first-trimester exposure with cardiac septal anomalies (1.81)
cards.summary: Bérard 2019: oral fluconazole in early pregnancy was associated with more spontaneous abortions at both low dose (adjusted odds ratio 2.23, relative) and high dose (3.20), and high-dose first-trimester exposure with cardiac septal anomalies (1.81)
cards.people: Three nested case-control studies within the Quebec Pregnancy Cohort (1998–2015), drawn from 441,949 pregnancies; 320,868 pregnancies contributed to the spontaneous-abortion analysis, 226,599 to major congenital malformations and 7,832 to stillbirths. Most exposed women (69.5%) received the common single 150 mg dose.
cards.result: Use of oral fluconazole in early pregnancy was associated with an increased risk of spontaneous abortion compared with no exposure (adjusted odds ratio for 345 cases exposed to low-dose treatment 2.23 [95% CI 1.96–2.54]; for 249 cases exposed to high-dose treatment 3.20 [95% CI 2.73–3.75] — both relative measures). First-trimester exposure did not increase overall major congenital malformations, but high-dose first-trimester exposure was associated with cardiac septal closure anomalies (adjusted odds ratio 1.81 [95% CI 1.04–3.14]; 13 exposed cases). No association was found with stillbirth. The record gives odds ratios without absolute risks, printed here plainly.
cards.watchOut: The comparator here is no exposure, not topical treatment, and miscarriage ascertainment in claims/registry data can misclassify; still, a dose-graded association (2.23 at 150 mg, 3.20 above it) is the pattern confounding alone explains least easily.
cards.source: Bérard A et al. Associations between low- and high-dose oral fluconazole and pregnancy outcomes: 3 nested case-control studies. CMAJ : Canadian Medical Association journal = journal de l'Association medicale canadienne. 2019. PMID: 30782643. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mølgaard-Nielsen 2013: oral fluconazole was not associated with birth defects overall (2.86% versus 2.60%; adjusted prevalence odds ratio 1.06, relative) or with 14 of 15 prespecified defect types — but tetralogy of Fallot was increased (odds ratio 3.16, relative; 7 exposed cases)
cards.summary: Mølgaard-Nielsen 2013: oral fluconazole was not associated with birth defects overall (2.86% versus 2.60%; adjusted prevalence odds ratio 1.06, relative) or with 14 of 15 prespecified defect types — but tetralogy of Fallot was increased (odds ratio 3.16, relative; 7 exposed cases)
cards.people: Registry-based cohort of liveborn infants in Denmark: 7,352 pregnancies exposed to oral fluconazole in the first trimester and 968,236 unexposed pregnancies. Most exposed women received common therapeutic doses of 150 mg (56%) or 300 mg (31%).
cards.result: Oral fluconazole exposure was not associated with an increased risk of birth defects overall (210 defects among 7,352 exposed pregnancies [2.86%] versus 25,159 among 968,236 unexposed [2.60%]; adjusted prevalence odds ratio 1.06 [95% CI 0.92 to 1.21], a relative measure), nor with 14 of the 15 specific defect types previously linked to azole antifungals. A significantly increased risk of tetralogy of Fallot was observed (7 cases in exposed pregnancies [0.10%] versus 287 in unexposed [0.03%]; adjusted prevalence odds ratio 3.16 [95% CI 1.49 to 6.71], relative).
cards.watchOut: The reassuring overall null and the single positive signal coexist: with 15 defect types tested, one positive can arise by chance, but the tetralogy signal is concordant with the cardiac-septal signal in the Quebec data (Bérard 2019) — and live-birth cohorts cannot see miscarriage risk at all.
cards.source: Mølgaard-Nielsen D et al. Use of oral fluconazole during pregnancy and the risk of birth defects. The New England journal of medicine. 2013. PMID: 23984730. cards.headline: Synthesis: topical clotrimazole is effective in pregnancy trials and carries none of the systemic signals; oral fluconazole's risks are small in absolute terms but recur across three large cohorts (miscarriage, musculoskeletal and cardiac-septal signals) — and the head-to-head effectiveness trial in pregnancy has never been done
cards.summary: Synthesis: topical clotrimazole is effective in pregnancy trials and carries none of the systemic signals; oral fluconazole's risks are small in absolute terms but recur across three large cohorts (miscarriage, musculoskeletal and cardiac-septal signals) — and the head-to-head effectiveness trial in pregnancy has never been done
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of 10 pregnancy treatment trials (topical comparisons only), and three large observational pregnancy cohorts totalling over 3 million pregnancies (1,969,954; 441,949 in the source cohort; 975,588 liveborn-infant pregnancies), with topical azoles as the direct comparator in the largest. No small-N labelling applies; the limitation is that safety evidence is observational and effectiveness evidence is indirect.
cards.result: Topical imidazoles are more effective than nystatin (odds ratio 0.21, relative) and clotrimazole more effective than placebo (odds ratio 0.14, relative) in pregnancy, with 7-day courses outperforming 4-day courses (Young 2001). Against topical azoles, oral fluconazole carried an adjusted relative risk of 1.30 (relative) for musculoskeletal malformations, an absolute difference of about 12 per 10,000 (Zhu 2020); against no exposure it carried dose-graded miscarriage odds (2.23 and 3.20, relative; Bérard 2019) and a tetralogy-of-Fallot signal (3.16, relative) despite an overall-defects null (Mølgaard-Nielsen 2013). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (topical safer; comparative effectiveness untested head-to-head in pregnancy) — observational only for the safety comparison.
cards.watchOut: Effectiveness and safety pull from different evidence types on this shelf: randomised trials prove topical treatment works in pregnancy, cohorts indict the oral alternative, and no trial bridges them — so 'as effective' is an inference from separate literatures, not a measured result.

shelves.title: Transdermal versus oral estrogen for hot flashes: equally effective — transdermal estradiol matched oral estrogen in KEEPS and the head-to-head trials (the route made no difference to relief)
shelves.question: For menopausal hot flashes, is transdermal estradiol as effective as oral estrogen?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Administration, Oral · Adult · Autonomic Nervous System Diseases · Drug Therapy, Combination · Estradiol · Estrogen Replacement Therapy · Estrogens · Estrogens, Conjugated (USP) · Female · Hot Flashes · Humans · Irritable Mood · Longitudinal Studies · Middle Aged · Postmenopause · Progesterone · Progestins · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders · Treatment Outcome · Vasomotor System
shelves.balance: LIKELY (equal benefit) — yes: in every carded head-to-head comparison, transdermal estradiol relieved hot flashes as effectively as oral estrogen, and the route made no difference to relief. In KEEPS (727 recently postmenopausal women), moderate-to-severe hot flashes at 6 months were 7.4% on transdermal estradiol 50 µg/day and 4.2% on oral conjugated estrogens 0.45 mg/day versus 28.3% on placebo — both routes clearly effective, not significantly different from each other, and sustained over 4 years (Santoro 2017). A double-blind, double-dummy trial in 321 highly symptomatic women found no significant differences between patch and pill at matched doses by week 12 (Good 1999). The 32-trial review's versus-placebo reductions (transdermal −22.4 versus oral estradiol −16.8 weekly flushes) did not differ significantly between agents (Nelson 2004), and the earliest patch-versus-pill studies agree (Gordon 1995). The reading is concordant non-significance across several trials rather than one formal non-inferiority trial, and it covers symptom relief only. PROPOSED LIKELY (equal benefit): transdermal estradiol is as effective as oral estrogen for menopausal hot flashes.

cards.headline: Santoro 2017 (KEEPS): moderate-to-severe hot flashes fell to 7.4% on transdermal estradiol and 4.2% on oral conjugated estrogens versus 28.3% on placebo at 6 months — with no significant difference between the two active routes, sustained over 4 years
cards.summary: Santoro 2017 (KEEPS): moderate-to-severe hot flashes fell to 7.4% on transdermal estradiol and 4.2% on oral conjugated estrogens versus 28.3% on placebo at 6 months — with no significant difference between the two active routes, sustained over 4 years
cards.people: Randomised trial in recently postmenopausal women (Kronos Early Estrogen Prevention Study): 727 women aged 42–58, within 3 years of their final menstrual period, randomised to oral conjugated estrogens 0.45 mg/day (n = 230), transdermal estradiol 50 µg/day (n = 225) — both with micronized progesterone 200 mg for 12 days each month — or placebo (n = 275). Symptoms were recorded at screening and at 6, 12, 24, 36 and 48 months.
cards.result: Moderate-to-severe hot flashes fell from 44% at baseline to 28.3% on placebo, 7.4% on transdermal estradiol and 4.2% on oral conjugated estrogens at 6 months, and night sweats from 35% to 19%, 5.3% and 4.7% respectively; both active treatments beat placebo (P < .001 for both symptoms) with no significant differences between the active treatment arms — the route made no difference to vasomotor relief. Reductions were sustained during 4 years. Insomnia fell intermittently versus placebo in both active arms; neither treatment significantly affected irritability. Symptom relief was not significantly modified by body mass index or race/ethnicity.
cards.watchOut: KEEPS used lower-than-conventional doses in young, recently postmenopausal volunteers and measured symptom proportions rather than flush counts; it answers the route question at these doses, not whether higher-dose regimens differ.
cards.source: Santoro N et al. Longitudinal changes in menopausal symptoms comparing women randomized to low-dose oral conjugated estrogens or transdermal estradiol plus micronized progesterone versus placebo: the Kronos Early Estrogen Prevention Study. Menopause (New York, N.Y.). 2017. PMID: 27779568. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Good 1999: in a double-blind head-to-head trial (321 women), transdermal estradiol 0.1 mg/day matched oral conjugated estrogens 1.25 mg/day at every time point, and the 0.05 mg/day patch matched the 0.625 mg/day pill by week 12
cards.summary: Good 1999: in a double-blind head-to-head trial (321 women), transdermal estradiol 0.1 mg/day matched oral conjugated estrogens 1.25 mg/day at every time point, and the 0.05 mg/day patch matched the 0.625 mg/day pill by week 12
cards.people: Randomised, parallel-group, double-blind, double-dummy trial: 321 highly symptomatic postmenopausal women treated for 12 weeks with an estradiol matrix transdermal system (0.05 or 0.1 mg/day, changed twice weekly) or oral conjugated equine estrogens (0.625 or 1.25 mg daily). The outcome was the frequency of moderate-to-severe hot flushes. (The transdermal system tested is named in the article's title, as published.)
cards.result: There were no statistically significant differences at any time point in mean frequency or mean percentage reduction of moderate-to-severe hot flushes between the transdermal 0.1 mg/day group and the oral 1.25 mg/day group — the treatments made no difference to each other at matched doses. Between the transdermal 0.05 mg/day and oral 0.625 mg/day groups, mean flush frequency also did not differ significantly at any time, although the oral group showed a statistically greater percentage reduction at weeks 3, 4 and 8; by week 12 the two were statistically indistinguishable. There were no serious or unexpected adverse events, local skin tolerability was excellent, and other estrogenic effects were comparable between routes except less unexpected vaginal bleeding on the lower-dose transdermal regimen. The record reports these comparisons without printing the underlying flush counts, stated here plainly.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week, industry-era equivalence reading based on non-significance rather than a prespecified equivalence margin: 'no significant difference' in 321 women over 12 weeks is weaker than a modern non-inferiority trial, though it points the same way as every other card on this shelf.

cards.headline: Nelson 2004: across 32 randomised trials, transdermal estradiol cut weekly hot flashes by 22.4 versus placebo and oral estradiol by 16.8 — differences between agents were not significant
cards.summary: Nelson 2004: across 32 randomised trials, transdermal estradiol cut weekly hot flashes by 22.4 versus placebo and oral estradiol by 16.8 — differences between agents were not significant
cards.people: Scientific review for JAMA of double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trials of conjugated equine estrogen and 17β-estradiol (oral and transdermal) for menopausal hot flashes: 32 trials met inclusion criteria, including 4 head-to-head comparisons; 14 trials entered the meta-analysis.
cards.result: All estrogen agents significantly reduced the weekly number of hot flashes compared with placebo: conjugated equine estrogen, mean change −19.1 (95% CI −33.0 to −5.1; 1 trial); oral 17β-estradiol, pooled weighted mean difference −16.8 (95% CI −23.4 to −10.2; 5 trials); transdermal 17β-estradiol, pooled weighted mean difference −22.4 (95% CI −35.9 to −10.4; 6 trials). Differences between agents were not significant. Breast tenderness and atypical vaginal bleeding were the most frequently reported adverse effects among estrogen users, and the review could not determine the influence of progestin use or regimen type.
cards.watchOut: The transdermal point estimate is numerically the largest and the oral the smallest, with wide overlapping intervals from few trials: the correct reading is 'no demonstrated difference', not 'transdermal is stronger' — and these are versus-placebo effects assembled across trials, not head-to-head estimates.
cards.source: Nelson HD et al. Commonly used types of postmenopausal estrogen for treatment of hot flashes: scientific review. JAMA. 2004. PMID: 15069049. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gordon 1995: a 7-day transdermal estradiol system beat placebo, and against oral conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg/day there were no statistically significant between-group differences (participant N not documented in the record)
cards.summary: Gordon 1995: a 7-day transdermal estradiol system beat placebo, and against oral conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg/day there were no statistically significant between-group differences (participant N not documented in the record)
cards.people: Two randomised studies of a seven-day transdermal estradiol delivery system in healthy postmenopausal women with hot flushes: the first randomised participants to a 0.05 mg/day patch, a 0.1 mg/day patch or a placebo patch; the second to either patch dose or oral conjugated estrogens 0.625 mg/day. Efficacy was assessed from diary records of hot-flush frequency and severity plus global assessments. Participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: In the first study, both patch doses were significantly more effective than placebo in reducing hot flushes, with higher global assessments. In the second study, all three active treatments produced a significant reduction in hot flushes compared with baseline, and there were no statistically significant between-group differences — although the response to the 0.1 mg patch was greater, and to the 0.05 mg patch less, than the response to conjugated estrogens (the treatments made no significant difference to each other). The patches were generally well tolerated; skin irritation was the most common adverse experience.
cards.watchOut: The oldest and least precisely reported card: no participant number and no effect sizes in the record, so it corroborates direction (patch works; no route difference detected) and can carry no weight beyond that.
cards.source: Gordon SF et al. Efficacy and safety of a seven-day, transdermal estradiol drug-delivery system: comparison with conjugated estrogens and placebo. The Transdermal Estradiol Patch Study Group. International journal of fertility and menopausal studies. 1995. PMID: 7663539. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: transdermal estradiol relieves hot flashes as effectively as oral estrogen in every carded comparison — no significant route difference in KEEPS, in the double-blind head-to-head trial, or in the 32-trial review
cards.summary: Synthesis: transdermal estradiol relieves hot flashes as effectively as oral estrogen in every carded comparison — no significant route difference in KEEPS, in the double-blind head-to-head trial, or in the 32-trial review
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large randomised route comparison (727 women, 4 years), one double-blind double-dummy head-to-head trial (321 women, 12 weeks), one systematic review of 32 randomised trials (14 meta-analysed, including 4 head-to-head), and two early patch studies whose participant N is not documented in the record (printed on that card's face). Totals exceed 30 by an order of magnitude; no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: In KEEPS, moderate-to-severe hot flashes at 6 months were 7.4% on transdermal estradiol versus 4.2% on oral conjugated estrogens versus 28.3% on placebo, with no significant difference between active arms (Santoro 2017). The head-to-head trial found no significant differences at matched doses by week 12 (Good 1999), and the review's versus-placebo effects (−22.4 transdermal versus −16.8 oral weekly flushes) did not differ significantly between agents (Nelson 2004); the early patch studies agree (Gordon 1995). PROPOSED LIKELY (equal benefit): transdermal estradiol is as effective as oral estrogen for menopausal hot flashes — the route made no difference to relief in the head-to-head evidence.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence here is read from concordant non-significance across several trials rather than from one prespecified non-inferiority trial, and the shelf answers symptom relief only: route differences that matter for other outcomes (for example clotting risk) are different questions with different shelves.

Climacteric : the journal of the International Menopause Society. 1999 (PMID: 11915854); Nelson HD et al. JAMA. 2004 (PMID: 15069049); Gordon SF et al. shelves.title: Group B streptococcus screening and treatment in pregnancy: yes for early-onset newborn infection — intrapartum antibiotics cut it in small trials (RR 0.17 relative) and universal screening beat risk-based care observationally (RR 0.43), but the trials are small and biased and no mortality effect is shown
shelves.question: Does screening and treatment for group B streptococcus in pregnancy reduce newborn infection?
shelves.mesh: Ampicillin · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Carrier State · Female · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Infectious Disease Transmission, Vertical · Labor, Obstetric · Penicillin G · Penicillins · Pregnancy · Streptococcal Infections · Streptococcus agalactiae
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised evidence is small and at high risk of bias, and the screening-strategy evidence is observational, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE despite consistent direction. The treatment half of the question rests on the Cochrane review (Ohlsson 2014): in three small trials (488 infants), intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis for colonised women reduced early GBS infection with a risk ratio of 0.17 relative (risk difference −0.04; NNTB 25), but did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality or deaths from GBS or other bacteria, and the reviewers warn the result may well be due to bias. The screening half rests on a meta-analysis of 17 observational studies (Hasperhoven 2020): universal screening was associated with less early-onset GBS disease than risk-based protocols (RR 0.43 relative) and than no policy (RR 0.31 relative), while risk-based protocols did not differ significantly from no policy (RR 0.86 relative, the treatment made no significant difference), and screening was not associated with higher antibiotic use (31% vs 29%). Surveillance of 309 residual US cases (Verani 2014) found most involved implementation errors, consistent with a programme that works when delivered. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): screening-based prophylaxis is associated with substantially less early-onset newborn GBS infection, on small high-bias trials for treatment and observational comparisons for the screening strategy.

cards.headline: Ohlsson 2014 (Cochrane): intrapartum antibiotics for colonised women reduced early GBS infection (RR 0.17 relative; NNTB 25) in three small trials — but mortality was not significantly reduced and bias risk was high
cards.summary: Ohlsson 2014 (Cochrane): intrapartum antibiotics for colonised women reduced early GBS infection (RR 0.17 relative; NNTB 25) in three small trials — but mortality was not significantly reduced and bias risk was high
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials, Cochrane (Ohlsson 2014)
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) in women with known maternal group B streptococcal colonisation: four trials involving 852 women; three trials (500 women, 488 infants) compared IAP with no treatment, and one trial (352 women) compared intrapartum ampicillin with penicillin.
cards.result: The incidence of early GBS infection was reduced with IAP compared with no treatment (risk ratio 0.17 relative, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.74, three trials, 488 infants; risk difference −0.04, 95% CI −0.07 to −0.01; number needed to treat to benefit 25, 95% CI 14 to 100). IAP did not significantly reduce all-cause mortality, mortality from GBS infection, or mortality from infections caused by other bacteria (the treatment made no significant difference on those outcomes), and late-onset disease, sepsis from other organisms and puerperal infection did not differ significantly. Ampicillin versus penicillin showed no significant difference in neonatal or maternal outcomes. The reviewers found a high risk of bias in one or more key domains and state the early-infection result may well be due to bias.
cards.watchOut: The entire randomised base is 852 women in old, small trials at high risk of bias, and the outcome it moves is early GBS infection, not mortality. The reviewers themselves conclude there is a lack of evidence from well designed trials — the shelf's POSSIBLE stamp reflects that verdict.
cards.source: Ohlsson A et al. Intrapartum antibiotics for known maternal Group B streptococcal colonization. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 24915629. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hasperhoven 2020: universal screening was associated with less early-onset GBS disease than risk-based protocols (RR 0.43 relative) and than no policy (RR 0.31) across 17 studies; risk-based protocols did not beat no policy
cards.summary: Hasperhoven 2020: universal screening was associated with less early-onset GBS disease than risk-based protocols (RR 0.43 relative) and than no policy (RR 0.31) across 17 studies; risk-based protocols did not beat no policy
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational comparisons (Hasperhoven 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 eligible studies comparing screening-based protocols (universal third-trimester GBS screening to identify women for intrapartum prophylaxis), risk-based protocols, and no policy, with early-onset GBS disease incidence in newborns as the outcome. The record does not document a total participant N.
cards.result: Screening was associated with a reduced risk of early-onset GBS disease compared with risk-based protocols (ten studies, RR 0.43 relative, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.56) and compared with no policy (four studies, RR 0.31 relative, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.84). Risk-based protocols versus no policy showed no significant effect (seven studies, RR 0.86 relative, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.20 — the treatment made no significant difference). In studies reporting antibiotic use, screening was not associated with higher antibiotic administration rates (31% versus 29%). Absolute incidence rates by strategy are not printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: These are comparisons of policies as implemented in different places and eras, not randomised comparisons: countries and periods adopting universal screening differ in other ways that also move newborn infection rates, so the relative risks are associations with a strategy, not pure strategy effects.
cards.source: Hasperhoven GF et al. Universal screening versus risk-based protocols for antibiotic prophylaxis during childbirth to prevent early-onset group B streptococcal disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BJOG : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 2020. PMID: 31913562. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Verani 2014: of 309 residual US early-onset GBS cases, 57.9% involved at least one implementation error — optimal delivery of the current strategy could cut cases a further 26–59%
cards.summary: Verani 2014: of 309 residual US early-onset GBS cases, 57.9% involved at least one implementation error — optimal delivery of the current strategy could cut cases a further 26–59%
cards.people: Population-based surveillance cases of early-onset GBS disease (infants under 7 days with GBS from a normally sterile site) at US surveillance sites in 2008–2009: 309 cases whose mothers' prenatal and labour records were reviewed for screening, laboratory, communication and prophylaxis errors.
cards.result: Among 309 cases, 179 (57.9%) had one or more implementation errors; the most common error type was prenatal screening in term case-patients (80 of 222, 36.0%) and intrapartum prophylaxis in preterm case-patients (46 of 85, 54.1%). The authors estimated that under optimal implementation, cases could be reduced by 26–59%, with the largest single-intervention benefit from improved intrapartum prophylaxis (16% decrease). They note that even with perfect adherence the further decline may be modest, and that novel approaches such as intrapartum assays and vaccines are also needed.
cards.watchOut: A case series of failures, not an effectiveness estimate: it shows where the screening-and-prophylaxis chain breaks in practice, and its 26–59% figure is a modelled estimate built on published screening sensitivity and prophylaxis effectiveness, not an observed reduction.
cards.source: Verani JR et al. Early-onset group B streptococcal disease in the United States: potential for further reduction. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2014. PMID: 24785612. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: yes — screening plus intrapartum treatment is associated with substantially less early-onset newborn GBS infection, but the trial base is small and biased and the strategy comparison is observational, so the stamp stops at POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes — screening plus intrapartum treatment is associated with substantially less early-onset newborn GBS infection, but the trial base is small and biased and the strategy comparison is observational, so the stamp stops at POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of 4 small randomised trials (852 women, 488 infants in the treatment comparison), one meta-analysis of 17 observational policy comparisons (total N not documented in its record), and one surveillance review of 309 residual cases. No large modern randomised trial of the screening strategy exists in the carded evidence.
cards.result: Intrapartum antibiotics reduced early GBS infection in the trials (RR 0.17 relative, risk difference −0.04, NNTB 25) without a significant mortality effect; universal screening was associated with lower early-onset disease than risk-based care (RR 0.43 relative) or no policy (RR 0.31 relative), while risk-based care did not differ significantly from no policy (RR 0.86 relative); and most residual US cases involved a break in the screening or prophylaxis chain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): screening-based prophylaxis is associated with substantially less early-onset newborn GBS infection, on small high-bias trials for treatment and observational comparisons for the screening strategy.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf shows a mortality reduction, and late-onset GBS disease is not prevented by intrapartum prophylaxis — the benefit claimed is confined to early-onset infection, which is the outcome the question asks about.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ohlsson A et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014 (PMID: 24915629); Hasperhoven GF et al. BJOG : an international journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 2020 (PMID: 31913562); Verani JR et al. Obstetrics and gynecology. 2014 (PMID: 24785612).

shelves.title: Rh(D) immune globulin in pregnancy: likely prevents hemolytic disease of the newborn by preventing alloimmunisation — postpartum anti-D cut alloimmunisation to RR 0.04 relative, and antenatal doses cut first-pregnancy alloimmunisation from about 1% to about 0.2%
shelves.question: Does Rh(D) immune globulin in pregnancy prevent hemolytic disease of the newborn in Rh-negative women?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Postpartum Period · Rh Isoimmunization · Rho(D) Immune Globulin
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two Cochrane reviews of randomised trials point the same way, and the mechanism is direct: hemolytic disease of the newborn in a later pregnancy is caused by the maternal alloimmunisation that anti-D prevents. Postpartum anti-D (Crowther 2000; six trials, over 10,000 women) cut alloimmunisation at 6 months to a relative risk of 0.04 and in a subsequent pregnancy to 0.12 relative. Antenatal anti-D (Crowther 2013; two trials, over 4,500 women) did not reach significance on immunisation itself (RR 0.42 relative, confidence interval crossing 1) but significantly reduced positive Kleihauer tests, and the review puts the underlying risk at about 1% in a first pregnancy falling to about 0.2% with 100 µg antenatal anti-D; the antenatal programme data assembled by Urbaniak 1998 show the same gradient in first pregnancies (for example 1.6% in controls to 0.18% with a single 300 µg dose at 28 weeks). The honest limit, printed on the face: the trials measured alloimmunisation — the necessary precursor — not hemolytic disease itself, which had already become too rare to be a trial outcome. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): Rh(D) immune globulin in pregnancy (antenatal plus postpartum) prevents the alloimmunisation that causes hemolytic disease of the newborn in subsequent pregnancies.

cards.headline: Crowther 2000 (Cochrane): postpartum anti-D cut alloimmunisation to RR 0.04 relative at 6 months and RR 0.12 in a subsequent pregnancy — six trials, over 10,000 women
cards.summary: Crowther 2000 (Cochrane): postpartum anti-D cut alloimmunisation to RR 0.04 relative at 6 months and RR 0.12 in a subsequent pregnancy — six trials, over 10,000 women
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials, Cochrane (Crowther 2000)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials in Rh-negative women without antibodies who had given birth to an Rh-positive infant: six eligible trials comparing postpartum anti-D immunoglobulin with no treatment or placebo, involving over 10,000 women; trial quality varied.
cards.result: Anti-D lowered the incidence of RhD alloimmunisation six months after birth (relative risk 0.04 relative, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.06) and in a subsequent pregnancy (relative risk 0.12 relative, 95% CI 0.07 to 0.23). The benefits were seen regardless of the ABO status of mother and baby and when anti-D was given within 72 hours of birth. Higher doses (up to 200 µg) were more effective than lower doses (up to 50 µg) in preventing alloimmunisation in a subsequent pregnancy, though the reviewers note the evidence on optimal dose is limited. Absolute alloimmunisation rates are not printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: The outcome is alloimmunisation, not hemolytic disease of the newborn itself: the causal chain (no antibodies, no immune hemolysis in the next Rh-positive baby) is direct, but no carded trial randomised women and counted hemolytic disease, which was already becoming rare when these trials were done.

cards.headline: Crowther 2013 (Cochrane): antenatal anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks — immunisation RR 0.42 relative (not significant), Kleihauer positivity significantly reduced; review puts risk at about 1% falling to about 0.2% with 100 µg
cards.summary: Crowther 2013 (Cochrane): antenatal anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks — immunisation RR 0.42 relative (not significant), Kleihauer positivity significantly reduced; review puts risk at about 1% falling to about 0.2% with 100 µg
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials, Cochrane (Crowther 2013)
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised trials in Rh-negative women without anti-D antibodies given anti-D after 28 weeks of pregnancy versus no treatment, placebo or a different regimen: two trials with moderate to high risk of bias, involving over 4,500 women.
cards.result: With anti-D at 28 and 34 weeks, the risk of immunisation was not significantly different from no antenatal anti-D during pregnancy (risk ratio 0.42 relative, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.17), after the birth of an Rh-positive infant (RR 0.42 relative, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.17), or within 12 months after birth (RR 0.39 relative, 95% CI 0.10 to 1.62). Women receiving antenatal anti-D were significantly less likely to register a positive Kleihauer test in pregnancy (RR 0.60 relative, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.88) and at the birth of an Rh-positive infant (RR 0.60 relative, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.79). No significant differences were seen for neonatal jaundice and no adverse effects were reported in either trial. The reviewers state the risk of alloimmunisation during or immediately after a first pregnancy is about 1%, and that 100 µg (500 IU) anti-D in a first pregnancy can reduce it to about 0.2%. No data were available for alloimmunisation in a subsequent pregnancy.
cards.watchOut: Only two trials, at moderate to high risk of bias, and the immunisation confidence intervals are wide and cross 1 — the antenatal increment over postpartum prophylaxis is supported by the Kleihauer results and the programme data on the next card, not by a significant immunisation result in these two trials alone.
cards.source: Crowther CA et al. Anti-D administration in pregnancy for preventing Rhesus alloimmunisation. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 23450526. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Urbaniak 1998: postpartum prophylaxis alone leaves 0.83–1.5% alloimmunised in the UK; adding antenatal anti-D cut first-pregnancy alloimmunisation from 1.6% to 0.18% (Canadian 300 µg study) and from 0.95% to 0.32% (English study)
cards.summary: Urbaniak 1998: postpartum prophylaxis alone leaves 0.83–1.5% alloimmunised in the UK; adding antenatal anti-D cut first-pregnancy alloimmunisation from 1.6% to 0.18% (Canadian 300 µg study) and from 0.95% to 0.32% (English study)
cards.type: Evidence review of controlled antenatal prophylaxis studies (Urbaniak 1998)
cards.people: Review of the scientific basis of antenatal prophylaxis, assembling the controlled antenatal studies: a Canadian study of a single 300 µg dose at 28 weeks (1,086 treated women, 2,768 concurrent non-randomised controls), a French study (362 treated, 360 controls) and an English study (1,238 treated, 2,000 controls) of two 100 µg doses at 28 and 34 weeks, all in first pregnancies.
cards.result: Standard post-delivery anti-D, with further doses for fetomaternal-haemorrhage-risk events, had reduced alloimmunisation to 0.83–1.5% in the UK, with residual cases mainly from missed or insufficient doses and from 'silent' fetomaternal haemorrhage during pregnancy (detectable in 3% of women in the first trimester, 12% in the second and 45% in the third). In first pregnancies, the Canadian single-dose study observed alloimmunisation falling from 1.6% (45/2,768) in controls to 0.18% (2/1,086) with treatment; the French two-dose study from 1.11% (4/360) to under 0.28% (0/362); and the English two-dose study from 0.95% (19/2,000) to 0.32% (4/1,238). The author notes there have been no systematic studies of the reduction in mortality from antenatal anti-D, but that if immunisation is largely prevented, fetal morbidity and mortality will be prevented with it.
cards.watchOut: The antenatal comparisons use concurrent non-randomised controls in the largest (Canadian) study, so their percentages carry more confounding risk than the Cochrane trial results; the review is also a single-author synthesis from 1998, carded for its primary study numbers, which are printed with their denominators on the face.
cards.source: Urbaniak SJ et al. The scientific basis of antenatal prophylaxis. British journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 1998. PMID: 9863973. Registry ID: none in the record.
