cards.headline: Synthesis: anti-D works by preventing alloimmunisation — postpartum prophylaxis is decisively effective in trials, antenatal prophylaxis adds a further reduction, and hemolytic disease is prevented by removing its cause
cards.summary: Synthesis: anti-D works by preventing alloimmunisation — postpartum prophylaxis is decisively effective in trials, antenatal prophylaxis adds a further reduction, and hemolytic disease is prevented by removing its cause
cards.people: The carded evidence: two Cochrane reviews covering eight randomised trials and over 14,500 women in total, plus a review assembling the controlled antenatal programme studies (over 7,000 women in the three first-pregnancy comparisons). Participants overlap between the reviews' underlying literatures and are not summed into a single N.
cards.result: Postpartum anti-D reduced alloimmunisation to RR 0.04 relative at 6 months and RR 0.12 relative in a subsequent pregnancy (over 10,000 women). Antenatal anti-D reduced Kleihauer positivity significantly (RR 0.60 relative) with a non-significant immunisation RR of 0.42 relative in two trials, and programme data show first-pregnancy alloimmunisation falling from 1.6% to 0.18% and from 0.95% to 0.32% when antenatal doses are added. No adverse effects were reported in the antenatal trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): Rh(D) immune globulin in pregnancy (antenatal plus postpartum) prevents the alloimmunisation that causes hemolytic disease of the newborn in subsequent pregnancies.
cards.watchOut: Prevention here protects the next pregnancy, not the current one: a woman already alloimmunised gains nothing from anti-D, and the carded trials' endpoint is alloimmunisation — hemolytic disease itself is prevented by implication of a direct causal chain, not counted as a trial outcome.
cards.source: Synthesis of Crowther C et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2000 (PMID: 10796089); Crowther CA et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013 (PMID: 23450526); Urbaniak SJ et al. British journal of obstetrics and gynaecology. 1998 (PMID: 9863973).

shelves.title: Earlier cataract surgery vs waiting: vision improves sooner (OR 7.22 for acuity gain) — quality-of-life benefit inferred, falls benefit unproven
shelves.question: In adults with cataracts, does surgery at an earlier stage improve quality of life compared with waiting?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Ambulatory Care · Cataract · Cataract Extraction · Female · Health Services for the Aged · Humans · Male · Visual Acuity · Persons with Visual Disabilities · Waiting Lists
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The timing trials are small but point the same way: a meta-analysis of expedited versus routine cataract surgery (Desapriya 2010) found expedited surgery increased the odds of improved visual acuity more than seven-fold (OR 7.22, 95% CI 3.16 to 16.55), while the pooled falls result — the outcome patients fear most from waiting — was a non-significant reduction (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.17, 2 RCTs, 535 participants), i.e. the treatment made no proven difference to falls. The Cochrane review of immediate versus 6-month-delayed surgery in patients with cataract and age-related macular degeneration (Casparis 2017, 2 RCTs, 114 participants) found better best-corrected visual acuity at 6 months with immediate surgery (mean difference −0.15 logMAR, 95% CI −0.28 to −0.02, moderate-certainty evidence). Quality of life itself is barely moved by timing in the carded evidence: in the 3,787-patient Quintana 2011 cohort, waiting over 5 months meant smaller visual-acuity gains than waiting under 3 months (P = .0348), but waiting time did not significantly influence VF-14 quality-of-life gains or complications — the benefit shown is better vision sooner, during the months waiting would otherwise spend impaired. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): earlier surgery improves vision sooner; a quality-of-life advantage is plausible and consistent with the acuity data but thinly measured, and no falls benefit is proven.

cards.headline: Desapriya 2010: expedited cataract surgery raised the odds of improved visual acuity over seven-fold (OR 7.22) versus routine waiting, but the falls reduction was not significant (OR 0.81)
cards.summary: Desapriya 2010: expedited cataract surgery raised the odds of improved visual acuity over seven-fold (OR 7.22) versus routine waiting, but the falls reduction was not significant (OR 0.81)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (737 participants in the review) of expedited versus routine cataract surgery in older people, including randomised trials and prospective cohorts from 12 databases (literature to 2008); the falls meta-analysis pools 2 RCTs with 535 participants.
cards.result: Three studies evaluated visual acuity after expedited versus routine surgery: the pooled estimate showed expedited surgery increased visual acuity improvement (odds ratio 7.22, 95% CI 3.16 to 16.55, P < .0001). Pooling 2 RCTs (535 participants) showed a non-significant reduction in falls after expedited surgery (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.17) — the treatment made no proven difference to falls. The authors conclude expedited surgery significantly enhances vision but is inconclusive for preventing falls.
cards.watchOut: 'Expedited versus routine' compares positions on a waiting list, not cataract stage as such, and the acuity odds ratio pools few studies — the direction is secure, the seven-fold size is not.
cards.source: Desapriya E et al. Vision improvement and reduction in falls after expedited cataract surgery Systematic review and metaanalysis. Journal of Cataract and Refractive Surgery. 2010. cards.headline: Cochrane 2017 (Casparis): immediate surgery beat 6-month-delayed surgery on acuity at 6 months (mean difference −0.15 logMAR) in cataract with macular degeneration — 2 RCTs, 114 participants
cards.summary: Cochrane 2017 (Casparis): immediate surgery beat 6-month-delayed surgery on acuity at 6 months (mean difference −0.15 logMAR) in cataract with macular degeneration — 2 RCTs, 114 participants
cards.people: Cochrane review of 2 randomised trials (114 participants, 114 study eyes) in people with visually significant cataract and age-related macular degeneration, randomised to immediate cataract surgery (within 2 weeks) or delayed surgery (6 months). Population has macular degeneration as well as cataract — printed plainly here.
cards.result: At 6 months (before the delayed group had surgery), the immediate-surgery group had better best-corrected visual acuity (mean difference −0.15 logMAR, 95% CI −0.28 to −0.02; 56 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). At 12 months in the second study, which group had better acuity was uncertain (very low-certainty evidence). No participant in one study developed exudative macular degeneration in the study eye over 12 months; choroidal neovascularisation developed in 1 of 27 immediate-surgery participants in the other. The record reports no quality-of-life outcome for the timing comparison.
cards.watchOut: A macular-degeneration population answers a narrower question than this shelf's: it shows delay costs acuity even when the retina is diseased, but says nothing directly about quality of life in ordinary cataract.
cards.source: Casparis H et al. Surgery for cataracts in people with age-related macular degeneration. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28206671. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Quintana 2011: in 3,787 patients, waiting over 5 months meant smaller visual-acuity gains than waiting under 3 months — but waiting time did not significantly change VF-14 quality-of-life gains or complications
cards.summary: Quintana 2011: in 3,787 patients, waiting over 5 months meant smaller visual-acuity gains than waiting under 3 months — but waiting time did not significantly change VF-14 quality-of-life gains or complications
cards.people: Prospective cohort of 3,787 consecutive patients scheduled for cataract removal by phacoemulsification at 12 ophthalmology units in Spain; visual acuity and Visual Function Index 14 (VF-14) collected before and after surgery, with waiting-list time analysed against outcomes.
cards.result: Patients who waited longer than 5 months for cataract extraction had smaller gains in visual acuity than those who waited fewer than 3 months (P = .0348). Time on the waiting list did not significantly influence changes in VF-14 results or surgical complications. Patients with contralateral visual acuity better than 0.5 and those with vision-related daily-living difficulties spent less time on the waiting list, while patients with social support waited significantly longer (1.04 times, P = .0188).
cards.watchOut: Observational waiting-time comparison: who waits longest is decided by triage and social factors, not chance, so part of the smaller acuity gain may reflect who was made to wait rather than the wait itself.
cards.source: Quintana JM et al. Waiting time for cataract extraction: Predictive factors and influence on outcomes. Journal of Cataract and Refractive Surgery. 2011. PMID: 21067891. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: earlier surgery buys better vision during the waiting months (OR 7.22 for acuity improvement; −0.15 logMAR at 6 months; smaller acuity gains after waits over 5 months) — quality-of-life gains did not vary with waiting time in the large cohort, and falls are unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: earlier surgery buys better vision during the waiting months (OR 7.22 for acuity improvement; −0.15 logMAR at 6 months; smaller acuity gains after waits over 5 months) — quality-of-life gains did not vary with waiting time in the large cohort, and falls are unproven
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of expedited versus routine surgery (737 participants in the review; 535 in the falls pooling), one Cochrane review of immediate versus delayed surgery (114 participants, all with macular degeneration), and one prospective waiting-time cohort (3,787 patients). Total carded participants exceed 4,600, so no small-N labelling applies; the limitation is that quality of life itself responds weakly to timing in the one large study that measured it.
cards.result: Expedited surgery: odds ratio 7.22 for improved visual acuity; falls OR 0.81, not significant (the treatment made no proven difference) (Desapriya 2010). Immediate versus 6-month-delayed surgery: acuity better by 0.15 logMAR at 6 months (Casparis 2017). Waiting over 5 months versus under 3: smaller acuity gains (P = .0348), no significant difference in VF-14 change or complications (Quintana 2011). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The quality-of-life instrument (VF-14) is measured after everyone has had surgery, so it cannot capture the months of impaired life that waiting imposes — the strongest quality-of-life argument for earlier surgery is time lived with better vision, which none of the carded studies measures directly.
cards.source: Synthesis of Desapriya E et al. Journal of Cataract and Refractive Surgery. 2010 (PMID: 20117700); Casparis H et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28206671); Quintana JM et al. Journal of Cataract and Refractive Surgery. 2011 (PMID: 21067891).

synthesis the carded evidence: one meta-analysis of expedited versus routine surgery (737 participants in the review; 535 in the falls pooling), one cochrane review of immediate versus delayed surgery (114 participants, all with macular degeneration), and one prospective waiting-time cohort (3,787 patients). total carded participants exceed 4,600, so no small-n labelling applies; the limitation is that quality of life itself responds weakly to timing in the one large study that measured it. expedited surgery: odds ratio 7.22 for improved visual acuity; falls or 0.81, not significant (the treatment made no proven difference) (desapriya 2010). immediate versus 6-month-delayed surgery: acuity better by 0.15 logmar at 6 months (casparis 2017). waiting over 5 months versus under 3: smaller acuity gains (p = .0348), no significant difference in vf-14 change or complications (quintana 2011). proposed possible (benefit). the quality-of-life instrument (vf-14) is measured after everyone has had surgery, so it cannot capture the months of impaired life that waiting imposes — the strongest quality-of-life argument for earlier surgery is time lived with better vision, which none of the carded studies measures directly. synthesis of desapriya e et al. journal of cataract and refractive surgery. 2010 (pmid: 20117700); casparis h et al. cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017 (pmid: 28206671); quintana jm et al. journal of cataract and refractive surgery. 2011 (pmid: 21067891).

shelves.title: How long can menopausal hormone therapy continue? (evidence types on the face: two randomised trials and one observational meta-analysis) — no duration is proven risk-free: breast cancer risk rises steadily with years of use, while 18-year mortality in the WHI trials was neutral
shelves.question: How long can menopausal hormone therapy be safely continued in women who started before age 60?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cardiovascular Diseases · Cause of Death · Double-Blind Method · Estrogen Replacement Therapy · Estrogens, Conjugated (USP) · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Medroxyprogesterone · Middle Aged · Mortality · Neoplasms · Postmenopause · Risk
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by regimen, named here and in the stamp; evidence types are labelled on each card's face (randomised trials versus observational meta-analysis), as this question requires. The randomised WHI evidence is reassuring on the hardest endpoint: after median treatment durations of 5.6 years (oestrogen plus progestagen) and 7.2 years (oestrogen alone), all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer mortality over 18 years were neutral (pooled HR 0.99; Manson 2017). But the same trials split on breast cancer over 20+ years (Chlebowski 2020): oestrogen alone was associated with lower incidence (HR 0.78) and mortality (HR 0.60) in women with hysterectomy, while oestrogen plus progestagen raised incidence (HR 1.28). The observational duration evidence (Collaborative Group 2019) is the direct answer to 'how long': breast cancer relative risk rises steadily with years of use — 1.60 in years 1–4 and 2.08 in years 5–14 for oestrogen-progestagen — and some excess persists for more than 10 years after stopping, scaled by how long therapy was used. No carded study randomised duration or proves any number of years 'safe'; the honest statement is that risk accumulates with duration for combined therapy while trial mortality stayed neutral at the durations tested. PROPOSED SPLIT (oestrogen-only: lower breast cancer incidence and mortality in the WHI trial; oestrogen plus progestagen: higher breast cancer incidence, rising with duration) — all-cause mortality neutral over 18 years in both trials; no duration of combined therapy is shown to be free of breast cancer risk.

cards.headline: Manson 2017 (WHI randomised trials): hormone therapy for a median of 5.6 years (combined) or 7.2 years (oestrogen alone) was not associated with all-cause, cardiovascular or cancer mortality over 18 years (pooled HR 0.99) — randomised evidence
cards.summary: Manson 2017 (WHI randomised trials): hormone therapy for a median of 5.6 years (combined) or 7.2 years (oestrogen alone) was not associated with all-cause, cardiovascular or cancer mortality over 18 years (pooled HR 0.99) — randomised evidence
cards.type: Randomised clinical trials with observational follow-up (WHI, Manson 2017)
cards.people: 27,347 postmenopausal women aged 50 to 79 years randomised in the two Women's Health Initiative trials (conjugated equine oestrogens (CEE) 0.625 mg/d plus medroxyprogesterone acetate 2.5 mg/d, n = 8,506 vs placebo n = 8,102, median 5.6 years; or CEE alone, n = 5,310 vs placebo n = 5,429, median 7.2 years), with mortality follow-up through December 31, 2014 for more than 98%; 7,489 deaths occurred over the cumulative 18-year follow-up.
cards.result: All-cause mortality was 27.1% with hormone therapy versus 27.6% with placebo (hazard ratio (HR) 0.99, 95% CI 0.94–1.03) in the pooled cohort; with CEE plus MPA the HR was 1.02 (0.96–1.08) and with CEE alone 0.94 (0.88–1.01). Cardiovascular mortality HR was 1.00 (8.9% vs 9.0%) and total cancer mortality HR 1.03 (8.2% vs 8.0%). Among women aged 50–59 years the mortality ratios were more favourable than in women aged 70–79 (ratio of HRs 0.61 during the intervention phase), but the trials randomised women aged 50–79 as a whole and tested fixed median durations of 5.6 and 7.2 years — not indefinite continuation.
cards.watchOut: Mortality neutrality over 18 years is reassuring but is not a duration licence: the trials stopped therapy after a median of 5.6–7.2 years, enrolled few women who continued beyond a decade, and mortality is a blunter endpoint than breast cancer incidence, which diverged by regimen (next cards).
cards.source: Manson JE et al. Menopausal Hormone Therapy and Long-term All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality: The Women's Health Initiative Randomized Trials. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28898378. Registry ID: NCT00000611. cards.headline: Chlebowski 2020 (WHI randomised trials, 20+ years): oestrogen alone lowered breast cancer incidence (HR 0.78) and mortality (HR 0.60), while oestrogen plus progestagen raised incidence (HR 1.28) — randomised evidence, opposite directions by regimen
cards.summary: Chlebowski 2020 (WHI randomised trials, 20+ years): oestrogen alone lowered breast cancer incidence (HR 0.78) and mortality (HR 0.60), while oestrogen plus progestagen raised incidence (HR 1.28) — randomised evidence, opposite directions by regimen
cards.type: Randomised clinical trials with long-term follow-up (WHI, Chlebowski 2020)
cards.people: Long-term follow-up of the same two WHI placebo-controlled trials: 27,347 postmenopausal women aged 50–79 with no prior breast cancer, enrolled 1993–1998 at 40 US centres, followed through December 31, 2017 (more than 20 years' median cumulative follow-up; mortality information for more than 98%).
cards.result: CEE alone versus placebo (10,739 women with prior hysterectomy): breast cancer incidence 238 cases (annualized rate 0.30%) versus 296 (0.37%); HR 0.78 (95% CI 0.65–0.93); breast cancer mortality 30 deaths (0.031%) versus 46 (0.046%); HR 0.60 (0.37–0.97). CEE plus MPA versus placebo (16,608 women with a uterus): incidence 584 cases (0.45%) versus 447 (0.36%); HR 1.28 (1.13–1.45); breast cancer mortality 71 deaths (0.045%) versus 53 (0.035%); HR 1.35 (0.94–1.95), not statistically significant. Intervention durations were a median of 5.6 years (combined) and 7.2 years (oestrogen alone).
cards.watchOut: The oestrogen-alone result applies only to women with prior hysterectomy taking conjugated equine oestrogens; it cannot be read across to combined therapy, other oestrogens, or to continuing any regimen indefinitely.
cards.source: Chlebowski RT et al. Association of Menopausal Hormone Therapy With Breast Cancer Incidence and Mortality During Long-term Follow-up of the Women's Health Initiative Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA. 2020. cards.headline: Collaborative Group 2019 (observational meta-analysis): every hormone therapy type except vaginal oestrogen raised breast cancer risk, rising steadily with duration — relative risk 1.60 in years 1–4 and 2.08 in years 5–14 for oestrogen-progestagen — observational evidence
cards.summary: Collaborative Group 2019 (observational meta-analysis): every hormone therapy type except vaginal oestrogen raised breast cancer risk, rising steadily with duration — relative risk 1.60 in years 1–4 and 2.08 in years 5–14 for oestrogen-progestagen — observational evidence
cards.type: Individual participant meta-analysis of prospective observational studies (Collaborative Group 2019)
cards.people: Individual participant meta-analysis of the worldwide prospective epidemiological evidence: 108,647 postmenopausal women developed breast cancer during prospective follow-up at mean age 65 years; 55,575 (51%) had used menopausal hormone therapy (MHT). Mean MHT duration was 10 years in current users and 7 years in past users; mean age at starting MHT was 50 years.
cards.result: Among current users, excess breast cancer risks were definite even during years 1–4 (oestrogen-progestagen relative risk (RR) 1.60, 95% CI 1.52–1.69; oestrogen-only RR 1.17, 1.10–1.26) and twice as great during years 5–14 (oestrogen-progestagen RR 2.08, 2.02–2.15; oestrogen-only RR 1.33, 1.28–1.37) — all relative measures. After stopping, some excess risk persisted for more than 10 years, its magnitude depending on duration of previous use, with little excess after less than 1 year of use. In absolute terms the authors estimate 5 years of MHT starting at age 50 would increase breast cancer incidence at ages 50–69 by about 1 in every 50 users of oestrogen plus daily progestagen, 1 in 70 with intermittent progestagen, and 1 in 200 with oestrogen-only; the excesses from 10 years of use would be about twice as great.
cards.watchOut: Observational duration gradients can be distorted by screening and prescribing patterns, and this analysis pools many preparations and eras; its oestrogen-only duration gradient also sits in tension with the WHI oestrogen-alone trial result above — the split is printed in the stamp rather than smoothed over.
cards.source: Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer Type and timing of menopausal hormone therapy and breast cancer risk: individual participant meta-analysis of the worldwide epidemiological evidence. cards.headline: Synthesis: there is no evidence-based 'safe' number of years — mortality was neutral after median 5.6–7.2 trial years, but breast cancer risk with combined therapy rises with duration from years 1–4 onward, while oestrogen alone diverged favourably in the one trial that tested it
cards.summary: Synthesis: there is no evidence-based 'safe' number of years — mortality was neutral after median 5.6–7.2 trial years, but breast cancer risk with combined therapy rises with duration from years 1–4 onward, while oestrogen alone diverged favourably in the one trial that tested it
cards.people: The carded evidence: two randomised WHI trial reports (27,347 women; median intervention 5.6 years combined, 7.2 years oestrogen alone; follow-up to 18 and 20+ years) and one individual-participant meta-analysis of prospective observational studies (108,647 breast cancer cases). Total carded participants exceed 130,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; evidence types are labelled on each card's face, as this question requires.
cards.result: All-cause mortality over 18 years: HR 0.99 pooled (Manson 2017) — the trials made no difference to mortality. Breast cancer diverged by regimen in the trials (Chlebowski 2020): oestrogen alone HR 0.78 for incidence and 0.60 for mortality; oestrogen plus progestagen HR 1.28 for incidence. Observationally, breast cancer relative risk rose steadily with duration for both regimen types, reaching 2.08 (oestrogen-progestagen) and 1.33 (oestrogen-only) in years 5–14, with some excess persisting more than 10 years after stopping (Collaborative Group 2019). PROPOSED SPLIT (oestrogen-only versus oestrogen plus progestagen on breast cancer): continuation is a balance that worsens with duration for combined therapy; no carded evidence identifies a duration that is risk-free.
cards.watchOut: None of the carded evidence randomised women to different durations of continuation, and none isolates women who started before age 60 as a randomised subgroup — the under-60 timing is addressed only by the WHI age-stratified mortality ratios and the meta-analysis's finding that risks were similar for starting ages 40–59 and attenuated after 60.
cards.source: Synthesis of Manson JE et al. JAMA. 2017 (PMID: 28898378); Chlebowski RT et al. JAMA. 2020 (PMID: 32721007); Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer Lancet (London, England). 2019 (PMID: 31474332).
